design.rule:
One-thread state stays on its thread. One-thread state is memory that changing or ending a value writes with no atomic and no lock, and that other names on the same thread also write. It comes in six kinds: (1) a `shares` value's owner count; (2) the weak count of a value that is not `thread_shared`, which is written when a link to it is made, ended or opened, and when the value ends; (3) a target that several `sharedref mut` holders change; (4) a place that changes while several names read it (`Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, a channel's `Receiver`); (5) a value bound to the thread that made it (a guard, a `Scope`, a raw pointer, a `threads(creator)` handle); (6) a module's `static mut`, which belongs to the module's home thread.

The compiler works out two facts for every type from what it holds or can reach, and from nothing else:
- `Send`: the value may be handed whole to one other thread while this thread goes on.
- `ThreadShared`: several threads may use it through read-only names at once.

A type that does not show what it holds has exactly the markers its written type promises: a `dyn` value, a function value, `AnyError`, and a `some I` result seen from outside its package. The line that puts a value into such a type checks the promise.

Every route to another thread needs the marker for what happens on it:
- A value shared by several threads at once needs `ThreadShared`: a `thread_shared` value, a `static`, an export under `threads=any`.
- A value handed over needs `Send`: a capture word or a function's state, a channel's element, a join's result, a guarded module variable, a module's state passing to a new `creator`.
- Some routes the compiler follows place by place: a scoped task's, a scope job's and a parallel body's use of the caller's own variables and of the loop's element through `ref t`. These need no marker. They get the per-place check, and they never touch another thread's hidden counts (kinds 1 and 2).

A module's `static mut` is reached only on its home thread. The export's `threads` word says how the caller's thread stands to it:
- `main`: the caller is the home thread, fixed for the whole process.
- `creator`: the caller is the home thread, which moves to each new initialisation, and the module's state moves with it as a hand-over. So whatever a `creator` export reaches must be `Send`, and no lock is needed.
- `any`: any thread, at once. So the variable is `guarded by` a lock and holds `Send` values.
design.spec_text:
Adds `[THR-22]` and `[THR-8a]`. Changes `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`, `[THR-2]`, `[THR-10]`, `[THR-11]`, `[THR-13]`, `[THR-15]` (J7-07's lead fix, unchanged), `[THR-20]`, `[STA-1]`, `[CLO-16]`, `[FFI-22]`, `[FFI-27]`/`[FFI-31]`, `[FFI-33]`, `[FFI-33c]`, `[RC-4]` point 4, `[ERR-1]`, `[ERR-8]` and `[HR-3]`. `[TYP-43]`'s two marker rows then read only "see `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`".

* `[THR-22]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **One-thread state stays on its thread.** One-thread state is memory that changing or ending a value writes with no atomic and no lock, and that other values or names on its thread also write. It comes in six kinds:
  1. a `shares` or `shares mut` value's owner count;
  2. the weak count of a value that is not `thread_shared`, written when a `weakref` link to it is made, ended or opened, and when the value ends (`[OBJ-3]`);
  3. a target that several `sharedref mut` holders may change (`[LT-46]`);
  4. a place changed while several names read it (`Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, a channel's `Receiver`);
  5. a value bound to the thread that made it (a lock's guard, a `Scope` or `JobScope`, a raw pointer, a `threads(creator)` handle);
  6. a module's `static mut`, which belongs to the module's home thread (`[THR-20]`).

  No route takes one-thread state to another thread. Nothing runs for this rule except the steps `[THR-2]` names.

* `[THR-8]` *(changed)* **`Send`**: a value of the type may be handed whole to one other thread while this thread goes on. A type is `Send` when nothing it holds or can reach is of kinds 1, 2, 3 or 5, by the table below.
* `[THR-9]` *(changed)* **`ThreadShared`**: several threads may use one value of the type through read-only names at once. A type is `ThreadShared` when it is `Send` and nothing it holds or can reach is of kind 4.

  Both markers are worked out from components, and nothing else decides them. Table:

  | holder | `Send` when | `ThreadShared` when |
  |---|---|---|
  | struct, enum, tuple, fixed array, collection, class object, `owns T`, `Option`, `Result`, `JoinHandle[R]`, a lambda's own type (its state), an iterator adapter, a generator (what it holds across a `yield`) | every component is | every component is |
  | `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `sharedref mut T`, `weakref T` to a value that is not `thread_shared` | never | never |
  | `thread_shared T`, `weakref T` to one | `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared` | the same |
  | `ref T`, `Span[T]` | `T` is `ThreadShared` | `T` is `ThreadShared` |
  | `ref mut T`, `MutSpan[T]` | `T` is `Send` | never |
  | `Cell[T]`, `UnsafeCell[T]`, `Receiver[T]` | `T` is `Send` | never |
  | `Mutex[T]`, `Sender[T]`, a `guarded by` field or `static mut` of type `T` | `T` is `Send` | `T` is `Send` |
  | `RwLock[T]` | `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared` | the same |
  | `Atomic[T]`, `Lock`, `Once`, `StrView`, scalars, `extern "C" fn` | always | always |
  | `fn()`, `once fn()` | never | never |
  | `thread_shared fn()` (`[CLO-16]`) | always | always |
  | `dyn I`, `AnyError`, a `some I` result outside its package | `[THR-8a]` | `[THR-8a]` |
  | a guard, `Scope`, `JobScope`, a raw pointer, a `threads(creator)` handle | never, unless vouched for in `unsafe` code as the vouching rule says | never, unless vouched for in the same way |

* `[THR-8a]` *(new)* **A type that does not show what it holds has the markers it says.**
  - A `dyn` value is `Send` (or `ThreadShared`) when an interface written after `dyn` is that marker or requires it: `owns dyn Task + Send`, or `interface Task: needs Send:`.
  - A function type is `Send` and `ThreadShared` when it is `thread_shared fn()`.
  - A `some I` result, seen from outside its package, has the markers written after it (`some Iterator[Item = int] + Send`). Inside its package it has the markers of the type it is.
  - `AnyError` has the markers its declaration gives (`[ERR-8]`).
  - A type parameter has the markers its bounds give: written on a `pub` function (verdict 108), worked out on a private one (verdict 113).

  The line that puts a value into such a type checks that the value has what the type promises: `owns Square(side=2)` given to `owns dyn Shape + Send`, a lambda given to `thread_shared fn()`, a `?` into `AnyError`. A broken promise is `E7015`, naming the field that breaks it.

* `[THR-2]` *(changed)* **Every route to another thread needs the marker for what happens on it.**
  (a) **Routes the compiler follows place by place**: a scoped task's, a scope job's and a `@parallel` body's use of the caller's own variables (no word), and of the loop's element through `ref t` (`[THR-17]`). They need no marker. `[THR-11]` checks every place they read or change, and they never touch kinds 1 and 2 of the caller's thread.
  (b) **Routes the value travels**:

  | route | needs |
  |---|---|
  | shared by several threads at once: a value made `thread_shared` (`[THR-1]`, checked at that line, verdict 165); a `static` (`E7002`); an export under `threads=any` | `ThreadShared` |
  | handed over: the state of a thread's, job's or task's function (its capture words); `tx.send(owns v)` and a channel's element type; a join's result `R`; a `ref` or `Span` sent to a scoped task; an object handed whole to another thread (verdict 114's one compare); a `guarded by` field or `static mut` that several threads reach under its lock; a module's state passing to a new `creator` (`[FFI-33]`) | `Send` |

  Each check is made where the route is written:
  - `E7015` for kinds 1 to 4;
  - `E7008` for kind 5;
  - `E7012` for kind 6.

  The message names the route's line and the field that holds the state ("`Watcher.target` is a `sharedref mut` link, which other holders change on this thread"). A route that carries an owner of a `thread_shared` value hands that owner over at that place (`[RC-4]` point 4). Verdict 114's hand-over and its fixes stay as written.

* `[THR-11]` *(changed)* A task uses the caller's variables with no marker.
  - Two tasks changing one place, or one reading a place another changes, is `E7007`. The exceptions are a reduction, a lock, or the place's own operations where the place is `ThreadShared`: an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender`, or a `guarded by` field under its lock. A `Receiver` or a `Cell` used by two tasks is `E7007`.
  - A task never touches kinds 1 and 2 of the caller's thread (`E7015`, verdict 166). It makes and ends no `shares` owner. It makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target. It ends no object, reached through the caller's variables, of a class family that some `weakref` link may name (`[OBJ-1]`). All of this is worked out from its body (`[EFF-24]`).
  - What the task's function captured with a word is handed to the task's thread, so it is `Send` (`E7015`).
  - `R` is `Send`.
* `[THR-13]` *(changed)* The fourth bullet reads "an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender` or `guarded by` field (a `ThreadShared` place): ordered by the atomic or by the lock".
* `[THR-10]` *(changed)* `R` is `Send`. An owner of a `thread_shared` value in the result is handed over at the `return` (`[RC-4]` point 4).
* `[RC-4]` *(changed)* Point 4 reads: "every route of `[THR-2]` (b) that carries an owner of a `thread_shared` value hands it over at that place", now including a join's result and a module variable that a later `creator` thread may reach.
* `[CLO-16]` *(changed)* A `thread_shared fn()` is `Send` and `ThreadShared`. Its state is `Send`: `thread_shared` owners, values handed over, and copies of `Send` values. So `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: ...)` is accepted.

  Several threads may call one such function at once: a function held by a `thread_shared` value or a `static`, or a C callback under `threads(any)` (`[FFI-22]`). There, a call does not change the function's own state, including the own operations of a captured `Receiver` or `Cell` (`rx.recv()`, `c.set(v)`) (`[CLO-18]`). For a C callback this is `E7015` at the registering line: "C may call `on_tick` from several threads at once (`threads(any)`), and it adds to its own `n`; count with `n: Atomic[int]`, or, if C calls it only on this thread, write `threads(creator)`".

* `[STA-1]`, `[THR-20]` *(changed)* A module's `static mut` belongs to its **home thread**: in a program, the thread that runs `main`; in a library, the thread of its initialisation (`[FFI-33]`).
  - It is reached only by its home thread and by the tasks of scopes that thread opens.
  - A function that may run on another thread and reaches it is `E7012`, unless the variable is `guarded by` a `static` `Lock` and used under that lock.
  - A variable reached that way holds a `Send` value, as a `Mutex` does (`E7015`: "`CACHE` is guarded by `CACHE_LOCK`, and `worker` reaches it from another thread, but it holds `shares` owners, which stay on one thread; hold the nodes whole: `Array[Node]`").

* `[FFI-33]`, `[FFI-33c]` *(changed)* `threads=` says how the calling thread stands to the module's home thread.
  - **`main`**: the caller is the home thread, for the life of the process. The home thread is the thread of the module's first successful initialisation. An initialisation on another thread after a shutdown stops: "`plugin` keeps its module variables on thread 1, where it was first initialised (its exports say `threads=main`), and this initialisation runs on thread 7; initialise it on thread 1, or write `threads=creator`".
  - **`creator`**: the caller is the home thread, which is the thread of the current initialisation (ODR-083). An initialisation after a shutdown, on another thread, makes that thread the home thread. The module's state passes to it whole, as a value handed over, ordered by the shutdown and the initialisation. So every `static mut` a `creator` export reaches is `Send`, with no lock (`E7015` for kinds 1 to 4, `E7008` for kind 5).
  - **`any`**: any thread, at once. Every `static` it reads is `ThreadShared`, and every `static mut` it reaches is `guarded by` a lock and holds a `Send` value.

  Under `main` and `creator`, each export's wrapper compares the caller with the home thread, one compare per call, in every profile (as today).

* `[FFI-27]`, `[FFI-31]` *(changed)* A module whose exports include `threads=main` or `threads=creator` is shut down on its home thread, outside any of its export calls. Anywhere else, the shutdown stops and names both threads (one compare).
* `[ERR-8]`, `[ERR-1]` *(changed)* `AnyError` holds an `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, so it is `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8a]`). It implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`. A `?`, `.context` or `AnyError.from` of an error that does not meet this is `E7015` at that line, in every program: "`LoadError` holds `entry`, a `shares` owner, which stays on one thread, and an `AnyError` may go to another thread; return `Result[Mesh, LoadError]`, or hold a copy: `entry: Entry`". In `[ERR-1]`, "takes any `E: needs Error`" reads "`E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`".
* `[HR-3]` *(changed)* A reload's work on the program's values reaches every thread's one-thread state from the polling thread: prepare's `migrate_from`, commit, and reclaim's ends of removed fields with their `drop`. So it runs while no other registered thread runs Ember code, from the poll's test until reclaim ends. A registered thread that enters Ember code in that time waits: it tests a reload mark after its depth increment (`[HR-42]`). This applies to reload builds only, and to `std.hot.checkpoint()` too.

answers.answer: Verdict 164, as a line of the rule. A `sharedref mut` link is kind 3 (a target that other holders change on this thread), so it is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared`, and so is any type holding one. A channel is a route the value travels on (tier b), so `channel[Watcher]` is refused. Scoped tasks still reach the link where it is, through the caller's variables, checked place by place (tier a). So verdict 77's reduction stands, in a loop too (`ref w`).
answers.code:
struct Watcher:
    target: sharedref mut Player

fn main():
    p = Player()
    w = Watcher(target=sharedref mut p)
    tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)     # E7015
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): w.target.hp -= 1)
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): p.hp -= 2)      # a reduction with the task above (verdict 77)
    println(p.hp)
answers.outcome: The channel line is refused: E7015, "`Watcher.target` is a `sharedref mut` link, which other holders change on this thread, so a `Watcher` cannot go through a channel; let the tasks use `w` where it is". Without that line the program compiles and prints 7 every time.

answers.answer: Verdict 165, as a line of the rule. Making a value `thread_shared` is a sharing route, so it needs `Send` and `ThreadShared`, checked at the making line. `RwLock[T]` is `ThreadShared` only when `T` is, and a `Cell` is kind 4. A raw-pointer wrapper of a thread-safe C object passes this check only through the vouching rule (J7-06, J2-12, group P04), so the two questions should be shown together.
answers.outcome: Refused at the making line: "`FrameStats.draws` is an `RwLock` of a `Cell`, and threads holding its read lock at once would change the `Cell` together; write `draws: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)` in `FrameStats`". With the `Atomic` it compiles and prints 2 every time.

answers.answer: Verdict 166, as a line of the rule. A task's use of the caller's variables needs no marker but never touches kinds 1 and 2 of the caller's thread. So ending `shares` owners from a task is refused. The same goes for making, ending or opening a `weakref` link to a one-thread value, and for ending an object, reached through the caller's variables, whose class some link may name. An object the task was handed, or made itself, it may end: verdict 114 moved the handed one away from its links.
answers.code:
with scope = thread.scope():
    scope.spawn(owns fn(): level.enemies.clear())   # E7015
    hud.target = Some(shares mut boss)

# compiles:
with scope = thread.scope():
    hud.target = Some(shares mut boss)
level.enemies.clear()
println(boss.hp)
answers.outcome: The task line is refused: "`level.enemies` holds `shares mut Enemy` owners, whose count is kept without atomics, and the task ends them on another thread; clear them after the scope: move this line below the `with` block". With the line moved, it compiles and prints 10.

answers.answer: `AnyError` does not show what it holds, so it has the markers its declaration promises (`[THR-8a]`), and the standard library declares it `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`. So `Result[int]` may be a thread's result or a channel's element. The promise is checked at the conversion: `?` (`From[E]`) takes `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`. The cost, stated: an error type holding one-thread state (a `shares` owner, a link to a one-thread object, a `sharedref mut` link, a `Cell`) cannot go into `AnyError`, in a program with one thread too. Such a program names its error type, or holds a copy. Concrete error types stay unrestricted.
answers.outcome: The worker program compiles and prints the file's length. `check(owns e)?` is refused: "`LoadError` holds `entry`, a `shares` owner, which stays on one thread, and an `AnyError` may go to another thread; return `Result[Mesh, LoadError]` from `open`, or hold a copy: `entry: Entry`". It compiles with either change.

answers.answer:
One rule for both words: a module's `static mut` lives on the module's home thread, and the export's word says how the caller's thread stands to it.
- `main`: the caller is the home thread, fixed at the first initialisation, for the process. An initialisation on another thread after a shutdown stops.
- `creator`: the caller is the home thread, which is the current initialisation's thread. The module's state passes to a new creator whole, ordered by the shutdown (on the home thread) and the initialisation, as a value handed over. So what a `creator` export reaches must be `Send`, and needs no lock.
- `any`: the caller is any thread, at once: the variable is guarded and holds `Send` values.
Today's `E7012` under `creator` goes: the lock it asks for orders nothing that the hand-over does not already order.
answers.outcome: `HITS` compiles under `creator` (today it is E7012) and under `main`. `MESHES`, if a `creator` export reaches it, is E7015: "`bump` may run on the thread of a later initialisation (`#! threads creator`, line 1), and `MESHES` holds `shares` owners, which stay on one thread; hold the meshes whole, `Map[String, Mesh]`, or write `#! threads main`". Under `main`, a host that re-initialises the module on another thread stops at that initialisation, naming both threads. Under `any`, `HITS` needs its lock (E7012, with the lock's lines in the help).

other_cases.case: A `dyn` value with no `needs Send`: `struct Job: task: owns dyn Task` sent through `channel[Job]`.
other_cases.settled: `[THR-8a]`: E7015, "`Job.task` is an `owns dyn Task`, and `Task` does not say it may go to another thread; write `task: owns dyn Task + Send`" (or `interface Task: needs Send:`). Each `owns Render(...)` stored there is then checked for `Send`. `owns dyn Error` in a program's own error type follows the same rule.

other_cases.case: Is `thread_shared fn()` ThreadShared? THR-9 does not list it, so under verdict 165 THR-1's and CLO-16's own help, `handlers: Array[thread_shared fn()] = []` in a `thread_shared Bus`, would not compile.
other_cases.settled: `[CLO-16]`: it is `Send` and `ThreadShared`. Its state needs only `Send`, and where several threads may run it at once, a call does not change its own state (`[CLO-18]`). So the help's line compiles, and a handler that adds to its own counter is refused at the loop that calls it.

other_cases.case: A consumer thread, `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: for v in rx: total += v)`, whose `Receiver` is `Send` but not `ThreadShared`.
other_cases.settled: It compiles. `thread.spawn` hands the function to one thread, so its state needs `Send` only.

other_cases.case: A C callback under `threads(any)` that changes its own state: `register(owns fn() owns n: n += 1)`.
other_cases.settled: Today it is undecided, and two threads would add to `n` at once. Under `[CLO-16]` it is E7015 at the registering line: count with `n: Atomic[int]`, or write `threads(creator)`.

other_cases.case: A guarded module variable holding one-thread owners, reached from a `thread.spawn` thread: `static mut CACHE: Array[shares Node] guarded by L`.
other_cases.settled: Today it races: an owner taken out under the lock is ended later on another thread. Under `[STA-1]`/`[THR-20]` it is E7015: a guarded variable holds `Send` values, as `Mutex[T]` does. The fix is `Array[Node]`.

other_cases.case: Channel ends: `channel[shares mut Player]` with its `Receiver` given to a thread.
other_cases.settled: Worked out from the table. `Sender[T]` is `Send` and `ThreadShared` when `T` is `Send`, and `Receiver[T]` is `Send` when `T` is `Send`. So it is E7015, naming the element type (J7-07's lead fix, now a consequence of the rule).

other_cases.case: A `Receiver` used by two scoped tasks of one scope.
other_cases.settled: E7007 (`[THR-11]`, `[THR-13]`). A place's own operations order two threads only when the place is `ThreadShared`. A `Sender` used by both is fine.

other_cases.case: Join results and job results: a worker returning `thread_shared` values it made, or a `shares` scene graph.
other_cases.settled: `R` is `Send`. A `thread_shared` owner in it is handed over at the `return` (`[RC-4]` point 4), which closes the stale-home-count hole after the worker ends. A `Level` holding `shares` owners built on a worker is E7015 (verdict 23, an understandable limitation). The help: build it on the thread that keeps it, or make it `thread_shared`.

other_cases.case: Verdict 77 in a loop: `for w in watchers: scope.spawn(owns fn() ref w: w.target.hp -= 1)`.
other_cases.settled: It compiles as a reduction: `ref t` is tier (a), checked place by place, needing no marker. `copy of w` is a hand-over of a `Watcher`, which is not `Send`, so E7015 with `ref w` as the help.

other_cases.case: A scoped task's capture words: `scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of team: ...)`, where `Team` holds a `shares Player`.
other_cases.settled: E7015. What a task's function captured with a word is handed to the task's thread and must be `Send`. The real variables it uses stay tier (a), so verdict 94's plain `fn()` is unchanged.

other_cases.case: A one-thread object's weak count: a task opening `cam.target` (a link to a one-thread player), or ending an enemy that such a link may name.
other_cases.settled: E7015 (`[THR-11]`, verdict 166). Handing the whole object to a thread keeps verdict 114's one compare and leaves the links behind.

other_cases.case: Statics: `static REG: Map[String, Cell[int]] = {}`.
other_cases.settled: A sharing route, so it must be `ThreadShared`: E7002 as today, now worked out from the table (`Cell` is kind 4).

other_cases.case: Iterators, generators and lambdas that hold one-thread values.
other_cases.settled: Worked out from their parts. A generator holding a `shares` value across a `yield` is not `Send`. A lambda given to a type parameter keeps its own type, so its markers are those of its captures. Converting it to `fn()` gives a type that is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared`.

other_cases.case: `pub fn tiles() -> some Iterator[Item = int]` used by another package's worker thread.
other_cases.settled: `[THR-8a]`: outside its package it has only what is written (`some Iterator[Item = int] + Send`), so the promise does not depend on the body (verdict 108). Inside the package it has the markers of the type it is. A private generic's `needs Send` is worked out (verdict 113).

other_cases.case: A value made in an `Arena` (P02, J5-05) handed to a thread or made `thread_shared`.
other_cases.settled: `[LT-4]` makes it keep a `sharedref mut` link to its arena instance. That link is kind 3, so the value is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared`, and both are refused (E7015, verdict 165), naming the arena. A one-instance manager adds no link, so the value is judged by its contents. Whether a thread-safe manager's link may be a `ref` to a `ThreadShared` instance is for P02 to say.

other_cases.case: A drop where the last owner ends, and a queued drop (P05).
other_cases.settled: A `drop`'s body is code that runs on each thread where the drop may run, and it is checked there (`[THR-20]`). Where queued drops run is P05's to decide. Whatever P05 decides, the drop is checked for that thread.

other_cases.case: Hot reload: prepare's `migrate_from` and reclaim's drops of removed fields run on the polling thread while other threads may enter Ember code again.
other_cases.settled: `[HR-3]`: the whole reload, through the end of reclaim, runs while no other registered thread runs Ember code, and a thread that enters waits. Today reclaim's drops can end another thread's `shares` owners concurrently with it.

other_cases.case: Callbacks C runs on threads C owns (`[FFI-22]`, `[HR-3a]`).
other_cases.settled: `threads(any)` gives a `thread_shared fn()` whose state is `Send` and which does not change its own state. `threads(main)` and `threads(creator)` give a plain function that may hold one-thread values, with the trampoline's one compare as today.

other_cases.case: A `threads(creator)` handle, or a `creator` callback's token, held in a `static mut` that a `creator` export reaches.
other_cases.settled: E7008: it is bound to the old home thread and cannot pass to a later initialisation's thread. Under `threads main` it is accepted.

other_cases.case: A module with `main` or `creator` exports shut down from another thread.
other_cases.settled: `[FFI-31]`: it stops, naming both threads (one compare). This makes the hand-over of the module's state ordered by Ember itself, not by the host.

other_cases.case: A raw-pointer wrapper of a thread-safe C logger used by scoped tasks or a `static` (P04's J7-06 and J2-12).
other_cases.settled: A raw pointer is kind 5, so the wrapper is neither marker until it is vouched for. After verdict 165 that vouch must reach `ThreadShared` and classes too, or correct C bindings pay an Ember lock they do not need. The spelling is P04's.

design.prior_art:
**Rust.**
- `Send` and `Sync` are auto traits worked out from fields; `unsafe impl` vouches for what the compiler cannot see.
- `dyn Trait + Send` at the use site; `Rc` and `Cell` are `!Send` and `!Sync`.
- `thread::scope` lets threads borrow, but `&T` needs `T: Sync` and `&mut T` needs `T: Send`.
- `anyhow::Error` requires `Send + Sync + 'static`; `Box<dyn Error>` does not, hence the `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` idiom.
- `static mut` needs `unsafe` (and references to it are denied in the 2024 edition); `thread_local!` serves per-thread state.
- Where it falls short:
  - scoped threads are judged by type, not place by place, so `&Cell<i32>` cannot be read by scoped threads even when nothing writes it;
  - an `Rc` cannot be handed over even when it is unique (Ember took the run-time compare, verdict 114);
  - `impl Trait` leaks auto traits, a semver hazard;
  - safe module variables are not possible.

**C++.**
- Nothing is checked, and a data race is undefined behaviour.
- `shared_ptr` counts are always atomic, so every copy pays an atomic even on one thread (Ember's `shares` count is plain, and `thread_shared` uses two counts).
- `thread_local` exists. A `mutable` member under a `const&` read from two threads is the J7-03 race, unchecked.

**Swift 6.**
- `Sendable` is inferred for non-public structs and enums, and must be written for public ones (Ember's verdict 108). `@unchecked Sendable` vouches.
- `protocol Error: Sendable`: every Swift error is `Sendable`, the direct precedent for J6-16 A.
- `some P` does not leak `Sendable` (Ember's `some I` rule).
- A global variable must be `Sendable` and isolated to a global actor such as `@MainActor`, or `nonisolated(unsafe)`. That is close to Ember's home thread.
- Region isolation (SE-0414) and `sending` (SE-0430) let a non-`Sendable` value that is not connected to anything else be handed over. Ember does not take this (verdict 23; see open_risks).

**Ada/SPARK.** Protected objects. SPARK's Ravenscar and Jorvik flow analysis proves that a variable two tasks reach is protected, atomic, or `Part_Of` one task: place by place, like tier (a), but only inside restricted tasking profiles.

**Go.** Nothing is checked when compiling. The race detector is a debug-only run-time check, at 2 to 20 times the run time, and finds only races that occur in that run.

**Zig.** Nothing is checked; there is `threadlocal`.

**C#.** No race safety; there are `[ThreadStatic]` and `ThreadLocal<T>`.

What this rule keeps of each: Rust's work-it-out-from-fields markers; Swift's erased promise, public promise and `Error`-may-travel; SPARK's place-by-place check for tasks that share the caller's variables; Swift's main-actor idea, as a module's home thread. It is safe like Rust, at C's run-time cost, with fewer refusals than Rust for scoped tasks and module variables.
design.cost:
**When compiling: everything.** Working out the markers, the conversion checks, the route checks, the place-by-place task checks, and which exports reach which module variables. Each is a fact in the existing per-function summaries (`[EFF-24]`). Nothing goes into any value or object: zero bytes.

**While running, per operation, against C** (which pays nothing and checks nothing):
- **Markers, erased promises, route checks, a scoped task's use of the caller's variables:** zero, as Rust.
- **A `shares` owner count:** plain add or subtract, as today. C++'s `shared_ptr` pays an atomic on every copy.
- **A hand-over of an object a `weakref` may reach:** one compare (verdict 114, existing).
- **A `thread_shared` owner carried by a route:** one atomic add when it is handed over, then two-count counting (verdict 101, existing). The measured 9 to 13% cost for objects passed back and forth applies only to values that really cross. The new routes this covers (a join's result, a module's state under `creator`) add no cost to anything else.
- **An export call under `main` or `creator`:** one thread-id compare (existing).
- **A `main` module initialised again:** one compare at the initialisation.
- **A module shutdown:** one compare (new; once per shutdown).
- **A module's state passing to a new creator:** zero. Initialisation and shutdown already publish and acquire the runtime's own state, and the module's variables are ordered by the same pair.
- **Module variables under `creator`:** today's required lock goes, so one lock and one unlock fewer per access.
- **Reload builds only:** one load of a mostly-read word when a thread enters Ember code (the reload mark), and a wait only while a reload runs. Zero in other builds.
- **`AnyError`:** zero; the check at `?` is made when compiling. It allocates once on the failure path, as today.

**Refusals, the cost a program may pay in its text:**
- An error holding one-thread state does not go into `AnyError`, in a one-thread program too (it names its error type).
- A worker cannot hand back a `shares` graph it built (verdict 23).
- A `creator` module's variables cannot hold one-thread state (write `main` for that).

readability.note: The after is four lines shorter and nothing in it is new. Ordinary code never writes `Send` or `ThreadShared`. The only thread words stay where they are today: `thread_shared`, `thread_shared fn()`, `+ Send` after a `dyn` that crosses threads, and an export's `threads`. Every refusal names the field that holds the one-thread state and gives a line that compiles. The game loop, the scoped-task loops (`ref t`, reductions through links) and single-thread `shares` code read exactly as before.

design.compiler_does:
- **Works out both markers for every type** from its components, as it works out `Copy` and needs-drop. Recursive types are solved to a fixed point. For each failed marker it records the chain of fields that holds the one-thread state, for the message.
- **Reads the written promise of each erased type** (`dyn I + Send`, `thread_shared fn()`, `some I + Send` across a package, `AnyError`'s declaration) and checks every conversion into it.
- **At every route of `[THR-2]` (b), as written:** checks the travelling value's marker. It also emits the hand-over at that place of any `thread_shared` owner the route carries.
- **For tier (a)**, extends the existing place-by-place task check (`[THR-11]`):
  - a place's own operations count as ordered only when the place is `ThreadShared`;
  - it adds one summary fact per function, worked out from bodies: whether it touches kinds 1 and 2 (makes or ends a `shares` owner; makes, ends or opens a link to a one-thread value; ends a caller-reached object of a class family some link may name).
- **Follows each export's summary to the module variables it reaches**, and checks them by its `threads` word: nothing for `main`, `Send` for `creator`, guarded with `Send` contents for `any`. It does the same for every function reachable from `thread.spawn`, `jobs.submit` or a `threads(any)` callback.
- **Applies `[CLO-18]`** to function values in holders several threads may use at once, a C callback under `threads(any)` included.
- **Emits the few run-time steps:** the existing export and trampoline compares, the initialisation and shutdown compares, verdict 114's compare, and the reload mark in reload builds.
design.verdicts:
- **3:** kept. A `sharedref mut` target on two threads is changed only under a lock, through an `Atomic`, or by a reduction from scoped tasks (tier a); it never travels (tier b).
- **23:** kept. A `shares` value is never used from two threads. This is why a value whose one-thread owners all stay inside it is still not handed over whole (see open_risks).
- **61:** kept, and generalised: a thread permission on a type that hides its contents is written in that type (`thread_shared fn()`, `dyn I + Send`, `AnyError`'s declaration, `some I + Send` across a package). Option E would reverse it. It is not really better: a `pub` type's thread promise would then depend on what each program puts in it, against verdict 108.
- **77:** kept, including in loop form through `ref w`.
- **93:** kept. `ref t` is tier (a); `copy of t` is a hand-over and needs `Send`.
- **94:** kept. `thread.spawn` takes a `thread_shared fn()`, whose state needs only `Send`, so consumer threads with a `Receiver` compile. `scope.spawn` keeps a plain `fn()`: its real variables are tier (a), and only what it captured with a word travels.
- **101:** kept. `[RC-4]` point 4 now reaches every route, so a join's result and a `creator` module's state are covered without a stale home count.
- **104:** kept.
- **114:** kept. Its compare is the one run-time step of the hand-over route.
- **164, 165, 166:** kept unchanged, each a line of the rule: kind 3; the sharing route needs `ThreadShared`, checked at the making line; tier (a) never touches kinds 1 and 2.

No verdict covers J6-16 or J8-10. ODR-083 (a lead ruling: a new creator after a shutdown) is kept. Today's `E7012` under `creator` is a rule of the spec, not a verdict, and changes under option A.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. The compiler works out both markers from what a type holds. A type that hides its contents keeps the promise its type writes. Every route is checked. Module variables live on a home thread (`main` fixed, `creator` hands the state over, `any` guarded). `AnyError` may go to another thread.

options_for_owner.outcome: The worker and the plugin compile as written. The unsafe cases nobody had asked about are refused when compiling (a guarded variable holding `shares` owners, a self-changing `threads(any)` callback) or settled (a `thread_shared fn()` in a shared object, a reload's drops). An error holding one-thread state is refused at its `?`, in every program.

options_for_owner.summary: The compiler follows every value of a type that hides its contents through the whole program, instead of a written promise. `thread_shared fn()` and `+ Send` go. This reverses verdict 61.

h = thread.spawn(fn() => load("level1.cfg"))
options_for_owner.outcome: More programs are accepted with no word. A one-thread error is refused only if it reaches another thread. But a far-away edit can break a `spawn` line, with the chain named. A library type's thread promise then depends on what each program puts in it (against verdict 108). The owner chose the written word in verdict 61.

recommendation.reason: One rule answers all five questions and the cases nobody had asked about, with no exception by construct or type. Ordinary code gets no new word. Every race is refused when compiling, and the run-time cost is that of C plus the existing compares. Verdicts 61 and 164 to 166 stand as lines of it. The two open members follow from it: `AnyError` keeps a written promise (with Swift and Rust's `anyhow` as precedent), and `creator` hands a module's state over instead of asking for a lock that orders nothing. J7-06 (the `ThreadShared` vouch, group P04) should be put to the owner beside it, since verdict 165 leaves it as the only way a C wrapper becomes `thread_shared`.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: which objects may move to, or be shared with, another thread. That covers a `shared_ptr` whose count is not atomic, a pointer several holders write through, a `mutable` member, and a module's global. The compiler works out "may move" (Rust's `Send`) and "may share" (Rust's `Sync`) from what each type holds, and checks every way a value can reach another thread.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | worker | `cache` keeps a mesh entry as a `shares` owner | the entry's count: 1 |
| 2 | worker | loading fails: `LoadError(entry=shares e)` makes a second owner, and `?` puts the error into an `AnyError` | count: 2 |
| 3 | worker | `tx.send(owns r)` sends the `Result[Mesh]` to main | count: 2 |
| 4 | main | ends `r`: reads the count (plain, no atomic) | reads 2, about to write 1 |
| 5 | worker | at the same moment `cache.evict()` ends its owner: also reads 2 | reads 2, about to write 1 |
| 6 | both | both write 1 | count 1 with no owner left: the mesh is never freed; in the other order, it is freed while main still uses it |
owner_short.today: The spec lists thread markers and routes one case at a time, and verdicts 164 to 166 fixed three holes. Still, `Result[int]` from a worker is refused by a rule the text never states, a `creator` export needs a lock that protects nothing, and four more cases are undecided or race: a `thread_shared fn()` in a shared object, a guarded module variable holding `shares` owners, a C callback changing its own state on several threads, and a reload's drops.
owner_short.options:
A: one rule. The compiler works out the markers from contents; hidden-content types keep their written promise; every route is checked; module variables live on a home thread; `AnyError` may cross threads (the step table's step 2 is refused).
B: as A, but `AnyError` stays on its thread, so workers name their error types.
C: as A, but `creator` exports keep today's lock around module variables.
D: as A, but `main` and `creator` mean the same thread, and module variables restart at each initialisation.
E: the compiler follows every hidden-content value instead of a written word (reverses verdict 61).
owner_short.recommendation: A: no ordinary program gets a word, every race is refused when compiling, verdicts 61 and 164 to 166 stand, and the worker and plugin programs compile as written. Ask J7-06's `ThreadShared` vouch beside it.

design.open_risks:
1. **Handing over a self-contained value is not taken.** A worker that builds a `shares` scene graph cannot hand it back, even though every owner is inside it, because verdict 23 says a `shares` value is never used from two threads. Swift 6's region isolation accepts this. It is sound in Ember today only because Ember has no thread-locals and no owner crosses to C, so it would break if thread-locals or async come later. If wanted, it is a separate question for the owner.
2. **Shutting down a `threads=any` module while another thread is inside one of its exports** is about the module's lifetime, not its markers. It is left to the FFI groups (P08 or P04).
3. **The reload exclusion** (`[HR-3]`) adds a wait for threads entering Ember code during a reload, and one load of the reload mark per entry in reload builds. P09 should word it together with `[HR-42]`.
4. **Raw-pointer wrappers.** After verdict 165, a wrapper of a thread-safe C object can be `thread_shared` or a `static` only if P04's vouch reaches `ThreadShared` and classes (J7-06, J2-12). Otherwise correct bindings must pay an Ember lock.
5. **Values made in an `Arena`.** `[LT-4]` calls a value's link to its arena a `sharedref mut`, so such a value is never `Send`. That is intended. A thread-safe memory manager needs P02 to say whether its link is a `ref` to a `ThreadShared` instance.
6. **Spelling after `dyn`.** `+ Send` after `dyn` uses today's `+` (a lead ruling in `decisions.md`). If P24 moves to brackets, the rule follows that spelling.
7. **`Cell` under a read guard.** `[CELL-1]` already requires a name that may change the place to set a `Cell`, so J7-03's race may already be refused by E3023. `Cell` staying out of `ThreadShared` is cautious, and verdict 165's outcome holds either way.
8. **Wording shared with P05.** `[RC-4]` point 4's widening and P05's queued-drop rules edit the same text, so word them together.
9. **Foreign values with no thread word.** Whether a foreign `owns T` with no `threads` word in its contract is `Send` is P04's to say. Until then the rule treats it as bound to its thread.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed memory
matrix.how_kept: One-thread counts are written only on their thread. Send excludes shares, shares mut, sharedref mut and a weakref to a one-thread value (THR-8). A task never makes or ends a shares owner, never makes, ends or opens a link to a one-thread value, and never ends a caller-reached object of a weakref-targeted family (THR-11, verdict 166). A whole object handed to another thread moves away from its links (verdict 114: one compare, fix 1 for owned objects). A thread_shared value keeps two counts with the queue and Rule Q (RC-4, verdict 101), and an owner on any tier-(b) route is handed over at that line (RC-4 point 4, widened). A view of a linked object is not used after a line that may end such an object (RC-5).
matrix.edge_cases: Holes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. A static's object, an object read through an RwLock guard, a class-object field of a thread_shared value, or an object reached under a lock: any read-only name may make a link to it (WK-11), so several threads write its plain weak count. weakref T's type does not say what kind of target it has. A task ends a static mut's object, or an object reached through a ref mut it was handed. A borrowed threads(any) callback. A channel send of a linked object. Reload reclaim racing a thread's entry (hole 6).

Tier (a) gets the per-place check (E7007), in which a place's own operations order two threads only when the place is ThreadShared (Atomic, Mutex, RwLock, Sender, or a guarded field under its lock). import std.thread

class Registry:
    names: Array[String] = []

static REG: Registry = Registry()      # ThreadShared by the table, so every thread may read it

fn peek():
    w = weakref REG                    # +1 on REG's weak count, a plain add: REG is not thread_shared
    if w exists as r:
        println(r.names.len())
                                       # w ends here: -1, a plain subtract

fn main():
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn(): peek())   # the function holds nothing, so every route check passes
    peek()                                # main adds and subtracts on the same count at the same moment
    h.join()

# the same through other holders the table calls ThreadShared:
#   hub = thread_shared Hub()  with  level: RwLock[Level]       (verdict 165 accepts it)
#   with g = hub.level.read(): keep = weakref g                 # two threads hold read guards at once
#   w = weakref hub.cfg                                         # a class-object field of a thread_shared value
#   with hub.lock: cam.target = weakref hub.levels[0]           # made under a lock, ended after it
holes.what_goes_wrong: Two threads make and end links to REG at the same moment, with plain adds and subtracts on one weak count. WK-11 lets any read-only name make a link ("not a change of the target"). So a one-thread object's weak count is a place that several read-only names write: kind 4 in fact. But the table reads a class object's markers from its fields only, so `Registry` is Send and ThreadShared. The [THR-2] rewrite keeps verdict 114's part and drops today's sentence that refuses a link "in any function that may run on another thread than its target's owner" (J6-06's checker relied on that sentence). [THR-11]'s link rule covers tasks only. A lost +1 lets a later -1 bring the count to 0 and free REG's block (OBJ-3) while REG still lives, and every later read of REG reads freed memory. The same happens to an object read through an RwLock guard, to a class field of a thread_shared value, and to an object reached under a lock whose link outlives the lock.
holes.fix_hint: Make kind 2 follow the value, not the route. A link to a value that is not thread_shared is made, ended or opened only on that value's home thread, and for a static's object that is the module's home thread. It is never made through a path that other threads can take at the same time: a static off its home thread, a lock, an RwLock guard, or a thread_shared value's interior. Make this E7015 at the line, in every function and not only in tasks. The alternative is to give such objects atomic link counts. J6-06 A needs the same owner named for a static's object.

fn main():

- Judged never Send: a thread_shared observer list (`listeners: Array[weakref Listener] guarded by lock` in a `thread_shared Bus`) is refused.

class Player:
    hp: int = 10

struct Team:
    captain: shares Player

unsafe extern "C":
    # C's tile pool runs `visit` on its own threads, several at once; no threads(...) word: threads(any)
    @ffi(param(visit, callback(borrowed, user_data=data)))
    safe fn for_each_tile(visit: extern "C" fn(*mut void), data: *mut void)

fn main():
    team = Team(captain=shares Player())
    boss = Player()
    fn visit():
        t = copy of team          # +1 on the player's owner count, a plain add, on one of C's threads
        w = weakref boss          # +1 on boss's plain weak count
        println(t.captain.hp)     # t and w end: two plain subtracts
    for_each_tile(visit)
holes.what_goes_wrong: A borrowed callback uses main's real variables (FFI-21), and under threads(any), the default, it runs on several threads at once. The design's tier (a) lists only scoped tasks, scope jobs and @parallel bodies, and tier (b) checks only what a function holds through its capture words. So this route is in neither tier. FFI-22 checks that what the callback holds is Send and that it changes the caller's variables only by their own operations. `copy of team` and `weakref boss` change no variable, so nothing refuses them. Today's catch-all ("reaches another thread by any route", and the link sentence for "any function that may run on another thread") is exactly what the rewrite removes. Several C threads then add to and subtract from one plain owner count and one plain weak count. The counts are corrupted, and the player can be freed while `team` still owns it. A `rx.recv()` on the caller's Receiver inside such a callback counts as "its own operations", and it makes several consumers of a one-consumer queue.
holes.fix_hint: Put a borrowed threads(any) callback's use of the caller's real variables into tier (a), as a body that may run on several threads at once and so clashes with itself. Every place it changes must then be a ThreadShared place's own operations, with Receiver and Cell excluded. It never touches kinds 1 and 2: it makes or ends no shares owner, and makes, ends or opens no link to a one-thread value. The refusal is E7015 at the registering call.

#! threads main
class Session:
    names: Array[shares String] = []     # the new image removes this field: reclaim ends it on the polling thread

static mut S: Session = Session()

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `tick`
@unsafe(export("tick"))
pub extern "C" fn tick() -> i32:
    for n in S.names:                    # the home thread walks the list
        println(n)
    return 0

# host, reload build: thread 1 calls tick() in a loop; thread 2 calls ember_reload_poll()
holes.what_goes_wrong: [HR-3]'s exclusion is a store-then-load handshake on each side. The entering thread raises its depth and then reads the reload mark; the poller sets the mark and then reads every depth. [HR-42] and [HR-42a] order an entry with "one relaxed increment and one acquire fence", which does not keep the increment ahead of the mark's load. This is the store-buffer case: x86 allows it for a plain store, and ARM allows it even for a relaxed add. Both sides can then read the other's old value. Thread 1 goes into `tick` while reclaim ends `S.names` on thread 2, so the walk reads freed Strings and the shares counts race.
holes.fix_hint: Say that the entry's depth increment and the poll's mark store are each followed by a sequentially consistent fence (or are seq_cst read-modify-writes). Say too that clearing the mark after reclaim is a release that the waiting thread acquires. In reload builds this costs nothing extra on x86 for a locked increment, and one dmb per entry on ARM.

holes.what_goes_wrong: From the poll's test until reclaim ends, "a registered thread that enters Ember code waits". Reclaim runs the removed field's drop on the polling thread. The @parallel loop hands its chunks to idle job workers, each worker waits at its entry for the reload mark, and the drop waits for its chunks. The reload never ends and the process hangs, with no message. The same happens for a drop or migrate_from that opens thread.scope() or jobs.scope(), or that spawns a thread and joins it.
holes.fix_hint: Exempt the reload's own work: tasks, jobs and chunks that the polling thread starts inside the reload run, since they are tier (a) of that thread and are checked place by place. Or run that work on the polling thread itself; PAR-4 already lets the calling thread run a chunk. Otherwise refuse, when compiling, a drop or migrate_from that a reload may run and that starts other threads or waits for them.

unsafe extern "C":

    safe fn host_run_later(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)

pub extern "C" fn start() -> i32:

    return 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `frame`
@unsafe(export("frame"))
pub extern "C" fn frame() -> i32:

    return 0

#       meanwhile the C library runs the once callback on thread 1
holes.what_goes_wrong: Under creator, the design moves FRAMES's home to thread 2 at the second initialisation, and drops the lock because "the caller is the home thread". But the callback's trampoline compares the caller with the callback's own thread contract (thread 1, where it was registered: FFI-53), not with the module's current home. Nothing ends a module's callbacks at shutdown either: FFI-31 only detaches threads and releases thread-local state. So C's later call on thread 1 passes the compare and adds to FRAMES while thread 2 does too: a data race, with no lock and no stop. The E7008 rule for a creator handle in a static mut does not reach a once callback, which has no handle on Ember's side.
holes.fix_hint: Shutting a module down ends every callback it registered, so a later call stops ("C called the callback registered on line 9 after its module was shut down"). A threads(creator) callback of a creator module compares the caller with the module's current home thread. Both are the existing one compare. Also say that shutdown happens while no Ember code of the module runs on that thread, callbacks included, not only outside its export calls.

The marker table has `fn()` and `once fn()` (never) and `thread_shared fn()` (always), but no once function that another thread may run. So the commonest worker shape, handing data over and getting the result back, has no type. The same holds for jobs.submit, and for scope.spawn's plain `fn()`.
holes.fix_hint: Add the once form of the thread word to the table: a once function any thread may run, Send when its state is Send (ThreadShared does not apply, since it is called once). Let thread.spawn and jobs.submit take it (CLO-6: a once parameter accepts both kinds), and let scope.spawn take `owns f: once fn() -> R`.

Process: one listing command I ran early on also included a trivial `python -c "print(1)"` and `which`. Both read and wrote nothing, and nothing else was run. No file was edited.

Verdict: broken. The four high holes share one root. A one-thread object's header, its weak count, can be written through read-only names (WK-11) and by every route that is not a capture. Yet the table reads a class object's markers from its fields only, and the [THR-2] rewrite drops today's catch-all link sentence ("any function that may run on another thread than its target's owner"). The routes that are then left unchecked:
- statics, RwLock guards, objects reached under a lock, and thread_shared interiors (hole 1);
- `weakref T`, whose type does not say what kind of target it has (hole 2);
- a task ending objects reached through a static mut or a view it was handed, where THR-11's clause is narrower than verdict 166 and than its own headline (hole 3);
- borrowed threads(any) callbacks, which are in neither tier (hole 4).

Verdicts 164 to 166 themselves hold. Each member's own program is decided correctly. Phase 3 has no conflict or verdict clash that touches P01's members.

Smaller points, not counted as holes:
1. J6-16's example: `fn open(owns e: shares Entry) -> Result[Mesh]:` never returns, so \"It compiles with either change\" is false as written; add a `return Ok(...)`.
2. J7-03's race is already refused by CELL-1 (`g.set` through a read guard is E3023), as open risk 7 says. Verdict 165's making-line check stands anyway.
3. Hole 3's fix should stop at tasks and jobs. A @parallel body that ends linked objects is safe, because the caller only waits in the loop and runs chunks, so refusing it there would be needless.
4. Open risk 2 (a threads=any export running on another thread while a mixed-word module shuts down) is still open, and the new [FFI-31] claim that the hand-over is \"ordered by Ember itself\" depends on it.
5. If P12 admits `thread_shared dyn I`, [THR-8a] would make it need `+ Send + ThreadShared` written after a word that already says it (principle 3). P12 and P24 should word that together.
6. The cost claims hold (zero bytes per value, the listed compares), plus hole 6's fence in reload builds and, if nested owners are handed over, one atomic per nested owner at a route (hole 16).

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule's function rows are `fn()`, `once fn()`: never, and `thread_shared fn()`: always. There is no `thread_shared once fn()`, and `thread.spawn`/`jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared fn() -> R`. So a worker that hands its captured value to an `owns` parameter (a server handing a connection to `serve(owns conn)`, a job runner calling `run(owns job)`) is E3013, 'runs it twice'. That is untrue: a thread runs its function once. The same holds for `scope.spawn(owns fn() owns chunk: process(owns chunk))`, since scope.spawn takes a plain `fn()`. Rust's spawn takes `FnOnce + Send`. This is an exemption caused by missing syntax (checklist 12).
holes.fix_hint: Spell the once form with the same word: `thread_shared once fn()`, Send and ThreadShared as its state allows. `thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R`, and `scope.spawn` and `s.submit` take `owns f: once fn() -> R`. [CLO-6] already says such a parameter accepts both kinds, so no existing call changes.

import std.thread
from std.sync import channel

struct Feeder:
    pull: thread_shared fn() -> Option[int]

@derive(Copy)
struct Ctx:
    feeder: ref Feeder

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[int](capacity=8)
    feeder = Feeder(pull=fn() owns rx => rx.recv())   # its state, a Receiver, is Send: accepted by [CLO-16]
    ctx = Ctx(feeder=ref feeder)
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of ctx: println(ctx.feeder.pull()))   # `ref Feeder` is Send: `thread_shared fn()` is 'always' ThreadShared
        scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of ctx: println(ctx.feeder.pull()))   # a second thread runs rx.recv() on the same Receiver
        tx.send(owns 1).expect("gone")
        tx.send(owns 2).expect("gone")
holes.what_goes_wrong: The table makes `thread_shared fn()` ThreadShared 'always', although its state only has to be Send (a Receiver). That breaks the rule's own sentence, 'worked out from components, and nothing else decides them'. The design patches it in [CLO-16] only for 'a function held by a thread_shared value or a static, or a C callback under threads(any)'. A `ref`, a `Span` or a Copy view struct carrying the function to several tasks by a tier-(b) route is outside that closed list. The marker says ThreadShared, so the route is accepted. Two threads then call recv on one single-consumer Receiver, a data race in safe code.
holes.fix_hint: Drop the list of holders. One [CLO-18] line: a call through a read-only name counts a captured non-ThreadShared place's own operations (a Receiver's recv, an UnsafeCell) as a change of the function's state, wherever it is called. Then no read-only name on two threads can run such a call, and `thread_shared fn()` is ThreadShared because of what it lets read-only names do, not by decree.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Kind 2 is defined as the weak count 'written when a link to it is made, ended or opened'. But [WK-12] makes opening a one-thread link 'one test of the header', a read, and the rule's own definition of one-thread state is memory that changing or ending a value writes. The parent waits for a @parallel loop. Verdict 166 already forbids every task to end such a Player or to make or end shares owners. So nothing writes that header while the chunks read it. A common parallel AI or steering loop is still refused. Its only fix, making Player `thread_shared`, forbids every direct change of a player (E7014) and adds 32-byte headers and atomic opens. No verdict covers opening (166 names making and ending).
holes.fix_hint: A task may open a link to a one-thread target while neither the parent nor another task, until the join, may end an object of that type or make or end an owner of one. Those are the type-level end facts [RC-5] point 1 already uses (EFF-24), so the check runs when compiling and costs nothing. A @parallel body meets it whenever its chunks meet 166.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [THR-11] keeps 'R is Send' for scoped tasks. A scoped task cannot make kind 1 or 2 state (166), and R reaches the parent only after the join (verdict 104). So a view into the parent's own data goes back to the very thread that owns it, with nothing one-thread crossing. The rule still refuses the ordinary 'search each half in a task' program whenever the element type holds a weakref, shares or sharedref mut field, which game entities usually do. Rust refuses this too. The design claims fewer refusals than Rust for scoped tasks, and verdict 93's 'permissible as long as there is no clash' points the other way.
holes.fix_hint: Make a scoped task's or scope job's result tier (a). Views of the caller's places in R are checked as any view is, living no longer than the place, and what the task made itself must be Send. Only a thread.spawn or jobs.submit result needs Send.

The fixes are a thread word in a program with no threads (`thread_shared fn(ref mut Game)`) or `static mut`, which says 'may change' about a table that never does (against verdict 8). Meanwhile `static mut` is judged by reach (E7012 only where a function that may run on another thread reaches it), and so are a `threads=any` export's statics. That is two rules for one question.
holes.fix_hint: Judge `static` by reach as `static mut` is. It must be ThreadShared only where a function that may run on another thread reads it (E7002 at that function, naming the chain). That is the summary fact [THR-20] already uses.

The table contradicts it for Mutex, RwLock and guarded by (which hold kind-4 state and are ThreadShared), for `ref mut T` (no kind 4, yet never ThreadShared) and for `thread_shared fn()` holding a Receiver. So the six kinds do not generate the table. The std rows are decided by name, the per-case listing this group was meant to remove. A program's own lock or lock-free queue (an `Atomic[bool]` plus an `UnsafeCell[T]`) can never become ThreadShared, while std's Mutex is by fiat. CStrView, JobHandle, ScopedJoinHandle and ObjectPtr have no row at all.

Make std's synchronising types vouch for themselves with the one vouching spelling P04 settles (`unsafe extend[T: needs Send] Mutex[T] implements ThreadShared:`), so a program's own lock gets the same, and every other row then follows from components.

from std.sync import channel

class Bullet:

# BulletPool: `unsafe extend BulletPool implements Allocator:` and `unsafe extend BulletPool implements FoundByAddress:`
# (verdict 107 (c)): it gives bullets back one by one, and its values keep no word naming the pool

fn main():

    tx, rx = channel[Bullet using BulletPool](capacity=4)   # Send by the table: a class object whose fields are Send
    with scope = thread.scope():

A value of a FoundByAddress manager, or of a manager a program declares with no fields, keeps no word (ALC-1, verdict 107), yet its end still gives memory back to that instance. Judged by 'what it holds', it is Send, so the channel accepts it. The task's end then runs the pool's deallocate while this thread allocates: a race on a one-thread pool. This is safety, and it crosses P02 ('on the thread where the value may end').
holes.fix_hint: Count, in 'what it can reach', the manager instance a value's memory goes back to. Its kind is in the type (verdict 24: `using BulletPool`), whether the address is stored or found from the address. An instance kind that is not ThreadShared makes the value neither marker, exactly as LT-4's link does today. Word it with P02.

import std.thread

holes.what_goes_wrong: The table has no row for an opaque foreign `owns T`. Open risk 9 says that until P04 answers, 'the rule treats it as bound to its thread', which makes this E7008. Today FFI-33b binds a foreign value only when its contract says `threads(creator)`, so an absent word means not bound. A written declaration then means more than it says (verdict 132's lesson). Every C handle held in a struct (a database connection, a decoder, a socket) can no longer be returned from a worker, sent through a channel or kept in a creator static. The rule claims to be finished, yet leaves the commonest FFI value undecided.
holes.fix_hint: Decide the default in the rule, with P04. One option is FFI-33b's meaning: only `threads(creator)` binds, and the overlay writer vouches for the rest, listed by `ember tcb`. The other is verdict 31's direction: bound unless the contract writes a word for any thread. Either way it is one line of the table, not an open risk.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Tier (a) is listed by construct ('a scoped task's, a scope job's and a parallel body's use of the caller's own variables'), not by the property 'a function other threads run while this call waits, using this thread's variables'. A borrowed `threads(any)` callback has exactly that property and may use the caller's real variables ([FFI-21]), but it is in neither tier. [FFI-22] limits only its changes, and making a `shares` owner is not a change of the value (RC-1, WK-11). So kinds 1 and 2 of the caller's thread are touched from C threads at once, a race on a plain count, which the rule's 'never touch kinds 1 and 2' was written to stop.
holes.fix_hint: Define tier (a) by the property, so a borrowed `threads(any)` callback gets [THR-11]'s per-place check and its kinds 1-2 ban, as a @parallel body does (one summary fact, no run-time cost).

holes.what_goes_wrong: The changed point 4 does not say whether 'carries' reaches owners inside the carried value. If it does, a join result or a creator module's state with 10,000 thread_shared owners costs 10,000 atomic adds and a walk at the return or the shutdown. The cost section says 'zero' and 'no cost to anything else', and verdict 101 fix 2 accepted the delay instead: 'the delay remains only for an object that travels inside another object'. If it does not, the claimed fix ('closes the stale-home-count hole', 'covered without a stale home count') holds only for direct owners. Owners nested in creator statics, homed on an old creator that no longer runs Ember code, are then queued to a thread that never drains them (P05).
holes.fix_hint: Say which. For the join result, keep verdict 101 (direct owners only) and drop the claim. For a creator shutdown, a one-time walk of the module's statics is a real, once-per-shutdown cost: state it, and tell the owner that it widens verdict 101's fix 2.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Verdict 166 says 'the same for a task that ends an object weakref links on this thread point at'. The design's [THR-11] makes it 'ends no object ... of a class family that some weakref link may name', anywhere in the program. That is the only compile-time reading, but it is wider than the owner's words. A weakref added in an editor module now refuses a physics task's clear in another module, a far edit with its chain named. Per the verdict-125 lesson, a widening is confirmed, not written silently.
holes.fix_hint: Keep the class-family rule, which OBJ-1 already uses for headers. Put it to the owner as a one-line confirmation quoting verdict 166, and have the message name the far `weakref` line that brings the class in.

class Pooled:
    buf: Buffer = Buffer()
    ret: Sender[Buffer]

    fn drop():

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new [HR-3] keeps every other registered thread out of Ember code from the poll's test until reclaim ends, and reclaim runs user drops (and prepare runs migrate_from). A drop or migrate_from that blocks on another thread (a bounded channel's send, a join, a lock another thread must enter Ember to release) waits for a thread that is itself waiting for the reload: a deadlock where today there was a race. Separately, the Dekker-style 'increment the depth, then test the mark' needs a StoreLoad fence on entry. HR-42a's 'one relaxed increment and one acquire fence' does not order them on ARM, so the stated 'one load' cost is wrong.
holes.fix_hint: Refuse in plan (E9030-style) a reload whose reclaim drops or migrate_from carry the Block effect, which is decided when compiling. State the entry fence: a seq_cst fence, or an asymmetric barrier on the poll side (membarrier, FlushProcessWriteBuffers) that keeps entry at a plain load. Word it with P09 and [HR-42].

from std.sync import Lock

class Node:

class Scene:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    nodes: Array[shares mut Node] guarded by lock = []

fn main():
    scene = Scene(nodes=[shares mut Node(), shares mut Node()])
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): with scene.lock: scene.nodes[0].visible = false)
