A guarded field or Mutex of non-Send contents is not, so two tasks changing nodes under the scene's own lock are E7007. Tier (a) already bans the only dangerous part (making or ending the shares owners, verdict 166). The lock orders the rest, and nothing crosses by a value route.
holes.fix_hint: In tier (a), a lock (Mutex, RwLock's write guard, or a guarded by field under its lock) orders tasks whatever it holds. The ThreadShared condition belongs to tier (b) routes, where the lock itself travels.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Under [THR-8a] a bare `owns dyn Error` has neither marker, so any error type that wraps a cause that way can no longer be `?`-ed into AnyError, in single-thread programs too. Every such field must be written `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`. The design cites Swift's `protocol Error: Sendable` as the precedent but puts the bound on AnyError's From instead, which moves the words into every wrapping error.
holes.fix_hint: Offer the Swift form beside option A: `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display, Send, ThreadShared)`, refused at the `@derive(Error)` line naming the field. Then `dyn Error` carries both markers with no word, and AnyError's From needs only `E: needs Error`. Or keep A and state the cost to wrapping error types plainly in the option.

holes.what_goes_wrong: `thread_shared T` needs T Send and ThreadShared, and `dyn System` has only what is written after it. So if P12 lets `thread_shared` stand before `dyn I` (its other_places), the permission 'several threads own it' is written twice, which breaks principle 3 (said once). `thread_shared fn()` is itself the written promise for function types, so the same word before `dyn I` is the consistent promise.
holes.fix_hint: Make `thread_shared` before `dyn I` the written promise, as for `fn()`. The making line checks that the value put in is Send and ThreadShared, and no `+ Send + ThreadShared` is needed. Word it with P12.

design.rule:
One-thread state stays on its thread. One-thread state is memory that changing or ending a value writes with no atomic and no lock, and that other names on the same thread also write. It comes in six kinds:
1. a `shares` value's owner count;
2. the weak count of a value that is not `thread_shared` (making or ending a link writes it, opening one reads it, ending the value writes it);
3. a target that several `sharedref mut` holders change, a memory manager's instance among them;
4. a place changed through read-only names: an `UnsafeCell`, and what is built on one (`Cell`, a channel's `Receiver`);
5. a value bound to the thread that made it: a raw pointer and what holds one (a guard, a `Scope`), and a foreign value whose contract does not say `threads(any)`;
6. a module's variables, which belong to the module's home thread.

**Kinds 1 and 2 follow their value.** A value that is not `thread_shared` belongs to one thread: the thread that made it or was handed it whole, and, for a module variable, the module's home thread. Only that thread's own code makes or ends an owner of it, makes, ends or opens a link to it, or ends it where a link may name it.
- A task running beside that code does none of this, whatever route reaches the value.
- Nothing does it through a value that other threads reach at the same moment: inside a `thread_shared` value, through an `RwLock` read guard, or through a `static` off its home thread.
- A link made under an exclusive lock lives only for the lock's block.
- Opening a link only reads, so a task may open the caller's links while the caller, until the join, writes no header of that class family.

The compiler works out two markers for every type from what it holds or can reach:
- `Send`: the value may be handed whole to one other thread while this thread goes on.
- `ThreadShared`: several threads may use it through read-only names at once, and nothing they do through those names writes memory, except through an atomic or under a lock.

Some types decide their markers in other ways:
- A type that hides what it holds has the markers its written type promises (`dyn I + Send`, `thread_shared fn()`, `AnyError`, `some I + Send`).
- A type built in `unsafe` code has what its writer vouches for, the standard library's locks and channel ends included.
- A link's type says which kind of target it has: `weakref T` for a one-thread value, `weakref thread_shared T` for a shared one.

Every route to another thread needs the marker for what happens on it:
- **Shared at once** (needs `ThreadShared`): a value made `thread_shared`, a `static` that a function off the home thread reads, and what an export under `threads=any` reads.
- **Handed over** (needs `Send`): a capture word, a channel's element, the result of `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit`, a store into a place other threads reach under a lock, the parts of a value made `thread_shared`, and a module's state passing to a new `creator`. An object that a link names leaves its links behind (verdict 114's one compare).
- **Followed place by place** (needs no marker): code that runs on other threads while the code that started it is still running, using that code's variables (a scoped task, a scope job, a `@parallel` body, a borrowed callback under `threads(any)`), and a scoped task's result.

A thread runs its function once, so `thread.spawn` takes a `thread_shared once fn()`.

A module's variables live on its home thread, and the export's `threads` word says how the caller stands to it:
- `main`: the caller is the home thread, for the whole process.
- `creator`: the home moves to each new initialisation, and the module's state moves with it as a hand-over. So the state holds `Send` values and needs no lock, and the shutdown ends the callbacks bound to the old thread.
- `any`: any thread, at once. So the variable is guarded and holds `Send` values.
design.spec_text:
Adds `[THR-22]` and `[THR-8a]`.

Changes `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`, `[TYP-43]` (with P04), `[THR-2]`, `[THR-10]`, `[THR-11]`, `[THR-13]`, `[THR-15]` (J7-07's lead fix, now a row of the table), `[THR-20]`, `[STA-1]`, `[WK-11]`, `[WK-12]`, `[CLO-7]`, `[CLO-16]`, `[CLO-18]`, `[JOB-2]`, `[PAR-2]`, `[FFI-22]`, `[FFI-27]`/`[FFI-31]`, `[FFI-33]`, `[FFI-33b]` (with P04), `[FFI-33c]`, `[RC-4]` points 3 and 4, `[LT-4]`/`[ALC-1]` (with P02), `[ERR-1]`, `[ERR-8]`, `[HR-3]`, `[HR-42]` and `[HR-42a]`.

`[TYP-43]`'s two marker rows then read only "see `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`".

* `[THR-22]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **One-thread state stays on its thread.** One-thread state is memory that changing or ending a value writes with no atomic and no lock, and that other values or names on its thread also write. It comes in six kinds:
  1. a `shares` or `shares mut` value's owner count;
  2. the weak count of a value that is not `thread_shared`: making or ending a `weakref` link to it writes it, opening one reads it, and ending the value writes it (`[OBJ-3]`);
  3. a target that several `sharedref mut` holders may change (`[LT-46]`), the memory manager instance that a value's memory goes back to among them (`[LT-4]`);
  4. a place changed through read-only names: an `UnsafeCell`, and a type built on one that nobody vouches for (`Cell`, a channel's `Receiver`);
  5. a value bound to the thread that made it:
     - a raw pointer;
     - a type holding one that nobody vouches for (a lock's guard, a `Scope`, a `JobScope`);
     - a foreign `owns T` whose contract does not say `threads(any)` (`[FFI-33b]`);
  6. a module's `static` and `static mut`, which belong to the module's home thread (`[THR-20]`).

  **Kinds 1 and 2 follow their value.**
  - **Which thread a value belongs to.** A value that is not `thread_shared` belongs to one thread: the thread that made it, or that was handed it whole (`[THR-2]` (b)). The value of a module variable belongs to the module's home thread. A value reached through an exclusive lock belongs to the thread holding it, for the lock's block.
  - **What only that thread does.** Only that thread's own code:
    - makes or ends an owner of the value;
    - makes, ends or opens a link to it;
    - ends it, where a link may name it (its class family, `[OBJ-1]`).

  The following are refused at the line (`E7015`, except where another code is named):
  - **Code that runs beside it.** Code of `[THR-2]` (a) makes and ends no `shares` owner and no link to a one-thread value (verdict 166). It ends an object that a link may name only if it made that object or was handed it whole; verdict 114 moved such an object away from its links. An object it reaches any other way is refused, whatever the route: the starting thread's variables, a `static mut`, or a view it captured or was sent.
  - **A value other threads reach at the same moment.** None of these is done through such a value:
    - inside a `thread_shared` value;
    - inside the state of a `thread_shared fn()` (not a `once` one, which runs on one thread);
    - through an `RwLock`'s read guard;
    - through a `static`, in a function that may run off the module's home thread.

    The message for the last: "`REG` is a module variable that other threads read at once (`peek` runs on the thread started on line 14), and `weakref REG` adds to its link count, which has no atomics; make the link in code that runs on the main thread".
  - **A link made through an exclusive lock** (a `Mutex`'s guard, an `RwLock`'s write guard, a `guarded by` field under its lock) does not leave the lock's block (`E3063`), as a view made through a guard does not (`[THR-3]`). The message: "`hub.levels` is guarded by `hub.lock`, and other threads make and end links to its levels under that lock; `cam.target` (line 7) would keep this link after the lock ends; make the levels shareable: `levels: Array[thread_shared Level] guarded by lock`".

  **Opening a link only reads its target's header.** So code of `[THR-2]` (a) may open a link to the starting thread's value while nothing beside it writes a header of that class family. That means the starting thread, until the join, ends no object of the family and makes or ends no link to one. Otherwise it is `E7007`, naming both lines.
  - A `@parallel` body always meets this: its caller waits in the loop.
  - A scoped task meets it when the parent's lines between the spawn and the join do.

  These facts are worked out from bodies (`[EFF-24]`), as `[RC-5]` point 1's "may end an object of that type" is. Because read-only names that several threads hold at once make no link, a class object is `ThreadShared` when its fields are. Nothing runs for this rule except the steps `[THR-2]` names.

* `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]` *(changed)* The two markers:
  - **`Send`**: a value of the type may be handed whole to one other thread while this thread goes on. Afterwards nothing of it is one-thread state of this thread (kinds 1, 2, 3 and 5).
  - **`ThreadShared`**: several threads may use one value of the type through read-only names at once. Nothing those names do writes memory, except through an atomic or under a lock the thread holds.

  Both are worked out from a type's components by the table below. Only two other things decide them:
  - the promise that a type hiding its contents writes (`[THR-8a]`);
  - a vouch made in `unsafe` code (`[TYP-43]`).

  A type that holds itself is solved to a fixed point.

  | holder | `Send` when | `ThreadShared` when |
  |---|---|---|
  | struct, enum, tuple, fixed array, collection, class object, `owns T`, `Option`, `Result`, a lambda's own type (its state), an iterator adapter, a generator (what it holds across a `yield`) | every component is | every component is |
  | a value whose memory comes from a manager (`using A`) | as its components, and `A` is `ThreadShared` (`[LT-4]`) | the same |
  | `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `sharedref mut T`, `weakref T` | never | never |
  | `thread_shared T`, `weakref thread_shared T` | `T` is `Send` and `ThreadShared` | the same |
  | `ref T`, `Span[T]` | `T` is `ThreadShared` | `T` is `ThreadShared` |
  | `ref mut T`, `MutSpan[T]` | `T` is `Send` | `T` is `ThreadShared` |
  | `UnsafeCell[T]` | `T` is `Send` | never |
  | `Atomic[T]`, scalars, `StrView`, `extern "C" fn` | always | always |
  | a raw pointer | never | never |
  | `fn()`, `once fn()` | never | never |
  | `thread_shared fn()`, `thread_shared once fn()` (`[CLO-16]`) | always | always |
  | `dyn I`, `AnyError`, a `some I` result outside its package, a type parameter | `[THR-8a]` | `[THR-8a]` |
  | a foreign `owns T` | its contract says `threads(any)` (`[FFI-33b]`) | vouched for (P04) |

  **Every other type** is a struct, enum or class built from these, the standard library's types included. It has what its fields give and what its writer vouches for.

  The standard library vouches for these:
  - `Mutex[T]`: both, for a `Send` `T`;
  - `RwLock[T]`: both, for a `T` that is `Send` and `ThreadShared`;
  - `Lock` and `Once`: both;
  - `Sender[T]`: both, for a `Send` `T`;
  - `Receiver[T]`: `Send`, for a `Send` `T`;
  - `JoinHandle[R]`, `ScopedJoinHandle[R]` and `JobHandle`: both, for a `Send` `R`;
  - `CStrView`: both, as `StrView`.

  Nobody vouches for `Cell[T]`, a guard, a `Scope` or a `JobScope`. So `Cell[T]` is `Send` for a `Send` `T` and never `ThreadShared`, and the others are neither. A program's own lock (an `Atomic[bool]` beside an `UnsafeCell[T]`) vouches in the same way.

* `[TYP-43]` *(changed, spelling with P04's J7-06)* A program may vouch for `ThreadShared` as it vouches for `Send`, for every kind of type, with the spelling P04 settles (`unsafe extend[T: needs Send] SpinLock[T] implements ThreadShared:` with a `# SAFETY:` note). The standard library's vouches above are written that way.

* `[THR-8a]` *(new)* **A type that does not show what it holds has the markers it says.**
  - A `dyn` value is `Send` (or `ThreadShared`) when an interface written after `dyn` is that marker or requires it: `owns dyn Task + Send`, or `interface Task: needs Send:`.
  - A function type is `Send` and `ThreadShared` when it is `thread_shared fn()` or `thread_shared once fn()`.
  - A `some I` result, seen from outside its package, has the markers written after it (`some Iterator[Item = int] + Send`). Inside its package, it has the markers of the type it is.
  - `AnyError` has the markers its declaration gives (`[ERR-8]`).
  - A type parameter has the markers its bounds give: written on a `pub` function (verdict 108), worked out on a private one (verdict 113).

  The line that puts a value into such a type checks that the value has what the type promises: `owns Square(side=2)` given to `owns dyn Shape + Send`, a lambda given to `thread_shared fn()`, a `?` into `AnyError`. A broken promise is `E7015`, naming the field that breaks it.

* `[THR-2]` *(changed)* **Every route to another thread needs the marker for what happens on it.**

  **(a) Code followed place by place.** This is a function that runs on other threads while the code that started it is still running, and that uses that code's own variables:
  - a scoped task;
  - a scope job;
  - a `@parallel` body;
  - a `callback(borrowed)` under `threads(any)` (`[FFI-22]`);
  - the result of a scoped task or job, which comes back to the starting thread after the join.

  Such code needs no marker. `[THR-11]` checks every place it reads or changes against everything that runs beside it until the join, and `[THR-22]` keeps it off the starting thread's kinds 1 and 2.

  **(b) Routes the value travels.**

  | route | needs |
  |---|---|
  | **shared by several threads at once**: a value made `thread_shared` (`[THR-1]`, checked at that line, verdict 165); a `static`, where a function that may run off the module's home thread reads it (`E7002` at that function, `[STA-1]`); what an export under `threads=any` reads | `ThreadShared` |
  | **handed over**: what a function another thread runs holds by its capture words (`thread.spawn`, `jobs.submit`, a kept callback, a scoped task's or job's capture words); `tx.send(owns v)` and a channel's element type; the result of `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit`; a value stored into a place other threads reach under a lock (a guarded field of a `thread_shared` value, a guarded `static mut` reached off its home thread); the parts of a value made `thread_shared`; a module's state passing to a new `creator` (`[FFI-33]`) | `Send` |

  **Every hand-over of (b) runs verdict 114's compare** at its line, for an object of a class family that some `weakref` link may name, with fix 1 for the objects it owns. Its links here are left behind and find it ended wherever it is received. That includes this thread itself, for a channel this thread both sends on and receives from: the program said `owns`, and Rust's `Rc` cannot be sent at all.

  Two hand-overs need no compare:
  - the result of `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit`: its function's links ended before its thread gave it back;
  - a module's state: it is `Send`, so it holds no one-thread link, and the shutdown ended the module's callbacks bound to the old thread (`[FFI-31]`).

  **Each check is made where the route is written:**
  - `E7015` for kinds 1 to 4;
  - `E7008` for kind 5;
  - `E7012` for kind 6.

  The message names the route's line and the field that holds the state ("`Watcher.target` is a `sharedref mut` link, which other holders change on this thread").

  **`thread_shared` owners on a route.** A route that hands over an owner of a `thread_shared` value itself hands that owner over at that place (`[RC-4]` point 4). An owner inside another value the route carries keeps verdict 101's delay. Verdict 114's hand-over and its fixes stay as written.

* `[THR-10]`, `[CLO-7]`, `[JOB-2]` *(changed)* The thread functions take the `once` form:
  - `thread.spawn` is `[R: needs Send]` above `pub fn spawn(owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R) -> JoinHandle[R]:`.
  - `jobs.submit` takes `owns f: thread_shared once fn()`.
  - `scope.spawn` takes `owns f: once fn() -> R`, and `s.submit` takes `owns f: once fn()`.

  A thread, task or job runs its function once. A function that gives its captures away is accepted, `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: run(owns job))`, and a function that runs twice still is, since such a parameter accepts both kinds (`[CLO-6]`). Every call written today compiles unchanged.

* `[THR-11]` *(changed)* A task uses the caller's variables with no marker.
  - **Clashes.** These are `E7007`: two tasks changing one place; one task reading a place another changes; the parent doing either before the task's join. The exceptions are a reduction, a lock, and a `ThreadShared` place's own operations (an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender`, or a `guarded by` field under its lock).
    - A `Receiver` or a `Cell` used so is `E7007`.
    - A task started in a loop counts as several tasks.
    - A read or change through a link counts for that field of every object of the class family (`[EXC-3]`).
  - **Kinds 1 and 2: as `[THR-22]` (verdict 166).** A task:
    - makes and ends no `shares` owner;
    - makes and ends no link to a one-thread value;
    - ends an object that a link may name only if it made it or was handed it whole;
    - opens a link to the caller's value only while the caller, until the join, ends none of that family and makes or ends no link to one.

    The message for a static mut: "the task on line 9 gives `CUR` a new `Level`, which ends the old one, and `weakref` links on this thread may point at it (`Camera.target`); give `CUR` its new level after the scope: move line 9 below the `with` block".
  - **Captures.** What the task's function captured with a word is handed to the task's thread, so it is `Send` (`E7015`), with verdict 114's compare.
  - **The result.** `R` comes back to the caller after the join, and needs no marker. A view in it is checked as any view of the caller's places is, and lives no longer than they do. It holds nothing bound to the task's thread (`E7008`). So `scope.spawn(owns fn() => weakest(left))`, returning `Option[ref Enemy]`, compiles.

* `[PAR-2]` *(changed)* A `@parallel` body follows `[THR-11]`. It opens links to one-thread values freely (`if e.target exists as p: e.aim = p.x - e.x`): its caller waits in the loop, and no chunk makes or ends such a link (`[THR-22]`).

* `[THR-13]` *(changed)* The bullets follow `[THR-2]`:
  - a place that code of (a) reads or changes (`[THR-11]`, `[THR-22]`);
  - a reduction;
  - an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender` or `guarded by` field (a `ThreadShared` place): ordered by the atomic or by the lock;
  - a value handed over;
  - a `thread_shared` value;
  - a module variable (`[THR-20]`);
  - a `sharedref mut` target.

* `[CLO-16]` *(changed)* `thread_shared fn()` and `thread_shared once fn()` are functions that any thread may run.
  - **Their state.** A value of either holds `Send` state: `thread_shared` owners, values handed over, and copies of `Send` values. This is checked at the line that makes it (`[THR-8a]`).
  - **`thread_shared fn()`.** Several threads may call one `thread_shared fn()` at once through read-only names, and `[CLO-18]` keeps those calls from changing its state. So the type is `Send` and `ThreadShared`, and no list of holders is needed.
  - **`thread_shared once fn()`.** It runs once, on the thread that holds it, so its state may change. So `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx => rx.recv())` is accepted.

* `[CLO-18]` *(changed)* **A call that changes its function's own state.**
  - **What counts.** A call changes its function's state when it changes a value the state holds, by any route. A place's own operations count (`rx.recv()`, `c.set(v)`), except a `ThreadShared` place's (an `Atomic`, `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Sender`, or a `guarded by` field under its lock), whose own operations any number of names may run at once.
  - **Where it may be made.** Such a call is made only through a name that may change the place holding the function (`E3023`), wherever that is. These are read-only names: a list walked read-only, a `static`, a `thread_shared` value, a `ref` given to tasks, and C's calls of a `threads(any)` callback.
  - **What does not count.** Making or ending a `weakref` link is not such a change (`[WK-11]`); `[THR-22]` says where it is done.

  The message: "`ctx.feeder.pull()` runs a function that takes from its own `Receiver` (line 9), and `ctx.feeder` only reads the feeder; give each task its own channel, or call it through `ref mut`".

* `[STA-1]`, `[THR-20]` *(changed)* A module's variables belong to its **home thread**: in a program, the thread that runs `main`; in a library, the thread of its initialisation (`[FFI-33]`).

  A function **may run off the home thread** when it is reachable from:
  - `thread.spawn`;
  - `jobs.submit`;
  - a kept callback that C may call on another thread;
  - an export under `threads=any`;
  - a `drop` that may run on another thread (a `thread_shared` value's, `[RC-4]`).

  Code of `[THR-2]` (a) is checked place by place instead.
  - **A `static` never changes.** Other threads read it at once only where a function that may run off the home thread reads it. There its type is `ThreadShared` (`E7002` at that function, naming the chain from where the thread starts). The message: "`WEAPONS` holds plain `fn(ref mut Game)` values, and `worker`, which runs on the thread started on line 30, reads it while the main thread does; write `on_fire: thread_shared fn(ref mut Game)` in `WeaponDef`". A program with no such function needs nothing of its statics' types.
  - **A `static mut`** is reached by its home thread and by the code of `[THR-2]` (a) that the home thread starts. A function that may run off the home thread and reaches it is `E7012`, unless the variable is `guarded by` a `static` `Lock` and used under that lock.
    - A guarded `static mut` holds `Send` values, as a `Mutex` does. The message: "`CACHE` is guarded by `CACHE_LOCK`, and `worker` reaches it from another thread, but it holds `shares` owners, which stay on one thread; hold the nodes whole: `Array[Node]`".
    - A value stored into it is handed over (`[THR-2]` (b)).
  - The rest of `[THR-20]` (where a `drop` runs) stays.

* `[WK-11]`, `[WK-12]` *(changed)* **A link's type says which kind of target it has.**
  - **Two types.** `weakref T` links to a value that is not `thread_shared`; `weakref thread_shared T` links to one held `thread_shared`. These are two types, as Rust's `rc::Weak` and `sync::Weak` are. `weakref x` makes the kind of what `x` is.
  - **Mixing them.** A link of one kind given to a place of the other is `E2020`. The message: "`listeners` holds links to one-thread `Listener`s, and `l` is `thread_shared`; write `listeners: Array[weakref thread_shared Listener]`".
  - **What the type decides.** Each making, ending and opening is compiled plain or atomic from the type.
  - **`weakref this`.** Inside a method, `weakref this` has the kind of the object the method is called on. The compiler compiles the method once for each kind it is called on, as verdict 88 makes a copy. A body that stores the link where the other kind is wanted is refused at the call that gives that kind.
  - **The last sentence of `[WK-11]`** reads: "Making, ending or opening a link touches its target's header, so it is done only as `[THR-22]` says."

* `[LT-4]`, `[ALC-1]` *(changed, worded with P02)* **A value reaches the manager instance its memory goes back to.** This holds whether it keeps the instance's address or the manager finds it from the value's own address (verdict 107 (c)).
  - For `[THR-8]` the value holds a `sharedref mut` link to that instance (kind 3). So it is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared`, unless the manager type is `ThreadShared`; then it is judged by its contents.
  - A `ThreadShared` manager is one whose `allocate` and `deallocate` order themselves, vouched for in its `unsafe extend`. `Global` and `System` are.
  - A one-instance manager that a program declares is reached as a module variable is: its `deallocate` is a call, checked on each thread where the value may end (`[THR-20]`).

  The message: "`Bullet using BulletPool` gives its memory back to `pool` when it ends, and a `BulletPool` is not safe for two threads at once; end the bullets on this thread, or send copies made with the built-in manager".

* `[FFI-22]` *(changed)* **A callback that C may call from any thread** (`threads(any)`, the default) is a `thread_shared fn()`, which C calls through read-only names, several at once.
  - **Its state** is `Send`, and a call changes none of it (`[CLO-18]`). Otherwise it is `E7015` at the registering line: "C may call `on_tick` from several threads at once (`threads(any)`), and it adds to its own `n`; count with `n: Atomic[int]`, or, if C calls it only on this thread, write `threads(creator)`".
  - **A `callback(borrowed)` one** may use the caller's real variables, as a scoped task does (`[THR-2]` (a)). It may run any number of times at once and has no reductions:
    - It changes a caller's place only by a `ThreadShared` place's own operations. A `Receiver`'s or a `Cell`'s are not.
    - It touches no kind 1 or 2 of the caller's thread (`[THR-22]`).

    So `copy of team`, where `Team` holds a `shares Player`, and `weakref boss` are `E7015` at the registering call: "C may run `visit` on several threads at once (`threads(any)`), and `copy of team` makes another owner of `team.captain`, whose count has no atomics; read `team.captain.hp` where it is, or, if C runs `visit` only on this thread, write `threads(creator)` in its contract".
  - **`threads(main)` and `threads(creator)` callbacks** are plain functions, checked by the trampoline's one compare, as today.

* `[FFI-33]`, `[FFI-33c]` *(changed)* `threads=` says how the calling thread stands to the module's home thread.
  - **`main`**: the caller is the home thread, for the life of the process. The home thread is the thread of the module's first successful initialisation. An initialisation on another thread after a shutdown stops: "`plugin` keeps its module variables on thread 1, where it was first initialised (its exports say `threads=main`), and this initialisation runs on thread 7; initialise it on thread 1, or write `threads=creator`".
  - **`creator`**: the caller is the home thread, which is the thread of the current initialisation (ODR-083).
    - After a shutdown, an initialisation on another thread makes that thread the home thread.
    - The module's state passes to it whole, as a value handed over, ordered by the shutdown and the initialisation.
    - So every `static` and `static mut` that a `creator` export reaches is `Send`, with no lock (`E7015` for kinds 1 to 4, `E7008` for kind 5).
  - **`any`**: any thread, at once. Every `static` it reads is `ThreadShared`, and every `static mut` it reaches is `guarded by` a lock and holds a `Send` value.

  Under `main` and `creator`, each export's wrapper compares the caller with the home thread, one compare per call, in every profile, as today.

* `[FFI-27]`, `[FFI-31]` *(changed)* **Shutting down a module whose exports include `threads=main` or `threads=creator`.**
  - **Where and when.** It is shut down on its home thread, while none of its code runs there, its callbacks included.
    - Each export wrapper and trampoline of such a module counts the module's calls running on the calling thread: a plain add and subtract, beside its existing compare.
    - A shutdown on another thread stops, naming the thread. So does one made while that count is above zero, naming the call.
  - **Callbacks.** The shutdown ends every callback the module registered whose contract binds it to a thread (`threads(creator)`, `threads(main)`). Its slot is retired, as `[FFI-53]` retires a worn-out one, and its state ends on the home thread. So a later call from C stops: "C called the callback registered on line 9 after its module was shut down".
  - **Detached threads.** A thread the shutdown detaches has ended for `[RC-4]` point 3. It empties its queue then. A `thread_shared` value it made, whose last owner ends later on another thread, is ended at once by that thread; the shutdown and the next initialisation order the home count it left. This is worded with P05.

* `[FFI-33b]` *(changed, with P04)* **A foreign `owns T`** (a `returns_owned` result) is `Send` only when its contract says `threads(any)`.
  - **With no word**, it is bound to the thread that made it, which is what `threads(creator)` says. It is not `Send` (`E7008`): "`db` is a `sqlite3` handle, and its contract (`sqlite3.overlay.em`, line 4) does not say another thread may have it; if the library allows it, write `threads(any)` on that result". In every profile it stops the program when it ends on another thread.
  - **A forgotten word** then refuses a line, instead of letting a thread-bound C object (a GL context, a COM object) reach another thread (verdict 31's direction).
  - **Whether several threads may use one at once** is a vouch (P04).

* `[RC-4]` *(changed)*
  - **Point 4** reads: "every route of `[THR-2]` (b) that hands over an owner of a `thread_shared` value itself hands it over at that place". This now includes the result of `thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` (verdict 101's fix 2). An owner inside another value that a route carries keeps verdict 101's delay (point 5).
  - **Point 3** adds: "a thread that its module's shutdown detached has ended (`[FFI-31]`)".

* `[ERR-8]`, `[ERR-1]` *(changed)*
  - `AnyError` holds an `owns dyn Error + Send + ThreadShared`, so it is `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8a]`).
  - It implements `From[E]` for every `E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`.
  - A `?`, `.context` or `AnyError.from` of an error that does not meet this is `E7015` at that line, in every program: "`LoadError` holds `entry`, a `shares` owner, which stays on one thread, and an `AnyError` may go to another thread; return `Result[Mesh, LoadError]`, or hold a copy: `entry: Entry`".
  - In `[ERR-1]`, "takes any `E: needs Error`" reads "`E: needs (Error, Send, ThreadShared)`".

* `[HR-3]` *(changed)* A reload's work on the program's values reaches every thread's one-thread state from the polling thread: prepare's `migrate_from`, commit, and reclaim's ends of removed fields with their `drop`.
  - **The exclusion.** From the poll's test until reclaim ends, no other registered thread runs Ember code, except the work the reload starts itself. A registered thread that enters Ember code in that time waits until reclaim ends.
  - **The reload's own work** is the tasks of scopes it opens, the jobs and `@parallel` chunks it submits, and the threads it starts. It is checked as that code's own tasks and threads are (`[THR-2]`).
  - **Scope.** This applies to reload builds only, and to `std.hot.checkpoint()` too.

* `[HR-42]` *(changed)* **Publication.**
  - **The handshake.** An entering thread increments its depth counter and then reads the reload mark. The poll sets the mark and then reads every depth counter. Each side's store comes before its load.
  - **How the order is kept.** The poll issues a process-wide barrier between its store and its loads (`membarrier` on Linux, `FlushProcessWriteBuffers` on Windows), so the entering side needs only a compiler barrier. On a platform with no such barrier, each side's store is a sequentially consistent read-modify-write.
  - **Leaving, and clearing the mark.** Leaving decrements with release. Clearing the mark after reclaim is a release store, which a waiting thread acquires before it runs.
  - **Commit** publishes as today.

* `[HR-42a]` *(changed)* The counter is not a lock. Entering Ember code costs:
  - one plain increment, a compiler barrier and one load of a mostly-read word, where the platform has a process-wide barrier;
  - one sequentially consistent increment, where it has none.

  The reload side pays the barrier and the scan over threads.

Verdict 164, as a line of the rule. A `sharedref mut` link is kind 3: a target that other holders change on this thread. So it is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared`, and neither is any type holding one.
- A channel is a route the value travels on (tier b), so `channel[Watcher]` is refused.
- Scoped tasks still reach the link where it is, through the caller's variables, checked place by place (tier a). So verdict 77's reduction stands, in a loop too (`ref w`).

    target: sharedref mut Player

fn main():
    p = Player()
    w = Watcher(target=sharedref mut p)
    tx, rx = channel[Watcher](capacity=1)     # E7015
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): w.target.hp -= 1)
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): p.hp -= 2)      # a reduction with the task above (verdict 77)

Verdict 166, as a line of the rule, worded by what is touched and not by the route. A task never touches kinds 1 and 2 of the caller's thread:
- It makes and ends no `shares` owner.
- It makes and ends no link to a one-thread value.
- It ends an object of a class family that some link may name only if it made that object or was handed it whole (verdict 114 moved that one away from its links).

This holds whatever route reaches the object: the caller's variables, a `static mut`, a view the task captured or was sent. So `CUR = Level()` from a task is refused too, and so is `r.clear()` on a captured `ref mut` list.

Opening a link only reads its target's header. A task may open the caller's links while the caller, until the join, ends no object of that family and makes or ends no link to one. A `@parallel` body always may, since its caller waits.

answers.answer:
One rule for both words: a module's variables live on the module's home thread, and the export's word says how the caller's thread stands to it.
- `main`: the caller is the home thread, fixed at the first initialisation, for the process. An initialisation on another thread after a shutdown stops.
- `creator`: the caller is the home thread, which is the current initialisation's thread. The module's state passes to a new creator whole, as a value handed over. It is ordered by the shutdown, which is made on the home thread with none of the module's code running there, and by the initialisation. So every `static` and `static mut` a `creator` export reaches must be `Send`, and needs no lock. The shutdown also ends the callbacks bound to the old thread, so C cannot run one there beside the new home.
- `any`: the caller is any thread, at once. The variable is guarded and holds `Send` values.

Today's `E7012` under `creator` goes: the lock it asks for orders nothing that the hand-over does not already order.

design.prior_art:
**Rust**
- **Markers.** `Send` and `Sync` are auto traits worked out from fields.
- **Vouching.** `unsafe impl` vouches for what the compiler cannot see, and the standard library vouches exactly the same way (`unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for Mutex<T>`). That is the precedent for std's rows here and for a program's own lock.
- **Two link types.** `rc::Weak<T>` and `sync::Weak<T>` are different types for one-thread and shared targets. That is the precedent for `weakref T` against `weakref thread_shared T`.
- **Spawning.** `thread::spawn` takes `F: FnOnce() -> T + Send`. That is the precedent for `thread_shared once fn()`.
- **`&mut T`.** `&mut T: Sync` holds when `T: Sync`.
- **Allocators.** `Box<T, A>` is `Send` only when `A: Send`. That is the precedent for a value reaching its manager instance.
- **Other precedents.** `anyhow::Error` requires `Send + Sync + 'static`. `Rc::try_unwrap` is verdict 114.
- **Where it falls short:**
  - Scoped threads are judged by type, not place by place: a scoped thread's result must be `Send`, and `&Cell<i32>` cannot be read by scoped threads even when nothing writes it.
  - An `Rc` cannot be handed over even when it is unique.
  - Every `static` must be `Sync`, even in a program with no threads, since Rust has no whole-program reach.
  - `impl Trait` leaks auto traits.

**C++**
- Nothing is checked, and a data race is undefined behaviour.
- `shared_ptr` and `weak_ptr` counts are always atomic, so every copy pays an atomic, even on one thread.
- A `mutable` member under a `const&` read from two threads is the J7-03 race, unchecked.

**Swift 6**
- `Sendable` is inferred for non-public types, `@unchecked Sendable` vouches, and `protocol Error: Sendable` is the precedent for J6-16 A.
- `some P` does not leak `Sendable`.
- A global variable must be `Sendable` or isolated to a global actor such as `@MainActor`: a declared home thread, which Ember works out by reach.
- Region isolation (SE-0414) is not taken (verdict 23).

**Hand-shake ordering**
- An asymmetric barrier makes the rare side pay and the common side pay nothing: Linux `membarrier(MEMBARRIER_CMD_PRIVATE_EXPEDITED)` and Windows `FlushProcessWriteBuffers`.
- .NET's thread suspension for its garbage collector, folly's `asymmetric_thread_fence_heavy` and userspace RCU use it this way.

**Ada/SPARK**
- Ravenscar and Jorvik flow analysis proves place by place that a variable two tasks reach is protected, atomic or owned by one task, as tier (a) does.

**Go**
- A debug-only race detector, at 2 to 20 times the run time.

**What this rule keeps**
- Rust's markers worked out from fields, its std-vouches-like-everyone, its two weak types and its `FnOnce` spawn.
- Swift's erased promise and error-may-travel.
- SPARK's place-by-place check.
- A home thread, as Swift's main actor.

It is safe like Rust, at C's run-time cost, with fewer refusals than Rust for scoped tasks, module variables and statics.
design.cost:
**When compiling: everything.** No value or object grows by a byte. The compiler:
- works out the markers;
- checks every conversion into a type that hides its contents;
- checks every route;
- checks tasks place by place;
- decides, for every owner, link and end, which thread its value belongs to and by which route it is reached;
- follows which functions reach which module variables.

Each of these is a fact in the existing per-function summaries (`[EFF-24]`). A method that makes `weakref this` and is called on both kinds of object is compiled twice (rare).

**While running, per operation, against C** (which pays nothing and checks nothing):
- **Markers, promises, route checks, the belongs-to rule, a task's use of the caller's variables:** zero.
- **A `shares` owner count:** a plain add or subtract, as today. C++'s `shared_ptr` pays an atomic on every copy.
- **A link to a one-thread value:** a plain add or subtract, now chosen from the link's type. A link to a `thread_shared` value: atomic, as today. Today's text does not say how one `weakref Player` type picks between them.
- **A hand-over of an object a link may name:** one compare (verdict 114). It is now made at every hand-over route: sends, stores into places other threads reach under a lock, and values made `thread_shared`, as verdict 114 says of "an object handed to another thread". A spawned thread's result needs none.
- **A `thread_shared` owner handed over itself:** one atomic add (fix 2), as today. Owners inside another value keep verdict 101's delay, with no walk.
- **An export call or trampoline under `main` or `creator`:** one thread compare (existing), plus a plain add and subtract of the module's call count on this thread (new, for the shutdown check).
- **A `main` module initialised again:** one compare.
- **A module shutdown:**
  - one compare and the count test;
  - one generation bump per thread-bound callback the module registered (once per shutdown);
  - no walk of the module's state, since a detached thread counts as ended for `[RC-4]` point 3.
- **A module's state passing to a new creator:** zero.
- **Module variables under `creator`:** one lock and one unlock fewer per access than today.
- **Reload builds only:**
  - Entering Ember code costs a plain increment, a compiler barrier and one load of a mostly-read word where the OS has a process-wide barrier (Linux, Windows).
  - Elsewhere it costs one sequentially consistent increment: on x86 a locked add, about 20 cycles; on ARM one `dmb`.
  - The poll pays the barrier and the scan.
  - The reload's own tasks and jobs run, instead of every thread hanging.
- **`AnyError`:** zero; the check at `?` is made when compiling.

**Refusals, the cost a program may pay in its text:**
- An error holding one-thread state does not go into `AnyError`, in a one-thread program too.
- A worker cannot hand back a `shares` graph (verdict 23).
- A `creator` module's variables cannot hold one-thread state.
- A handler that takes from its own `Receiver` is called through `ref mut`.
- No link is made to a `static`'s object off the home thread, or through what several threads read at once.
- A foreign handle with no thread word stays on its thread until the overlay says `threads(any)`.
- A value made in a pool that is not `ThreadShared` stays on its thread.

readability.ordinary_before:
# plugin.em: a plugin (cdylib) counting calls
#! threads creator
from std.sync import Lock

static HITS_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut HITS: int guarded by HITS_LOCK = 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `bump`
@unsafe(export("bump"))
pub extern "C" fn bump() -> i32:
    with HITS_LOCK:
        HITS += 1
    return 0

# game.em: a weapon table, a loader and a job runner
struct WeaponDef:
    name: StrView
    on_fire: thread_shared fn(ref mut Game)    # a thread word in a table no thread reads (E7002 without it)

static WEAPONS: Array[WeaponDef] = [WeaponDef(name="pistol", on_fire=fire_pistol)]

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))   # refused by rules the text never states
    println(h.join()?)
    job = Job()
    w = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: run(owns job))  # E3013: "runs it twice"
    w.join()
    return Ok(())
readability.ordinary_after:
# plugin.em
#! threads creator
static mut HITS: int = 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `bump`
@unsafe(export("bump"))
pub extern "C" fn bump() -> i32:
    HITS += 1
    return 0

# game.em
struct WeaponDef:
    name: StrView
    on_fire: fn(ref mut Game)

static WEAPONS: Array[WeaponDef] = [WeaponDef(name="pistol", on_fire=fire_pistol)]

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() => load("level1.cfg"))   # compiles
    println(h.join()?)
    job = Job()
    w = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: run(owns job))  # compiles: a thread runs its function once
    w.join()
    return Ok(())
readability.note:
The after is shorter: no lock and no thread word in a table that no thread reads. Nothing in it is new, and two lines that are refused today compile.

Ordinary code never writes `Send` or `ThreadShared`. The thread words stay where they are today: `thread_shared`, `thread_shared fn()`, `+ Send` after a `dyn` that crosses threads, and an export's `threads`. The only new spelling, `weakref thread_shared T`, appears only in an observer list that crosses threads.

Every refusal names the field or the route that holds the one-thread state, and gives a line that compiles. The game loop, scoped-task loops (`ref t`, reductions through links, a `@parallel` loop opening its targets) and one-thread `shares` and `weakref` code read exactly as before.

design.misuse:
**Refused when compiling**, at the route's or the operation's line. Each message names the field chain or the route, and gives a line that compiles.
- One-thread state on a route that values travel: E7015.
- A thread-bound value handed over, a foreign handle with no `threads(any)` among them: E7008.
- A module variable reached off its home thread without a guard: E7012.
- A `static` read off its home thread whose type is not `ThreadShared`: E7002, at the reading function.
- Two tasks, a task and the parent, or a callback's calls with themselves clashing on a place: E7007. This includes a task opening a link while the parent writes that family's headers.
- Code beside a thread touching that thread's kind 1 or 2, by any route: E7015.
- A link made through what several threads reach at once: E7015. A link made through an exclusive lock that leaves its block: E3063.
- A link of one kind stored where the other is wanted: E2020.
- An erased type given a value that breaks its promise, an `AnyError` conversion included: E7015.
- A call that changes a function's own state through a read-only name: E3023, or E7015 at the registering line for a `threads(any)` callback.
- A `creator` module variable holding one-thread state: E7015 or E7008.

**Stopped at run time**, with a clear message naming both threads or the call, in every profile, only where the fact comes from C and so cannot be known when compiling:
- a `main` or `creator` export or callback called on the wrong thread (existing);
- a `main` module initialised again on another thread;
- a `main` or `creator` module shut down off its home thread, or while its code runs there;
- a thread-bound callback called after its module was shut down;
- a bound foreign handle ended on another thread (existing).

**Never a hang:** a reload's own tasks, jobs and threads run while every other thread waits.

A false vouch is `unsafe` code's own promise (P04), listed by `ember tcb`. No program the rule accepts in safe code races or has undefined behaviour.
design.verdicts:
- **3:** kept. A `sharedref mut` target on two threads is changed only under a lock, through an `Atomic`, or by a reduction from scoped tasks (tier a). Channel ends still take no word at the call: `[CLO-18]` speaks of a function's own state, not of call words.
- **23:** kept. A `shares` value is never used from two threads, so a self-contained one is not handed over (open risk 1).
- **31:** its direction is applied to a foreign handle with no thread word: a forgotten word refuses a line and never crashes. Option F keeps today's FFI-33b meaning.
- **61:** kept, and applied to the types that hide what they hold (`dyn I + Send`, `AnyError`, `some I + Send`).
  - Its spelling reaches the once form, `thread_shared once fn()`, and the link to a shared target, `weakref thread_shared T`.
  - Option E would reverse it. That is not really better: a `pub` type's thread promise would then depend on what each program puts in it, against verdict 108.
- **77:** kept, in loop form too, through `ref w`.
- **88:** its way is reused: a method making `weakref this` is compiled once for each kind of object it is called on.
- **93:** kept. `ref t` is tier (a); `copy of t` is a hand-over and needs `Send`.
- **94:** kept. `thread.spawn` takes a function any thread may run, and `scope.spawn` takes one that is not `thread_shared` and may use the caller's variables.
  - Each gains `once`, since a thread runs its function once and `[CLO-6]` says such a parameter accepts both kinds. Every call written today compiles unchanged, and handing a capture on now compiles too.
- **101:** kept as measured.
  - Its fix 2 applies to an owner a route hands over itself, a spawned thread's result included.
  - Owners inside another value keep the delay.
  - A thread that a module shutdown detached counts as ended, so no walk is added.
  - My earlier claim that every nested owner is handed over is withdrawn.
- **104:** kept, and extended: a scoped task's result comes back after the join, checked as a view.
- **107:** kept. A value of a manager that keeps no word still reaches its instance for the markers, as it does for its life.
- **108, 113:** kept. A type parameter has the markers its bounds give.
- **114:** kept. Its one compare is now named at every hand-over route (sends, stores into places other threads reach under a lock, values made `thread_shared`). Its own words are \"an object handed to another thread\".
- **164, 165, 166:** kept unchanged, each a line of the rule.
  - 164 is kind 3.
  - 165 is the sharing route, checked at the making line.
  - 166 is tier (a)'s ban on making and ending, now worded by what is ended so that a `static mut` or a captured view is covered too. Opening, which 166 does not name, is a read and follows the place rule (option G keeps today's refusal).

No verdict covers J6-16, J8-10, STA-1's unconditional `ThreadShared` (option H keeps it), a foreign handle's default, or the type of a link to a `thread_shared` target. ODR-083 (a lead ruling: a new creator after a shutdown) is kept. Today's `E7012` under `creator` is a rule of the spec, not a verdict.

options_for_owner.summary:
The rule, as repaired:
- The compiler works out both markers from what a type holds, and std's locks vouch for themselves as a program's own lock does.
- Owners and links follow the thread their value belongs to, by any route.
- A link's type says whether its target is shared.
- Threads take a `once` function.
- Code beside a thread is checked place by place, borrowed C callbacks included.
- Statics are judged by which threads read them.
- Module variables live on a home thread.
- `AnyError` may cross threads.
options_for_owner.code:

w = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: run(owns job))  # a once function

#! threads creator
static mut HITS: int = 0              # no lock

fn peek():                            # run by a spawned thread
    w = weakref REG                   # E7015: REG belongs to the main thread

check(owns e)?                        # E7015: LoadError holds a `shares` owner
options_for_owner.outcome:
The worker, the job runner, the plugin and the weapon table compile as written.

Every race found is refused when compiling: links to one object made from two threads, a task ending objects through a module variable, a C callback copying an owner on C's threads, a function taking from its own `Receiver` on two threads, a pool's values sent away.

A reload's drops no longer hang. An error holding one-thread state is refused at its `?`, in every program.

recommendation.reason:
One rule answers the five questions, the nineteen holes the two breakers found, and the cases nobody had asked about. It has no list of constructs, holders or types:
- Owners and links follow the thread their value belongs to, whatever the route.
- The markers follow from what types hold, with std vouching as a program does.
- Code beside a thread is checked place by place, defined by what it is.

The cost of A:
- Ordinary code gets no new word, and two lines refused today compile.
- Every race found is refused when compiling.
- The run-time cost is C's plus the existing compares, one plain count per export call, and, in reload builds only, an entry that pays nothing extra on Linux and Windows.

Verdicts 61, 94, 101, 114 and 164 to 166 stand as lines of it.

The two open members follow from it:
- `AnyError` keeps a written promise, with Swift and `anyhow` as precedent.
- `creator` hands a module's state over instead of asking for a lock that orders nothing.

Put J7-06 (the `ThreadShared` vouch, P04) beside it: std's locks and a program's own lock use the same vouch.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: which objects may move to, or be shared with, another thread. The cases are a `shared_ptr` or `weak_ptr` whose count is not atomic, a pointer several holders write through, a `mutable` member, and a module's global. The compiler works out "may move" (Rust's `Send`) and "may share" (Rust's `Sync`) from what each type holds, and checks every way a value or its count can reach another thread.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | worker | `cache` keeps a mesh entry as a `shares` owner | the entry's count: 1 |
| 2 | worker | loading fails: `LoadError(entry=shares e)` makes a second owner, and `?` puts the error into an `AnyError` | count: 2 |
| 3 | worker | `tx.send(owns r)` sends the `Result[Mesh]` to main | count: 2 |
| 4 | main | ends `r`: reads the count (plain, no atomic) | reads 2, about to write 1 |
| 5 | worker | at the same moment, `cache.evict()` ends its owner: it also reads 2 | reads 2, about to write 1 |
| 6 | both | both write 1 | count 1 with no owner left: the mesh is never freed; in the other order, it is freed while main still uses it |
owner_short.options:
- **A:** one rule. Owners and links follow the thread their value belongs to. The markers are worked out from contents, with std's locks vouching as a program does. Links say whether their target is shared, and threads take a `once` function. Code beside a thread is checked place by place, and statics are judged by who reads them. Module variables live on a home thread, and `AnyError` may cross threads (the step table's step 2 is refused).
- **B:** as A, but `AnyError` stays on its thread.
- **C:** as A, but `creator` keeps today's lock.
- **D:** as A, but `main` and `creator` mean the same thread, and module variables restart at each initialisation.
- **E:** the compiler follows every hidden-content value instead of a written word (reverses verdict 61).
- **F:** as A, but a C handle with no thread word may cross threads.
- **G:** as A, but no task opens a one-thread link.
- **H:** as A, but every `static` must be shareable even with no threads.
owner_short.recommendation: A. No ordinary program gets a word, every race found is refused when compiling, verdicts 61 and 164 to 166 stand, and the worker, job runner, plugin and weapon table compile as written. Ask J7-06's `ThreadShared` vouch beside it.

repairs.hole: Safety (high): `weakref REG` on a `static`, through an `RwLock` read guard, on a `thread_shared` value's class field, or under a lock with the link kept after it. Plain adds and subtracts from two threads on one weak count.
repairs.answer:
Real. `[THR-22]` makes kinds 1 and 2 follow their value. A value belongs to the thread that made it or was handed it, a module variable's value to the home thread, and a lock-reached value to the lock holder for the block.
- A link is refused (E7015) through a `static` off its home thread, inside a `thread_shared` value or a `thread_shared fn()`'s state, and through a read guard.
- A link made through an exclusive lock does not leave the block (E3063, as a guard's view).

This restores, worded by the value, the sentence today's `[THR-2]` had ("any function that may run on another thread than its target's owner"). It is also what makes a class object honestly `ThreadShared`. It costs nothing at run time, and gives P03's J6-06 its owner: the home thread.

repairs.hole: Safety (high): `weakref Player` is one type for one-thread and `thread_shared` targets, so `Watch` cannot be judged.
repairs.answer:
Real. A link's type says its target's kind: `weakref T` and `weakref thread_shared T`, as Rust's `rc::Weak` and `sync::Weak`.
- `weakref x` makes x's kind, and E2020 is given between the two.
- Each operation is compiled plain or atomic from the type, which today's text leaves unsaid although `[EFF]`'s cost row says "atomic for a `thread_shared` target".
- A method making `weakref this` is compiled once for each kind of object it is called on (verdict 88's way).

The spelling is the owner's (open risk 9).

repairs.hole: Safety (high): a task ends an old `Level` through a `static mut`, or clears through a captured `ref mut` view, while main links to it.
repairs.answer:
Real. `[THR-22]`/`[THR-11]` are worded by what is ended: a task ends an object of a weakref-named family only if it made it or was handed it whole. Any other route is E7015: the caller's variables, a `static mut`, a view captured or sent. This is verdict 166's own wording.

`ref mut T` stays `Send`, since handing the view over is harmless and ending through it is the act refused. The suggested relaxation for `@parallel` ends is not taken: verdict 166 refused that shape, and the parent need not wait for it to be safe.

repairs.hole: Safety (high): a borrowed `threads(any)` callback runs on C's threads and does `copy of team` and `weakref boss` on the caller's variables.
repairs.answer:
Real. Tier (a) is now defined by what it is: code running on other threads while its starter is still running, using the starter's variables. A borrowed `threads(any)` callback is such code:
- It is checked place by place.
- It clashes with itself, since any number of calls may run at once.
- It has no reductions.
- It changes the caller's places only by a `ThreadShared` place's own operations (not a `Receiver`'s or a `Cell`'s).
- It touches no kind 1 or 2: E7015 at the registering call.

repairs.hole: Safety (medium): it is not said whether `tx.send(owns e)` runs verdict 114's compare.
repairs.answer:
Real. Every hand-over route of `[THR-2]` (b) runs verdict 114's compare and fix 1 at its line: a capture word, a send, a store into a place other threads reach under a lock, the parts of a value made `thread_shared`. Verdict 114 says it of "an object handed to another thread".

The links are left behind wherever the value is received, the same thread included. That is an understandable limitation: the program said `owns`, and Rust refuses the send outright. A spawned thread's result and a module's state need no compare, and the reason is stated.

repairs.hole: Safety (medium): `[HR-3]`'s store-then-load handshake is not ordered by a relaxed increment and an acquire fence (the store-buffer case).
repairs.answer:
Real. `[HR-42]` makes each side's store come before its load.
- The poll issues a process-wide barrier (`membarrier` on Linux, `FlushProcessWriteBuffers` on Windows), so an entry pays only a compiler barrier.
- Elsewhere, each store is a sequentially consistent read-modify-write.
- Clearing the mark is a release that a waiting thread acquires.

This applies to reload builds only.

repairs.hole: Fault (medium): reclaim runs a removed field's `drop` that uses `@parallel`, a scope, or a spawn and join; its workers wait at entry and the reload hangs.
repairs.answer:
Real. `[HR-3]`: the reload's own work does not wait. That is the tasks of scopes it opens, the jobs and chunks it submits, and the threads it starts, all checked as that code's own tasks and threads are. Every other registered thread waits.

This is safe by the ordinary rules: tier (a) for its tasks, and `Send` values for its threads. Refusing such drops when compiling cannot work, since which fields a reload removes is not known then.

repairs.hole: Safety (medium): a `threads(creator)` once callback of a `creator` module, run by C on the old thread after re-initialisation on a new one, races on `FRAMES`.
repairs.answer:
Real. The shutdown happens on the home thread while none of the module's code runs there, its callbacks included. Each wrapper and trampoline keeps a plain count of the module's calls running on this thread; elsewhere the shutdown stops.

The shutdown ends every thread-bound callback the module registered, retiring its slot. A later call stops ("... after its module was shut down"), with the existing generation compare.

repairs.hole: Needless refusal (medium): `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns mesh => optimise(owns mesh))` is E3013, since spawn takes a function that may run twice.
repairs.answer: Real, and it is checklist 12. `thread.spawn` and `jobs.submit` take `owns f: thread_shared once fn() -> R`, and `scope.spawn` and `s.submit` take `owns f: once fn()`. `[CLO-6]` says such a parameter accepts both kinds, so no existing call changes. A `thread_shared once fn()` is `Send` and `ThreadShared`, with `Send` state.

repairs.hole: Needless refusal (high): `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns job: run(owns job))` is E3013.
repairs.answer: The same repair as the previous hole: the once form of the thread word, as Rust's `FnOnce + Send`.

repairs.hole: Unsafe (high): `thread_shared fn()` is `ThreadShared` by decree although its state is only `Send`. Two tasks then call `rx.recv()` through `ref Feeder`, a route outside `[CLO-16]`'s list of holders.
repairs.answer:
Real. The list of holders is dropped. `[CLO-18]` now says: a call changes its function's state when it changes a captured value, a place's own operations included, unless that place is `ThreadShared`. Such a call needs a name that may change the holder, wherever it is. So `ctx.feeder.pull()` is E3023, and `thread_shared fn()` is `ThreadShared` because of what read-only names may do.

The one-thread consequence is stated in open risk 12.

repairs.hole: Needless refusal (medium): a `@parallel` body opening `e.target` (a link to a one-thread `Player`) is refused.
repairs.answer:
Real. Opening only reads the header. Code of tier (a) may open the starter's links while the starter, until the join, ends no object of that family and makes or ends no link to one.
- A `@parallel` body always meets this.
- A scoped task meets it when the parent's lines before the join do (E7007 otherwise).

Verdict 166 names only making and ending, which stay refused. Option G keeps today's refusal of opening.

repairs.hole: Needless refusal (medium): a scoped task returning `Option[ref Enemy]` needs `Enemy` `ThreadShared`.
repairs.answer: Real. A scoped task's or job's result comes back to the starting thread after the join, so it is tier (a). It is checked as a view of the caller's places, with no marker, and holds nothing bound to the task's thread. Only a `thread.spawn` or `jobs.submit` result needs `Send`.

repairs.hole: Needless refusal (medium): `static WEAPONS` holding `fn(ref mut Game)` is E7002 in a program with no threads, while a `static mut` is judged by reach.
repairs.answer: Real. A `static` is judged by reach too: it needs `ThreadShared` only where a function that may run off the home thread reads it, with E7002 at that function naming the chain. This is the fact `[THR-20]` and `[FFI-33]`'s `any` already use, so there is one rule for module variables. Option H keeps STA-1 as it is.
