Real. It reaches direct owners only, which is verdict 101's fix 2: an owner a route hands over itself, a spawned thread's result included. Nested owners keep the delay, and the claim that every nested owner is handed over is withdrawn.

For `creator`, no walk is added. A thread that the module's shutdown detached counts as ended for point 3, so a value it made is ended at once by whoever ends its last owner. The shutdown and the initialisation order the home count it left. This is worded with P05.

design.open_risks:
1. **A self-contained value is not handed over.** A worker cannot hand back a `shares` graph whose every owner is inside it (verdict 23). Swift's region isolation accepts this; for Ember it would be a separate question.
2. **Shutting down a `threads=any` module while another thread is inside its exports or its `threads(any)` callbacks** is about the module's lifetime. It is left to P08/P04.
3. **The reload exclusion and its handshake** (`[HR-3]`, `[HR-42]`) should be worded with P09. macOS has no documented process-wide barrier, so it pays the sequentially consistent increment per entry, in reload builds only.
4. **The `ThreadShared` vouch** needs P04's spelling (J7-06). If vouching for `ThreadShared` is refused, std's lock rows stay by name, an exception the rule would then have to state, and a program's own lock can never be shared.
5. **A value's manager instance** (`[LT-4]`/`[ALC-1]`) is worded with P02, including which managers are `ThreadShared`.
6. **The spelling after `dyn`:** `+ Send` after `dyn` uses today's `+`. If P24 moves to brackets, the rule follows that spelling.
7. **A `Cell` under a read guard:** `[CELL-1]` may already refuse J7-03's race by E3023. Verdict 165's outcome holds either way.
8. **Wording shared with P05:** `[RC-4]` points 3 to 5, a detached thread's queue (values queued at the moment of detachment), and where queued drops run.
9. **The spelling of a link to a shared target** is the owner's: `weakref thread_shared T`, or `thread_shared weakref T` after verdict 61's word order. P12's `weakref dyn I` follows whichever is chosen.
10. **Verdict 166, read as written,** also refuses a task's own `shares` values and links, made and ended inside it, which race with nothing. Widening it is the owner's; it is not proposed.
11. **Code size:** a method called on both kinds of object that makes `weakref this` is compiled twice. This is rare.
12. **A new one-thread refusal:** `[CLO-18]` refuses, in one-thread code too, a call through a read-only name of a handler that takes from its own `Receiver` (write `ref mut h`). This is consistent with `Cell`.

design.rule: One property, from which every case follows: memory that a memory manager's instance gave out is reached only while the instance still holds it for that use. A value "reaches" an instance in two cases: it holds an address in memory the instance gave, or it will call the instance later. That covers a value made in the instance, an owner of it, a weakref link to it (the link keeps the block through the weak count in the block's header), a view into such memory, and anything that holds or captures one of these: a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token. Four consequences follow. (1) Bound: a value that reaches an instance lives no longer than the instance. Keeping it longer is E3063, and handing it to C, which keeps it, is such a keeping. (2) Exact ends: such a value is ended by exactly the operation that gives back the memory it reaches, and by nothing else. The instance's end and reset() give back everything. A scope's end gives back only what that scope gave. Allocating and opening a scope give back nothing. (3) Thread: a value's growth and its end call its instance, so the value holds a link to the instance. The link is never written, and it is stored only where verdict 47/107 keep the word. It is a changing link (sharedref mut, one thread, verdict 164) when the manager's allocate/deallocate/reallocate change their object, as an Arena's move its cursor. It is a read-only link (ref) when the manager changes its state only through Atomic or a lock, or has no state. So where the value may go, a thread_shared value included, follows from P01's own rule: markers come from contents, and verdict 165 checks at the making line. (4) Which types: `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker. That is a holder that may give a block back (owns, shares, shares mut, thread_shared, weakref), a class, and any type that says it takes one (`struct SlotMap using A:`). The library's String and collections say it the same way, so a program's own container takes `using` as theirs do. The kind of manager is named only where a value may be grown, replaced or ended; a name that can do neither (a plain parameter, a view) accepts a value from any manager.
design.spec_text:
NEW [ALC-6] **Memory a manager gave is reached only while the manager holds it.** A value *reaches* an instance of a memory manager when it holds an address in memory the instance gave out, or will call the instance: a value made in it ([ALC-1]); an owner of such a value; a `weakref` link to one, which keeps its block through the weak count ([OBJ-3]); a view into such memory ([ARN-1], [LT-1]); and every value that holds or captures one of these (a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token). A value that only names a position (a `Handle`, an index) reaches nothing. Every value that reaches an instance:
1. lives no longer than the instance. Keeping or returning it where it would outlive the instance is `E3063` ([LT-4], [LT-45]). A hand-over to C that keeps it ([FFI-54], [OWN-12]) is such a keeping: "C keeps `w` after `level` ends; make it without `using level`". A value put in through a `ref mut` parameter reaches what it reached in the callee ([LT-47]).
2. is ended by exactly the operation that gives back the memory it reaches, and by no other. The instance's end and `reset()` give back all of the instance's memory. The end of a scope ([ARN-6]) gives back what that scope gave. Allocating, and opening a scope, give back nothing. A use after the memory it reaches was given back is `E3060`. Giving that memory back while such a value is still used is `E3021` ([ALC-5]).
3. holds a link to the instance. The link is written nowhere and is stored only where [ALC-1] keeps the word. It is a changing link, a kept `sharedref mut` ([LT-46]), when the manager's `allocate`, `deallocate` or `reallocate` change their object (worked out from their bodies, [EXC-15]), as an `Arena`'s move its cursor. Otherwise it is a kept `ref`: the manager changes its state only through `Atomic` or a lock (verdict 3), or has none. So a value made in an instance its methods change stays on one thread (verdict 164; `E7015`, `E7008`). Scoped tasks use it where it is, and its growth and end count as changes of the instance ([THR-11], [EFF-24]; two tasks: `E7007`). A value made in an instance that its methods only read is `Send` and `ThreadShared` exactly as a `ref` of the manager is ([THR-8], [THR-9]). A manager with one instance holds no link, and its methods are checked as any call wherever a value's growth or end may run them ([THR-20]).

CHANGED [TYP-46] / [ALC-1] (the closed list goes). `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker:
* a holder that may give a block back (`owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` before a type: `target: weakref Enemy using LevelArena`);
* a class type;
* a type that says it takes one, with `using` after its name in its declaration (`[T]` above `struct SlotMap using A:`; `class Level using A:`). In its body `A` names the manager kind, and a field typed `using A` takes its memory from the instance the value is made in. The standard library's `String`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, `BitSet`, `RingBuffer` and `Pool` are declared this way.

`enemies: SlotMap[Enemy] using LevelArena`, made `SlotMap[Enemy]() using current`, makes in `current` its field defaults and what its methods make for those fields without naming an instance. A type takes at most one manager. After any other type, `using` is `E2114`. The message for a struct whose fields have memory but which takes no manager: "`Level` does not say it takes a memory manager, and its fields say where their memory comes from; to give it one, write `struct Level using A:` and `using A` after the fields that take it, or remove `using`". The message for a view: "a view gives nothing back to a manager; remove `using`". A manager written in brackets (`SlotMap[Enemy, LevelArena]`) is `E1010`, whose help gives `SlotMap[Enemy] using LevelArena`, as for `Array[T, A]`. The kind must match only where a value may be grown, replaced or ended: a field, a local, an `owns` or `ref mut` parameter, a `weakref` place (`E2020` otherwise). A plain parameter or a view accepts a value from any manager. `thread_shared T using A` is allowed exactly where the value's end may run on any thread under [ALC-6] 3: an instance its methods only read that is `ThreadShared`, or a manager with one instance whose methods reach no one-thread state. Anything else is `E7015` at the making line ([THR-1], verdict 165).

CHANGED [LT-4]: "A value made in a memory manager's instance, and every value that reaches it ([ALC-6]), lives no longer than that instance". "That address is a kept `sharedref mut` link" becomes "that address is the link of [ALC-6] 3".
CHANGED [LT-47]: "a view, or a value that reaches an instance ([ALC-6]), put in through `ref mut`".
CHANGED [ALC-5]: "While a value that reaches an instance lives ([ALC-6]), the instance is changed only by …".
CHANGED [ARN-1]: "`reset()` and the arena's end give back all of its memory and end every view into it. The end of a scope ends the views into what that scope gave ([ARN-6]). Opening a scope ends none: the scope holds a view of the arena's cursor, not of its memory, as `alloc*` does."
CHANGED [ARN-6]: add "Reading or changing a value in memory the parent gave before the scope is not using the parent. Allocating from the parent, resetting it, or opening another scope of it while the scope lives is `E3096`. An inner scope's end ends only the views into what the inner scope gave."
CHANGED [ARN-7]: "… while a view into the bytes it lowers past or reuses is used: every such operation ends every view into those bytes".
CHANGED [OBJ-1] / [RC-4] point 4: "A `thread_shared` value whose block a manager gave ([TYP-46]) is made handed over: from its first owner, every thread counts its owners in the away count, so no making thread is read for it and its end never waits in a queue. The making thread of a block from the runtime's allocator is read from its chunk, never from the value (verdict 101, fix 1)."
CHANGED [THR-2] (verdict 114): "the new block for an object made in an instance is taken from that instance".
CHANGED [HEAP-7] / [WK-11]: "a `weakref` place that links objects made in a manager names its kind (`weakref Enemy using LevelArena`), as an owner's place does ([TYP-46]); its last link gives the block back to the target's instance".
CHANGED [UNS-4]: add "a raw pointer into memory a manager gave is not used after that memory is given back ([ALC-6] 2)".
GRAMMAR: struct_decl and class_decl take an optional `"using" NAME` after the name.
CODES: E2114 row becomes "`using` after a type whose declaration leaves no manager to its maker (a number, a view, a struct that does not say `using A`)". E2020 row: add "a `weakref` place given a link to an object made in another kind of manager". E3063 row: "a value that reaches a memory manager's instance ([ALC-6]) kept or returned where it would outlive it, a hand-over to C included". E7015 row: add "a value made in an instance whose methods change it, sent to another thread or made `thread_shared`".

answers.answer: Decided: the link reaches the instance, because it keeps the boss's block, weak count included, in the arena's memory. So it lives no longer than the arena (E3063), and resetting the arena while the link is still used is E3021 ([ALC-6] 1, 2). The camera's field names the kind, as an owner's field does (verdict 24). After the boss ends, opening the link finds it ended, because the block is still in memory the arena holds.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 500, then gone. The draft's original program, with the arena made inside load_level and the field without `using`, is refused at `cam.target = weakref boss`. First comes E2020: "`cam.target` links enemies from the built-in manager, and `boss` was made in `level`, an `Arena`: write `target: weakref Enemy using Arena = None` in `Camera`". With the field fixed, E3063: "`cam.target` keeps a link to `boss`, whose block is in `level` (line 9), and `level` ends when `load_level` returns while `cam` lives on in `main`; make the arena in the caller: `fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):`, and in `main` write `level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)` above `cam = Camera()`". `level.reset()` in main while `cam.target` is still used is E3021, as a reset under a live value is.

answers.answer: Decided with no exception for thread_shared. A thread_shared value may end on any thread, and its end gives its block back to its instance, so the instance must be one every thread may give memory back to ([ALC-6] 3). An Arena's allocate moves its cursor, so its link is a changing link that stays on one thread (verdict 164). That makes `thread_shared ... using level` E7015 at the making line, by verdict 165's check. A manager with one instance and no one-thread state (System, Global), or a several-instance manager whose state sits behind a lock or Atomic, is allowed. Such a value is made handed over (RC-4 point 4): every owner is counted in the away count, so no making thread is read and fix 1's 'never from the value' holds.
answers.code:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using System    # a manager every thread may give memory back to
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))
    println("done")
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints done. Every owner of `stats` is counted with one atomic add, as Rust's Arc counts. The example's `thread_shared Stats() using level` is E7015 at that line: "`stats` is shared between threads, so its last owner may end on any of them and give its block back to `level` there; `level` is an `Arena`, whose `allocate` moves its cursor, so only this thread may use it; make `stats` without `using level`". A program's own pool whose free list sits in a `Mutex` (`static SLAB: Slab`, then `thread_shared Session() using SLAB`) compiles the same way.

answers.answer: Decided: a scope's end gives back only what the scope gave, so it ends only views into that memory ([ALC-6] 2). Opening a scope gives back nothing. The root, taken from the arena before the scope, stays valid inside the scope and after it. Allocating from the parent while the scope lives stays E3096.
answers.code:
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))   # kept for the whole parse
    with s = frame.scope():                          # scratch memory, given back when the block ends
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind                    # root is below the scope's memory
    return root.kind

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    println(parse(ref mut frame))
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 3. The scope's end lowers the cursor to where the scope began, and root lies below that. `frame.alloc(...)` inside the `with` block is E3096 (allocate from `s`). `toks` used after the block is E3060.

answers.answer: Decided, as phase 3 restated it. `using` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker. The standard library's String, Array, Map, Set, Deque, SmallArray, BitSet, RingBuffer and Pool all say it in their declarations (`struct Deque using A:`), and a program's own container says it the same way. So no path exists that only the library can take. thread_shared is decided by the thread consequence, not left out by type.
answers.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:                         # takes a memory manager, called A in its body
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []        # from the instance the map is made in
    free: Array[int] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

struct Level:
    names: Array[String] using Arena
    title: String using Arena
    enemies: SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena

fn load(ref mut current: Arena) -> Level:
    return Level(names=[String("orc")] using current, title=String("Cave") using current, enemies=SlotMap[Enemy]() using current)

fn main():
    level_mem = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    lvl = load(ref mut level_mem)
    println(lvl.title, lvl.names.len())
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints Cave 1. The title's text, the names list's buffer and both of the SlotMap's lists come from `level_mem`. `lvl` lives no longer than `level_mem` (E3063 otherwise). `using Arena` after `int`, after a view, or after a struct that does not say `using A` is E2114, whose help gives the declaration line.

answers.answer: Decided: String declares that it takes a manager, as Array does. So `text: String using Arena` is allowed, and its growth goes back to the arena, as ALC-1's own sentence already says.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints let. A StrView of `t.text` reaches the arena too: it is ended by `arena.reset()` and refused past the arena's end (E3060, E3063).

other_cases.case: A StrView into an arena-made String, used after `arena.reset()`.
other_cases.settled: The view reaches the arena's memory ([ALC-6]), so the reset ends it. The use after the reset is E3060; with the use placed before the reset, the program compiles.

other_cases.case: Two scoped tasks each pushing to its own list, both lists made in one Arena.
other_cases.settled: Growth calls `level.allocate`, which moves the cursor: both tasks change the instance through a changing link. That is E7007 (two tasks change `level`). One task alone pushing, or the pushes done after the join, compiles. Reads of arena lists from many tasks compile, because a read never touches the manager.

other_cases.case: An arena-made widget handed to C through an `owns` contract (`widget_take(owns w)`), or captured by `thread.spawn`.
other_cases.settled: C, or an unscoped thread, keeps it past every local instance. That is E3063 for C and E7015 for the thread (its instance link stays on one thread). The help says to make it without `using`. `w.into_raw()` inside `unsafe:` is the block's vouching: [UNS-4] now says a raw pointer into a manager's memory is not used after that memory is given back.

other_cases.case: A program's struct `Level` with list fields, written `lvl: Level using Arena`, without `struct Level using A:`.
other_cases.settled: E2114: Level's fields already say where their memory comes from (the built-in manager), and a written field means only what it says (verdict 132's lesson). The help gives `struct Level using A:` plus `using A` on the fields.

other_cases.case: A helper `fn total(xs: Array[int]) -> int` called with an arena-made list, and `fn fill(ref mut xs: Array[int])` called with one.
other_cases.settled: `total` compiles for a list from any manager, because a plain parameter can neither grow nor end the list. `fill` may push, so the kind must match: E2020, with help `ref mut xs: Array[int] using Arena`, or a generic `[A: needs Allocator]` with `using A`.

other_cases.case: A class object made in a lock-based pool, with a weakref link on this thread, handed whole to another thread (verdict 114).
other_cases.settled: The pool's methods only read it, and it is ThreadShared, so the object is Send. Verdict 114 moves its contents to a new block taken from the same pool instance. The old block stays here until its last link ends, then goes back to the pool (allowed from this thread).

other_cases.case: Nested scopes: `with a = frame.scope():` then `with b = a.scope():`, with a view from `a` used after `b` ends.
other_cases.settled: b's end gives back only what b gave, so the view from `a` stays valid until a's end. Views from b used after b's end are E3060.

other_cases.case: A Pool's Handle kept after the pool ends.
other_cases.settled: A handle is a number and reaches no memory, so nothing bounds it. Without the pool it cannot be looked up. A `ref T` from `pool.get(h)` is a view into the pool and is bounded by it, as today.

other_cases.case: A closure capturing an arena-made value, stored in a static, or an AnyError holding an error that views arena text, returned with `?` past the arena.
other_cases.settled: Both reach the instance, so both are E3063. The closure's state block and AnyError's box come from the built-in manager; no declaration names a manager for them, so `fn() using A` is E2114. A program that wants type-erased state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`.

other_cases.case: A static instance (`static LEVEL: LockedPool`), with values made in it kept in other statics.
other_cases.settled: A static instance outlives everything, so its values may be kept anywhere, unscoped threads included if its link only reads. A reset of it is E3021 while any value that reaches it may still be used, which is never for a value held in a static.

other_cases.case: A FixedArena over a buffer (`Arena.fixed(ref mut buffer)`), with values made in it.
other_cases.settled: The FixedArena holds a kept ref mut view of the buffer ([ARN-4]), so its values reach the buffer through it, and each is bounded by both.

other_cases.case: A shares mut value made in an Arena, with a sharedref mut link to it held elsewhere.
other_cases.settled: Owners hold the block and the link views it, so both reach the arena and both are bounded. The count block is in arena memory, which the arena keeps until its end or reset, and a reset is refused while either lives.

design.prior_art: C++ std::pmr: a container holds a memory_resource* (8 bytes). Program types opt in by declaring allocator_type and getting uses-allocator construction, the same idea as `struct SlotMap using A:`. allocate_shared puts the control block, weak count included, in the resource's memory, so a weak_ptr that outlives a released monotonic_buffer_resource is undefined behaviour (exactly J5-02). A string_view into a released resource is also undefined behaviour. Nothing is checked. Rust (allocator_api, still unstable): Box<T, A>, Vec<T, A>, Rc<T, A> and Weak<T, A> take the allocator as a type parameter. With A = &'a Bump the lifetime 'a bounds every holder, the Weak included, which is facet 1. Send follows the allocator: Box<T, &Bump> is Send only if Bump is Sync, and bumpalo's Bump is not, which is facet 3. bumpalo's reset takes &mut self, so no allocation may be live, which is ALC-5. Rust's shortfalls: unstable for years, and the type parameters are written everywhere (Vec<T, &'a Bump>), which is a readability loss Ember avoids with `using` and inferred regions. A Rust scope API that borrows the arena mutably also refuses J5-19's program, which Ember accepts because a view points into memory, not into the cursor. Ada: a storage pool is named per access type (`for Node_Ptr'Storage_Pool use Level_Pool;`), the place naming the kind, as in verdict 24. Accessibility levels bound the access values, partly with run-time checks. Ada 2012 subpools free a subpool at once with Unchecked_Deallocate_Subpool, an erroneous program if references remain. Zig: an Allocator interface passed explicitly and an ArenaAllocator; containers (ArrayListUnmanaged) take the allocator per call; no lifetime or thread checking, so a use after reset is illegal behaviour that is often not detected. Go: GOEXPERIMENT=arenas checked a use after Free at run time by unmapping pages, and the proposal is on hold. Swift and C#: class instances always come from the runtime heap. Swift's withUnsafeTemporaryAllocation and C#'s stackalloc with scoped Span give scratch buffers only. Where they fall short of safe, C-fast and readable: C++ and Zig are fast but unsafe; Go's check costs at run time and was abandoned; Ada checks partly at run time; Swift and C# give no arenas for objects; Rust is safe and fast but unstable and wordy. The rule takes Rust's two facts (the allocator's lifetime and its thread-safety reach every holder), keeps C++'s one-word cost, and the compiler infers both with nothing written.
design.cost: Bound and exact ends (facets 1 and 2): zero at run time, because both are compile-time region checks. A scope's end is one pointer store (the cursor lowered), the same as C. Thread (facet 3): zero at run time; the markers are worked out when compiling. `using` on any declared type: one call of the manager's allocate (static dispatch, inlinable), plus the instance word, 8 bytes per value, only where verdict 107 does not remove it. That matches C++ pmr's pointer per container and Rust's &Bump per Vec. Where verdict 107 removes the word it costs nothing extra, and its measurement stands: a million small values took 191 ms and 28.2 MB against C's 191 ms and 28.2 MB. A weakref link to an arena object costs as any link: one plain add and one subtract of the weak count. The block it keeps is reclaimed at the arena's end or reset, as C's arena reclaims everything. A plain parameter that accepts a list from any manager: zero; the compiler makes one copy of the function per layout, or reads the common fields. A thread_shared value made in a manager is the one case that differs. It is made handed over, so each owner +1 or -1 is one atomic read-modify-write, as Rust's Arc and C++'s shared_ptr pay, instead of biased counting's plain add on the making thread. The measured mechanism (measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md, 'own' pattern) shows a thread's own objects at 43.6 ms with one atomic count against 32.3 ms biased, so 1.35x for this case only. Cross-thread patterns cost the same as the atomic column, and a pipeline is 27% faster than biased_pub on one thread. Memory: the same 32-byte header as every thread_shared value, so zero extra; its home and queue fields stay unused. Reading the maker's id from the value instead, J5-05 B's idea, was measured 13% to 44% slower on cross-thread copying, and fix 1 excludes it. C pays nothing for counting because C has no safe sharing. Nothing in this rule adds a check that runs.

readability.ordinary_before:
# a parser: a tree kept for the whole parse, scratch memory per statement
# today the scope ends every view into `frame`, so the tree's root must be made after the scratch work
fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    kind = 1                                         # kept in a local instead of the tree
    with s = frame.scope():
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        kind += toks[0].kind
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=kind)) # made after the scope
    return root.kind

struct Token:
    kind: int
    text: String                                     # `String using Arena` is E2114 today
readability.ordinary_after:
fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))    # the tree, made first, as the program means
    with s = frame.scope():
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind
    return root.kind

struct Token:
    kind: int
    text: String using Arena                         # the token's text in the parse's arena
readability.note: The after version is the same length and reads in the order the program means. A program with no arena (a game loop, a server handler using the built-in manager) is identical before and after: no new word, nothing new to write. The rule's cost falls only on the rare program that links into an arena from something that outlives it: the camera's field then names its kind (`weakref Enemy using Arena`), as an owner's field already must. A program's own container writes `using A` once in its declaration, reusing the language's word. Its users write exactly what they write for the library's types (`SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena`).

design.compiler_does: 1. It gives each instance a region, and every value made in it that region. It then follows the region, as it follows views today (LT-45), through every holder of an address in the instance's memory: owners, weakref links, views, iterators, captures, errors, tokens, and values put in through ref mut (LT-47). It refuses a keeping past the instance with E3063, and treats a hand-over to C as a keeping. 2. It splits an arena's memory into nested regions, one per open scope, and treats each give-back as ending exactly the regions it frees: reset and the end free all, a scope's end frees its own. An alloc and a scope's opening touch only the cursor, so they end no view (ARN-1 already separates memory from cursor). 3. It infers whether the manager's allocate, deallocate and reallocate change `this` (EXC-15, the inference every method already gets) and makes the hidden instance link a sharedref mut or a ref accordingly. From that link it derives Send and ThreadShared by THR-8/9 and verdict 164, and checks verdict 165 at a thread_shared making line. It counts a value's growth and end as calls of those methods wherever they may run (EFF-24 for scoped tasks, P05's rule for ends the program does not write). 4. For a block a manager gives to a thread_shared value, it emits the handed-over count sequence from the first owner, chosen statically from the place's `using` kind, so no run-time branch and no maker read. 5. For a type declared `using A`, it fills A from the place's `using M`, defaulting to Global. It makes the parts the making line makes (field defaults, and init's making of `using A` fields) in the named instance, and finds `this`'s instance for later parts from the word verdict 47/107 keep. It places the instance word of a block a weakref may keep inside the block, so the last link can give it back. It dispatches deallocate statically by the kind the place names, weakref places included. 6. For a plain parameter given values from several managers, it makes one copy per layout. Nothing is written by the programmer for any of this, except the `using` that names a kind where a value may grow or end.
design.misuse: Every mistake is refused when compiling; nothing in safe code reaches freed or reused memory. A weakref, view, owner, iterator, closure or error that reaches an instance and is kept past it: E3063 at the line that keeps it, with the line that makes the arena in the caller. A hand-over to C of an arena-made value: E3063. A reset, or another give-back, while such a value is still used: E3021, with `mem.drop(owns x)` or the reorder. A use after the give-back: E3060, naming the give-back line. A weakref place without the kind for an arena target: E2020, with the field line. `using` after a number, a view, or a struct that does not declare one: E2114, with the declaration line or 'remove using'. An allocator in brackets: E1010, with the `using` spelling. An arena-made value sent to another thread, captured by thread.spawn, put in a channel, or made thread_shared: E7015, naming the arena and why only its thread may use it (its allocate moves its cursor). Two scoped tasks growing or ending values of one Arena: E7007. Allocating from a parent while its scope lives: E3096. What only unsafe code can do stays the vouching code's promise, never undefined behaviour in safe code: into_raw of an arena value used after the reset (UNS-4), and an Allocator implementation that frees memory through a lock under live values (ALC-2's unsafe promise).
design.verdicts: Kept as given: 19 (`using` names a manager; now also in a type's own declaration, the same word). 24 (the field names the kind and the making line names which one; no value outlives its arena), made complete: weakref places name the kind too, and links, tokens and captures are bounded. 47 and 107 (the instance word where needed, none where the manager can do without), kept: the instance link is checked when compiling and stored only where they say. 101 (fix 1, the maker's id from the runtime chunk, never from the value), kept: a thread_shared block from a manager is made handed over, so no maker is read and fix 1's 'never from the value' holds; J5-05 B, which would read it from the value, contradicts fix 1, and the 13% to 44% cross-thread cost was measured. Reused, not revisited: 164 (a sharedref mut link never goes to another thread) is the instance link of a manager whose methods change it. 165 (thread_shared refused at the making line when something in it is not ThreadShared) decides J5-05. 114 (a handed-over object moves) takes its new block from the same instance. 3 (Mutex, Atomic and channels need no ref mut) is why a manager changed only through a lock is read, not changed, by its methods. 86 and EXC-15 (what a method changes is inferred) decide the link's kind. 132 (a written declaration means only what it says) is why a struct's unannotated field stays on the built-in manager and the type must say `using A`. One point the lead should put to the owner plainly: J5-05's draft recommended A (refuse `using` after thread_shared), and phase 3 resolved that the list be 'the property minus thread_shared'. The reason given for that exception, 'the block must come from the built-in manager that every thread may give memory back to', is untrue for a lock-based or one-instance manager, so under principle 6 it cannot stand as an exception. The general rule refuses the Arena case anyway (E7015, by verdict 165) and accepts only what is safe.

options_for_owner.summary: The one rule. Whatever points into or is served by a manager's memory lives no longer than the manager and ends exactly when its memory is given back. Where it may go follows from the hidden link to the manager. `using` follows every type that says it takes a manager, the library's and the program's alike.
options_for_owner.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy using Arena = None

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    cam.target = weakref boss
    names = String("Ogre") using level
    enemies = SlotMap[Enemy]() using level
    with s = level.scope():
        tmp = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[u8](256)    # scratch; `names` stays valid
    println(names)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam, ref mut level)
    if cam.target exists as e:
        println(e.hp)
    else:
        println("gone")
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using level    # E7015: an Arena is used by one thread
options_for_owner.outcome: Without the last line it compiles and prints Ogre, then gone. With the arena made inside load_level, `cam.target = weakref boss` is E3063. The last line is E7015 ("its last owner may end on any thread and give its block back to `level` there"); `thread_shared Stats() using System` compiles. A program's own SlotMap, and String, Deque and the rest, take `using` as Array does.

options_for_owner.summary: The bound and the scope fix only, with `using` staying a list. weakref links are bounded (J5-02 A) and a scope ends only its own views (J5-19 A). `using` may follow the owner words but not thread_shared (J5-05 A), a class, String, and the standard collections by name. A program's own container cannot take `using`.

The list must be edited for every new library collection.

options_for_owner.summary: The narrow answer. A weakref link may only name an object from the built-in manager (J5-02 B). Opening a scope keeps ending every view into the arena, as today (J5-19 B). Only String joins the list (J5-09 A, J2-02 B), and thread_shared is refused (J5-05 A).

options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles. Every `weakref` of an arena-made object is refused ("a `weakref` link needs an object from the built-in manager"), so a camera can never follow a level's enemy, even while the level lives. A tree taken before a scope cannot be used inside it or after it (E3060), so parsers reorder their code. `Deque[int] using Arena` stays E2114.

recommendation.reason: A is the only option that is one rule. The same sentence settles weakref links, views, scopes, tokens, C hand-overs, threads and which types may take `using`, for the library's types and the program's alike, with no exception by type. It refuses exactly the programs that would read freed or reused memory or race on a manager, all when compiling, and accepts the correct ones that B and C refuse: a camera following an arena enemy, a tree kept across scratch scopes, an engine's own SlotMap in a level arena, a thread_shared value in a manager every thread may use. Nothing runs for it. The one run-time difference, Arc-style counting for a thread_shared value in a manager, falls only on that rare case and costs what Rust and C++ pay. Ordinary programs are unchanged. It reuses verdicts 164 and 165 and the inference every method already gets, instead of adding a list.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: what may outlive a std::pmr arena or reach another thread through it. A weak_ptr whose control block is in the arena, a string_view taken before a nested scope, a shared object made in a one-thread arena, and which containers, yours included, can take the arena at all.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `load_level` makes `level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)` | 64 KiB that `level` owns |
| 2 | main | `boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level` | boss's block (header with weak count 1, then `hp` 500) sits inside `level`'s 64 KiB |
| 3 | main | `cam.target = weakref boss` (`cam` belongs to `main`) | weak count 2; `cam` now points into `level`'s memory |
| 4 | main | `load_level` returns: `boss` ends | boss ended, weak count 1; the link keeps the block, still inside `level` |
| 5 | main | then `level` ends | all 64 KiB given back, the boss's block with it |
| 6 | main | `if cam.target exists as e:` in `main` | reads the weak count and header in freed memory: a use after free (C++: `weak_ptr::lock()` on a control block in a released pmr arena) |
owner_short.today: Only a value made in an arena and what holds one are tied to the arena. A weakref escapes (step 6 compiles), a scope ends views it never touched, thread_shared in a one-thread Arena is undecided, and only Array, Map and Set may take `using`.
owner_short.options:
A: one rule. Whatever points into an arena's memory lives no longer than the arena and ends exactly when that memory goes back. Threads follow from the arena (an Arena is one thread's). Any type that says `using A`, yours too, can take one.
B: bound links and fix scopes, but keep `using` a list. thread_shared is refused, and your own containers can never take an arena.
C: a weakref may only name a heap object, scopes keep ending every view, and only String joins the list.
owner_short.recommendation: A: one rule settles every case, all checked when compiling, nothing runs, ordinary code unchanged; it refuses only what would read freed memory or race on an arena.

design.open_risks: 1. `struct SlotMap using A:` is a new declaration form, though it reuses the word. The owner may prefer an ordinary type parameter `[T, A: needs Allocator = Global]` filled by `using`, which is existing syntax but leaves a second, bracket spelling to refuse. This is a spelling sub-question to show beside A. 2. A thread_shared value in a manager is made handed over and loses biased counting's 25% gain for its own thread's objects. This exact case is not measured; the 1.35x comes from REPORT.md's 'own' pattern, a mechanism measured on runtime blocks. 3. The instance link's kind is inferred from the manager's method bodies, so a library manager's thread-safety follows its bodies, as EXC-15 already makes every pub method's effects do. The owner may judge this against verdict 108's 'a library's promise does not depend on its body'. If so, the alternative is to require that a manager be ThreadShared and change only through lock or Atomic for its values to be Send. 4. Function values' state blocks and AnyError's box take no `using`, because no declaration names a manager for them. A program wanting closure state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`. If the owner wants `fn() using A`, that is checklist 12's 'add the syntax' and a further question. 5. C-kept addresses: facet 1 reaches what C keeps only through a holder on Ember's side. P08's token for retained non-callback pointers (J8-12) must be such a holder, or an arena object given to a `retained` parameter is bounded only by FFI-35a. Answer P08 consistently. 6. Weakref places now name their kind (`weakref Enemy using Arena`). One weakref field cannot mix links to heap and arena objects, as one owner field cannot (verdict 24). 7. P01 (markers from contents) and P05 (an end counts as a call where it may run) are assumed: facet 3 is their rule applied to the instance link, so their wording must name 'what a value reaches' to avoid a gap between groups. 8. Verdict 114's new block taken from the same instance can fail for lack of memory at a hand-over, which is a stop ('out of memory', ALC-4). That is the same as any allocation, but it is a new place where a hand-over may stop.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed or reused memory through anything that holds an address in a manager's memory (owner, weakref link, view, iterator, capture, error, token).
matrix.how_kept: [ALC-6] 1 ties every value that reaches an instance to the instance's life (E3063, a C keeping included). [ALC-6] 2 and the changed [ALC-5] refuse a give-back (reset, the instance's end) while such a value is used (E3021), and any use after it (E3060). A weakref link counts because its weak count keeps the target's block in the instance's memory ([OBJ-3]). A scope's end ends only views into what the scope gave ([ARN-6]), and opening a scope ends none.
matrix.edge_cases: The J5-02 target ended but its block kept by the weak count. A root taken before a scope (J5-19). Nested scopes. FixedArena over a caller's buffer (bounded by both). A value put in through ref mut (LT-47). Closures, AnyError, iterators and generators holding arena views. Static instances. A Handle (reaches nothing). A holder that let go before the give-back (`cam.target = None`, a list replaced by an empty one): hole. A parent-made list growing inside a scope: hole. A lock- or static-backed manager whose reset the compiler does not see as a change: hole. Moving the instance: the hidden link is a kept view, so BCK-4 ends it.

matrix.guarantee: No data race on a manager's state (an Arena's cursor, a free list).
matrix.how_kept: [ALC-6] 3: the hidden instance link is a kept sharedref mut when allocate/deallocate/reallocate change their object, so by verdict 164 the value is neither Send nor ThreadShared (E7015, E7008). It is a kept ref when the manager changes only through Atomic or a lock, so Send/ThreadShared follow ref M's markers (M ThreadShared). In scoped tasks a value's growth and end count as changes of the instance (THR-11, EFF-24; two tasks: E7007). A one-instance manager's methods are checked wherever they may run (THR-20). thread_shared using A is checked at the making line (verdict 165).
matrix.edge_cases: Two tasks growing their own lists from one Arena. Parent allocating while one task grows. THR-21 reductions (push) into a using place: hole. copy of / clone / String + of an arena value inside tasks: hole. Lock-based pools. A one-instance manager touching a static mut. System/Global. UnsafeCell- or raw-pointer-based managers: not ThreadShared, so the ref link is not Send. A ThreadShared local pool reaches only scoped tasks, because the ref link is a view (THR-8).

matrix.guarantee: No double end, and no give-back to the wrong manager: each block goes back once, to the instance and kind it came from.
matrix.how_kept: E2020 requires the kind to match wherever a value may grow, be replaced or end: fields, locals, owns and ref mut parameters, weakref places. deallocate is dispatched statically by the kind the place names. A block that a weakref may keep holds its instance word inside it. Under verdict 114 the old block is marked ended and its drop does not run; the new block's drop runs once. `using A` on declared types reuses the same place-names-kind rule.

A plain parameter or read-only `this` that 'accepts any manager' and then makes a holder from the value (a link, an owner), and `owns this` methods: hole, through dyn, virtual and function-value paths compiled once. Values from verdict 107 (b)/(c) managers that keep no word, when a later step needs the instance (a `using A` type's methods, a verdict-114 move): hole. Values swapped between two instances of one kind: each keeps its own word, and regions bound both.

Allocator stays an unsafe interface whose implementer vouches (ALC-2).

holes.program:
class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Bus:
    watchers: Array[weakref Enemy] = []        # links to enemies from the built-in manager

interface Listener:
    fn listen(ref mut bus: Bus)

extend Enemy implements Listener:
    fn listen(ref mut bus: Bus):
        bus.watchers.push(weakref this)        # `this` is only read: under the changed [TYP-46] it accepts an Enemy from any manager

fn hook(l: dyn Listener, ref mut bus: Bus):     # one body for every kind of listener
    l.listen(ref mut bus)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    bus = Bus()                                 # made after `level`, so it ends first: no E3063
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    hook(boss, ref mut bus)
    println(bus.watchers.len())
holes.what_goes_wrong: The design checks the kind (E2020) per place, and says a plain parameter or a view, a read-only `this` included, 'accepts a value from any manager'. `Enemy.listen` is one entry in a method table, compiled once. So neither the line nor 'one copy per layout' (compiler_does 6) can see that `this` came from `level`. The link lands in a Global-kind weakref place. When main ends, `boss` ends first (its block is kept by the weak count), then `bus`. The link's end takes the weak count to 0 and gives the block back 'statically by the kind the place names' (compiler_does 5), which is Global. So `ember_free` runs on an address inside the arena's chunk, which corrupts the heap. The same gap appears in two more places. An `owns this` method of a class made `using level` ends `this`, and nothing says which deallocate runs (or whether `boss.retire()` is E2020). A `thread_shared` owner made from a plain parameter, in code compiled once (a function value, a dyn method), needs a count sequence that the design chooses 'statically from the place's using kind'. For a manager's block, the Global sequence reads a making thread from a runtime chunk header that does not exist (verdict 101, fix 1).
holes.fix_hint: Say that a value reached through `this`, a plain parameter or a view has the caller's manager kind. Every step that depends on the kind and is made from such a value (an owner or link made from it, an `owns this` end, the deallocate dispatched, the count sequence) is checked at each call through the callee's summary. That is how [LT-1] already decides a `dyn` call: 'by the code of each kind that may reach it'. Here that means E2020 at `hook(boss, ref mut bus)`, naming line 10. Direct calls get per-kind copies. Alternatively, a block that a weakref may keep records its kind beside its instance word.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Nothing says which manager gives the memory for a value made from another value: `copy of`, `clone`, String's `+` under P06's J2-04 A, `to_string`. Rust's `Vec<T, A>::clone` uses the same allocator. The design's own facet-4 sentence (a `using A` type's methods make 'in the instance the value is made in') invites that reading. Under it, both tasks call `level.allocate` at once, race on the arena's cursor, and can be handed overlapping blocks. The design states the opposite: 'Reads of arena lists from many tasks compile, because a read never touches the manager'. If the compiler takes that sentence at face value, it counts no change of `level`, and the race compiles. If it counts the clone's allocation (EFF-24), the program is E7007, which contradicts the design's statement and refuses a correct program whose copies could come from Global.
holes.fix_hint: State where a value made from another value takes its memory. The consistent rule is that the place it goes to names the kind, so `copy of names` into a place with no `using` comes from Global, as C++ pmr's copy construction uses the default resource. A copy into a `using A` place is made in the instance named on the line. Otherwise, count such a making as a change of the source's instance (E7007) and remove the 'a read never touches the manager' claim.

holes.what_goes_wrong: THR-21 makes `push` from several tasks into one local a reduction. Each task fills a private accumulator 'of the place's type', and the accumulators are combined at the join. Here that type is `Array[int] using Arena`, but nothing says which instance the accumulators are made in. If they are made in `level`, each task's pushes call `level.allocate` on its own thread. THR-11's 'other than by a reduction' and LT-46's 'by a reduction from scoped tasks' (sharedref mut on two threads) can be read as covering those instance changes, which gives a race on the cursor. If they are not covered, the design's 'growth and end count as changes ... two tasks: E7007' refuses a correct parallel collect. The design decides neither.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a reduction's private accumulator for a `using` place takes its memory from Global, and that the combine at the join grows the place on the parent's thread. Or say that a reduction's accumulators count as values made in the place's instance, so two tasks are E7007, with help to collect into a list with no `using` and extend after the block.

Facet 2 says a value is ended only by the operation that gives back the memory it reaches, so this empty list, which reaches no memory, survives the reset and later grows into the reset arena. That is safe. The changed ALC-5 refuses any change 'while a value that reaches an instance lives', so the reset is E3021. The camera case is the same: `cam.target = None`, then `level.reset()` or a new level arena. The design does not say whether reaching is decided per value at each point, as views in locals are (non-lexical lifetimes), or by the place's type. A value that only will call the instance (an empty list, a link set to None, a type made `using` with nothing given out yet) is bound by the instance's life only (E3063) and survives a reset. State that this is decided per place at each point where the compiler follows the place, and by type elsewhere.

from std.sync import Mutex
from std.mem import Allocator, Layout

struct Slab:                                   # several instances; changes only through its Mutex
    chunks: Mutex[Array[Array[u8]]] = Mutex([])

    fn clear_all():                            # no `ref mut`: a Mutex changes through itself (verdict 3)
        with g = this.chunks.lock():
            g.clear()                          # frees every chunk, blocks still given out included

# SAFETY: every block lies in a chunk the instance keeps until it is given back or the instance ends
unsafe extend Slab implements Allocator:
    fn allocate(layout: Layout) -> *mut u8:
        ...                                    # carves the block from the last chunk, under the lock
    unsafe fn deallocate(p: *mut u8, layout: Layout):
        pass
    unsafe fn reallocate(p: *mut u8, old: Layout, new_size: usize) -> *mut u8:
        ...

fn main():
    slab = Slab()
    name = String("orc") using slab
    slab.clear_all()                           # reads `slab` only, so [ALC-5] sees no change
    println(name)                              # reads a freed chunk
holes.what_goes_wrong: The design makes managers that change only through a lock first-class (a ref link, Send values, `thread_shared ... using SLAB`). By verdict 3 and EXC-15, a method that frees memory through the Mutex does not change `this`, so ALC-5's E3021 never sees it. ALC-2's promise, 'stays valid until it is given back or the instance ends', read beside facet 2's own words ('The instance's end and reset() give back all of the instance's memory'), lets an implementer believe a reset through a lock is a give-back. The SAFETY note is then 'true', and safe code reads freed memory. The other case 'A reset of it [a static LockedPool] is E3021' is untrue for such a reset. A manager with one instance whose memory sits in a `static mut` and is reset by a free function is the same case.
holes.fix_hint: Tighten ALC-2's obligation. Memory given out stays valid until deallocate or reallocate gives that block back, the instance ends, or a change of the instance that ALC-5 sees. No method of the manager that changes it through a lock, an Atomic or a static frees a block still out. Optionally, let ALC-5 count a lock-mediated write that EXC-15 infers in a manager's own method as a change (E3021).

safety.notes:
The rule's core holds up under the safety lens:
- The weakref bound (J5-02).
- The scope-only end (J5-19).
- The J5-05 decision mechanism: a thread_shared block from a manager is made handed over, so verdict 101 fix 1 holds, and verdict 165's check applies at the making line.
- `using` for every declared type (J2-02, J5-09).

The hidden link is a kept view, so moving an instance and C or unscoped-thread keepings are refused by BCK-4, THR-8 and E3063. Lock-based and UnsafeCell-based managers get the right markers because Send for a ref link needs the manager to be ThreadShared.

Nine holes, two of them high:
1. The design lets plain parameters and a read-only `this` accept any manager. But kind-dependent steps made from such a value (a weakref put in a Global place, an `owns this` end, the thread_shared count sequence) are dispatched 'statically by the place's kind'. Through a dyn method or a function value that gives heap corruption, because ember_free runs on an arena block. The fix is summary-checked kinds, as [LT-1] already does for dyn.
2. Nothing says where `copy of`, `clone` or `+` of an arena value takes its memory. Under the source-instance reading, two tasks race on the cursor, which contradicts the design's 'a read never touches the manager'.

Medium:
- THR-21 reduction accumulators for a `using` place.
- The changed ARN-6's 'changing a value is not using the parent' lets a parent-made list grow into the scope's region.
- The changed ALC-5 and ARN-7 still omit scope(), so the design's own option-A program is E3021.
- 'Reaches' merges 'holds memory' with 'will call the instance', so ALC-5 and facet 2 disagree on the per-frame reset and camera-across-levels patterns.
- Verdict 107's no-word values when a `using A` type's method or a verdict-114 move needs the instance.
- ALC-2's promise does not forbid a reset through a lock or a static, which ALC-5 cannot see.

Low: an Arena's empty deallocate is still counted as a change (thread_shared using level refused, two tasks ending their own arena values refused).

None of these reopens verdicts 164 to 166; the fixes are statements of where memory comes from and when 'reaching' holds.

class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None             # links enemies from the built-in manager

fn follow(ref mut cam: Camera, e: Enemy):    # a plain parameter: 'accepts a value from any manager'
    cam.target = weakref e                   # any name may make a link ([WK-11])

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    cam = Camera()                           # made after `level`, so it ends first: the bound holds
    hero = Enemy(hp=100)
    follow(ref mut cam, hero)                # the ordinary heap program: compiles today
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    follow(ref mut cam, boss)                # the same function, an arena enemy
    mem.drop(owns boss)
    cam.target = None                        # the last link gives the boss's block back
holes.what_goes_wrong: A view of a class object is one pointer whatever its manager ([OBJ-2]), so 'one copy per layout' compiles `follow` once, and inside it the kind of `e` is unknown. Either the compiler refuses `cam.target = weakref e` from every plain parameter into a place of a fixed kind, and the first, ordinary heap call stops compiling. Or it accepts both calls, and the last link gives an arena block back through the built-in manager's free: undefined behaviour. The same happens with `fn keep(p: shares Player): LIST.push(shares p)`, and with `weakref e` stored in a static, where LT-47 does not carry the bound back to the call.
holes.fix_hint: The function's summary (EFF-24) records which plain parameters' values it links, owns or keeps, and where. The kind (E2020) and the bound (E3063) are checked at each call against the caller's value, as LT-47 does for ref mut. Make copies per manager kind, not per layout, wherever a body depends on the kind (verdicts 88, 128).

engineering.notes:
The design holds up in what it sets out to do. One sentence settles J5-02, J5-19, J2-02 and J5-09. Its J5-05 answer follows from verdict 165 and verdict 101 fix 1. Its case against phase 3's 'minus thread_shared' exception is right: that exception's reason is untrue for System and for lock-based pools, so under principle 6 it cannot stand. The two high holes are not in the idea but in two sentences. First, 'one copy per layout' for plain parameters: class objects of every manager share one layout, so the kind is lost inside the callee (hole 1). Second, 'and by no other' in ALC-6 2, which read word for word overrides BCK-4 (hole 2). Both have general fixes: summaries checked at the call, and the sentence scoped to the instance's operations. Several medium holes come from the design writing down the kind, or the instance, where the compiler knows it (ref mut parameters, weakref places, constructor arguments). Others come from two rules of the design disagreeing ('used' against 'lives'; 'changing a value is not using the parent' against 'allocating is E3096'). The rest are its edges against THR-21, THR-8 with verdict 164, and LT-47.

Numbers checked. 43.6 ms against 32.3 ms (1.35x, own pattern, 1 thread) and '13% to 44%' match measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md. 191 ms and 28.2 MB match verdict 107. One number is misquoted: 'a pipeline is 27% faster than biased_pub on one thread'. REPORT.md has pipe at 1 thread: atomic 98.9 ms, biased_pub 124.8 ms. So biased_pub is 26% slower, and the atomic count takes 21% less time. Correct it before the owner sees it.

Not holes, but for the lead. Risk 3 (the link kind inferred from a pub manager's bodies) is the cost verdict 86 already accepted for EXC-15. Verdict 108 concerns pub generic needs. Risk 5 (P08's retained token) stands as written.
