design.rule: One property, from which every case follows: memory that a manager's instance gave out is reached only while the instance still holds it, and every step that takes memory from a manager or gives it back goes to the manager the memory came from. All of it is decided when compiling. A value *holds into* an instance when it holds an address in memory the instance gave: a value made in it, an owner of one, a weakref link to one (the link keeps the block through its weak count), a view into such memory, and anything that holds or captures one of these. A value *will call* an instance when it holds none of that memory yet, but its growth, replacement or end, or a making for its parts, would call the instance (an empty list made in it). Both are decided for each place at each point, from what the place last got, as a view's life is, and through a call by the callee's summary. Five consequences follow. (1) Bound: such a value lives no longer than the instance (E3063). Handing it to C, which keeps it, counts as a keeping. (2) Exact ends: of the instance's own operations, only one that gives back memory a value holds into ends that value. Its end and reset() give back all of it, a scope's end gives back what that scope gave, and allocating or opening a scope gives back nothing. This is added to the ends every other rule gives. Giving the memory back while the value lives (a view until its last use, an owner or a link until its end) is E3021. A value that only will call the instance survives a reset. (3) New memory: a value takes its memory from the instance its making line names. Else, for a part its type ties to its own manager, it takes it from the instance its whole value is made in. Else it takes it from the built-in manager. So a copy, a sum or a task's accumulator never takes its source's instance unless the line says so, and a read never calls a manager. (4) Threads: only an owner or a ref mut name makes a value call its instance. So the hidden link to the instance counts toward Send and never toward ThreadShared. It stays on one thread (verdict 164) when the manager's allocate, deallocate or reallocate change their object, as an Arena's do. (5) Kinds: the kind is part of a value's type. Every place that keeps a value beyond a call names it, and none means the built-in manager. A function's parameter takes its caller's kind, and the compiler makes a copy of the function for each kind where its body depends on the kind. A block's type index names its kind, so a dyn or virtual call reaches the method compiled for that kind, and a weakref link, which names no kind, gives the block back there. `using` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker: a holder that may end a value (owns, shares, shares mut, thread_shared), a class, and a struct, class or enum declared `using A`. The library's String and collections are declared that way.
design.spec_text:
NEW [ALC-6] **Memory a manager gave is reached only while the manager holds it.** A value *holds into* an instance of a memory manager when it holds an address in memory the instance gave out. That covers a value made in it ([ALC-1]); an owner of such a value; a `weakref` link to one, which keeps its block through the weak count ([OBJ-3]); a view into such memory ([ARN-1], [LT-1]); and every value that holds or captures one of these (a struct, a list, an iterator, a function value's state, an error, a token). A value *will call* an instance when it holds none of the instance's memory, but its growth, replacement or end, or a making for its parts ([ALC-7] 2), would call the instance. Examples are an empty value made in it (`Array.new_in(frame)` and `[] using frame` take no memory until they first grow) and a value of a type made `using` it whose parts hold nothing yet. A value that only names a position (a `Handle`, an index) does neither. What a place holds into or will call is decided at each point, from what the place last got, as a view's life is ([BRW-2]). Where the compiler follows the place (a local, a part of a local or of a parameter, and through a call by the callee's summary, [EFF-24], [LT-47]), it is decided by what the place holds there. Elsewhere (an element reached by position, a part reached through a link or a shared owner, a static) it is decided by what the program may put there. Every value that holds into or will call an instance:
1. lives no longer than the instance. Keeping or returning it where it would outlive the instance is `E3063` ([LT-4], [LT-45]). A hand-over to C that keeps it ([FFI-35a], [OWN-12]) is such a keeping: "C keeps `w` after `level` ends; make it without `using level`".
2. if it holds into the instance's memory, is ended by the instance's operations that give that memory back, and by no other of the instance's operations. The instance's end gives back all of its memory, and so does any change of it that [ALC-5] allows only while no value holds into its memory (an `Arena`'s `reset()`). A scope's end ([ARN-6]) gives back what that scope gave. Allocating and opening a scope give back nothing. This is added to the ends every other rule gives the value ([BCK-4], [BRW-17]): a view of a list's element ends when the list is cleared, whatever manager gave the list. A use after the memory it holds into was given back is `E3060`. Giving that memory back while the value lives is `E3021`; a view lives until its last use, and an owner or a link until its end, which writes the block's counts. A value that only will call the instance is not ended by a reset: it holds none of the memory, and its next growth takes new memory from the instance.
3. calls the instance's methods only through an owner or a `ref mut` name, by the operations that call it: growth, replacement, end, and a making for its parts. A read-only name never makes its value call the instance: a value made from what it reads takes its memory by [ALC-7]. A link or an owner made from it ([WK-11], [RC-1]) is a value of its own, and a scoped task makes one only to a `thread_shared` target ([THR-2], verdict 166). So the instance link of [LT-4] counts toward `Send`, because an owner may be handed over, and never toward `ThreadShared`, because readers never use it. `T using A` is `ThreadShared` exactly when `T` is. It is `Send` when `T` is and the link may go to another thread: the link is a kept `ref` of the instance when `A`'s `allocate`, `deallocate` and `reallocate` change their object only through `Atomic` or a lock, or not at all (worked out from their bodies, [EXC-15]), and the instance is `ThreadShared`. Otherwise the link is a kept `sharedref mut` (an `Arena`'s methods move its cursor), which stays on one thread (verdict 164, `E7015`, `E7008`). Scoped tasks use such a value where it is. Its growth and end there count as changes of the instance ([THR-11], [EFF-24]; two tasks: `E7007`), and a task's reduction into it uses an accumulator of the task's own ([THR-21]). A manager with one instance holds no link. Its methods are checked as any call wherever a value's growth or end may run them ([THR-20]).

NEW [ALC-7] **Where a new value takes its memory.** Every value made takes its memory, and the kind in its type, from the first of these that applies. That covers a literal, a constructor, `copy of x`, and every value made from another: a clone, a `+` that makes a new `String`, `to_string()`, a conversion, `collect()`, a task's accumulator.
1. The instance named after it on its line: `[0.0, 1.0] using current`; `copy of names using level` makes the copy, and every part of it of that kind, in `level` ([GRM-43]).
2. Else, for a part that a type's declaration ties to its own manager (a field, an element type or a payload written `using A` in a type declared `using A`), the instance its whole value is made in. That covers a field's default; a constructor argument (`SlotMap[int](free=[]) using level` makes `free` in `level`); and what `init`, the type's methods (from the word the value keeps, [ALC-1]) and its `clone` make for such a part.
3. Else the built-in manager, or the one instance of the place's kind when the place's type names a manager with one instance.
A value made for a place whose kind may have several instances, which gets no instance by 1 or 2, is `E2020`: "`x` takes its memory from an `Arena`, and nothing names which; say which: `copy of names using level`". So a value made from another never takes its source's instance unless its line names it. `snapshot = copy of names` is an `Array[String]` from the built-in manager, which may outlive `level`, as C++'s `pmr` copy takes the default resource. The compiler gives a derived or library `clone`, and a hand-written one's makings, the instance the copy is made in.

CHANGED [TYP-46] / [ALC-1] (the closed list goes) **The kind of manager is part of a value's type. A place that keeps the value names it, and a parameter takes its caller's.** `using A` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker:
* a holder that may end a value: `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` before a type (`mesh: owns Mesh using LevelArena`);
* a class type;
* a struct, class or enum that says it takes one, with `using` after its name, or for a class after its base list: `[T]` above `struct SlotMap using A:`; `class Level using A:`; `class Boss(Enemy) using A:`; `enum Expr using A:`. In its body `A` names the manager kind, and a part written `using A` takes its memory from the instance the value is made in ([ALC-7] 2). A derived class takes its base's manager, so `using` on a class whose base takes one is `E2114`. Before such a type, `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` with `using A` gives the block and the type's `A` one manager. The standard library's `String`, `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, `BitSet`, `RingBuffer` and `Pool` are declared this way.
A type takes at most one manager. After any other type, `using` is `E2114`, with these messages:
* a number;
* a view: "a view gives nothing back to a manager; remove `using`";
* a `weakref` link: "a link takes no memory of its own, and its target's block goes back to the manager it came from; remove `using`";
* a struct that does not say it takes one: "`Level` does not say it takes a memory manager, and its fields say where their memory comes from; to give it one, write `struct Level using A:` and `using A` after the fields that take it, or remove `using`".
A manager written in brackets (`SlotMap[Enemy, LevelArena]`, `Array[T, A]`) is `E1010`, whose help gives the `using` spelling.

Every place that keeps a value beyond a call names its kind, and none means the built-in manager: a field, a static, an element type, a payload, a result, a local whose type is written, and a function type's parameter. A value of another kind given to one is `E2020`: `return [String("orc")] using level` under `-> Array[String]` gets the help `-> Array[String] using Arena`. A local whose type is not written takes its value's kind.

A function's parameter (`this` included) whose type has no `using` takes the kind its caller's value has. The function is compiled once for each kind its callers pass where its body depends on the kind, and once where it does not (verdict 88's copies). The body depends on the kind when it grows, replaces, ends or hands over the value, makes an owner of it, sends it to another thread, or makes values for its `using A` parts. A line of the function that puts the value where another kind is named is `E2020` at the call, naming that line. A call that one body serves for every caller (through a function value, or a `dyn` or `virtual` method) takes the kind each parameter's type says. It accepts any kind where no function that may be reached depends on it ([LT-1]: by the code of each kind that may reach it). `this` of a class object reaches the method compiled for its block's kind ([OBJ-2]). `thread_shared T using A` is allowed exactly where `T using A` is `Send` and `T` is `ThreadShared` ([ALC-6] 3, verdict 165). Otherwise it is `E7015` at the making line.

CHANGED [ALC-1] (the instance word): "A value whose manager may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, wherever a later step takes memory from the instance or gives memory back to it. Such steps are its growth, its end, a making for its `using A` parts ([ALC-7] 2), a move to a new block at a hand-over ([THR-2]), and a link's give-back of its block. Verdict 107's two kinds of manager keep the word only where such a step remains. In a manager that frees nothing one by one (its `deallocate` empty), a value that grows, makes values for its parts or may be moved keeps the word, and one that does none of these keeps none. A manager that implements `FoundByAddress` finds the instance from the address, and no value keeps the word."

CHANGED [OBJ-1] / [OBJ-2]: "A block's type index names its type and the kind of manager that gave the block. An object or a shared value of one type made in two kinds has two indices, which every type test (`is`, `cast`) reads as its one type. Each index's interface tables reach the methods compiled for that kind ([TYP-46]). This adds no memory."

CHANGED [OBJ-3] / [HEAP-7] / [WK-11]: "A `weakref` place names no manager, because a link takes no memory of its own. The last end of a block's counts, an owner's or a link's, gives the block back to the kind its type index names, and to the instance found from the word [ALC-1] keeps in the block. Where every object of a class family that a link may name comes from one kind, that give-back is a direct call. One camera may follow a player from the built-in manager and an enemy from a level arena."

CHANGED [OBJ-1] / [RC-4] point 4: "A `thread_shared` value whose block a manager gave is made handed over. From its first owner, every thread counts its owners in the away count, and its end never waits in a queue. Every count sequence reads the handed-over mark before the making thread, so the making thread of a value marked handed over is never read. A block a manager gave therefore needs no chunk header, and one sequence serves an owner, or a view opened from a link, of a `thread_shared` value from any manager. The making thread of a block from the runtime's allocator is read from its chunk, never from the value (verdict 101, fix 1)."

CHANGED [LT-4]: "A value made in a memory manager's instance, and every value that holds into or will call it ([ALC-6]), lives no longer than that instance …". The sentence "That address is a kept `sharedref mut` link" becomes "That address is the link of [ALC-6] 3".

CHANGED [LT-47]: "A view, or a value that holds into or will call an instance ([ALC-6]), put in through `ref mut` …". Add: "The callee's summary says what the caller's place holds after the call. It records each part the callee leaves holding nothing (set to `None`, given an empty value, or with its links ended), and each part it gives a value that reaches another argument or a static ([EFF-24]). After `cam.forget()`, whose body is `this.target = None`, `cam` holds into nothing."

CHANGED [EFF-24], the summary also records: "for each parameter, `this` included: whether the body depends on the value's manager kind ([TYP-46]); where the body keeps a link, an owner or a view made from the value (a part of another parameter, a static, a capture, its result); and which parts of a `ref mut` parameter it leaves holding into no instance ([LT-47])".

CHANGED [ALC-5]: "**An instance stays as its values need it.** While a value holds into memory an instance gave ([ALC-6]), the instance is changed only by operations that give none of that memory back: the `Allocator` methods a value's growth and end call, the making of other values in it, an `Arena`'s `alloc*` ([ARN-1]), and opening a scope ([ARN-6]). Any other change through a name that may change the instance is `E3021`: '`frame.reset()` (line 26) gives back memory `names` holds (line 25), and `names` still lives; end it first: write `mem.drop(owns names)` above line 26'; for a link, 'end the link first: write `cam.target = None` above line 15'. While values only will call an instance, the instance may be reset, and its end stays bounded by [ALC-6] 1."

CHANGED [ALC-2] (the implementer's promise): "… valid, aligned, unaliased memory, which stays valid until `deallocate` or `reallocate` gives that block back, the instance ends, or the instance is changed through a name that may change it. [ALC-5] refuses that last while a value holds into the memory. Nothing else frees or reuses a block still given out: no change made through a lock, an `Atomic`, a static or C, and no method reached through a read-only name. So an implementer keeps the state that holds its memory where only those operations reach it."

CHANGED [ARN-1]: "`reset()` and the arena's end give back all of its memory and end every value that holds into it ([ALC-6] 2). The end of a scope ends what holds into what that scope gave ([ARN-6]). Opening a scope ends nothing: the scope holds a view of the arena's cursor, not of its memory, as `alloc*` does."

CHANGED [ARN-6], add: "Reading or changing a value in memory the parent gave before the scope is not using the parent, except a change that calls the parent's `allocate` or `reallocate`. A growth of a value made in the parent, or a making in it ([ALC-7]), is allocating from the parent, which is `E3096`: '`toks.push(owns 7)` (line 6) grows `toks`, made in `frame` (line 2), while `s` holds `frame` (line 3); push before the `with` block or after it, or make `toks` from `s`'. The parent's `deallocate` does nothing, so ending a value made in the parent stays allowed. Allocating from the parent, resetting it, or opening another scope of it while the scope lives is `E3096`. A scope's end ends only what holds into memory that scope gave, and an inner scope's end only what the inner scope gave."

CHANGED [ARN-7]: "No operation lowers an arena's allocation pointer or reuses its bytes while a value holds into those bytes. Each such operation ends every value holding into them ([ALC-6] 2), and [ALC-5] says which changes of the arena are allowed while one lives."

CHANGED [THR-2] (verdict 114): "the new block for an object made in an instance is taken from that instance, whose word the object keeps ([ALC-1])".

CHANGED [THR-8] / [THR-9]: "A value made in a manager's instance is `Send` and `ThreadShared` as [ALC-6] 3 says."

CHANGED [THR-21]: "A task's private accumulator for a place a manager serves has the place's type with its memory from the built-in manager ([ALC-7] 3), since a task never calls the instance of a place it reduces into. The combine at the join runs on the parent's thread and moves the accumulator's contents into the place, whose growth goes to the place's instance."

CHANGED [GRM-43]: "`using` after a value the line does not make (a name, a part) names the instance of the value that the words before it make: `copy of names using level` makes the copy in `level`."

CHANGED [UNS-4], add: "A raw pointer into memory a manager gave is not used after that memory is given back ([ALC-6] 2)."

GRAMMAR: `struct_decl := "struct" IDENT ["using" IDENT] [implements] [where_clause] ":" type_body`; `class_decl := ["open" | "abstract"] "class" IDENT ["(" type ")"] ["using" IDENT] [implements] [where_clause] ":" type_body`; `enum_decl := "enum" IDENT [generic_params] ["using" IDENT] [implements] [where_clause] ":" …`.

CODES:
* E2114 row: "`using` after a type whose declaration leaves no manager to its maker (a number, a view, a `weakref` link, a struct that does not say `using A`), or on a derived class whose base already takes one".
* E2020 row, add: "a value put in a place that names another kind of manager, a result included; a function's line that does so with a caller's value, reported at the call; a value made for a place whose kind may have several instances when nothing names which".
* E3063 row: "a value that holds into or will call a memory manager's instance ([ALC-6]), kept or returned where it would outlive it, a hand-over to C included".
* E3021 row, add: "a give-back of memory a value holds into while the value lives".
* E3096 row: "allocating from, resetting or scoping a parent arena, or growing or making a value in it, while a scope of it lives".
* E7015 row, add: "a value made in an instance whose methods change it, sent to another thread or made `thread_shared`".

answers.answer: Decided. The link holds into the arena, because it keeps the boss's block, weak count included, in the arena's memory. So the link lives no longer than the arena (E3063), and giving that memory back while the link lives is E3021 ([ALC-6] 1, 2). The link names no manager: a link takes no memory of its own. Its last end gives the block back to the kind the block's type index names, here the arena, whose `deallocate` does nothing. After the boss ends, opening the link finds it ended, because the block is still in memory the arena holds.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 500, then gone. When `cam` ends, its link's end gives the boss's block back to `level`. The draft's own program, with the arena made inside `load_level`, is E3063 at `cam.target = weakref boss`: "`cam.target` keeps a link to `boss`, whose block is in `level` (line 9), and `level` ends when `load_level` returns while `cam` lives on in `main`; make the arena in the caller: `fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):`, with `level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)` above `cam = Camera()` in `main`, or end the link before it returns: `cam.target = None`". `level.reset()` in `main` while `cam.target` keeps the block is E3021, and after `cam.target = None` it is allowed. The camera's field is the one written today.

answers.answer: Decided with no exception for thread_shared. A thread_shared value may end on any thread, and its end gives its block back to its instance, so every thread must be able to use that instance ([ALC-6] 3). An Arena's allocate moves its cursor, so its link is a changing link that stays on one thread (verdict 164). That makes `thread_shared ... using level` E7015 at the making line, by verdict 165's check. A manager with one instance and no one-thread state (System, Global) is allowed. So is a several-instance manager whose methods change it only through a lock or an Atomic. Such a value is made handed over (RC-4 point 4): every owner is counted in the away count. Every count sequence reads the handed-over mark before the making thread, so no chunk header is read, and fix 1's 'never from the value' holds.
answers.code:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using System    # a manager every thread may give memory back to
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))
    println("done")
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints done. Every owner of `stats` is counted with one atomic add, as Rust's Arc counts. The example's `thread_shared Stats() using level` is E7015 at that line: "`stats` is shared between threads, so its last owner may end on any of them and give its block back to `level` there; `level` is an `Arena`, whose `allocate` moves its cursor, so only this thread may use it; make `stats` without `using level`". A program's own pool whose free list sits in a `Mutex` (`static SLAB: Slab`, then `thread_shared Session() using SLAB`) compiles the same way.

answers.answer: Decided. A scope's end gives back only what the scope gave, so it ends only what holds into that memory ([ALC-6] 2). Opening a scope gives back nothing. The root, taken from the arena before the scope, stays valid inside the scope and after it. Reaching it is not using the parent. Allocating from the parent, or growing or making a value in it, while the scope lives stays E3096 ([ARN-6]).
answers.code:
@derive(Zeroable)
struct Tok:
    kind: int

struct Node:
    kind: int

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))   # kept for the whole parse
    with s = frame.scope():                          # scratch memory, given back when the block ends
        toks = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        toks[0].kind = 2
        root.kind += toks[0].kind                    # root is below the scope's memory
    return root.kind

fn main():
    frame = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    println(parse(ref mut frame))
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 3. The scope's end lowers the cursor to where the scope began, and root lies below that. Inside the `with` block, `frame.alloc(...)` is E3096 (allocate from `s`), and so is a `push` to a list made in `frame`, which would grow it from `frame`. `toks` used after the block is E3060.

answers.answer: Decided, as phase 3 restated it. `using` follows every type whose declaration leaves a manager to its maker. The standard library's String, Array, Map, Set, Deque, SmallArray, BitSet, RingBuffer and Pool all say it in their declarations (`struct Deque using A:`). A program's own struct, class or enum says it the same way. So no path exists that only the library can take. thread_shared is decided by the thread consequence, not left out by type.
answers.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:                         # takes a memory manager, called A in its body
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []        # from the instance the map is made in
    free: Array[int] using A = []

    fn insert(owns v: T) -> int:
        this.slots.push(owns Some(owns v))      # grows `slots` in the map's instance
        return this.slots.len() - 1

class Enemy:
    hp: int

struct Level:
    names: Array[String] using Arena
    title: String using Arena
    enemies: SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena

fn load(ref mut current: Arena) -> Level:
    return Level(names=[String("orc")] using current, title=String("Cave") using current, enemies=SlotMap[Enemy]() using current)

fn main():
    level_mem = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    lvl = load(ref mut level_mem)
    println(lvl.title, lvl.names.len())
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints Cave 1. The title's text, the names list's buffer and both of the SlotMap's lists come from `level_mem`, and `insert` grows `slots` there. `lvl` lives no longer than `level_mem` (E3063 otherwise). `using Arena` after `int`, after a view, after a `weakref` link, or after a struct that does not say `using A` is E2114, and the help gives the declaration line.

answers.answer: Decided: String declares that it takes a manager, as Array does. So `text: String using Arena` is allowed, and its growth goes back to the arena, as ALC-1's own sentence already says.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints let. A StrView of `t.text` holds into the arena too, so `arena.reset()` ends it, and it may not outlive the arena (E3060, E3063). `copy of t.text` is a String from the built-in manager, which may outlive the arena.

other_cases.case: A StrView into an arena-made String, used after `arena.reset()`.
other_cases.settled: The view holds into the arena's memory ([ALC-6]), so the reset ends it. The use after the reset is E3060. With the use placed before the reset, the program compiles.

other_cases.case: A renderer kept for the whole game, with `r.cmds = Array.new_in(frame)` and then `frame.reset()` every frame.
other_cases.settled: After the assignment, `r.cmds` holds no memory of `frame` and only will call it ([ALC-6]), so the reset is allowed. The next push takes new memory from `frame`. If the reset comes while `r.cmds` still holds pushed commands, it is E3021, with `r.cmds = Array.new_in(frame)` above it as the help.

other_cases.case: One camera following the player (no `using`) and then an arena enemy, through `fn follow(ref mut cam: Camera, e: Enemy): cam.target = weakref e`.
other_cases.settled: Both calls compile. A link names no manager, and `follow` does nothing that depends on the kind, so it is compiled once. The second call makes `cam` hold into `level` (follow's summary), which is allowed because `cam` ends before `level`. When the last link ends, the enemy's block goes back to the kind its type index names. `fn keep(p: shares Player): LIST.push(shares p)` given an arena player is E2020 at the call, naming line 2: LIST's owners are from the built-in manager. A `weakref e` stored in a static is E3063 at the call, because a static outlives `level`.

other_cases.case: An arena-made Enemy registering itself through a `dyn Listener` method: `bus.watchers.push(weakref this)`.
other_cases.settled: Compiles. `this` reaches the method compiled for its block's kind through its type index. The link is kind-free. The callee's summary (`[LT-1]`: by the code of each kind that may reach it) makes the caller's `bus` hold into `level`. `bus` must end before `level`, which is E3063 otherwise, at the call, naming the method's line.

other_cases.case: An `owns this` method (`fn retire() owns this`) on a class object made `using level`, called directly and through `dyn`.
other_cases.settled: Both end the object through the Arena's `deallocate`. The direct call compiles the Arena copy of `retire`, and the dyn call reaches it through the block's per-kind type index.

other_cases.case: Tasks each taking `(copy of names).len()` of a list made in `level`.
other_cases.settled: Compiles. Each copy names no instance, so it comes from the built-in manager ([ALC-7]), and no task calls `level`. `copy of names using level` in two tasks is E7007 (two tasks change `level`). Inside a scope of `level`, it is E3096.

other_cases.case: Tasks pushing into a caller's `hits: Array[int] using Arena` (a reduction, [THR-21]).
other_cases.settled: Compiles. Each task's accumulator comes from the built-in manager, and the combine at the join grows `hits` in `level` on the parent's thread. A push made through a helper call, which is not a reduction, grows the list from the task's thread: one such task is allowed, and two touching `level` is E7007.

other_cases.case: An arena-made widget handed to C through an `owns` contract (`widget_take(owns w)`), or captured by `thread.spawn`.
other_cases.settled: C, or an unscoped thread, keeps the widget past every local instance. That is E3063 for C and E7015 for the thread, because its instance link stays on one thread. The help says to make it without `using`, or to hand over `copy of w`, which is a copy from the built-in manager. `w.into_raw()` inside `unsafe:` is vouched for by the block: [UNS-4] now says a raw pointer into a manager's memory is not used after that memory is given back.

other_cases.case: A helper `fn add_token(ref mut toks: Array[Tok], kind: int)` called with an arena list.
other_cases.settled: Compiles, with nothing written. `add_token` is compiled once more for Arena lists, and its push grows `toks` through the Arena's reallocate. A helper whose body does `toks = []` is E2020 at an arena call, naming that line: the new list is from the built-in manager. The help offers `toks.clear()`. The same helper stored in a `fn(ref mut Array[Tok])` value is compiled for the built-in manager, because a function type's parameter names its kind. Calling the stored value with an arena list is E2020.

other_cases.case: A function returning an arena list under `-> Array[String]`.
other_cases.settled: E2020 at `return`, with the help `-> Array[String] using Arena`. A result keeps its value beyond the call, so its type names the kind.

other_cases.case: A program's struct `Level` with list fields, written `lvl: Level using Arena` without `struct Level using A:`.
other_cases.settled: E2114. Level's fields already say where their memory comes from (the built-in manager), and a written field means only what it says (verdict 132's lesson). The help gives `struct Level using A:`, with `using A` on the fields. `owns Level using Arena` is allowed: the block comes from the arena, and the fields come from where they say.

other_cases.case: A parser tree `enum Expr using A:` with `Add(owns Expr using A, owns Expr using A)`, returned as `owns Expr.Add(owns Expr.Num(1), owns Expr.Num(2)) using frame`.
other_cases.settled: The outer block and both children are made in `frame` ([ALC-7] 2). With `enum Expr:` and `Add(owns Expr, owns Expr)`, the children come from the built-in manager, as the declaration says.

other_cases.case: A generic `[T: needs Clone] fn dup(x: T) -> T: return copy of x` given an `Array[int] using Arena`.
other_cases.settled: E2020 at the call, naming line 2. The result's type is a list from some Arena, and nothing names which. This is an understandable limitation, stated clearly, and the help is to name the arena or to pass a list from the built-in manager.

other_cases.case: A program's own Slab manager whose `clear_all()` frees its chunks through its Mutex while values made in it live.
other_cases.settled: Safe code cannot see this change (verdict 3), so the Slab's `unsafe extend ... implements Allocator` promise covers it ([ALC-2] as changed): nothing but deallocate, reallocate, the end, or a change through a name that may change the instance frees a block still given out. So the SAFETY note is false, and the fault is in the vouching code, as it is with an unsound `unsafe impl GlobalAlloc` in Rust.

other_cases.case: A class object made in a lock-based pool, with a weakref link on this thread, handed whole to another thread (verdict 114).
other_cases.settled: The pool's methods only read the pool, and the pool is ThreadShared, so the object is Send. Verdict 114 moves its contents to a new block taken from the same pool instance, from the word the object keeps for that ([ALC-1]). The old block stays here until its last link ends, then goes back to the pool, through the block's type index.

other_cases.case: Nested scopes: `with a = frame.scope():` then `with b = a.scope():`, with a view from `a` used after `b` ends.
other_cases.settled: b's end gives back only what b gave, so the view from `a` stays valid until a's end. Views from b used after b's end are E3060.

other_cases.case: A Pool's Handle kept after the pool ends.
other_cases.settled: A handle is a number and holds into nothing, so nothing bounds it. Without the pool it cannot be looked up. A `ref T` from `pool.get(h)` is a view into the pool and is bounded by it, as today.

other_cases.case: A closure capturing an arena-made value, stored in a static, or an AnyError holding an error that views arena text, returned with `?` past the arena.
other_cases.settled: Both hold into the instance, so both are E3063. The closure's state block and AnyError's box come from the built-in manager, because no declaration names a manager for them, so `fn() using A` is E2114. A program that wants type-erased state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`.

other_cases.case: A static instance (`static POOL: LockedPool`), with values made in it kept in other statics.
other_cases.settled: A static instance outlives everything, so its values may be kept anywhere, unscoped threads included if its link only reads. Its changes through its lock free no block still given out, by the [ALC-2] promise. Safe code cannot reset it under its values, because a change through a name that may change it needs a name that is not a static's.

other_cases.case: A FixedArena over a buffer (`Arena.fixed(ref mut buffer)`), with values made in it.
other_cases.settled: The FixedArena holds a kept ref mut view of the buffer ([ARN-4]), so its values hold into the buffer through it, and each is bounded by both.

other_cases.case: A shares mut value made in an Arena, with a sharedref mut link to it held elsewhere.
other_cases.settled: The owners hold the block and the link views it, so both hold into the arena and both are bounded. The count block is in arena memory. The arena keeps that memory until its end or a reset, and a reset is refused while either lives.

design.prior_art:
**C++ std::pmr.** A container holds a memory_resource* (8 bytes). Program types opt in by declaring allocator_type and getting uses-allocator construction, the same idea as `struct SlotMap using A:` with its parts made in the holder's instance ([ALC-7] 2). A copy does not propagate the resource: polymorphic_allocator::select_on_container_copy_construction returns the default resource, which is [ALC-7]'s rule that a copy names its instance or uses the built-in manager. allocate_shared stores the allocator in the control block, and the last weak release gives the block back through one virtual call. So weak_ptr<T> names no allocator, which is how a weakref link names no manager here; Ember finds the kind through the block's existing type index and adds no memory. Nothing is checked in C++: a weak_ptr or string_view that outlives a released monotonic_buffer_resource is undefined behaviour (exactly J5-02).

**C++20 abbreviated templates.** `void f(auto& v)` compile one copy per argument type, which is how a parameter takes its caller's kind here; Ember writes not even `auto`.

**Rust (allocator_api, still unstable).** Box<T, A>, Vec<T, A>, Rc<T, A> and Weak<T, A> take the allocator as a type parameter. With A = &'a Bump, the lifetime 'a bounds every holder, the Weak included, which is facet 1. Vec::clone keeps the same allocator, which Ember does only when the line names it, so copies made in tasks never race. Send follows the allocator: Box<T, &Bump> is Send only if Bump is Sync, and bumpalo's Bump is not, which is facet 4. A &Vec<T, &Bump> is still not Send, a refusal Ember avoids because a read never calls the manager. bumpalo's reset takes &mut self, so no allocation may be live. Because the lifetime sits in the holder's type, even an empty Vec<T, &'a Bump> in a long-lived struct blocks the reset, and Rust programs rebuild the holder every frame, a refusal Ember's per-place 'will call' avoids. Rust's other shortfalls: the API has been unstable for years, and the type parameters are written everywhere (Vec<T, &'a Bump>, Weak<T, A>), so one Weak field cannot hold links from two allocators.

**Ada.** A storage pool is named per access type (`for Node_Ptr'Storage_Pool use Level_Pool;`), the place naming the kind as in verdict 24. Accessibility levels bound access values, partly with checks while running. Ada 2012 subpools are freed at once with Unchecked_Deallocate_Subpool, which leaves the program erroneous if references remain.

**Zig.** An Allocator interface is passed explicitly, with an ArenaAllocator and containers (ArrayListUnmanaged) that take the allocator per call. There is no lifetime or thread checking, so a use after reset is illegal behaviour that often goes undetected.

**Go.** GOEXPERIMENT=arenas checked a use after Free while running, by unmapping pages, and the proposal is on hold.

**Swift and C#.** Class instances always come from the runtime heap. withUnsafeTemporaryAllocation and stackalloc with scoped Span give scratch buffers only.

**Where they fall short of safe, C-fast and readable.** C++ and Zig are fast but unsafe. Go's check costs time while running and was abandoned. Ada checks partly while running. Swift and C# give no arenas for objects. Rust is safe and fast but unstable and wordy. This rule takes Rust's two facts (the allocator's life and its thread-safety reach every holder) and C++'s one word, its non-propagating copy and its allocator-free weak pointer. The compiler infers all of it, and nothing extra is written.
design.cost:
**Bound and exact ends (facets 1 and 2).** Zero while running: both are region checks made when compiling, per place and per point, as for views today. A scope's end is one pointer store (the cursor lowered), the same as C.

**Where new memory comes from (facet 3).** One call of the named manager's allocate (static dispatch, inlinable). A copy that names no instance costs what a heap copy costs, as C++'s pmr copy does, and `copy of x using level` gets the arena's speed. A reduction into a place a manager serves takes its accumulators from the built-in manager, and at the join it pays one growth of the place and a move of the elements per task, which is what any reduction into a list pays.

**Threads (facet 4).** Zero while running; the markers are worked out when compiling.

**Kinds (facet 5).** A function whose body depends on the kind is compiled once more for each kind its callers pass. That is code size, not time, the same as Rust's monomorphised Vec<T, A> and C++'s templates, and a body that does not depend on the kind is compiled once. A block's type index naming its kind adds no memory (the same 32 bits). A type test ignores the kind, and dyn and virtual calls stay one table load. A weakref link costs what any link costs: one plain add and one subtract of the weak count. The last give-back of a block is a direct call where every object of the family comes from one kind (unchanged from today). Where a family comes from several kinds, it is one load and one indirect call, at that last end only, as C++'s control block pays.

**The instance word.** 8 bytes per value that needs it, the same as C++ pmr's pointer per container and Rust's &Bump per Vec. It is kept only where a later step takes memory from the instance (growth, a making for `using A` parts, a verdict-114 move, a link's give-back in a manager whose deallocate does something). Where verdict 107 removes it, nothing extra is paid, and its measurement stands: a million small values took 191 ms and 28.2 MB, against C's 191 ms and 28.2 MB (and 241 ms and 44.7 MB with the word). A `struct Tree using A` whose methods make nodes keeps one word for the tree, not one per node.

**thread_shared in a manager.** This is the one case that differs while running. The value is made handed over, so each owner +1 or -1 is one atomic read-modify-write, as Rust's Arc and C++'s shared_ptr pay, instead of biased counting's plain add on the making thread. measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md, 'own' pattern on one thread: 43.6 ms with one atomic count against 32.3 ms biased (biased_chunk), so 1.35x for this case only. In the one-thread pipeline the atomic column is 98.9 ms against biased_pub's 124.8 ms. Memory: the same 32-byte header as every thread_shared value, so zero extra. Reading the mark before the making thread uses the loads the sequence already makes to learn of a hand-over. Reading the maker's id from the value instead, J5-05 B's idea, was measured at 13% to 44% slower on cross-thread copying, and fix 1 excludes it.

C pays nothing for counting because C has no safe sharing. Nothing in this rule adds a check that runs.

readability.ordinary_after:
fn add_token(ref mut toks: Array[Tok], kind: int):      # a list from any manager
    toks.push(owns Tok(kind=kind))

fn parse(ref mut frame: Arena) -> int:
    root = ref mut frame.alloc(owns Node(kind=1))       # the tree first, as the program means
    toks: Array[Tok] using Arena = Array.new_in(frame)
    add_token(ref mut toks, 2)
    with s = frame.scope():                              # scratch; root and toks stay valid
        scratch = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[Tok](64)
        root.kind += scratch[0].kind + toks[0].kind

readability.note: The after version is the same length and has one word fewer: the helper no longer names the kind. It reads in the order the program means. The camera's field is unchanged, and it may follow an enemy from any manager. A program with no arena (a game loop, a server handler using the built-in manager) is identical before and after: no new word and nothing new to write. The rule's cost falls only on rare programs: a program's own container writes `using A` once in its declaration, reusing the language's word, and its users write exactly what they write for the library's types (`SlotMap[Enemy] using Arena`). A copy wanted inside the arena writes `copy of x using level`.

design.compiler_does:
1. Regions. It gives each instance a region, and every value made in it that region. It then follows, per place at each point, what holds into the region and what will call it, as it follows views (LT-45, BRW-2): owners, weakref links, views, iterators, captures, errors and tokens. It follows them through calls by the callee's summary, which now records where a body keeps a link, owner or view made from a parameter, and which ref mut parts it leaves holding nothing (LT-47, EFF-24). It refuses a keeping past the instance (E3063), a hand-over to C included. Where it cannot follow a place (an element reached by position, a part reached through a link, a static), it decides by what the program may put there.
2. Give-backs. It splits an arena's memory into nested regions, one per open scope, and treats each give-back as ending exactly the values that hold into the memory it frees: reset and the end free all, and a scope's end frees its own. Allocating and opening a scope end nothing. The ends that BCK-4 and BRW-17 give stay in force. A give-back while a holder lives (a view until its last use, an owner or a link until its end) is E3021. A value that only will call the instance is not ended.
3. New memory. It picks each new value's instance: the one the line names, then the holder's (from the word the holder keeps), then the built-in manager. It refuses a value made for a several-instance kind when nothing names its instance (E2020). It gives derived and library clones, and a hand-written clone's makings, the instance the copy is made in. It makes a reduction's accumulators from the built-in manager and combines them into the place on the parent's thread.
4. Kinds. It treats the kind as part of the type and checks every keeping place's kind, results included (E2020). It compiles each function once per kind its callers pass where its body depends on the kind, and once otherwise, as for verdict 88's copies. It checks a call compiled once by every body that may be reached (LT-1). It gives a block's type index its kind, so dyn and virtual calls on `this` reach the per-kind method, and a link's last end gives the block back to that kind, by a direct call where the family comes from one kind.
5. Threads. It infers from the manager's Allocator bodies (EXC-15) whether the instance link changes the instance or only reads it. It counts the link toward Send for owners and ref mut names, and never toward ThreadShared. It checks verdict 165 at a thread_shared making line. It counts a value's growth and end in a task as a change of the instance (EFF-24, THR-11). It makes a thread_shared block a manager gave handed over, and every count sequence reads that mark before the making thread.
6. Words. It keeps the instance word exactly where a later step takes memory from the instance or gives memory back to it, and nowhere else (verdict 107).
7. Scopes. It refuses a growth of a value made in the parent, or a making in the parent, while a scope of it lives (E3096).
The programmer writes nothing for any of this, except `using` where a value is made in an instance, or where a keeping place's kind is not the built-in manager.
design.misuse:
Every mistake is refused when compiling, and nothing in safe code reaches freed or reused memory or races on a manager.
* A weakref, view, owner, iterator, closure or error that holds into or will call an instance and is kept past it: E3063 at the line that keeps it, or at the call whose callee keeps it, naming the callee's line. The help is to make the arena in the caller or to end the link before the arena ends.
* A hand-over to C of an arena-made value: E3063.
* A reset, or another give-back, while a value holding into that memory lives: E3021, with `mem.drop(owns x)`, `cam.target = None` or the reorder as the help.
* A use after the give-back: E3060, naming the give-back line.
* A value put where another kind is named, a result included: E2020, with the line to write (`-> Array[String] using Arena`).
* A helper's line that does this with a caller's value: E2020 at the call, naming the line.
* A value made for a several-instance kind with nothing naming which instance: E2020, with `using level`.
* `using` after a number, a view, a weakref link, a struct that does not declare one, or a derived class whose base already takes one: E2114, with the declaration line or 'remove using'.
* A manager in brackets: E1010, with the `using` spelling.
* An arena-made value sent to another thread, captured by thread.spawn, put in a channel or made thread_shared: E7015, naming the arena and why only its thread may use it (its allocate moves its cursor), with `copy of x`, which comes from the built-in manager, as the help.
* Two scoped tasks growing, ending or making values in one Arena outside a reduction: E7007.
* Allocating from a parent arena, or growing or making a value in it, while its scope lives: E3096.
Only unsafe code can do the following, and they stay the vouching code's promise, never undefined behaviour in safe code: into_raw of an arena value used after the reset (UNS-4), and an Allocator implementation whose own state frees memory still given out, through a lock or otherwise (ALC-2's promise, as changed).
design.verdicts:
**Kept as given.**
* 19: `using` names a manager. It now also stands in a type's own declaration, with the same word.
* 24: the field names the kind and the making line names which one; no value outlives its arena. It is made complete: every keeping place, a result included, names the kind, and the holder's making line names the instance once for the parts its type ties to its manager. It is not extended to links. A weakref field names no kind, because a link takes no memory of its own. This withdraws round 0's extension, which refused a camera following both a heap player and an arena enemy.
* 47 and 107: the instance word where needed, none where the manager can do without it. 107's own condition, 'when the manager can do without it', of which 'a value that grows cannot be made in it this way' is one case, is now applied to every later step that needs the instance: a making for `using A` parts, a verdict-114 move, a link's give-back. This applies 107's stated reason and widens nothing. Its measured case, a million small values with no word, is unchanged.
* 101, fix 1: the maker's id comes from the runtime chunk, never from the value. A thread_shared block from a manager is made handed over, and every count sequence reads the mark before the making thread, so no maker is read for it. J5-05 B would read the id from the value, which contradicts fix 1, and its 13% to 44% cross-thread cost was measured.
* 132: a written declaration means only what it says. A keeping place's type with no `using`, a result's included, is the built-in manager. A struct's field without `using` stays on the built-in manager, and the type must say `using A` to take one.

**Reused, not revisited.**
* 88 and 128: the compiler makes a copy of a function, and a callable parameter holds what its callers pass. A parameter likewise takes its caller's kind, with a copy per kind where the body depends on it.
* 164: a sharedref mut link never goes to another thread. It covers the instance link of a manager whose methods change it, and only owners and ref mut names use that link.
* 165: thread_shared is refused at the making line when something in it is not ThreadShared. It decides J5-05.
* 166: a scoped task makes no shares owner. It is why a read-only view in a task cannot make an owner that would call the instance.
* 114: a handed-over object moves, and it takes its new block from the same instance, through a kept word.
* 3: Mutex, Atomic and channels need no ref mut. It is why a manager changed only through a lock is read, not changed, by its methods. It is also why ALC-2's promise must cover changes made through a lock.
* 86 and EXC-15: what a method changes is inferred. They decide the link's kind.
* 159: a constructor's argument takes no word. [ALC-7] 2 changes where a new argument's memory comes from, not the word.

**One point the lead should put to the owner plainly.** J5-05's draft recommended A (refuse `using` after thread_shared), and phase 3 resolved that the list be 'the property minus thread_shared'. The reason given for that exception, 'the block must come from the built-in manager that every thread may give memory back to', is untrue for a lock-based or one-instance manager. So under principle 6 it cannot stand as an exception. The general rule refuses the Arena case anyway (E7015, by verdict 165) and accepts only what is safe.

options_for_owner.summary: The one rule. Whatever points into, or is served by, a manager's memory lives no longer than the manager, and ends exactly when its memory is given back. A new value takes the manager its line names, or else the built-in one. Where a value may go follows from its hidden link to the manager. A helper takes a list from any manager. A link names no manager. `using` follows every type that says it takes one, the library's and the program's alike.
options_for_owner.code:
[T]
struct SlotMap using A:                          # takes a memory manager, called A in its body
    slots: Array[Option[T]] using A = []

class Enemy:
    hp: int

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None                 # a link names no manager

fn add_name(ref mut names: Array[String], n: StrView):   # a list from any manager
    names.push(owns String(n))

fn load_level(ref mut cam: Camera, ref mut level: Arena):
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level
    cam.target = weakref boss
    names: Array[String] using Arena = Array.new_in(level)
    add_name(ref mut names, "Ogre")
    enemies = SlotMap[Enemy]() using level
    with s = level.scope():
        tmp = ref mut s.alloc_zeroed[u8](256)    # scratch; `names` stays valid
        tmp[0] = 1
    println(names[0])

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)
    cam = Camera()
    load_level(ref mut cam, ref mut level)
    if cam.target exists as e:
        println(e.hp)
    else:
        println("gone")
    cam.target = None                            # the link ends: the boss's block goes back to `level`
    level.reset()
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints Ogre, then gone. Without `cam.target = None`, `level.reset()` is E3021 ("`level.reset()` gives back the boss's block, which `cam.target` still keeps; end the link first: write `cam.target = None` above it"). With the arena made inside `load_level`, `cam.target = weakref boss` is E3063. The same camera may follow a player made with no `using`. `thread_shared Stats() using level` is E7015, and `using System` compiles. String, Deque and a program's own SlotMap take `using` as Array does.

options_for_owner.summary: The same safety rules as A (the bound, the exact ends, where new memory comes from, threads, and links naming no manager), but `using` stays a list: the owner words but not thread_shared (J5-05 A), a class, String, and the standard collections by name. A parameter that may grow or end a value names its kind. A program's own container cannot take `using`.

options_for_owner.summary: The narrow answer, with A's rules for copies and threads. A weakref link may only name an object from the built-in manager (J5-02 B). Opening a scope keeps ending every view into the arena, as today (J5-19 B). Only String joins the list (J5-09 A, J2-02 B), and thread_shared is refused (J5-05 A).

Every `weakref` of an arena-made object is refused ("a `weakref` link needs an object from the built-in manager"), so a camera can never follow a level's enemy, even while the level lives. A tree taken before a scope cannot be used inside it or after it (E3060), so parsers reorder their code. `Deque[int] using Arena` stays E2114.

recommendation.reason: A is the only option that is one rule. The same sentence settles weakref links, views, scopes, copies, task reductions, tokens, C hand-overs, threads, helpers, and which types may take `using`, for the library's types and the program's alike, with no exception by type. It refuses exactly the programs that would read freed or reused memory or race on a manager, all when compiling. It accepts correct programs that B and C refuse, or that round 0 refused: a camera following a heap player and an arena enemy, a renderer reset every frame, a tree kept across scratch scopes, a helper given an arena list, tasks copying arena data, an engine's own SlotMap in a level arena, and a thread_shared value in a manager every thread may use. Nothing runs for it. The one difference while running, Arc-style counting for a thread_shared value in a manager, falls only on that rare case, and it costs what Rust and C++ pay. Ordinary programs are unchanged, and arena programs lose a word. It reuses verdicts 88, 128, 164 and 165 and the inference every method already gets, instead of adding a list.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: what may outlive a std::pmr arena or reach another thread through it. That covers a weak_ptr whose control block is in the arena, a string_view taken before a nested scope, a copy made inside a task, a shared object made in a one-thread arena, and which containers, yours included, can take the arena at all.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `load_level` makes `level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)` | 64 KiB that `level` owns |
| 2 | main | `boss = Enemy(hp=500) using level` | boss's block (header with weak count 1, then `hp` 500) sits inside `level`'s 64 KiB |
| 3 | main | `cam.target = weakref boss` (`cam` belongs to `main`) | weak count 2; `cam` now points into `level`'s memory |
| 4 | main | `load_level` returns: `boss` ends | boss ended, weak count 1; the link keeps the block, still inside `level` |
| 5 | main | then `level` ends | all 64 KiB given back, the boss's block with it |
| 6 | main | `if cam.target exists as e:` in `main` | reads the weak count and header in freed memory: a use after free (C++: `weak_ptr::lock()` on a control block in a released pmr arena) |
owner_short.today: Only a value made in an arena, and what holds one, is tied to the arena. A weakref escapes (step 6 compiles). A scope ends views it never touched. Nothing says where a copy's memory comes from. thread_shared in a one-thread Arena is undecided. Only Array, Map and Set may take `using`.
owner_short.options:
A: one rule. Whatever points into an arena's memory lives no longer than the arena and ends exactly when that memory goes back. A copy comes from the heap unless its line names the arena. Threads follow from the arena (an Arena belongs to one thread). Helpers take lists from any arena with no word. A link names no arena. Any type that says `using A`, yours too, can take one.
B: the same safety, but `using` stays a list: helpers name the arena, thread_shared is refused, and your own containers can never take an arena.
C: a weakref may only name a heap object, scopes keep ending every view, and only String joins the list.
owner_short.recommendation: A: one rule settles every case, all checked when compiling. Nothing runs for it, ordinary code is unchanged, and it refuses only what would read freed memory or race on an arena.

repairs.hole: 1 (safety, high): an arena Enemy registers `weakref this` through a `dyn Listener` method compiled once, into a link place of a fixed kind, and its block is later freed with ember_free. The same gap appears for `owns this` ends and for thread_shared count sequences in code compiled once.
repairs.answer: Closed by facet 5, with no refusal. A weakref place names no kind, and a link's last end gives the block back to the kind the block's type index names ([OBJ-1], [OBJ-3] as changed), so `bus.watchers.push(weakref this)` is the same code for every kind. Each kind has its own type index and interface tables, so a dyn or virtual call on `this` reaches the method compiled for its block's kind, and an `owns this` end runs that kind's deallocate (`boss.retire()` directly, or through dyn). The bound comes from the summary: after `hook(boss, ref mut bus)`, `bus` holds into `level` (LT-1's 'by the code of each kind that may reach it'). Here `bus` ends before `level`, so the program compiles and prints 1, and bus's end gives the block back to the Arena. With `bus` made before `level`, it is E3063 at the call, naming line 10. Every count sequence reads the handed-over mark before the making thread ([RC-4] point 4 as changed), so one sequence serves a thread_shared value from any manager, in code compiled once too, and no chunk header is read for a manager's block.

repairs.hole: 2 (safety, high): nothing says where `copy of`, clone, String `+` or to_string take their memory. If copies are made in the source's arena, two tasks race on its cursor, against the claim that 'a read never touches the manager'.
repairs.answer: Closed by NEW [ALC-7]. A new value takes its memory from the instance its line names, else from the holder's instance for a part its type ties to its manager, else from the built-in manager, as C++ pmr's copy takes the default resource. So `(copy of names).len()` in each task is a copy from the built-in manager: no task calls `level`, and the program compiles and prints 4. `copy of names using level` from two tasks is E7007 (a making in `level` is a change of it), and inside a scope of `level` it is E3096. The claim is now true by rule: no value made from another takes its source's instance unless its line names it.

repairs.hole: 3 (safety, medium): THR-21's private accumulators for a `using` place have no stated instance, so tasks either race on `level` or are refused.
repairs.answer: Closed in [THR-21] as changed. A task's accumulator for a place a manager serves has the place's type, with its memory from the built-in manager ([ALC-7] 3), because a task never calls the instance of a place it reduces into. The combine at the join runs on the parent's thread and grows the place in its instance. The program compiles.

repairs.hole: 4 (safety, medium): ARN-6's 'changing a value in memory the parent gave is not using the parent' lets `names.push` grow from `frame` inside a scope, and the scope's end then frees the grown buffer.
repairs.answer: Closed in [ARN-6] as changed. A change that calls the parent's allocate or reallocate, which is a value's growth or a making in the parent, is allocating from the parent (E3096), with the help to push before or after the `with` block or to make the list from `s`. Ending a parent-made value stays allowed, because an Arena's deallocate does nothing. The program is E3096 at `names.push(owns 5)`.

repairs.answer: Closed. [ALC-5] as changed adds opening a scope to what may change an instance while a value holds into it, because it gives none of that memory back. [ARN-7]'s second clause now points to ALC-5. The program compiles and prints Ogre.

A value keeps its instance word wherever a later step takes memory from the instance or gives memory back to it: its growth, a making for its `using A` parts, a verdict-114 move, and a link's give-back where deallocate does something. It keeps none where no such step remains, so 107's measured cases are unchanged. The Tree keeps one word, `plant` makes its node in `level`, and the program prints true. repairs.answer: Closed by tightening [ALC-2]'s promise, which the `unsafe extend ... implements Allocator` vouches for (principle 11). Memory given out stays valid until deallocate or reallocate gives that block back, the instance ends, or the instance is changed through a name that may change it (ALC-5 refuses that under live values). design.open_risks:
1. `struct SlotMap using A:` (and `enum Expr using A:`, `class Boss(Enemy) using A:`) is a new declaration form, although it reuses the word. The owner may prefer an ordinary type parameter, `[T, A: needs Allocator = Global]`, filled by `using`. That is existing syntax, but it leaves a second, bracket spelling to refuse. This spelling sub-question should be shown beside A.
2. A parameter takes its caller's kind (hole 14). A missing `using` then means the built-in manager on a keeping place and 'the caller's' on a parameter. The owner may see that as one absence with two meanings (checklist 5), although a parameter already means 'the caller's value' for `dyn I` and for regions. The alternative is round 0's rule (owns and ref mut parameters name the kind, or are made generic), which costs a word on every arena helper. Whether a call to a `pub` function compiles may then depend on its body, as verdict 86's inferred changes already do. Under verdict 108's 'a library's promise does not depend on its body', the owner may want `pub` parameters that grow a value to write `using A` generics. Show this beside A.
3. Copies default to the built-in manager (C++ pmr), not to the source's instance (Rust). This is what keeps reads and copies in tasks race-free and lets a copy outlive its arena, but `copy of x` may then differ in kind from `x`. A generic `[T: needs Clone]` function given an arena-kinded T cannot make its copy, which is E2020 at the call. That is an understandable limitation, stated clearly. Show this beside A.
4. A thread_shared value in a manager is made handed over, and it loses biased counting's 25% gain for its own thread's objects. This exact case is not measured: the 1.35x comes from REPORT.md's 'own' pattern, a mechanism measured on runtime blocks. Reading the mark before the making thread is said to use the loads the sequence already makes, and that ordering is not separately measured either.
5. The kind of the instance link is inferred from the manager's method bodies, so a library manager's thread-safety follows its bodies, as EXC-15 already makes every pub method's effects do. The owner may judge this against verdict 108. If so, the alternative is to require that a manager be ThreadShared and change only through a lock or Atomic for its values to be Send.
6. Per-kind type indices: type tests ignore the kind and dyn calls stay one table load, but neither this nor the code size of per-kind function copies has been measured. It is the same mechanism as monomorphisation.
7. Function values' state blocks and AnyError's box take no `using`, because no declaration names a manager for them. A program that wants closure state in an arena writes `owns dyn I using A`. If the owner wants `fn() using A`, that is checklist 12's 'add the syntax', and a further question.
8. C-kept addresses: facet 1 reaches what C keeps only through a holder on Ember's side. P08's token for retained non-callback pointers (J8-12) must be such a holder, or an arena object given to a `retained` parameter is bounded only by FFI-35a. P08 should be answered consistently.
9. Neighbouring groups: P01 (markers from contents) and P05 (an end counts as a call where it may run) must use 'holds into or will call'. P16 decides which spellings are reductions and their start values; this group decides only where an accumulator's memory comes from. P10's J5-07 must keep WK-11's 'any name may make a link', which hole 1's answer relies on.
10. Verdict 114's new block, taken from the same instance, can fail for lack of memory at a hand-over, which is a stop ('out of memory', ALC-4). That is the same as any allocation, but it is a new place where a hand-over may stop.
11. Where the compiler cannot follow a place (an element of a list of cameras reached by position, a static), it decides by what may be put there. Clearing one camera's link then does not let the arena be reset while the list may hold others. This is a conservative, understandable limitation, and the message says to end the links first.

holes.what_goes_wrong: ALC-6 decides a place the compiler follows, here a local, by what it last got, and decides 'a part reached through a link' by what the program may put there. In main, `cam.target` is reached through the local `cam`, which last got `Camera()`, so `cam` holds into nothing. aim's summary keeps the link in 'a part of another parameter', `rig`, whose life ends at its last use, the call. So nothing refuses `level.reset()` (no E3021), and the bound passes (no E3063 for `cam`). The opening then reads the reset memory, and `cam`'s end, after `level` ends, subtracts the weak count in freed memory. The same happens when the camera is retargeted through `for w in CAMS: if w exists as ref mut c: c.target = weakref e`, or when `cam.forget()` is followed by a call that retargets cameras through links. It breaks the misuse claim that every mistake is refused.

Per-point tracking should hold only for places no other name can write. A callee's summary that keeps a value in a part reached through a link should taint every object of that type.

It gives no static kind to four kinds of name: a view opened from a weakref place (which names no manager), a name bound by `is ... as` or `cast` (which read a type's per-kind indices as one type), a name given objects of two kinds on two paths, and the target of a kept `sharedref mut` or `ref` field. Each call then checks them against its arguments' instances, as BRW-21 checks ends, and reports E3096 or E3021 at the call, naming the callee's line.

    x: f32

struct BulletPool:                            # hands out 64 KiB pieces, its own address in each piece's first word
    pieces: Array[usize] = []

# SAFETY: every block lies in a piece that starts at a multiple of PIECE and holds this pool's address in its first word
unsafe extend BulletPool implements FoundByAddress:
    pass

# SAFETY: blocks stay valid, aligned and unaliased until given back or the pool ends
unsafe extend BulletPool implements Allocator:
    pass                                      # allocate, deallocate and reallocate as [ALC-2] declares them, carving blocks from `pieces`

fn main():

    shots: Array[Bullet] using BulletPool = Array.new_in(pool)   # no block yet, and no word

So `shots` holds neither the pool's address nor an address inside one of its pieces. Its first push cannot reach `pool`: masking its null buffer reads the word at address 0, which is undefined behaviour in safe code. A `struct ... using A` value, such as a SlotMap whose parts are still empty, cannot make its parts in such a manager for the same reason. Repair 7 says a value keeps the word 'wherever a later step takes memory from the instance', which the spec_text contradicts for FoundByAddress. Verdict 107 (c) was measured on growing lists, so this is its ordinary case.

For a FoundByAddress manager, at no extra memory: while a value holds no block, its buffer field holds the instance's address, and capacity 0 marks that. The first growth reads it from there. Otherwise the making takes the first block (and the value then holds into the instance, so a reset is refused).

struct Bump:
    buf: Array[u8]
    at: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)              # its only changing state is an Atomic

    fn allocate(layout: Layout) -> *mut u8:

    a: Array[int] using Bump = Array.new_in(bump)
    b: Array[int] using Bump = Array.new_in(bump)
    with scope = thread.scope():

safety.notes:
The rule is sound for the cases it names. I walked its five answers and its 22 other cases, and each does what it says: J5-02's camera, J5-05's Arena refusal, System and lock pool, J5-19's tree under a scope, J2-02's SlotMap, and J5-09's tokens.

Four high holes remain. Each comes from one of four mechanisms:
1. The per-place follower decides a local by what it last got and ignores writes made through other names. A local class object whose part a sharedref mut or weakref link writes therefore escapes E3021 and E3063.
2. Views have no static kind when they come from a weakref place (which names no manager), from is/cast (which read the per-kind indices as one type), from two paths, or from kept view fields. Direct, non-virtual kind-dependent calls on them have no rule, and 'none means built-in' picks the wrong allocator.
3. Copies per kind hide which instance a parameter is in. E3096 and E3021 inside a callee are stated only for known making lines, and the summary carries nothing for the call to check.
4. A FoundByAddress manager keeps no word, so an empty or will-call value has neither a word nor an address. This is what remains of repair 7.

Mediums: the summary cannot tell a result that holds a block from one that only will call (new_in against with_capacity, and clear()); the Layout of a give-back through a base-class owner or a link; a null from allocate outside standard containers; and `using level` after a call that makes its value inside the callee.

Checked and safe:
- Moving, replacing or swapping the instance: the link is a kept view of the instance's place, so BCK-4 and BRW-17 end its holders. A will-call value after mem.replace calls a live instance of its kind at the same place.
- @parallel chunks: PAR-2 (c) refuses them, since the instance is reached through a sharedref mut link.
- Channels, jobs and unscoped threads with a local lock pool: bounded by THR-8's Send-view rule.
- Statics.
- mem.swap of values from two instances: the words move with the values.
- Reductions: accumulators from the built-in manager, combined on the parent's thread.
- No double end: one give-back at the last count.
- RC-4 point 4's mark read first.
- Verdict 114's old and new blocks.
- into_raw: covered by UNS-4.
- A fieldless manager with static mut state: THR-20, E7012.

Wording that does not cause a hole: 'only an owner or a ref mut name makes a value call its instance' and 'readers never use it' are untrue for a link's own end, and for a view opened from a link to a thread_shared target, which holds a count and may end the value, and so give its block back, on a task's thread. No hole follows, because verdict 165's Send check at the making line already covers the block's manager.

For the engineering lens, not reported as holes:
- Two scoped tasks ending Arena values are E7007, and `owns arena_object` to a task is E7015, although Arena's deallocate is empty.
- mem.take(ref mut r.cmds) on an arena-kinded place is E2020, with clear() or new_in as the way out.
- J5-05's `using System` writes a type where an instance goes.
- Verdict 108 applied to pub parameters that take their caller's kind (open risk 2).
