Anywhere in a parameter or result, a raw pointer or an `unsafe extern "C" fn`, and in what C fills, a view-typed field or a handle field (a field states no life), make `safe fn`, an entry asserting the function safe, or `@ffi(safe)` `E5002`, naming the field: "`PixelBuf.data` is a raw pointer, and nothing states how many bytes `clear_pixels` writes through it; declare `@safety("…") unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, and give safe callers a function that builds the `PixelBuf` from a `MutSpan[u8]` in an `unsafe:` block". A function-pointer result or `out` slot of an `@ffi(safe)` typedef states its life as a pointer result does (`from(p)`, `from(static)`; `E5002` without), and the value carries that region, so a function of an unloaded library is never called. One C passes into Ember lives for that call.

[FFI-31b], [FFI-26] (changed): What C passes to an export is typed by the export's own signature, which is its statement: its C prototype is made from it (`--emit-header`), so no words map it.
- The `# SAFETY:` note above `@unsafe(export(…))` vouches for the name and for every fact the signature states about what the host passes, and `ember tcb` lists each: `msg: Option[CStrView]` is NULL or a NUL-terminated string that lives for the call, and `done: extern "C" fn(i32)` is a function safe to call with one `i32`.
- A view parameter is lent for the call. A `Span` or `MutSpan` parameter names its length with `@ffi(param(data, count(n)))`, `n` written at its C ABI position as in a hand declaration ([FFI-10], ODR-074). A safe function-pointer parameter passes [FFI-56]'s list. A raw parameter is what C can send.
- An export whose body relies on more than its types say is an `unsafe` export: `@safety("…")` above `pub unsafe extern "C" fn`. The note vouches that C's calls make its `@safety` true, and Ember's callers make it true in unsafe code ([UNS-13] point 4).
- `char`, a range type, or an enum that is not `@non_exhaustive`, in a parameter, is `E5054`, since C may pass any value of its C type.
- The same holds for every function of an `@export_table`; an `unsafe` one fills an `unsafe extern "C" fn` field.

[FFI-40], [FFI-17a] (changed): A C++ reference is a pointer whose count and nullability C++ fixes: it names one object and is never null. Its other facts are stated as a C pointer's are ([FFI-11]).
- Ember calling C++: a `T&` parameter imports as `ref mut x: T`, its being the only name of its place for the call coming from Ember's own check of the argument, and a `const T&` one as `x: T`, passed by address ([LT-1a]). Neither is kept after the call ([FFI-35a]).
- C++ calling an override or a `std::function` target: C++ does not fix that a reference is the only name of its object (it may pass `*this`, or one object twice). A `T&` argument is `ref mut` alone, compiled with noalias, only when the virtual's entry writes `exclusive` for it. Otherwise it, `this` and the call's other reference arguments of one type may be one place, as two paths through links may be ([BCK-3]), and none is compiled with noalias, as `this` never is ([EXC-15]). What it points into is memory C++ reaches by itself ([UNS-13] point 5).
- A reference result's lifetime is never derived ([FFI-2a]). Its entry writes `-> from(this)`, `from(p)` or `from(static)`; without one it is `E5002`, whose help gives the line read from the declaration or from `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` ([FFI-11f]). A `T&` result is a `ref mut T` view only when the entry writes `exclusive`, and a `ref T` view otherwise.
- A reference result called with no entry, in unsafe code, is `*mut T` or `*T`.
- The same holds for `std::span` results, fixed extent included, and `std::string_view` results.

[FFI-8] static row, [FFI-41], [STA-1] (changed): A foreign global (of a C header, or of a C++ namespace or class) is read safely, as an Ember `static` is, when two things hold:
- its own language fixes that it changes only as a `static` may: never, for an object declared `const` with no `mutable` and no `volatile` part at any depth; only through its atomic operations, for an `_Atomic` one that maps to `Atomic[T]`;
- its type is `ThreadShared`.
Any other foreign global is read and written in `unsafe` (ODR-163), unless its declaration vouches with `@ffi(immutable)` (ODR-082). That is a hand declaration's `static`, or an overlay's `static NAME` entry, written under the class section for a static data member. A vouched global that is read safely must be `ThreadShared` too. The binding reads an imported global through the header's own declaration.

[FFI-42] (changed): A C++ operator or `begin`/`end` implements `Index`, `IndexMut`, `Iterable` or read-through only when its overlay entry asserts it safe and states its result's lifetime (`-> from(this)`, with `exclusive` for `IndexMut` and `get_mut()`). How an entry names an operator is P07's. Without an entry the type implements none of these, and the operator is called only as an `unsafe` method. These interfaces are safe, so their implementation is safe ([UNS-13] point 4): an `operator[]` that does not check its index has no true entry.

[GRM-35] (changed):
- `overlay_item` gains `"static" IDENT NEWLINE`, and so does `overlay_class`; a `static` entry with `@ffi(immutable)` states a fact (`E5067` applies).
- A function-pointer typedef's `type` entry takes `@ffi(safe, param(name, words…), result(words…))`.
- A `callback(…)` word takes `param(name, words…)` for the callback's own parameters.
- A `type` entry takes `@ffi(handle, null=NAME, destroys(f, p=CONST…))` and `retained`; a result takes `immutable` after `from(static)`; a handle slot takes `nullable(NAME)`.
- An overlay's `extend_decl` may be `unsafe extend T implements Send:` or `ThreadShared:` for a type the overlay describes ([TYP-43]).

[FFI-57] (new) **Handles.** `@ffi(handle)` on a `type` entry makes the type a handle: an opaque value with the C typedef's representation (a pointer or an integer). It is passed and returned by value, compared with `==`, and never read through by Ember. Its facts (`handle`, `null=`, `destroys`, `retained`, a vouched marker) are facts of the C type ([FFI-30]). In one build they come from one place: two packages that state them differently for one type, or one that states them and one that uses the type without them, are `E5010`, naming both.
- **Null.** A handle's null value is the all-zero one (`NULL`, `VK_NULL_HANDLE`) unless its entry names another (`@ffi(handle, null=INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE)`). A plain `H` never holds it, which gives `Option[H]` C's layout on every target. A slot whose "none" is another value names it, `nullable(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE)`, and Ember tests it with one compare where the value arrives. A handle C passes with no word (a callback's argument) is `Option[H]`.
- **Making one.** A handle value comes only from a foreign call's result or `out` slot, a constant of the header (which lives for the program), a loan of an owner, or unsafe code. A handle type has no default and is not `Zeroable`, and a cast to or from one is unsafe ([UNS-1]): `7 as g.Buf` outside unsafe code is `E3100`.
- **Slots.** A slot of a handle type is no pointer slot. It takes the words about the life of what it names: `returns_owned(destructor=f)`, `nullable`, `from(p)`, `from(this)`, `from(static)`. A word about memory Ember reads (`borrowed`, a count, `exclusive`, `aliased`) is `E5002` on it: "`device` is a handle (`@ffi(handle)`, line 3), passed by value; remove `borrowed`". A handle parameter with no word gives C the handle for the call.
- **Life.** A safe entry's handle result or `out` slot states its life (`E5002` without), and the stated life decides what the value is, whatever the type: `returns_owned` gives an `owns H`; `from(p)`, `from(this)` or `from(static)` give a loan, a plain `H` that is `Copy` within that region, as `ref T` is. A handle C passes into Ember lives for that call.
- **Owners and loans.** A type with a stated end (`@ffi(handle, destroys(f))`) has owners and loans. An `owns H` is not `Copy`, and it is ended once, by `f`, which in safe code only that end calls. Wherever a value of type `H` is wanted (an argument, a field, an element of a list or a span, a copy), an `owns H` lends a plain `H` bound to its region, and a struct or list holding one is a view of it, as one holding a `Span` is.
- **What `destroys(f)` vouches.** It vouches that `f`'s `@safety` holds at every point an owner may end, so what `f` asks must follow from the owner's own existence (made by the making call, not ended yet, ended once), as for the calls the compiler makes for a `using` value ([ALC-2]). A destructor whose precondition rests on state the end cannot see (the GPU done with a buffer) gives the type no stated end.
- **Kept arguments.** `f`'s other parameters take the making call's arguments of the same name, as a token's do ([FFI-11]), or a constant the entry fixes (`destroys(vkDestroyBuffer, pAllocator=None)`). The owner keeps each one it takes from the making call, one word each. Each one that was a loan (a handle `from(p)`, one an owner lent, a `borrowed` pointer) makes the owner carry its region: `mem.drop(owns dev)` while `buf` lives is `E3060` ("`buf` keeps `dev` for `buf_free` (line 9) and ends at the end of `main`; end `buf` first: write `mem.drop(owns buf)` above line 14").
- A type with no stated end has no owners: its values are plain `Copy` handles whose life is their source's, and unsafe code that ends one vouches for every copy ([UNS-4]).
- `threads(creator)` on a handle type binds it to its thread ([FFI-33b]).

[FFI-30a] (changed): an overlay never changes a type's identity, layout or fields; a type's handle facts and vouched markers are facts of its C declaration, one per build ([FFI-57]).

[FFI-36a] (changed): "…so an `owns T` foreign value stays one word, plus one for each argument its destructor keeps ([FFI-57])".

[FFI-51], [TCB-4] (changed): An import is written `unsafe import c` or `unsafe import cpp`, with a `# SAFETY:` note, exactly when what Ember compiles for it (the C shim, [FFI-29]; the C++ thunks, [FFI-3]) defines a function or variable under a name the whole process shares, which the linker does not merge with identical copies: a C source file, `implementation = [...]`, or a definition in a header that is neither `inline` nor `static`. That is the hazard `@unsafe(export)` vouches for ([FFI-26]): the name may replace one the process defines elsewhere. The importer finds each one in that translation unit, for every target the manifest builds. Without `unsafe` the import is `E3100`, naming each: "`import c "counters.h"` defines `g_calls` (counters.h:4), a name the whole process shares, and the compiler cannot see whether another library defines it too; say that you vouch for it: write `unsafe import c "counters.h"` with a `# SAFETY:` note above it". An import that defines none, on every target, needs no word, and `unsafe` on it is `L3010`. Code that runs with no call (a dynamic initialiser, a static's destructor, a constructor or destructor function) is foreign code like a linked library's: it needs no word, and `ember tcb` lists each one with its line in the external-library section, as it lists each `unsafe import c` and `unsafe import cpp` in the unsafe section.

XVI.4's overlay is rewritten:

```ember,overlay
# SAFETY: matches vulkan.h 1.3 and the Vulkan specification's valid-usage rules
unsafe overlay c "vulkan/vulkan.h":
    @ffi(handle)
    type VkDevice
    @ffi(handle)
    type VkCommandBuffer
    @ffi(handle)
    type VkBuffer
    @ffi(status=VkResult, ok=VK_SUCCESS, error=VkError)
    enum VkResult

    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    fn vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties(pLayerName: nullable borrowed nul_terminated,
                                              pPropertyCount: inout_count(pProperties),
                                              pProperties: nullable count(pPropertyCount)) -> status

    @safety("the chain at `pCreateInfo.pNext` and `pQueueFamilyIndices` are valid for the call")
    unsafe fn vkCreateBuffer(device, pCreateInfo: borrowed one,
                             pAllocator: nullable borrowed one, pBuffer: out one) -> status
    @safety("`commandBuffer` is recording")
    unsafe fn vkCmdSetViewport(commandBuffer, firstViewport, viewportCount,
                               pViewports: borrowed count(viewportCount))
    @safety("`buffer` was made from `device`, and the GPU is done with it")
    unsafe fn vkDestroyBuffer(device, buffer, pAllocator: nullable borrowed one)

    rename VkPhysicalDeviceFeatures2 as PhysicalDeviceFeatures2
    hide vkAllocationFunction
```

`vkEnumerateInstanceExtensionProperties` is safe: its contract covers every state. The others are `unsafe fn` entries, because Vulkan's rules for them rest on state Ember does not track (a create-info's `pNext` chain, a command buffer that is recording, the GPU done with a buffer), and `VkBuffer` states no end for the same reason ([UNS-13] point 1, [FFI-57]). The handles' parameters take no `borrowed`. The safe layer is the GPU module ([GPU-1], [GPU-2], [GPU-4]).

answers.answer: Points 1 to 3: the compiler follows the safe-call list into every field, and into what C writes through a parameter. `PixelBuf.data` is a raw pointer. No contract word can stand on a field ([FFI-30a]), so nothing states how many bytes C may write through it or for how long. `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is therefore E5002, naming the field. The same holds behind a contracted pointer, for an `@ffi(safe)` typedef and for an overlay entry: XVI.4's `vkCreateBuffer`, whose create-info holds `pNext` and `pQueueFamilyIndices`, becomes an `unsafe fn` entry. The list is necessary, not sufficient: an entry is safe only if no call within its contract, in any state, breaks memory safety. The safe interface is an ordinary function that builds the struct from a `MutSpan` it was given. This is phase 2's option A, made general by the walk through every part.
answers.code:
@layout(c)
struct PixelBuf:
    data: *mut u8      # C writes `len` bytes here
    len: usize

# SAFETY: these declarations match pixels.h
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`buf.data` points at `buf.len` writable bytes")
    @ffi(no_callbacks)
    unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

fn clear(ref mut bytes: MutSpan[u8]):
    # SAFETY: the struct describes exactly the bytes of `bytes`
    unsafe:
        clear_pixels(PixelBuf(data=bytes.as_mut_ptr(), len=bytes.len()))

fn main():
    pixels: Array[u8] = [7, 7, 7, 7]
    clear(ref mut pixels)
    println(pixels)
answers.outcome: The original `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` is E5002: "`PixelBuf.data` is a raw pointer, and nothing states how many bytes `clear_pixels` writes through it; declare `@safety("…") unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)` …". This version compiles and prints `[0, 0, 0, 0]`. Safe code can no longer give C an address and a length that disagree. Nothing extra runs: the wrapper builds the same struct and makes the same call.

answers.answer: Point 2: what C passes an export is what C can send, unless a statement narrows it. Point 6 and [FFI-31b]: an export's C prototype is made from its Ember signature (`--emit-header`), so there is no C type for contract words to map from, and the signature itself is the statement. The `# SAFETY:` note above `@unsafe(export(...))` vouches for it as well as for the name, and `ember tcb` lists each fact. `msg: Option[CStrView]` states that the host passes NULL or a NUL-terminated string that lives for the call. `done: extern "C" fn(i32)` states that it passes a function safe to call with one int, which [FFI-56]'s list allows. Point 4: a body that needs more than its types say is an `unsafe` export. A safe `game_log` that took `done: unsafe extern "C" fn(i32)` and called it in `unsafe:` would be wrong, because any Ember caller may pass it any `unsafe fn`; the compiler warns, as it does for a safe export that writes through a raw-pointer parameter. Phase 2's A typed everything as the widest, and the earlier draft asked for contract words that only repeated the types; both are replaced.
answers.code:
from std.ffi import CStrView, c_int

# SAFETY: the host defines no other `game_log`; it passes NULL or a NUL-terminated string that lives for the call, and a `done` safe to call with one int
@unsafe(export("game_log"))
pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: Option[CStrView], done: extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:
    ok: i32 = 0
    if msg exists as m:
        match m.to_str():
            Ok(text):
                println(text)
                ok = 1
            Err(_):
                pass
    done(ok)
    return 0

@layout(c)
struct Counter:
    hits: c_int

# SAFETY: the host defines no other `counter_hit`, and passes back the address `counter_new` gave it
@unsafe(export("counter_hit"))
@safety("`ctx` is an address `counter_new` gave out and nothing has freed")
pub unsafe extern "C" fn counter_hit(ctx: *mut Counter) -> c_int:
    ctx.write(Counter(hits=ctx.read().hits + 1))
    return 0
answers.outcome: Both compile. `ember tcb` lists `game_log`'s two facts and `counter_hit`'s `@safety`, and `--emit-header` writes that `@safety` above `counter_hit`'s prototype. An Ember call `counter_hit(null[*mut Counter]())` outside unsafe is E3100. The same export written as a safe `fn` compiles with a warning naming `ctx`. A NULL `msg` is `None`, prints nothing and still calls `done(0)`; the test is one compare. The original example (`msg: CStrView`) compiles too: its type now states that the host never passes NULL, and the note vouches for that, listed by `ember tcb`.

answers.answer: Points 1, 2 and 5: C++ fixes two facts of a reference, that it names one object and is never null. It does not fix where a returned reference points or how long that lives. So [FFI-2a]'s "a result's lifetime is never derived" reaches C++ references, as [FFI-17a] already says for `std::span`, and [LT-1]'s first-line rules no longer decide a foreign call. The entry writes `from(this)`, `from(p)` or `from(static)`. A `T&` result becomes `ref mut T` only with `exclusive`, as a C pointer result does ([FFI-11]); otherwise it is a read-only `ref T`. A parameter that `from(p)` names is passed as the address of the caller's own place, never of a copy, so `from(v)` over a `const Vec3&` points into the caller's `Vec3`. `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` is the header's claim, not C++'s rule, so it only writes the help's line (verdict 132). This is phase 2's option B with the aliasing half added. It reads verdict 137's "a C function" as the entry, which plays the first line's part.
answers.outcome: `fn root()` or `fn first_child(parent)` with no lifetime word is E5002. Its help gives `-> from(parent) exclusive`, read from the declaration, or from `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` on `parent`, which supplies nothing else. With the words, the program compiles and prints the child's id. Had `level = sc.Scene.new()` come before `println(child.id())`, it would be refused, because `child` points into the old `level`. Without `exclusive` the results are read-only `ref Node` views. A `const Vec3& clamped(const Vec3& v)` entry written `-> from(v)` points into the caller's own `Vec3`, which Ember passes by address. Nothing runs for this rule.

answers.answer: Point 4: `drop` is the `Drop` interface's method, and it runs wherever a `Window` ends: a block's end, a list cleared, a field replaced. None of those lines can vouch. So `unsafe fn drop()` is refused. So is an `unsafe` override or implementation of any safe method, which a safe `virtual` or `dyn` call, an operator, `for`, `copy of` or a map hashing its keys reaches. An `unsafe gen fn` is refused for the same reason, since its body is its generator's `next`. An implementation or override takes its interface's or base's signature, safety included. One of an `unsafe fn` may be safe, or `unsafe` with the declaration's own `@safety`. The C call goes in an `unsafe:` block inside `drop`. Its note rests on what `Window`'s module makes true of its private `handle`, which point 4 allows. This is phase 2's option A.
answers.code:
# SAFETY: these declarations match window.h
unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn create_window() -> *mut u8
    @safety("`w` came from `create_window` and is destroyed once")
    unsafe fn destroy_window(w: *mut u8)

class Window:
    handle: *mut u8

    fn drop():
        # SAFETY: `this.handle` came from `create_window` in this module, and drop runs once
        unsafe:
            destroy_window(this.handle)

fn main():
    w = Window(handle=create_window())
    println("open")
answers.outcome: In the original, `unsafe fn drop():` is refused at its line: "`drop` runs wherever a `Window` ends, where no line can vouch for it, so it cannot be an `unsafe fn`; write `fn drop():` and put line 12 in an `unsafe:` block with a `# SAFETY:` note". This version compiles, prints `open` and destroys the window when `w` ends. The same code runs as before.

answers.answer: Point (a): changing an object declared `const` is undefined behaviour in C (C11 6.7.3p6, with 6.2.7 requiring the definition to match) and in C++ ([dcl.type.cv]), `mutable` members aside. So the header's `const` fixes that the global never changes. A `const` global with no `mutable` and no `volatile` part, whose type is `ThreadShared`, therefore reads as an Ember `static` does, in C and C++ alike. A raw pointer is not `ThreadShared`, so [FFI-41]'s "holds no pointer" is part of the same test. A C++ `mutable` member changes through a read-only name in C++ code, as a `Cell` does in Ember, so `STATS` is read in `unsafe`. A non-`const` global is vouched with `@ffi(immutable)`, and an overlay gains a `static` entry for it, so imported globals get the spelling hand declarations have (ODR-082). The same word after `from(static)` says a result points into memory that never changes (point 5). This is phase 2's option A, with B's overlay line kept for non-`const` globals.
answers.outcome: Both `MAX_PLAYERS` reads compile with no `unsafe`, and so does `cf.VERSION` once the overlay line vouches for it; `ember tcb` lists the assertion. `lp.game.STATS.hits` outside `unsafe:` is E3100, naming `mutable long hits` ("C++ may change it through a `const` method, so it is not a value that never changes"). Each read is one load, as in C.

answers.answer: Point 6: an import needs `unsafe` exactly when what Ember compiles for it (the C shim or the C++ thunks) defines a function or variable under a name the whole process shares, which the linker does not merge with identical copies: a C source file, `implementation = [...]`, or a definition in a header that is neither `inline` nor `static`. That is the hazard `@unsafe(export)` already vouches for: the name may replace another one the process defines. Code that runs with no call (a dynamic initialiser, a static's destructor, a constructor function) is foreign code under the floor, the same as a linked library's, which needs no word today ([FFI-51]). So it gets no word either, and `ember tcb` lists each one with its line. The earlier draft made start-up code need the word. Then the word followed where a library put that code and which standard library the machine had (libstdc++ before GCC 13 defines an initialiser in every file that includes `<iostream>`), and nothing in it was a memory-safety fact a note could vouch for. Phase 2's A (every `import cpp`) has the same fault.
answers.outcome: `config.hpp` and `vec3.hpp` need no word, and `unsafe` on either is L3010. `ember tcb` lists `g_default_path`'s initialiser (config.hpp:1) in the external-library section. `counters.h` without `unsafe` is E3100, naming `g_calls`. A libstdc++ upgrade that adds or removes `<iostream>`'s initialiser changes only the `ember tcb` listing. Nothing changes at run time, and the check rides the importer's existing parse.

answers.answer: Point 6: `ThreadShared` is vouched the way `Send` is: `unsafe extend Logger implements ThreadShared:`, with its note. The compiler walks every part. The parts it cannot read (a raw pointer here) are what the vouching rests on. Every other part must have the marker by inference, or the vouching is E2040 naming it: that is the walk's result, not a list. Scoped tasks may then read `lg`. A `static` or a `thread_shared` value of `Logger` is allowed too: this is how a thread-safe C wrapper gets past verdict 165's refusal at the making line. A foreign type is vouched the same way, in its overlay. This is phase 2's option A.
answers.code:
import std.thread
from std.ffi import c_int

# SAFETY: these declarations match logger.h
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("call it once, at start-up")
    unsafe fn logger_open() -> *mut void
    @safety("`logger` came from logger_open; the C library takes its own lock")
    unsafe fn logger_write(logger: *mut void, event: c_int)

struct Logger:
    raw: *mut void

    fn write(event: c_int):
        # SAFETY: raw came from logger_open in this module, and the C logger locks inside
        unsafe:
            logger_write(this.raw, event)

# SAFETY: the C logger may be handed to any thread
unsafe extend Logger implements Send:
    pass

# SAFETY: every logger_write takes the C logger's own lock, so threads may share one logger
unsafe extend Logger implements ThreadShared:
    pass

fn open_logger() -> Logger:
    # SAFETY: this module calls it once, at start-up
    unsafe:
        return Logger(raw=logger_open())

fn main():
    lg = open_logger()
    events: Array[c_int] = [1, 2, 3]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for e in events:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of e: lg.write(e))
answers.outcome: This compiles, and the three tasks log at once with no Ember lock. `static LOGGER: Logger = open_logger()` is also allowed, and so is `thread_shared` of a `Logger` (E7002 and E7015 no longer apply). Adding `hits: Cell[int]` to `Logger` makes the `ThreadShared` line E2040, naming `Logger.hits`; adding a `sharedref mut` field makes both lines E2040. `ember tcb` lists both vouchings. There is no lock on top of C's own.

answers.answer: The same edit to [TYP-43]: any struct, enum or class of the program's own package may be vouched `Send` or `ThreadShared`, and a foreign type in its overlay. The vouching is about the parts the compiler cannot read, not about the kind of type that holds them. Classes were left out only because ODR-111 (a delegation ruling) gave classes `@sync`, which [THR-1] has since removed (E0104). This is phase 2's option A.
answers.code:
import std.thread

class GpuTexture:                          # wraps a driver handle
    handle: *mut u8
    size: int

# SAFETY: the driver's texture handles may be used from any thread
unsafe extend GpuTexture implements Send:
    pass

fn main():
    tex = GpuTexture(handle=null[*mut u8](), size=0)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tex: tex.size)
    println(h.join())
answers.outcome: This compiles and prints `0`. If `GpuTexture` also held a `shares` or `sharedref mut` field, the vouching would be E2040, naming that field. The class's own header counts are handled by verdict 114's hand-over, as for any class.

This compiles and prints `true`. At the end `refs` ends, then `buf` (`buf_free(dev, buf)`), then `dev` (`dev_close`). `mem.drop(owns dev)` above the `println` is E3060: "`buf` keeps `dev` for `buf_free` (line 9) and ends at the end of `main`; end `buf` first". A copy of `refs[0].buf` used after `mem.drop(owns buf)` is refused, as a view is. `g.BufRef(buf=7 as g.Buf, offset=0)` outside unsafe is E3100. `fn dev_bind(d: borrowed, …)` is E5002 ("`d` is a handle (`@ffi(handle)`, line 3), passed by value; remove `borrowed`"). A `Buf` owner is one word plus the `Dev` it keeps; a loan is the handle alone, in a register as in C.

other_cases.case: A C function pointer arriving from C (a struct field, a typedef, a result, an extern static) [FFI-56]
other_cases.settled: Point 2: its type is `unsafe extern "C" fn(…)`. `@ffi(safe)` on its typedef vouches for it only when every part of every parameter and result passes [FFI-10]'s list. A safe one returned or written into an `out` slot states its life (`-> from(p)`), so a function of an unloaded library is never called, and one C passes in lives for that call.

other_cases.case: The arguments C passes to a callback
other_cases.settled: Point 2: they have the type of what C can send. A `const char*` arrives as `*c_char`, read in `unsafe:`, unless `param(msg, borrowed, nul_terminated)` inside its `callback(…)` word, or on its typedef's `@ffi(safe, …)` entry, states the facts, which makes it `CStrView`. A handle arrives as `Option[H]` and lives for the call. `char` and an exhaustive enum are E5054. A callback is vouched by the code that gives it to C, and an `unsafe fn` reaches C only through an unsafe call.

other_cases.case: Out-parameters
other_cases.settled: An `out` slot is a result, and so is what C writes through an `exclusive` pointer, a `MutSpan` or an `inout_count`. A pointer, handle or function pointer written there states its life (`from(p)`, `from(static)`, `returns_owned`), and E5002 is given without it.

other_cases.case: C struct fields in general
other_cases.settled: Fields take no contract words ([FFI-30a]), so a pointer field Ember reads from a C struct is raw and is used in `unsafe:`. A struct holding one is not a safe-call type (J8-08). In what C fills, a view field or a handle field is refused too, since a field cannot state a life.

other_cases.case: Unions
other_cases.settled: Which field is live is unknown, so fields are read in `unsafe` ([FFI-8], unchanged). A union passed by value is a safe-call type only when every field passes the list. One holding a pointer does not.

other_cases.case: Variadic C calls (E5013)
other_cases.settled: What C reads from `...` is unknown, so the call is made only in `unsafe` ([FFI-8], unchanged), and E5013 still names C's promotion (verdict 123).

other_cases.case: C strings returned
other_cases.settled: A `const char*` result is `CStrView` or `Option[CStrView]` only with `borrowed nul_terminated`, `nullable` if C may return NULL, and a lifetime word ([FFI-15], [FFI-10]); otherwise it is `*c_char`. One valid until the next call (`strerror`, `getenv`, `dlerror`, `SDL_GetError`) is `from(static)` without `immutable`, so its view does not live across another foreign call (point 5). A version string that never changes is `from(static) immutable`.

other_cases.case: Extern statics C writes
other_cases.settled: Such a global is not fixed as unchanging, so it is read and written in `unsafe` (ODR-163). `@ffi(immutable)` vouches for it, on a hand declaration or on an overlay `static` entry. An `_Atomic` global maps to `Atomic[T]` and is used safely through its atomic operations when it is `ThreadShared`. A `const volatile` global is not unchanging, so it is read in `unsafe`.

other_cases.case: C++ `mutable` members and `const_cast`
other_cases.settled: A `mutable` member changes in C++ bodies the compiler cannot read, so it is an opaque part. A type holding one is not `ThreadShared` by inference and a `const` object of it is not unchanging, but a vouching may rest on it. `const_cast` on a `const` object is undefined behaviour in C++, below the floor. On a non-`const` object it is why `const` on a pointee fixes nothing: a safe entry's `const T&` parameter is read-only because the entry vouches for it.

other_cases.case: C++ virtual calls and exceptions
other_cases.settled: C++ calls an Ember override, which takes its base's signature and safety. Its reference parameters are the only names of their objects only with `exclusive` on the virtual's entry; otherwise they and `this` may be one place. An `unsafe` override is vouched by the entry's `@safety`, and refused without one. Ember calling a C++ virtual is vouched by its entry for every C++ override it may reach. `noexcept` is fixed by C++ (a throw calls terminate), so it is derived; `@ffi(noexcept)` is asserted and still caught ([FFI-24], [FFI-24b]).

other_cases.case: `[[clang::lifetimebound]]`
other_cases.settled: It is the header author's claim, which C++ does not enforce, so it is no fact (verdict 132). It writes the help's line for a reference result with no word, and a call with no entry keeps a raw pointer.

other_cases.case: Header-only libraries and static initialisers in any compiled foreign code
other_cases.settled: J8-11's rule covers C and C++ alike: `unsafe import` exactly when what Ember compiles defines a process-wide name the linker does not merge. `implementation = [...]` and C source files always do ([FFI-29b], [FFI-51]). Start-up and exit code needs no word and is listed by `ember tcb` with its line, as a linked library's is.

other_cases.case: Another package's overlays ([FFI-30c])
other_cases.settled: An `unsafe overlay` from a dependency is that package's vouching item. `ember tcb` lists it under that package, and its function entries apply only to the header it was written for ([FFI-55]). A C type's handle facts and vouched markers are one per build: they come from one package's overlay, which other packages depend on, and two that differ are E5010.

other_cases.case: Send, ThreadShared and other markers for every kind of type
other_cases.settled: `Send` and `ThreadShared` can be vouched on a struct, enum or class, on a generic type per its bounds, and on a foreign type in its overlay, but only over opaque parts. `Copy` comes only from `@derive(Copy)`, whose fields are checked. `Sized` is never written.

other_cases.case: An unsafe implementation of a safe interface method reached through `dyn`
other_cases.settled: Point 4: it is refused at the implementation, since a safe `dyn` call cannot vouch. An implementation of an `unsafe fn` interface method may be safe, or `unsafe` with the interface's `@safety`.

other_cases.case: Interfaces whose correctness memory safety relies on (Hash and Eq for maps)
other_cases.settled: Point 4's last bullet: the standard library's `Map`, `Set` and sorting stay memory-safe whatever a safe `Hash`, `Eq` or `Ord` returns; a wrong one gives wrong lookups or a stop. An abstraction that must rely on an implementation's behaviour declares an `unsafe interface`, as `Allocator` is, implemented only by `unsafe extend`.

other_cases.case: Unsafe code at compile time (P17)
other_cases.settled: This is P17's to decide. This rule adds nothing at compile time: a vouched fact is still a vouched fact, and P17's checker sees each access.

other_cases.case: GPU bindings
other_cases.settled: XVI.4's Vulkan overlay has handles with no stated end, and its create functions and commands are `unsafe fn` entries, because their safety rests on state Ember does not track (point 1). The standard library's GPU module ([GPU-1], [GPU-2], [GPU-4]) is the safe layer, vouched in its own unsafe code. A program's binding of a library whose destructors need only the handle and its maker uses `destroys(f)` ([FFI-57]).

other_cases.case: An export written `unsafe fn`, or an `@export_table` function
other_cases.settled: Allowed: `@safety("…")` above `pub unsafe extern "C" fn`, vouched for the host by the note above `@unsafe(export(…))` and written into the generated header as a comment. Ember's calls of it are in unsafe code. In a table it fills an `unsafe extern "C" fn` field.

other_cases.case: An Ember enum as an export or callback parameter
other_cases.settled: C may pass any value of its `@repr`, so it is E5054 (as `char` is) unless the enum is `@non_exhaustive`.

other_cases.case: `std::string_view` and `std::span` results
other_cases.settled: Each needs a lifetime word, the same rule as `T&` results ([FFI-17a] made complete).

other_cases.case: Vouching over a known-false part
other_cases.settled: `unsafe extend Cache implements ThreadShared:` on a struct holding a raw pointer and a `Cell[int]` is E2040, naming the `Cell`. So is a vouching over a `sharedref mut` field (verdict 164), or over an `UnsafeCell[shares Enemy]`.

other_cases.case: A `retained` raw-pointer parameter
other_cases.settled: It has no safe type and the call stays `unsafe` ([FFI-11], unchanged). The spelling J8-12 needs is P07's and P08's.

other_cases.case: A generator over raw memory
other_cases.settled: `unsafe gen fn` is refused (point 4), since its body runs at each `next`, which `for` calls. It takes a `Span` and reads in `unsafe:` blocks inside.

other_cases.case: C++ operators and iterators ([FFI-42])
other_cases.settled: Only an entry that asserts the operator safe and states its result's lifetime makes the class `Index`, `IndexMut` or `Iterable`. Without one the operator is an unsafe method call.

other_cases.case: C++ singletons and C libraries with internal tables
other_cases.settled: `Engine::get()` written `-> from(static)` gives a view of the whole object, which lives for the program. A view into its parts (a name, a span of its table) does not live across another foreign call, which may change them (point 5). The program reads it again after the call, or copies it before.

other_cases.case: Win32 handles
other_cases.settled: `HANDLE` is `@ffi(handle)` with null 0. `GetStdHandle` returns `-> nullable(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE) from(static)`, so -1 arrives as `None`. A `CreateFileW` handle is `returns_owned(destructor=CloseHandle) nullable(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE)`.

design.prior_art:
**C++** has no safety boundary: every `extern "C"` declaration and every header is trusted. It offers aids rather than checks:
- `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` gives warnings only, which is why Ember takes it as help text, not as a fact.
- Clang's `-fbounds-safety` adds `__counted_by(len)` on struct fields, checked at run time in C.
- Changing a `const` object is undefined behaviour except for `mutable` members, which is what J8-07 derives from.
- Vulkan-Hpp's `vk::UniqueBuffer` keeps the device, the allocation callbacks and the dispatcher beside each handle, so RAII over a two-argument destructor costs the words [FFI-57]'s kept arguments cost.
- C's "valid until the next call" results (`strerror`, `getenv`, `localtime`, `dlerror`, `SDL_GetError`) are the case point 5 refuses.

**Rust** trusts whoever writes the declaration:
- Edition 2024's `unsafe extern` blocks with `safe fn` and `safe static` (RFC 3484) take the declarer's word. A `safe fn` may even take raw pointers, which Ember refuses, and a `#[repr(C)]` struct holding raw pointers passes freely.
- `unsafe impl Send` and `unsafe impl Sync` are accepted for any type, a `Cell`-holding one included: nothing refuses a vouching the compiler knows is false. The orphan rule keeps one implementation per type, which [TYP-43]'s E2041 keeps for foreign types.
- Soundness is judged at the module: a safe function must be sound for every safe caller, and unsafe code may rely on its module's private fields, which is point 4. Clippy's `not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref` (deny by default) flags a public safe function that dereferences a raw-pointer argument; Ember's warning is the same check.
- `pub unsafe extern "C" fn` is how Rust exports a function whose soundness rests on its C caller.
- `Drop::drop` is safe, and an impl may not add `unsafe` to a safe trait method, which is J5-16's rule.
- I/O safety (RFC 3128) has `OwnedFd` and `BorrowedFd<'a>`, `OwnedHandle` and `BorrowedHandle<'a>`: an owner, and a loan bound to a lifetime, which is [FFI-57]'s model. `OwnedFd` excludes -1, so `Option<OwnedFd>` keeps C's layout. `HandleOrInvalid` and `HandleOrNull` exist because Win32 reports failure with either value, which `nullable(INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE)` answers.
- Unsafe traits such as `GlobalAlloc` and `TrustedLen` cover cases where the standard library relies on an implementation, and `HashMap` stays memory-safe under any `Hash` or `Eq`.
- Cargo's `links` key lets one package link a given native library, so a C library's types have one binding; [FFI-57]'s one place per build asks the same.

**Swift** imports C pointers as `UnsafePointer`, unsafe by name. Swift 6.2's opt-in strict memory safety (SE-0458) flags such uses, and Swift can read `__counted_by` and `__lifetimebound` to generate safe `Span` overloads.

**Zig** translates C pointers to `[*c]T`, which may be null and of any length: point 2's "type of what C can send", with no safe layer above it.

**C#**: `SafeHandle` is an owned OS handle released once, counted against early release at run time. Ember checks the same when compiling.

**Go** checks cgo's pointer rules partly at run time (`cgocheck`), and C strings cross by copy (`C.GoString`).

**Ada and SPARK**: an imported subprogram's contracts are assumed, not proven.

**Where each falls short**: C++ and Zig are not safe. Rust's and Swift's safe layers rest on words that nothing checks against what the compiler knows. C# and Go pay at run time. Ember keeps Rust's vouching model (an `unsafe` item, a note, the trusted computing base) and its module soundness boundary, adds Zig's widest type by default and Rust's owned and borrowed handles, refuses a vouching the compiler can see is false, and runs nothing.
design.cost:
Run time, per operation, against C:
- **J8-08** (structs holding pointers): zero. The wrapper builds the same struct and makes one call, as C does.
- **J8-09** (export arguments): zero for the types. `Option[CStrView]` costs one compare per call for its NULL test, which a robust C function pays too.
- **J8-06** (C++ reference results): zero. A view is the same pointer, and a `const T&` parameter is passed as an address, as C++ passes it.
- **J5-16** (`drop`): zero. The `unsafe:` block inside `drop` compiles to the same call.
- **J8-07** (foreign globals): one load, as C; an `_Atomic` global one atomic load, as C.
- **J8-11** (imports): zero. What runs before `main` is unchanged; the rule only says who vouches for what.
- **J7-06** (vouching `ThreadShared`): zero, and it removes a cost. Without it, the only route is an Ember `Mutex` around a C logger that locks itself: a lock and an unlock on every call, each an atomic operation even when uncontended, plus the `Mutex`'s word.
- **J2-12** (vouching a class): zero.
- **J8-14** (handles): a handle travels in a register, as in C, and a loan is the handle itself. An `owns H` is one word, plus one for each argument its destructor keeps: two words for a buffer freed with its device, where a C program keeps one device for all its buffers and Vulkan-Hpp's `UniqueBuffer` keeps three. A constant argument (`pAllocator=None`) costs nothing. A binding that wants C's layout states no end and keeps the device once, in a struct of its own. `nullable(X)` costs one compare where the value arrives.
- **Point 4** (who vouches): zero.
- **Point 5** (foreign memory across a foreign call): zero at run time. Where a view is refused, the program reads the value again after the call (one call) or copies it before, which is what correct C does with a "valid until the next call" result.
- **Inbound C++ references**: an override's reference parameters without `exclusive` are compiled without `restrict`, as `this` always is and as C++ compiles the same function.

Memory is zero everywhere, except the arguments an `owns H` keeps for its destructor.

Compile time:
- The safe-call walk runs once per type, as `Send` is inferred.
- The importer's scan for process-wide definitions and start-up code rides the libclang parse it already makes.
- Point 5 checks, for each view of foreign memory, the foreign calls in its life, which the summaries already record ([BCK-8]).
- The vouching check reads the markers the compiler already infers.

readability.ordinary_before:
import std.thread
from std.ffi import c_int
from std.sync import Mutex
import engine.log as log          # the binding: struct Logger wraps a C logger that locks itself

fn log_one(lg: Mutex[log.Logger], e: c_int):
    with g = lg.lock():
        g.write(e)

fn main():
    lg = Mutex(log.open())
    events: Array[c_int] = [1, 2, 3]
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for e in events:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of e: log_one(lg, e))

design.compiler_does:
The compiler:
- Walks every part of each foreign parameter and result at any depth, and what C writes through a parameter as a result. It refuses a safe call whose value holds a raw pointer or an `unsafe extern "C" fn`, or, in what C fills, a view or handle field, naming the field. The same walk serves `safe fn`, overlay entries and `@ffi(safe)`.
- Types every value arriving from foreign code by the facts stated for its slot, whichever route it takes. It types an export's parameters by its written signature, which `ember tcb` lists as the export note's facts, and refuses `char`, range types and exhaustive enums in what C sends (E5054).
- Warns on a `pub` function, export or override that is not `unsafe fn` and reads or writes through a raw-pointer parameter, or calls an `unsafe` callable parameter, in its unsafe code.
- Checks every C++ entry that returns a reference, span or string_view for its lifetime word, giving the line from the declaration or from `[[clang::lifetimebound]]`. It makes `T&` a `ref mut` view only with `exclusive`, and passes a parameter `from(p)` names as the caller's own address.
- Checks an override C++ may call with its reference parameters and `this` as possibly one place unless `exclusive` is stated, and compiles it without `restrict` on them.
- Ends, at a foreign call, each view that reads foreign memory foreign code reaches by itself, or points into a part of it that may end, unless that memory is `const` or stated `immutable`, naming the call.
- Derives safe reads of foreign globals from `const` or `_Atomic`, with no `mutable` or `volatile` part at any depth and a `ThreadShared` type. It accepts `@ffi(immutable)` on hand and overlay `static` entries.
- Scans each import's translation unit, for every target the manifest builds, for definitions of process-wide names the linker does not merge. It asks for `unsafe import` naming each, gives L3010 when there is none, and lists start-up and exit code in `ember tcb`.
- Judges `unsafe extend T implements Send|ThreadShared:` by its walk: accepted over opaque parts; E2040 naming any other part that lacks the marker, or a non-`Send` type inside an opaque part; a type parameter there held to its bound, or to the marker.
- Refuses `unsafe` on `drop`, on `gen fn`, and on overrides and implementations of safe methods. It checks implementation and override signatures, safety included, gives an `unsafe` override its base's `@safety`, and refuses an `unsafe` override of a C++ virtual whose entry states no `@safety`.
- Gives handle types their C representation and by-value passing, a niche at their null value, owners and region-bound loans by the stated life, kept destructor arguments with their regions, no default, no `Zeroable`, and unsafe casts. It refuses pointer words on handle slots, and differing handle facts for one C type in a build (E5010).
- Makes a C++ class implement `Index`, `IndexMut`, `Iterable` or read-through only from a safe entry with a lifetime word.
- Lists every new statement in `ember tcb` under its section.
design.verdicts:
The rule keeps these verdicts:
- **31** (a forgotten mark refuses, never crashes): kept and generalised. A silent declaration gives the widest type, a view that ends at the next foreign call, or E5002.
- **60** (anything that can break safety only inside `unsafe`): kept. It is the rule's root.
- **118 and 119** (an `unsafe fn` is unsafe as a whole; everything inside unsafe code is unsafe): kept. Point 4 follows from them: an `unsafe fn`'s obligation goes to callers who vouch, so a method no caller can vouch for is safe. A `gen fn` written in unsafe code would be an `unsafe gen fn`, so it is written in a `safe:` block. An `unsafe` export, callback or override is an `unsafe fn` like any other, and Ember's calls of it are in unsafe code.
- **120, 125, 130, 133, 136** (the spellings for unsafe C and C++ declarations): kept unchanged. Every example uses `@safety` above `unsafe fn`, `safe fn` or `unsafe fn` and never a plain `fn`, and C++ members vouched by entries. An `unsafe` implementation takes its method's `@safety` instead of repeating it, which is principle 3 (a marking said once), not a change to 120.
- **126** (lambdas carry `@safety`): kept.
- **132** (an entry means only what it writes): kept and carried to three more places. A C++ reference result's lifetime is one of the entry's words (J8-06). `[[clang::lifetimebound]]` in the header supplies no fact the entry does not write, so [FFI-11f] changes. An export's string facts are its written types.
- **164** (`sharedref mut` never goes to another thread): carried into [TYP-43]: no vouching covers such a link, by the walk rather than by a list.
- **165** (`thread_shared` refused when not `ThreadShared`): kept. Vouching `ThreadShared` (J7-06) is how a thread-safe C wrapper passes it legitimately.

One verdict is read narrowly:
- **137**: kept for Ember code. Its parenthetical says LT-1's first-line rules decide a call to "a C function". This design changes [LT-1] so that a foreign function's result points where its entry's word says. Nothing checks a C++ body, so rules 1 to 3 would supply an unwritten fact there, and [FFI-2a] already says so for C pointer results ("never derived"). The evidence: under the literal reading, J8-06's `first_child(parent)` is taken to point into the scene, and safe code reads a freed node. The lead should put this to the owner plainly, with that program.

Rulings that are not verdicts:
- **ODR-111** (a delegation ruling, not the owner's): its `Send|Sync` is restored as `Send` and `ThreadShared`. Its exclusion of classes rested on `@sync`, which has since been removed (E0104).
- **ODR-163** (the owner's ruling): kept. A foreign static read only in `unsafe` need not be `ThreadShared`.
- **ODR-082**: kept. Its `@ffi(immutable)` gains the overlay `static` entry and, as `immutable`, the place after `from(static)`.
- **ODR-024**: [BRW-8]'s copy of a small `Copy` parameter is never made for a parameter a foreign entry's `from(p)` names, as it is already never made for the object of a view-returning method.
- **ODR-074**: an export's `Span` parameter names its length witness as a hand declaration does.
- **ODR-075** (`ref_to_ptr`): untouched; P07 decides its spelling.

Phase 2's recommendations this design changes (none is an owner verdict):
- **J8-09**: phase 2 recommended A (the widest types, a function pointer always unsafe). This design takes its B, made precise: the export note's reach is stated, `ember tcb` lists each fact, an export whose body relies on more is `unsafe` with `@safety`, and the compiler warns where a safe one visibly rests on its callers. The reason: the C prototype is made from the export's signature, so its types are the statement. Under A, a safe export that calls its `unsafe extern "C" fn` argument lets an Ember caller break an `unsafe fn`'s `@safety` from safe code.
- **J8-11**: phase 2 recommended A (every `import cpp` is `unsafe`). This design takes neither A nor B: `unsafe import` marks process-wide names, and start-up code is listed like a linked library's.
- **J8-14**: from always `Copy` to owners and region-bound loans by the stated life, because copies let safe code destroy twice.
- **J8-06**: adds `exclusive` and the by-address rule.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule: a fact counts only if C or C++ fixes it, or an `unsafe` item states it. Every part and every route is followed, foreign memory C reaches by itself may change at any foreign call, a safe function is sound for every caller, and one spelling per fact covers every item and type.
options_for_owner.code:
class Window:
    handle: *mut u8
    fn drop():
        # SAFETY: `handle` came from create_window in this module, and drop runs once
        unsafe:
            destroy_window(this.handle)

# SAFETY: the C logger locks inside, so threads may share one
unsafe extend Logger implements ThreadShared:
    pass

# SAFETY: these declarations match pixels.h
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`buf.data` points at `buf.len` writable bytes")
    unsafe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

# SAFETY: no other `game_log`; the host passes NULL or a NUL-terminated string, and a `done` taking one int
@unsafe(export("game_log"))
pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: Option[CStrView], done: extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:
options_for_owner.outcome: This compiles, with nothing extra at run time beyond the NULL compare and one word per argument a handle's destructor keeps. Each of these is refused at its line with the fix: `unsafe fn drop`, `safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)`, a C++ `fn root()` entry with no `from`, `device: borrowed` on a handle, a buffer that outlives its device, a vouching over a `Cell`, and a view of `SDL_GetError()` used after another SDL call. The tasks share the logger with no Ember lock.

options_for_owner.summary: Phase 2's drafts, item by item. Each item is answered on its own: J8-09 takes `Option[CStrView]` and an `unsafe extern "C" fn` called inside a safe export, every `import cpp` is `unsafe` while C headers never are, handles are always `Copy`, and a C++ `T&` result is `ref mut` with only `from`.
options_for_owner.code:
pub extern "C" fn game_log(msg: Option[CStrView], done: unsafe extern "C" fn(i32)) -> i32:
    # SAFETY: the host's `done` takes one int
    unsafe:
        done(0)

# SAFETY: vec3.hpp has only inline maths
unsafe import cpp "vec3.hpp" with (project="engine") as v3

b2 = buffer                                  # VkBuffer is always Copy
vk.vkDestroyBuffer(device, buffer, None)     # a safe entry
vk.vkDestroyBuffer(device, b2, None)         # compiles
options_for_owner.outcome: It compiles what A compiles, plus unsafe programs. An Ember caller passes `game_log` an `unsafe fn` as `done`, and that function's `@safety` is broken from safe code. Copies of a handle destroy one buffer twice. A `T&` result is a `ref mut` view that C++ may reach by another name. Every `import cpp` says `unsafe`, `vec3.hpp`'s included, for nothing.

options_for_owner.summary: Rust's model: the declarer's word covers everything. `safe fn` covers struct fields, a C++ entry's lifetime defaults into `this`, and `unsafe extend` may vouch any marker for any type. `drop` stays safe.
options_for_owner.code:
# SAFETY: these declarations match pixels.h
unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn clear_pixels(buf: PixelBuf)

unsafe overlay cpp "scene.hpp":
    class Scene:
        fn first_child(parent)                 # taken to point into the scene

# SAFETY: trust me
unsafe extend Cache implements ThreadShared:   # Cache holds a Cell[int]
    pass
options_for_owner.outcome: Everything compiles. J8-08's example writes 4,095 bytes past `x` from safe code. `first_child` reads a freed node. Two threads race on the `Cell`. Each of these is listed in `ember tcb`, but none is refused.

options_for_owner.summary: Everything foreign is unsafe. No `safe fn`, no safe overlay entries, no safe foreign globals: every C or C++ call and read is in `unsafe:`, and the safe interface is always an Ember wrapper (Rust's bindgen and ash style).
options_for_owner.outcome: It is sound, with nothing to vouch per fact. But every binding, down to Part XVI's opening `abs` and `cos`, needs a hand-written wrapper. This undoes the design of [FFI-2] (overlays make calls safe) and verdicts 125 and 130, and it does not settle J5-16, J7-06 or J2-12, which are about Ember code.

recommendation.reason: A is the rule Ember already states for C pointers ([FFI-2a]'s "never derived", [FFI-56]'s unsafe function pointers, E5054's "C may pass any value"), carried to every route, every type and every kind of item. It closes the nine members' holes, and the twenty-six the breakers found, with refusals at the line. It costs nothing at run time beyond a NULL compare and the words a handle's destructor keeps, which C++'s RAII pays too. B leaves holes open: an export can break an `unsafe fn`'s promise from safe code, and handles are destroyed twice through copies. C corrupts memory from safe code whenever a word is wrong. D gives up the safe bindings the language promises. Under A, ordinary programs write nothing new, and a binding that shares a thread-safe C object makes its callers shorter.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: C++ trusts every `extern "C"` declaration and every header. Ember lets safe code trust a C or C++ fact only if C or C++'s own rules fix it (a `const` object, a reference that is never null) or someone wrote it under `unsafe`. Today nine places let an unwritten fact through.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `x: u8 = 7` | `x` is 7: one byte on the stack |
| 2 | main | `buf = PixelBuf(data=ref_to_ptr(ref mut x), len=4096)`, all safe code | `buf.data` is the address of `x`; `buf.len` is 4096 |
| 3 | main | `clear_pixels(buf)`: a `safe fn`, so no `unsafe:` anywhere | C writes 4,096 zero bytes, starting at `x` |
| 4 | main | `println(x)` | `x` is 0, and the 4,095 bytes after it (other locals, the return address) are overwritten |
owner_short.today: Each construct has its own list of what it trusts. So a raw pointer inside a struct, the arguments C passes to an export, a C++ reference result, an `unsafe fn drop`, a C++ `const` global with a `mutable` member, a C string that changes at the next call, and a Vulkan handle copied after its buffer is destroyed all reach safe code with nobody vouching for them.
owner_short.options:
A: one rule. A fact counts only if C or C++ fixes it, or an `unsafe` item states it. The holes are refused at their line, at no run-time cost beyond a NULL compare and a word per argument a handle's destructor keeps.
B: the nine drafts, item by item. They let an export break an `unsafe fn`'s promise from safe code, let copied Vulkan handles be destroyed twice, and mark every `import cpp` `unsafe` for nothing.
C: Rust's model, where the declarer's word covers everything. More compiles, and memory is corrupted from safe code whenever a word is wrong.
D: everything foreign is unsafe and safe only through wrappers. Sound, but every binding needs a wrapper.
owner_short.recommendation: A: it is the rule Ember already applies to C pointers, carried to every route, type and item. Ordinary programs write nothing new, and a binding that shares a thread-safe C object gets shorter.

repairs.hole: 1. Exports, callbacks and C++-called overrides could not be `unsafe fn`, so a raw-pointer export had no true note and any safe Ember line could call it with any pointer (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: Point 4 now says who vouches. A safe function is sound for every call code outside its module can make, so one whose soundness rests on its callers is an `unsafe fn` with `@safety`, whoever calls it. Only callers that call a safe interface or base method (an end, `dyn`, an operator, `for`, `with`, `copy of`, a collection, a generator's `next`) force safety. Foreign callers are vouched where the function is handed over: the note above `@unsafe(export(…))` vouches for an `unsafe` export's `@safety`; an `unsafe` callback reaches C only as an `unsafe extern "C" fn` through an unsafe call, whose block vouches; an override C++ calls is vouched by its virtual's entry. An Ember call of any of them is in unsafe code. `counter_hit` becomes `@safety("…") pub unsafe extern "C" fn`. The compiler warns on a `pub` function or export that writes through a raw-pointer parameter, or calls an `unsafe` callable parameter, without being `unsafe` (Clippy's `not_unsafe_ptr_arg_deref`). J8-09's `done` is now a safe `extern "C" fn(i32)`, so no Ember `unsafe fn` can be passed to it.

repairs.hole: 2. An inbound C++ `T&` became an exclusive `ref mut`, though C++ may pass `*this` or one object twice (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: [FFI-40] splits the routes. Outbound, a `T&` is `ref mut` because Ember's own argument check makes it alone. Inbound (C++ calling an override or a `std::function` target), it is alone and compiled with noalias only when the virtual's entry writes `exclusive`. Otherwise it, `this` and the other reference arguments of one type may be one place, as two paths through links may be ([BCK-3]), and none gets noalias, as `this` never does ([EXC-15]). What it points into is memory C++ reaches by itself (point 5). The `on_touch` loop is refused at `push_back`, which may change the vector the loop reads.

repairs.hole: 3. `from(v)` over a `const T&` of a `Copy` type let the thunk return the address of its own copy (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: [LT-1a] and [BRW-8]: a parameter that a foreign entry's `from(p)` names is one the declaration passes by address, and Ember passes the address of the argument's own place, never of a copy, since the foreign declaration fixes the ABI ([FFI-9]). `clamped(a)` then points into `a`. `from(p)` naming a by-value parameter is E2031, as for an Ember function. The same holds for a C `borrowed one` parameter of a `Copy` type.

repairs.hole: 4. Nothing said what a view of foreign memory may assume across a foreign call (the `Registry` singleton and `reload_names`) (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: Point 5: foreign code changes by itself only what it reaches by itself: what a `from(static)` result or a foreign global points into, objects it keeps, objects of a `retained` type, C++-held Ember objects, and what it passes in. A foreign call, or an Ember call whose summary makes one, may change, end or move any of it. Across such a call a view that reads it does not live (E3021), nor does a view into a part that may end (E3060), as a view through a link does not live across a call that may change its type ([BCK-7]). Memory that is `const` in C or C++, or stated `immutable` (after `from(static)`, or `@ffi(immutable)` on a global), is excepted. A view of a whole opaque object relies only on its life, so `reg` lives, and `n` is refused after `reload_names()`, naming that call. [UNS-13](a) no longer counts `const` on a pointee as fixed by C: the read-only fact of a `const T*` parameter is part of what asserting the call safe vouches. P10 should state the same promise for its own routes.

repairs.hole: 5. An owner's end could call a destructor whose `@safety` the end cannot meet (`vkDestroyBuffer` while the GPU still reads) (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: [FFI-57]: `destroys(f)` vouches that `f`'s `@safety` holds at every point an owner may end, so what it asks must follow from the owner's own existence (made by the making call, not ended, ended once), as for the calls the compiler makes for a `using` value ([ALC-2]). A destructor whose precondition rests on state the end cannot see gives the type no stated end. XVI.4's `VkBuffer` is now a plain `@ffi(handle)`, and `vkDestroyBuffer` an `unsafe fn` called after the fence. Point 1 adds that asserting a function safe covers every state the program can be in, so the safe-call list is necessary, not sufficient.

repairs.hole: 6. An owner kept its destructor's other arguments (the device) past the loan that gave them, so a device could end before its buffers (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: [FFI-57]: an owner keeps each argument its destructor takes from the making call, matched by name as [FFI-11] already matches a token's, unless the entry fixes it as a constant (`destroys(vkDestroyBuffer, pAllocator=None)`). Each kept argument that was a loan makes the owner carry its region, so `mem.drop(owns dev)` while `buf` lives is E3060 ("`buf` keeps `dev` for `buf_free`"). [FFI-36a]'s "one word" becomes one word plus one per kept argument, and the cost line says so.

repairs.hole: 7. Nothing said how a handle value comes to exist (`7 as g.Buf`, defaults, `zeroed`), or how an owner lends one into a field (safety lens, high).
repairs.answer: [FFI-57]: a handle comes only from a foreign result or `out` slot, a header constant, a loan of an owner, or unsafe code. A handle type has no default and is not `Zeroable`, and a cast to or from one is unsafe ([UNS-1]). Wherever an `H` is wanted (an argument, a field, a list, a span, a copy), an `owns H` lends a plain `H` bound to its region, and a struct or list holding one is a view of it, as one holding a `Span` is. `r` used after `mem.drop(owns b)` is E3060. [UNS-4] adds that every handle safe code holds names a live object, so unsafe code that ends a handle with no stated end vouches for every copy.

repairs.hole: 8. Two [FFI-57] bullets disagreed on a `from(p)` result of a type with a stated end, and two overlays could give one C type different handle facts (safety lens, medium).
repairs.answer: The stated life decides: `returns_owned` gives an owner, and `from(p)`, `from(this)` or `from(static)` give a loan in that region, whatever the type. `ctx_staging` returns a loan of `ctx`, so nothing frees it twice. Handle facts (`handle`, `null=`, `destroys`, `retained`, a vouched marker) are facts of the C type ([FFI-30]). In a build they come from one place, and two packages that state them differently, or one with them and one without, are E5010 naming both. [FFI-30a] says so.

repairs.hole: 9. What C writes through a parameter (`exclusive`, a `MutSpan`, `inout_count`) was walked as outbound, so C could leave a view in a field that safe code then reads (safety lens, medium).
repairs.answer: Point 2 and [FFI-10]: what foreign code writes through a parameter is a result, typed and walked as one. A view field, or a handle field (a field states no life), in it is E5002, naming the field (`Label.text`). A `MutSpan` or `inout_count` that C fills takes a lifetime word, as an `out` slot does.

repairs.hole: 10. E2040 was a closed list that left out `sharedref mut`, `JobScope`, `ref T` of a non-`ThreadShared` `T`, `dyn I` without `needs Send`, and closures holding these (safety lens, medium).
repairs.answer: [TYP-43] states E2040 as the walk's result.
