design.rule:
Ending a value runs its `drop` at one point of one thread. At that point the end counts as a call of the `drop` for every rule: locks held, walks, views and contracts.

(1) Where the program's text fixes the point (the end of a block or a statement, a replacement, a `clear()`, the line that ends the last owner, on whichever thread it runs), the call is checked there. A clash is refused, with the line to write.

(2) A `thread_shared` value whose drop may wait (`Block`: a lock, a bounded `send`, a receive, a `join`, a sleep) or may call C (`FFI`) always ends at such a point. It is handed over where it is made, so the thread that ends its last owner runs the drop at that line, as C++ and Rust do. What such a drop does depends on what other threads, or C, hold when it runs, and only a line the program wrote shows that.

(3) Any other `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on another thread, after it travelled inside another object, goes back to its making thread. That thread ends it only at a clear point: one where a call of its drop, written there, would be accepted by every rule. Such a drop never waits and never calls C, so a placed end waits for nothing. Only a contract, a walk or a view can keep it out. Check points sit where a running thread reaches one after a bounded number of loop rounds, outside every such clash.

(4) A thread at rest has ended, has gone back to C, is waiting for work, or is asleep in a blocking call or in a foreign call that may block. While it rests, the thread that ends the last owner of one of its values ends that value at once, at its own line. That thread merges the counts first, and runs the drop only afterwards, with nothing of the queue held.

Nothing is refused for an end the compiler places. The programmer writes nothing.
design.spec_text:
Adds `[RC-8]`, `[RC-4]` point 6 and `[JOB-6]`. Changes `[RC-4]` points 1 to 5, `[OBJ-1]` (the home field), `[WK-3]`, `[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-1]`, `[THR-20]`, `[THR-16]`, `[FFI-22]`, `[HR-2a]`, `[HR-3b]`, `[RT-8]`, and two rows of `[COST-3]`.

* `[RC-8]` *(new)* **Where an end runs.** Ending a value runs its `drop`, and the drops of what it owns (`[DRP-8]`), at one point of one thread. At that point the end counts as a call of those drops for every rule that checks a call: a lock this thread holds (`[THR-19]`), a walk (`[BRW-18]`), a view (`[BRW-17]`, `[RC-5]`), the contracts of the functions running (§X.2), and every other rule.
  1. **A point the source fixes.** These are: the end of a block, for its locals (`[DRP-2]`); the end of a statement, for its temporaries (`[DRP-3]`); a value replaced; a collection cleared; `mem.drop`; and the line that ends a value's last owner, on whichever thread it runs (`[THR-20]`). Each end is checked as a call where the source puts it. A clash is refused there, with the line to write (`E7018`, `E3020`, `E3060`, or the contract's code). Example: a `Conn` whose `drop` takes `pool.lock` is made inside `with pool.lock:`. It ends where the block ends, before the lock is let go, so that point is `E7018`. The message says to make the `Conn` above the `with` line, so that it ends after the lock is let go.
  2. **A drop that may wait or call C runs where the source ends its value.** This covers a `thread_shared` value whose drops may wait (`Block`: a lock, a bounded channel's `send`, a receive, a `join`, a sleep, the first access to a static that another thread is initialising) or may call C (`FFI`; freeing memory is the runtime's work, `[RT-1]`, not `FFI`). Such a value is handed over where it is made (`[RC-4]` point 4): every thread counts its owners in the away count from the start. So the thread that ends its last owner ends it at that line, as C++'s `shared_ptr` and Rust's `Arc` do, and point 1 checks the end there. What such a drop does depends on what other threads, or C, hold at the moment it runs, and only a line the program wrote shows that.
  3. **A point the compiler or the runtime picks.** This covers every other `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on a thread that did not make it, and that was not handed over. Such a value is queued to its making thread (`[RC-4]`), which ends it only at a **clear point**: one where a call of its drops, written there, would be accepted by every rule of the first paragraph.
     * The drops that decide this are those of every type whose values may be queued to the thread; the compiler may use every such type in the program.
     * These drops never wait and never call C. So such an end waits for nothing and adds no order between locks. What keeps it out of a point is a contract it would break (an allocation inside `@noalloc`), or a walk or a view it would change or end.
     * No line is refused for such an end, and it is part of no function's effects or summary (`[EFF-1]`).
     * Which values a point ends depends on other threads. That alone is not `Nondet` (`[DET-6]`); whether what the drops change is `Nondet`, `[DET-2]` decides as for any code.
  4. **When.** A queued value is ended at the first clear point its making thread reaches after the value becomes due (`[RC-4]` point 3). While the making thread rests, the thread that ends the value's last owner ends it at once (`[RC-4]` point 6). A thread that runs for ever where no point is clear (an endless loop inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) keeps its queued values until it leaves that code.
  5. **A reload's reclaim.** The fields a reload removes are ended where `[HR-2a]` says, each as a call at that point.

* `[RC-4]` *(changed)*
  1. ... "Only the making thread reads both, or, while that thread rests, the one thread taking over that value (point 6)."
  2. ... "marking it queued in the same atomic step as its subtract. Only the making thread then ends it, at a clear point (`[RC-8]`), or, while the making thread rests, the thread whose subtract queued it (point 6). The making thread empties its queue at each of its check points: ..." (the rest unchanged).
  3. **Check points.** The compiler places them, only at clear points (`[RC-8]` point 3), so that a running thread never runs a loop for an unbounded number of rounds without reaching one:
     * at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts;
     * once every N rounds of a loop whose trip count is known when it starts. N is fixed by the compiler, so the rounds between two tests stay one loop that the C compiler can vectorise;
     * before every call that may block the thread, a foreign call that may block (`[EFF-3]`) included;
     * where a region that kept points out ends, if it kept one out. Such a region is a call of a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or a walk or a view they would change or end;
     * before each job a job worker runs, and when the thread ends, returns from its outermost Ember call to C, or waits for work.

     A function called from inside such a region runs no check point during that call:
     * A direct call goes to a copy of the function that has none, as verdict 88 makes a copy.
     * The following calls set a mark on the thread for the call's length: a call through a function value or a `dyn` or `virtual` method; a foreign call that may run the callbacks C keeps (`[FFI-52]`); and a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread (a blocking call, `join`, the end of a `with scope` block, `jobs.wait`, a `@parallel` loop). Every point tests the mark, the points the runtime places included.

     At each point the thread tests its queue. When the queue holds values, the thread empties it there (point 2), and their `drop`s run there. The runtime places no point while it holds a lock of its own. A recursion with no loop reaches a point when it returns to one.
  4. ... adds: "A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2)."
  5. **So a value's end is delayed only** when three things hold: its last owner ends on a thread that did not make it; it was not handed over, either at a place of point 4 or where it was made; and its making thread is not at rest. It is then ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point that thread reaches. Until then it is intact, and a `weakref` link opened on another thread may still find it (`[WK-3]`).
  6. *(new)* **A thread at rest.** A thread rests when it has ended, has returned from its outermost Ember call to C (`[FFI-22]`), waits for work in the job system (`[JOB-6]`), or sleeps inside a blocking call or a foreign call that may block. Before it rests, it empties its queue if that point is clear. A value it cannot end there stays queued until the thread's first clear point after it rests. While it rests, the thread reads and writes no home count.
     * **Code that may touch a home count** is code that may make, end or open an owner of a `thread_shared` value, end a value that owns one, or hand one over (point 4). Such code runs only after the thread has left rest.
     * **Taking over.** A thread whose subtract would queue a value to a resting thread registers as a taker of that thread's queue instead. It adds the value's home count into its away count, marks the value ended when the sum is zero, and deregisters. Only then, holding nothing of the queue, does it run the value's drops, at its own line that ended the owner; `[THR-20]` already checks that line as possibly running them. No user code runs while a taker is registered, so an end inside those drops takes the ordinary path. Several threads may take over values of one resting thread at once: rule Q gives each value to one of them, and each touches only its own value's counts and marks.
     * **Leaving rest.** A thread leaving rest first marks its queue as leaving; after that, a thread that would queue a value there pushes it as usual. The thread leaving rest then waits until no taker is registered. A taker runs a few instructions and no user code.
     * **Callbacks.** A callback that C runs while its thread rests leaves rest on entry when its code may touch a home count. When it returns, it empties its queue there (its return is a check point) and rests again. A callback whose code may not touch a home count leaves the thread at rest.

     This replaces point 3's sentence "A value whose making thread has ended is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner": an ended thread is at rest for good.

* `[OBJ-1]` *(changed)* The `home` field: "read and written only by that thread, with plain instructions; while that thread rests, by the one thread taking over that value (`[RC-4]` point 6)".

* `[WK-3]` *(changed)* The last sentence becomes: "A `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on a thread that did not make it, and that was not handed over, is ended at its making thread's next check point, the first clear point that thread reaches (`[RC-4]` points 3 and 5), and its `drop` runs there. While the making thread rests, the thread that ends the last owner ends the value at once (`[RC-4]` point 6). A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made, and ends where its last owner ends (`[RC-8]` point 2)."

* `[DRP-8]` *(changed)* Adds: "The end counts as a call of the `drop` at the point where it runs, the locks it may take included (`[THR-19]`). For a `thread_shared` value whose last owner ends on another thread, `[RC-8]` says which point that is."

* `[EFF-1]` *(changed)* Adds: "An end that `[RC-8]` point 3 runs at a point the compiler or the runtime picks is part of no function's effects or summary: it runs only where every rule accepts it."

* `[THR-20]` *(changed)* "A `drop` runs where the last owner ends, or, for a value queued to its making thread, at a clear point of that thread (`[RC-8]`). A value whose drops may wait or call C is never queued." The rest is unchanged.

* `[THR-16]` *(changed)* "When `main` returns, its locals end and it empties its queue (`[RC-4]`). Then the process ends: other threads stop without running destructors, no static is freed and no other drop runs. `process.exit` ends the process at once: no drop runs and no queue is emptied."

* `[JOB-6]` *(new)* "A job worker tests its queue before each job, and empties it before it waits for work. While it waits it is at rest (`[RC-4]` point 6), so a value it made is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner. A worker may run a job or a chunk while it waits inside another job's call (`[PAR-4]`, a scope's end). It runs that job at a point that tests the thread's mark (`[RC-4]` point 3)."

* `[FFI-22]` *(changed)* Adds: "When a thread's outermost Ember call returns to C, the thread empties its queue and rests (`[RC-4]` point 6) until it calls into Ember again. An outermost call whose code may touch a home count (`[RC-4]` point 6) leaves rest on entry; a call whose code may not leaves the thread at rest. A foreign call that may block rests the thread for its length in the same way: by its declared effects, or, when none are declared, every effect (`[EFF-3]`). A callback C runs during such a call leaves and re-enters rest as an outermost call does. `ember_rt_shutdown()` ends what is still queued to each thread."

* `[HR-2a]` *(changed)* "Reclaim frees each migrated instance's old version field by field without the type's own `drop`, since the instance lives on in its new form. It ends removed fields, running their `drop`, each as a call (`[RC-8]`):
  * at a host's poll, where no thread runs Ember code, at once;
  * at `std.hot.checkpoint()`, when that call is accepted there, judged with `[HR-44]`'s facts of the frames below the checkpoint: the locks they hold, what they walk and view, and their contracts;
  * otherwise at the first later poll or checkpoint where the call is accepted.

  Under `ember run --hot`, whose only polls are checkpoints (`[HR-33]`), the reload report names each drop that waits and what keeps it out: \"12 removed `Log` values wait: `Log`'s `drop` takes `world.lock`, which `main` holds at the checkpoint on line 21; call `std.hot.checkpoint()` after the `with world.lock:` block\". Prepare runs no check point: a `migrate_from` is compiled with none, since prepare ends nothing (`[HR-2]`)."

* `[HR-3b]` *(changed)* Adds: "`std.hot.checkpoint()` is a check point (`[RC-4]` point 3), and it empties its thread's queue first when it is clear. A layout change of a type whose values may be queued to this thread applies only when that queue is empty. Every other thread is outside Ember code, so it is at rest and has nothing queued. Otherwise the change is not applied at this checkpoint: the report names the line that kept the queue from being emptied, and the change applies at the next checkpoint or poll where the queue is empty."

* `[RT-8]` *(changed)* Adds:
  * "Entering rest is one compare-and-exchange of the thread's queue word, from empty to at rest. It is a release. When values arrived, the thread empties them and tries again.
  * A taker registers with one atomic add to the thread's taker count, then reads the queue word again. When it finds the thread leaving rest, it deregisters and pushes as usual.
  * Leaving rest is one atomic or of the leaving mark into the queue word, then a wait until the taker count is zero.
  * Registering and the read after it, and the leaving mark and the wait after it, are sequentially consistent, so each side sees the other. Deregistering is a release, and the wait reads the count with acquire, so the thread leaving rest sees every count and mark a taker wrote.
  * The protocol is stress-tested as rule Q was (`stress.c`)."

* `[COST-3]` *(changed)*
  * The owner-count row: "... for `thread_shared` on the thread that made the value until it is handed over (`[RC-4]`). A value whose drops may wait or call C is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2) ..."
  * The two-count row:
    * "A test of the thread's queue at each check point: at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts, and once every N rounds of a loop whose count is known, so that the rounds between two tests stay vectorisable.
    * There is no test inside a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or inside a walk or a view they clash with (`[RC-8]`).
    * One compare-and-exchange to enter rest, and one atomic or with a load to leave it. These are paid only when a job worker sleeps for lack of work, on a blocking call's sleeping path, around a foreign call that may block, and around an outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count; and only on a thread whose code may make a value that can be queued.
    * One thread-local add and one subtract, around a call made inside such a region that may reach code with check points and has no copy without them.
    * A value whose drops may wait or call C pays one atomic add or subtract for every owner made or ended, on every thread, as `shared_ptr` does (43.6 ms against 32.6 ms for a thread's own objects in the measurement), and it is never queued.
    * Nothing is paid per object."

answers.answer:
`Conn`'s drop takes a lock, so it may wait (`Block`). So a `Conn` is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2): every thread counts its owners in the atomic count from the start, as with a `shared_ptr`. Its drop runs where its last owner ends: on the worker, when `b` ends at the end of the worker's function. `[THR-20]` already checks that line as running `~Conn()`, and the worker holds no lock there. `~Conn()` waits for `pool.lock` until main's `with` block ends, then pushes 1.

Main never runs `~Conn()`. A drop that main does run for another thread (one that neither waits nor calls C) waits for nothing, so main's walk under `pool.lock` is never interrupted by a wait for that lock, nor by a change to the walked list. Nothing is refused and nothing is written.
answers.code:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # takes a lock, so it may wait
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # counted like a shared_ptr from here
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the worker ends the Conn's last owner and runs ~Conn() there
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            for id in pool.free:              # no drop main runs for another thread waits here
                println(id)
    println(h.join())
answers.outcome: Compiles. While the worker runs, frames print nothing, because `pool.free` is empty. When the worker's function ends, `b` ends and with it the `Conn`'s last owner, so the worker runs `~Conn()`. It waits for `pool.lock` until main's current `with` block ends, then pushes 1. Every later frame prints 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. `~Conn()` never runs on main, so main never waits for its own lock, and the list it walks never changes under it. Every count change of a `Conn` is one atomic add or subtract, as a `shared_ptr`'s is.

answers.answer:
A job worker that waits for work is at rest (`[JOB-6]`). So is a host thread whose outermost Ember call has returned to C (`[FFI-22]`), and a thread asleep in a blocking call or in a foreign call that may block. Each first empties its queue. While it rests, the thread that ends the last owner of one of its values ends that value at once, at its own line.

This `Texture`'s drop neither waits nor calls C, so it is queued to the worker that made it. Main's `bundles.clear()` ends it at once if that worker already waits for work. Otherwise the worker ends it before it waits or before its next job.

An engine's `Texture` gives its GPU memory back through C. It is handed over where it is made (`[RC-8]` point 2), so main ends it during `bundles.clear()` whatever the worker is doing.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. "texture 1 freed" and "texture 2 freed" are printed as soon as `bundles.clear()` runs. Main prints a texture's line during the clear when the worker that made it already waits for work. Otherwise that worker prints it just before it waits, which may come after the first frames. No texture is held while the game runs.

On a host thread: a value queued to it during a callback is ended before the callback returns to C. A value queued while the thread is in C is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner.

other_cases.case: A local made inside `with pool.lock:` (`c = Conn(id=2, pool=thread_shared pool)`) ends where the block ends, inside the lock, and `Conn`'s drop takes `pool.lock`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1. The block's end is a written point, checked as a call of `~Conn()`: `E7018` there. The message says to make `c` above the `with` line, so that it ends after the lock is let go. C++'s `{ lock_guard g(m); Conn c; }` deadlocks here; Ember refuses it when compiling (verdict 43).

other_cases.case: A temporary under a lock: `with pool.lock: n = Conn(id=3, pool=thread_shared pool).id`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1. The temporary ends at the end of the statement (`[DRP-3]`), inside the lock: `E7018`. The fix is `c = Conn(...)` above the `with` line.

other_cases.case: `enemies.clear()` or `enemies[0] = Enemy(hp=5)` inside `for line in LOG:`, where `Enemy`'s drop pushes to `LOG`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1 and verdict 57, as today: `E3020` at the clear, with the advice to move it below the loop (`[DRP-8]`). Unchanged.

other_cases.case: A worker ends the last owner of a `Conn` that main made, inside the worker's own `with pool.lock:`.
other_cases.settled: Point 2 makes that line a written end on the worker: it runs `~Conn()`, which takes `pool.lock`, so the line is `E7018` there (`[THR-19]`, `[THR-20]`). The message says to end the owner below the block.

other_cases.case: A check point inside `@realtime fn mix(ref mut out: MutSpan[f32])`, or inside a function it calls, while queued drops allocate.
other_cases.settled: No point is placed in `mix`, or in what it calls during that call. A direct callee runs as a copy with no points, and the thread's mark covers an indirect callee. The queue is emptied at the first clear point after `mix` returns. Nothing is refused, and `mix` keeps its contract.

other_cases.case: `@deterministic fn simulate(inputs: Receiver[int], out: Sender[Bundle])` sends each turn's `thread_shared Frame` inside a `Bundle` to a network thread, which ends it; the sim thread sleeps in `recv` every turn.
other_cases.settled: The sim thread rests in every `recv` that sleeps (point 6 needs no clear point), so the network thread ends each `Frame` at once, at its own line, and memory does not grow. Points inside `simulate` are clear, because `Frame`'s drop only frees memory. Timing alone is not `Nondet` (`[DET-6]`). Whether a drop that changes what `simulate` reads would make it `Nondet` is `[DET-2]`'s question, decided with P14's J6-07.

other_cases.case: Main holds an unrelated lock (`with stats.lock: for s in stats.samples: total += s`), and a value whose drop takes `pool.lock` was let go on another thread.
other_cases.settled: That value was never queued (point 2): its drop ran on the thread that let it go. A queued drop, which neither waits nor calls C, may run inside main's block. It takes no lock, so the program gets no lock order it did not write.

other_cases.case: Main walks a generator that is suspended inside `with POOL_LOCK:` (`for id in busy_ids(): println(id)`), while a `Conn` whose drop takes `POOL_LOCK` is let go on a worker.
other_cases.settled: The `Conn` is never queued, so the worker runs `~Conn()`. It waits until main's generator finishes its walk and lets the lock go. No queued drop takes a lock, so nothing can wait at main's back edge for the lock the generator holds. A written end, or a written `with POOL_LOCK:`, in main's loop is a different gap: `[THR-19]` misses a lock held across a `yield`. It is raised to the lead separately (see open risks).

other_cases.case: A subscription whose drop calls C's `bus_unsubscribe`, which locks the bus mutex, while main's back edges run inside C's `bus_dispatch()` callbacks.
other_cases.settled: `~Sub()` calls C (`FFI`), so a `Sub` is handed over where it is made and ends where its last owner ends: on the worker, when `b` ends. That is what the drop's `# SAFETY:` note says. No queued drop calls C, so a queued drop that runs inside a callback touches nothing of C's.

other_cases.case: A drop that sends its id back on a bounded channel that only its making thread receives from (`Conn.back.send(...)`, `Job.done.send(...)`).
other_cases.settled: `send` on a bounded channel may wait (`Block`), so the type is handed over where it is made, and the worker runs both drops. The second send waits until main receives the first, and the program finishes, as it does with `shared_ptr` or `Arc`. A placed drop would have made main wait for itself.

other_cases.case: A worker clears its batch (the `Conn`'s last owner), then holds `pool.lock` while it receives main's ids; main sends them.
other_cases.settled: `~Conn()` runs on the worker at `b.conns.clear()`, before the worker takes `pool.lock`, and nothing hangs. No placed drop takes a lock, so the rule adds no wait between threads that the program does not write.

other_cases.case: A job worker holds `pool.lock` inside a job, or runs under a contract, and runs a chunk itself, or another job, while it waits for a `@parallel` loop.
other_cases.settled: Locks do not matter: no queued drop takes one. Under a contract that the queued drops would break, the wait sets the thread's mark (`[RC-4]` point 3), and the points the runtime places there (before a job, on the sleeping path) test it. The queue is emptied after the job returns.

other_cases.case: A server's accept thread waits an hour in `listener.accept()`, or in a C library's `net_accept()` declared `@ffi(no_callbacks)`, while values it made are ended on session threads.
other_cases.settled: Point 6. A blocking call's sleeping path, and a foreign call that may block (`net_accept` declares no effects, so it may), rest the thread for their length. Each session thread ends such a value at once, at its own line.

other_cases.case: Main sits in C's event loop (`run_event_loop()`, which runs a kept callback per input) while a worker ends the last owners of two `Session`s main made.
other_cases.settled: `run_event_loop` may block, so main rests for its whole length. The callback touches no `thread_shared` count, so it leaves main at rest, and the worker ends both `Session`s at once. A callback whose code does touch one leaves rest on entry, and at its return empties its queue and rests again.

other_cases.case: A thread inside `with q.lock:` waits in `rx.recv()` while values it made are ended elsewhere.
other_cases.settled: It rests while it sleeps, whatever it holds. The threads that end those values run their drops on their own threads, and those drops never wait, so none of them waits for `q.lock`.

other_cases.case: A job worker idle for the rest of the process (pool workers end only with it, `[THR-16]`).
other_cases.settled: `[JOB-6]`: the worker rests while it waits, so every value it made is ended at once by the thread that ends its last owner. A value queued while the worker runs a job is ended within that job, or before the worker next waits.

other_cases.case: A C audio driver calls an exported Ember function on its own thread. The function makes a `thread_shared Buffer`, which travels inside a `Mix` to an Ember mixer thread, and the mixer ends it while the driver thread is back in C.
other_cases.settled: `[FFI-22]` and point 6. The driver thread emptied its queue and rested when the callback returned, so the mixer ends the `Buffer` at once. An exported function whose code touches no `thread_shared` count pays nothing on entry or on return.

other_cases.case: An exported `on_flush` makes, ends and opens nothing, but hands a saved `thread_shared Frame` into a `Mutex` other threads read.
other_cases.settled: A hand-over at a place of point 4 touches the home count, so `on_flush`'s code may touch a home count (point 6), and it leaves rest on entry. No other thread can merge that count while `on_flush` writes it.

other_cases.case: A callback C runs during `glfwPollEvents()`, which Ember calls inside `with ui.lock:`.
other_cases.settled: Queued drops may run at the callback's points, since they take no lock. If the caller is under a contract the drops would break, the foreign call sets the thread's mark and they wait for the end of that region.

other_cases.case: `fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[float], vel: Span[float], dt: float)` loops `for i in 0..pos.len():`.
other_cases.settled: The trip count is known when the loop starts, so the queue is tested once every N rounds, not every round (`[RC-4]` point 3). The rounds between two tests are one loop the C compiler can vectorise.

other_cases.case: `std.hot.checkpoint()` is reached while a `thread_shared Conn` of a type the reload changes waits in main's queue.
other_cases.settled: `[HR-3b]`: the checkpoint empties main's queue first when it is clear, and only then is the layout change applied. When the checkpoint is not clear, the change is not applied there, and the report names the line. No point runs while prepare runs: a `migrate_from` has none.

other_cases.case: A reload at `std.hot.checkpoint()`, called inside `with world.lock:`, removes a field whose type's drop takes `world.lock`.
other_cases.settled: `[HR-2a]`. By `[HR-44]`'s facts, a frame below holds `world.lock`, so the drop's call is not accepted at the checkpoint. The removed values are kept and ended at the first later poll or checkpoint where that call is accepted. Under `ember run --hot`, the report names the drop that waits and the lock that keeps it out. The new code still runs from the checkpoint on.

other_cases.case: Program exit: `main` returns while a worker still holds a `Conn` that main made; or `process.exit(1)` is called inside a lock.
other_cases.settled: `[THR-16]`. When main returns, its locals end, then it empties its queue (no frame is left, so the point is clear), then the process ends. What other threads hold is not ended, as for every object of another thread. `process.exit` runs no drop and empties no queue, as today.

other_cases.case: A generator is abandoned mid-iteration: `g = d.replay()`, one `next`, then `g` ends.
other_cases.settled: Point 1. Its end is a written point, checked as the drops of its frame's locals (`[EFF-1]`, ODR-057). Check points inside a generator's body follow the context of the `next` call that runs them.

other_cases.case: A queued drop ends the last owner of a `thread_shared Buffer` that a third thread made.
other_cases.settled: That end follows the same rule on the thread running the drop. If `Buffer`'s drop may wait or call C, it was handed over and ends there. Otherwise it goes into its maker's queue, or is ended at once if its maker rests.

other_cases.case: A parent at the end of `with scope = thread.scope():`, while a task ends an owner of a value the parent made.
other_cases.settled: The scope's end may sleep, so the parent rests while it waits, and the task ends the value at once, at its own line, which `[THR-20]` checks.

other_cases.case: A static whose initialiser runs under `Once` (`[STA-3]`) contains a loop.
other_cases.settled: No queued drop waits, so a point inside the initialiser cannot wait on `Once`'s lock. A value whose drop would read a static another thread is initialising may wait, so it is handed over where it is made.

other_cases.case: A `Receiver` ends while values are still queued in its channel (`[THR-15]`).
other_cases.settled: Point 1: a written end. It already ends the values after letting the channel's lock go, which is what this rule asks.

other_cases.case: A drop that spins on an `Atomic` flag until its making thread clears it (a lock built by hand).
other_cases.settled: An `Atomic` loop is not an operation the compiler sees as waiting, so such a value may be queued. If its making thread holds the flag at a clear point, the drop spins there for ever, as a spin lock taken twice does in C. This is stated as a limitation in `misuse`. std's locks and channels are seen.

other_cases.case: A later `await` (§XI.6), or any other point the compiler adds in the future.
other_cases.settled: `[RC-8]` decides it with no new text: a queued drop runs at such a point only where the point is clear, and a drop that may wait or call C is never queued.

design.prior_art:
**C++ and Rust.** A `shared_ptr`'s destructor, and an `Arc`'s drop, run where the last owner ends, on that thread, with an atomic count on every thread. Point 2 gives exactly that to a drop that waits or calls C: it runs at the place a programmer can see. In both languages, a self-wait there is found only at run time. A destructor that locks a `std::mutex` its own thread holds is undefined behaviour, and Rust's `Mutex` docs say that locking it twice "might panic or deadlock". Ember refuses that self-wait when compiling (`[THR-19]`).

**Python.** CPython runs `__del__` wherever a count reaches zero or the collector runs. Its data-model documentation warns that `__del__` may run in the middle of arbitrary code, on any thread, so one that takes a lock or waits can deadlock on the code it interrupted. Point 2 removes exactly that hazard.

**Swift.** SE-0371's isolated deinit queues the deinit of an actor-isolated object released elsewhere as a job on the actor's executor, so it runs between jobs. That is the shape of point 3, but only for actor classes, and with no compile-time check.

**Go, Java, .NET.** Finalisers and cleaners run on a runtime thread. Go runs all of them in one goroutine, in order, and its docs tell a long finaliser to start its own goroutine. There is no time bound, and a collector is needed. This is option D.

**crossbeam-epoch.** It runs deferred destructors during a later `pin()` on any thread, with no time bound.

**Biased counting** (Choi, Shull and Torrellas, PACT 2018), where Ember's two counts come from, leaves it to the runtime when the owner thread processes its queue. The BRC report says the placement is "still to design".

**Threads in native code.** The JVM treats a thread running native code as being at a safepoint: the VM goes on without it, and the thread checks on its way back. Go's scheduler hands a goroutine's processor on while it sits in a blocking system call or a cgo call. Point 6's rest is the same idea, applied to the queue.

**Loop polls.** HotSpot polls at loop back edges. In counted loops it polls once every so many rounds (loop strip mining), so the rounds in between stay optimisable. Point 3 places tests the same way.

**Linux.** The last `fput()` of a file defers the release to task_work, which runs when the task returns to user mode, where it holds no kernel lock. RCU callbacks must not sleep. These are the two halves of the rule: a deferred end runs where it clashes with nothing, and only an end that does not wait is deferred.

**Objective-C/Cocoa.** An autorelease pool is drained at the top of each run-loop turn.

**C#.** `await` inside a `lock` statement is refused (CS1996). This bears on the lock-across-`yield` question raised for `[THR-19]`.

**Where each falls short.**
* C++ and Rust pay an atomic count for every type and leave self-waits to run time.
* The finaliser-thread languages give no bound and need a collector.
* Swift, Cocoa and Linux get the right shape, but by convention or for one kind of object.

The rule decides, when compiling, which ends may be deferred at all (those that neither wait nor call C). It places them where they clash with nothing, and keeps the two-count speed for them.
design.cost:
**Against what.** C has no deferred ends and pays nothing here. The relevant comparison is one atomic count (C++ `shared_ptr`, Rust `Arc`). Verdict 101's two counts beat it by 25% on a thread's own objects: 32.6 ms against 43.6 ms (`measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md`, own pattern, one thread). The rule keeps that gain for every type whose drop neither waits nor calls C. A type whose drop does either pays exactly C++'s and Rust's cost.

**Per operation.**
1. **A check point outside a clash:** one thread-local load of the queue word, and a branch not taken. It sits at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts. A loop whose trip count is known gets one every N rounds, so the rounds in between stay one loop the C compiler can vectorise. This is fewer tests than today's test at every back edge.
2. **Inside a function under a contract the queued drops would break, or a walk or view they clash with:** zero, because no point is placed there. A lock no longer keeps points out: queued drops take none.
3. **Where such a region ends, if it kept a point out:** one thread-local load and a branch.
4. **A direct call from such a region into a function that has points:** zero time. The cost is one more copy of the function, in code size, as with verdict 88's copy, and only for callees that have points.
5. **Calls from such a region that may reach points:** one plain thread-local add before the call and one subtract after. This covers a call through a function value or a `dyn`/`virtual` method, a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, and a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread. The points read the mark only when the queue holds values.
6. **Rest:** one compare-and-exchange to enter it, and one atomic or with a load to leave it. It is paid only:
   * when a job worker sleeps for lack of work;
   * on a blocking call's sleeping path, beside the system call that sleeps;
   * around a foreign call that may block, beside the call;
   * around an outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count.

   And it is paid only on a thread whose code may make a value that can be queued. A foreign function that declares no effects counts as one that may block (`[EFF-3]`). Declaring its effects without `Block` removes the cost.
7. **Taking over a resting thread's value:** one atomic add and one subtract to register and deregister, plus the merge (one atomic add) that the maker would have done. Then comes the drop the value needs anyway. This is paid only on the path that would otherwise queue.
8. **A value whose drop may wait or call C:** one atomic add or subtract for every owner made or ended, on every thread, as `shared_ptr` does: 43.6 ms instead of 32.6 ms on the measurement's own-objects loop, for those types only. They have no queue, no placed point and no rest.
9. **A job worker before each job:** one thread-local load and a branch.

**Memory.** Zero per object: the 32-byte header already holds the queue link, and a type of item 8 keeps the same header. Per thread: the rest state in spare bits of the existing queue word, one taker count and one mark.

**Where it is zero.** Every count change of a type that may be queued; every check point outside a clash; every direct call; every exported function whose code touches no `thread_shared` count; every blocking call that does not sleep; every foreign call that neither may block nor runs callbacks inside a clash.

**Not measured:** items 6, 7 and 8 on real programs, and the choice of N. They must be measured on the laptop (P-cores, mains) before the rule goes in, and the rest protocol must be stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q.

readability.note: Not a character changes: the rule adds no word, attribute or line. The same text now has one meaning, and it is the meaning a C++ or Rust programmer expects. A destructor that takes a lock, waits, or calls C runs where its last owner ends. Any other destructor runs on its making thread, at a point that clashes with nothing, or at once while that thread is idle. The work belongs to the compiler (which types may be queued, and where the points go) and to the runtime (rest). The programmer never writes or sees any of it. A connection pool, a texture cache, a game loop and a C event loop read exactly as before. Option A would make the loop copy the list out of the lock.

design.compiler_does:
1. **Which types are handed over where they are made.** For each `thread_shared` type, the compiler works out its drop chain's effects: its drop and the drops of what it owns (`[DRP-8]`, `[EFF-24]`), with every implementation that may sit in an `owns dyn` field. A type whose chain may wait (`Block`) or call C (`FFI`) is handed over at every line that makes a value of it: the header starts with the owner in the away count and the handed-over mark, and every count change is atomic.
2. **Which types may be queued.** For every other `thread_shared` type, the compiler works out whether its values may be queued: whether an owner may reach another thread inside another object (by `[THR-2]`'s routes) without point 4's hand-over. For each thread entry (main, each `thread.spawn` and job function, each export and kept callback), it works out which such types the entry's code may make. Then it takes the summary of those queued drops: what they change and end, and their effects. One program-wide set is allowed.
3. **Which points are clear.** For each candidate point, it decides from each function's own code whether the point is clear: the function has no contract the drops' effects would break, and no live walk or view that they change or end. There is no lock condition.
4. **Context in callees.** It carries the caller's context into callees. A direct call made inside a region where the drops cannot run goes to a copy with no points. An indirect call, a foreign call that may run kept callbacks, or a call that may sleep or run jobs on this thread, made there, is bracketed by the thread-local mark.
5. **Where points go.** It places points at the back edges of loops whose trip count is not known when they start, and once every N rounds of counted loops (strip-mined). It also places them before blocking calls (blocking foreign calls included), where a region that kept a point out ends, at thread end, at the return to C, at a worker's wait, and before each job.
6. **Rest transitions.** It emits them at these places, and only on threads whose code may make a value that can be queued:
   * the return to C from an outermost call, with leaving rest on entry when the export's or callback's code may touch a home count;
   * around a foreign call that may block, with callbacks inside it leaving and re-entering rest when their code may touch a home count;
   * on a blocking call's sleeping path;
   * at a worker's wait;
   * at thread end.
7. **No effect from placed ends.** It keeps placed ends out of every effect set and summary, and refuses nothing because of them.
8. **Written ends.** It checks written ends as calls (point 1), every end of a handed-over type's last owner on any thread included (`[THR-20]`).
9. **Hot reload.** It records whether each `std.hot.checkpoint()` call is clear. It records `[HR-44]`'s facts for the frames below each checkpoint (the locks they hold, what they walk and view, their contracts), so that plan can time the drops of removed fields. It compiles each `migrate_from` with no points.
10. **Inspection (optional).** `ember inspect` lists each type handed over where it is made, with the operation in its drop that waits or calls C, and each point left out, with what kept it out.
design.misuse:
**Nothing new can be misused.** No program can write, call or skip a check point, choose which types are queued, or read the header (`[OBJ-1]`).

**Refused when compiling:** a written end that clashes.
* A local or a temporary ends inside `with pool.lock:`, and its drop takes `pool.lock`: `E7018`, with the line to write.
* The last owner of a `Conn` ends inside `with pool.lock:` on any thread. That line runs `~Conn()` (point 2), so it is `E7018` there.
* A `clear()` inside a walk of something its drops change: `E3020`.

**Never undefined behaviour, and no hidden wait.**
* A drop the compiler places never waits for anything and never calls C, because a drop that may do either is never placed. So neither C++'s self-wait on a `std::mutex` (undefined) nor a C call inside C's own locked dispatch can happen at a line the program did not write.
* A placed drop never runs inside a walk, a view or a contract it clashes with.
* Another thread reads a home count only while that count's thread rests, after a release. A taker runs no user code while it is registered.

**Not refused, and stated:**
* A thread that runs for ever where no point is clear (an endless loop inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) keeps its queued values until it leaves. Only memory is held, since those drops neither wait nor call C.
* A drop that waits runs where its last owner ends, and waits there, as in C++ and Rust. A self-wait on a std lock there is refused (`[THR-19]`). A cycle between threads built from the program's own waits is the program's, as in C++ and Rust; the debug lock-order report (`[THR-4]`) and `L7001` point at it.
* A wait built by hand from an `Atomic` (a spin loop) is not an operation the compiler sees as waiting. A queued drop that spins until its own making thread lets go hangs, as a spin lock taken twice does in C. std's locks and channels are seen.
design.verdicts:
**43 kept, and made stronger.** No placed drop waits for any lock: a drop that may take one is never queued, and it runs where its last owner ends, at a line `[THR-19]` checks. A written end inside a lock, whose drop takes that lock, is refused when compiling (point 1), as 43 refuses any such call.

**56 kept.** A queued value is marked ended before its drop runs, on the making thread and on a taker alike, and links then find it gone.

**57 kept, and carried to every end.** Ending a value is a call of its drop where the drop runs. For an end the compiler places, the compiler puts it only where that call is accepted, so 57 holds for queued drops with nothing refused.

**101: the placement it left open, plus two changes that need the owner's yes.**
* **Kept:** the two numbers. The making thread deletes a queued value at its next check point, "placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends". The BRC report says the placement is "still to design", and decisions.md section 6 records the back-edge placement as a lead choice.
* **Widened:** "or the other thread deletes it at once if the making thread has ended" becomes "... is at rest". At rest means: ended, back in C, waiting for work, or asleep in a blocking call or a foreign call that may block. The evidence:
  * J7-02: a pool worker never ends, and a C thread may never call in again. Under 101's letter, a value queued to either is held for the life of the process.
  * A resting thread touches no home count, exactly like an ended one, so the same takeover is safe.
  * It costs nothing on any fast path.
* **Narrowed:** a type whose drop may wait or call C is handed over where it is made. This is 101's own fix 2 ("a hand-over the compiler sees moves A into B"), applied at the making line. All its counts are atomic, and it ends where its last owner ends. The evidence: three programs that work with `shared_ptr` and `Arc` fail under every placement on the making thread, because the making thread is the wrong thread to do the waiting:
  * a drop that sends on a bounded channel only its maker drains: the maker waits for itself;
  * a drop that takes a lock another thread holds while that thread waits for the maker: a cycle the text does not show;
  * a drop that calls C inside C's own locked dispatch: undefined behaviour, against a true `# SAFETY:` note.

  The cost: those types pay `shared_ptr`'s count, 43.6 ms against 32.6 ms on the measured own-objects loop. Every other type keeps 101's speed. This is narrower than option C, which counts every type whose drop reaches outside its fields, and everything a worker makes, atomically.

**114 kept.** An object moved to another thread has its drop run once there: a written end on that thread.

**164 to 166 untouched.** The rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]`: a `thread_shared` value's drop reaches only what any thread may reach.

**Not decided here:**
* Whether what a queued drop changes makes a `@deterministic` function `Nondet` is `[DET-2]`'s question, under P14's J6-07. The rule says only that timing alone is not `Nondet` (`[DET-6]`).
* A lock held across a `yield` is `[THR-19]`'s gap, raised separately.

options_for_owner.summary: Refuse: a check point counts as a call of every queued type's drop, so a loop whose back edge may run `~Conn()` under the lock that drop takes is E7018; J7-02 is handled by threads at rest, as in B
options_for_owner.code:
# the J7-01 program is refused at the inner `for` line (E7018):
#   "this loop's back edge may end a `Conn` another thread let go of, and `Conn`'s drop takes
#    `pool.lock`, which this thread holds (line 21); walk a copy after the lock"
# the programmer writes instead:
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            ids = copy of pool.free
        for id in ids:
            println(id)
options_for_owner.outcome: The original does not compile. The rewrite does, and `~Conn()` runs on main at a back edge outside the lock. Every loop under a lock, or walking a list, that some queued type's drop may touch is refused the same way, although the compiler, not the programmer, chose to put a check point there (principle 7). A queued drop that waits for its own thread (a bounded `send` only main drains) still hangs unless B's point 2 is added.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule: a drop that may wait or call C runs where its last owner ends (its type is counted atomically from the start, as `shared_ptr` is); every other queued drop runs only at a point where it clashes with nothing, and at once while its making thread rests
options_for_owner.code:
# the J7-01 and J7-02 programs, unchanged: no word, no line
#   `~Conn()` takes a lock, so a Conn is counted like a shared_ptr: the worker runs it when `b` ends
#   a Texture whose drop neither waits nor calls C goes back to its worker; a worker waiting for work,
#   a thread back in C, one asleep or one that ended is at rest: the thread that ends the last owner ends it
options_for_owner.outcome: Both compile. J7-01: the worker runs `~Conn()` when `b` ends. It waits for `pool.lock` until main's block ends, then pushes 1; later frames print 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. Main never waits for its own lock, and the walked list never changes. J7-02: both textures are freed as soon as `bundles.clear()` runs, by main if their worker is waiting, otherwise by the worker before it waits. Nothing is refused. Every type whose drop neither waits nor calls C keeps verdict 101's speed; the types whose drop does pay `shared_ptr`'s cost.

options_for_owner.summary: Never queued (J7-01 C and J7-02 B as one): a type whose drop reaches outside its own fields, and anything a job worker or a C thread makes, is counted atomically on every thread from the start
options_for_owner.code:
# the J7-01 and J7-02 programs, unchanged
# `Conn` (its drop reaches the pool) and every `Texture` (made on a worker) count every owner with
# an atomic add, on their own thread too; the thread that ends the last owner runs the drop
options_for_owner.outcome: Both compile. J7-01 behaves as in B. J7-02: main prints both lines during `bundles.clear()`. The 25% that verdict 101 bought for a thread's own objects (43.6 ms against 32.6 ms) is lost for most types with a real drop (a log line, a cache entry), and for everything a worker or a C thread makes, even where deferring is harmless. Types whose drop only frees their fields still queue, so their check points still need B's placement.

options_for_owner.summary: The making thread only merges counts at a check point, which runs no user code; a value whose count reaches zero has its drop run on a thread the runtime starts (threads at rest as in B)
options_for_owner.code:

options_for_owner.outcome: Both compile. J7-01: the drop thread waits for `pool.lock` until main's `with` block ends, then pushes 1. J7-02 behaves as in B. A thread the program never started runs every queued drop, one after another, so a drop that waits holds up all the rest. Each queued end costs one wake (a system call when the drop thread sleeps). Verdict 101's 'that thread deletes it' no longer holds.

recommendation.reason:
B is verdict 101 with the placement 101 left open. Ends that cannot safely be moved are not moved. A drop that may wait or call C runs where its last owner ends, as `shared_ptr` and `Arc` run it, because only there are the wait and C's state visible in the program's text. Every other queued drop runs at the first point where it clashes with nothing, or at once while its making thread is idle, in C, asleep or ended.

Compared with the other options:
* B refuses nothing; A refuses correct loops the programmer never put a point in, and still hangs on a drop that waits for its own thread.
* B keeps 101's speed for every type whose drop neither waits nor calls C; C gives it up for most types with a drop and for everything a worker makes.
* B needs no hidden thread, which D does, and no word from the programmer.

It changes verdict 101 twice, both said plainly: 'has ended' becomes 'is at rest', and a type whose drop waits or calls C is handed over where it is made.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: when the last `shared_ptr<Conn>` dies on a worker thread, Ember's two counts (verdict 101) run `~Conn()` later, on the thread that made the `Conn`. Where may that thread run it, by when, and should a `~Conn()` that takes a lock or waits be run there at all?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])` | a `Conn` made on main; today main counts its owner in its own plain count. `~Conn()` takes a lock, so under B it is counted like a `shared_ptr` from here |
| 2 | main | `h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())` | `b` goes to the worker with the `Conn` inside it; nothing hands the `Conn` itself over |
| 3 | main | `with pool.lock:` then `for id in pool.free:` | main holds the pool's lock and walks `pool.free` |
| 4 | worker | its function returns and `b` ends | today: the `Conn`'s last owner ends here, so the `Conn` goes into main's queue. Under B: the worker runs `~Conn()` here; it waits for `pool.lock` until main's block ends, then pushes 1 |
| 5 | main | today: the walk's back edge is a check point (`[RC-4]`) | today `~Conn()` runs here: it waits for ever for the lock main holds, and its `push` would change the list main walks |
| 6 | main | under B: the next frames | they print 1, and `h.join()` prints 1; `~Conn()` never runs on main |
| 7 | a job worker | makes a `Texture` whose drop only prints, then waits for work (J7-02) | today it waits in the worker's queue for ever; under B the worker is at rest, so main ends it at once in `bundles.clear()` |
owner_short.today: `[RC-4]` (a lead choice, not verdict 101) runs queued destructors at every loop's back edge. So `~Conn()` can run inside main's `with pool.lock:` walk, where it waits for ever for the lock main holds, or changes the list main walks. A queued destructor that sends on a full channel only main reads makes main wait for itself. One that calls C can run inside C's own locked callback. A value queued to an idle job worker, or to a thread back in C, may never be freed.
owner_short.options:
A: a check point counts as a call of every queued drop, so the inner `for` under the lock is refused (E7018), and you copy the list out first.
B: a destructor that may wait or call C runs where its last owner ends, as with `shared_ptr` (its type counts atomically); any other destructor runs on the making thread only where it would compile, and at once while that thread is idle, back in C, asleep or ended.
C: every type whose destructor reaches outside itself, and everything a job worker or a C thread makes, is counted atomically from the start, and loses verdict 101's 25%.
D: the making thread only merges the counts at a check point, and the destructors run on a thread the runtime starts.
owner_short.recommendation: B. Nothing is refused and no word is written. `~Conn()` takes a lock, so it runs on the worker where its last owner ends, as in C++ and Rust. Every destructor that neither waits nor calls C keeps verdict 101's speed. B changes verdict 101 twice, which needs your yes: 'the making thread has ended' becomes 'is at rest', and a type whose destructor waits or calls C is counted like `shared_ptr` from the start (those types give up the 25%).

repairs.hole: Safety, high: main's generator is suspended inside `with POOL_LOCK:`, so RC-8's 'this thread holds no lock' test passes at main's back edge, and `~Conn()` waits for the lock main's own frame holds.
repairs.answer: Closed for this rule by construction. A drop that may take a lock may wait (`Block`), so it is never queued: its type is handed over where it is made (RC-8 point 2), and `~Conn()` runs on the thread that ends its last owner, at a written line. Queued drops take no lock, so no placed drop can wait for POOL_LOCK at main's back edge, whatever a suspended generator holds, and the 'holds no lock' condition is gone from the clear-point test. The breaker's second half is real but not P05's: a lock held across a `yield` hides from `[THR-19]` (a written `with POOL_LOCK:` in the consumer's loop, or a written end there whose drop takes it, is not refused). It goes to the lead as its own question, beside CORO-13. The options are to refuse a `yield` inside a lock's block or with a live guard (as CORO-13 refuses a `@must_drop` value across a `yield`, and as C# refuses `await` in `lock`), or to count the lock as held while the frame may be suspended there.

repairs.hole: Safety, high: point 6's order runs the drop while the taker holds main's queue, so a drop that ends an owner main counted (or one that waits for a lock whose holder needs main's queue) waits for itself; cost item 7 gave a different order.
repairs.answer: Fixed, with one order written in RC-4 point 6, RT-8 and cost item 7. A taker registers (one atomic add), merges the home count into the away count, marks the value ended, and deregisters (a release). Only then does it run the drop chain, on its own thread, at its own line. No user code runs while a taker is registered, so ends inside the drop take the ordinary path, and a nested takeover of the same resting thread just registers again. Takers never wait for one another: each touches only its own value's counts (rule Q gives each value to one thread). The maker leaving rest waits only for registered merges. Both deadlocks in the hole need a queue held across user code, which no longer happens. `~Conn()` is not queued at all now.

repairs.hole: Safety, high: `~Sub()` calls C's `bus_unsubscribe` at a back edge inside C's `bus_dispatch` callback, where C holds the bus mutex: undefined behaviour at a site no `# SAFETY:` note can cover; the same at an outermost return still inside C's call.
repairs.answer: Closed by RC-8 point 2. `~Sub()` calls C (`FFI`), so a `Sub` is handed over where it is made and ends where its last owner ends: on the worker, when `b` ends. That is exactly what the drop's `# SAFETY:` note says. No queued drop calls C, so a queued drop at a callback's back edge, or at an outermost return inside C's call, touches nothing of C's. Principle 11 holds: a vouch only ever covers lines the program wrote. The breaker's mark-only fix was not taken. It would still run vouched C calls at compiler-picked lines whenever no foreign frame is below, and a C lock held across Ember code (a `bus_lock()`/`bus_unlock()` pair, a GIL, a current GL context) breaks that.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: entering rest by one exchange either loses a value pushed just before it or leaves the resting thread holding a list while other threads take its queue; the give-back was not ordered.
repairs.answer:
Fixed in RC-4 point 6 and RT-8.
* Entering rest is a compare-and-exchange from the empty queue to 'at rest' (a release). When values arrived, the thread empties them and tries again.
* A putter that finds the thread running, or leaving rest, does the ordinary push.
* Leaving rest marks the queue as leaving, then waits for registered takers, reading their count with acquire, so it sees every count and mark they wrote.
* A value that was queued before rest, at a point that was not clear, stays in the list, which takers never touch, and is ended at the thread's first clear point after it rests.
* The stress test is kept.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: FFI-22's 'make, end or open' misses a hand-over at a place of point 4 (`on_flush` hands a frame into a Mutex at rest), so two threads write one home count; COST-3 said something else.
repairs.answer: There is now one condition, defined once in RC-4 point 6 and used by FFI-22 and COST-3: code that may touch a home count, meaning code that may make, end or open an owner of a `thread_shared` value, end a value that owns one, or hand one over at a place of point 4. `on_flush` hands a frame over, so it leaves rest on entry.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: a queued drop that waits for something other than a lock (a bounded `send` only its maker drains, a join, a spin lock) hangs on its maker; C++ and Rust run it on the worker.
repairs.answer: Closed by RC-8 point 2. Every drop that may wait (`Block`: a lock, a bounded channel's `send`, a receive, a `join`, a sleep) is never queued. In the example, the worker runs both `~Conn()`s, and the second waits until main receives, as with C++ and Rust. A wait built by hand from an `Atomic` (a spin loop) is not an operation the compiler sees as waiting. It is stated in `misuse`, as a spin lock taken twice is a hang in C. That a bounded `send` is `Block` follows from the table's 'an operation that may wait'; P14 is told, because the row lists receives and not sends.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: `~Conn()` placed before main's `tx.send` waits for `pool.lock`, while the worker holds it waiting for main's sends: a cycle the text never writes.
repairs.answer: Closed by RC-8 point 2. `~Conn()` takes a lock, so it runs on the worker at `b.conns.clear()`, before the worker takes `pool.lock`, and nothing hangs, as in C++ and Rust. No placed drop takes a lock, so the rule adds no wait between threads that the program does not write. Round 1's open risk 2 is gone.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: a job worker inside `pool.lock` runs a chunk itself, or another job, while it waits (PAR-4, stealing); the runtime's points cannot see the frame's lock or contract.
repairs.answer: Locks: no queued drop takes one, so a point the runtime places inside `pool.lock` waits for nothing. Contracts: RC-4 point 3 now sets the thread's mark around every call made inside a region where queued drops cannot run that may sleep or run jobs on this thread (a blocking call, `join`, the end of a `with scope` block, `jobs.wait`, a `@parallel` loop). Every point the runtime places (before a job, on a sleeping path, at a wait for work) tests the mark (JOB-6). The cost is one thread-local add and one subtract, only for such calls inside such a region.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: main sits an hour in a blocking foreign call (`net_accept`), which is not a rest, so values queued to it wait until the next client.
repairs.answer: Fixed in RC-4 point 6 and FFI-22. A foreign call that may block rests the thread for its length, as a blocking call's sleeping path does; it may block by its declared effects, and an undeclared foreign function counts as one that may (EFF-3). A callback C runs meanwhile leaves and re-enters rest as an outermost call does. In this example the `Conn`s are not queued anyway (their drop takes a lock), so their ids go back at once. A queued value would be ended at once by the session thread.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium: a hot-reload checkpoint migrates a value still in main's queue while the queue points at the old block; a `migrate_from` with a loop can end a queued instance in mid-prepare.
repairs.answer: Fixed in HR-3b and HR-2a. `std.hot.checkpoint()` is a check point, and it empties its thread's queue first when it is clear. A layout change of a type whose values may be queued to that thread applies only when that queue is empty. Every other thread is outside Ember code, so at rest with nothing queued. Otherwise the change is not applied at that checkpoint, and the report names the line. No point runs while prepare runs: a `migrate_from` is compiled with none, since prepare ends nothing (HR-2). So no queue link ever points at a migrated block.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: main sits in a C event loop (`run_event_loop`); its callbacks have no point and are not outermost, so `Session`s are freed only when the user quits.
repairs.answer: Fixed by the rest around a foreign call that may block. `run_event_loop` declares no effects, so it may block, and main rests for its whole length. The callback touches no `thread_shared` count, so it leaves main at rest, and the worker ends both `Session`s at once ('session 1 closed' is printed by the worker). A callback whose code does touch such a count leaves rest on entry, and at its return (a check point) empties its queue and rests again. A call marked `@ffi(no_callbacks)` that does not block pays nothing. The cost is stated in COST-3, and is to be measured.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: a `@deterministic` lock-step sim thread never rests, because rest needed a fully clear point and the queue's work was 'Nondet' by fiat; memory grows each turn, and P14's J6-07 was decided ahead of P14.
repairs.answer:
Both needless conditions are removed.
* Rest needs no clear point. While a thread rests, its values are ended on other threads by drops that never wait and never call C, which touch nothing its frames walk, view or are contracted for. So any blocking call's sleeping path rests the thread, and the sim thread rests in every `recv`.
* 'Counted as Nondet' is gone. Which values a point ends depends on timing, which DET-6 leaves out. Whether what the drops change makes a result `Nondet` is DET-2's question, decided under P14's J6-07. Nothing is decided here ahead of P14, and DET-2 needs no new entry.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: `~Job()` sends on a one-slot channel that only main receives from; placed on main, the second send waits for main itself.
repairs.answer: Same answer as the bounded-`send` hole: `~Job()` may wait, so the worker runs both drops where it ends `b`. Its second send waits until main receives 1, and the program finishes, as with `shared_ptr` or `Arc`. This narrows verdict 101 for such types; the verdicts section says so for the owner, with the evidence.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: RC-4 point 6 says 'end the value, then give the queue back', so the queue word becomes a lock held across user code (w1 inside `~Conn()` waiting for `pool.lock` while main cannot leave rest); item 7 of the cost section gave the opposite order.
repairs.answer: Same answer as the high-severity order hole. There is one order, written in RC-4 point 6, RT-8 and cost item 7: merge and set the ended mark while registered, deregister with a release, then run the drop at the line that ended the last owner. A thread that finds the queue in use never waits: a taker registers beside the others, and a putter to a running thread pushes as usual. `~Conn()` is not queued in this program.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: a test at every loop's back edge stops the C compiler from vectorising a counted loop like `integrate`.
repairs.answer: Fixed in RC-4 point 3. Points are placed so that a running thread never runs a loop for an unbounded number of rounds without one: at the back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known when it starts, and once every N rounds of a loop whose count is known (strip-mined, as HotSpot does). So `integrate`'s rounds between two tests are one loop that the C compiler can vectorise. COST-3 says so. N and the cost go on the laptop.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium: RC-8 point 3 put reload reclaim at 'the first clear point its thread reaches', which means nothing for removed fields of every thread; under `ember run --hot` the only poll is inside the same lock every frame, so the removed `Log` never ends.
repairs.answer: Fixed. Reload reclaim is out of RC-8's placed ends (RC-8 point 5 refers to HR-2a), and HR-2a decides its time. Removed fields are ended as a call at a host's poll, or at a checkpoint where that call is accepted with HR-44's facts of the frames below. Otherwise they are kept, and ended at the first later poll or checkpoint where the call is accepted. Under `ember run --hot`, the reload report names each drop that waits and what keeps it out, as HR-33 does for a missing checkpoint. 'Its thread' is no longer used for them. This is to be agreed with P09.

design.open_risks:
1. **A lock held across a `yield` (outside P05, real).** A generator suspended inside a lock's `with` block holds that lock while its consumer runs. A written `with` of the same lock, or a written end whose drop takes it, in the consumer's loop is then a self-wait that `[THR-19]` does not see. This rule no longer depends on it, but the gap needs its own owner question. One option is to refuse a `yield` inside a lock's block or with a live guard, as CORO-13 does for `@must_drop` and as C# does for `await` in `lock`. The other is to count the lock as held while the frame may be suspended there.
2. **Speed of the types handed over where they are made.** It is unmeasured on real programs; the only number is the own-objects loop (43.6 against 32.6 ms). Every `thread_shared` wrapper of a C resource, and every type whose drop takes a lock or sends on a bounded channel, counts atomically. If std's console printing waits or calls C, every drop that prints is handed over too. That is correct, but it widens the set. Measure on the laptop (P-cores, mains).
3. **The rest protocol is a new concurrent protocol** on the queue word: compare-and-exchange to enter, takers that register, a leaving mark. It must be stress-tested the way `stress.c` tested rule Q (the race found there was in this very hand-over). Rest around foreign calls that may block and around callbacks must be measured. A foreign function that declares no effects counts as possibly blocking, so it pays rest on threads that may have queued values. No number here is measured.
4. **Code size.** Copies of functions called inside contract regions cost code size. Where size matters, the compiler may use the mark instead, at one thread-local add and one subtract per call.
5. **N for strip-mined counted loops** is unmeasured. A recursion with no loop reaches a point only when it returns to a loop or ends.
6. **Coordination with other groups.**
   * P14: `Block` must carry every operation that may wait. The table's row names receives and reads, not a bounded `send` or a static's first access. Whether what the queued drops change is `Nondet` is J6-07's question.
   * P09: the time of reclaim. Removed fields that are one-thread values of other threads must be ended before those threads enter Ember again (HR-42's publication).
   * P01: the rule relies on `[THR-8]` and `[THR-20]`.
7. **Output from a drop may come from main or from a worker**, depending on timing. That was already so.
8. **A thread that sleeps where its queue cannot be emptied** (a blocking call inside `@noalloc` whose queued drops allocate) rests with those values still queued. They wait for its first clear point after it wakes.

The value is marked ended before its drop runs (verdict 56), on the maker and on a taker. A written end is checked as a call of the drop where it runs (verdict 57, point 1: E3020, E3060). # J7-01, unchanged: Conn's drop takes pool.lock, so a Conn is handed over where it is made
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())
    for frame in 0..1000:

                println(id)
    println(h.join())

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Log:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    lines: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

class Enemy:
    name: String

class Squad:
    leader: owns Enemy
    log: thread_shared Log
    fn drop():                                    # takes a lock: handed over where it is made (point 2)
        with this.log.lock:
            this.log.lines.push(owns String("squad gone"))

class Batch:
    squads: Array[thread_shared Squad] = []

class Camera:
    target: weakref Enemy = None

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    b = Batch(squads=[thread_shared Squad(leader=Enemy(name=String("boss")), log=thread_shared log)])
    cam = Camera()
    cam.target = weakref b.squads[0].leader       # a plain link on main to a one-thread Enemy the Squad owns
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.squads.clear())   # the worker runs ~Squad() and ends the Enemy
    for frame in 0..1000:
        if cam.target exists as p:                # main tests the Enemy's plain header, with no count
            println(p.name)                       # the worker may be freeing this String
    h.join()
# point 6, with a Squad whose drop neither waits nor calls C:
#     if cam.target exists as p:
#         rx.recv()          # main rests; the worker takes the Squad over and ends the Enemy at once
#         println(p.name)    # reads the freed String
holes.what_goes_wrong: Squad's drop takes a lock, so point 2 hands every Squad over where it is made, and the worker runs ~Squad() when it clears `b`. The Squad's field drops end the Enemy on the worker. Today the Squad travels inside `b`, so it is queued back and ended on main, which is safe. The Enemy is a one-thread object. Its weak count is plain, and `if cam.target exists as p:` tests its header and gives a view with no count, because RC-5 point 2 counts only for a thread_shared target. So main's test and the worker's end race on a plain field, and `p.name` may read the String the worker frees. Point 6 opens the same hole for a Squad whose drop neither waits nor calls C. Main rests in `rx.recv()` while `p` is live, the worker takes the Squad over and ends the Enemy at once, and `p.name` after the call reads freed memory. The point before `recv` was correctly kept out (a view the drop ends), but 'rest needs no clear point'. The design claims a resting thread's frames view nothing the takers' drops end, and that is false for this view. It also goes against verdict 166's reason: another thread must not end an object that weakref links on this thread point at. Nothing refuses the link today: WK-11 and WK-16 accept `weakref b.squads[0].leader` (a class object lives on its own), and THR-2 guards only links that travel, not targets that do.
holes.fix_hint: Settle it in P01, as verdict 166 settles it for tasks. A weakref link to a one-thread object that a thread_shared value owns is E7015 at the line that makes it ('another thread may end the leader; make it shared between threads: `leader: thread_shared Enemy`'). Then every object another thread may end counts its links atomically, and a view opened from such a link holds a count. Then state the invariant in RC-8: nothing a thread_shared value owns is linked with a plain count or viewed without one. If P01 does not take it, a type whose drop chain ends an object of a class that some weakref may name (the compiler knows these classes, as verdict 114 fix 1 uses them) is neither handed over at its making nor taken over.

# package `events`, compiled on its own
pub interface Handler: needs (Send, ThreadShared):
    fn handle(n: int)

pub class Sub:
    h: owns dyn Handler

pub fn subscribe(owns h: owns dyn Handler) -> thread_shared Sub:
    return thread_shared Sub(h=h)        # the making line: events knows no Handler whose drop waits

# the program, another package
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock
import events

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class PoolHandler:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

extend PoolHandler implements events.Handler:
    fn handle(n: int):
        pass

class Batch:
    subs: Array[thread_shared events.Sub] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(subs=[events.subscribe(owns PoolHandler(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool))])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.subs.len())
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            for id in pool.free:          # main hangs here
                println(id)
    println(h.join())
holes.what_goes_wrong: Whether `thread_shared Sub(...)` is handed over where it is made depends on Sub's drop chain. That chain runs the drop of whatever implementation sits in `h` (compiler_does 1: 'every implementation that may sit in an owns dyn field'). `subscribe` is compiled with `events`, which knows no implementation that waits. So its making line starts the header with the Sub on the home count, and the Sub can be queued. In the program, PoolHandler's drop takes `pool.lock`, so the program's compile treats Sub as a type that is never queued. The Sub travels inside `b`, so the worker's end queues it to main all the same. Main ends it at the inner walk's back edge, which counts as clear because a queued drop 'takes no lock'. ~PoolHandler() then waits for the lock main holds. Main hangs at a line nobody wrote, which is J7-01's own failure, reached through an ordinary library call. With a drop that calls C, it is the bus_dispatch case's undefined behaviour. Clear points have the same flaw. A package compiled alone places its points against the queued drops it knows, so a later package's allocating drop runs inside its `@noalloc` functions. I.6 rules out 'a correctness property that depends on whole-program optimisation or LTO', and packages are compiled separately (MONO-1, MNG-6, EFF-4).
holes.fix_hint: Make both decisions sound for code compiled alone. The making line reads the type's 'drop may wait or call C' bit from its TypeInfo (RT-3). The program's build sees every package's interface file (EFF-4), so it writes that bit, at the cost of one load per making line. Equivalently, a type whose drop chain reaches a `dyn`, a function value or a type parameter that another package may fill counts as possibly waiting. A package compiled alone places no point inside a contract region, or inside a walk or view of state that another package's code can reach, and uses the thread's mark for every call into another package.
