import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

class Texture:
    id: int

class Bundle:
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn finish(owns b: Bundle, tx: Sender[int]):
    b.textures.clear()                   # away -1; main rests, so this thread takes over: home 2 + away -1 = 1
    tx.send(owns 1).expect("main is gone")

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[int](capacity=1)
    t = thread_shared Texture(id=1)      # home count 1
    b = Bundle()
    b.textures.push(thread_shared t)     # home count 2
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b, owns tx: finish(owns b, tx))
    rx.recv()                            # main sleeps: at rest
    println(t.id)                        # main's own owner is still live
    h.join()
holes.what_goes_wrong: The resting maker still holds an owner, so the taker's merge gives 1, not 0. RC-4 point 6 and RT-8 say only 'adds the value's home count into its away count, marks the value ended when the sum is zero, and deregisters. Only then ... does it run the value's drops'. Nothing says what happens to the home count, to the queued mark, or to the handed-over mark when the sum is above zero. OBJ-1's change says the taker 'reads and writes' the home field, but not what it writes. Read literally, the taker runs ~Texture() anyway, and `t.id` reads a freed object. If the taker leaves the home count at 2 without marking the value handed over, main's plain decrement at its end reaches 1 and the Texture leaks. If it zeroes the home count without the mark, the decrement wraps the u32. Only 'zero the home count, clear the queued mark, set the handed-over mark, all before the release that deregisters' is correct. A protocol that was stress-tested for rule Q needs it written.
holes.fix_hint: Write the else branch in RC-4 point 6 and RT-8: when the sum is above zero, the taker stores the sum in the away count, sets the handed-over mark and clears the queued mark in one atomic step, zeroes the home count, deregisters with a release, and runs no drop. The maker, after its acquire on leaving rest, counts that value in the away count. Add this path to the stress test.

holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-4 point 6 says a thread rests even where it cannot empty its queue: 'A value it cannot end there stays queued until the thread's first clear point after it rests'. RT-8 says 'Entering rest is one compare-and-exchange of the thread's queue word, from empty to at rest ... When values arrived, the thread empties them and tries again'. Here the queue holds a Texture that main may not end inside `@noalloc`. The exchange from empty always fails, and 'empties them and tries again' cannot succeed. Followed literally, main spins in the rest entry instead of sleeping in `recv`, or it never rests, and other threads queue to it instead of ending at once. HR-3b's 'every other thread ... is at rest and has nothing queued' also depends on which reading holds.
holes.fix_hint: Write one entry protocol. A compare-and-exchange from 'running, list L' to 'at rest, list L' keeps the values that could not be ended in a list that takers never touch. The thread ends them at its first clear point after rest. Better, a thread entering rest with such a list hands it to the next thread that takes one of its values over, so a C thread that never calls back in does not keep them for ever. Say that HR-3b holds because a return to C is always clear for the values left.

from std.sync import Mutex

class Note:
    pitch: int

class Chord:
    notes: Array[thread_shared Note] = []

static PENDING: Mutex[Array[Chord]] = Mutex([])

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `on_midi`
@unsafe(export("on_midi"))
pub extern "C" fn on_midi(pitch: i32) -> i32:   # the driver's real-time thread; leaves rest on entry
    with g = PENDING.lock():
        g.push(owns Chord(notes=[thread_shared Note(pitch=pitch)]))
    return 0

fn drain():                                      # a low-priority Ember thread
    while true:
        with g = PENDING.lock():
            g.clear()       # ends Notes the driver thread made while it rests in C: this thread takes them over
holes.what_goes_wrong: Leaving rest is 'one atomic or of the leaving mark into the queue word, then a wait until the taker count is zero'. A taker runs only a few instructions, but the OS may preempt it between registering and deregistering. The driver thread's next `on_midi` then waits for the drain thread's time slice before its first line. That wait is in no line, no effect set (`Block`) and no contract. If the wait is a spin, a real-time driver thread on the same core as the drain thread (SCHED_FIFO, or one core) never lets the taker run, and it spins for ever. If the wait is a sleep, every exported call whose code may touch a home count may sleep on entry, which a `@noblock` or `@realtime` export cannot allow. It is a priority inversion the program never wrote, in the very C-audio case the design lists.
holes.fix_hint: Make leaving rest wait-free. Keep the home count a relaxed atomic (a plain load and store on every mainstream ISA) and use a sequence lock instead of waiting. Leaving rest increments the thread's rest epoch. A taker reads the epoch, merges, and confirms the epoch with one compare-and-exchange on the value's away word. If the epoch changed, the taker undoes its merge and pushes the value as usual. The maker then never waits. Measure it against today's protocol in stress.c.

from std.sync import Mutex

class Grain:
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println(f"grain {this.id} freed")    # allocates; may be queued to the driver thread

class Bank:
    grains: Array[thread_shared Grain] = []

class Voice:
    left: int

static BANKS: Mutex[Array[Bank]] = Mutex([])
static DONE: Mutex[Array[thread_shared Voice]] = Mutex([])

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `load`
@unsafe(export("load"))
pub extern "C" fn load(id: i32) -> i32:
    with g = BANKS.lock():
        g.push(owns Bank(grains=[thread_shared Grain(id=id)]))   # made on the driver thread
    return 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `mix`
@noalloc
@unsafe(export("mix"))
pub extern "C" fn mix(frames: i32) -> i32:
    with g = DONE.lock():
        g.clear()            # ends Voice owners: mix may touch a home count, so the thread is not at rest while it runs
    return frames            # an Ember thread clears BANKS meanwhile: the Grains are queued, and mix's return empties them
holes.what_goes_wrong: While `mix` runs, the driver thread is not at rest, so the Grains another thread ends are queued to it. No point inside `mix` is clear, because their drops allocate. 'Where a region that kept points out ends' is mix's return, and FFI-22's change says that when an outermost call returns to C the thread 'empties its queue'. So ~Grain() builds f-strings in the trampoline, after mix's last line but still inside the C driver's call to a `@noalloc` export, within its deadline. The contract the export's author wrote, and the C caller relies on, is broken by work nobody wrote. The design's own audio-driver case meets it as soon as an export both touches a home count and carries a contract.
holes.fix_hint: An outermost call's contracts cover its return to C. There the thread ends only the values whose drops those contracts allow. It rests with the rest still listed (hole 4's entry), and they are ended at its next clear point, or by the next thread that takes one of its values over.

import std.jobs
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:                  # waits: handed over where made, runs where the last owner ends
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = jobs.submit(owns fn() owns b: println(b.conns.len()))   # the job's state holds the last owner
    jobs.wait(h)
    with pool.lock:
        println(pool.free.len())
holes.what_goes_wrong: The job's captured `b` lives in its queue slot (JOB-1). It is ended by the job system on the worker after the job's function returns, at no line of the program. Point 1 checks ends 'where the source puts them', but no source line is there. THR-20's 'a function that ... holds such a count' is the job's function, whose body has already returned. The J7-01 answer itself relies on such an end ('the worker runs ~Conn() when b ends at the end of the worker's function'), which really happens where std or the runtime drops the function value. Before P05 this Conn would have been queued back to main. Under point 2, every drop that waits or calls C whose last owner a job, a thread's function or a kept callback holds now runs in that runtime path. The spec does not say what the runtime holds there (its queue or completion lock: a drop that submits or waits on a job then waits for itself). It does not say whether this runs before or after the HR-3 depth counter falls to zero (a host's ember_reload_poll() may swap code under ~Conn()), or before or after the thread rests or takes its next job.
holes.fix_hint: State it once. The end of a function value the runtime runs (a thread's, a job's, a scoped task's, a callback's after its once) is the end of that function's body block, on that thread. It is a written end, checked there as the block's locals are (point 1, THR-19, contracts). It happens before the thread rests, ends, returns to C, takes its next job or lowers its Ember depth, and with none of the runtime's own locks held, as THR-15 already says for a channel's values.

# Pool has `lock`, `free: Array[int] guarded by lock` and `closed: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)`
# image 1
class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        this.pool.closed.fetch_add(1)     # neither waits nor calls C: a Conn may be queued

# image 2, after a reload that changes only the drop's body
class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:              # now it waits
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

# main, not rebuilt, below `std.hot.checkpoint()` in its frame loop:
#     with pool.lock:
#         for id in pool.free:   # a point placed as clear against image 1's drop
#             println(id)
holes.what_goes_wrong: Conns made before the reload were made without the handed-over mark, so a worker's end still queues them to main. Main's inner walk keeps the point compiled against image 1, which judged it clear because no queued drop took a lock. The next queued Conn runs image 2's ~Conn() there, and it waits for the lock main holds: J7-01's hang, brought back by a reload. HR-44 refuses a reload that changes a fact 'code not rebuilt was checked against'. But the design keeps placed ends out of every summary (the EFF-1 change). The fact that decided both the hand-over at making and the clear points (whether a type's drop chain may wait or call C, and the queued drops' effects) is not among the facts a reload compares. A reload that adds an allocating drop to a queued type does the same to points inside `@noalloc` code not rebuilt.
holes.fix_hint: Add to HR-44's facts, for each thread_shared type, whether its drop chain may wait or call C. Add, for each point placed as clear, the queued drops' effects and summary it was judged against. Plan refuses (E9030) a reload that makes a type wait or call C while values of it made without the mark may live, or that makes a point in code not rebuilt unclear, naming the type, the drop and the line.

import std.thread

struct Pixels:
    data: Array[u8]

class Texture:
    pixels: owns Pixels using Pool       # Pool: a manager kind that frees values one by one

class Bundle:
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn main():
    pool = Pool.with_capacity(1024 * 1024)
    b1 = Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(pixels=owns Pixels(data=[0, 0]) using pool)])
    b2 = Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(pixels=owns Pixels(data=[1, 1]) using pool)])
    with s = thread.scope():
        s.spawn(owns fn() owns b1: b1.textures.clear())
        s.spawn(owns fn() owns b2: b2.textures.clear())
    # main rests at the scope's end: each task takes its Texture over at once and frees its Pixels into `pool`
holes.what_goes_wrong: Before P05, both Textures went back to main and were freed into `pool` one after the other, on the thread that owns the manager. Under point 6, the two tasks take their values over at the same moment ('several threads may take over values of one resting thread at once') and free into one one-thread manager together: a data race on its free list. Under point 2 the same happens for any value whose drop waits. P02's principle bounds a manager's values 'on the thread where the value may end', and its K05 question (thread_shared and `using`) was framed on today's rule that such a value ends on its maker. P05 makes that thread any thread, and several of them at once.
holes.fix_hint: State in RC-8 that a thread_shared value, and everything it owns, may end on any thread, and several of one maker's values at once. P02 then takes that as its 'thread where the value may end': a manager that serves any part of a thread_shared value must be ThreadShared, or `using` there is E7015 at the making line, as verdict 165 does for the value's contents. Show the two together to the owner.

# SAFETY: run_event_loop runs the window's callbacks until the user quits
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("call only on the thread that opened the window")
    unsafe fn run_event_loop()

fn main():
    open_window()
    # a worker ends the last owners of two Sessions main made
    unsafe:
        # SAFETY: this is the thread that opened the window
        run_event_loop()
holes.what_goes_wrong: FFI-22's change rests a thread during a foreign call that may block, 'by its declared effects, or, when none are declared, every effect (EFF-3)'. EFF-3 says an extern function carries the effects its contract declares, 'FFI at least', and EFF-3 is not among the rules the design changes. Read with EFF-3, `run_event_loop` carries FFI only, so main never rests in it, and the Sessions a worker ends stay in main's queue until the user quits. The design's own C-event-loop and accept-thread cases then fail. Read with FFI-22, the two rules disagree, and EFF-2 already gives every effect to a foreign function pointer with none declared.
holes.fix_hint: Change EFF-3 with this rule and list it: an extern function whose effects are not declared has every effect, as EFF-2 says for a foreign function pointer. A declared effect set without Block is a vouched fact (TCB-1).

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2's test is `Block` or `FFI`. A drop that only tries a lock is neither, so it may be queued and placed. At main's points inside its own `with g = pool.free.lock():`, the try always fails and the id is silently dropped. Run where its last owner ends, as C++ and Rust run it, it would usually succeed. What the drop does now depends on where the compiler put it (principle 7). The design's prose says 'a destructor that takes a lock, waits, or calls C runs where its last owner ends', but its rule says `Block`.
holes.fix_hint: Put `Lock` (any lock taken, try_lock included) beside Block and FFI in point 2's set, as the prose says. A drop that touches a lock then always runs where its last owner ends.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Points sit at back edges, every N rounds of counted loops, before blocking calls and at region ends. 'A recursion with no loop reaches a point when it returns to one.' A long recursive computation (a tree walk, a recursive-descent parser, a search) can run for hours with no loop, so queued values, and the memory they hold, are kept that long. The principle's bound ('before the thread waits idle, leaves Ember for C, or ends') holds, but the design's own bound ('a running thread never runs ... without reaching one') holds only for loops.
holes.fix_hint: Also place a point at the entry of each function in a recursive call group (HotSpot polls at method entry and return). Test it once every N calls if the cost matters, as counted loops do.

holes.what_goes_wrong: When main empties its queue it runs ~Cache(), and the loop inside that drop has a check point. Values queued meanwhile are emptied there, inside the outer pass. RC-4 point 2 says the thread 'empties its queue' but not that it takes the whole list before ending anything. An implementation that walks the list by the headers' `next` links while running drops can free, in the nested pass, a header the outer pass reads next. Round 0 raised this, and the repaired text still does not say it.
holes.fix_hint: Say in RC-4 point 2 and RT-8 that a thread takes its whole queue with one exchange, the acquire, before it ends any value in it. A nested point then sees only values queued afterwards.

holes.what_goes_wrong: There are three regions the clear test misses. (1) A function checked against a contract through its function type (verdict 106) or an interface method (EFF-2) is not 'a function under a contract' by its own attribute. So its points may run allocating drops while a plain caller runs it through `cb`. (2) The first access to a lazily initialised static inside a region runs the initialiser through `Once`. That is neither a direct call (no copy) nor in the mark's list, so its loops' points run queued drops inside the region. (3) The test asks whether 'a call of its drops, written there' is accepted. But ending a queued value is itself an atomic merge and a thread_shared end, which is `Sync` in the effect table. So points inside `@nosync` code pass the test and run atomics there.
holes.fix_hint: Under a contract means every contract a function is checked against, its type's and its interface method's included. Static initialisers reached inside a region run as a copy with no points, or under the mark. The clear test judges the whole end, its merge's `Sync` included, so no point is placed inside `@nosync`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Each Texture names its maker through its chunk's header, and every taker reads that thread's queue word, taker count and mark. The design says 'an ended thread is at rest for good'. It does not say that the thread's record lives as long as any value it made, or what happens when the allocator hands its chunks, or the OS its id, to a new thread. Such a thread would merge and end values another entry made, at points placed for the types its own entry makes (compiler_does 2 allows per-entry sets). Separately, FFI-22's change has `ember_rt_shutdown()` 'end what is still queued to each thread' with no condition that those threads are at rest. It may then merge the home counts of a thread still running, a data race.
holes.fix_hint: A thread's record (queue word, taker count, mark) lives until no chunk names it and is never given to another thread. A chunk is never handed to a thread of another entry while per-entry sets are used, or one program-wide set is required. ember_rt_shutdown ends only the queues of threads at rest, and waits (or reports) while a thread runs Ember code.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock, channel

class Pool:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    tx, rx = channel[thread_shared Conn](capacity=64)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: for c in rx: println(c.id))
    for i in 0..1000000:
        c = thread_shared Conn(id=i, pool=thread_shared pool)
        if i % 1000 == 0:
            tx.send(owns c).expect("receiver is gone")   # a hand-over of RC-4 point 4
    mem.drop(owns tx)
    h.join()
holes.what_goes_wrong: No `Conn` can ever be queued: the only route to another thread is the channel, a hand-over the compiler sees (verdict 101 fix 2, RC-4 point 4), and no `Conn` travels inside another object. Yet RC-8 point 2 (and compiler_does step 1) hands every `Conn` over at its making line only because `~Conn()` takes a lock, so the 999,000 Conns that live and end on main pay an atomic count instead of the plain home count. That is the design's own 43.6 ms against 32.6 ms on the own-objects loop, for a type whose waiting drop is never at risk. Step 2 already works out which types may be queued and does not use it here. P03's principle also chooses storage at the making line from what the program later does with the value.
holes.fix_hint: Hand a type over where it is made only when its drop chain may wait or call C AND its values may be queued (step 2's analysis: an owner may reach another thread inside another object without a point-4 hand-over). Every other lock-taking or C-calling type keeps 101's two counts. State it in RC-8 point 2, the COST-3 owner-count row and `ember inspect`'s list.

holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-4 point 3 and compiler_does step 5 place a test of the thread's queue at every back edge of a loop whose trip count is not known, and every N rounds of a counted loop, in every function of every program. The two-count COST-3 row keeps it 'guaranteed present'. The compiler already works out, per thread entry, which queueable types the entry's code may make (step 2), and uses that only to skip rest transitions (step 6). So a program with no queueable type, or a function reachable only from such threads, still pays a load of a word other threads write and a branch on every round of every `while`. C pays nothing. The C compiler may not hoist that load, so it also stops vectorising early-exit search loops like this one. The cost section contradicts itself: item 1 prices a check point outside a clash at one load and a branch, while 'Where it is zero' lists 'every check point outside a clash'.
holes.fix_hint: Place no check point (and no strip mining) in code that runs only on threads to which no value can be queued; with no queueable type in the program, place none at all. Make the COST-3 row 'guaranteed elided' there, and correct 'Where it is zero'.

holes.program:
from std.ffi import c_double

unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn hypot(x: c_double, y: c_double) -> c_double      # no @ffi(effects=[...])

fn lengths(xs: Span[f64], ys: Span[f64], ref mut out: MutSpan[f64]):
    for i in 0..xs.len():
        out[i] = hypot(xs[i], ys[i])
# main also makes thread_shared Texture values that reach a worker inside a Bundle (J7-02's shape)
holes.what_goes_wrong: A foreign function that states no effects has every effect (FFI-10, EFF-3), so under RC-4 point 6 and FFI-22 it 'may block'. On a thread whose code may make a queueable value, every one of the n calls is wrapped in a compare-and-exchange to enter rest and an atomic or with a load to leave it, all sequentially consistent (RT-8). C, Rust and COST-3's own 'FFI call' row ('one direct call for an ABI-direct C function', which the design leaves unchanged) pay one call. The cost buys nothing for safety, only a shorter wait for values queued during the call. It falls on the ordinary game or numeric loop, and the only way out is a word the programmer must add, `@ffi(effects=[], no_callbacks)`. The same two atomics are paid at the entry and return of every outermost call from C whose code may touch a home count, such as a per-entity `on_update` export.
holes.fix_hint: Rest around a foreign call only when its effects include Block as declared; an undeclared call leaves the thread running, and values queued meanwhile end at its first point after the return. Or give rest a fast path of plain thread-local stores, with the rare taker paying a process-wide barrier (FlushProcessWriteBuffers or membarrier, as HotSpot's and .NET's native-state transitions do), reusing HR-42's Ember-depth counter, which already marks a thread outside Ember code. Either way, update COST-3's FFI and export rows.

holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-8 point 3 calls a point clear when 'a call of its drops, written there, would be accepted'. `~Texture()` has no Sync, so the strip-mined points inside `scale` are clear. When the worker's end queues the Texture, main empties its queue inside `scale`: an acquire exchange of the queue word, and an atomic add merging the home count into the away count (ending a thread_shared owner). Both are the Sync that `@nosync` forbids (EFF table; EFF-1 counts an operation's count changes as its effects). An end written there would be E4002. `@nosync` is in EFF-14's usual inner-loop set, so the contract is broken at lines the program never wrote, against P14's principle that a contract means all of what it says.
holes.fix_hint: Test a point as 'the end of such a value, written there': the drops plus the end's own work (the queue's exchange and the merge, Sync). Then no point is placed inside @nosync code, and those inner loops carry no test at all.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Main empties its queue at a point and runs a Mesh's drop. Its loop over 1000 names reaches a strip-mined check point, which is clear and finds more Meshes the worker has just ended, so it empties the queue again inside that drop. That drop's loop does the same. Nothing in RC-4 points 2, 3 or 6 stops a point inside a drop the emptying runs from emptying again. While the worker ends Meshes faster than main finishes N names, the nesting deepens. Main never returns to its own loop, and the stack grows until 'stack overflow' aborts the program (RT-12). A flat emptying, or C++ freeing each Mesh on the worker, finishes.
holes.fix_hint: The emptying sets the thread's mark (RC-4 point 3) for its length. A point inside a drop it runs then leaves newly queued values for the emptying loop, which takes them after each drop, or for the next point once this snapshot is done. That gives constant stack, main keeps making progress, and the fast path costs nothing.

holes.what_goes_wrong: `~GpuBuffer()` has neither Block nor FFI, so it is queued to main. It then runs at a back edge of main's frame loop and spins until main sets `done`, which main does only after the loop: the program hangs. In C++ or Rust the worker spins until main sets the flag, and the program finishes. A drop that takes a lock without waiting has the same problem: `try_lock` has the Lock effect (EFF-21), but point 2 looks only at Block. Run at main's point inside main's own `with pool.lock:`, it always fails, so the id is silently never given back. That contradicts the design's 'no queued drop takes a lock'. The design lists the spin as a limitation, but the compiler can see the cause: a loop in the drop chain whose exit test reads memory another thread writes (an Atomic load, try_lock, try_recv).
holes.fix_hint: Count as 'may wait' in RC-8 point 2 every drop chain that takes a lock in any form (the Lock effect, try_lock included), or that contains a loop whose exit depends on a value another thread may write (an Atomic load, try_lock, try_recv in the condition). Such types end where their last owner ends, as C++ runs them. The limitation then leaves `misuse`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2 decides what a making line does (all counts atomic from the start, and which thread runs the drop) from facts worked out from drop bodies, including every implementation that may sit in an `owns dyn` field. EFF-25 and BLD-14 say a fact worked out from a body 'never changes what a line does: it decides only whether a line compiles, or removes a test'. Here an edit inside `~Saver()` silently moves drops between threads and changes their cost. Across a package edge the decision cannot be made at all: `make_host`'s making line is generated with the library, which cannot see the program's `Saver`. So a `Host` that travels inside an object is queued to main with a drop that may wait. Since RC-8 point 3 has 'no lock condition', that drop can run at main's back edge inside `with journal.lock:`, which is J7-01's self-wait again.
holes.fix_hint: State point 2 as an exception to EFF-25, with its reason (principle 6). Record 'drop may wait or call C' per type in the interface file. Decide it where the making line is compiled: either an `owns dyn` field of an interface other packages may implement counts as may-wait unless every implementation is known there, or the making line reads one flag from the type's information, which the program's final link sets from every implementation.

holes.program:
from std.sync import Receiver

class Buffer:
    samples: Array[f32] = []

static RETURNED: Receiver[thread_shared Buffer] = audio_returns()   # buffers the mixer gives back

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `on_audio`
@unsafe(export("on_audio", threads=any))
@realtime
pub extern "C" fn on_audio(frames: i32) -> i32:
    if RETURNED.try_recv() exists as b:     # b, a thread_shared owner, ends at the block's end
        return frames
    return 0
holes.what_goes_wrong: `on_audio`'s code may end a thread_shared owner, so by RC-4 point 6 and FFI-22 it 'leaves rest on entry': an atomic or of the leaving mark, then 'a wait until the taker count is zero'. Another thread may have registered as a taker of this driver thread's queue an instant before, and been preempted inside its few instructions. Then the @realtime (@noblock) callback waits on another thread's progress at a line the compiler placed. Placed work is in no effect set, so no contract sees it. This is the one wait the count protocol adds; rule Q's push and the merge are lock-free.
holes.fix_hint: Make leaving rest wait-free. A taker publishes the value it is merging in a per-taker slot, and the thread leaving rest completes that merge itself with the same CAS steps (helping), instead of waiting. Or takers claim each value with a CAS on its away word, so the maker never waits for another thread.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Points are placed so that a running thread never runs an unbounded number of loop rounds without one. Unbounded work without loops is not covered: 'a recursion with no loop reaches a point when it returns to one'. For the whole of `fib(50)`, or a recursive tree walk or recursive-descent parse of a large input, main reaches no point and does not rest. Every value queued to it meanwhile is held until the computation ends. The rule's own claim, a bound on when a queued value ends, does not hold for this ordinary shape.
holes.fix_hint: Also place a point at the entry (or return) of every function in a recursive group, tested like a back edge, as HotSpot polls at method returns. Strip it like a counted loop (every N calls, with a thread-local counter) if the test shows on calls.

holes.program:
import std.thread

class Texture:
    id: int

class Bundle:
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn main():
    t = thread_shared Texture(id=1)
    b = Bundle(textures=[thread_shared t])           # main's home count: 2
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.textures.len())
    println(h.join())   # main sleeps in join, so it rests; the worker's end of b takes over: 2 + (-1) = 1
    println(t.id)       # t ends at main's end
holes.what_goes_wrong: RC-4 point 6 says the taker 'adds the value's home count into its away count, marks the value ended when the sum is zero, and deregisters'. It says nothing for a non-zero sum, like this one. Main still owns `t`, and its later `-1` is a plain subtract of the home count (RT-10), which the taker has already folded into the away count. Read as written, either main's owner is counted twice and the Texture never ends (a leak), or an implementation that zeroes only one side ends it while `t` still points at it. Today's point 2 has the same gap for the maker's own merge, and the design copies it into the new take-over path.
holes.fix_hint: State that after any merge, by the maker or by a taker, the home count is zero and the value is marked handed over, so every later owner end (the maker's included) is an atomic subtract of the away count, and the subtract that reaches zero ends it at its line.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2's list of what 'may wait' (a lock, a bounded send, a receive, a join, a sleep, a static's first access) leaves out a blocking write or flush. The EFF table's Block row names only 'a blocking receive or read', so this drop is Io, not Block, and is queued to main. When the pipe is full, `~Report()` waits at main's back edge for a reader that is main: the bounded-send self-wait again, through a file. Where main is not the reader, the write still stalls main's loop, where C++ would stall the worker. The design tells P14 only about the bounded send and the static.
holes.fix_hint: Define 'may wait' by what the operation does, as P14's principle asks: a blocking write or flush (file, pipe, socket, console) included. List it in RC-8 point 2, and give it to P14 with the bounded send. If console output can wait, J7-02's Texture is then handed over too, and its answer text should say so.

engineering.notes:
Design B holds in its core. It refuses no correct program that compiles today: every refusal it names already exists through verdict 57, THR-19 and THR-20. The ordinary program is the same text, and the programmer writes nothing. Verdicts 43, 56, 57, 88, 114 and 164-166 are kept.

The two changes to verdict 101 are stated plainly with evidence, and both are really better than the alternatives:
- 'has ended' becomes 'is at rest': a take-over needs no wake, and a thread in C cannot be woken, so this beats J7-02 A's wake-ups.
- Atomics from the start for a drop that waits or calls C: this is the only way to run such a drop where C++ and Rust run it.

The holes are engineering ones:
- Medium, cost:
  - Point 2 is applied to every lock-taking or C-calling type, even ones that can never be queued (hole 1).
  - Check points are placed even where nothing can be queued (hole 2).
  - Rest surrounds every undeclared C call, and COST-3's FFI row is left saying one direct call (hole 3).
- Medium, rule clashes:
  - The clear-point test ignores the emptying's own Sync work, so @nosync loops get atomic read-modify-writes (hole 4).
  - The hand-over decision is a body fact that changes what a line does (EFF-25, BLD-14), and it cannot be made across a package edge (hole 7).
- Medium, robustness:
  - Nested emptying can grow the stack without bound under a steady producer (hole 5).
  - Hand-built waits and try_lock in a drop are queued and can hang or silently fail on the making thread (hole 6).
- Low: the leave-rest wait (hole 8), recursion with no loop (hole 9), the unstated non-zero merge (hole 10), blocking writes missing from 'may wait' (hole 11).

Every fix stays inside the rule's own mechanisms: step 2's queueability analysis, the thread mark, the interface file, P14's definition of 'may wait'. No fix adds a word for the programmer.

I ran no measurement. The 43.6 ms and 32.6 ms figures are the design's, from measure-0.9.15/brc/REPORT.md. No other number is given.

design.rule:
There is one rule for every call and every argument. The word before an argument says what happens to the caller's value, and it means the same for every callee: a function or method of the program, of std or of C, an operator, or a constructor.

* No word lends the argument. The callee gets a view of it, and the caller keeps it.
* `ref mut` lends it to be changed.
* `owns` hands it over, and the caller's name ends. `owns copy of x` hands over a copy. A value made in the call takes `owns`, or the word that makes it (`shares mut game`, `weakref this`).

A loan can fill an `owns` parameter only where the view is itself a value of the parameter's type, never by copying. That means:
* a function value that calls a function (a named one, a local one, or one held in a variable or field);
* a `StrView` of a `String`;
* a `Span` of an `Array`.

What the callee keeps of a loan lives no longer than the value lent. That covers an adapter it returns, a list element, a field, a thread, a job, a channel and C. The compiler works out from the callee's body what it keeps. A loan that would outlive its value is refused at the call, and the message gives `owns x` and `owns copy of x`.

An operator is a call of its interface's method, with both operands lent. So `a + b` reads both and makes a new value, and `a += b` changes `a` in place. String is no exception.

A construction `Name(...)` works as `=` (verdict 159). Each argument goes into the constructor's place, a field or a written init's parameter, the way `=` would put it there:
* a field or an `owns` parameter takes a whole name over;
* a plain parameter views it;
* `ref mut` is written for a `ref mut` parameter.

The object before the dot is not marked. Its method's first line (`owns this`) or its body says what happens to it (verdict 1).
design.spec_text:
Changes [FN-2a], [GRM-15], [OWN-9], [OWN-12], [STD-19], [CLO-7], [CLO-10], [CLO-12], [GRM-28], [TYP-21], [TXT-11], [STR-1], [STR-6] and [CLS-2]. Adds [FN-2b], [FN-2c] and [OWN-8a].

[FN-2a] (changed) **The word before an argument says what happens to it, for every callee.** This holds alike for a function or method of the program, of the standard library or of C, for an operator (`[TYP-21]`) and for a constructor (`[FN-2c]`).
* No word **lends** the argument (`[FN-2b]`).
* `ref mut` lends it to be changed, with the parameter's words, `const` included: `bump(ref mut a)` for `fn bump(ref mut c: Counter):`, and `mem.take(ref mut this.items)`.
* `owns` **hands it over**, and the caller's name ends: `take(owns xs)` for `fn take(owns xs: Array[int]):`.
* `owns copy of xs` hands over a copy and keeps `xs`.
* `owns` before a value made in the call hands that value over: `take(owns [1, 2])`; `names.push(owns p.name)`, a part (`[OWN-11]`); `xs.iter().for_each(owns fn(x: int): println(x))`.
* A value made in the call by a word that makes an owner or a link takes that word and no `owns`: `setup(shares mut game)`, `ROSTER.push(weakref this)`, `start_logger(thread_shared log)`.

The word must be one the parameter takes:
* for an `owns` parameter, `owns`, or a loan that `[FN-2b]` lets it hold;
* for a plain parameter, no word;
* for a `ref mut` parameter, `ref mut`.
Anything else is `E3028`, with the messages of verdict 157.

A plain `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or channel-end parameter takes no word, like every plain parameter. `ref mut` before one is `E3028`, because its own 'only me' is the lock's block. An `owns` one takes `owns`: `start_worker(owns rx)`.

The object before the dot is not marked. Its method's first line (`owns this`) or its body says what happens to it (`[FN-4]`, `[EXC-15]`).

`return a` takes no word. Neither does `e?`, which hands `e` over the way `return` does (`[OWN-9]`).

Removed: 'A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word'. `[FN-2b]` replaces it for every callee.

[FN-2b] (new) **A loan, and what a callee keeps of it.** A name or place given with no word is lent. The callee gets a view of it, and the caller's name stays the caller's.

A plain parameter reads through the view for the call.

An `owns` parameter holds the view itself as its own value, where the view is a value of the parameter's type made from the argument without copying it (`[TYP-5]` rules 4, 6, the first half of 7, and 10). That is:
* a function value that calls a named function, a local function, or a function held in a variable or a field, given to a callable type or to a type parameter with a callable bound (`fn()`, `thread_shared fn()`, `[F: needs fn(Item)]`);
* a `StrView` of a `String`;
* a `Span` of an `Array`;
* a `ref T` of a place.

A function with no state is lent as itself, since its code lives as long as the program (`[CLO-1]`).

A function that changes its own state when it runs (`[CLO-18]`) is lent with `ref mut`: `xs.iter().for_each(ref mut tally)`.

In every other case a loan is not a value of an `owns` parameter, and the call is `E3028`. This covers a number, a `String`, an `Array`, a class object, and a view held in a name, which lending would copy. So `take(xs)` and `names.push(p.name)` are refused, and so is `words.push(w)` for `w: StrView`, whose fix is `owns w`. A type parameter with no callable bound is never made a view to fit a loan: `mem.drop(g)` is `E3028`, with the help 'write `mem.drop(owns g)`'. A value made in the call has no owner to lend from, so for an `owns` parameter it takes `owns`.

**Whatever the callee keeps of a loan lives no longer than the value lent** (`[TYP-15]`, `[CLO-4]`). This covers what it keeps in its result (as an iterator adapter does), in a list, a map, a field or a static, on a thread or in a job, in a channel, and in C.

The compiler works out from the callee's body which parameters it keeps and where. Within a package this is the callee's summary (`[EFF-24]`); across a package's edge it is the interface file (`[EFF-4]`). The compiler follows the keeper as it follows every view. A `thread.spawn` thread, an unscoped job, and C count as never ending, unless Part XVI ties C's hold to a token Ember owns.

A loan kept where it would outlive its value is refused at the call. The message names the keeper and both ways out:
* `E7004` for a thread, a job or C: 'the thread may outlive `main` (dropping `a` lets it run on), so it cannot call `main`'s `push_a`; hand it over: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, or keep yours and give it a copy: `thread.spawn(owns copy of push_a)`';
* `E3026` for a kept function value;
* `E3063` for a kept view.
`owns copy of h` is offered only where `h` can be copied (`[CLO-10]`).

These are loans and compile:
* `xs.iter().for_each(h)`;
* `total = xs.iter().map(h).sum()`;
* `it = xs.iter().map(h)`, used inside the function;
* `b.handlers.push(beep)`, for a `b` that ends with `beep`;
* `words.push(line)`, for `words: Array[StrView]`;
* `scope.spawn(task)`, whose tasks end with their scope (`[THR-11]`).

These are refused, with `owns push_a` and `map(owns h)` as the help:
* `thread.spawn(push_a)` of a local function with state;
* `return xs.iter().map(h)` of a local `h`.

A function of the module is lent anywhere with no word: `thread.spawn(worker)`, `b.on_click(log_click)`, `xs.iter().map(double)`. `owns` before one is `E0109`: 'nothing owns `worker`, a function of the module, and it never ends; remove `owns`'.

While a keeper may still call a lent function, no other name changes the function or what it reads (`[BRW-1]`).

[FN-2c] (new) **A construction works as `=`.** `Name(…)` puts each argument into the constructor's place, the way `=` puts a value into a place of that kind. This holds for:
* a memberwise constructor (`[STR-1]`, `[CLS-3]`);
* a written `init` (`[STR-6]`, `[CLS-2]`);
* a base's `init`, through `super.init(…)` or `[CLS-10]`;
* `Self(…)`;
* an enum variant, such as `Some(x)`.

Each argument goes as follows:
* A field, or an `owns` parameter of a written `init`, takes a whole name over, and copies a value that `=` copies.
* A plain parameter of a written `init` views it, as every view does.
* An `init`'s `ref mut` parameter takes `ref mut` before its argument, as `r = ref mut x` does.
* `owns` stays on the line that makes a value for a place that owns it in a block of its own (`[OWN-10]`): `Entity(mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0]))`.

So:
* `Emitter(title)` for `fn init(owns name: String):` hands `title` over;
* `Label(caption)` for `fn init(text: String):` lends `caption`;
* `Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over;
* `Point(x=a)` copies `a`;
* `Emitter("fountain")` makes the `String`.

`owns` before a whole name at a construction is `E0109`: 'a construction already hands `title` over (`Emitter`'s `init` takes `owns name`); remove `owns`: `Emitter(title)`'. Before an argument for a plain `init` parameter it is `E3028`. A later use of a name that a construction took over is `E3040`, and the message names the constructor's parameter or field.

[OWN-8a] (new) **A copy of what is not used again.** A function may make `copy of` a plain parameter or of `this` while the caller's argument is a value of the caller's own that nothing uses afterwards: a temporary, or a name at its last use. The compiler may then hand the function that value to use as the copy. This applies when ending the value would run no code except releasing its memory, meaning it has no `drop` of its own, all the way down. Nothing the program can observe changes, and any allocation it still needs is counted (`Alloc`).

[TYP-21] (changed) An operator's operands are lent, as every argument with no word is (`[FN-2a]`), and an implementation takes them the way the interface's method does. `bool` and `char` implement none of the operator interfaces. `String` implements `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, which reads both operands and gives a new `String`, and `AddAssign[StrView]`, which appends in place (`[TXT-11]`). Removed: '`String` implement[s] none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)'.

[TXT-11] (changed) `a + b` for `a: String, b: StrView` reads both and gives a new `String`, and `s += t` appends to `s`. Where `a` is not used again (`s = s + t`, or the `a + b` inside `a + b + c`), the new `String` is built in `a`'s buffer (`[OWN-8a]`). `StrView + StrView` is `E2040`, and its help is an f-string.

[CLO-10] (added) `copy of` a function value copies its state field by field, the way `[OWN-8]` copies a value that holds links:
* an `owns` or `copy of` capture is copied itself;
* a `shares` or `thread_shared` capture becomes one more owner;
* a `weakref` capture becomes one more link.
The real variables it uses are the same ones. A state that holds something that cannot be copied makes `copy of` `E2116`.

[STD-19] (changed) A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word (`[FN-2b]`), as it is to every callee, and an adapter made from a lent function lives no longer than that function. After `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is still the caller's and `h(5)` runs it (ODR-240). `return xs.iter().map(h)` of a local `h` is `E3063`, with the help `map(owns h)`.

[CLO-7] (changed) Add: a function from a variable given to one of these functions is lent (`[FN-2b]`). A thread, a job or a registry that may outlive the function does not keep a loan of it: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)` hands a local function over, while `scope.spawn(task)` lends one, since its tasks end with the scope.

[CLO-12], [GRM-28] (changed) The example becomes '... then `a = thread.spawn(owns push_a)`'.

[GRM-15] (changed) '... before an argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given, unless the argument is a loan the parameter holds (`[FN-2b]`) or a value made by a word that makes an owner or a link (`[FN-2a]`) ...'.

[OWN-9] (changed) 'and a construction works as `=` (`[FN-2c]`)' replaces 'and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does'.

[OWN-12] (changed) The text becomes 'takes it by an ordinary hand-over, `widget_take(owns first)`', by verdict 147. `[OWN-6]`'s message already writes it that way.

[STR-1], [STR-6], [CLS-2] (added) 'A call of it works as `=` (`[FN-2c]`).'

answers.answer: The rule lends `push_a`, as it lends every argument given with no word. `thread.spawn` keeps its function on a thread that may outlive `main`, because dropping the handle detaches the thread (THR-10). So the loan is refused at the call, and the hand-over has to be written: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, or `owns copy of push_a` to keep main's own. Verdict 51's two ways of writing a thread body both still compile; the local-function way is now spelled with `owns`, as verdict 147 spells every hand-over. A local function with no state, or a function of the module (`thread.spawn(worker)`), is lent with no word, because nothing it points at can end. `scope.spawn(push_a)` lends it, since its tasks end with the scope.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Mutex

class Log:
    lines: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([])

    fn add(line: StrView):
        with g = this.lines.lock():
            g.push(owns String(line))

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    fn push_a() thread_shared log:
        log.add("a")
    a = thread.spawn(owns copy of push_a)     # the thread gets a push_a of its own
    push_a()                                  # main's push_a still runs here
    a.join()
answers.outcome: It compiles, and the log gets "a" twice. `push_a`'s state is one `thread_shared` owner of `log`, so its copy is one more owner. `thread.spawn(push_a)` with no word is E7004: 'the thread may outlive `main` (dropping `a` lets it run on), so it cannot call `main`'s `push_a`; hand it over: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, or keep yours and give it a copy: `thread.spawn(owns copy of push_a)`'. With `thread.spawn(owns push_a)` the line compiles, and the `push_a()` after it is E3040 ('`push_a` was handed to `thread.spawn` on line 15').

answers.answer: Lent. `push`'s parameter, `owns value: Handler`, has a callable type, and a callable value may call a function it does not own. So the loan itself becomes the element: a function value that calls `beep`. The list keeps it no longer than `beep` lives. `beep` holds no state, so it is lent as itself, and here the list could even outlive `main`. A handler with state bounds the list. Verdict 149's own line (`names.push(p.name)`) is still an error, because a loan of a `String` is not a `String`. Verdict 150's 'a function from a variable given to std is borrowed' reaches `push`, as its words say.

type Handler = fn()

class Button:
    handlers: Array[Handler] = []

fn main():
    b = Button()
    beep = fn(): println("beep")
    b.handlers.push(beep)              # lent: the list holds a function that calls beep
    beep()                             # beep is main's still
    for h in b.handlers:
        h()

fn make_button(who: String) -> Button:
    b = Button()
    greet = fn() copy of who: println(f"hi {who}")
    b.handlers.push(owns greet)        # b is returned and greet ends here: handed over
    return b
answers.outcome: `main` compiles and prints "beep" twice. In `make_button`, writing `b.handlers.push(greet)` with no word is E3026 at the push: '`b.handlers` keeps a function that calls `greet`, and `b` is returned on line 18 while `greet` ends there; hand it over: `b.handlers.push(owns greet)`, or give it a copy: `b.handlers.push(owns copy of greet)`'. The line as written, with `owns greet`, compiles.

So String implements `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, which reads both and gives a new String, and `AddAssign[StrView]`, which appends in place. The built-in path and its hidden hand-over go. A generic `Add` bound now accepts a String.

A construction works as `=`: verdict 159's words name every constructor ('a constructor's argument ... works as `=` does'). Each argument goes into the constructor's place the way `=` would put it there.
* The init's `owns name` is an owning place, so `Emitter(title)` hands `title` over with no word, as `Words(names=xs)` does.
* Label's plain `text` is a view place, so `Label(caption)` lends `caption`.
* An init's `ref mut` parameter takes `ref mut`, as `r = ref mut x` does.
The overview's `Emitter("fountain")` stays as it is.
answers.code:
class Emitter:
    name: String
    rate: f32 = 100.0

    fn init(owns name: String):          # this init takes the name over
        this.name = name

class Label:
    text: String

    fn init(text: String):               # this init only reads what it is given
        this.text = copy of text

fn main():
    title = String("fountain")
    fountain = Emitter(title)            # handed over, as = would
    caption = String("smoke")
    sign = Label(caption)                # lent: the init only reads it
    println(fountain.name)
    println(sign.text)
    println(caption)
answers.outcome: It compiles and prints `fountain`, `smoke`, `smoke`. A `println(title)` after line 16 would be E3040: '`title` was handed to `Emitter` on line 16 (its `init` takes `owns name`); to keep it, write `Emitter(copy of title)`'. `Emitter(owns title)` is E0109: 'a construction already hands `title` over; remove `owns`'. `Label(owns caption)` is E3028: '`Label`'s init only reads `text`; remove `owns`'.

design.prior_art:
**C++.** The callee's signature decides: `const T&` lends, a by-value parameter copies, and `T&&` takes over. The call writes `std::move(x)` to hand over, but nothing for a copy or a loan. Nothing checks what a callee keeps of a reference: `std::thread t([&f]{ f(); }); t.detach();` compiles and calls a dead `f`. `std::function` copies its target. `std::string` has a `const&` and a `&&` overload of `operator+`, so a temporary left side is appended to. A constructor is an ordinary call, so a by-value `std::string` parameter copies unless the caller moves.

**Rust.** A call with no word moves, so the hand-over is not written in the line. Its `String + &str` consumes the left operand silently, which is exactly Ember's TXT-11 today. `&f` and `&mut f` lend, and lifetimes check what a callee keeps of a loan (`Vec<&dyn Fn()>`, a returned `iter().map(&f)`); this is the same check FN-2b reuses. `thread::spawn` requires `F: 'static`, so it refuses any loan even when the thread is joined, while `thread::scope` lends. Struct literals move their fields.

**Swift.** Arguments are borrowed by default, and `consuming` parameters and `consume x` (5.9) hand over. Initialisers take their arguments owned (+1) by convention, as FN-2c does. A closure parameter is lent (non-escaping) unless the callee writes `@escaping`, and escaping closures are reference-counted. `String + String` reads both sides and makes a new String; `+=` appends.

**Ada.** Parameter modes (in, in out, out) say what a callee does. `'Access` of a local subprogram is checked against accessibility levels when compiling, so it cannot escape (FN-2b's refusal), but `'Unchecked_Access` bypasses the check.

**Go and C#.** Closures capture by reference, and escape analysis or the collector keeps them alive. That is safe, but each escaping closure is a heap object. Strings are immutable, so every `+` allocates.

**Zig.** There are no closures: a function pointer plus an explicit context pointer. That is Ember's stored loan without the check.

**Where each falls short of safe, as fast as C, and readable:**
* C++ is fast but unchecked.
* Rust is checked, but it moves with no word and refuses `thread::spawn` loans even when they would be safe.
* Swift makes the programmer write `@escaping`, a fact its compiler could read from the body, and pays reference counts for it.
* Go and C# pay a collector.

FN-2b takes Rust's lifetime check, Swift's default loan and initialiser convention, and C++'s speed, and the compiler reads from the callee's body what Swift asks the programmer to write.
design.cost:
Every check is made when compiling; nothing runs while the program runs.

**A loan to a callee that runs it now** (`for_each(h)`, `map(h).sum()`): the callee is compiled for the lent function's own type and calls it directly, and the call can be inlined (CLO-14). The cost is zero. That is cheaper than a C callback in the style of `qsort`, which pays one indirect call per item and cannot be inlined.

**A loan kept as a function value** (`push(beep)`, `on_click(handler)`, an adapter in a field):
* It is two words, a call stub for the lent function's own type and the function's address, with no allocation and no count.
* A call is one indirect call, which is what a C function pointer with a context pointer costs. That is followed by one direct call into the lent function, which is inlined into the stub when its own type is known (a lambda or a local function).
* A function with no state is kept as itself: one word of code and no address.
* When the lent value is itself a `fn()` that is already erased, the stub makes a second indirect call.

**`owns h`:** a move of two words.

**`owns copy of h`:** a copy of h's state, which is one allocation when the state has a block.

**String `a + b` where `a` is used again:** one allocation of `len(a) + len(b)` and two copies. That is what C pays (`malloc` and two `memcpy`) and what C++'s `const std::string& + const char*` pays.

**String `a + b` where `a` is not used again** (the inner `a + b` of `a + b + c`, or `s = s + t`): OWN-8a lets `add` extend `a`'s own buffer, an amortised append. That is what C's `realloc` plus `memcpy` and C++'s `std::string&& + ...` pay.

**`s += t`:** an amortised append, as `std::string::append` is.

**An f-string:** one allocation for the whole text.

**A construction:** each argument moves as `=` does (a copy of its words). That costs nothing beyond the object's own block, as C's struct initialisation.

**Memory:** two words per kept loan, the size of any function value, and nothing for a loan that is used and ended in the call.

These are mechanisms only. Nothing has been measured on the laptop.

design.compiler_does:
At each call, the compiler resolves the callee: a function, a method, the interface's method for an operator, or the constructor for `Name(...)`. It then reads each argument's word against the parameter's word.

**A name given with no word to an `owns` parameter.** The compiler asks whether a view of the name is a value of the parameter's type: TYP-5 rules 4, 6 and 10, the first half of rule 7, or a callable bound. If it is not, the call is E3028, with `owns x` and `owns copy of x` as help. It never makes a bare type parameter into a view.

**Following a loan.** The compiler reads the callee's summary (EFF-24), or the interface file across a package (EFF-4). The summary says which parameters the callee keeps and where: in its result, in a field or element of another argument, in a static, on a thread, in a job, in a channel, or in C. The compiler treats the keeper as holding a view of the argument. TYP-15 and CLO-4 then check that the keeper ends before the argument; a `thread.spawn` thread, an unscoped job and C count as never ending. A refusal is reported at the call, naming the keeper's line, and `owns copy of h` is offered only where h's state can be copied. Verdicts 122, 128 and 129 then follow the lent function's effects into the place that holds it.

**Building the kept value.** For a type parameter, the callee is compiled for the lent function's own type. Otherwise the kept value is two words: a call stub for the argument's own type, and the argument's address. A function with no state is kept as itself, and a loan of a `once fn` is refused.

**Constructions.** The compiler treats each argument as `=` into a field or an init's parameter.

**Operators.** The compiler calls the interface's method with both operands lent. Where the left operand is a temporary or a name at its last use, owned by the caller, and ending it would run no code except freeing memory (worked out from its drop), the compiler gives a callee that copies it the value itself (OWN-8a).

None of this runs while the program runs.
design.misuse:
Every misuse is refused when compiling, at the line, and none can produce undefined behaviour. Every help line compiles (checklist 9).

**A loan kept past its value:**
* `thread.spawn(push_a)` is E7004.
* `b.handlers.push(greet)` with `b` returned is E3026.
* `return xs.iter().map(h)` of a local `h` is E3063.
* `register_cb(on_tick)` with C keeping a local function is E7004.
Each message names the keeper and gives `owns x`, and gives `owns copy of x` only where the function's state can be copied.

**A loan given to an `owns` parameter whose type a view is not:** `take(xs)`, `names.push(p.name)`, `mem.drop(g)`, and `words.push(w)` for a view held in a name are E3028, with verdict 157's messages.

**`owns` where it does not belong:**
* before a module function is E0109;
* before an operand (`(owns label) + \"!\"`) is E3028;
* before a whole name at a construction is E0109;
* before an argument for a plain init parameter is E3028.

**Other misuses:**
* Changing a lent function, or something it reads, while a keeper may still call it, is refused by the read-only rules (verdict 5, BRW-1).
* A lent function that changes its own state, given without `ref mut`, is E3023 (CLO-18).
* A loan of a `once fn` is E3013.
* A later use of a name that a construction, an `owns this` method or `?` took over is E3040, naming that line.
design.verdicts:
**Kept:**
* **Verdict 1:** the object before the dot is not marked.
* **Verdict 3:** a lock or channel end takes no word for a plain parameter, and `ref mut` before one stays E3028. Its reason concerns `ref mut`, so an `owns` parameter of one takes `owns` (J3-04, a one-line confirmation).
* **Verdict 5:** a loan never copies and never aliases a changeable value.
* **Verdict 51:** both ways of writing a long thread body compile. Say plainly to the owner that the spec's local-function line `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` becomes `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, because the thread may outlive what it borrows and verdict 147 writes every hand-over.
* **Verdict 80:** a function that outlives its maker owns what it keeps. FN-2b is the same rule at the call.
* **Verdicts 84, 145, 146, 148, 158 and 161:** kept as written.
* **Verdict 149:** `names.push(p.name)` is still an error, because a loan of a String is not a String.
* **Verdict 94:** kept, and no longer an exception: `scope.spawn`'s tasks end with the scope, so a loan to them is kept no longer than its value.
* **Verdict 160:** kept. Its reason, 'the word that makes the value says what is given', is applied to `thread_shared x` and `sharedref mut x` made in the call (J1-06, a one-line confirmation).
* **Verdicts 122, 128 and 129:** a lent function stored in a list is followed the exact way.
* **Verdict 159:** kept, and carried by its own words ('a constructor's argument ... works as `=` does') to every constructor. A written init's `owns` parameter takes a whole name over and its plain parameter views it (J1-07; option F would narrow 159 to memberwise constructors).
* **Verdicts 164 to 166:** untouched.

**Revisited under option A: verdicts 150 and 147.** Verdict 150's loan is given to every callee, not only to std's functions. Verdict 147's 'whatever is passed' still holds wherever a loan is not a value of the parameter's type, so every example shown with 147 is unchanged: an `Array`, a list literal, `owns copy of`.

The evidence that this is really better:
1. The same first line, `[F: needs fn(Item)] fn ...(owns f: F)`, means a loan in std and a hand-over in a program (J3-03). That breaks 'a written declaration means only what it says' (checklist 15).
2. The compiler decides what a call means from the callee's module path (D-963: 'a function value is lent only to a function of the standard library's (its symbol's module path)'). That is a hidden path only std can take (checklist 13).
3. A program cannot write a library as convenient as std: an ECS's `world.each(update)` would need `owns update`.
4. A module function given by name (`apply(double, 3)`) would need `owns double`, a word that says something untrue, since nothing owns it and it never ends (principle 6).

Option B keeps verdicts 147 and 150 word for word.

recommendation.reason: A is one rule for every callee and every argument. The word before an argument says what happens to it, and a loan is kept no longer than its value, which the compiler reads from the callee's body as it already does for views (verdict 137) and for function values (CLO-4). It keeps every example the owner was shown: `take(xs)` and `names.push(p.name)` are still errors, `for_each(h)` still lends, `Words(names=xs)` still hands over, and `Emitter("fountain")` is unchanged. It refuses only the lines that would dangle: a thread or a returned adapter keeping a local function. It removes the one path only std may take (the compiler's module-path test, D-963) and the one hand-over written with no word (String's `+`). The ordinary program stays the same length. It does widen verdict 150 and narrow verdict 147; B keeps both word for word, at the price of that std-only path.

| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `start(log)` runs `fn push_a() thread_shared log:` | `push_a`'s state block holds one owner of `log` |

B: as A, but a function is lent only to std, and a program's own `owns f` needs `owns`.

design.open_risks:
1. **Verdicts.** Option A widens verdict 150 beyond std and narrows verdict 147, so it is the owner's decision. Option B is the literal alternative, and J3-03's 'already decided' changes under A.
2. **Constructions (J1-07).** Under the rule, whether a construction ends a name depends on the constructor's first line: an owning place takes it, a view place views it. That already depends on a memberwise field's type today. The E3040 message must name the init's parameter.
3. **Cost of a stored loan.** A loan stored as a `fn()` costs a call stub, whose inner call is inlined when the lent function's own type is known, and two indirect calls when the lent value is already an erased `fn()`. That is the mechanism only, not measured on the laptop.
4. **OWN-8a.** OWN-8a's elision is a permission and has not been measured. Without it, `a + b + c` makes one String per `+`. It applies only to values whose end runs no code.
5. **Library changes.** What a callee keeps is read from its body, and across a package from its interface file. A library change that starts keeping a parameter breaks callers' lines, with the chain named; verdict 86 accepted that cost.
6. **Missing pieces.** The rule needs P04's missing rule that an interface implementation's parameter words match the interface, so that no `Add` takes `owns this`. It also needs the CLO-10 sentence on copying a function value, so that the `owns copy of h` help compiles.
7. **Copying a view.** Keeping a `StrView` held in a name while giving a copy of it waits on P11's J2-01.
8. **The method's object.** The object of an `owns this` method stays unmarked (verdict 1). The only fully uniform alternative, `(owns it).sum()`, is not offered, because it lengthens every iterator chain and every `join()`.
9. **Dependants.** P08 builds on FN-2b for callbacks C keeps (J8-01: `register_cb(owns on_tick)`, with a module function lent), and on FN-2c for adopted objects. P15's J3-05 relies on FN-2c's `super.init(id=id)` taking no word.
10. **One-line confirmations.** J1-06 (`thread_shared` and `sharedref mut` made in the call) and J3-04 (an `owns` channel end) each need a one-line confirmation, as phase 3 said.

holes.program:
fn shout(line: String) -> String:
    loud = copy of line
    loud.push_str("!")
    println(line)                 # the parameter, read after its copy changed
    return loud

fn main():
    bar = String("=-")
    for i in 0..4:
        bar = bar + bar           # bar += bar is E3021 (BRW-11); this is its plain fix
    println(bar)
    println(shout(String("hey")))
holes.what_goes_wrong:
`bar + bar` lends both operands. BRW-11 sees two reads and lets the line through. `bar` is at its last use, since it is given a new value, so OWN-8a lets `add` take bar's own buffer as its copy and then `push_str` the right operand into it. That right operand is a view of the same buffer. Doubling the text goes past the capacity, so push_str reallocates. It frees the buffer the right operand still points into, then copies from it: a read of freed memory in a loop meant only to double a string.

In `shout`, the temporary is handed over as `loud`. `loud.push_str("!")` changes, or reallocates, the very text `line` views. `println(line)` then prints `hey!`, or reads freed memory.

OWN-8a states 'Nothing the program can observe changes' as a fact, with no condition that makes it true. The design widened phase 3's 'a temporary' to 'or a name at its last use', and that widening is what lets the aliasing operand in. Neither version requires the copy to be the parameter's last use in the callee.
holes.fix_hint:
State OWN-8a's conditions in the rule.
(1) During the call, no other argument views or reaches any part of the value, and neither does any real variable or state of a function argument.
(2) The `copy of` is the parameter's last use in the callee on every path. The compiler reads this from the body and records it in the summary, as BRW-21 does for views.
(3) The value is owned alone (hole 4).
Or keep phase 3's 'a temporary' and add (2). `bar = bar + bar` then makes one new String (malloc and two memcpy, as C does). `s = s + t` still extends s's buffer wherever t does not view s.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The loan bounds `d` by `say`. By name, `d` is last used before `say` ends, so the call is accepted, as the design accepts 'b.handlers.push(beep), for a b that ends with beep'. But a class is never a view type (TYP-14/15), so `weakref Doc` carries no bound, and the link made from `d` does not know that `d` holds a loan.

At main's end, `say` and `tag` end first. Then `c` ends, and its drop opens the link. `d` is still alive, because it was declared first, so the drop runs `say` through the kept loan and reads its freed copy of `tag`. DRP-7 does not fire: `c` holds links, not views, and `d` has no drop.

The same route exists through `shares d`, or a `sharedref mut` link, given to anything that outlives `say`. This is the ordinary handler and observer shape of UI and game code (P12's J5-13). FN-2b makes it the normal path, where CLO-4 had it only for function values that use real variables.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a value holding a kept loan, a class object included, is bounded by the lent value, and that every owner or link made from it (shares, thread_shared, weakref, sharedref mut) carries that bound. `c.watch.push(weakref d)` is then E3063 where `c` may outlive `say`, or c's drop is E3060 by DRP-7 read through its links. Write the exception into TYP-14/15's 'a class is never a view type', with its reason (Rust's Weak<Doc<'a>> carries the same bound). Ask with P12, whose observer lists must keep compiling where the bound holds.

holes.program:
import std.thread

fn main():
    total = 0
    fn count_one():
        total += 1                 # uses the real `total`
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(count_one)     # lent: the scope's tasks end with the block
        scope.spawn(count_one)     # the same function on a second thread
    println(total)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
FN-2b accepts `scope.spawn(task)` as a loan. The kept value is a stub that calls `count_one`'s one compiled body through its address. THR-21 makes a task's `total += e` a reduction, with a private accumulator per task. The compiler can do that for a lambda written in the call, because it compiles that body as the task's own.

Here both tasks run the same body, and that body adds into main's `total` itself. Two threads write one int with no lock, which is a data race, unless the compiler makes each spawn its own instance of `count_one`. No rule says it does.

If THR-21 does not see the `+=` instead, because it sits in another function, the program is E7007. The same body written in the call compiles, so one program gets two answers depending on how it is spelled.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a function lent to `scope.spawn`, or to a scoped job, is compiled as that task's own instance, as a type parameter's instance is (CLO-14). THR-11's checks and THR-21's accumulators then apply to its body. The cost is unchanged: a direct call that can be inlined. Coordinate with P16, which unifies reductions for loops and tasks.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
`deck` is a name at its last use, and Deck has no drop all the way down. So OWN-8a lets `extended` take deck's object itself as `d`. The link `seen` made from `deck` then reaches `back`.

The program prints `[1, 2, 3, 4]` where the language says `[1, 2, 3]`, because `deck` lives to the end of main (OWN-2). `back` can also be changed through a link the program made to a different object, which is silent aliasing (verdict 5).

For a `thread_shared` owner at its last use, ending it releases nothing while other threads still hold owners. 'A value of the caller's own' does not exclude such an owner, so the 'copy' would be the very object other threads read: a data race.

struct Tally:
    marks: Array[int]

extend Tally implements Add[int]:
    type Output = Tally
    fn add(rhs: int) owns this -> Tally:
        this.marks.push(owns copy of rhs)
        return this

fn main():
    t = Tally(marks=[])
    u = t + 1
    println(t.marks)
    println(u.marks)

The rule says 'an operator is a call of its interface's method, with both operands lent'. It also says 'the object before the dot is not marked. Its method's first line (owns this) or its body says what happens to it' (verdict 1, FN-4). For `t + 1` the left operand is add's object, so the two sentences disagree.

Under FN-4, `t` is handed over with no word. `println(t.marks)` is then E3040, pointing at a line that says no `owns`: the hidden hand-over the rule removes from String. An `add` whose body changes `this` without `owns this` silently changes `t`.

Nothing in the rule refuses such an implementation. It waits on P04's missing rule that an implementation's words match its interface (open risk 6).
holes.fix_hint: Write it into this rule. An operator interface's method takes its object read-only and its other parameters as the interface declares them. An implementation that writes `owns this`, or whose body changes `this`, is refused at the implementation, naming the interface's line. So `a + b` always only reads `a`.

fn main():

CLO-4 lets a class object that never leaves the function hold a function value bounded by a local, so `d.hooks.push(say)` compiles. One rule ('a loan is kept no longer than its value') gives two answers by type.

TYP-15's 'a function value holds a view only as a ref capture or as a real variable it uses' does not list a loan. J6-12's own `Button` is a class, so whether its stateful line compiles depends on which rule the loan follows.

It could follow CLO-4's function-value rule, with TYP-15's third bullet extended to 'or a loan it was given ([FN-2b])' and hole 2's bound carried through links. unsafe extern "C":
    # C runs `each` for every element, only during the call
    @ffi(param(each, callback(borrowed, user_data=ud)))
    safe fn visit_all(each: extern "C" fn(*mut void, i32), ud: *mut void)

fn main():

    show = fn(x: i32) copy of bonus: println(x + bonus)
    visit_all(show)                # lent, as for every callee, C's included

holes.what_goes_wrong: FN-2a and FN-2b lend `show` with no word. FFI-21 says the trampoline moves 'the function value, its code and its state' into a block of its own, and that 'the block is freed when the call returns'. Read with a loan, that ends main's `show` at the call, with no word saying so. `show(1)` then runs on freed state, and main's own end of `show` frees that state a second time: a double end. The rule never says what the block holds for a loan. (The declaration's spelling, raw pointers on a safe fn and one argument for two, is P08's J8-01.)
holes.fix_hint: Change FFI-21 so the block holds the argument as given. For a loan, that is a stub (the code and the lent function's address), and ending it ends nothing (DRP-6). For `owns`, it is the value itself.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
FN-2b says 'the compiler works out from the callee's body which parameters it keeps'. A call through `dyn`, a virtual method or a stored function value has a body per kind. EFF-24's 'every function the program can put there' would refuse `s.add(bump)` even when the input picks Runner. Verdicts 152 and 163 (`runtime`, lines checked while running) give a keep no meaning: the program might be refused, stopped at the call when s is a Keeper, or let through.

Across a package's edge, a library's `s.add(h)` has implementers the library cannot see. If its interface file records 'keeps nothing', a later package's Keeper puts the loan in LATER, and `f()` runs install's ended `bump`.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a keep reached through dyn, virtual or a function value is the union over every function the program can put there (EFF-24). Across packages it is recorded as 'flows to I.add's parameter' and resolved where the implementers are known (EFF-4). Under `runtime`, the kind is checked at the call, and the program stops there, naming the keeper, when that kind keeps the loan past its value.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The C parameter `cb` is declared plain. FN-2a says 'for a plain parameter, no word ... Anything else is E3028'. FN-2b's E7004 help for a loan C keeps is `register_cb(owns on_tick)`, which is then E3028. The help line does not compile (checklist 9, verdict 73). 'The word means the same for every callee ... of C' has no rule giving a C parameter its word.
holes.fix_hint: In FN-2a, say that a C parameter whose contract says `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` is an `owns` parameter for the call word, because C takes the function over, and that one saying `callback(borrowed)` is a plain parameter. Ask it together with P08's J8-01.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CLO-10 makes two function values equal 'when they call the same function with the same state'. A kept loan is a stub plus an address, and a stub made through an erased `fn()` parameter differs from one made for greet's own type. The rule does not say whether a loan is `==` to the function it lends. If it is not, the unregistering line removes nothing, and the button still prints `hi ann`: a silent wrong result in the common way of removing a handler.
holes.fix_hint: In CLO-10, say that a kept loan is `==` to the function it lends, comparing the target whatever path the loan took. Or say that `==` between a loan and a function value is E2040, so this line is refused and its help names the way that works.

holes.what_goes_wrong: OWN-8a is a permission ('may'), and says 'any allocation it still needs is counted (Alloc)'. Where the compiler applies it, `first_three` allocates nothing and `tag` meets `@noalloc`. Where it does not, `copy of` allocates and `tag` is E4001. So whether a contract accepts the program depends on the compiler's choice, against P14's principle that an effect is fixed by the language. TXT-11's 'a + b + c makes one String' rests on the same 'may'.
holes.fix_hint: Either OWN-8a never removes an effect (the call carries the copy's Alloc whether or not the copy is elided), or the elision becomes a rule ('does', under hole 1's conditions), so the effect and the cost are fixed by the language. Ask together with P14.

holes.fix_hint: Offer `owns x` and `owns copy of x` only where the function holds nothing but its own state. Otherwise give THR-17's capture-word fix, or verdict 166's, by verdict 73: the error whose fix compiles.
