safety.notes:
Read: owner-bar.md, brief.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, P06 and the other groups' principles in phase1-groups.json, phase2 drafts (J3-02, J6-12, J2-04, J6-14, J1-07, J1-06, J3-03, J3-04, J8-01), phase3 K12/K18/K19 with conflicts, recommendation changes and verdict clashes, JOB.md verdicts 1, 3-5, 21-23, 38, 51, 61, 80-86, 94, 145-166, and spec parts p03 (GRM-15/28), p04 (TYP-5/14/15/21, Add), p05 (FN-1..9, STR-1/6, CLS-1..3/10), p06 (CLO-1..19, CTL-6/8), p07 (OWN-1..13, BRW-1/11/21, DRP-2..8), p10 (EFF-4/24/25), p11 (THR-5/10/11/17/21), p15 (TXT-5..11, STD-19), p16 (FFI-21), p26 (ODR-102). I made no edits and ran nothing. I used one python call to read the JSON keys, then only Read and Grep.

Main findings:

1. **OWN-8a (holes 1, 4 and 11).** The rule says 'Nothing the program can observe changes' as a fact, with no condition that makes it true. The design also widened phase 3's 'a temporary' to 'a name at its last use'.
   * `bar = bar + bar`, the plain fix for the refused `bar += bar`, reads freed memory.
   * A callee that reads its parameter after `copy of` sees the change.
   * A weakref link, or another thread_shared owner, sees the 'copy'.
   * As a 'may', OWN-8a also makes Alloc the compiler's choice (P14).

2. **Bounded holders (holes 2 and 6).** FN-2b makes it normal for class objects to hold loans. TYP-14/15 say a class is never a view, so `weakref` and `shares` drop the bound. A drop elsewhere can then run a lent function after it has ended. CLO-4 already has this route for function values that use real variables, so this hole is not new, but the rule makes it the common path. TYP-15 and CLO-4 also disagree on whether a class field may hold a loan, and J6-12's `Button` is a class.

3. **Lent scoped tasks (hole 3).** One compiled body serves several tasks, so THR-21's private accumulators cannot apply, and two tasks race on a real variable. Coordinate with P16.

4. **Rest.** The other holes are a missing piece of the rule (P04's 'implementation matches interface' for operators), rules that clash (FFI-21's block, the word for a plain C parameter for P08), cases left undecided (dyn and runtime keeps, `==` of a loan), and low items (help lines, THR-5's join order, `owns` into a view parameter, an untyped `[]`).

**Kept as designed:** no word lends; owns hands over; constructions work as =; String's + reads both operands; refusals at the call; module functions and stateless functions lent as themselves; ref mut for self-changing functions; once fn loans refused; E0109 and E3028 at constructions. The thread_shared fn() markers of a loan stub are not stated, but THR-11 still catches the change, so I did not count it as a separate hole.

**Text mismatch:** the rule's summary lists three kinds of view that a loan can fill, and spec_text adds a fourth, `ref T` of a place.

holes.program:
fn tagged(d: String) -> String:
    r = copy of d
    r.push_str("!")
    println(d)                       # reads d after its copy was changed
    return r

fn main():
    println(tagged(String("hi")))    # a temporary: nothing uses it afterwards
holes.what_goes_wrong: OWN-8a's conditions are all on the caller's side (a temporary or a last-use name) and on the type (no drop all the way down). Its own example meets them, so the compiler may hand the temporary to `tagged` 'to use as the copy'. `r` is then the caller's String. Two things can happen at `println(d)`. If `d` and `r` share storage, it prints `hi!` instead of `hi`. If the String was moved out of `d`, `d`'s pointer is left at a buffer that `push_str` may have reallocated, and it reads freed memory. Written plainly, the program prints `hi` and then `hi!`. 'Nothing the program can observe changes' is claimed, but nothing in the rule makes it true. OWN-8a is general (any function that copies a plain parameter or `this`), so this reaches every program, not only String's `add`.
holes.fix_hint: Add the callee's condition: on every path, the `copy of` is the parameter's last use in the callee, so nothing reads the parameter or a view of it after the copy. Or state OWN-8a as a transformation the compiler makes only when it proves both sides unobservable. Say it costs one more instance of each such function, as verdict 88's copy does.

holes.program:
static mut CLONES: int = 0

struct Doc:
    text: String

extend Doc implements Clone:
    fn clone() -> Doc:
        CLONES += 1
        return Doc(text=copy of this.text)

fn stamped(d: Doc) -> Doc:
    r = copy of d
    r.text.push_str("!")
    return r

fn main():
    x = stamped(Doc(text=String("a")))
    println(CLONES)                  # 1 as written; 0 once OWN-8a hands the temporary over
holes.what_goes_wrong: OWN-8a excludes only types with a `drop`. `copy of` runs the type's `Clone` (OWN-8), and a hand-written `clone` replaces the implicit one (STR-5). Under OWN-8a, `stamped` silently skips `clone`, and the program prints 0. The same holds for a class object with no `drop` that a `weakref` points at. `n = copy of this` in a method called on a last-use object hands the old object over as the copy, so a link that should keep seeing the unchanged original (until that original ends at the end of its scope) sees the changed copy instead. A rule that makes code compile but do something not meant is wrong (JOB.md, 'First, the intent').
holes.fix_hint: Limit OWN-8a to types whose Clone is the implicit field-wise one all the way down. Exclude class objects, or any type a weakref may target (the compiler knows those classes, verdict 114 fix 1).

holes.what_goes_wrong: The changed FN-2a says its rule 'holds alike ... for a constructor (FN-2c)'. It also says the word for an `owns` parameter is `owns` or a loan FN-2b lets it hold, and 'anything else is E3028'. A String name is not such a loan, so `Emitter(title)` is E3028. FN-2c says the same line hands `title` over, and that `Emitter(owns title)` is E0109. The changed GRM-15 ('before an argument for an owns parameter, whatever is given, unless ... a loan ... or a value made by a word that makes an owner or a link') drops the construction exception that J1-06's lead fix carried. So `Emitter("fountain")` also needs `owns` by GRM-15. The spec text being written gives every class with an init two opposite answers. The rule's headline ('it means the same for every callee: ... or a constructor') is not what FN-2c does.
holes.fix_hint: Write constructions into FN-2a and GRM-15 as the one place that follows `=`, with verdict 159 as its reason, and remove 'a constructor' from FN-2a's 'holds alike' list.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Verdict 159 says a constructor's argument 'works as `=` does', and `=` with a whole owning name hands it over (OWN-3). Read literally, `Label(a)` ends `a` (option G). FN-2c's 'a plain parameter of a written init views it' is therefore a new reading, yet the design reports verdict 159 as 'kept, and carried by its own words'. In the call line, nothing shows whether `a` or `b` survives: the init's first line, often in another file, decides. That fails the owner's test behind verdict 147 ('for every name, point at the word in the line'), and checklist 15. Two identical lines end one name and keep the other. That is the 'signature decides' model the design's own prior-art section criticises in C++.
holes.fix_hint: Tell the owner plainly that the design's reading departs from verdict 159's literal words for plain init parameters. Offer the hybrid that passes his test: a whole name given to a written init's `owns` parameter says `owns` (`Emitter(owns title)`), as every call does. A value made in the call and a memberwise field keep verdict 159's no-word form (`Emitter("fountain")`, `Words(names=xs)`), and a plain parameter lends.

holes.program:
type Handler = fn()

fn main():
    n = 3
    shout = fn() copy of n: println(n)
    handlers: Array[Handler] = []
    handlers.push(shout)             # push is `owns value: T`, T a type parameter of Array with no bound
    line = String("a b")
    words: Array[StrView] = []
    words.push(line)                 # the same parameter
    g: Handler = fn() copy of n: println(n + 1)
    mem.drop(g)                      # [T] fn drop(owns x: T), T = Handler
holes.what_goes_wrong: FN-2b says 'a type parameter with no callable bound is never made a view to fit a loan'. Array's `push(owns value: T)` has exactly such a parameter, so the text refuses both of the rule's flagship examples (`b.handlers.push(beep)` for J6-12, `words.push(line)`). Read instead after substitution (T = Handler, a callable type), `mem.drop(g)` takes a loan and drops nothing, which is the silent no-op the sentence was written to refuse. The meaning of the most common call in the language then rests on an unstated distinction: where the type parameter's value comes from.
holes.fix_hint: State it: a type parameter fixed without this argument (by the receiver's type, another argument or a written type argument) counts as that type, and a loan may fill it. One inferred only from this argument is the argument's own type, and a loan never fills it (`mem.drop(g)` is E3028).

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Mutex

class Log:
    lines: Mutex[Array[String]] = Mutex([])
    fn add(line: StrView):
        with g = this.lines.lock():
            g.push(owns String(line))

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    fn push_a() thread_shared log:
        log.add("a")
    a = thread.spawn(push_a)         # E7004 under the rule
    a.join()                         # joined on the only path
    push_a()
holes.what_goes_wrong: FN-2b counts every `thread.spawn` thread as never ending. This program joins `a` on its only path. A panic aborts and nothing unwinds (p06 484), so no path drops `a` and detaches the thread. The thread ends before `push_a`, and the loan is safe. The rule still refuses it, and its E7004 text ('dropping `a` lets it run on') is untrue for this program. That costs an `owns`, plus the allocation of `push_a`'s state block when it becomes a `thread_shared fn()` value (CLO-10). It rewrites verdict 51's own line, where it could have kept it. The design faults Rust for refusing exactly this ('refuses thread::spawn loans even when they would be safe'), and Ember already tracks a scoped task's end at its join (verdict 104).
holes.fix_hint: A `thread.spawn` thread ends at its handle's `join` when the handle is joined on every path of the function and never moved or stored. A handle dropped, moved or kept counts as never ending. Then scoped and unscoped joins follow one rule, and J3-02's program compiles as verdict 51 wrote it.

fn main():
    a = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
    b = [4.0, 5.0]
    parts: Array[MutSpan[float]] = []
    parts.push(ref mut a)            # TYP-5 rule 6: an Array given with ref mut is a MutSpan
    parts.push(ref mut b)
    for ref mut p in parts:
        p[0] = 0.0
    println(a, b)
holes.what_goes_wrong: FN-2b lets `ref mut` fill an `owns` parameter only for a function that changes its own state (`for_each(ref mut tally)`). The second half of TYP-5 rule 6 (an Array given with `ref mut` is a `MutSpan`) and `ref mut T` of a place are left out, although each is a view made without copying, which is the rule's own test. So `parts.push(ref mut a)` is E3028. No spelling compiles: `owns a` would hand an Array to a MutSpan slot, and `owns ref mut a` is not a form. Rust writes `parts.push(&mut a[..])`. One kind of loan gets the word and its siblings do not, with no reason given (principle 6).
holes.fix_hint: A `ref mut` loan fills an `owns` parameter whose type is the `ref mut` view the argument gives: a self-changing function, a MutSpan of an Array, or a `ref mut T` of a place. While it is kept, nothing else touches the value (BRW-1). Write the list as 'TYP-5 rules 4, 6 (both halves), 7a and 10, with the parameter's word'.

holes.what_goes_wrong: TYP-15 says 'a class object is never a view': a class's view field must say what it points into (`from`). Yet FN-2b keeps a loan of a stateful function in `b.handlers` and calls it bounded (J6-12: 'a handler with state bounds the list'). 'Lives no longer than the value lent' is not defined for an object that other names reach, or one that outlives the value by declaration order. Locals end in reverse order (DRP-2), so `shout`'s state is freed before `c` and `b`. Read by scope, the rule refuses the common order (the button first, then the handler, then the push), with `owns` as the help. Read by last use, as views are, with DRP-7 (Button has no drop), the program compiles. Then `c`'s drop opens ROSTER's link to `b`, which still exists, and calls the loan into freed state. CLO-4's 'objects that never leave the function' does not say whether a `weakref` or `shares` made to the keeper makes it leave.
holes.fix_hint: One rule for kept loans in any object. A loan kept in a class object counts as used wherever code may reach that object: its own end (DRP-7), and every call that may read that class's fields through a link or a second owner, by type, as verdict 82 does. Or: a link or owner made to an object that keeps a loan is E3026 at that line. Reword TYP-15's class bullet to match CLO-4, so that StrView and function loans follow the same rule.

    return word.trim() + " (" + kind + ")"    # E2040, help an f-string
holes.what_goes_wrong: TXT-11 keeps 'StrView + StrView is E2040' after the rule makes `+` read both operands and make a new value. The old reason, that `+` took its left operand over to extend it, is gone. `String + StrView` and `StrView + StrView` are now the same operation, one allocation. A parser or formatter writing `word.trim() + ":"` is refused, though `String(word.trim()) + ":"` compiles at the same cost. An exception with no stated reason fails principle 6.
holes.fix_hint: `StrView` implements `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, reading both sides with one allocation (Alloc, as for String). Or, if the owner wants the refusal kept, state the reason in TXT-11.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design says every help line compiles (checklist 9, verdict 73), but E7004 and E3026 always offer `owns x`. That is E3013 where `x` does not own its value: a plain parameter (OWN-11), or a class object's field (verdict 78's class rule). The working lines are `fn start(owns h: thread_shared fn())`, `owns copy of h` and `owns mem.take(ref mut this.on_close)`. The same goes for `scope.spawn(task)` with `task` declared inside the `with` block. There the help `owns task` fails at a second `scope.spawn(owns task)` (E3040), while moving `fn task` above the `with` line lets both spawns lend. And for a thread body that also uses a real variable the thread outlives, `owns push_a` still fails at CLO-4; the variable needs a capture word.
holes.fix_hint: Choose the help by what the argument is. `owns x` only where `x` owns its value. Otherwise give the parameter's `owns` on the caller's first line, `owns copy of x`, or `mem.take`. For a scope, move the declaration above the `with`. Name any real variable the keeper would outlive with its capture word.

holes.what_goes_wrong: A loan of an already-erased `fn()` is a stub plus an address, so each call is two indirect calls where C's function pointer plus context costs one. The design states this but takes it as given, when one record per function type would avoid it. The cost section also says `owns h` is 'a move of two words', but a local function given to `owns f: fn()` (spawn, push) gets its state put in a block of its own (CLO-10, Alloc). OWN-8a needs a second instance of every function that copies a plain parameter, and it does not reach generic callers (`with_suffix(shown, "?")` allocates where C++'s forwarding would not). None of this has been measured.
holes.fix_hint: Give each function type's code record a borrowed twin whose end does nothing, so that lending an erased `fn()` copies its two words and a call stays one indirect call. State `owns h`'s allocation and OWN-8a's code-size cost in the cost section.

Read in full: owner-bar.md, brief.md, docs/OWNER-DIRECTION.md, phase1-groups.json (all 28 principles), the phase2.json drafts of J3-02, J6-12, J2-04, J6-14, J1-07, J3-03, J3-04 and J1-06, and phase3.json's K12, K18 and K19, its conflicts, recommendation changes, verdict clashes and reroutes. I read JOB.md verdicts 1 to 166. Spec rules read in the parts: FN-2/2a/3/4/6/9, STR-1/6, CLS-2/3/7/10/11, OWN-1 to OWN-13, BRW-12 to BRW-15, TYP-5, TYP-14/15/34/45, CLO-1 to CLO-19, STD-19, TXT-8 to TXT-11, THR-10/11/21, EFF-24, GRM-15 and DRP-1 to DRP-8. I also checked p06 484: panics abort and nothing unwinds.

What holds well. FN-2b reuses an existing mechanism, CLO-4's 'every function it is handed to keeps it no longer, by that function's summary'. So a loan is the same as a lambda that uses the real variable, which is general and costs nothing at run time. It removes D-963's std-only path, routes String `+` through Add, and turns verdict 94 into a consequence. E0109 before a module function gives its reason (principle 6). The verdict-150 widening, the verdict-147 narrowing, and the rewrite of verdict 51's line are disclosed and routed to the owner with evidence. I list them as clashes only where the design mislabels one (159).

Broken, for two high and seven medium holes.
- High 1: OWN-8a's conditions do not stop a callee from reading its parameter after changing the copy. That gives wrong output, or a read of freed memory.
- High 2: a loan kept in a class object. TYP-15 says a class object is never a view, CLO-4 accepts the loan, and neither defines when an object reached through a weakref or a second owner ends. One reading calls a freed function's state from another local's drop.
- Medium: FN-2a and GRM-15 contradict FN-2c on `Emitter(title)`; verdict 159 is reinterpreted while being reported as kept; the bare-type-parameter sentence refuses the rule's own `push` examples; a joined `thread.spawn` is refused; `ref mut` loans exist only for self-changing functions; StrView + StrView keeps an exception with no reason; OWN-8a is observable through a written `clone` and through weakref identity.

Each fix is a sentence or a narrowing of a condition. None needs a new word in ordinary code. Two fixes make ordinary code shorter: join tracking keeps verdict 51's line without `owns`, and StrView `+` drops an f-string rewrite.

design.rule:
There is one rule for every call and every argument. The word before an argument says what happens to the caller's value, and it means the same for every callee: a function or method of the program, of std or of C, and an operator.

* No word lends the argument. The callee gets a view of it, and the caller keeps it.
* `ref mut` lends it to be changed.
* `owns` hands it over, and the caller's name ends. `owns copy of x` hands over a copy. A value made in the call takes `owns`, or the word that makes it (`shares mut game`, `weakref this`).

A loan can fill an `owns` parameter only where the view is itself a value of the parameter's type, never by copying:
* with no word: a function value that calls the lent function, a `StrView` of a `String`, a `Span` of an `Array`, or a `ref T` of a place;
* with `ref mut`: a function that changes its own state, a `MutSpan` of an `Array`, or a `ref mut T` of a place.

The parameter's type is the one the call fixes apart from this argument, such as a list's element type or a callable bound. A type parameter that only this argument fixes asks for the argument itself, so a loan never fills it.

What the callee keeps of a loan lives no longer than the value lent, and so does whatever holds it. That includes a class object, and every owner and link made from that object. The compiler reads what a callee keeps from its body. For a `dyn`, `virtual` or stored-function call, it reads each kind or function that may be there. It follows the keeper as it follows a view.

A thread or job ends at its handle's `join` where the handle is joined on every path. Otherwise an unscoped thread or job never ends, and neither does C without a token. A loan that would outlive its value is refused at the call, and the message gives `owns x` and `owns copy of x`.

An operator is a call of its interface's method, with both operands lent, and that method only reads its object. So `a + b` reads both and makes a new value, and `a += b` changes `a` in place. String is no exception.

A construction `Name(...)` puts each argument into its place as `=` would (verdict 159):
* a field or an `owns` init parameter takes a whole name over;
* a plain init parameter is a read-only view place, so it views the name;
* a `ref mut` parameter takes `ref mut` before its argument.

The object before the dot is not marked. Its method's first line (`owns this`) or its body says what happens to it (verdict 1).

Some functions copy a plain parameter at its last use. When the caller passes a plain value that nothing uses afterwards and nothing else reaches, the function uses that value as the copy. So `s = s + t` extends `s`, and the result is the same as with a real copy.
design.spec_text:
Changes [FN-2a], [GRM-15], [OWN-9], [OWN-12], [STD-19], [CLO-7], [CLO-10], [CLO-12], [GRM-28], [TYP-15], [TYP-21], [TYP-34], [TXT-11], [DRP-7], [THR-10], [THR-11], [JOB-2], [FFI-21], [STR-1], [STR-6] and [CLS-2]. Adds [FN-2b], [FN-2c] and [OWN-8a].

[FN-2a] (changed) **The word before an argument says what happens to it, for every callee.** This holds alike for a function or method of the program, of the standard library or of C, and for an operator (`[TYP-21]`). A construction `Name(…)` is the one call whose arguments go as `=` puts a value into a place (`[FN-2c]`, verdict 159).
* No word **lends** the argument (`[FN-2b]`).
* `ref mut` lends it to be changed, with the parameter's words, `const` included: `bump(ref mut a)` for `fn bump(ref mut c: Counter):`, and `mem.take(ref mut this.items)`.
* `owns` **hands it over**, and the caller's name ends: `take(owns xs)` for `fn take(owns xs: Array[int]):`.
* `owns copy of xs` hands over a copy and keeps `xs`.
* `owns` before a value made in the call hands that value over: `take(owns [1, 2])`; `names.push(owns p.name)`, a part (`[OWN-11]`); `xs.iter().for_each(owns fn(x: int): println(x))`.
* A value made in the call by a word that makes an owner or a link takes that word and no `owns`: `setup(shares mut game)`, `ROSTER.push(weakref this)`, `start_logger(thread_shared log)`.

The word must be one the parameter takes:
* for an `owns` parameter, `owns`, or a loan that `[FN-2b]` lets it hold;
* for a plain parameter, no word;
* for a `ref mut` parameter, `ref mut`.
Anything else is `E3028`, with the messages of verdict 157.

A C function's parameter has the word its declaration writes. A function-pointer parameter whose contract says `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` is declared `owns`, because C takes the function over, as verdict 91's `owns widget` is: `owns cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void)`. Declared plain, it is refused at the declaration, and the message names the word (`E5002`). A `callback(borrowed)` parameter is plain, so its argument is lent. (P08's J8-01 settles the rest of the declaration's spelling.)

A plain `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Atomic` or channel-end parameter takes no word, like every plain parameter. `ref mut` before one is `E3028`, because its own 'only me' is the lock's block. An `owns` one takes `owns`: `start_worker(owns rx)`.

The object before the dot is not marked. Its method's first line (`owns this`) or its body says what happens to it (`[FN-4]`, `[EXC-15]`).

`return a` takes no word. Neither does `e?`, which hands `e` over the way `return` does (`[OWN-9]`).

Removed: 'A function from a variable given to a standard-library function that takes one is lent and takes no word'. `[FN-2b]` replaces it for every callee.

[FN-2b] (new) **A loan, and what a callee keeps of it.** A name or place given with no word, or with `ref mut`, is lent. The callee gets a view of it, and the caller's name stays the caller's. A plain or `ref mut` parameter uses the view for the call.

An `owns` parameter holds the view itself as its own value. It does so where the view is a value of the parameter's type, made from the argument without copying it (`[TYP-5]` rules 4, 6, 7 and 10).

With no word, the view is one of these:
* a function value that calls a named function, a local function, or a function held in a variable or a field, given to a callable type or to a type parameter with a callable bound (`fn()`, `thread_shared fn()`, `[F: needs fn(Item)]`);
* a `StrView` of a `String`;
* a `Span` of an `Array`;
* a `ref T` of a place.

With `ref mut`, the view is one of these:
* a function that changes its own state when it runs (`[CLO-18]`): `xs.iter().for_each(ref mut tally)`;
* a `MutSpan` of an `Array`: `parts.push(ref mut a)` for `parts: Array[MutSpan[float]]`;
* a `ref mut T` of a place: `targets.push(ref mut boss)` for `targets: Array[ref mut Enemy]`.
While a `ref mut` loan is kept, nothing else touches the value (`[BRW-1]`).

The parameter's type is the one the call fixes apart from this argument. It is fixed by one of these:
* the receiver's type: `push`'s `T` is `Handler` for `b.handlers: Array[Handler]`, and `StrView` for `words: Array[StrView]`;
* another argument;
* a written type argument;
* a callable bound.

A type parameter that only this argument fixes, with no callable bound, asks for the argument itself, so a loan never fills it. `mem.drop(g)` for `[T] fn drop(owns x: T)` is `E3028`, with the help 'write `mem.drop(owns g)`'.

A function with no state is lent as itself, since its code lives as long as the program (`[CLO-1]`).

In every other case a loan is not a value of an `owns` parameter, and the call is `E3028`. This covers a number, a `String`, an `Array`, a class object, and a view held in a name, which lending would copy. These are refused, with their fixes:
* `take(xs)`: write `owns xs`;
* `names.push(p.name)`: write `owns p.name`;
* `words.push(w)` for `w: StrView`: write `owns w`.
A value made in the call has no owner to lend from, so for an `owns` parameter it takes `owns`.

**What a callee keeps of a loan, and whatever holds that, lives no longer than the value lent** (`[TYP-15]`, `[CLO-4]`). This covers what it keeps in its result (as an iterator adapter does), in a list, a map, a field or a static, on a thread or in a job, in a channel, and in C. It is checked by last use, as views are. A keeper may outlive the value where nothing uses it afterwards and no `drop` reaches it (`[DRP-7]`).

A class object that keeps a loan is bounded by it as a whole object. Two more things carry the same bound:
* every owner and link made from that object, before or after the loan is put in (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`, `sharedref mut`);
* every value that holds one of those (`[TYP-34]`).
A use through any of them counts as a use of the loan. So does the `drop` of any value that may reach the loan through them. Take a `static mut ROSTER`: `ROSTER.push(weakref b)` followed by `b.handlers.push(shout)` is refused at the push, because `ROSTER` may open its link to `b` after `shout` ends.

The compiler works out from the callee's body which parameters it keeps and where, as it works out which views a result points into (verdict 137). Within a package this is the callee's summary (`[EFF-24]`); across a package's edge it is the interface file (`[EFF-4]`). The compiler follows the keeper as it follows every view.

A call through `dyn`, `virtual` or a stored function value keeps what each kind or function that may be there keeps. It is read as every such call is (verdicts 122, 151):
* A kind known when compiling is checked as itself.
* A kind known only while running is the compile error of verdict 152, unless a `runtime` word covers it (verdicts 152, 162, 163). Then the program stops at the call, naming the keeper, when the kind there keeps the loan past its value.
* A library's call through an interface is recorded as 'keeps what `I.add` keeps of its parameter'. It is resolved where the kinds are known.

A keeper ends as follows:
* A scoped task or job ends at its join, or at the end of its scope (verdict 104).
* A `thread.spawn` thread, or a job submitted outside a scope, ends at its handle's `join` (`h.join()`, `jobs.wait(h)`). This holds where that handle is joined on every path of the function that made it and is never moved, stored or returned. Otherwise it never ends, because dropping the handle lets the thread run on (`[THR-10]`). A panic aborts and nothing unwinds (`[PAN-1]`), so a join on every path always runs.
* C keeps a loan until the token that Part XVI ties its hold to ends. With no token, it keeps it for ever.

A loan kept where it would outlive its value is refused at the call. The message names the keeper and both ways out:
* `E7004` for a thread, a job or C: 'the thread started on line 23 may still run after `push_b` ends, because its handle is dropped on that line; hand it over: `thread.spawn(owns push_b)`, or give it a copy: `thread.spawn(owns copy of push_b)`'.
* `E3026` for a kept function value. Where a link or owner reaches the keeper, the message names it: '`b.handlers` would keep a function that calls `shout`, and `ROSTER` keeps a link to `b` (line 17) for the whole program; hand it over: `b.handlers.push(owns shout)`'.
* `E3063` for a kept view.
`owns copy of h` is offered only where `h` can be copied (`[CLO-10]`).

A loan changes nothing about what the lent function may do. `[THR-2]`, `[THR-17]`, `[CLO-16]` and `[FFI-22]` read a lent function as they read one handed over.

These are loans and compile:
* `xs.iter().for_each(h)`;
* `total = xs.iter().map(h).sum()`;
* `it = xs.iter().map(h)`, used inside the function;
* `b.handlers.push(beep)`, where nothing that reaches `b` outlives `beep`;
* `words.push(line)`, for `words: Array[StrView]`;
* `parts.push(ref mut a)`, for `parts: Array[MutSpan[float]]`;
* `scope.spawn(task)`, whose tasks end at their join or with their scope (`[THR-11]`);
* `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`, where `a` is joined on every path.

These are refused, with `owns push_b`, `map(owns h)` and `owns shout` as the help:
* `thread.spawn(push_b)` of a local function with state, where the handle is dropped, moved or returned;
* `return xs.iter().map(h)` of a local `h`;
* `b.handlers.push(shout)` of a function with state, where a link to `b` is kept past `shout`.

A function of the module is lent anywhere with no word: `thread.spawn(worker)`, `b.on_click(log_click)`, `xs.iter().map(double)`. `owns` before one is `E0109`: 'nothing owns `worker`, a function of the module, and it never ends; remove `owns`'.

While a keeper may still call a lent function, no other name changes the function or what it reads (`[BRW-1]`).

[FN-2c] (new) **A construction works as `=`.** `Name(…)` puts each argument into the constructor's place, the way `=` puts a value into a place of that kind (verdict 159). This holds for:
* a memberwise constructor (`[STR-1]`, `[CLS-3]`);
* a written `init` (`[STR-6]`, `[CLS-2]`);
* a base's `init`, through `super.init(…)` or `[CLS-10]`;
* `Self(…)`;
* an enum variant, such as `Some(x)`.

Each argument goes as follows:
* A field, or an `owns` parameter of a written `init`, is an owning place. It takes a whole name over, as `snapshot = items` does, and copies a value that `=` copies.
* A plain parameter of a written `init` is a read-only view place, as a `ref T` place is (`[TYP-5]` rule 7). It views its argument, as `v: StrView = line` views `line`.
* An `init`'s `ref mut` parameter takes `ref mut` before its argument, as `r = ref mut x` does.
* `owns` stays on the line that makes a value for a place that owns it in a block of its own (`[OWN-10]`): `Entity(mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0]))`.

So:
* `Emitter(title)` for `fn init(owns name: String):` hands `title` over;
* `Label(caption)` for `fn init(text: String):` views `caption`;
* `Words(names=xs)` hands `xs` over;
* `Point(x=a)` copies `a`;
* `Emitter("fountain")` makes the `String`.

`owns` before a whole name at a construction is `E0109`: 'a construction already hands `title` over (`Emitter`'s `init` takes `owns name`); remove `owns`: `Emitter(title)`'. `owns` before an argument for a plain `init` parameter is `E3028`. A later use of a name that a construction took over is `E3040`, and the message names the constructor's parameter or field.

[OWN-8a] (new) **A copy of what is not used again.** Sometimes a function makes `copy of` a plain parameter or of `this`. The call then gives the function the caller's own value to use as that copy, when all four of these hold:
1. Nothing uses the caller's value after the call, by its name or through any view, link or owner made from it. It is a temporary, or a name at its last use.
2. No other argument of the call views or reaches any part of it. Neither does any real variable used by a function given as an argument.
3. In the callee, on every path, the parameter's last use is that `copy of`, or an argument to a call for which these four hold again. The callee keeps no view of the parameter. The compiler reads this from the callee's body and records it in its summary, as it does `[BRW-21]`'s facts.
4. The value is plain all the way down. It holds no class object, no `shares` or `thread_shared` owner, no `weakref` or `sharedref mut` link, and no `Clone` or `drop` written by hand. So its copy is the field-by-field one, and ending it only frees memory.

Where the four hold, the compiler always does this, so the language fixes what the call costs and which contracts it meets. The call's effects are those of the code that then runs (`[EFF-1]`): a copy that is not made does not allocate. Nothing else the program can observe changes. The callee is compiled once more for such calls, with that parameter as its own value. That is the cost verdict 88 accepted.

So `s = s + t`, and the inner `a + b` of `a + b + c`, extend the left `String`'s buffer. The copy is made in these cases:
* `bar = bar + bar`, whose right operand views `bar`;
* a callee that reads its parameter after copying it;
* a class object;
* a type with a hand-written `clone`.

[TYP-21] (changed) An operator's operands are lent, as every argument with no word is (`[FN-2a]`), and **an operator reads its object**. These methods take their object read-only and their other parameters as the interface declares them:
* the methods of `Add`, `Sub` and the other operator interfaces that are not `…Assign` forms;
* the methods of `Neg`, `Not`, `Eq`, `Ord`, `Index` and `Contains`.
An implementation that writes `owns this`, or whose body changes `this`, is refused at the implementation, and the message names the interface's line. The reason: nothing in `a + b` could say that `a` ends or changes. Verdict 1 leaves a method's object unmarked because the method's name and first line are in the line, and for an operator neither is.

The `…Assign` forms, `IndexMut` and `IndexSet` change their left side. The operator names that side as `=` names its place.

`bool` and `char` implement none of the operator interfaces. `String` and `StrView` implement `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, which reads both operands and gives a new `String`. `String` implements `AddAssign[StrView]`, which appends in place (`[TXT-11]`).

Removed: '`String` implement[s] none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)'.

[TXT-11] (changed) `a + b` reads both operands and gives a new `String` of their text. Here `a` is a `String` or a `StrView`, and `b` is a `StrView`; a `String` given as `b` is read as one (`[TYP-5]` rule 4). `s += t` appends to `s`.

The implementation is `r = copy of this`, then `r.push_str(rhs)`, then `return r`, which any program could write. So where `a` is a `String` that nothing uses afterwards, the new `String` is `a`'s own buffer, extended (`[OWN-8a]`). That is the case in `s = s + t`, and for the `a + b` inside `a + b + c`.

Removed: '`StrView + StrView` is `E2040`, and its help is an f-string'. Its reason was that `+` extends its left side, which no longer holds.

[CLO-10] (added) `copy of` a function value copies its state field by field, the way `[OWN-8]` copies a value that holds links:
* an `owns` or `copy of` capture is copied itself;
* a `shares` or `thread_shared` capture becomes one more owner;
* a `weakref` capture becomes one more link.
The real variables it uses are the same ones. A state that holds something that cannot be copied makes `copy of` `E2116`.

A loan kept as a function value (`[FN-2b]`) is `==` to the function value it lends, and to every other loan of it, whatever path it took, since it calls that function with that state. A loan of a loan is the same loan. So `b.handlers.retain(owns fn(h) => h != greet)` removes the handler lent from `greet`.

[TYP-15] (changed) The third bullet becomes: 'a function value holds a view only as a `ref` capture, as a real variable it uses, or as a loan it is (`[FN-2b]`), and does not outlive what it views (`E3026`, `[CLO-2]`, `[CLO-4]`)'.

Added to the class bullet: 'A class's declared type carries no bound, so a view field of a class says what it points into. A class object that is given a bounded function value is bounded by it as a whole object. The function value may use real variables (`[CLO-4]`), or it may be a loan (`[FN-2b]`). Every owner and link made from that object carries the same bound. The two kinds of field differ for a reason. A view field's type always views, so the field says where. A callable field (`fn()`) holds bounded and unbounded functions alike, so the bound belongs to the value and is read from the program. (Rust's `Weak<Doc<'a>>` carries the same `'a`.)'

[TYP-34] (changed) '… and a class is never a view type: a view field of a class says what it points into, and a class object that holds a bounded function value is bounded as an object (`[TYP-15]`)'.

[DRP-7] (changed) 'A value must be dropped while what its `drop` may reach is valid (`[FN-2b]`). That covers a view it holds that the `drop` may read through, a loan it holds that the `drop` may call, and either one reached through a link or owner it holds.'

[THR-10] (changed) Added after 'Dropping a `JoinHandle` detaches the thread': 'so a thread whose handle is not joined on every path of the function that made it may outlive that function, and keeps no loan (`[FN-2b]`)'.

[THR-11] (changed) Added: **A task's function is compiled for that task**, whichever way it is given: written in the call, given by name and lent, handed over, or copied. `[THR-11]`'s checks and `[THR-21]`'s accumulators read its body, and the bodies it calls, as they read a lambda written in the call. Each task's reductions go into its own accumulators. The body is compiled with each reduced place read from the task, as verdict 88 compiles a function with one name replaced. So two `scope.spawn(count_one)` of a local `fn count_one(): total += 1` leave `total` at 2.

Sometimes the function is a function value of a callable type, not known at the spawn: one taken from a list, a field or a `fn()` parameter. It is checked as every function the program can put there (`[EFF-24]`). A change it makes to a place that another task or the parent changes is `E7007`, because no accumulator can be given to code that is not known at the spawn. The message: 'two tasks run `hooks[0]`, which may add to `total`; give each task the function itself, `scope.spawn(count_one)`, or guard `total` with a lock'. `[CLO-14]` draws the same line between a type parameter and a callable type.

[JOB-2] (changed) `jobs.wait(h)` ends a job for `[FN-2b]`, as `join` ends a thread.

[FFI-21] (changed) 'the function value, its code and its state, is moved into a block of its own' becomes 'the argument, as given, is put into a block of its own'.
* For a loan, the block holds the loan: a call stub and the lent function's address. It owns nothing, so ending the block ends nothing (`[DRP-6]`).
* For `owns`, the block holds the function value, and the block's end ends its state.
* With `callback(borrowed)`, a plain parameter (`[FN-2a]`), the block is freed when the call returns. The caller's function is still the caller's: `visit_all(show)`, then `show(1)` runs `show`.
* With `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)`, an `owns` parameter, a loan is kept as `[FN-2b]` says, until the token's end.

[STD-19] (changed) A function from a variable is lent to the call and takes no word (`[FN-2b]`), as it is to every callee. An adapter made from a lent function lives no longer than that function. After `xs.iter().for_each(h)`, `h` is still the caller's and `h(5)` runs it (ODR-240). `return xs.iter().map(h)` of a local `h` is `E3063`, with the help `map(owns h)`.

[CLO-7] (changed) Added: a function from a variable given to one of these functions is lent (`[FN-2b]`). A thread, a job or a registry that may outlive the function does not keep a loan of it. `thread.spawn(owns push_b)` hands a local function over where the handle is not joined on every path. `scope.spawn(task)` lends one, and so does `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` with `a` joined on every path.

[CLO-12], [GRM-28] (changed) The example stays '… then `a = thread.spawn(push_a)`', and adds that `a.join()` runs before the function returns. A thread whose handle is not joined on every path takes `thread.spawn(owns push_a)` (`[FN-2b]`).

[GRM-15] (changed) '… before an argument for an `owns` parameter, whatever is given, unless the argument is one of these:
* a loan the parameter holds (`[FN-2b]`);
* a value made by a word that makes an owner or a link (`[FN-2a]`);
* an argument of a construction, which goes as `=` does (`[FN-2c]`, verdict 159) …'.

[OWN-9] (changed) 'and a construction works as `=` (`[FN-2c]`)' replaces 'and so does a constructor's argument, as `=` does'.

[OWN-12] (changed) The text becomes 'takes it by an ordinary hand-over, `widget_take(owns first)`', by verdict 147. `[OWN-6]`'s message already writes it that way.

[STR-1], [STR-6], [CLS-2] (added) 'A call of it works as `=` (`[FN-2c]`).'

The rule lends `push_a`, as it lends every argument given with no word, and `thread.spawn` keeps it on its thread. That thread ends at `a.join()`, because `a` is joined on every path of `main` and never moved or stored. `push_a` lives past that line, so the loan is kept no longer than `push_a`. The line compiles as verdict 51 wrote it.

Where the handle is dropped, moved or returned, the thread may outlive `push_a`, because dropping a handle detaches its thread (THR-10). Then the loan is refused at the call, and the hand-over is written: `thread.spawn(owns push_a)`, or `owns copy of push_a` to keep the maker's own.

A function of the module, or a local function with no state, is lent with no word in both cases, because nothing it points at can end. `scope.spawn(push_a)` lends it too, since its tasks end at their join or with the scope.
answers.outcome:
It compiles. The log gets `a` twice, and `start_logging`'s thread adds `b` while it runs. `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` is a loan, because the thread ends at `a.join()`, before `push_a` ends.

In `start_logging`, `thread.spawn(push_b)` with no word is E7004: 'the thread started on line 23 may still run after `push_b` ends, because its handle is dropped on that line; hand it over: `thread.spawn(owns push_b)`, or give it a copy: `thread.spawn(owns copy of push_b)`'. After `thread.spawn(owns push_b)`, a later `push_b()` is E3040.

Lent. `push`'s parameter is `owns value: T`. The call fixes `T` as `Handler` through the type of `b.handlers`, apart from this argument. `Handler` is a callable type, and a callable value may call a function it does not own. So the loan itself becomes the element: a function value that calls `beep`.

The list keeps it no longer than `beep` lives, and so does `b`, which holds the list. So does every owner and link made from `b`, so a link to `b` kept past a handler with state would refuse the push. `beep` holds no state, so it is lent as itself, and here the list could even outlive `main`. A handler with state bounds the list.

Verdict 149's own line (`names.push(p.name)`) is still an error, because a loan of a `String` is not a `String`. Verdict 150's 'a function from a variable given to std is borrowed' reaches `push`, as its words say.
answers.code:
type Handler = fn()

class Button:
    handlers: Array[Handler] = []

fn main():
    b = Button()
    beep = fn(): println("beep")
    b.handlers.push(beep)              # lent: the list holds a function that calls beep
    beep()                             # beep is main's still
    for h in b.handlers:
        h()

fn make_button(who: String) -> Button:
    b = Button()
    greet = fn() copy of who: println(f"hi {who}")
    b.handlers.push(owns greet)        # b is returned and greet ends here: handed over
    return b
answers.outcome:
`main` compiles and prints `beep` twice.

In `make_button`, writing `b.handlers.push(greet)` with no word is E3026 at the push: '`b.handlers` keeps a function that calls `greet`, and `b` is returned on line 18 while `greet` ends there; hand it over: `b.handlers.push(owns greet)`, or give it a copy: `b.handlers.push(owns copy of greet)`'. The line as written, with `owns greet`, compiles.

A handler with state pushed into a `b` that a static's `weakref` reaches is E3026 too, and the message names the line that made the link.

answers.answer:
`+` is a call of `Add.add` with both operands lent, which is TYP-21's own 'both operands read in place', and an operator method only reads its object. So `String` and `StrView` implement `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, which reads both sides and gives a new String. `String` implements `AddAssign[StrView]`, which appends in place.

The built-in path and its hidden hand-over go. So does `StrView + StrView`'s E2040, whose reason (that `+` extends its left side) is gone. A generic `Add` bound now accepts a String. Where the left side is a String that nothing uses afterwards, OWN-8a builds the result in its buffer.
answers.code:
[T: needs Add[StrView, Output = T]]
fn with_suffix(a: T, b: StrView) -> T:
    return a + b

fn main():
    label = String("hp: ")
    label += "10"                    # appends in place
    shown = label + "!"              # reads label, makes a new String
    println(label)
    tagged = with_suffix(shown, "?")
    println(tagged)
    unit = "k" + "g"                 # two views make a new String
    println(unit)
answers.outcome:
It compiles and prints `hp: 10`, then `hp: 10!?`, then `kg`.
* `label += "10"` appends in place.
* `label + "!"` makes one new String, because `label` is used again.
* `with_suffix(shown, "?")` gives `shown` at its last use, so the result is built in `shown`'s buffer (OWN-8a, through `with_suffix` to `add`).

Writing `(owns label) + "!"` is E3028: '`+` only reads its operands; remove `owns`'.

answers.answer: The same rule settles it. `+` reads both sides and makes a new String. Nothing is handed over without a word, and a read-only parameter may be the left side. Where the left side is not used again and nothing else reaches it, OWN-8a builds the result in its buffer.
answers.code:
fn greet(name: String) -> String:
    return name + "!"

fn main():
    first = String("Ada")
    full = first + " Lovelace"
    println(full)
    println(first)
    println(greet(full))
answers.outcome:
It compiles and prints `Ada Lovelace`, `Ada` and `Ada Lovelace!`.

`return name + "!"` on a read-only parameter is accepted, because it only reads `name`. `full = first + " Lovelace"` makes a copy, because `first` is printed afterwards. In `s = s + t`, or in the `a + b` inside `a + b + c`, the left String is not used again, so the result is built in its buffer and costs what `+=` costs.

A construction works as `=`. Verdict 159's words name every constructor ('a constructor's argument ... works as `=` does'). Each argument goes into the constructor's place the way `=` would put it into a place of that kind.
* The init's `owns name` is an owning place, so `Emitter(title)` hands `title` over with no word, as `Words(names=xs)` does.
* Label's plain `text` is a read-only view place, as a `ref String` place is (TYP-5 rule 7), so `Label(caption)` views `caption`.
* An init's `ref mut` parameter takes `ref mut`, as `r = ref mut x` does.
The overview's `Emitter("fountain")` stays as it is.

Said plainly: verdict 159 was decided on fields, and reading a plain parameter as a view place is this design's reading. Read literally, `=` with a whole name hands it over (OWN-3), which is option G.
answers.code:
class Emitter:
    name: String
    rate: f32 = 100.0

    fn init(owns name: String):          # this init takes the name over
        this.name = name

class Label:
    text: String

    fn init(text: String):               # this init only reads what it is given
        this.text = copy of text

fn main():
    title = String("fountain")
    fountain = Emitter(title)            # handed over, as = would
    caption = String("smoke")
    sign = Label(caption)                # viewed: the init only reads it
    println(fountain.name)
    println(sign.text)
    println(caption)
answers.outcome:
It compiles and prints `fountain`, `smoke`, `smoke`.
* A `println(title)` after line 16 would be E3040: '`title` was handed to `Emitter` on line 16 (its `init` takes `owns name`); to keep it, write `Emitter(copy of title)`'.
* `Emitter(owns title)` is E0109: 'a construction already hands `title` over; remove `owns`'.
* `Label(owns caption)` is E3028: '`Label`'s init only reads `text`; remove `owns`'.

other_cases.case: J3-03: a program's own `[F: needs fn(int)]` above `fn each_score(xs: Array[int], owns f: F)`, called `each_score(scores, show)`
other_cases.settled: Lent, exactly like std's `for_each(h)`. The same first line means the same thing wherever it is written, and the compiler no longer reads the callee's module path to decide (D-963's test). `show(1)` after the call prints. Under option B this stays E3028, as J3-03 records it.

other_cases.case: `a = thread.spawn(push_a)` then `a.join()` on every path; the same with `a` returned, pushed into a list, or dropped
other_cases.settled: Where `a` is joined on every path and never moved or stored, the thread ends at the join. So `push_a` is lent with no word (verdict 51's line). Where `a` is returned, stored or dropped, the thread may outlive `push_a`: E7004, with `owns push_a` or `owns copy of push_a` as the help. Handles kept in a list count as never joined. Threads started that way each take `owns copy of task`, or run in a `with scope` block.

other_cases.case: `scope.spawn(task)` of a local function declared before the `with scope` block, and two `scope.spawn(count_one)` of a `fn count_one(): total += 1`
other_cases.settled:
Lent and accepted, because the scope's tasks end at their join or with the block, before `task` ends. Verdict 94's plain `fn()` follows from this rule rather than being an exception.

Each task runs its own instance of the function. So `count_one`'s `total += 1` is a reduction into each task's own accumulator, and `total` is 2 after the block.

A `task` declared inside the block, after the scope, ends before the scope joins its tasks. So it is refused, with `owns task` as the help.

other_cases.case: `scope.spawn(hooks[0])` twice, for `hooks: Array[fn()]` holding a function that adds to `total`
other_cases.settled: E7007. The function is not known at the spawn, so no task can be given an accumulator for it, and the two tasks would change `total` at once. The help gives the function by name, or a lock.

other_cases.case: A module function given by name: `xs.iter().map(double)`, `b.on_click(log_click)`, `thread.spawn(worker)`, `apply(double, 3)`
other_cases.settled: Lent with no word, everywhere. A function of the module has no state and lives as long as the program (CLO-1), so nothing can outlive it. `owns worker` is E0109: 'nothing owns `worker`, a function of the module, and it never ends; remove `owns`'.

other_cases.case: `return xs.iter().map(h)`, and an adapter kept in a local or a field
other_cases.settled:
It depends on what `h` is.
* With a local `h`, the returned adapter would outlive it: E3063 at the return, labelled at `map(h)`, with the help `map(owns h)`.
* With `h` a plain parameter, it compiles, and the result points into the caller's function (FN-3).
* With a module function, it compiles.

`total = xs.iter().map(h).sum()` and `it = xs.iter().map(h)` used inside the function are loans, bounded by `h`. So is a struct field holding the adapter.

other_cases.case: A function that changes its own state: `tally = fn(x: int) copy of n: n += x`, then `xs.iter().for_each(tally)`
other_cases.settled: Running `tally` changes `tally` itself, so it is lent to be changed: `xs.iter().for_each(ref mut tally)` (verdict 1, CLO-18). With no word it is E3023, and the help names `ref mut tally`. A function that changes only the real variables it uses (`fn(x): total += x`) is lent with no word, and the change is inferred (verdict 86).

other_cases.case: `parts.push(ref mut a)` for `parts: Array[MutSpan[float]]`, and `targets.push(ref mut boss)` for `targets: Array[ref mut Enemy]`
other_cases.settled: Lent to be changed. The element is the `MutSpan` or `ref mut` view the word gives. While the list keeps it, nothing else touches `a` or `boss` (BRW-1). After the list's last use, `a` is the caller's again.

other_cases.case: J3-04: `fn start_worker(owns rx: Receiver[Job])`, called `start_worker(rx)`
other_cases.settled: The call is `start_worker(owns rx)`: a hand-over is a hand-over for every type (verdict 147). Verdict 3's no-word rule holds for plain parameters, and `ref mut` before one stays E3028. Verdict 3's reason ('only me' would be untrue) concerns `ref mut` only. This needs the one-line confirmation phase 3 asked for.

other_cases.case: `words.push(line)` for `words: Array[StrView]` and `line: String`; `keep(name)` for `fn keep(owns s: StrView)`
other_cases.settled: Lent. The element is a view of `line`'s text, and `words` lives no longer than `line` (TYP-15). `words.push(w)` for a `w: StrView` held in a name is E3028, because lending would copy the view; the fix is `owns w` (verdict 145). Keeping `w` while giving a copy waits on P11's J2-01, whether `copy of` copies a view.

other_cases.case: `a == b`, `a < b`, `x in xs`, `m[k]`, `print(x)`, `a[i] = v`, `m[k] += 1`, and an `Add` implementation that writes `owns this` or changes `this`
other_cases.settled: Every operand and argument is lent, and nothing is taken. `a[i] = v` and `m[k] = v` hand `v` over as `=` does. `+=` changes its left side, which is the place the operator names, so it is not marked, like the left side of `=`. An implementation of an operator method that takes `owns this`, or changes `this`, is refused at the implementation (TYP-21). So `t + 1` never ends or changes `t`.

other_cases.case: `v = r?` for a named `r: Result[T, E]`, with its `From` conversion
other_cases.settled: `?` hands its operand over as `return` does (verdict 148), with no word, and the From conversion is part of that return. A later use of `r` is E3040, naming the `?`. (P11 decides the binding of the Ok value.)

other_cases.case: `producer.join()`, `it.sum()`, `h.finish()` on a named object: methods with `owns this`
other_cases.settled: The object before the dot is not marked (verdict 1, FN-4). The method's first line, `owns this`, says the object is taken over, and a later use is E3040 naming that line.

other_cases.case: `Button(label="ok", on_click=beep)` (a memberwise field of type `fn()`), `x.on_click = beep`, and `b.on_click(beep)`
other_cases.settled: A construction and an assignment work as `=`: a `beep` with state is handed over (CLO-10), and one with no state is copied. `b.on_click(beep)` is a method call, so it lends `beep`, bounded by `b`.

other_cases.case: `mem.drop(g)` for `[T] fn drop(owns x: T)`, against `b.handlers.push(beep)`
other_cases.settled: `mem.drop(g)` is E3028: 'write `mem.drop(owns g)`'. Only this argument fixes `T`, and `T` has no callable bound, so it asks for `g` itself. A call never silently drops a loan and leaves `g` as it was. `b.handlers.push(beep)` differs, because the type of `b.handlers` fixes `push`'s `T` as a callable type.

other_cases.case: `super.init(id=id)`, CLS-10's `Door(entity)`, `Self(...)`, `Some(x)`, `Shape.Circle(radius=r)`
other_cases.settled: These are constructions: each argument goes as `=` into the constructor's place (FN-2c). A memberwise base's `super.init(id=id)` takes no word, as P15's J3-05 needs. `Some(owns Tree(...))` keeps verdict 85's `owns` for a place that owns its value in a block of its own.

other_cases.case: A C function that keeps a callback (`register_cb(on_tick)`), one that runs it only during the call (`visit_all(show)`), `tx.send(h)` on a channel of functions, `jobs.submit(h)`
other_cases.settled:
`register_cb`'s parameter is declared `owns` (`callback(retained)`), so a lent `on_tick` is kept until the token's end. That is accepted where the token ends before `on_tick`. Otherwise it is E7004, with `register_cb(owns on_tick)` as the help, which compiles.

`visit_all`'s parameter is plain (`callback(borrowed)`), so `show` is lent for the call and `show(1)` runs afterwards.

A channel outlives anything the compiler can bound (E3026), and so does an unscoped job unless it is waited for on every path (E7004). Both take `owns h` as the help. A module function is lent.

other_cases.case: `run_once(f)` for `owns f: once fn()`
other_cases.settled: A `once fn` is used up when it is called, so a loan of one can never be run: E3013, 'run_once uses `f` up; hand it over: `run_once(owns f)`' (CLO-6).

other_cases.case: J1-06: a value made in the call with `thread_shared` or `sharedref mut`: `start_logger(thread_shared log)`, `w = Watcher(target=sharedref mut players[0])`
other_cases.settled: It takes only that word, like verdict 160's `setup(shares mut game)`. Verdict 160's own reason, 'the word that makes the value says what is given', covers every word that makes an owner or a link. This is the one-line confirmation phase 3 asked for.

other_cases.case: Unregistering a handler: `b.handlers.retain(owns fn(h) => h != greet)` after `add_handler(ref mut b, greet)`
other_cases.settled: A kept loan is `==` to the function it lends, whatever path it took (CLO-10). So the line removes it, and the button no longer greets.

other_cases.case: OWN-8a's limits: `bar = bar + bar`; `deck.extended()` for a class with a `weakref` to it; `stamped(Doc(...))` with a hand-written `clone`; a callee that prints its parameter after copying it

A handler with state lent to an object that a link reaches. Two programs: `ROSTER.push(weakref b)` (a static), then `b.handlers.push(shout)`; and `c.watch.push(weakref d)` for a `d` holding a loan, with `c` declared before the lent function
other_cases.settled: The first is E3026 at the push, naming line 17's link, because the static may open it after `shout` ends. The second is E3060 at `c`'s end where `c`'s drop opens its links; where nothing opens them after the lent value ends, it is accepted. In both, the help is `owns` at the push, which compiles.

other_cases.case: `unit = "k" + "g"` and `word.trim() + " (" + kind + ")"`
other_cases.settled: Both compile. `StrView` implements `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, so two views make a new String with one allocation. Each later `+` extends that String's buffer (OWN-8a).

design.prior_art:
**C++.** The callee's signature decides:
* `const T&` lends, a by-value parameter copies, and `T&&` takes over.
* The call writes `std::move(x)` to hand over, but nothing for a copy or a loan.
* Nothing checks what a callee keeps of a reference. `std::thread t([&f]{ f(); }); t.detach();` compiles and calls a dead `f`. The same with `t.join()` is safe, but only because the programmer remembered the join.
* `std::function` copies its target.
* `std::string` has a `const&` and a `&&` overload of `operator+`, so a temporary left side is appended to. Ember gets that from one body, with no overloading (OWN-8a).
* C++17 made prvalue copy elision mandatory, so the language, not the compiler, fixes whether a copy runs. OWN-8a's 'always' does the same.
* A constructor is an ordinary call, so a by-value `std::string` parameter copies unless the caller moves.

**Rust.**
* A call with no word moves, so the hand-over is not written in the line.
* Its `String + &str` consumes the left operand silently, which is exactly Ember's TXT-11 today.
* `&f` and `&mut f` lend, and lifetimes check what a callee keeps of a loan (`Vec<&dyn Fn()>`, a returned `iter().map(&f)`). FN-2b reuses this check.
* A `Weak<Doc<'a>>` or `Rc<Doc<'a>>` carries `Doc`'s `'a`, so a link to an object holding a borrow is bounded too, as FN-2b's links are.
* Non-lexical lifetimes and `#[may_dangle]` let a holder outlive a borrow when nothing uses it and its drop does not read it. That is DRP-7's reading.
* `thread::spawn` requires `F: 'static`, so it refuses a loan even when the handle is joined on every path, while `thread::scope` lends.
* Struct literals move their fields.

**Swift.**
* Arguments are borrowed by default, and `consuming` parameters and `consume x` (5.9) hand over.
* Initialisers take their arguments owned (+1) by convention, as FN-2c does for `owns` init parameters.
* A closure parameter is lent (non-escaping) unless the callee writes `@escaping`, and escaping closures are reference-counted.
* `withoutActuallyEscaping` lets the programmer vouch that a closure does not escape.
* `String + String` reads both sides and makes a new String; `+=` appends.

**Ada.** Parameter modes (in, in out, out) say what a callee does. `'Access` of a local subprogram is checked against accessibility levels when compiling, so it cannot escape (FN-2b's refusal). `'Unchecked_Access` bypasses the check.

**Go and C#.** Closures capture by reference, and escape analysis or the collector keeps them alive. That is safe, but each escaping closure is a heap object. Strings are immutable, so every `+` allocates.

**Zig.** There are no closures, only a function pointer plus an explicit context pointer. That is Ember's stored loan without the check.

**Where each falls short of safe, as fast as C, and readable:**
* C++ is fast but unchecked.
* Rust is checked, but it moves with no word, and it refuses `thread::spawn` loans even when the thread is joined.
* Swift makes the programmer write `@escaping`, a fact its compiler could read from the body, and pays reference counts for it.
* Go and C# pay a collector.

FN-2b takes Rust's lifetime check, carried through links and through joins, and Swift's default loan and initialiser convention. It keeps C++'s speed: the rvalue append and the elision, made by the compiler from one body. The compiler reads from the callee's body what Swift asks the programmer to write.
design.cost:
Every check is made when compiling. Two things run while the program runs: a `runtime` kind check, where the program asks for one, and the extra test when two function values are compared.

**A loan to a callee that runs it now** (`for_each(h)`, `map(h).sum()`): the callee is compiled for the lent function's own type and calls it directly, and the call can be inlined (CLO-14). The cost is zero. That is cheaper than a C callback in the style of `qsort`, which pays one indirect call per item and cannot be inlined.

**A loan kept as a function value** (`push(beep)`, `on_click(handler)`, an adapter in a field):
* It is two words: a call stub for the lent function's own type, and the function's address. There is no allocation and no count.
* A call is one indirect call, which is what a C function pointer with a context pointer costs. Then comes one direct call into the lent function, which is inlined into the stub when its own type is known (a lambda or a local function).
* A function with no state is kept as itself: one word of code and no address.
* When the lent value is itself a `fn()` that is already erased, the stub makes a second indirect call.
* A loan of a loan copies the stub's two words, so a call never goes through more than one stub.

**A loan kept by a thread joined on every path:** the two words go into the thread's start block. The function's state stays where it is, where `owns copy of` would allocate a copy.

**A task's own instance:** one more compiled body for each function given to tasks whose body reduces. While running, the task runs as a lambda written in the call does, with its accumulator in the task's own block.

**Comparing function values** (`h != greet`): two words are compared. Where either side is a loan, add a test of its code word and a read of the lent value's two words.

**`owns h`:** a move of two words.

**`owns copy of h`:** a copy of h's state, which is one allocation when the state has a block.

**String `a + b` where `a` is used again:** a copy of `a`, then the append. A copy that is appended to straight after is made at the size the append needs, since a String's room is only 'at least' its length (ODR-098). The result is one allocation of `len(a) + len(b)` and two copies. That is C's `malloc` and two `memcpy`, and C++'s `const std::string& + const char*`. Without that sizing, the append grows the copy once more.

**String `a + b` where `a` is not used again** (`s = s + t`, the inner `a + b` of `a + b + c`): OWN-8a hands `add` `a`'s own buffer, which it extends with an amortised append. That is C's `realloc` and `memcpy`, and C++'s `std::string&& + ...`. It costs one more compiled instance of `add` (and of each function that copies a parameter at its last use and is called this way), as verdict 88's copy does.

**`s += t`:** an amortised append, as `std::string::append` is.

**`StrView + StrView`:** one allocation of the joined length and two copies.

**An f-string:** one allocation for the whole text.

**A construction:** each argument moves as `=` does (a copy of its words). That costs nothing beyond the object's own block, as C's struct initialisation.

**These cost nothing while running:** the operator implementation check, the bounds carried through objects and links, and the check that a thread is joined on every path.

**Memory:** two words per kept loan, the size of any function value. A loan that is used and ended in the call costs nothing.

These are mechanisms only. Nothing has been measured on the laptop.

readability.ordinary_before:
class Button:
    label: String
    handlers: Array[fn()] = []

    fn init(owns label: String):
        this.label = label

fn main():
    ok = Button("ok")                    # a written init: owns or not? two answers
    beep = fn(): println("beep")
    ok.handlers.push(beep)               # lent (verdict 150) or E3028 (verdict 149)?
    hp = String("hp: ")
    hp += "10"
    shown = hp + "!"                     # takes hp over, with no word

    for h in ok.handlers:
