design.prior_art:
**C++.** Ad hoc overloading by parameter types, by the `const`-ness of `this` and by ref-qualifiers, resolved by conversion ranking plus argument-dependent lookup.
* Zero run-time cost, but the reader has to rank conversions to know which body runs.
* A newly added overload silently changes existing calls.
* `f(0)` against `f(NULL)`, and a `bool` overload catching pointers, are classic traps.
* The `const`/non-`const` pair is duplicated code; C++23's deducing `this` (P0847) exists to fold it into one function.

**Rust.** No ad hoc overloading: several functions of one name exist only as trait instances (`impl Mul<f32> for Vec3` beside `impl Mul<Vec3> for Vec3`, `Index<usize>` beside `Index<Range<usize>>`, `From<T>` for many `T`), picked by type when compiling.
* Read/change pairs are two names (`get`/`get_mut`, `iter`/`iter_mut`, `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr`).
* A pointer from a reference is the cast `&x as *const T`, or `&raw const x`.
* Safe and fast, and it is the model Ember already follows (`[TYP-24]`, ODR-096, the `_mut` names across std).
* It falls short only at C++. bindgen names overloads `draw`, `draw1`, `draw2`; autocxx adds numbered suffixes; cxx makes the programmer declare each overload under a Rust name of their own (`#[cxx_name = "draw"] fn draw_mesh`). The names come from nothing.

**Swift.** Real overloading by types and argument labels.
* Its C++ interop imports overloads as Swift overloads, a `const`/non-`const` `operator[]` as one `subscript` (the getter from the `const` one, the setter from the other), and `operator()` as `callAsFunction`.
* Readable, but solving overloads together with literals is known for "expression too complex" compile times.

**C#.** Overloading by types and by `ref`/`out`. This is the model of J2-11's option C and of option B here.

**Ada.** Overloading by parameter types and by result type, with named association. Precise, but resolution needs the whole surrounding context.

**Go and Python.** No overloading. SWIG for Go and pybind11 for Python reach C++ overloads through a dispatcher that tries the overloads at run time (a type switch, or each overload in order), which costs every call.

**Zig.** No overloading: one function taking `anytype` that branches on the type at compile time. This is the model of "one name, cases chosen when compiling", but Zig has no C++ import.

**What A takes.** Rust's model: one function per declaration, instances picked by type when compiling, `_mut` twins, and the cast. It fills Rust's gap at C++ with Swift's result (the C++ name kept, overloads picked by the arguments), using Rust's single selection rule instead of C++'s ranking, so it is safe, as fast as C and readable at once.
design.cost:
Zero at run time, in every part of the rule.

* **Choosing a case** happens when compiling. The call is one direct call of that case's thunk (`[FFI-17]`), which is exactly what C++'s static overload resolution leaves and what C pays: one call. With LTO the thunk is inlined (`[BLD-FFI-4]`).
* **A default argument.** C++'s default expression runs in the thunk for that call, the same work C++ does at its own call site. There is one extra thunk per case and per number of arguments left out, for the shapes actually used; C++ emits that same code inline.
* **`_mut` pairs.** Two functions, as C++ has two; nothing is added.
* **The cast `ref x as *T`.** The address itself (one `lea`, or nothing), as C's `&x`, and the same code `ref_to_ptr` compiled to.
* **Memory.** No byte is added to any object, call or method table. Cases are not table entries, except C++'s own virtuals, which are unchanged.
* **Compile time.** Each call filters its name's cases. The set is bounded by the header's overload set, usually 2 to 5 cases, which is negligible beside libclang's parse.

readability.note:
The program text is the same; it now has a meaning, and it reads as the C++ library's own documentation does.

An ordinary Ember program with no C++ (a game loop, a server handler, a parser) does not change at all: the rule adds no word, annotation or ceremony anywhere.

The only line that grows is a raw-pointer line in FFI code: `ref_to_ptr(ref mut info)` becomes `ref mut info as *mut VkBufferCreateInfo`. That line now states the pointer's type, as `null[*i32]()` already must (ODR-076). It is unsafe-adjacent code, not an ordinary program.

design.compiler_does:
**The importer**
* Collects each C++ name's cases from Clang's lookup: overloads, constructors as `new`, listed template instances, using-declarations, and hiding.
* Names each `const`/non-`const` pair `name`/`name_mut`.
* Maps operators to interface instances where the signature fits (one instance per right-hand type), and skips the rest with `W5002`, naming why.
* Maps the copy constructor to `Clone`.
* Records C++ default arguments as defaults, with one thunk per shape used.
* Gives each case its own thunk, its own `ember.overlays` fingerprint (`[FFI-55]`) and its own facts.

**The checker**
* Resolves every call of a name with cases by `[TYP-24]`'s three steps (bind by number, names and defaults; take an exact match before a coercion; refuse a tie or no fit).
* Resolves a name used as a value through the expected callable type.
* Writes `E2070` with each case's Ember signature and a call that compiles.
* Applies the read-only rules per case: `E3023` when the chosen case changes its object.

**The overlay checker**
* Matches every entry, `rename` and `hide` to exactly one case (names, `_`, types, type arguments).
* Refuses an item that fits no case or several with `E5010`, giving the typed lines. This includes an old entry that a newly added overload makes ambiguous.
* Refuses `@ffi(const)` on an entry whose result is a `ref mut` view into its object.

**Everywhere**
* Refuses a second declaration of one name in Ember source (`E1030`), the library's own included.
* Refuses `ref_to_ptr` with the cast as help; `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites `ref_to_ptr(x)` to `ref x as *T` with `x`'s type.

The programmer invents no name and writes no annotation in ordinary code. The facts the compiler cannot know (whether a C++ case is safe to call, or only reads) stay where they already are: in the overlay entry for that case.
design.misuse:
Refused when compiling:
* **A call that no case fits, or that two fit equally:** `E2070`. It lists each case with its Ember parameter types and gives a call that compiles (the argument written with its type, `grid.set(5 as c_int)`).
* **A name with cases used as a value with no expected callable type:** `E2070`, giving the typed line.
* **A case called outside `unsafe` without its own entry:** `E5002`/`E3100`, naming the case and the entry line. Vouching for one overload vouches for no other.
* **An overlay item that fits no case or more than one:** `E5010` with the line for each case. A header that adds an overload which an old entry also fits makes that entry `E5010`, so a new overload is never vouched for silently.
* **`@ffi(const)` on `index_mut`, `at_mut`, or any entry returning a `ref mut` view into its object:** `E5010`.
* **Ember source declaring a name twice:** `E1030`, in a program, an overlay `extend` or the library. The help gives another name, or an interface implemented once per type.
* **`ref_to_ptr(x)`:** `E1010`, with the cast in the help.
* **An `override fn` that matches no virtual case:** `E5057`.

Reported, never silently absent:
* An operator that no Ember type can have (`operator()`, conversion operators, `==` against another type) is `W5002` at the import. Using it is the "skipped" diagnostic of `[FFI-20a]`, never "unknown identifier".
* A `_mut` name collision is `W5002`, with the `rename` line.

Nothing is decided while running, and no program the rule accepts picks a different C++ function from the one its types select. When Ember's rule and C++'s ranking would disagree, Ember refuses with a fix rather than silently choosing. An overlay that wrongly vouches for an unchecked C++ `operator[]` as safe is an asserted fact, listed by `ember tcb` (`[TCB-1]`), exactly as any other entry is; J8-05's answer shows the honest `unsafe fn index(i)` with `@safety`.
design.verdicts:
**Kept**
* **125:** each case is unsafe to call until its own entry vouches for it, members, constructors and operators included.
* **131:** operator and constructor entries go under their class (`class Grid:` holds `fn index(i)`).
* **132:** `@ffi(const)` above `fn index(i)` keeps the `const` `operator[]` reading, and an entry without it makes `index` a method that changes its object. Extended by refusing `@ffi(const)` on an entry that returns a `ref mut` view into its object, which would otherwise break verdict 5's read-only promise.
* **1:** `ref mut g[3]` reaches `index_mut`.
* **12:** the copy constructor is reached by `copy of`, not by a second spelling.
* **130 and 133:** an unsafe operator entry is `@safety` above `unsafe fn index(i)`.
* **ODR-219 (owner):** the construction order at `super.init`.

**Applied**
* Checklist items 11 and 16, and verdict 133's lesson: `ref_to_ptr` is a second spelling of the cast, so it goes everywhere it is written (IV.5, `[FFI-21a]`, P04's J8-08 example, P08's J8-12).

**Revisited: rulings that are not owner verdicts**
* **ODR-075 (lead, Hardened_32)** kept two spellings of one idea, and a library overload a program may not write. It is removed. The evidence: STD-13 ("there is no second name"), TYP-26, and checklist 11.
* **ODR-096 (delegated)** is kept, and extended by the binding step and by names used as values; it now picks among every kind of case, which is what makes A one rule rather than a C++ exception.
* **ODR-149 (delegated):** "a second entry for one name" becomes "for one case".
* **ODR-252 (delegated):** `get`/`get_mut` becomes one instance of the read/change pair rule.
* **§I.6's non-goal** (overloading) is kept for Ember source; its wording now says what remains.

No owner verdict is reversed or widened.

recommendation.reason:
A settles every member and every other case with one selection rule that Ember already has (ODR-096's, for `Mul[f32]` beside `Mul[Vec3]`).

* C++ code stays as readable as C++ (`r.draw(mesh)`), with no names to invent and no overlay needed before a call compiles.
* It costs nothing at run time.
* Ember source keeps one declaration per name (§I.6, STD-13).
* It removes the library's only twins: `ref_to_ptr`, a second spelling of the cast, and `range`'s three forms, which become one function.

B buys uniform declarations at the price of a non-goal and new rules for cases in five other places. C and D give up C++'s readability for every overloaded header.

A: one name, one function. A C++ name's overloads (like an interface's instances) are its cases, picked by the arguments' Ember types when compiling. `const`/non-`const` pairs become `name`/`name_mut`, operators are their interface's methods, and `ref_to_ptr` goes in favour of the cast.

owner_short.recommendation: A: `r.draw(mesh)` reads as in C++ and costs nothing, Ember's own programs and its no-overloading rule are unchanged, and the one selection rule Ember already uses for `Mul[f32]` beside `Mul[Vec3]` also picks among C++'s cases.

design.open_risks:
1. **`grid.set(5)` with an `int` case and a `float` case is `E2070`.** The literal reaches both through a coercion, while C++ picks the `int` one. The fix in the help is `5 as c_int`. A refinement in which an integer literal prefers integer types would accept the call, but a case added later could then switch existing calls silently, so it is left out. The owner may want it.

2. **A header that adds a closer overload switches calls.** A call that reached a case through a coercion moves to the new exact case, as in C++ (exact before coercion, ODR-096). Only entries the overlay already has are checked against such additions (`E5010`). The calls themselves are not reported, though `ember bind --report` could list them as API changes.

3. **Skipped operators.** `operator()`, conversion operators (`explicit operator bool`) and `==` against another type are skipped because no Ember type has them, so functor objects and validity checks need a named C++ member. If Ember classes ever gain a call operator, imports would follow.

4. **Contract-word clash in typed overlay parameters.** A C++ type named like a contract word (`handle`, `status`, `one`) must be written with its namespace path in a typed parameter. One in the global namespace has no such path and needs a spelling; this touches P22's raw identifiers.

5. **`_mut` naming flips with the header.** When a header adds the `const` twin of a lone non-`const` member, `v.at(3)` then reaches the `const` one. Reads are unchanged, and `ref mut v.at(3)` becomes refused rather than silently different.

6. **`_` for unnamed header parameters** is a new form in overlays (patterns already use `_`).

7. **Dependencies on other groups.**
   * P08's J8-12 must take the cast form, which needs `ObjectPtr[C]` added to IV.5's cast list; that is P08's question.
   * P04's J8-08 example and `[FFI-21a]` are rewritten to the cast.
   * The `@ffi(const)`-on-`ref mut`-result refusal overlaps P10's read-only principle and P04's vouching; present it with them.

8. **`range`'s one signature** has an awkward first parameter name for named calls (`range(first, stop=None)`).

9. **Not checked on the real compiler** (this was a read-only design task, checklist 14). The importer does not build cases yet, and E2070's typed help is unbuilt; both are implementation gaps, not spec gaps.

matrix.how_kept: A case's result view takes its lifetime from that case's own entry (`-> from(this)`, `from(p)`, [FFI-11]), as any import does. The cast `ref x as *T` makes an untracked raw pointer that only unsafe code may use ([UNS-4]). C++ objects behind a pointer move as pointers, never as bytes.

A header adding the `const` twin of a lone member, so `v.at(3)` switches to it (reads are unchanged; `ref mut` becomes refused).

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-42] (changed) says an operator 'implements the Ember operator interface of its operator', whatever its entry says, and [FFI-17g] makes the copy constructor implement Clone and begin/end implement Iterable. So Grid implements Index through a case that is unsafe to call. `first(g)` reaches the unchecked `operator[]` from code with no `unsafe`, and reads past the end of an empty buffer. The same holds with no entry at all: `xs.contains(v)` reaches an unvouched `operator==` through Eq; `copy of` inside `@derive(Clone)`, or `[T: needs Clone]`, reaches an unvouched copy constructor; and `for x in v` over Iterable reaches unvouched begin/end. Verdict 125 ('members included') is then kept only for direct calls.
holes.fix_hint: An imported case implements its interface only when its own entry vouches it safe (a plain `fn index(i)`, `fn eq(other)`, `fn clone()`). With no entry, or an `unsafe fn` entry, its operator spelling (`g[3]`, `a == b`, `copy of g`) is a direct call of that case, allowed in unsafe code only. Every bound, `dyn`, `@derive` or std use that would reach it is refused when compiling, with E3100 naming the case and its entry line ('`first(g)` reaches Grid's `index`, which is unsafe to call'). Present this with P04's J5-16, whose option A refuses an unsafe implementation of a safe method and would refuse J8-05's own `unsafe fn index(i)` entry.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-17g] says a C++ default argument is an Ember default, and that 'C++ evaluates its default expression for that call, in the thunk'. The `Style()` temporary is therefore made and destroyed inside the thunk, and the reference `checked` returns points at it once the thunk returns. The entry's `from(s)` is honest for every call that writes `s`, but no rule says what `from(s)` means when the call leaves `s` out, so `st` is not bounded by anything and `st.size()` reads a destroyed object. This is safe code under an honest overlay. The same goes for `retained` on a defaulted parameter, and for the common `const std::string& get(key, const std::string& fallback = "")` shape.
holes.fix_hint: State that a defaulted C++ argument lives only for the call, so it can be the source of nothing that outlives it. A call that leaves out a parameter named by the case's result lifetime (`from(s)`), or by a `retained`/`owns` contract, is refused (E3063: 'the result views `s`, which this call leaves to C++'s default `Style()`, made and ended inside the call; pass one: `gui.ui.checked(s)`'). Alternatively the importer gives such a parameter no Ember default.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-17g] matches an override to its virtual case 'by writing its parameter types', and E5057 only covers an override that matches no case. No rule makes the override's parameter words match the import's ([FFI-40]: `const T&` is plain, `T&` is `ref mut`, `T&&` is `owns`), and CLS-4 states no signature match either. So `owns e` is accepted. Ember ends C++'s Event when `on` returns, running the destructor and freeing what is a C++ stack object; `dispatch` then destroys it again. That is a double end and a free of a non-heap address, from safe code. Writing `ref mut e` instead lets the Ember override write through a reference C++ passed as `const`.
holes.fix_hint: An override writes its case's parameters exactly as the import gives them, words included. A differing word is E5057 naming the case and the line to write (`override fn on(e: evs.ev.Event)`). Give an interface method's implementation the same rule; P04's J5-16 notes it is missing.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The two cases import as `add(m: Mesh)` and `add(owns m: Mesh)`: the same number of parameters, the same names, the same Ember types. [TYP-24] step 1 binds 'by their number, their names and the parameters' defaults', not by the word, so every call ties (E2070), even inside `unsafe:`. The promised help, 'the argument written with its type', cannot tell them apart. FN-2a already requires the word at the call, but no rule lets it choose the case. `overlay_param` has no word slot, so no entry, `rename` or `hide` can name either case, and neither can ever be vouched. [TYP-26] meanwhile says functions that 'differ only in the word on one parameter' are a read/change pair with `_mut`, while [FFI-17g] applies `_mut` only to `this`. That is three answers for the commonest modern C++ shape (`push_back`, setters, `insert`, `emplace`), so the API is unusable.
holes.fix_hint: Bind by the call's words as well: [TYP-24] step 1 becomes 'by their number, their names, their words (none, `ref mut`, `owns`, as FN-2a requires at every call) and defaults'. Then `s.add(m)` reaches `add(const Mesh&)` and `s.add(owns m)` reaches `add(Mesh&&)`. Give `overlay_param`/`fn_ref` the word (`fn add(owns m)`). Limit [TYP-26]'s read/change-pair sentence to `this`, the one argument a call does not mark.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-17g] says move constructors are not imported 'since Ember's hand-over and `=` move and replace an owner without them'. THR-2 (verdict 114) breaks that premise: an object handed to another thread while a `weakref` points at it has 'its contents move to a new block'. The contents include the C++ base subobject, moved as bytes without C++'s move constructor. `title_`'s internal pointer still points into the old block, which is freed when `w` ends; the other thread's `Widget` destructor then touches freed memory. A Send vouch says the object may live on another thread, not that its bytes may be relocated. [FFI-35a]'s 'never moves' covers only objects given to a `retained` parameter. Hot reload's relocation (HR-20, P09) has the same issue.
holes.fix_hint: Never move an object holding a C++ subobject (a class with a C++ base, or a value holding a C++ object inline) by hand-over or reload. Mark it in OBJ-1 as [FFI-35a] marks an object C keeps, so a hand-over with a link stops the program with that message. Alternatively run C++'s move constructor through a thunk when moving. Either way, [FFI-17g]'s sentence then becomes true. Coordinate with P03/P09.

holes.what_goes_wrong: With version 1, `n` widens to i64 and reaches `read_into(char*, int64_t)`. After the header update, `n` is exactly `i32`, so by exact-before-coercion the same line silently reaches the new case and writes `4 * n` bytes into an `n`-byte buffer. The new overload has no overlay entry, but entries fence only safe code; in unsafe code the `# SAFETY:` note, written for the old case, now silently covers a case it never vouched for. The design's 'a new overload is never vouched for silently' holds for overlay entries only, and its open risk 2 calls this an API change, not a safety hole.
holes.fix_hint: Record the case each call reaches alongside the overlay fingerprints ([FFI-55]). A build in which an existing call would reach a different case then stops, E5010-style, naming the call and both cases with the line that keeps the old one (`n as i64`). At the least, refuse the switch inside unsafe code, whose note was written for the old case.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-24] makes every function that is not noexcept return `Result[T, CppError]`. `Add.add` returns `Output` and `Eq.eq` returns `bool`, and [FFI-42] imports an operator only 'where its signature fits'. No rule says which happens: the operator is skipped (then `a + b` and `a == b` fail for most real headers, since few mark their operators noexcept), it imports with `Output = Result[...]` (then Eq cannot fit), or a throw stops the program. A throw inside `+` reached from std code (`sum`, `contains`) therefore has no stated behaviour, rather than a clear stop at its line. The same holds for a copy constructor that may throw (any class with a `std::vector` member) and Clone.
holes.fix_hint: Say once, for every case an interface method reaches: a case whose C++ declaration may throw implements the interface only with `@ffi(noexcept)` in its entry. A throw then stops the program naming the declaration and the line ([FFI-24b]). Without it the case is skipped with W5002, giving that entry line.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new [FFI-40a] sentence refuses `@ffi(const)` only above an entry 'whose result is a `ref mut` view into its object'. That keys on the result's spelling, not on whether the object can change through it. A `MutSpan`/`exclusive` result carries the same broken promise and is accepted, so `peak` changes, through read-only `b`, the floats that `first` is viewing (verdict 5). Meanwhile a view class's `float& operator[](size_t) const` truly only reads its object, but [FFI-40] counts its `T&` result as a view 'into the object'. Its true `@ffi(const)` is refused, so `v[i]` through a read-only name is E3023, while C++ allows it (span, mdspan and Eigen::Map are all shaped like this).
holes.fix_hint: Word the refusal by what the result lets a caller do: refuse `@ffi(const)` above any entry whose result may change its object (`ref mut`, `MutSpan`, `exclusive`, or an Option or tuple of those, from `this`). Accept it where the result points into something other than the object (`from(p)`, `from(static)`). The view-class case needs P04's J8-06 answer on where a C++ reference points.

holes.what_goes_wrong: `c_int`, `c_long`, `c_char` and `c_wchar` are aliases (std.ffi: 'c_int and the other C aliases'). Two C++ overloads whose types are distinct in C++ can therefore have equal Ember parameter lists on one target: `long`/`long long` on LP64, `char`/`signed char` where `c_char` is i8, `wchar_t`/`char16_t` on Windows. Every call then ties, the help's typed argument fits both, and no overlay item or `rename` can name either case, so a common overload set (`std::to_string`, JSON setters, stream `<<`) is unusable even in unsafe code. The pick also depends on the target: with `f(int)` beside `f(long)`, Linux's `f(5)` exactly reaches `f(long)` (c_long = i64 = int), which C++ would not call, while Windows ties (c_long = c_int = i32). This is the collision the design charges against option D.
holes.fix_hint: When two cases' Ember parameter lists are equal on the build target, report them at the import with W5002, and let an overlay item name a case by its C++ declaration (`rename put(long long) as put_i64`), so each stays reachable. Or keep the C aliases distinct types for case selection and typed entries on every target.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Step 2 counts an untyped literal 'as its default type, int'. `int` is i64, so `out.put(5)` exactly reaches `put(int64_t)` and writes 8 bytes. C++'s documented `w.put(5)` reaches `put(int32_t)` and writes 4, so a file or wire format written from Ember silently differs from the same-looking C++ call. This contradicts the design's own promises: 'When Ember's rule and C++'s ranking would disagree, Ember refuses with a fix rather than silently choosing', and J8-04's 'one direct call of the thunk of the overload C++ would call'. It is also inconsistent with `grid.set(5)` being refused for int/float.
holes.fix_hint: Let an untyped integer literal fit every integer case equally (LEX-16: it is not a value yet), so `out.put(5)` is E2070 offering `5 as i32` and `5 as i64`, as `grid.set(5)` already is. Otherwise drop the two promises and say plainly that Ember picks by its own `int`, with `ember bind --report` listing the calls whose pick differs from C++'s.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-42] (changed) says 'a free operator function implements its interface for its operands wherever its namespace is'. Vec3 is one entity across both imports ([FFI-30]), so the program has two `Add[Vec3]` implementations for Vec3. Under [TYP-20] that is E2041 'anywhere in a program', so a game is refused merely for depending on both libraries, even if it never writes `+`. No rule says which package may write `Add` for an imported C++ type ([TYP-20]'s E2121 knows only packages that declare `I` or `T`). With separate compilation each package keeps its own `+`, which is the incoherence [TYP-20] exists to rule out. In C++ neither operator is found for `gfx::Vec3` outside its own namespace.
holes.fix_hint: Follow C++'s associated namespaces: a free operator implements its interface only when it is declared in the namespace of one of its operand types (or as a hidden friend), and implementations belong to the import of the header that declares that type. Any other free operator is a plain function, called by its path.

holes.program:
interface Shape:
    fn area() -> f64

interface Drawable:
    fn area() -> f64            # the pixels it covers

struct Circle:
    r: f64

extend Circle implements Shape:
    fn area() -> f64:
        return 3.14159 * this.r * this.r

extend Circle implements Drawable:
    fn area() -> f64:
        return 4.0 * this.r * this.r

fn main():
    c = Circle(r=2.0)
    println(Shape.area(c), Drawable.area(c))
holes.what_goes_wrong: The new [TYP-26] reads: 'Two functions of one name in one scope are E1030, in a program ... A type's methods are one scope, whichever block declares them'. Its only lawful cases are 'the instances of one generic interface' and C++ names. So this program, which [TYP-24]'s kept first paragraph allows ('When two interfaces supply a method of one name for one type, the call is E2070 and is written I.m(recv, …)'), is E1030 by the letter. The same reading refuses an inherent method beside an interface's (IV.11: 'an inherent method beats an interface method of the same name'), the two `fn mul` that implement `Mul[f32]` and `Mul[Vec3]` (Ember source writing one name twice in Vec3's one scope), and the design's own two `override fn on(...)` in one class.
holes.fix_hint: Say that implementing a declaration made elsewhere declares no new name: an interface method's implementation and an `override fn` of a C++ virtual case are not second declarations. E1030 is two declarations of one name that implement nothing, and IV.11's inherent-first rule stays.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Step 3 promises a message that 'gives the call that reaches each: the argument written with its type (`grid.set(5 as c_int)`)'. `as` converts scalars only (TYP-6), and no spelling upcasts a class or turns an Array into a Span, so the help for `p.add(t)` has no line that compiles. For `draw()` beside `draw(int = 0)`, no call can ever reach `draw()`. Both break checklist 9 ('every message gives a line that compiles'), and the second is an import that is silently unreachable.
holes.fix_hint: Give step 3 a spelling for every coercion it can meet: a typed local (`b: ref gui.ui.Button = ref t`, if [TYP-5] rule 8 holds there) or an explicit upcast. Report a case that no call can reach with W5002 at the import, with its `rename` line.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-17g] says 'the copy constructor implements Clone, so `copy of g` runs it', and C++ counts `T(T&)` as a copy constructor. `copy of b` reads `b`, yet this one changes the caller's buffer through a read-only name (verdict 5) and leaves it hollow, which C++ code may later dereference.
holes.fix_hint: Only a copy constructor taking `const T&` implements Clone. One taking `T&` is a case of `new` with `ref mut other`, or is skipped with W5002.

holes.program:
fn total(xs: Span[int], start: int, stop: Option[int]) -> int:
    sum = 0
    for i in range(start, stop):     # stop None: counts 0..start, not from start
        sum += xs[i]
    return sum
holes.what_goes_wrong: With `fn range(first: T, stop: Option[T] = None, step: T = 1)`, an `Option` value given for `stop` is indistinguishable from leaving it out. When it is None at run time, `first` silently becomes the stop, and the loop counts a different range from the one written. That is a silent wrong result (bounds checks stop any read past the end); Python refuses `range(5, None)`.
holes.fix_hint: Refuse an `Option` value for `stop`: only a number, or nothing written. Then the meaning of `range`'s first argument never depends on a run-time value.

holes.program:
# a program's own helper, kept from before
[T]
fn ref_to_ptr(r: T) -> *T:
    return ref r as *T

fn main():
    x = 5
    p = ref_to_ptr(x)
holes.what_goes_wrong: IV.5 (changed) says flatly that '`ref_to_ptr(x)` is E1010'. Read as written, this refuses a call of the program's own function, or of a C header's `ref_to_ptr`, giving one name a hidden special path (checklist 13).
holes.fix_hint: Give E1010's help only when no `ref_to_ptr` is in scope (the unknown-name diagnostic). A program's or a header's own `ref_to_ptr` is an ordinary function.

holes.what_goes_wrong: [FFI-42] reaches `operator*`/`->` 'through `get()` and `get_mut()`'. [FFI-17g]'s collision rule skips 'a member that would import under a name another member already has', but does not say which of the two `get`s is skipped. If the C++ `T* get()` wins, read-through goes through a raw, possibly null pointer; if the operator wins, the C++ member vanishes. This shape is common in user smart pointers (intrusive_ptr, Ref<T>).
holes.fix_hint: Say that the operator's read-through `get`/`get_mut` (views) wins, and the C++ member is skipped with W5002 giving `rename get as raw`; or state the reverse.

safety.notes:
The rule's core holds for the members' own programs. J8-04's calls, J8-05's direct `g[3]` inside `unsafe:`, and J2-11's cast keep every guarantee. Choosing a case is decided when compiling. Each case is vouched for on its own (verdict 125). E5010 catches overlay drift, so an old entry never vouches for a new overload. `const`/non-`const` pairs become `name`/`name_mut`. `ref x as *T` parses as `(ref x) as *T`, since `as` binds looser than `ref`. An unsafe case cannot become a safe function value (ODR-115). A generic Ember body cannot reach a C++ case. A non-override Ember method named like a base's is already E2110/E2111 (CLS-4).

The holes sit where a case is reached by something other than a direct call:
- through its interface (high: an unvouched or `unsafe fn` operator, copy constructor or begin/end is reached from safe generic or std code);
- through a C++ default argument (high: a result whose lifetime names a defaulted parameter views a temporary the thunk has already ended);
- through an override (high: matched by types only, so `owns` or `ref mut` on a `const T&` parameter gives a double end, or a write through const);
- through verdict 114's relocation (medium: an object with a C++ base is moved as bytes, with no move constructor).

The design's own selection data has three more gaps:
- the call's word is not part of binding, and overlays have no word slot, so `const T&` beside `T&&` (high) is unusable even in unsafe code;
- the C aliases (`c_long`, `c_char`, `c_wchar`) make some overloads identical on one target (medium);
- an integer literal counted as i64 silently picks a different overload than C++ (medium), against the design's promise to refuse rather than diverge.

Coordination:
- Hole 1 and the override hole need P04's J5-16, which is the general 'an implementation must match and may not be unsafe' rule. J5-16 A would also refuse J8-05's own `unsafe fn index(i)` entry, a clash between the two groups to present together.
- The `@ffi(const)` hole needs P04's J8-06 (where a C++ reference points).
- Relocation touches P03/P09.
- Send for C++-based classes is P01/P04's.

Outside P07 but adjacent: the destructor of a C++ base or opaque class runs at every end with no entry. The special-members list says nothing of it, and it is J5-16's question for drop.

Wording only:
- [FFI-30c]'s `override` still says 'for that name' rather than 'for that case'.
- [FFI-55]'s record is keyed by name; cases need keys (tooling, not an ODR).
- The cast form repeats the pointee type the compiler knows (`ref mut info as *mut VkBufferCreateInfo`). That is an engineering-lens readability cost in unsafe-adjacent code, not a safety hole.

No owner verdict is broken by the rule. Severities follow the bar: high where safe code, or a common C++ shape, goes wrong.

holes.what_goes_wrong: TYP-24 step 1 binds by number, names and defaults only, not by the word at the call. The two cases have the same Ember parameter type, so both calls tie and are E2070, though verdicts 146 and 147 (and 1 for `const T&` against `T&`) already let each word fit exactly one case. E2070's help, "the argument written with its type", cannot separate them. FFI-12 names a case by names, types and type arguments, never by a word, so neither entry can be written: both cases stay unsafe for good. This `const T&`/`T&&` pair is in nearly every modern C++ container, setter and constructor (`push_back`, `insert`, `set_name(const std::string&)` / `set_name(std::string&&)`). The new TYP-26 sentence ("differ only in the word on one parameter ... are a read form and a change form") would instead name the `T&&` case `add_mut`, a wrong name since it hands over and changes nothing, while FFI-17g applies `_mut` only to `this`. The two texts disagree. It also clashes with P06: the word at the call says what the call does, for every callee.
holes.fix_hint: Add the word to step 1: an argument binds only to a parameter whose word it carries (none for a plain parameter, `ref mut`, `owns`), as verdicts 1, 146 and 147 already require. Let FFI-12 name a case by its parameter's word where names and types tie (`fn add(owns m)`). Restrict TYP-26's read/change sentence to the word on `this`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: C++ overloads on types that are distinct in C++ but one type in Ember (`c_long` is an alias of `i64` on LP64 and of `i32` on LLP64; `c_char` is `i8` or `u8`; `c_wchar` is `i32` on Linux, the same type as `c_int`) give two cases with identical Ember signatures. Every call ties, whatever `as` the help suggests. The typed overlay lines fit two cases each (E5010), so neither case can be named, vouched, renamed or hidden. Which overloads are unreachable depends on the target, so one source compiles on Windows and is refused on Linux. `std::to_string`, `std::abs`, `std::ostream::operator<<` (char, signed char, unsigned char, int, long, long long) and Qt's `QString::number` all have such sets. The design itself names this collision as option D's flaw.
holes.fix_hint: Give each C type that C++ distinguishes a distinct Ember type: `c_long`, `c_ulong`, `c_char` and `c_wchar` as nominal types, as `@ffi(newtype)` already makes for a typedef, still converting by rule 12 and `as`. Or let FFI-12 and E2070's help name a case by its C++ parameter type where the Ember types coincide.

        println(v)
holes.what_goes_wrong: The new TYP-26 drops today's exception for operator-interface implementations and allows cases only for instances of one generic interface and for C++ names. As written, it makes E1030 of three things other rules keep legal: an inherent method beside an interface method of the same name (IV.11), two different interfaces declaring one method name for one type (TYP-24's first sentence, which the design keeps word for word), and the two `override fn on` that the design's own other case writes for C++ overloaded virtuals.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a method implementing an interface instance belongs to that instance, and that an override of a base's case belongs to that case, not to the type's own scope. E1030 is then for two inherent declarations of one name on one type, or two implementations of one instance (E2041).

holes.what_goes_wrong: An operator with no fitting interface is skipped, and only an imported operator can be renamed (FFI-42). So `operator<`, `operator<=>`, `operator()` (every functor and hasher), `explicit operator bool` and a mixed `operator==` cannot be called at all, not even as plain methods. An overlay's `extend Key implements Ord:` therefore has nothing to call, and the only workaround is a C++ shim. This is inconsistent within the design: the `_mut` name collision is also skipped with W5002, but its message gives the `rename` line that rescues it. Leaving these operators out because the syntax to name them is missing is the exemption that checklist 12 (ODR 13) forbids.
holes.fix_hint: Import every skipped operator as a plain method under a stated name (`operator()` as `call`, `operator<` as `lt`, `operator bool` as `to_bool`), reachable by `rename`, so an overlay `extend` may implement `Ord` or `Hash` over it, as FFI-42 already allows for a renamed `index`. Map `operator<=>` to `Ord`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: FFI-24 makes every function not declared non-throwing return `Result[T, CppError]`. FFI-42 maps an operator only "where its signature fits that interface's method", and FFI-17g says unconditionally that "the copy constructor implements Clone". By the letter, then, every non-noexcept `operator==`, `operator[]` and `operator+=` is skipped, and the copy constructor's `clone` does not have Clone's type. That covers most real C++, including `std::vector`'s `operator[]` and nearly every copy constructor. J8-05's example works only because its header writes `noexcept`. It is also not stated whether an overlay's `@ffi(noexcept)` (FFI-24b) is applied before the fit test.
holes.fix_hint: State that the fit is judged with the overlay's facts, so `@ffi(noexcept)` (whose thunk turns a throw into a panic) makes the operator or copy constructor fit. With no overlay, the W5002 should give that line. Alternatively, say that a throwing copy constructor implements Clone with a throw as a panic, the way allocation failure is.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Step 2 counts every TYP-5 rule as a coercion. Reading through a view or an `owns` (rule 7) therefore makes a case inexact, so the same value resolves when held as a plain parameter and is refused when held in an `owns` field or reached through a view. Upcasts are not ranked, so a derived argument ties between a near base and a far one, where C++ (and Ember's own method lookup, IV.11, "base classes nearest first") takes the nearest. E2070 must give a call that compiles (checklist 9), but Ember has no explicit upcast (`as` converts scalars only, TYP-6), so for `lg.log(d)` no such line exists.
holes.fix_hint: In step 2, compare an argument's type with its views and one owner level read through, as IV.11 step 1 strips them from a receiver. Rank a base class by nearness, nearest first as IV.11 does, so the case for the nearest base wins; refuse only cases at equal distance.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The safe cast may produce only one pointee type, the view's own (IV.5: "when the pointee type is unchanged"). The compiler knows that type, yet after the change every pointer line must write it out, and FFI lines grow (`ref mut out as *mut vk.VkBuffer`). This is what the owner's bar calls a last resort. A value whose type cannot be written (an iterator pipeline, a lambda, a `some I` result) loses its safe pointer altogether, a capability `ref_to_ptr` gave. The precedent cited, `null[*i32]()` (ODR-076), has no source to infer from; the cast does. Rust, the model cited, added `&raw const x`, which needs no type, and its linter flags `&x as *const T`.
holes.fix_hint: Keep one spelling, but let it take the pointee from the view when the programmer leaves it out (for example `ref mut out as *mut`), with the type written only where the programmer wants it checked. Otherwise keep a single inferring form and let the typed cast be its checked spelling.

holes.program:
fn ticks(n: u8):
    for i in range(1, n):          # T from `first` (the literal, resolved last) or from `stop: Option[T]` given a u8?
        println(i)
    whole: Range[int] = range(10)   # Hardened_11: `range(n)` is `0..n` (STD-26)
    println(len(range(0, 100, 7)))
holes.what_goes_wrong: `fn range(first: T, stop: Option[T] = None, step: T = 1)` returns one type for all three forms. A Python-style negative step cannot be held in `Range[T]` (`start`/`end` only, CTL-3), so `range(n)` stops being `0..n`, and the design's STD-26 text does not say what it returns. Inferring `T` from a `u8` given to `stop: Option[T]` needs inference through rule 11, which TYP-18 ("inferred from the arguments") does not state, so the loop variable's type in `range(1, n)` is undecided. Unless the step is constant, `len()` and `x in range(...)` now need it (a division and a modulo). The design's claim of "at no cost" covers the loop only.
holes.fix_hint: State range's one result type and how `T` is inferred (from `first` and from `stop` read as its `Some`), and keep `range(n)` and `range(a, b)` as values of `0..n`'s type. Alternatively drop the third argument for the existing `.step_by(k)`, which CTL-3b already lowers.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Effects are computed per function body (EFF-1), and EFF-15 lists no proof that removes an effect behind a constant default. Folding the twins into one function with defaults therefore puts every form's effects on every call: the `step == 0` panic (or at least a check no proof removes) on each `for i in range(n)`, and `Alloc` on `String()`. `@realtime` code (its default set includes `@noalloc @nopanic(explicit)`) that is correct today is refused. This clashes with P14: effects belong to exactly the operations that do them.
holes.fix_hint: Either add to EFF-15's proofs that a branch on a parameter whose value at the call is a constant (a default or a literal) is decided, or keep the forms whose effects differ apart, for example `range(a, b).step_by(k)` and an empty `String()` that is `Default`'s, with a stated empty effect set.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-12 lists how every special member is named (a constructor by `new`, the copy constructor by `clone`, operators by their methods) but leaves out the destructor, which runs at every end of an imported object in safe code. Under verdict 125 it is either unsafe until vouched, with no line able to vouch for it, so every C++ object in safe code is refused at its end, or it is silently exempt, an unstated exception to verdict 125.
holes.fix_hint: Name it `fn drop()` in the class section (Ember's `Drop`), and state with P04 whether an end with no entry is unsafe or is vouched by the class's first entry.

holes.what_goes_wrong: A literal is more ambiguous than a variable holding the same value: `k.set(5)` is refused where `k.set(n)` compiles, for the common `set(int)`/`set(double)` pair. The ordinary call gets longer (`5 as c_int`). The design rejects "an integer literal prefers integer types" because a case added later could switch calls silently, yet its kept exact-before-coercion rule switches calls the same way (its own risk 2). Separately, `k.scale(2)` reaches a different overload from the one C++ calls, which contradicts J8-04's stated outcome, "the overload C++ would call".
holes.fix_hint: In step 2, rank an untyped integer literal at an integer type before a float type, its own kind, as LEX-16 gives it `int` by default. Say plainly that Ember picks by Ember's `int`, or else count a literal at C++ cases as C++'s literal type, and fix J8-04's wording either way.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new TYP-26 states that a read form and a change form have two names, "the change form's name ending `_mut`", and calls this Ember's own pattern. Ember's library breaks it in about twenty places (`as_span`/`as_mut_span`, `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr`). The rule is then either false of the library it governs or a silent rename of every such example. This touches P24's one spelling per idea.
holes.fix_hint: Say that `_mut` is the importer's name for a C++ change form, or rename std's pairs (`as_span_mut`, `as_ptr_mut`) everywhere with `ember fmt --migrate`, and settle the choice with P24.

holes.what_goes_wrong: `clamp` takes three arguments and `map`'s function takes one, so step 1 binds no case and the line is E2070. The design's other case says this line picks `clamp<float>`, which its own rule does not give.
holes.fix_hint: Replace the example with one whose callable type has the case's number of parameters (`f: fn(f32, f32, f32) -> f32 = eng.clamp`), or show the E2070 it gives.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule does not say whether an Ember class that overrides one case of a C++ virtual name hides the base's other cases. If the design's nearest-first rule applies, Ember inherits C++'s name-hiding trap and has no `using Button.on` to undo it. If it does not, that is unstated.
holes.fix_hint: Say that an `override fn` replaces only the case it names, and that the class's cases of that name are the base's with the overridden ones replaced.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Under the new FFI-12, a first word after the `:` that is in FFI-11's vocabulary is a contract. A global C++ type named `handle`, `one`, `out`, `status` or `owns` therefore cannot be written, so its case cannot be told apart from another and stays unvouchable (the design's own risk 4).
holes.fix_hint: Let a raw identifier (`r#handle`, P22) name such a type in an overlay parameter, and say so in FFI-12.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Smart-pointer-like classes (`Ref<T>`, `ComPtr<T>`) have a lone `const` `operator*` returning `T&`. engineering.notes:
Engineering review of P07 (read only; no edits, builds or scripts). Two high holes, both common C++ programs that are refused with no way out:

1. TYP-24 step 1 ignores the word at the call. `const T&`/`T&&` (and `const T&`/`T&`) overload pairs import with equal Ember types (FFI-40). Every call ties, and no overlay line can name either case. Verdicts 1, 146 and 147 already make each word fit exactly one case, so the fix is to bind by the word. This also clashes with P06.
2. Distinct C++ integer and character types map to one Ember alias (`c_long` is `i64` on LP64 and `i32` on Windows; `c_char`; `c_wchar`). The cases then have identical signatures: unreachable, unvouchable, and different on each target.

Medium holes:
* The new TYP-26 sentence "a type's methods are one scope" contradicts IV.11 (inherent before interface method), TYP-24 (two interfaces with one method name) and the design's own two `override fn on`.
* Skipped operators cannot be renamed, though the `_mut` collision skip can (checklist 12).
* FFI-24's `Result` for throwing members makes most real C++ operators and copy constructors misfit their interfaces.
* Upcasts and read-through count as coercions, so hierarchies tie and E2070's help has no line that compiles.
* `ref_to_ptr`'s removal makes the programmer write a pointee type the compiler knows, and loses safe pointers to values whose type cannot be written.
* Merging `range` and `String()` into one function each: range's result type and inference are undecided, and per-function effects (EFF-1, EFF-15) put `Panic`/`Alloc` on forms that never run them, refusing `@realtime` code (clash with P14).
* The destructor has no overlay name under verdict 125.
* Literals: `k.set(5)` ties for int/double cases, and int/long long picks a different overload from C++.

Checked and fine:
* Zero run-time cost of case choice.
* Not importing move constructors is safe, because FFI-32 keeps non-trivially-copyable classes opaque behind a pointer.
* The at/at_mut flip when a header gains a const twin is caught by FFI-55's per-declaration fingerprint.
* A generic Ember body calling C++ cases is refused, consistent with TYP-17.
* A new overload making an old entry E5010 works as designed.
* `super.init` reuses the rule.
* Default-argument ties match C++.
* P08's cast form is consistent with phase 3's resolution.

The cross-group items to put to the owner together: P06 (call words), P14 (effects of merged defaults), P24 (`as_mut_span` against the `_mut` rule), P22 (contract-word type names), P10 (`@ffi(const)` with `ref mut` results) and P04 (destructor vouching). Files read:

design.rule:
One name in one scope is one function. Ember source (a program, the library, an overlay's `extend` block) declares a name once there. A declaration that implements another declares no name of its own: an interface method's implementation belongs to its instance, and an `override fn` belongs to what it overrides. A name stands for several functions, its **cases**, only where each case comes from a declaration of its own: the instances of one generic interface (`Mul[f32]` beside `Mul[Vec3]`), and, in an import, the functions a C++ header declares under one name. A second form of one function is written with defaults, and a call that leaves a default out, or passes a constant, is checked with that value, so a default costs no effect the call does not have.

At every call one rule picks a case when compiling. It binds by the arguments' number, names and words, the words being the ones every call already writes (`ref mut`, `owns`). It then fits each argument: exactly (an untyped literal fits exactly every type of its own kind), through a base class nearer first, or through another coercion. The case that fits every argument at least as well as each other, and one better, is the one called. Otherwise the call is refused, and the message lists the cases and gives, for each, a call that compiles, written with `as`, which now spells every coercion. Nothing is chosen while the program runs. C++'s own ranking is never used. Where C++ would rank two conversions that Ember counts alike (a 32-bit `int` literal, a promotion), Ember refuses instead of choosing differently. A header that gives a name a new case never moves an existing call to it silently.

Only the call's unmarked object cannot choose, so a `const` member and a non-`const` member of one name are a read form and a change form with two names, the second ending `_mut`. Where an idea already has a spelling, that spelling is the only one: a pointer from a view is the cast `ref x as *`, with the pointee taken from the view unless it is written.

Every C++ operator imports under a name. An operator is its Ember interface's method where one exists. It implements the interface only where its case is vouched safe, its signature fits as its entry states it, and C++'s lookup finds it for its operands. Otherwise it is a plain method of that name, as is every operator with no interface (`lt`, `call`, `to[T]`). A case unsafe to call is therefore never reached through an interface, a bound, `dyn`, `@derive` or std.

An overlay names each case exactly as the importer does: by name, words and parameter names, then by Ember types or type arguments, and only where Ember's types cannot, by its C++ parameter types. A case that no call can reach is reported at the import with the line that reaches it. The special members follow Ember's own interfaces: the copy constructor is `clone`, and the destructor is `drop`, vouched like any member. An object holding a C++ base inline never moves.
design.spec_text:
Changes for P07.
* Rules added: `[FFI-17g]`.
* Rules changed: `[TYP-26]`, `[TYP-24]`, `[TYP-18]` (a sentence), `[TYP-6]` (a paragraph), §IV.5 with the grammar's `conversion`, `[FFI-21a]` (wording), `[FFI-42]`, `[FFI-39]` and `[THR-2]` (a sentence each), `[FFI-39b]`, `[FFI-48]`, `[GRM-35]`, `[FFI-12]`, `[FFI-30c]`, `[FFI-40a]`, `[FFI-55]` (a sentence), `[CLS-4]` (a sentence), `[EFF-15]` (a proof), §I.6, `[STD-26]`, `[TXT-11]` (wording).

`[TYP-26]` *(changed)* **One name, one function.** A declaration names one function. Ember source (a program, the library, an overlay's `extend` block) declares a name once in a scope; a second declaration of it there is `E1030`. A type's own methods are one scope, whichever blocks declare them, and methods of one name on different types are in different scopes.

A declaration that implements another declares no name of its own. An interface method's implementation belongs to its interface's instance, and an `override fn` to the method, or the C++ case (`[FFI-17g]`), it overrides. So:
* `extend Vec3 implements Mul[f32]` and `extend Vec3 implements Mul[Vec3]` each write `fn mul`;
* an inherent `area` beside the `area` of `Shape` and of `Tile` is three functions: the inherent one is found first (§IV.11), and the others are written `Shape.area(r)` (`[TYP-24]`);
* two implementations of one instance for one type are `E2041` (`[TYP-20]`).

A name stands for several functions, its **cases**, only where each comes from a declaration of its own:
* the implementations of one generic interface's method in several of its instances (`Mul[f32]` and `Mul[Vec3]`; `From[IoError]` and `From[ParseError]`);
* in an import, the functions a C++ header declares under one name (`[FFI-17g]`).

`[TYP-24]` picks among a name's cases at each call, when compiling.

What would be a second form of one function is written with defaults (`[TYP-25]`). `range` (`[STD-26]`) and `String`'s `init` (`[TXT-11]`) are each declared once, and a call is checked with the constants it passes or leaves to defaults (`[EFF-15]`).

A function whose last positional parameter takes a pack's values ... (unchanged).

`[TYP-24]` *(changed)* **Which function a call reaches.** An interface method is found through any implementation visible in the program; the interface need not be imported. When two interfaces supply a method of one name for one type, the call is `E2070` and is written `I.m(recv, …)`.

A call of a name with cases (`[TYP-26]`), whether an interface's instances or a C++ name's functions, picks one when compiling, by this rule and no other:
1. **Binding.** It takes the cases its arguments bind to: by their number, their names and the parameters' defaults (`[TYP-25]`), and by their words. An argument binds only to a parameter whose word `[FN-2a]` asks it to carry: `ref mut` (or `const ref mut`), `owns`, or none. So `s.add(m)` binds to `add(m: Mesh)`, and `s.add(owns m)` to `add(owns m: Mesh)`.
2. **Fit.** Each argument fits its parameter in one of three ways, the better first:
   a. *exactly*: its type is the parameter's, read through its views and one level of owner as §IV.11 step 1 strips a receiver's, so a `ref Mesh` or an `owns Mesh` fits `Mesh` exactly. An untyped literal has no type until its context gives one (`[LEX-16]`, `[LEX-17]`), so it fits exactly every type of its own kind that holds it: an integer literal every integer type, a float literal every float type.
   b. *through a base class*, a nearer base before a farther one, in §IV.11's order.
   c. *through any other coercion* of `[TYP-5]` (`[RNG-5a2]`), an integer literal given to a float type included.
   Of the bound cases that every argument fits, the one called fits each argument at least as well as every other, and some argument better.
3. **No choice.** No such case is `E2070`. The message lists each case with its Ember parameter types and gives the call that reaches each: the argument converted with `as` (`[TYP-6]`: `out.put(5 as i32)`, `p.add(t as gui.ui.Button)`, `show(c as dyn Shape)`), or `I[A].m(recv, …)` for an interface's instance.

For example, with `set(c_int)` and `set(f64)`, `k.set(5)` reaches `set(c_int)` (2a before 2c). With `put(i32)` and `put(i64)`, `out.put(5)` is `E2070`, since `5` fits both exactly, and `out.put(n)` for `n: int` reaches `put(i64)`. With `add(Widget)` and `add(Button)`, `p.add(toggle)` reaches `add(Button)`, the nearer base.

A name with cases used as a value rather than called (`f: fn(f32, f32, f32) -> f32 = eng.clamp`, or an argument for a callable parameter or bound) takes the case that the callable type expected there picks by steps 1 to 3, its parameters standing for the arguments. Where no callable type is expected it is `E2070`.

An operator chooses among instances as its method's call does (`[TYP-21]`, ODR-096). Inside a generic body ... (unchanged).

`[TYP-18]` *(added sentence)* An argument for a parameter of type `Option[T]` that is not itself an `Option` gives `T` its own type, as `[TYP-5]` rule 11 then makes it `Some` of it. So `range(1, n)` with `n: u8` has `T = u8`, the literal being resolved last (`[TYP-23]`).

`[TYP-6]` *(added paragraph)* `x as T` also writes out a coercion that `[TYP-5]` makes: to a base class (`t as gui.ui.Button`), to an interface (`c as dyn Shape`), to a view (`xs as Span[int]`), to a wider number (`n as i64`). It converts exactly as that coercion does where it is written, a value read in place staying read in place, and it is how a call names the case it means (`[TYP-24]`). Any other `as` between non-scalar types is `E2020`, and a cast to a raw pointer is §IV.5's.

§IV.5 *(changed)* `*T` and `*mut T` are nullable, possibly unaligned, untracked pointers. Making one from a view is safe, and is written as the conversion it is: `ref x as *T`, `ref mut x as *mut T`, or `r as *T` for a view `r`. It is allowed when the pointee is unchanged and the cast does not strengthen mutability (`ref T` to `*T`, or `ref mut T` to `*T` or `*mut T`).

The pointee may be left out, as in `ref x as *` and `ref mut x as *mut`. It is then the view's own type; where it is written, it is checked to be that type. So a pointer to a value whose type cannot be written (an iterator pipeline, a `some I` result) is made safely too. A cast between raw pointers that keeps the pointee may leave it out as well (`p as *mut`, in `unsafe`, `[TYP-7]`).

There is no second spelling (`[TYP-26]`). `ref_to_ptr(x)` is `E1010`: "`ref_to_ptr` is not Ember: a pointer from a view is the conversion `ref x as *`". `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites it. ODR-075's library name is removed. Grammar: `conversion := unary {"as" cast_type}` and `cast_type := type | "*" ["mut"]`, the second form only where no type follows. The rest of IV.5 is unchanged.

`[FFI-21a]` *(wording)* "one made from a view of it or of a part of it (`ref value as *`, `ref value.field as *`)".

`[FFI-17g]` *(new)* **A C++ name with several functions.** The functions that C++'s lookup finds for one name in one scope import as that name's cases (`[TYP-26]`). The scope is a namespace, or a class together with what a using-declaration brings in from a base; a name the class declares itself hides a base's, as in C++. The cases are:
* its overloads;
* its constructors, which are the cases of `new`;
* the instances of a function template listed in `instantiate=[…]` (`[FFI-17b]`), one of which an explicit type argument may also pick (`make[c_int]()`).

A call picks by `[TYP-24]`, from the arguments' Ember types and words, never by C++'s resolution. A call that C++ resolves and `[TYP-24]` leaves tied is `E2070`. `new` and `super.init` are called as functions, so their arguments take the words of their parameters (`[FN-2a]`).

Each case is its own import. It has its own thunk (`[FFI-17]`), its own overlay entry, which alone makes it safe to call (`[FFI-2]`, verdict 125), and its own facts (`@ffi(const)`, contract words, effects, exception policy). Importing a name (`from eng.gfx import draw`) imports all its cases.

**Every case reachable.** A case that no call can reach, because every argument list that fits it fits another case equally well, is reported at the import with `W5002`. The message names both cases and gives the overlay line that renames one. Until then, a call that fits both is `E2070`, giving that line. Examples:
* `put(long)` beside `put(long long)` where `c_long` is `i64`;
* `draw()` beside `draw(int layer = 0)`;
* `f(Mesh)` beside `f(const Mesh&)`.

An overlay names such a case by its parameter count where that differs (`rename draw() as draw_plain`). Otherwise it names it by its C++ parameter types, written as `instantiate=[…]` writes C++: `@ffi(cpp="put(long long)")` above `rename put(v) as put_wide`. That form may name only a case that Ember's types cannot (elsewhere it is `E5010`, giving the typed line), and the same line serves every target.

**Defaults.** A C++ default argument is a default (`[TYP-25]`). A call may leave it out, and C++ evaluates its expression for that call in the thunk, where its value ends when the call returns. So a parameter whose value must outlive the call has no default in Ember, and a call writes it. That is a parameter the case's result views (`-> from(s)`), or one that C keeps (`retained`). The message: "`checked`'s `s` has no default here: C++'s `Style()` would end when the call returns, and the result views `s`; make one and pass it: `s = gui.ui.Style.new()`, then `gui.ui.checked(s)`". A converting constructor is a case of `new` and never an implicit conversion (`[TYP-5]` is complete).

**`const` and non-`const` members.** A call does not mark its object (`[FN-2a]`, verdict 1), so it cannot choose between a `const` member and a non-`const` one with the same parameters. They import as a read form and a change form: the `const` one keeps the name, and the other takes `_mut` after it (`at` and `at_mut`; `operator[]`'s are `index` and `index_mut`, `[FFI-42]`). A member with no such twin keeps its name.

A member that would import under a name another member already has, with the same parameters, is skipped with `W5002` (a non-`const` `at` beside a member named `at_mut`). Its message gives the overlay's `rename` line.

Every other parameter's word is written at the call. So `add(const Mesh&)` and `add(Mesh&&)` stay two cases of `add`, reached by `s.add(m)` and `s.add(owns m)` (`[TYP-24]` step 1).

**Special members.**
* The copy constructor implements `Clone` where `[FFI-42]`'s conditions hold, so `copy of g` runs it. It is no case of `new`, and an overlay names it `clone`.
* The destructor is the class's `drop`, which runs wherever an object ends (verdict 57). It is unsafe to call until the class section says `fn drop()` (verdict 125). So an object that ends outside unsafe code without that line is `E3100`, naming the end and the line. A class whose destructor is trivial runs no C++ code at its end and has no `drop` case.
* Move constructors and copy or move assignment are not imported. Ember's hand-over and `=` move and replace an owner, never the object, and an object holding a C++ object inline never moves (`[FFI-39]`).
* A deleted special member gives nothing: with a deleted copy constructor there is no `Clone`, and `copy of g` is `E2116`.

**Overrides.** An Ember class derived from a C++ class overrides a case of a virtual name by writing its parameters exactly as the import gives them, types and words, one `override fn` per case (`[CLS-4]`):
* `override fn on(e: evs.ev.Event)` for `on(const Event&)`;
* `override fn on(code: c_int)` for `on(int)`.

One that matches no case, a word included, is `E5057`, naming the nearest case and its line: "`on(owns e: Event)` overrides nothing: `on(const Event&)` is `override fn on(e: evs.ev.Event)`".

**Changing headers.** `ember.overlays` records each case of every C++ name with several cases that the package calls (`[FFI-55]`). When a build finds that the header has a case the record lacks, it re-resolves each call of that name with the recorded cases as well. A call that would now reach another case is `E5010`, naming the call, both cases, and the line that keeps the old one (`io.io.read_into(p, n as i64)`); `ember bind <header> --merge` records the new case once the calls are checked. A new case that no call reaches is added to the record. So a header update never moves a call to another case silently, in safe code or in unsafe.

`[FFI-42]` *(changed)* **Operators.** A C++ operator, a member or a free function, imports under the name of its Ember interface's method where one exists, each of its functions a case of that name (`[FFI-17g]`):

| C++ | Ember name (interface) |
|---|---|
| binary `+ - * / % & \| ^ << >>` | `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `rem`, `bitand`, `bitor`, `bitxor`, `shl`, `shr` (`Add[R]` and the rest, one instance per right-hand type `R`) |
| `+=` and the other compound assignments | `add_assign` and the rest (`AddAssign[R]` …) |
| unary `-`, `~` | `neg`, `not` |
| `==` with an operand of its own type | `eq` (`Eq`) |
| `<=>` returning `std::strong_ordering`, beside `Eq` | `cmp` (`Ord`) |
| `[]` | `index`, `index_mut` (`Index[I]`, `IndexMut[I]`; a lone non-`const` one serves both, as a method that may change its object, `[FFI-40]`) |
| `*` and `->` on a smart-pointer-like class | `get`, `get_mut` (read-through, ODR-252) |
| `begin` and `end` with an iterator type | `Iterable` |

**When a case implements its interface.** A case implements its interface (or gives read-through) where all three hold:
* its signature fits the interface's method as its entry states it;
* it is vouched safe, by an entry that is not `unsafe fn` (verdict 125: an implementation of a safe method is safe, as J5-16's answer has it for Ember's own);
* so is every C++ function the interface's use runs (an `Iterable`'s `begin` and `end`, and its iterator's `++`, `*` and `!=`).

A case that does not is a plain method of that name: `g.index(3)`, called in unsafe code when its entry is `unsafe fn` or missing. Then `g[3]`, `a == b`, `copy of g`, `for x in v`, a bound (`[C: needs Index[usize]]`), a `dyn`, an `@derive` and a std function that would reach it are each refused when compiling, because the type does not implement the interface. The message names the case and its entry line: "`Grid` has no `Index`: its `operator[]` is unsafe to call (`unsafe fn index(i)`, overlays/grid.em line 9); call `g.index(3)` in unsafe code, or vouch for a checked operator with `fn index(i)`".

A C++ declaration that may throw gives `-> Result[T, CppError]` (`[FFI-24]`), which fits no operator interface. `@ffi(noexcept)` above its entry makes it `-> T`, and a throw then stops the program naming the declaration (`[FFI-24b]`), so it fits. Without that line it stays a plain method, `a.add(b)?`.

**Operators with no interface.** An operator with no Ember interface imports as a plain method of a stated name:
* `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` as `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`;
* another `<=>` as `cmp`;
* `==` against another type as a further case of `eq`;
* `()` as `call`;
* a conversion `operator T()` as a case of `to`, picked by its type argument (`k.to[bool]()`);
* unary `+` and `!` as `pos` and `logical_not`;
* `++` and `--` as `inc` and `dec`, the postfix form taking its dummy `c_int`;
* `&&`, `||` and `,` as `logical_and`, `logical_or` and `comma`;
* an `operator=` other than copy or move assignment as `assign`.

So an overlay's `extend` may implement an interface over them (`extend Key implements Ord:` calling `this.lt(o)`), and `rename` reaches them. A class's own `operator new` and `delete` belong to C++, used by its constructors and destructor, and import as nothing.

**Free operators.** A free operator implements its interface only where C++'s argument-dependent lookup finds it for its operands: when it is declared in the namespace of one of its operand types, or is a friend defined in the class. It belongs to the import of that type (`[FFI-30]`'s one entity), so two packages that import it give one implementation. A free operator declared anywhere else is a plain function of its namespace, called by its path (`phys.p.add(v, w)`).

An overlay names an operator by its Ember name (`fn index(i)`, `fn add(rhs)`, `fn eq(other)`, `fn lt(o)`, `[FFI-12]`). `rename` gives a case another name and makes it a plain method of that name, so the overlay's `extend` may then implement the interface itself (a checked `index` over C++'s unchecked one).

`[FFI-39]` *(added sentence)* An object of an Ember class derived from a C++ class holds its C++ base inline, whose bytes C++ may point into (a short `std::string`, a `this` that C++ keeps), so it never moves. Handed to another thread while a `weakref` link on this thread points at it, it stops the program as an object C keeps does (`[THR-2]`, `[FFI-35a]`, verdict 114), and a reload does not relocate it (Annex B).

`[THR-2]` *(wording)* "An object whose address C keeps (`[FFI-35a]`), or whose class has a C++ base (`[FFI-39]`), never moves".

`[FFI-39b]` *(changed)* `super.init(…)` picks the C++ base constructor among the base's `new` cases by `[TYP-24]`, its arguments taking their parameters' words, and runs it at `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-11]`). A base with no default constructor and no declared `init` is `E5058`.

`[FFI-48]` *(changed)* The row "overloads differing only in return type" is removed. C++ cannot declare such overloads, and template instances that differ only in their result are told apart by their type arguments (`[FFI-17g]`).

`[GRM-35]` *(changed)*
```text
overlay_item  := {attribute} ["override"] (overlay_fn | "type" IDENT NEWLINE | "enum" IDENT NEWLINE
                 | "rename" fn_ref "as" IDENT NEWLINE | "hide" fn_ref NEWLINE | extend_decl
                 | overlay_class)
overlay_class := "class" IDENT ":" NEWLINE INDENT {{attribute} ["override"] (overlay_fn
                 | "rename" fn_ref "as" IDENT NEWLINE | "hide" fn_ref NEWLINE)} DEDENT
overlay_fn    := ["unsafe"] "fn" IDENT [type_list] "(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")"
                 ["->" contract {contract}] NEWLINE
fn_ref        := IDENT [type_list] ["(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")"]
type_list     := "[" type {"," type} "]"
overlay_param := [param_word] (IDENT | "_") [":" [type] {contract}]
```

`[FFI-12]` *(changed)* An overlay item that names a function (an entry, a `rename`, a `hide`, and `override` before one) names exactly one of its cases:
* by its name and its parameters' words and names (`fn add(owns m)`), with `_` for a parameter the header leaves unnamed;
* where those fit more than one case, also by each parameter's Ember type, written as the import names it and placed before its contract words (`fn set(value: f32)`, `fn load(path: *c_char borrowed nul_terminated)`; `ember bind --explain` prints each case's line). After the `:`, a first word that belongs to `[FFI-11]`'s vocabulary is a contract word, and any other first word is the type;
* a template's instance, by its type arguments (`fn make[c_int]()`);
* a case Ember's types cannot tell from another, by `@ffi(cpp="…")` (`[FFI-17g]`).

An operator is named by its Ember name (`[FFI-42]`), a constructor by `new`, the copy constructor by `clone` and the destructor by `drop`. A case may have one entry and one `rename`.

An item that matches no case, or that fits more than one, is `E5010`. The message names each case it fits and the line that names each: "`fn set(value)` fits two of `Grid`'s `set`: write `fn set(value: c_int)` or `fn set(value: f32)`". So overlays cannot drift: a header that gains a case which an existing entry also fits makes that entry `E5010` at the next build. A new overload is never vouched for by an entry written before it.

An entry outside a class section that names only members of classes is `E5010` too (verdict 131, unchanged).

`[FFI-30c]` *(changed)* "… and any other second entry for one case is `E5010` (ODR-149)."

`[FFI-40a]` *(added sentence)* `@ffi(const)` above an entry whose result lets its caller change the object is `E5010` (`index_mut`, `at_mut`, `samples_mut`). Such a result is a `ref mut`, `MutSpan` or `exclusive` result into the object (`from(this)`, or no lifetime word, `[FFI-40]`), or an `Option` or tuple holding one. Through a name that only reads the object, it would hand out a way to change it (verdict 5). A result that points elsewhere (`from(p)`, `from(static)`) changes nothing of the object, so `@ffi(const)` above it stands. Where a C++ reference points is the entry's to say (`[FFI-11]`).

`[FFI-55]` *(added sentence)* For every package that imports a C++ header, with an overlay or without one, the record also holds the cases of each C++ name with several cases that the package calls (`[FFI-17g]`).

`[CLS-4]` *(added sentence)* An `override fn`, and a method that implements an interface's method, writes exactly the parameters (their types and words), `owns this` and the result of what it overrides or implements. One that differs is refused, the message giving that first line (`E5057` for a C++ case, `[FFI-17g]`).

`[EFF-15]` *(a proof added to the list)* **Constant arguments.** A call is checked as the function in which each parameter whose argument is a constant holds that value. The constant is written as a literal or a `const`, or left to a default that is one. The check is the same as for a generic's instance, which is checked for its types (`[TYP-16]`). A branch whose condition compile-time evaluation (`[CT-1]`) then decides is taken or not as it evaluates, and the operations of a branch not taken contribute no effect. So:
* `range(n)`, whose `step` is 1, has no step check;
* `String()`, whose text is empty, has no `Alloc`;
* `String.with_capacity(0)` has no `Alloc` either.

The package that compiles the call works this out, as it does a generic instance (`[EFF-4]`). Like every proof here, it only removes effects.

§I.6 *(changed)* "… function overloading, in the sense of declaring one name twice in one scope (a name reaches several functions only as the cases of `[TYP-26]`) …".

`[STD-26]` *(changed)* "`range` is one function, `fn range(first: T, stop: Option[T] = None, step: T = 1) -> RangeStep[T]`, with `T` inferred by `[TYP-18]`:
* `range(stop)` counts from 0, `first` then being the stop;
* `range(start, stop)` and `range(start, stop, step)` count from `start`, as Python's do, a negative `step` included;
* `step == 0` panics.

`RangeStep[T]` is a prelude struct with public `start`, `stop` and `step`, `Copy` when `T` is. It is iterated as a counted loop (`[CTL-3b]`), and has `len()` and `x in r` as Python's `range` has them. `range(n)` counts as `0..n` does. A call that leaves `step` out, or passes a constant one, has no step check (`[EFF-15]`)."

`[TXT-11]` *(wording)* "`String(s = "")`, one `init`: `String()` is empty and allocates nothing (`[EFF-15]`), and `String(s)` is a `String` of your own made from text".

`operator[]` imports under the name of its Ember interface's method: the `const` one is `index` and the non-`const` one is `index_mut`. They are a read/change pair, because the call does not mark its object (`[FFI-17g]`). An overlay names them that way, under the class (verdict 131), with `@ffi(const)` above `index` (verdict 132).

A case implements `Index` or `IndexMut` only where its entry vouches it safe (`[FFI-42]`), since an implementation of a safe method is safe. So:
* **A C++ operator that checks its bound** gets `fn index(i)`, and `g[3]` is safe anywhere: in a bound, through `dyn`, in std.
