The message names the case and its entry line. The case stays callable as a plain method (`g.index(3)`) in unsafe code.

other_cases.case: A throwing operator: `Amount operator+(const Amount&) const` without `noexcept`, or a copy constructor that may throw.
other_cases.settled: It imports as the plain method `add(other) -> Result[Amount, CppError]` (`[FFI-24]`), so `a.add(b)?` works and `a + b` is refused with the fix. `@ffi(noexcept)` above `fn add(other)` makes it `-> Amount`, and a throw then stops the program naming the declaration (`[FFI-24b]`). With that, it is `Add`, and `a + b` compiles. The same holds for `fn clone()` and `Clone`.

other_cases.case: `operator<`, `operator<=>`, `operator()`, `explicit operator bool()`, and `operator==(const char*)`.
other_cases.settled:
* **`<`** imports as `lt`, so `extend Key implements Ord:` in the overlay may call `this.lt(o)`.
* **`<=>`** returning `std::strong_ordering` is `Ord` beside `Eq`.
* **`()`** is `call`.
* **`operator bool`** is `k.to[bool]()`.
* **The mixed `==`** is a further case of `eq` (`k.eq(c"x")`); `==` itself stays `Eq`'s.

Each can be renamed.

other_cases.case: The destructor of an imported class.
other_cases.settled: It is the class's `drop`, which runs wherever an object ends (verdict 57). The overlay vouches for it with `fn drop()` under the class (verdict 125). Without that line, an end in safe code is `E3100`, naming the end and the line. A trivial destructor runs no C++ code and needs no line.

other_cases.case: Copy and move constructors, copy and move assignment.
other_cases.settled:
* **The copy constructor** implements `Clone` where `[FFI-42]`'s conditions hold: `copy of g` runs it, and an overlay names it `clone`. A deleted one gives no `Clone` (`E2116`).
* **Moves and assignments** are not imported: Ember moves and replaces owners, never objects.

other_cases.case: An Ember class with a C++ base handed to another thread while a `weakref` on this thread points at it (verdict 114's relocation).
other_cases.settled: It never moves (`[FFI-39]`): the hand-over stops the program, naming the link, as for an object C keeps. A short `std::string` in the base, or a `this` C++ keeps, is never left pointing at freed memory. Coordinated with P03 (placement) and P09 (reload).

other_cases.case: A named `const`/non-`const` pair: `T& at(size_t)` and `const T& at(size_t) const`; also `data()` and `begin()`.
other_cases.settled: They import as `at` and `at_mut`, and as `data` and `data_mut`. `x = v.at(3)` reads, and `v.at_mut(3)` gives a view that may change `v`, through a name that may change it. A lone member of either kind keeps its C++ name.

other_cases.case: `@ffi(const)` above `fn index_mut(i)`, above `fn samples_mut() -> from(this) exclusive`, or above a view class's `float& operator[](size_t) const` whose entry says `-> from(p)`.
other_cases.settled:
* **The first two** are `E5010`: each result lets a caller change the object through a read-only name (verdict 5).
* **The third** stands: its result points elsewhere. Where a C++ reference points is the entry's to say (P04's J8-06).

other_cases.case: An override or an interface implementation with other words: `override fn on(owns e: Event)` over `on(const Event&)`.
other_cases.settled: `E5057`, giving `override fn on(e: evs.ev.Event)`. Overrides and implementations write exactly the parameters and words of what they replace (`[CLS-4]`), so C++'s stack object is never ended by Ember, and a `const` reference is never written through.

other_cases.case: Ember source with names that look alike: an inherent `area` beside `Shape.area` and `Tile.area`; two `extend Vec3 implements Mul[...]` blocks each writing `fn mul`; two `override fn on`.
other_cases.settled: All allowed. An implementation or override declares no name of its own (`[TYP-26]`). `r.area()` is the inherent one (IV.11), and `Shape.area(r)` names another (`[TYP-24]`). Two inherent `len` on one type are `E1030`.

other_cases.case: An Ember class derived from a C++ class, overriding overloaded virtuals `on(int)` and `on(float)`.
other_cases.settled: `override fn on(code: c_int)` and `override fn on(v: f32)`, one per case, each written as the import gives it. An `override fn on(s: StrView)` matching no case is `E5057`.

other_cases.case: A header update adds `void read_into(char*, int32_t)` beside `read_into(char*, int64_t)`, and an existing unsafe call passes an `i32`.
other_cases.settled: The package's record (`[FFI-55]`) lacks the new case. The build re-resolves the call against the recorded cases: before, it reached the `int64_t` case through widening; now the `int32_t` case fits exactly. The build stops with `E5010`, naming the call, both cases and `n as i64`. No `# SAFETY:` note silently comes to cover a case it was not written for. An old overlay entry the new case also fits is `E5010` too.

other_cases.case: Upcasts: `Panel.add(const Widget&)` and `add(const Button&)` given a `Toggle` (a `Button`, which is a `Widget`); `log(const KeyEvent&)` given an `owns KeyEvent` field.
other_cases.settled:
* `p.add(t)` reaches `add(const Button&)`, the nearer base, as IV.11 and C++ do.
* `lg.log(p.ev)` fits `KeyEvent` exactly, read through its owner.
* Where two cases tie, the help writes the conversion: `p.add(t as gui.ui.Widget)`.

other_cases.case: std's `range(stop)`, `range(start, stop)`, `range(start, stop, step)`, and `String()` beside `String(s)`.
other_cases.settled:
Each is one function with defaults. `range` returns `RangeStep[T]` in every form, and `range(1, n)` with `n: u8` counts in `u8` (`[TYP-18]`).

A call is checked with the constants it leaves to defaults or passes (`[EFF-15]`):
* `for i in range(n)` in a `@nopanic(explicit)` function has no step check;
* `String()` in a `@noalloc` one allocates nothing.

Every form of `range` compiles to the same counted loop (`[CTL-3b]`).

other_cases.case: A name with cases used as a value: `f: fn(f32, f32, f32) -> f32 = eng.clamp`, or `xs.iter().map(eng.clamp)`.
other_cases.settled: The expected callable type picks the case by the same rule, here `clamp<float>`. `f = eng.clamp` with no expected type is `E2070`, which gives the typed line.

other_cases.case: A generic Ember function calling a C++ name with cases on a type parameter: `[T]` above `fn log_all(xs: Span[T])`, whose body calls `eng.log(x)`.
other_cases.settled: Refused. A generic body is checked once, for any `T` (`[TYP-17]`), and no case takes any `T`. The program writes an interface implemented for each type, which is Ember's own way to have cases.

other_cases.case: An overlay `extend` block adds `fn draw(c: Circle)` beside C++'s `draw` cases.
other_cases.settled: `E1030`: Ember source never adds a case. Name the wrapper (`draw_circle`), or implement an interface for `Circle`.

other_cases.case: Unnamed header parameters: `void set(int); void set(float);`.
other_cases.settled: The entries name them `fn set(_: c_int)` and `fn set(_: f32)`. Unnamed parameters are passed by position only.

other_cases.case: Inherited C++ overloads and name hiding: `Base::draw(float)` and `Derived::draw(int)`, with or without `using Base::draw;`.
other_cases.settled: `Derived`'s cases are what C++'s lookup in `Derived` finds: `draw(int)` alone, or both with the using-declaration. This is the same nearest-first rule as IV.11.

other_cases.case: A pointer made from a class object for C (P08's J8-12), and Vulkan's `pBuffer` (P04's J8-08).
other_cases.settled:
The spelling is the cast:
* `ref body as ObjectPtr[Body]`, if P08 adds `ObjectPtr` to IV.5's list;
* `ref mut out as *mut`.

Never a third `ref_to_ptr`.

design.prior_art:
**C++.** Ad hoc overloading by parameter types, by the `const`-ness of `this` and by ref-qualifiers, resolved by a ranking of conversions (exact, promotion, conversion, user-defined) and by argument-dependent lookup over the operands' namespaces. It has zero run-time cost. Its weaknesses:
* The reader has to rank conversions to know which body runs.
* A newly added overload silently changes existing calls.
* `f(0)` against `f(NULL)`, and a `bool` overload catching pointers, are classic traps.
* The `const`/non-`const` pair is duplicated code; C++23's deducing `this` (P0847) exists to fold it into one function.

The `const T&`/`T&&` pair is the commonest modern overload, chosen by value category.

**Rust.** No ad hoc overloading: several functions of one name exist only as trait instances (`impl Mul<f32> for Vec3` beside `impl Mul<Vec3> for Vec3`), picked by type when compiling.
* Read/change pairs are two names (`get`/`get_mut`, `as_ptr`/`as_mut_ptr`).
* `Index` is always safe; an unchecked access is a named `unsafe fn get_unchecked`, wrapped by a checked `Index`. This is the shape J8-05 now takes.
* A pointer from a reference is `&x as *const T`, `&x as *const _`, or, since 1.82, `&raw const x`, which needs no type. Clippy's `ref_as_ptr` prefers forms that cannot change the pointee, which Ember's checked cast cannot do anyway.
* At C++ it falls short: bindgen names overloads `draw`, `draw1`; cxx makes the programmer declare each overload under a name of their own.

**C#.** Overloading by types and by the `ref`/`out`/`in` modifiers that calls also write. That is the precedent for binding by the call's word (`s.add(owns m)`).

**Swift's C++ interop.** It imports overloads as Swift overloads, a `const`/non-`const` `operator[]` as one `subscript`, `operator()` as `callAsFunction`, and other operators as functions. Solving overloads together with literals is known for \"expression too complex\" compile times. Ember's literal rule (own kind fits exactly, ties refused) avoids that search.

**Ada.** Overloading by parameter and result types, with named association. Precise, but resolution needs the whole surrounding context.

**Go and Python.** No overloading. SWIG for Go and pybind11 for Python reach C++ overloads through a dispatcher that tries them at run time, which costs every call. Python's `range` is one callable with optional arguments; that is the model the library now follows.

**Zig.** No overloading: one function taking `anytype` branches on the type at compile time, and its comptime arguments decide branches. That is the model of `[EFF-15]`'s constant-argument proof.

**What A takes:**
* Rust's model: one function per declaration, instances picked by type when compiling, `_mut` twins, and a cast that never changes the pointee.
* Swift's result at C++: the C++ name is kept and overloads are picked by the arguments.
* C#'s binding by the written word.
* C++'s own nearest-base rule and associated namespaces, where they agree with Ember's types.
* A refusal wherever C++ would rank two conversions Ember counts alike.

So it is safe, as fast as C, and readable at once.
design.cost:
Zero at run time, in every part of the rule.

* **Choosing a case** happens when compiling. The call is one direct call of that case's thunk (`[FFI-17]`), which is exactly what C++'s static overload resolution leaves and what C pays: one call. With LTO the thunk is inlined (`[BLD-FFI-4]`).
* **A C++ default argument.** C++'s default expression runs in the thunk for that call, the same work C++ does at its own call site. There is one extra thunk per case and per number of arguments left out, for the shapes actually used; C++ emits that same code inline.
* **`_mut` pairs, operator names, `drop` and `clone`.** Each is the C++ member it names; nothing is added.
* **The cast `ref x as *`.** The address itself (one `lea`, or nothing), as C's `&x`, and the same code `ref_to_ptr` compiled to.
* **`RangeStep[T]`.**
  * Iteration is the same counted loop as `0..n` (`[CTL-3b]`). With `step` left out or constant there is no check, and a non-constant step is checked once before the loop.
  * `len()` and `x in r` cost one division and one modulo by the step when the step is not a constant, as Python and C pay for a stepped count. A constant step folds.
  * Memory: three numbers instead of `Range`'s two.
* **An object with a C++ base never moving.** It costs nothing on the path that does not stop. Verdict 114's one compare at a hand-over already reads the weak count.
* **Memory.** No byte is added to any object, call or method table. Cases are not table entries, except C++'s own virtuals, which are unchanged.
* **Compile time.**
  * Each call filters its name's cases, usually 2 to 5, which is negligible beside libclang's parse.
  * The constant-argument proof computes one effect set per distinct constant shape a function is called with, as monomorphisation does per instance, and only where a body branches on such a parameter.
  * The case-set record adds one re-resolution of each call of a name whose header gained a case.

readability.ordinary_before:
import cpp "renderer.hpp" with (project="engine", overlay="overlays/renderer.em") as eng

fn draw_frame(ref mut r: eng.gfx.Renderer, meshes: Span[eng.gfx.Mesh], hud: eng.gfx.Sprite):
    for m in meshes:
        r.draw(m)          # Hardened_11: no rule says what `draw` is (TYP-26: no overloading)
    r.draw(hud)

fn main():
    r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)   # which of two constructors? undecided
    level = load_level("forest")
    draw_frame(ref mut r, level.meshes, level.hud)
    for i in range(level.layers):          # Hardened_11: range's three forms, a name declared three times
        println(i)
readability.note:
The program text is the same; it now has a meaning, and it reads as the C++ library's own documentation does.

An ordinary Ember program with no C++ (a game loop, a server handler, a parser) does not change at all: the rule adds no word, annotation or ceremony. `range(n)` and `String()` read as before and carry no effect they do not have.

What grows is confined to rare or dangerous code:
* **An overlay** gains one `fn drop()` per class used from safe code, since the destructor is C++ code like any member.
* **An unchecked C++ operator** is called `g.index(3)` inside `unsafe:`, or wrapped once in a checked `extend`.
* **A literal given to a C++ name with two integer widths** writes its width (`5 as i32`), as a variadic C call already must.
* **A raw-pointer line** reads `ref mut info as *mut`, as short as `ref_to_ptr(ref mut info)` was.

design.compiler_does:
**The importer**
* Collects each C++ name's cases from Clang's lookup: overloads, constructors as `new`, listed template instances, using-declarations, and hiding.
* Names each `const`/non-`const` pair `name`/`name_mut`.
* Gives every operator its name: an interface method or one of `[FFI-42]`'s plain names.
* Finds free operators by argument-dependent lookup.
* Maps the copy constructor to `clone` and the destructor to `drop`, a trivial destructor to nothing.
* Records C++ default arguments as defaults, except where a case's result or contract needs the value past the call; one thunk per shape used.
* Reports with `W5002` every case no call can reach (equal Ember types, a default overlapping another case), giving the rename line.
* Gives each case its own thunk, its own `ember.overlays` fingerprint (`[FFI-55]`) and its own facts.
* Records the case set of every C++ name with several cases that the package calls.

**The checker**
* Resolves every call of a name with cases by `[TYP-24]`: bind by number, names, defaults and words; fit each argument exactly (read through views and one owner level; a literal at every type of its kind), through a nearer base, or through another coercion; take the dominant case or refuse.
* Resolves a name used as a value through the expected callable type.
* Writes `E2070` with each case's Ember signature and an `as` line that compiles.
* Decides whether each imported case implements its interface: it is vouched, it fits as its entry states it (`@ffi(noexcept)` included), and every function the interface's use runs is vouched too.
* Refuses every operator, bound, `dyn`, `@derive` and std use that needs a missing implementation, naming the case and its entry line.
* Applies the read-only rules per case (`E3023` when the chosen case changes its object).
* Treats the end of an object as a call of its `drop` (`E3100` when the destructor is unvouched).
* Checks overrides and interface implementations against exactly the parameters, words and result of what they replace.
* Checks each call as the function with its constant arguments fixed, deciding the branches compile-time evaluation decides (`[EFF-15]`).
* On a header that gained a case, re-resolves each call of the name against the recorded set and stops on any call that would move.

**The overlay checker**
* Matches every entry, `rename` and `hide` to exactly one case: names, words, `_`, types, type arguments, and `@ffi(cpp=…)` only where Ember's types cannot.
* Refuses an item that fits no case or several with `E5010`, giving the lines. This includes an old entry that a newly added overload makes ambiguous.
* Refuses `@ffi(const)` above an entry whose result lets a caller change the object.

**Everywhere**
* Refuses a second declaration of one name in Ember source (`E1030`), the library's own included, while implementations and overrides declare none.
* Accepts `ref x as *` with the pointee taken from the view.
* Refuses `ref_to_ptr`, with the cast as help; `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites it.
* Never relocates an object with a C++ base: a hand-over with a link stops.

The programmer invents no name and writes no annotation in ordinary code. The facts the compiler cannot know (whether a C++ case is safe to call, whether it only reads, whether a throw may stop the program) stay where they already are: in that case's overlay entry.
design.misuse:
**Refused when compiling**
* **A call that no case fits, or that two fit equally:** `E2070`. This includes a literal given to two cases of its kind (`out.put(5)` beside `put(i32)`/`put(i64)`) and two cases whose Ember types coincide. The message lists each case and gives a call that compiles (`5 as i32`, `t as gui.ui.Widget`, or the overlay line).
* **A name with cases used as a value with no expected callable type:** `E2070`, giving the typed line.
* **A case called outside `unsafe` without its own entry:** `E5002`/`E3100`, naming the case and the entry line. Vouching for one overload vouches for no other.
* **An object ending in safe code whose destructor no `fn drop()` vouches for:** `E3100`.
* **An interface reached through a case that is unvouched, `unsafe fn` or throwing:** refused wherever it would be reached (`g[3]`, `a == b`, `copy of g`, `for x in v`, a bound, `dyn`, `@derive`, std), naming the case and its entry line. An unchecked C++ operator is never reached from safe code.
* **A call that leaves out a parameter whose value must outlive the call** (`from(s)`, `retained`): refused, since that parameter has no default.
* **An overlay item that fits no case or more than one:** `E5010`, with the line for each case. A header that adds an overload which an old entry also fits makes that entry `E5010`.
* **A header that would move an existing call to a new case:** `E5010`, naming the call, both cases and the line that keeps the old one.
* **`@ffi(const)` above an entry whose result can change the object** (`index_mut`, `at_mut`, an `exclusive` `MutSpan`): `E5010`.
* **An override or an implementation whose parameters, words or result differ from what it replaces:** `E5057` for a C++ case, and refused with the line for Ember's own.
* **Ember source declaring a name twice:** `E1030`, in a program, an overlay `extend` or the library. Implementations and overrides are not declarations of a name.
* **`ref_to_ptr(x)`:** `E1010`, with the cast in the help.

**Stopped at the line**
* An object with a C++ base handed to another thread while a `weakref` link on this thread points at it stops the program, naming the link, as an object C keeps does (verdict 114). It is never relocated byte by byte.
* A throw from an operator vouched `@ffi(noexcept)` stops the program, naming the declaration (`[FFI-24b]`).

**Reported, never silently absent**
* A case no call can reach is `W5002` at the import, with the line that reaches it.
* A `_mut` name collision is `W5002`, with the `rename` line.
* Every operator has an Ember name, so no operator is silently unreachable.

**Nothing is decided while running.** Ember's choice never depends on C++'s ranking. Where both rules choose, they agree:
* an exact fit is exact in both;
* a nearer base is nearer in both.

Where C++ would rank two conversions that Ember counts alike (a 32-bit `int` literal, a promotion against a widening), Ember refuses with a fix rather than choosing differently. An overlay that wrongly vouches for an unchecked C++ `operator[]` as safe is an asserted fact, listed by `ember tcb` (`[TCB-1]`). J8-05 shows the honest form: `unsafe fn index(i)` under a checked `extend`.
design.verdicts:
**Kept**
* **125:** each case is unsafe to call until its own entry vouches for it: members, constructors, operators, the copy constructor and the destructor. It now holds through every route, an interface, a bound, `dyn`, `@derive` and std included, not only through direct calls.
* **57:** destroying an object counts as calling its `drop`. With 125, the destructor of an imported class is vouched by `fn drop()`.
* **1, 146 and 147:** the word at the call is the parameter's. It now also binds the argument to a case, so `add(const Mesh&)` and `add(Mesh&&)` are told apart by `s.add(m)` and `s.add(owns m)`.
* **131:** member entries go under their class.
* **132:** an entry means only what it says. Whether a case implements its interface is judged on its entry (its vouch, its `@ffi(noexcept)`), and `@ffi(const)` without it makes the method one that changes its object. The refusal of `@ffi(const)` reads only the entry's result.
* **5:** a read-only name hands out no way to change its object. This is the reason for that refusal, now worded by what the result allows.
* **12:** the copy constructor is reached by `copy of`.
* **114:** an object that cannot move stops the hand-over. This now covers an object with a C++ base, as it covers one C keeps.
* **121 and 127:** the record Ember keeps also holds the case sets of called C++ names, for every package that imports C++ (one model for every program).
* **123:** a width that the foreign side reads and Ember cannot know is written, not guessed. This is the precedent for refusing `out.put(5)` between two integer widths.
* **130 and 133:** an unsafe operator entry is `@safety` above `unsafe fn index(i)`.
* **ODR-219 (owner):** the construction order at `super.init`.

**Applied**
* Checklist items 11 and 16, and verdict 133's lesson: `ref_to_ptr` is a second spelling of the cast, so it goes everywhere it is written (IV.5, `[FFI-21a]`, P04's J8-08 example, P08's J8-12).
* Checklist 12: every operator, and every case no call reaches, gets a spelling instead of being skipped.
* Checklist 1 (principle 1): the pointee is taken from the view.

**Tension, for the owner**
* **159** (\"a constructor's argument takes no word\") was about `T(…)`, which sets fields. An imported constructor is the function `new` (`[FFI-17]`), whose `T&&` parameter is `owns` (`[FFI-40]`). This design reads `new` and `super.init` as function calls, whose arguments take their parameters' words, so `Scene.new(owns m)`. If the owner reads 159 as covering them, `new(const Mesh&)` and `new(Mesh&&)` tie and need a `rename` each. That is P06's J1-07 question as well.

**Revisited: rulings that are not owner verdicts**
* **ODR-075 (lead, Hardened_32)** kept two spellings of one idea, and a library overload a program may not write. It is removed. The evidence: STD-13 (\"there is no second name\"), TYP-26 and checklist 11.
* **ODR-096 (delegated)** is extended with binding by words, ranking by base distance, read-through, and names used as values. Its literal clause changes: a literal counted as `int` or `f64` and preferred becomes a literal that fits every type of its kind exactly. The evidence: LEX-16 (\"not a value yet\") and verdict 123. The cost: `big + 5` beside `Add[i32]` and `Add[i64]` writes `5 as i64`.
* **ODR-149 (delegated):** \"a second entry for one name\" becomes \"for one case\".
* **ODR-252 (delegated):** `get`/`get_mut` becomes one instance of the read/change pair rule.
* **§I.6's non-goal** (overloading) is kept for Ember source; its wording now says what remains.

No owner verdict is reversed or widened.

options_for_owner.summary:
The rule. One name is one function, and Ember source declares each name once; implementations and overrides declare none.
* **Cases.** An interface's instances, and a C++ name's overloads, constructors and template instances, are that name's cases.
* **Picking.** One rule picks a case when compiling: by the arguments' words and Ember types, nearest base first, a literal of its own kind fitting exactly, and a refusal with an `as` line where two fit.
* **Pairs.** `const`/non-`const` pairs become `name`/`name_mut`.
* **Operators.** Operators are their interface's methods only where vouched and found by C++'s lookup, and plain methods otherwise.
* **Pointers.** `ref_to_ptr` goes in favour of the cast `ref x as *`.
options_for_owner.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new(1280, 720)        # Renderer(int, int)
r.draw(mesh)                                # draw(const Mesh&)
scene.add(m)                                # add(const Mesh&)
scene.add(owns m)                           # add(Mesh&&)
x = v.at(3)                                 # const at; v.at_mut(3) is the non-const one
return g[3]                                 # Index: only where operator[] is vouched or wrapped checked
p = ref mut info as *mut                    # ref_to_ptr is gone
out.put(5 as i32)                           # put(int32_t): the literal's width written

# overlay
class Grid:
    fn new(n)
    fn drop()                               # the destructor, vouched like any member
    fn set(value: c_int)                    # names fit two cases: the type tells them apart
    fn set(value: f32)
options_for_owner.outcome: Every call compiles to one direct call of the case Ember's rule picks, or it is refused with the cases listed and a line that compiles. No unchecked C++ code is reached from safe code by any route. Ember source still declares each name once (`E1030`); a program that wants cases implements one interface for each type, as `Mul[f32]` and `Mul[Vec3]` do.

options_for_owner.summary: Overloading for everyone, C#'s model. Ember source may declare cases too, by types and by a parameter's word; the selection rule is A's.
options_for_owner.code:
fn draw(m: Mesh):
    println(m.vertices)
fn draw(s: Sprite):                          # allowed in Ember source too
    println(s.frame)

[T]
fn addr(r: T) -> *T:
    return ref r as *
[T]
fn addr(ref mut r: T) -> *mut T:             # cases by a parameter's word
    return ref mut r as *mut

q = ref_to_ptr(ref mut pos)                  # stays: two cases
options_for_owner.outcome: It compiles, and C++ imports work as in A. But §I.6's non-goal is reversed: any Ember name may stand for several bodies. A function value, an `@export` symbol (one C name per case), `[IFC-6]`'s inferred bounds, a `dyn` method table and a reload's identity would each need a rule for cases. A case added later in a program or a dependency can also change which body an existing call reaches.

options_for_owner.summary: Strictly one function per name, C++ included. Each overload is skipped until an overlay renames it.
options_for_owner.code:
unsafe overlay cpp "renderer.hpp":
    class Renderer:
        rename new(width, height) as sized
        rename draw(mesh) as draw_mesh
        rename draw(sprite) as draw_sprite

r = eng.gfx.Renderer.sized(1280, 720)
r.draw_mesh(mesh)
r.draw_sprite(hud)
options_for_owner.outcome: Without the overlay, `r.draw(mesh)` is "skipped: `draw` is overloaded" (`W5002`). Every C++ class with overloads or two constructors (nearly all of them) needs an overlay before any call to it compiles, and the Ember names differ from the C++ documentation.

options_for_owner.summary: Each overload is imported under a name built from its C++ parameter types.
options_for_owner.code:
r = eng.gfx.Renderer.new_int_int(1280, 720)
r.draw_Mesh(mesh)
r.draw_Sprite(hud)
options_for_owner.outcome: It compiles with no overlay. But every overload gets a name built from types the program never wrote, which changes when the header renames a type or a `typedef`. Two overloads whose types map to one Ember type (`long` and `long long` on Linux) still collide.

recommendation.reason:
A settles every member and every other case with one selection rule that Ember already has (ODR-096's, for `Mul[f32]` beside `Mul[Vec3]`). It is extended only by what every call already writes (its words) and what C++ itself agrees with (nearest base).

* C++ code stays as readable as C++ (`r.draw(mesh)`, `scene.add(owns m)`), with no names to invent and no overlay needed before a call compiles.
* Where Ember and C++ could disagree, Ember refuses instead of guessing.
* No unchecked C++ code is reached from safe code by any route, whether an operator, a bound, `dyn`, `@derive`, a destructor, a default argument, an override's word or a header update.
* It costs nothing at run time.
* Ember source keeps one declaration per name (§I.6, STD-13), and the library loses its only twins: `ref_to_ptr`, a second spelling of the cast, and `range`'s and `String`'s forms, which become one function each with no effect they do not have.

B buys uniform declarations at the price of a non-goal and new rules for cases in five other places. C and D give up C++'s readability for every overloaded header.

owner_short.one_line: C++ overloading: what Ember does with `draw(const Mesh&)` beside `draw(const Sprite&)`, with `add(const Mesh&)` beside `add(Mesh&&)`, with several constructors, and with a `const`/non-`const` `operator[]` pair, given that Ember itself has no overloading; and with the two `ref_to_ptr` that std declares.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `import cpp "renderer.hpp"` reads `Renderer()`, `Renderer(int, int)`, `draw(const Mesh&)`, `draw(const Sprite&)` | two functions named `new`, two named `draw` |
| 2 | main | `[TYP-26]`: "two functions of one name in one scope are `E1030`"; `[FFI-48]` refuses only return-type overloads | the import breaks Ember's own rule, and no rule says how |
| 3 | main | `r = Renderer.new(1280, 720)` | which `new`? undecided |
| 4 | main | `r.draw(mesh)`; `scene.add(m)` beside `scene.add(owns m)` | one `draw` that picks by type, two names, or skipped? undecided |
| 5 | main | overlay entry `fn operator[](i)` to make `g[3]` safe | not overlay grammar: `g[3]` can never be vouched for |
| 6 | main | std's `ref_to_ptr(x)` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` | the library has the overload a program may not write, beside the cast `ref x as *T`, which does the same |
owner_short.today: Ember says one name is one function, yet C++ headers bring several functions under one name and std declares two `ref_to_ptr`. Nothing says how they import, how a call picks one, or how an overlay names one.
owner_short.options:
A: one name, one function. A C++ name's overloads, like an interface's instances, are its cases, picked by the arguments' words and Ember types when compiling, with a refusal wherever two fit. `const`/non-`const` pairs become `name`/`name_mut`. Operators are their interface's methods only where vouched. `ref_to_ptr` goes in favour of the cast `ref x as *`.
B: overloading for everyone (C#'s model). Ember source may declare cases too, by type and by a parameter's word, and `ref_to_ptr` stays.
C: one function per name, C++ included. Each overload is skipped until an overlay renames it.
D: each overload is imported under a name built from its C++ parameter types (`draw_Mesh`).
owner_short.recommendation: A. `r.draw(mesh)` and `scene.add(owns m)` read as in C++ and cost nothing. Where Ember and C++ could disagree, Ember refuses rather than guesses. Ember's own programs and its no-overloading rule are unchanged, and the one selection rule Ember already uses for `Mul[f32]` beside `Mul[Vec3]` also picks among C++'s cases.

repairs.hole: Safety 1 (high): an imported case implements its interface whatever its entry says, so `first(g)` over `[C: needs Index[usize]]` reaches an unchecked `operator[]` from safe code, and `contains`, `copy of`, `@derive(Clone)` and `for` reach unvouched `==`, copy constructors and `begin`/`end`.
repairs.answer:
Closed by `[FFI-42]`'s new condition. A case implements its interface only where it is vouched safe by an entry that is not `unsafe fn`, its signature fits as its entry states it, and every C++ function the interface's use runs is vouched too. Otherwise it is a plain method of that name, callable in unsafe code (`g.index(3)`).

The type then has no `Index`, `Eq`, `Clone` or `Iterable`, so every operator, bound, `dyn`, `@derive` and std use that would reach the case is refused by the ordinary rule (`E2040`). No extra path is needed. The message names the case and its entry line.

This is J5-16 A's "an implementation of a safe method is safe" for imports; under it, J8-05's `unsafe fn index(i)` is legal, because it is no implementation. J8-05 now shows the checked `extend` over the renamed unchecked case.

repairs.hole: Safety 2 (high): a C++ default argument is evaluated in the thunk, so `checked()` returns a reference to a `Style()` that ended inside the call; the same holds for `retained` and for `get(key, fallback = "")`.
repairs.answer: Closed in `[FFI-17g]` Defaults: a default's value ends when the call returns, so a parameter whose value must outlive the call (one the result views, `from(s)`, or one C keeps, `retained`) has no default in Ember. The call writes it, and the message gives the two lines that make and pass one. The rule follows the entry's own words (verdict 132), and needs no analysis at the call.

repairs.answer: Closed in `[FFI-17g]` Overrides and `[CLS-4]`. An `override fn`, and an implementation of an interface method, writes exactly the parameters, their words, `owns this` and the result of what it replaces. A differing word is `E5057`, naming the nearest case and the line to write. That is also the signature rule P04's J5-16 notes is missing, stated once for every override and implementation.

repairs.answer:
Closed:
* `[TYP-24]` step 1 binds by the call's words as well (`[FN-2a]`, verdicts 1, 146 and 147), so `s.add(m)` reaches `add(const Mesh&)` and `s.add(owns m)` reaches `add(Mesh&&)`.
* `[GRM-35]`'s `overlay_param` takes `param_word`, so an overlay names `fn add(owns m)`.
* The read/change pair rule now applies only to `this`, the one argument a call does not mark (`[FFI-17g]`); it is gone from `[TYP-26]`.

repairs.hole: Safety 5 (medium): verdict 114's hand-over moves an object's contents byte by byte when a `weakref` points at it, so an Ember class with a C++ base (a short `std::string` pointing into itself) is relocated without its move constructor; the same holds for a reload.
repairs.answer:
Closed by `[FFI-39]`'s added sentence and `[THR-2]`'s wording. An object whose class has a C++ base holds C++ bytes that C++ may point into, so it never moves: the hand-over with a live link stops the program, naming the link, as for an object C keeps (verdict 114, `[FFI-35a]`). A reload does not relocate it.

Running the move constructor instead was rejected: C++ may hold the object's `this`, which no move constructor updates. `[FFI-17g]`'s sentence that Ember moves owners, never objects, is then true. Coordinated with P03 and P09.

repairs.hole: Safety 6 (medium): a header adds `read_into(char*, int32_t)` and an existing unsafe call passing an `i32` silently moves to it; its `# SAFETY:` note now covers a case it never vouched for.
repairs.answer:
Closed in `[FFI-17g]` Changing headers and `[FFI-55]`. Every package that imports C++ records the cases of each C++ name with several cases it calls, with or without an overlay. When the header gains a case, every call of that name is re-resolved against the recorded set too, and a call that would move is `E5010`, naming both cases and `n as i64`. A new case no call reaches is just recorded.

This is general (safe and unsafe code, every name) and needs no per-call record, since the old set reproduces the old pick.

repairs.hole: Safety 7 (medium): every non-`noexcept` C++ function returns `Result[T, CppError]`, so throwing operators and copy constructors either do not fit their interfaces or fit with no stated behaviour.
repairs.answer:
Closed in `[FFI-42]`: the fit is judged on the case as its entry states it.
* **Without `@ffi(noexcept)`**, a throwing operator is the plain method `add(other) -> Result[…]` (`a.add(b)?` works), and `a + b` is refused with the line to write.
* **With it**, the case returns `T`, a throw stops the program naming the declaration (`[FFI-24b]`), and the case implements `Add`.

The same holds for `fn clone()` and `Clone`. No `W5002` is raised at the import, since nothing is skipped.

repairs.hole: Safety 8 (medium): `[FFI-40a]`'s refusal keyed on a result spelled `ref mut`, so an `exclusive` `MutSpan` result escapes, while a view class's `float& operator[](size_t) const` is refused although it reads only its object.
repairs.answer:
Closed by rewording the refusal by what the result lets a caller do. `@ffi(const)` above an entry whose result can change the object is `E5010`; that covers a `ref mut`, `MutSpan` or `exclusive` result into it, or an `Option` or tuple holding one. A result that points elsewhere (`from(p)`, `from(static)`) stands.

The view class follows whatever lifetime word its entry writes, which is P04's J8-06 to require. Under J8-06 B it says `from(…)` and stands; with no word it is taken to point into the object (`[FFI-40]`) and is refused, as the entry says.

repairs.hole: Safety 9 (medium): `c_long`, `c_char` and `c_wchar` are aliases, so `put(long)`/`put(long long)`, `char`/`signed char` and `wchar_t`/`int` have equal Ember parameter lists on some targets; every call ties and no overlay item can name either case.
repairs.answer:
Closed in `[FFI-17g]` Every case reachable. A case that no call can reach (equal Ember types on the target, or a default overlapping another case) is `W5002` at the import, naming both cases and the line that renames one. Such a case is named by its C++ parameter types, `@ffi(cpp="put(long long)")`, the way `instantiate=[…]` already names C++ entities Ember cannot spell; this is allowed only where Ember's types cannot name it. The same line serves every target.

Making the C aliases nominal types was weighed and left out: it would change every C call that passes an `int`, and still would not separate `string_view` from `span<const char>` or a by-value parameter from a `const&` one.

repairs.hole: Safety 10 (medium): an untyped literal counted as `int` (i64), so `out.put(5)` reached `put(int64_t)` where C++ calls `put(int32_t)` and writes 4 bytes; this contradicted the design's promises.
repairs.answer:
Closed in `[TYP-24]` step 2a: an untyped literal has no type yet (`[LEX-16]`), so it fits exactly every type of its own kind that holds it. `out.put(5)` is `E2070`, offering `5 as i32` and `5 as i64`, as a variadic C call already must write its width (verdict 123).

The promises are reworded: where both rules choose, they agree, and where C++ would rank conversions Ember counts alike, Ember refuses (misuse). This changes ODR-096's delegated literal clause for Ember's own instances too, stated in verdicts and open risk 1.

repairs.hole: Safety 11 (medium): a free operator implemented its interface "wherever its namespace is", so `phys::operator+` and `hud::operator+` for `gfx::Vec3` gave two `Add[Vec3]` (`E2041`) in any program depending on both.

A free operator implements its interface only when declared in the namespace of one of its operand types, or as a friend defined in the class, and it belongs to the import of that type (`[FFI-30]`'s one entity). Any other free operator is a plain function called by its path (`phys.p.add(v, w)`). The game compiles, and `v + v` is refused because neither library gives `Vec3` an `Add`, as in C++.

An interface method's implementation belongs to its instance, and an `override fn` to what it overrides. `E1030` is a second declaration of a name in a scope; two implementations of one instance are `E2041`. On the target-dependence: a call that compiles on one target and is `E2070` on another names, on both, the overlay line that makes it portable. Fully nominal C types are left to an owner question (open risk 4).

repairs.answer: The same hole as Safety 12, closed by "a declaration that implements another declares no name of its own".

Closed in `[FFI-42]`: every operator now imports under a stated name.
* `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `!=` are `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge`, `ne`.
* `<=>` with `strong_ordering` is `Ord`.
* `()` is `call`.
* A conversion is `to[T]()`.
* A mixed `==` is a further case of `eq`.

`rename` reaches each, and an overlay's `extend Key implements Ord:` may call `this.lt(o)`. Only class-specific `new`/`delete` import as nothing, since C++'s own constructors and destructor use them; they are not operations on an object.

The message at the refused use (`a + b`, `copy of g`) gives that line. A throwing copy constructor is not silently treated as a panic without the entry, since that would be a fact the reader of the overlay cannot see (verdict 132).

Closed in `[TYP-24]` step 2:
* An argument's type is compared read through its views and one owner level, as IV.11 step 1 strips a receiver's, so `p.ev: owns KeyEvent` fits `KeyEvent` exactly.
* Bases are ranked nearer first, so `lg.log(d)` reaches `log(const KeyEvent&)`.

* Lines are as short as `ref_to_ptr` (`ref mut out as *mut`).
* A pipeline or `some I` value gets its pointer.
* The cast still never changes the pointee, so Clippy's reason against `as` does not apply.

This matches Rust's `&raw const x`; `null[P]()` keeps its written type (ODR-076), having no source to infer from.

Closed in `[STD-26]` and `[TYP-18]`:
* **Result type.** `range` returns `RangeStep[T]` (public `start`, `stop`, `step`) in every form, iterated as the same counted loop. `range(n)` counts as `0..n`, which is all a program observes of it.
* **Inference.** An argument for an `Option[T]` parameter gives `T` its type through rule 11, so `range(1, n)` counts in `n`'s `u8`.
* **Cost.** `len()` and `in` cost a division and a modulo when the step is not a constant, as Python's and C's stepped counts do, and nothing extra otherwise.

Dropping the third argument for `.step_by(k)` was rejected: it would lose Python's negative step, which STD-26 promises.

Closed by a proof added to `[EFF-15]`. A call is checked as the function with its constant arguments fixed (literals, `const`s, defaults), the way a generic instance is checked for its types. * `range(n)` (step 1) has no step check, and `String()` (empty text) no `Alloc`.
* As a bonus, `String.with_capacity(0)` has no `Alloc`: a contract means only what the call does (P14's principle).

Like every proof it only removes effects. It is a language revision of EFF-15's list, so it is part of this ODR, coordinated with P14.

Ending an object counts as calling its `drop` (verdict 57), and an unvouched C++ function is unsafe to call (verdict 125), so without the line an end in safe code is `E3100`, naming the end and the line. A trivial destructor runs no code and needs none.

Whether an `unsafe fn drop()` entry is refused is P04's J5-16; under its option A it is.

Closed in `[TYP-24]` step 2a:
* An integer literal fits integer types exactly and float types only through its typing, so `k.set(5)` reaches `set(int)`.
* `k.scale(2)` with `scale(int)` and `scale(long long)` is `E2070`, giving `2 as c_int` or `2 as i64`, never a pick that differs from C++.

J8-04's outcome now reads "the case Ember's rule picks, which here is the one C++ calls", and the general promise is worded as agreement where both choose, refusal where they would differ.

design.open_risks:
1. **The literal rule refuses some calls that compile in Hardened_11.** An Ember type with two integer-width instances (`big + 5` beside `Add[i32]` and `Add[i64]`) now writes `5 as i64`, and so does a float literal beside `f32` and `f64` cases. This is ODR-096's delegated clause changed, for one rule with C++ imports and for verdict 123's no-guessing. The owner may prefer Ember's own instances to keep the `int` preference, but that would be an exception by origin.

2. **The destructor needs a line.** Every C++ class used from safe code writes `fn drop()` in its overlay; this follows verdicts 57 and 125. If the owner reads verdict 125 as excluding destructors, ends become an unwritten exemption, which checklist 15 argues against. P04's J5-16 decides `unsafe fn drop()`.

3. **The constant-argument proof is a new item in `[EFF-15]`'s list.** It is a language revision in P14's territory.
   * Compile time grows with the distinct constant shapes a function is called with, only where its body branches on such a parameter.
   * Across packages it needs the callee's body, as a generic instance already does (`[EFF-4]`).

   Without it, folding `String()` and `range` into defaults would add effects to their calls, and they would have to stay separate declarations, against `[TYP-26]`.

4. **C type aliases.** `@ffi(cpp=\"…\")` is a C++ spelling in an overlay, allowed only where Ember's types cannot name a case, as `instantiate=[…]` already is. The alternative, nominal `c_long`, `c_char` and `c_wchar` on every target (one source compiling everywhere), is a wider question about all C FFI and is left to the owner as its own question.

5. **`as` now writes every coercion.** This widens `[TYP-6]`, which is P25's group (J2-14); present them together.

6. **The case-set record** extends `ember.overlays` to every package that imports C++, overlay or not, which is verdict 121's record under verdict 127's every-program model. `ember bind --merge` acknowledges a checked move.

7. **Importer names for operators.** `lt`, `call`, `to[T]`, `logical_not` and the rest are new names the importer gives. A C++ member already named so becomes a further case, or `W5002` with the `rename` line.

8. **Verdict 159 and `new`.** An imported constructor's arguments take their parameters' words here (`Scene.new(owns m)`). If the owner reads verdict 159 as covering `new`, the `const T&`/`T&&` constructor pair needs a `rename`. This is P06's J1-07 too.

9. **Relocation.** An object with a C++ base never moves, so a hand-over with a live `weakref` link stops, as for an object C keeps. A compile-time refusal would refuse programs whose link is gone by then. P03 and P09 coordinate (reload relocation).

10. **`RangeStep[T]`** is a new prelude type. `range(n)` is no longer of type `Range[T]`; it counts the same. A program that wrote `r: Range[int] = range(10)` writes `0..10`.

11. **Typed overlay parameters and contract words.** A C++ type named like a contract word (`handle`, `status`, `one`) must be written with its namespace path in a typed parameter. One in the global namespace needs a spelling; this touches P22's raw identifiers.

12. **`_mut` naming flips with the header.** When a header adds the `const` twin of a lone non-`const` member, `v.at(3)` then reaches the `const` one. Reads are unchanged, and `ref mut v.at(3)` becomes refused rather than silently different.

13. **Dependencies on other groups:**
    * P04: J5-16, the unsafe-implementation rule this extends; J8-06, where a C++ reference points, which `[FFI-40a]` follows; J8-08's example, rewritten to `ref mut out as *mut`.
    * P06: call words.
    * P08: J8-12 takes the cast and needs `ObjectPtr[C]` in IV.5's list.
    * P14: `[EFF-15]`.
    * P24: one idea, one spelling.
    * P25: `[TYP-6]`.
    * P03 and P09: relocation.

14. **Not checked on the real compiler** (this was a read-only design task, checklist 14). The importer does not build cases yet, and E2070's help, the case-set record and the constant-argument proof are unbuilt. These are implementation gaps, not spec gaps.

design.rule:
Whatever crosses between Ember and C has exactly one owner at every moment, written in Ember's own words, and every type has one end, which every owner of it runs. Every owner also lives in memory that end gives back.

(1) C takes it for good (`owns`). C may take a value for good only if C can run that value's end: a foreign type's value, or an object of a C++-derived class that C++ deletes. Anything else is refused when compiling.

(2) C holds it while Ember owns it (`retained`, `callback(retained)`, `callback(once)`). The value is handed over at the call (`owns`, or made `shares`/`shares mut`/`thread_shared` in the call) to a token the call returns, `Retained[T]`. The token is the one Ember owner of C's hold. It keeps what C holds alive and at the address C was given. Its end calls the declared unregister function `destroys(f)` exactly once, then ends what it kept.
- The token may be one of several owners only of a class object. C holds such an object's address and reaches it only through calls Ember already counts.
- Data C reads or writes itself (a buffer, a `@layout(c)` value, a callback's state) is the token's alone. `into_inner()` gives it back once C lets go.
- Every hold has an end Ember can reach. `retained` must name its `destroys(f)`. A one-shot (`once`) callback's hold ends at its one run, so its call returns a token exactly when a cancel function is named.

(3) Ember takes it from C. It becomes one owner whose end is its type's own:
- an Ember type: its drop and Ember's free, so `adopt` takes back what `into_raw()` gave;
- a C type: the `destroys(f)` its declaration names;
- a C++ class: its overlay's `destroys(f)`, else C++'s `delete`.
design.spec_text:
NEW [FFI-57] Every hold across the boundary has one owner, and every type one end.
At every moment, what crosses between Ember and foreign code is owned by exactly one side, and Ember's side is written in Ember's own words. Every type has one end, which every owner of it runs, and every owner of it lives in memory that end gives back:
- an Ember type's end is its `drop`, its fields' ends and Ember's free;
- a foreign C type's end is the `destroys(f)` its declaration names;
- a C++ class's end is the `destroys(f)` its overlay names, else C++'s `delete` (its destructor, then its `operator delete`).
A parameter's or result's ownership word ([FFI-11]) decides which of three crossings a call makes.

1. Foreign code takes it for good (`owns`).
   - The parameter is `owns p: T`; its argument says `owns` (verdict 147). The name ends, and Ember never ends the value.
   - Only a value whose end foreign code runs crosses so: a foreign type's value, or an object of a class declared `@ffi(trampoline, owner="foreign")`, whose `delete` runs its Ember end ([FFI-17d]).
   - Any other value is `E5060`, for C as for C++ ([FFI-39c]): "`take_buffer` keeps `buf` and frees it itself, and `buf` is an Ember list, which only Ember can free; let C read it during the call (`borrowed`), let C hold it while Ember keeps it (`retained`, with `destroys(f)`), or give C memory C made".

2. Foreign code holds it while Ember owns it (`retained` on any pointer, `callback(retained)`, `callback(once)`).
   - The parameter is `owns p: T`: a callback's `owns cb: fn(...)`, or `owns cb: thread_shared fn(...)` under `threads(any)` ([FFI-22]).
   - Its argument says `owns` (verdicts 147, 158), or is made with `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` in the call (verdict 160).
   - A function from a variable given with no word is lent ([FN-2a], verdict 150). A callee that keeps it past the call is refused at the call: "C keeps `on_tick` after the call (`callback(retained)`); hand it over: `register_cb(owns on_tick)`, or keep yours: `register_cb(owns copy of on_tick)`".
   - The call hands what C holds to its token, `Retained[T]` ([FFI-23]). The token is one more output of the call, placed as [FFI-11b] places outputs (`Result[Retained[T], N]` for a `status` result).
   - The token is the one Ember owner of C's hold. It keeps what C holds alive and at the address C was given. Its end calls the declared `destroys(f)` exactly once, then ends what it kept.
   - The token may be one of several owners (`shares mut`, `thread_shared`) only of what C reaches through calls alone, which Ember counts ([FFI-39d], [FFI-52]). That is a class object: its layout is Ember's ([OBJ-1]), so C holds its address and nothing else.
   - What C reads or writes itself (a `@layout(c)` value, a counted buffer, a callback's state) is the token's alone, so no Ember name reads, changes or moves it while C holds it. A `shares` parameter there is `E5002`: "C reads and writes `buf` after the call returns, so nothing else may reach it until C lets it go: take it whole, `owns buf: Array[u8]`, and get it back with `held.into_inner()`".
   - A link (`weakref`, `sharedref mut`) or a view keeps nothing alive and is never what C holds (`E5002`).
   - Every hold has an end Ember can reach. A `retained` contract names `destroys(f)`; without one it is `E5041`: "C keeps `cb` with no way to give it back: name the function that unregisters it, `destroys(unregister)`; a function that captures nothing needs no token: pass an `extern "C" fn`".
   - A `callback(once)` hold ends at its one run, so the call returns a token exactly when `destroys(f)` is declared. That token's end calls `f` before the run, and does nothing after it (the slot's used-up mark, [FFI-53]). With no `destroys(f)`, the call returns nothing, and the trampoline ends the function after its run.

3. Ember takes it from foreign code (`returns_owned`, `adopt`, `std::unique_ptr`, a C++ class by value, `T&&`). It becomes one owner, `owns T` (for a class `C`, its owner `C`), ended by its type's end.

CHANGED
- [FFI-10]: An ABI witness (`count(n)`'s length, or a callback's `user_data`) is written at its C ABI position with its C type and is absent from the callable signature. The compiler supplies it at the call, so a raw type there exposes nothing and is no `E5002`. A `safe fn` that registers a hold writes its token result.
- [FFI-11], ownership row:
  - `retained` (any pointer): an `owns p: T` parameter whose value the call's token keeps ([FFI-57] point 2).
  - `owns`: a value whose end the callee runs (point 1).
  - "on any other pointer no safe type" goes.
- [FFI-21]: A `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` parameter is `owns cb: fn(...)`, called with `owns`. Tokens follow [FFI-57] point 2. The help lines of `E7004` and of [FFI-22]'s `E7015` write `register_cb(owns fn() owns game: ...)`.
- [FFI-23]:
  - `Retained[T]` keeps what C holds, on Ember's side. `T` is `ForeignCallback` for a callback (its function, whatever its type), and otherwise the kept parameter's type (`Retained[shares mut Body]`). It gives no object away.
  - Its end counts as a call of `f` and as ending what it kept (verdict 57, [FFI-52]).
  - It keeps `f`'s other arguments as the call was given them. A value handed over is its own; a copied one (a number, a `Copy` handle) is copied; one lent to the call is viewed, so the token does not outlive it ([LT-1]).
  - `held.into_inner()` (`owns this`, as `Cell`'s) calls `f`, then gives back what the token kept.
  - A `destroys(f)` with a `status` result is checked at the token's end, and an error stops the program in every profile: "`world_remove` failed (`WorldError(3)`) for the body given to `world_add` on line 14; C may still hold it, so it cannot be ended".
  - A token's thread markers follow from what it keeps and from its contract's `threads(...)` ([THR-8], [FFI-33b]).
- [FFI-35a]: An object a token keeps is kept by C from the registering call to the token's end, which is known when compiling. An object given to a `retained` parameter of an `unsafe fn` (its address in P07's spelling, never a third `ref_to_ptr`) is marked in its header for good (lead fix J6-03's bit). Either way, if it is handed to another thread while a `weakref` link here points at it, the program stops (verdict 114 fix 3).
- [FFI-36a] and Annex C [FFI-36]:
  - `std.ffi.adopt[T](p)` (`unsafe fn`) makes point 3's owner from an address, for every type: one foreign code made, and one `into_raw()` gave ([FFI-54]). That means an `ObjectPtr[C]` for a class `C`, or the `*mut T` of an `owns T`. An `owns dyn I`'s `*mut u8` no longer says its kind, so it is taken back as the type it was made of: `adopt[Mesh](p as *mut Mesh)`.
  - The owner is ended by `T`'s end, and nothing else is read.
  - `adopt` is `E5002` for a C type with no `destroys(f)`, for a C++ class with no public destructor, and for a class with virtual functions whose destructor is not virtual and which is not `final` (`delete` could end only part of a derived object). The message names the `destroys(f)` to write. [FFI-36b] is unchanged.
- [FFI-32]: A C++ class returned by value is moved into an object C++'s `new` makes (the one allocation it already costs), so every owner of the class ends with `delete`. For a class whose overlay names `destroys(f)`, a by-value result is `E5002`.
- [FFI-39c]: `E5060` is [FFI-57] point 1. A C++ parameter contracted `retained` takes its object as point 2 says (ODR-156's token, now returned by the call).
- [FFI-52]: The example declares `safe fn register_cb(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]` and calls `register_cb(owns fn() owns game: game.add_point())`.
- [FFI-54] and [OWN-12]: write `widget_take(owns first)` (verdict 147). `into_raw()` is for a C function whose declaration cannot name how it gives the value back; `adopt` takes it back.

answers.answer:
Point 2 of the rule: C keeps the function, so it is handed over.
- The declaration writes the Ember side: `owns cb: fn()` (`thread_shared fn()` under `threads(any)`), and the user data `ud` at its C position.
- `ud` is an ABI witness: the compiler supplies the tagged number, as it supplies `count(n)`'s length (ODR-074). It is absent from the call.
- The result is written: the token that ends C's hold.
- The call says `owns` before the function (verdicts 147, 158).
- A `callback(borrowed)` parameter stays a plain `cb: fn()`. It is lent for the call, with no word and no token.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. `poll_events()` may run the kept callback ([FFI-52]), so it changes `game.score`, and `println` prints the points C's events added.

`token` ends at the end of `main`: `unregister` runs once, then the callback's state (setup's owner of the game) ends.

Refused:
- `register_cb(fn() owns game: ...)` without `owns` is verdict 147's error ("say so at the call: `register_cb(owns fn() ...)`").
- `register_cb(on_tick)` with a named function is refused at the call: "C keeps `on_tick`; hand it over: `owns on_tick`, or `owns copy of on_tick`".
- `register_cb(f, ud)` is too many arguments.
- A declaration with no result is E5002: "`register_cb` returns the token that ends C's hold: write `-> Retained[ForeignCallback]`".

answers.answer:
Option C, from point 2's rule that every hold has an end Ember can reach.
- A `once` hold ends at its one run.
- So the call returns a token exactly when `destroys(f)` names a way to end the hold earlier (a cancel function).
- That token's end calls `f` before the run, and does nothing after it (the slot's used-up mark).
- With no `destroys(f)`, the call returns nothing, and the function ends after C's one call.
- `retained` differs only because C never ends a retained hold by itself, so it must name `f` (E5041 stays).
answers.code:
from std.ffi import CStrView, ForeignCallback, Retained

class Loader:
    loaded: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    # C calls `cb` once, with `req`, when the read finishes or fails; the library has no cancel function
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(once, user_data=req), threads(creator)))
    safe fn fs_read_async(path: CStrView, owns cb: fn(i32), req: *mut void)
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `http_get` was given")
    unsafe fn http_cancel(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void, i32), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(once, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(http_cancel))
    safe fn http_get(url: CStrView, owns cb: fn(i32), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn run_loop()

fn main():
    loader = shares mut Loader()
    fs_read_async(c"save.dat", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.loaded += n)
    pending = http_get(c"http://example.com/a", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.loaded += n)
    run_loop()
    println(loader.loaded)
answers.outcome:
Both declarations compile. The program prints the bytes the two requests delivered.
- `fs_read_async` returns no token; its function ends after C's one call.
- `pending` ends at the end of `main`. If the reply has not come, `http_cancel` runs once and the function ends. If it has, nothing runs.

Refused:
- Writing `-> Retained[ForeignCallback]` on `fs_read_async` is E5002: "no `destroys(f)` names a way to cancel it, so there is no token: remove the result".
- Leaving the result off `http_get` is E5002: "`http_get` returns the token that cancels it: write `-> Retained[ForeignCallback]`".

A second call by C stops the program at the trampoline, as today ([FFI-53]).

answers.answer:
Point 2: the address C keeps is held on Ember's side by the call's token.
- The declaration names how C gives the body back (`destroys(world_remove)`), so the call is a safe call with no `unsafe` and no address spelling: the call passes the address.
- The token keeps one owner of the body. A body is a class object, which C reaches only through calls, so the program keeps its own owner too.
- The token's end calls `world_remove` once, then lets its owner go.
- An object whose token holds its only owner may go to another thread with the token. If a `weakref` here points at it, the program stops (verdict 114 fix 3, now reachable from safe code).
- A C function that cannot name how it gives the body back is called in `unsafe:`, with the address in P07's spelling (the cast, never a third `ref_to_ptr`), and the object is marked kept by C for good.
answers.code:
from std.ffi import Retained

class Body:
    mass: f32 = 1.0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` was given to `world_add` and not removed yet")
    unsafe fn world_remove(p: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(p, retained, one, threads(creator)), destroys(world_remove))
    safe fn world_add(owns p: shares mut Body) -> Retained[shares mut Body]

fn main():
    body = shares mut Body()
    held = world_add(shares mut body)    # C keeps the body's address; `held` keeps one owner
    body.mass = 2.0                       # the program keeps its own owner
    println(body.mass)
    # `held` ends first: `world_remove` runs, then its owner ends; then `body`
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints 2.0. `world_remove` runs once at the end of `main`, before the body is freed, so C never holds a freed body.

Refused when compiling:
- `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns body: body.mass)`: E7015 (a `shares` owner stays on one thread).
- Without `destroys(...)`: E5041.

With a one-owner variant (declared `owns p: Body` with the default `threads(any)`, called `held = world_add(owns body)`), after `w = weakref body`, the line `thread.spawn(owns fn() owns held: held.into_inner().mass)` stops the program: "`held` goes to another thread with the `Body` C keeps the address of (`world_add`, line 12), while `w` points at it, so it cannot move; end the link first: `w = None`". With `w = None` first, the body goes at the same address, and `into_inner()` calls `world_remove` on that thread.

answers.answer:
Point 3, option A. `adopt` takes back what `into_raw()` gave, for every type, and ends it by the type's own end: `Game`'s drop and Ember's free.
- There is no second word for taking ownership.
- Where the C side can name how it gives the address back, point 2 is the safe route instead: `held = set_user_pointer(owns game)` with `destroys(clear_user_pointer)`, and `held.into_inner()` gives the game back.
answers.code:
from std.ffi import ObjectPtr, adopt

class Game:
    score: i32 = 0

    fn drop():
        println("game over")

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` stays valid until `take_user_pointer` gives it back")
    unsafe fn set_user_pointer(p: ObjectPtr[Game])
    @safety("a pointer was set and not taken back yet")
    unsafe fn take_user_pointer() -> ObjectPtr[Game]

fn main():
    game = Game()
    # SAFETY: the window keeps the address until `take_user_pointer` hands it back
    unsafe:
        set_user_pointer(game.into_raw())
    # SAFETY: the address C hands back is the one `into_raw()` gave
    unsafe:
        back = adopt[Game](take_user_pointer())
    println(back.score)
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints 0, then "game over" at the end of `main`, when `back` ends and its block is freed.
- Adopting the address a second time while `back` lives stops the program, naming both lines ([FFI-36b]). On one local in one function it is refused when compiling (E5068).
- `adopt[Level](take_user_pointer())` is a type error: an `ObjectPtr[Game]` is not an `ObjectPtr[Level]`.
- Never taking it back leaves the game in the `debug` leak report, as kept by unsafe code ([WK-15]).

answers.answer:
Point 3, option A. A C++ class's end is its overlay's `destroys(f)`, else C++'s `delete`, as `std::unique_ptr`'s default deleter does. So `adopt[f.Enemy](p)` needs nothing written.
- A by-value `Enemy` is moved into an object `new` makes, so every owner of `Enemy` ends the same way.
- `adopt` is refused where `delete` could be wrong: no public destructor, or virtual functions with a destructor that is not virtual on a class that is not `final`.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. `e`'s end runs `delete` on the enemy through a generated thunk, which LTO inlines ([BLD-FFI-4]).
- An overlay's `@ffi(destroys(free_enemy))` on `type Enemy` replaces `delete` for every owner of `Enemy`.
- A class with a private destructor gets E5002: "`Enemy` has no public destructor, so Ember cannot end it; name the function that does: `@ffi(destroys(f))`".
- So does a class with virtual functions, a destructor that is not virtual, and no `final`: "deleting an `Enemy` runs only `~Enemy`, and `make_enemy` may give a derived object; ...".

other_cases.case: A `std::unique_ptr<T>` result.
other_cases.settled: Point 3: an `owns T` ended by the deleter the header states ([FFI-17a]); a deleter that holds state stays refused (E5034). Unchanged.

other_cases.case: A `std::shared_ptr<T>` result.
other_cases.settled: Point 3 with C++'s own count: `CppShared[T]`, ended by `shared_ptr`'s destructor through a thunk. It is never `shares` ([WK-14], E5065). Unchanged.

other_cases.case: A C++ class returned by value ([FFI-32]).
other_cases.settled: Point 3 with one end per type. The result moves into an object C++'s `new` makes (the one allocation it already costs). So every owner of the class ends with `delete`, and a by-value object may go to a `std::unique_ptr<T>` or `T*`-owns parameter. A class whose overlay names `destroys(f)` cannot be returned by value (E5002), since `f` ends only objects the library made.

other_cases.case: A buffer Ember made that C frees (manager mismatch): `take_buffer(owns buf)` with an Ember `Array[u8]` to a C function that later calls `free`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1: C takes for good only what it can end. This is E5060 when compiling, with three ways out: let C read it during the call, hold it with a token, or give C memory C made. A `free()` of Ember memory never happens.

other_cases.case: User-data pointers: `glfwSetWindowUserPointer(window, p)` and `glfwGetWindowUserPointer(window)`.
other_cases.settled:
The setter is a `retained` parameter (point 2).
- Declared by hand with its Ember type and the function that clears it (`destroys(clear_user_pointer)`), it returns a token and needs no `unsafe`.
- With no such function, it is called in `unsafe:` with P07's address spelling, and the object is marked kept by C.
- The getter's `void*` is a raw result, read only in `unsafe:` ([FFI-2a]).
- Ember callbacks capture their own state, so they need no user pointer.

other_cases.case: A buffer C fills after the call returns (an async read, io_uring- or libuv-style).
other_cases.settled: Point 2: data C writes is the token's alone. `held = read_async(owns buf, ...)`, and once C has finished, `buf = held.into_inner()` (which calls the declared wait or cancel first) gives the bytes back. No Ember name reads the buffer while C may write it. This is the ownership-passing I/O of Rust's tokio-uring.

other_cases.case: A token ended after C has finished.
other_cases.settled:
- A `once` token after the run does nothing (the used-up mark).
- A `retained` token always calls `f` once. Its declaration asserts `f` is valid for the token's life (an asserted fact, `ember tcb`).
- The token keeps `f`'s lent arguments as views, so it ends before them (checked when compiling).

other_cases.case: A token ended on another thread.
other_cases.settled:
Its markers follow from what it keeps and its contract's `threads(...)`.
- Under `threads(creator)` it never leaves its thread (E7008, compile time).
- Under `threads(any)`, with `Send` contents, it may leave, and `f` runs there. A callback still running is waited for ([FFI-53]).

other_cases.case: An unregister function that fails (`destroys(f)` with a `status` result).
other_cases.settled: The status is checked at the token's end. An error stops the program in every profile, naming `f`, its error and the registering line. Nothing C may still hold is freed.

other_cases.case: An object C keeps, then handed to another thread.
other_cases.settled:
- A `shares` owner held by a token never goes (E7015, compile time).
- A token holding the only owner goes with it, without moving the object, unless a `weakref` here points at it; then the program stops (verdict 114 fix 3).
- An object given to C in unsafe code carries the header mark, with the same stop.

other_cases.case: A callback C keeps forever with no unregister (`atexit` with captures, a signal handler).
other_cases.settled: E5041: a retained hold needs an end. A function that captures nothing goes as an `extern "C" fn` with no token ([FFI-21]) and reaches module state. There is no deliberate leak (verdict 58).

other_cases.case: A C++ listener list that keeps an Ember-owned object (`button.add_listener(p)`, `remove_listener(p)`).
other_cases.settled:
Point 2 for C++: `@ffi(param(p, retained, one), destroys(remove_listener))` on the overlay entry.
- `held = button.add_listener(shares mut panel)` keeps one owner, and the program keeps `panel`.
- The overrides C++ runs are counted ([FFI-39d]).
- This brings back ODR-156's token, now returned by the call.

other_cases.case: A C++ `T&&` parameter.
other_cases.settled: Point 1 for the value, point 3 for the memory. C++ moves the value out; the emptied object stays Ember's owner and is ended after the call by its destructor and `delete`.

other_cases.case: A borrowed C result.
other_cases.settled: Ownership does not cross. The result is a view whose life the contract names (`from(p)`, `from(static)`), or a raw pointer read in `unsafe:` ([FFI-2a]). Unchanged.

other_cases.case: The callback table's capacity (P27, J8-18).
other_cases.settled: Only callbacks take slots; objects C keeps take none. What a full table does is P27's rule. This rule changes nothing in it, and J8-18's example already uses J8-01's spelling.

other_cases.case: A `once` callback C never calls (a library shut down with requests pending).
other_cases.settled: Its function stays alive while C may still call it, so it is never freed. The `debug` leak report lists it as kept by foreign code ([WK-15]). C's `once` contract is the vouched fact.

other_cases.case: One registration that keeps several values (a callback and an object, or two callbacks).
other_cases.settled: One token keeps every value the call hands C to keep, and calls `f` once.

design.prior_art:
C++
- C gets a `void* user_data` and a function pointer; the context is `new`ed and unregistered by hand. `unique_ptr::release()` and `unique_ptr(T*)` (`default_delete` calls `delete`) cross ownership.
- Nothing ties C's hold to an owner, so a missing unregister or a freed context is a use-after-free.

Rust
- `Box::into_raw` / `Box::from_raw` and `Rc::into_raw` / `Rc::from_raw` are unsafe. `from_raw` is untyped: a `Box<Level>` taken back as a `Box<Game>` is undefined behaviour.
- Callbacks are a `Box<Box<dyn FnMut>>` given as user data with an `extern "C"` trampoline. Unregistering and freeing are manual; wrapper crates add RAII guards one library at a time.
- The `cxx` crate's `UniquePtr::from_raw` ends a C++ object with C++ `delete`, the precedent for J8-16 A.
- No crossing is safe without an `unsafe` block, and nothing records that C holds an address.

Swift
- `Unmanaged.passRetained(obj).toOpaque()` gives C a +1 hold; `takeRetainedValue()` balances it. `passUnretained` gives the address with no keep-alive.
- An imbalance is a leak or undefined behaviour. `@convention(c)` closures cannot capture, so context always goes through `Unmanaged` by hand.

C#
- `GCHandle.Alloc` (Normal or Pinned), `ToIntPtr` / `FromIntPtr`, and `Free()` once. A delegate given to C through `Marshal.GetFunctionPointerForDelegate` must be kept alive by hand; otherwise the program crashes (CallbackOnCollectedDelegate).
- `SafeHandle.ReleaseHandle` ends an adopted handle exactly once, which is the token idea for C results, but the release is written per type.

Go
- cgo forbids C keeping a Go pointer after the call. `runtime.Pinner` pins one.
- `cgo.NewHandle(v)` gives C an integer; `h.Value()` panics after `h.Delete()`. This is the closest to Ember's tagged slot, but `Delete` is manual and a forgotten one leaks.

Zig and Ada
- Zig: `*anyopaque` user data and `defer`, with no tracking.
- Ada: controlled types (`Finalize`) wrap an adopted handle, and accessibility checks refuse giving C a nested subprogram, a static approximation of the closure-lifetime problem.

Where they all fall short
In every one, C's hold is bookkeeping by hand outside the type system. None derives the release from a declaration written once, and runs it from the owner's end.

Ember's rule
The call itself returns the owner of C's hold (C#'s SafeHandle plus Go's handle plus Swift's passRetained, as one object). The unregister is named once, in the declaration. The words at the call are checked, the end is placed by the compiler, and C pays nothing it would not pay by hand.
design.cost:
Each operation, against what C pays:

- **Hand-over to C for good (`owns`):** zero. A pointer passed; the name ends.
- **Callback C keeps:** unchanged from [FFI-53].
  - One allocation of the function's state at registration (C mallocs a context struct too).
  - One generation compare per registration.
  - 1.02x to 1.05x of a plain call through a function pointer, per call C makes.
  - The token is the slot number plus `f`'s other arguments (8 to 24 bytes, no allocation). Its end is the one call of `f` that C makes too.
- **Object C keeps:**
  - The token is one pointer plus `f`'s arguments (8 to 16 bytes).
  - `owns` costs nothing. `shares mut` costs one add at registration and one subtract at the token's end; a class object already has its block and header, so no memory.
  - Every access goes through the program's own owner, as before: zero.
  - The kept-by-C fact for a token is known when compiling: zero header cost. Only the unsafe route writes one spare header bit, once (lead fix J6-03).
  - A thread hand-over: verdict 114's one compare, nothing new.
- **`once` without a token:** zero beyond the state, which is freed after the run, as C frees its context in the callback.
- **`once` with a token:** its end is one compare of the used-up mark, or the call of `f`.
- **A data hold given back by `into_inner()`:** the call of `f`, then a move. Zero per access, since nothing reads it meanwhile.
- **A `status` from `f`:** one compare at the token's end; C code that checks pays the same.
- **`adopt`:**
  - Zero beyond the type's end. An Ember type ends by its drop and free (C: `free`). A C++ class ends by `delete` through one thunk call, inlined under LTO ([BLD-FFI-4]), the same as `unique_ptr`'s default deleter.
  - [FFI-36b]'s live-adopted check is unchanged.
- **A C++ by-value result:** the same one allocation, made by C++'s `new` instead of Ember's allocator.
- **Every refusal (E5060, E5041, E5002, E7015, E7008):** compile time, zero.

Memory: no header grows, no table entry is added for objects, and a token is 8 to 24 bytes on the stack or in a field.
