readability.note:
A program that never calls C is untouched.

The C-calling program after the rule is shorter:
- the two `unsafe:` blocks, their notes and the hand-written `world_remove` call go;
- the release can no longer be forgotten or run twice.

It gains `owns` before the function C keeps. That is the hand-over word verdicts 147 and 158 already require at every hand-over, and `shares mut` is the existing sharing word of verdict 160. Every name still says what it is: `held` is the owner of C's hold, and `body` is the program's own.

design.compiler_does:
From the declaration:
- It reads each foreign parameter's and result's contract words and works out the crossing: `borrowed` is lent; `owns` is for good; `retained`, `callback(retained)` and `callback(once)` are a hold.
- It checks the Ember signature written for it (E5002 naming the slot): `owns p` for a hold, a token result, a witness at its C position.
- It drops ABI witnesses (`user_data`, `count(n)`) from the callable signature and supplies them at the call.

At the call:
- It checks the argument's word under P06's rule: `owns`, or made with `shares` or `weakref` in the call, else the loan is refused when C keeps it.
- It refuses a hold whose value C would read or write while other Ember owners may reach it.
- It refuses a link or view as the held value, a `retained` contract with no `destroys(f)`, and an `owns` hand-over of a value C cannot end (E5060, for C as for C++).

The token:
- It generates the token type and its end: the call of `f` once, with the arguments the token kept as the call gave them, then the end of what it kept.
- It counts that end as a call of `f` and a drop for the loop, view and lock rules ([FFI-52], verdict 57).
- It checks a `status` from `f`, places the token's end on every path out (an ordinary owner), and works out the token's thread markers from its contents and `threads(...)` (P01).

Kept by C:
- It knows when compiling which objects a token keeps, for verdict 114's hand-over stop.
- It writes the header bit on the unsafe route.

`adopt` and C++ results:
- For `adopt[T]` it picks `T`'s own end: an Ember type's drop and free; a C type's `destroys(f)`; a C++ class's `destroys(f)`, else a `delete` thunk.
- It refuses a type with no end, a private destructor, or a polymorphic class whose non-virtual destructor `delete` would misuse.
- It allocates C++ by-value results with `new`, so each class has one end.
design.misuse:
Refused when compiling:
- `register_cb(fn() ...)` without `owns`: verdict 147's error, with the line to write.
- `register_cb(on_tick)`, a lent function C would keep: "hand it over: `owns on_tick`, or `owns copy of on_tick`".
- `register_cb(f, ud)`: too many arguments (the compiler supplies `ud`).
- A hold's declaration with no token result, or a token on a `once` with no `destroys(f)`: E5002, with the exact result line.
- `retained` with no `destroys(f)`: E5041, offering a function that captures nothing as the way for a forever registration.
- `owns buf` of an Ember value to a C function that frees it: E5060.
- A `shares` parameter for data C reads or writes: E5002, "take it whole, get it back with `into_inner()`".
- A `weakref` or view as the held value: E5002.
- A token holding a `shares` owner sent to another thread: E7015.
- A `threads(creator)` token sent to another thread: E7008.
- `adopt` of a type with no end, or a C++ class whose `delete` could end only part of an object: E5002, naming the `destroys(f)` to write.
- Adopting one live object twice on one local: E5068.

Stopped at the line, with a clear message, in every profile:
- A one-owner object C keeps, handed to another thread while a `weakref` here points at it (verdict 114 fix 3).
- `f` reporting failure at the token's end.
- C calling a callback after its token ended, or a `once` one twice ([FFI-53]).
- Adopting a live object twice across functions ([FFI-36b]).

Inside `unsafe` code, vouched by its note and `@safety`, as for every unsafe call:
- `into_raw()` never taken back: a leak, listed in the debug report.
- `adopt` of an address `into_raw()` never gave.
- A C library breaking its declared contract.

Nothing the rule allows in safe code reads freed memory or races.
design.verdicts:
Kept:
- **31:** a C call may run the callbacks C keeps. A token's end also counts as a call of its `destroys(f)`.
- **39 and 86:** what kept callbacks change is inferred.
- **57:** a token's end counts as calling `f` and ending what it kept.
- **58:** no deliberate leak. `retained` keeps E5041; `once` ends at its run.
- **62:** a callback that ends its own token runs to its end ([FFI-53] unchanged).
- **91:** `into_raw()` only in unsafe and built in. `adopt` is its inverse, also unsafe.
- **102:** `owns` is C's take-over word.
- **114:** kept, and fix 3 is made reachable from safe code. A one-owner object in a token, handed to another thread while a `weakref` here points at it, stops. The unsafe route keeps the header mark.
- **147 and 158:** `owns` at the call before what C keeps, a function written in the call included.
- **150:** a function from a variable is lent; C keeping it is refused at the call (P06's K12 rule).
- **160:** `world_add(shares mut body)` takes no `owns`.
- **164 to 166:** the token's markers follow from its contents (P01).

One widening, said plainly:
- `Retained` grows from callbacks to every hold C keeps. [FFI-23]'s "keeps none for C" becomes "keeps what C holds, on Ember's side".
- Verdict 91's correction describes `Retained` as keeping an object on Ember's side while C holds a callback, and giving nothing away. The rule keeps both halves and applies them to every hold.
- Evidence it is the owner's direction: ODR-156, the owner's own answer, gave a C++ parameter that keeps a pointer a `Retained` token (`Retained.pin(self)`). It was removed when [FFI-39c] moved to hand-over and `into_raw()`, and that removal left "C holds it while Ember owns it" with no safe form at all (J8-12).

Lead's text, not a verdict:
- ODR-074's witness rule is extended to `user_data`, a lead ruling.
- [OWN-12] still writes verdict 91's old `widget_take(first)`. Verdict 147 makes it `widget_take(owns first)`, a lead fix like J8-02.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule: every hold C keeps is a token the call returns. The token keeps what C holds, and its end calls the declared unregister once. A callback is `owns cb: fn()` with the user data supplied by the compiler. A one-shot callback gives a token only when a cancel function is named. Every owner Ember takes ends by its type's own end: drop, the declared `destroys(f)`, or C++ `delete`. `adopt` takes back what `into_raw()` gave.

recommendation.reason:
A gives one owner at every moment, which is the group's principle, written in words the language already has (`owns`, `shares mut`, the `Retained` token, `adopt`, `into_inner`). It holds for every type and crossing with no case-by-case path.

- It makes the commonest engine registrations safe with no `unsafe` block.
- It costs nothing per access, and per registration and removal only what C pays by hand.
- It makes verdict 114's decided stop reachable from a program that compiles.
- It keeps every owner verdict. Its one widening (`Retained` for every hold) returns to the owner's own ODR-156 choice of a token for a kept pointer.

B leaves the most frequent pattern as hand-written, unchecked bookkeeping. C adds a second spelling and refuses correct one-shot APIs.

owner_short.one_line: When a C library keeps something of ours (a callback, as a `std::function` behind `void* user_data`, or an object's `this` pointer in a physics world or listener list), or hands us an object to own (C++: `unique_ptr<T>(raw)`, the inverse of `release()`), who owns it at each moment and what ends it.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `body = Body()` | a `Body` with one owner, `body` |
| 2 | main | `world_add(...)` gives the physics world (C) the body's address; today this is only possible inside `unsafe:`, and no spelling keeps `body` | C holds the address; Ember's only owner is `body` |
| 3 | main | `body` ends (its block ends, or `body = Body()` replaces it) | freed: nothing on Ember's side knew C held it |
| 4 | main | `world_step()` (C) reads the body through the address it kept | freed memory read: undefined behaviour, from a program whose only safeguard was a `# SAFETY:` note |
owner_short.today: Only a callback C keeps has an owner on Ember's side (its token), and the spec's own declaration of one does not compile. An object C keeps has no safe spelling. `into_raw()` has no way back. A one-shot callback's token is undecided. `adopt` of a C++ object needs a free function no C++ class names.
owner_short.options:
A: everything C keeps is held by a token the call returns. The token's end calls the declared unregister once, and every owner Ember takes ends by its type's own end (drop, the declared free function, or C++ `delete`).
B: as A, but an object C keeps stays unsafe, with its address given and removed by hand in `unsafe:` blocks.
C: Rust's way: `Game.from_raw(p)`, `adopt` only with a written free function, and every one-shot callback needs a cancel function.
owner_short.recommendation: A: one owner at every moment, in words the language already has. No unsafe block for the common engine registrations, nothing new per call, and verdict 114's decided stop gets a program that compiles.

design.open_risks:
1. **Overlay entries for a `void*` C keeps.** An overlay entry for a `void*` that C keeps has no place to write its Ember type: overlay parameters take contract words, not types. A hand declaration ([FFI-10]) can write it. Reusing `@ffi(macro_fn)`'s `p: Body` form needs one grammar line (GRM-35) from the lead.
2. **Tokens beside their anchor.** A token keeps `f`'s lent arguments as views. So a token whose `f` needs an anchor (`uv_timer_stop(handle)`) cannot be stored in the same object as that anchor unless the anchor is shared (`shares mut`). This is a cost in that one pattern; say it to the owner if it comes up.
3. **Copy handles.** A `Copy` handle (J8-14 A) given to `f` carries no lifetime, so `f`'s validity after the handle's object ends rests on the vouched contract (P04's domain).
4. **A failing `f` stops the program.** No handled form (a `try_` end) is given. Add one if a real API needs it; P27's 'stop plus try_' pattern would be the model.
5. **Call words for `into_inner()`.** `into_inner()` is reused from `Cell`/`UnsafeCell` (`owns this`). Its call words follow P06's rule for methods taking `owns this`.
6. **Data C only reads.** Data C only reads (`const T*`) that Ember wants to keep changing is the token's alone under this rule. The program takes it back with `into_inner()`, changes it, and registers again. Sharing it would need C's later reads counted by the view rules: a larger rule, not proposed.
7. **The class-object line.** The owner may read 'a class object may be shared, data may not' as an exception by type. Its reason is stated: C reaches a class object's contents only through calls Ember counts, and data it reads or writes itself.
8. **C++ by-value results and `new`.** [FFI-32]'s by-value results become `new`-allocated, so each class has one end. A class whose overlay names `destroys(f)` then cannot be returned by value. That is rare, but it is a change to what imports.
9. **Lead fixes the edit needs.** [OWN-12]'s `widget_take(first)` (verdict 147) and the help messages of E7004 and E7015 need `owns` written. The examples of J8-18 (P27) and FFI-52 follow J8-01's spelling.
10. **Order with P06 and P07.** It depends on P06's K12 rule (a loan kept past the call is refused) and on P07's address spelling for the unsafe route. Ask them first, as phase 3 orders.

matrix.how_kept: The contract word decides the crossing. owns hands over for good. retained, callback(retained) and callback(once) make a token. returns_owned, adopt, unique_ptr, a by-value C++ class and T&& are point 3. Every Ember side is written and checked against the contract (E5002 naming the slot). Call words follow verdicts 147, 158 and 160.
matrix.edge_cases: A foreign type whose end is a C function, made by Ember in its own block (hole 2). A C++ type with two ends (hole 3). Trampoline and constructor memory (hole 6). One registration keeping a callback and an object: Retained[T] has one T, and the type of a two-value token is not stated. A failing status registration: what happens to the value handed over (hole 17).

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2 lets the token be one of several owners of 'a class object', on the ground that 'its layout is Ember's, so C holds its address and nothing else' and that C++ reaches it only through calls Ember counts (FFI-39d, FFI-52). A class with a C++ base breaks both claims. Its C++ part has C++'s layout, and C++ reads and writes it itself: set_title is a non-virtual member, run inside any C++ call, @ffi(no_callbacks) ones included. FFI-39d and FFI-52 count only the Ember overrides. So no rule sees `win.relayout()` change `label`. The view `s` lives across the call and reads a freed buffer, in safe code. With `thread_shared` and threads(any), the same write races with this thread's read. This is the rule's own showcase ('Point 2 for C++ ... held = button.add_listener(shares mut panel)'). Today there is no safe way for C++ to hold an object Ember still names, so the rule opens this route.
holes.fix_hint: State the true dividing line: what C reaches only through Ember code (a plain Ember class) may be shared, and what foreign code reads or writes itself may not. An object whose class has a C++ base is then the token's alone, like data. Or, the general alternative: while C++ holds it, every foreign call counts as changing and possibly reshaping its C++ part, @ffi(no_callbacks) ones included, so no view of that part lives across one (BCK-3, BCK-7).

holes.program:
unsafe extern "C":
    # `queue_push` keeps `ev` and frees it with free() after dispatching it
    @ffi(param(ev, owns, one), no_callbacks)
    safe fn queue_push(owns ev: owns Event)    # Event: the header's complete `struct Event`, a @layout(c) value type

fn main():
    ev: owns Event = owns Event(kind=1)        # an owned block from Ember's allocator (IV.1, OBJ-4)
    queue_push(owns ev)                         # point 1: 'a foreign type's value', so no E5060
holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 1's test is the type ('a foreign type's value'), not where the owner lives. An `owns T` is always 'a pointer to a heap block it owns alone' from Ember's allocator, and that allocator may be a host's own (FFI-27), an arena, or another C runtime's heap on Windows. C then calls free() on Ember memory: heap corruption, in safe code. This is the very case the rule says it closes ('A free() of Ember memory never happens'). The same happens without crossing at all: with `@ffi(destroys(event_free))` on `type Event`, or a `returns_owned(destructor=event_free)` (FFI-36a makes that Event's one end), the Ember-made owner's own end calls event_free on an Ember block. This breaks the rule's own sentence 'every owner lives in memory that end gives back', and no CHANGED line refuses it.
holes.fix_hint: Let the type's one end decide both directions. A foreign type whose end is a C function (destroys(f) or returns_owned) gets owners only from C (returns_owned, adopt). `owns Event(...)` is then E5002, naming the C function that makes one. A foreign type with no C end is ended by Ember's free, so `owns ev` to a C taker is E5060, with the same three ways out.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule says a C++ class has one end (its overlay's destroys(f), else delete) and that 'every owner of the class ends with delete'. Yet it keeps 'A std::unique_ptr<T> result ... ended by the deleter the header states ... Unchanged', and FFI-17a accepts any stateless deleter. Read the first way, the pooled particle is deleted: memory the pool owns goes to operator delete, heap corruption from an automatic import with no unsafe. Read the second way, `owns Particle` no longer has one end, and an `owns T` 'holds one address' (FFI-17a), so a list that mixes the two sources cannot end both correctly. FFI-36a already refuses two destructors for one C type (E5002). Nothing does so for C++.
holes.fix_hint: Carry FFI-36a's 'a foreign type has one destructor' to C++. A unique_ptr<T, D> whose D is not T's one end (default_delete<T>, or the overlay's destroys(f)) is E5002, naming both. Or the overlay names D's function as T's destroys(f), and every other source of an owns T (by-value results, adopt) must then match.

holes.program:
# ui.hpp: class Panel { public: void add_child(Widget* w) noexcept;   // takes w over
#                               void clear() noexcept; };            // deletes every child
# overlay: class Panel:  fn add_child(w: owns one)  and  fn clear()
import cpp "ui.hpp" with (project="game", overlay="overlays/ui.em") as ui

@ffi(trampoline, owner="foreign")
class Button(ui.Widget):
    codes: Array[i32] = []

fn main():
    panel = ui.Panel()
    b = Button()
    w = weakref b
    panel.add_child(owns b)          # point 1: C++ takes it for good; `delete` runs its Ember end
    if w exists as btn:
        panel.clear()                # C++ deletes the button here
        println(btn.codes.len())     # btn reads a freed Button
holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 1 keeps owner="foreign": C++'s delete 'runs its Ember end' at a moment chosen inside C++. BCK-7 keeps `btn` alive only while 'no line and no call in its life may end an object of its type'. A foreign call's summary is 'those of the Ember functions C may run' (BCK-8, FFI-52). FFI-52's list names kept callbacks, exports, overrides and extern "C" fn values, but not the end that C++'s delete runs. So nothing says `panel.clear()` may end a Button, `btn` lives across it, and the program reads freed memory in safe code. The same hole lets an override go on using `this` after a C++ call that deletes it (BCK-8's 'uses after a line that may end'). If clear() is marked @ffi(no_callbacks), the mark is false, since delete runs Ember code, yet E5069 cannot see that.
holes.fix_hint: Write it into point 1 and FFI-52: every foreign call, no_callbacks or not, counts as possibly ending every object of a class C++ takes for good, with its drop's changes (DRP-8, verdict 57). So BCK-7 ends views opened from links across it, BCK-8 refuses `this` after it, and no_callbacks keeps meaning 'runs no other Ember code'.

holes.program:
from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Game:
    score: i32 = 0
    token: Option[Retained[ForeignCallback]] = None

    fn add_point():
        this.score += 1

fn main():
    game = shares mut Game()
    on_event = fn() shares mut game:
        back = mem.take(ref mut game.token).unwrap().into_inner()   # calls `unregister`, then gives back this very function
        mem.drop(owns back)                                           # ends its state: the block this call is running in
        game.add_point()                                              # reads `game` from the freed block
    game.token = Some(register_cb(owns on_event))
    poll_events()
holes.what_goes_wrong: FFI-53 (verdict 62) delays freeing a running callback's block only when the callback 'ends its own token'. The rule adds `into_inner()`, which 'calls f, then gives back what the token kept', and for a callback that is the function itself (ForeignCallback). Inside its own run, the callback takes back the block it runs in and ends it. The rest of its body reads `game` from freed memory. This is verdict 62's exact pattern (a callback that removes its own registration and goes on), reached by the new operation, in safe code.
holes.fix_hint: Make verdict 62's rule cover every end of a running callback's state, not only the token's. A function that into_inner() gives back while it runs keeps its block until that run returns, so its end is deferred as the token's is. Otherwise, offer into_inner() only for holds that are not callbacks.

@ffi(trampoline, owner="foreign")
class Button(ui.Widget):
    codes: Array[i32] = []

fn main():
    panel = ui.Panel()
    b = Button()                 # OBJ-4: Ember's runtime allocator makes the block, its header at offset 0
    w = weakref b
    panel.add_child(owns b)
    panel.clear()                # `delete`: ~Button, then operator delete on the C++ subobject's address
    if w exists as btn:          # the weak count is read from a header C++ has just freed
        println(btn.codes.len())
holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule's principle is 'every owner lives in memory that end gives back', and it defines a C++ class's end as 'its destructor, then its operator delete'. But no CHANGED line places that memory. Not FFI-17d or FFI-39, where a trampoline object is allocated (OBJ-4 says Ember's allocator) and what its operator delete frees. Not OBJ-3's rule that the block stays while weak links hold it. Not imported constructors (FFI-17's constructor thunks): only FFI-32's by-value results are moved into `new`. Read literally, C++'s global operator delete frees an interior pointer of an Ember block, and frees it even while a weakref link holds it, so opening `w` reads freed memory. Also, a class whose operator new is deleted or private cannot be `new`ed by the by-value or constructor thunk, and the rule states no refusal for it.
holes.fix_hint: A trampoline class's operator new and operator delete are Ember's block allocation and free. delete ends the object, and the block stays while its weak count holds it (OBJ-3). Imported constructors construct with `new`, as by-value results do. A class whose operator new or operator delete is not public is E5002 for by-value results and constructors.

# a reloadable build
class Body:
    mass: f32 = 1.0
    # the next build adds `spin: f32 = 0.0`, so the new size does not fit

class Level:
    held: Option[Retained[shares mut Body]] = None

fn main():
    level = Level()
    body = shares mut Body()
    level.held = Some(world_add(shares mut body))
    run_game(ref mut level)       # a reload is committed while C's world keeps the body's address
holes.what_goes_wrong: HR-20 refuses a reload that must move 'an object C holds', and today it knows which objects those are from FFI-35a's header mark. The rule's changed FFI-35a drops that mark for the token route ('known when compiling: zero header cost'). HR-15 rewrites every owner it can enumerate, a token's `shares mut` owner in `level.held` and `body` included, and moves the Body. The C world still holds the old address and writes freed memory at the next world_step. HR-15a excuses only owners the runtime cannot enumerate, and a token's owner is enumerable.
holes.fix_hint: Name HR-15 and HR-20 in the rule. An owner inside a Retained counts as C holding what it keeps, so the reload treats it as one it cannot rewrite and refuses the move (decided in plan, HR-15b). Or, in reload builds, which already carry the 24-byte header (HR-12), the registering call sets the kept-by-C bit.

holes.program:
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `req` are a pair `fs_read_async` was given, its callback not run yet")
    unsafe fn fs_cancel(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void, i32), req: *mut void)
    # libuv's rule: a cancelled request still gets its one callback later, with -125 (UV_ECANCELED)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(once, user_data=req), threads(creator)), destroys(fs_cancel))
    safe fn fs_read_async(path: CStrView, owns cb: fn(i32), req: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn run_loop()

fn main():
    loader = shares mut Loader()
    pending = fs_read_async(c"save.dat", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.loaded += n if n > 0 else 0)
    mem.drop(owns pending)    # the token's end: fs_cancel runs, then the function is ended
    run_loop()                # libuv delivers the one call (-125): the trampoline stops the program
holes.what_goes_wrong: A once token's end 'calls f before the run, and ... then ends what it kept', which assumes a cancel means C will never call. libuv's uv_cancel, the async API J8-03 is modelled on, promises the opposite: 'cancelled requests have their callbacks invoked some time in the future', and it is not safe to free what the request holds until then. So C's one call meets an ended slot and the program stops ('C called the callback registered on line N after its token ended'), a correct program stopped. If the request is already running, uv_cancel fails (EBUSY). As a status f, that stops the program at the token's end. The rule fits only one kind of cancel API, although it presents option C as covering 'both real kinds of one-shot API'.
holes.fix_hint: A once hold ends at its one run, whatever the cancel does. The token's end calls f and leaves the function to that run (the trampoline ends it afterwards). A failing cancel of a running once hold is not an error, since the run will come. If the owner also wants APIs whose cancel suppresses the call, the contract must say so, because leaving it to a guess either stops correct programs or leaks.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 2 ends a hold when f returns: 'Its end calls the declared destroys(f) exactly once, then ends what it kept'. A buffer that C or the kernel fills after the call is released at a later completion, not when cancel returns. The rule's other case claims 'This is the ownership-passing I/O of Rust's tokio-uring', but tokio-uring parks the buffer in its driver until the completion arrives. Under the rule an author has no honest declaration. A cancel that only asks makes destroys(f) false, and the worker writes freed memory. A cancel that reports busy (uv_cancel's EBUSY as a status) stops a correct program at the token's end. The headline async-I/O case is not covered.
holes.fix_hint: Let a hold end at a later completion: the callback's one run, or a completion the library reports. The token's end calls f, then parks what C holds until that completion and ends it there, as tokio-uring does. The debug leak report lists a hold whose completion never comes.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The compiler places a token's end wherever the token ends, here inside a callback that C runs from space_step. So space_remove runs re-entrantly while C walks its body list. Chipmunk aborts ('cannot remove during a step'), and Box2D v2's DestroyBody corrupts its lists when its assert is compiled out. The program has no unsafe block. f's @safety precondition ('not inside space_step') is text the compiler cannot read, and the rule gives the declaration no way to say it. FFI-52 counts the change, but nothing refuses or delays it. Physics worlds are the rule's headline 'commonest engine registrations'. The same reaches a token ended by a queued drop at a check point inside a callback (P05).
holes.fix_hint: With no new word: a token whose end comes while a foreign call is running on this thread (inside a callback or an override C runs) calls f when the outermost foreign call returns. That is Chipmunk's post-step callback, done by the compiler and runtime. What the token keeps ends then. Cost: a per-thread depth count at the attach the trampoline already does (FFI-22) and a short queue, against the hand-written post-step lists C programs keep.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule: 'Under threads(any), with Send contents, it may leave, and f runs there'. J8-12's one-owner variant shows it as intended. For an object hold no callback runs, so leaving the threads word out is natural. The default then lets the compiler call f, an unsafe fn whose @safety the compiler cannot read, on a thread the declaration never named, racing inside a C library that is not thread-safe. Verdict 31's lesson ('a forgotten mark lets a crash through') points the other way. For callbacks, FFI-22's default `any` is the restrictive side for the callback's contents, but it is the permissive side for where f runs: one word now carries two facts. This rests partly on P04: Ember does not model a C function's thread safety.
holes.fix_hint: Make forgetting safe. A token ends on the thread that made it (E7008 when sent) unless the hold's contract writes `threads(any)`. A callback's own markers keep FFI-22's default. Present it with P04's vouching of C thread facts.

# overlay: class Button:
#     @ffi(param(l, retained, one, threads(creator)), destroys(remove_listener))
#     fn add_listener(l)
#     fn remove_listener(l)
#     fn set_label(text: borrowed nul_terminated)
class Panel(ui.Listener):
    clicks: i32 = 0
    override fn on_click():
        this.clicks += 1

fn main():
    button = ui.Button()
    panel = shares mut Panel()
    held = button.add_listener(shares mut panel)   # the token keeps `button`, remove_listener's receiver, as a view
    button.set_label(c"Start")                      # E3021: set_label changes `button` while `held` views it
holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule says of f's arguments 'one lent to the call is viewed, so the token does not outlive it'. A view carries verdict 5's promise that what it reads does not change while it is used (BCK-3). So for the token's whole life nothing may change the anchor: no non-const C++ method of the button (every entry without @ffi(const) changes its object, verdict 132), no `ref mut world` step of a physics world, no write to a window. The rule's own showcase, the C++ listener, then compiles only for a button nobody touches again. The physics case compiles only if no step is declared `exclusive`. Open risk 2 names only storing the token beside its anchor, which understates this.
holes.fix_hint: Keep the anchor as a tie on its life only. The compiler checks that the anchor is not ended, moved or replaced before the token's end and is not lent ref mut where the token ends (f is an ordinary call there). Changes through other names are allowed in between. No new word, and nothing at run time.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule: 'a copied one (a number, a Copy handle) is copied'. So nothing ties the token's life to the window's, and the compiler places f's call after the window ended, at a line the program never wrote. Open risk 3 hands this to P04. But the dangling call is made by the token, at a point the rule chooses, using the rule's own glfwSetWindowUserPointer case. Because the program text shows no later use of `window`, no reader can see it.
holes.fix_hint: A token keeps an anchor only as a tie to an owner (the previous hole's tie), never as a bare Copy handle. A hold whose f takes a handle whose type has an owner (`owns GLFWwindow` with destroys) ties that owner. A bare Copy handle in f's arguments is E5002, naming the owner to pass. Decide it together with J8-14.

struct Point:
    x: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` came from into_raw()")
    unsafe fn stash(p: *mut Point)
    @safety("a pointer was stashed and not taken back")
    unsafe fn unstash() -> *mut Point

fn main():
    for i in 0..2:
        p: owns Point = owns Point(x=i)
        # SAFETY: unstash gives back the address stash was given
        unsafe:
            stash(p.into_raw())
            back = adopt[Point](unstash())   # round 2: the allocator reuses the address round 1's `back` freed
        println(back.x)
holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule keeps FFI-36b ('Adopting one live object twice is caught at run time in every profile') 'unchanged' and costs adopt at 'zero beyond the type's end'. For an Ember owns T, a pointer with no header (OBJ-1 allows no flags), 'live' means the check must learn when an adopted owner ends. Either every `owns T` end in the program looks the address up, a cost on every free that the rule does not state, or nothing removes it and round 2 stops a correct program with a false 'adopted twice'.
holes.fix_hint: For what into_raw() gave, record the address at into_raw() and remove it at adopt. A second adopt finds nothing and stops. That costs only at the two calls and nothing at any end. Keep the live set for foreign pointers as today.

holes.what_goes_wrong: 'Every hold has an end Ember can reach. A retained contract names destroys(f); without one it is E5041'. A hold of something that lives for the whole program (a c"..." literal, a static) needs no end, yet the only way out is to declare the function unsafe.
holes.fix_hint: A retained parameter whose value lives for the whole program (a view `from(static)`: a c"..." literal, a static's data) needs no token and no destroys(f).

safety.notes:
The rule is broken. It has 5 high holes, 8 medium and 7 low.

The direction is sound for safety. Point 1 refuses an Ember list C would free (E5060). Point 2 gives every hold an Ember owner whose end calls f once, which matches verdicts 57, 58 and 114. Point 3's one end per type is the right general principle. The call words follow verdicts 147, 150, 158 and 160 exactly (`world_add(shares mut body)` with `owns p: shares mut Body` is verdict 160's own shape).

**High holes.**
- **Hole 1 (C++ base fields).** The claim that a class object is reached by C only through calls Ember counts is false for a class with a C++ base. C++ writes that part itself, and FFI-39d counts only the Ember overrides. So the rule's own listener case is a use after free in safe code.
- **Hole 2 (Ember-made foreign owners).** Point 1's test is the type. An Ember-made `owns Event` of a foreign struct reaches C's free(), or its own end calls event_free on Ember memory.
- **Hole 3 (`unique_ptr` deleters).** 'One end per type' and 'every owner ends with delete' clash with 'unique_ptr<T, D> unchanged'.
- **Hole 4 (C++ delete not counted).** C++'s delete of an owner="foreign" object is missing from FFI-52's list. BCK-7 and BCK-8 therefore do not see the end.
- **Hole 5 (`into_inner()` inside its own callback).** It escapes verdict 62's deferral.

**Medium holes.** Hole 6 is trampoline and constructor memory. Hole 7 is reload: the changed FFI-35a removes the header mark that HR-20 relies on. Holes 8 and 9 are cancel APIs whose hold ends after f returns (libuv's uv_cancel, io_uring), which the rule says it covers. Hole 10 is f run re-entrantly inside a physics step. Hole 11 is a default thread word that lets f run on another thread. Hole 12 is an anchor kept as a view, which locks it against change for the token's life (the listener's `set_label`, a world step). Hole 13 is a Copy-handle anchor that dies before the token.

**What the matrix checked and found fine.**
- E5041, E5060, E5002 and E7015 refuse what they should.
- The trampoline's generation, once and thread stops.
- The status-f stop.
- The kept-object hand-over stop.
- adopt-twice on one local (E5068).
- C++ T&& (the moved-from object is ended once).
- shared_ptr, borrowed results and the capacity case (P27).
- The once-never-called leak report.
- Owner loops through a token: WK-1 already follows function values' state, and the registering line is visible.

Unstated but implied: a Retained must be neither Copy nor Clone. The type of a token that keeps two values is undecided.

**Cross-group.** Holes 11 and 13 rest partly on P04 (vouching C thread facts and handles, with J8-14). Hole 10 reaches P05 (queued drops at check points). Hole 7 is P09's. Hole 20 is P02's. The THR-2 routes into threads(any) callbacks are P01's. The unsafe route's spelling waits on P07 (J2-11).

**Verdicts.** No owner verdict is contradicted. The widening of verdict 91's correction (Retained for every hold) is stated plainly by the design. Verdict 114 fix 3 holds as worded.

matrix.how_kept: Three crossings, chosen by the contract's ownership word (owns for good, retained/once as a token-held hold, returns_owned/adopt taken back). One end per type (drop and Ember's free, the declared destroys(f), or C++ delete). Retained[T] for every hold, adopt for every type.
matrix.edge_cases: Slot APIs where a new registration replaces the old one. Holds that end when another C object ends (setvbuf until fclose). Destroy-notify APIs where C ends the value through a function Ember gives (GLib, SQLite, Lua). Cancel that still delivers the one completion (uv_cancel, IOCP, io_uring), and async close (uv_close). Callback and user data in a struct field or in two calls (SDL_AudioSpec, curl). unique_ptr<T, D> with a non-default deleter. The class-object line drawn by type rather than by layout. Overlay entries that cannot write the Ember type.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The design says a token keeps f's lent arguments as views ("one lent to the call is viewed, so the token does not outlive it"). So `held` views `world` for its whole life, and `world_step(ref mut world, 0.016)` is refused: it changes what a live view looks at (verdicts 2 and 5).

Every real registration names its anchor in its unregister function: cpSpaceRemoveBody(space, body), uv_timer_stop(timer), epoll_ctl(epfd, DEL, fd), g_signal_handler_disconnect(instance, id). So the ordinary engine loop does not compile. Keeping `held` in a `Scene` beside `world` is refused as well; open risk 2 names only this second effect.

If the anchor is instead a Copy `@ffi(handle)` (J8-14 A), the token copies it with no bound. Then ending or replacing `world` before `held` (`world = world_new()` for the next level) makes the token's end call `world_remove` on a freed world, from safe code.
holes.fix_hint: Keep a lent argument of f in the token only as a bound on the token's life. The token must end before that argument's owner ends or is replaced (checked when compiling, as LT-4 bounds a value by its manager), but the anchor may be changed meanwhile. The token reads it only at its end, and an opaque foreign value or a class object does not move when changed. Apply the same bound to a Copy handle that names an owned foreign object.

from std.ffi import adopt

@layout(c)
struct Event:
    kind: i32
    code: i32

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("returns an `Event` made with `malloc`, which the caller frees with `free`")
    unsafe fn next_event() -> *mut Event

fn main():
    # SAFETY: `next_event` hands over a new `Event` C made, which nothing else frees
    unsafe:
        e = adopt[Event](next_event())
    println(e.kind)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
The design lets `adopt` take an address "for every type: one foreign code made, and one into_raw() gave". It ends an Ember type with "its drop, its fields' ends and Ember's free".

`Event` is the program's own `@layout(c)` struct, so it is an Ember type. `e`'s end therefore hands C's malloc block to Ember's allocator, which [RT-1] and [FFI-27] allow to differ from malloc: heap corruption.

The SAFETY note is true; the language chose the wrong end. A `*mut T` from `into_raw()` and a `*mut T` C made have the same type, so nothing tells the two apart. Today's text reads the end from destroys(f) and so does not do this.
holes.fix_hint: Give what `into_raw()` produces a type that only `into_raw()` makes: the class object's `ObjectPtr[C]`, and an own pointer type for an `owns T`. Let `adopt` end a value with Ember's free only when it comes from that type. A `*mut T` C made is adopted only for a type whose declaration names destroys(f) (`@ffi(destroys(free))` on the struct), and is E5002 otherwise, as for a C type.

from std.ffi import ObjectPtr, adopt

class Enemy:
    hp: i32 = 100

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`p` stays valid until `take_user_pointer` gives it back")
    unsafe fn set_user_pointer(p: ObjectPtr[Enemy])
    @safety("a pointer was set and not taken back yet")
    unsafe fn take_user_pointer() -> ObjectPtr[Enemy]

fn load(ref mut current: LevelArena):
    boss = Enemy(hp=500) using current
    # SAFETY: the window keeps the address until `take_user_pointer` hands it back
    unsafe:
        set_user_pointer(boss.into_raw())

fn main():
    current = LevelArena()
    load(ref mut current)
    # SAFETY: the address C hands back is the one `into_raw()` gave
    unsafe:
        back = adopt[Enemy](take_user_pointer())
    println(back.hp)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
`into_raw()` takes any class object with one owner ([FFI-54]), including one made in `current`. Its result is one pointer, so the instance word that ALC-1 and LT-4 keep is lost.

`adopt[Enemy]` returns a plain `Enemy`. Its end is "its drop and Ember's free", so the arena's block goes to Global's free (corruption), and `back` is no longer bounded by `current` (LT-4), so it may outlive the arena.

Both SAFETY notes are true. "Every owner lives in memory that end gives back" fails, and P02 already lists "into_raw and C-kept addresses of arena objects" as open.
holes.fix_hint: Either refuse `into_raw()` of a value made in a manager other than Global (E-code naming the manager and the making line), or keep the instance in what `into_raw()` gives and make `adopt[T using A](p)` end the value through that instance, with LT-4's bound. Ask this together with P02.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The rule gives every type one end ("a C++ class: its overlay's destroys(f), else C++'s delete"), yet other_cases keeps [FFI-17a]'s "ended through the deleter" unchanged.

Both elements of `enemies` are `owns g.Enemy`. One must end with PoolDelete and the other with delete, and an `owns T` "holds one address" (E5034's own reason), so `clear()` cannot tell which is which.

Ending the pooled one with delete frees pool memory in safe code, since the unique_ptr import is automatic. Following each value's deleter would need a hidden word per owner, which the rule says does not exist.
holes.fix_hint: Under one end per type, import `std::unique_ptr<T, D>` as `owns T` only when D is T's one end: `std::default_delete<T>`, or the deleter the overlay names as T's destroys(f). Refuse any other D (E5034), naming D and the overlay line that would make it T's end.

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Counter:
    n: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    # C keeps one filter; a new one replaces the old one (SDL_SetEventFilter, sqlite3_busy_handler)
    @safety("`ud` is the user data `set_filter` was given")
    unsafe fn clear_filter(ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(clear_filter))
    safe fn set_filter(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn pump_events()

fn main():
    hits = shares mut Counter()
    tok = set_filter(owns fn() shares mut hits: hits.n += 1)
    tok = set_filter(owns fn() shares mut hits: hits.n += 10)
    pump_events()
    println(hits.n)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
The second `tok =` evaluates the new registration first, so C replaces filter 1 with filter 2. Then the old token ends ([OWN-5]) and calls `clear_filter`, which clears C's single slot. Filter 2 is gone, and the program prints 0 with no message, where it means 10 per event.

The destroys(f) model gives each hold its own release, but a slot API releases the old hold at the next registration. The only correct f is a hand-written C shim that clears the slot only if `ud` is still the current one.

SQLite's busy, progress and commit hooks, SDL_SetEventFilter, lua_atpanic, png_set_error_fn and glfwSetWindowUserPointer (the design's own user-data case, which has no separate clear function) all have this shape.
holes.fix_hint: Let a contract say the hold lives in a slot keyed by some of the call's arguments: `callback(retained, user_data=ud, slot(db))`, or `slot()` for a global one. A new registration on the same slot ends the old hold's state without calling f, and marks the old token used so its end does nothing. f is called only by the token whose registration is still current.

from std.ffi import CStrView, ForeignCallback, Retained

class Loader:
    done: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    # C calls `cb` exactly once: with the bytes read, or with -125 (cancelled) after `fs_cancel`
    @safety("`cb` and `req` are a pair `fs_read` was given")
    unsafe fn fs_cancel(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void, i32), req: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(once, user_data=req), threads(creator)), destroys(fs_cancel))
    safe fn fs_read(path: CStrView, owns cb: fn(i32), req: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]
    safe fn run_loop()

fn main():
    loader = shares mut Loader()
    pending = fs_read(c"big.dat", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.done += 1)
    pending = fs_read(c"small.dat", owns fn(n: i32) shares mut loader: loader.done += 1)
    run_loop()
    println(loader.done)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
By the design, the first token's end calls `fs_cancel` and then ends the function before it runs. But libuv's uv_cancel, Win32 CancelIoEx and io_uring's cancel all still deliver the request's one completion (with ECANCELED or ERROR_OPERATION_ABORTED).

So `run_loop()` makes C call the first callback, and the trampoline stops the program: "C called the callback ... after its token ended". A correct program stops, and the only alternative, declaring no destroys(f), gives up cancelling.

Data holds have the same shape. libuv's `uv_close(handle, close_cb)` lets go of the handle only when close_cb runs, so a token whose end calls uv_close and then frees the handle leaves C writing freed memory. No declaration can say "the hold ends at C's next call". The other_cases claim of tokio-uring style I/O hits this too: `into_inner()` calls cancel on an already finished request.
holes.fix_hint: Let a contract say that C still calls once after f; this can be once's meaning, since once says C calls exactly once. The token's end then calls f and leaves the block to the one run, which ends it. Let a data hold name the once callback whose run ends it (`retained(until(cb))`), and give the kept value to that run.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
This is E5041, because no destroys(f) is named. But the hold has no unregister function: C lets go of `buf` when `f` is closed, and that close is run by `f`'s own end.

Naming `destroys(fclose)` here would close the stream at the token's end and again at `f`'s end. The token would have to end after `f`, the reverse of every token in the rule, so this correct program has no safe form.

Expat's XML_SetUserData (until XML_ParserFree), sqlite3_bind_blob with SQLITE_STATIC (until finalize) and every API that keeps a pointer for the life of one of its own objects have this shape.
holes.fix_hint: Let the contract name the foreign owner whose end ends the hold: `param(buf, retained(until(f)), count(n))`. The call then hands the kept value to that owner, with no token, and the owner's end runs its destroys(f) and then ends what it keeps. The cost is one block per owner that keeps something; state it in COST-3.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
This is E5041. Naming `destroys(disconnect)` (g_signal_handler_disconnect(instance, id)) instead gives a token whose end calls disconnect on a button C may already have destroyed when its window closed. C then reads a freed object, from safe code; under J8-14 A the handle is copied with no bound.

The real APIs take the value for good and end it through a function Ember gives them: GLib's g_signal_connect_data, g_idle_add_full and g_object_set_data_full, sqlite3_create_function_v2's xDestroy, sqlite3_bind_blob's destructor, Lua's __gc.

That is "C can run that value's end", the rule's own test for point 1. Yet point 1 lists only foreign values and `owner="foreign"` classes.
holes.fix_hint: Let point 1 also cover a value whose end Ember hands to C. A `notify=` word on the contract (`callback(owned, user_data=ud, notify=notify)`, `param(data, owns, notify=free_fn)`) makes the compiler pass a generated thunk that ends the value by its own end (drop and Ember's free, or the function's state), with no token. C's one call of the thunk ends the hold, and a second call stops, as FFI-53's used-up mark does.

class Synth:
    phase: f32 = 0.0

@layout(c)
struct AudioSpec:
    freq: i32
    callback: Option[unsafe extern "C" fn(*mut void, *mut u8, i32)]
    userdata: *mut void

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`spec.callback` and `spec.userdata` are a pair C keeps until `close_audio`")
    unsafe fn open_audio(spec: *mut AudioSpec) -> i32
    safe fn close_audio()

fn main():
    synth = shares mut Synth()
    # no spelling gives C `fn(out: MutSpan[u8]) shares mut synth: ...` through `spec`
holes.what_goes_wrong:
The rule says a hold C keeps is a token the call returns. But [FFI-21] names `user_data` only as a parameter of the same call, so two common shapes have no contract word:
- a callback C finds in a struct field (SDL_AudioSpec, miniaudio's ma_device_config, Vulkan's VkDebugUtilsMessengerCreateInfoEXT);
- a callback given in a different call from its user data (libcurl's WRITEFUNCTION and WRITEDATA).

A capturing function cannot be handed over (E5040), the pair stays raw inside `unsafe`, and there is no token to end the hold.
holes.fix_hint: Let `callback(..., user_data=f)` name a field of the same `@layout(c)` parameter, for example `param(spec, borrowed, one, field(callback, callback(retained, user_data=userdata)))`. The field's Ember type is then `owns fn(...)`, and the call returns the token as it would for a parameter. A two-call API is wrapped once in an overlay `extend` method that makes both calls ([FFI-13]).

from std.sync import Atomic

class Stats:
    ticks: Atomic[i32] = Atomic(0)

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `on_tick` was given")
    unsafe fn off_tick(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(any)), destroys(off_tick))
    safe fn on_tick(owns cb: thread_shared fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]

fn main():

holes.fix_hint: Put the thread kind in the token's type: either the kept function's type (`Retained[thread_shared fn()]`, `Retained[fn()]`), or two erased kinds, one-thread and any-thread. P01's type rule then decides the markers, and a list of mixed tokens holds the one-thread kind.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The token holds a `shares mut` owner of `panel`, and `panel` holds the token: a loop of owners. [WK-5] lists only `Retained[ForeignCallback]` (to the callback's state) as an owner edge, and the design widens Retained without adding `Retained[T]` to T.

So WK-6's refusal (E3032) does not fire. `panel` is never ended, `remove_listener` never runs, and C keeps the address for good: a leak in safe code, which [WK-15] says cannot happen.
holes.fix_hint: Add to [WK-5]: a `Retained[T]` token is an owner edge to every owner it keeps, as well as to a callback's state. The line is then E3032, with help to hold a `weakref` instead or to keep the token outside `Panel`.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The token is a temporary, so it ends at the end of its statement ([OWN-2]). `world_remove` runs at once, and C simulates nothing, with no message. The program compiles and does something the programmer did not mean (OWNER-DIRECTION principle 7).

Today's callback registrations have the same trap. The rule turns every C function that keeps something into one that returns a token, so the trap reaches every hold. Retained is not even @must_use, and W2190 would only be a warning ([ERR-5]).
holes.fix_hint: Make a token result that ends in its own statement an error, not W2190: "`world_add` returns the token that keeps C's hold, and it ends here, so `world_remove` runs at once; keep it: `held = world_add(shares mut body)`". Registering and ending in one line is never meant.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The design checks f's status at the token's end and stops the program in every profile on an error, with no handled form (open risk 4).

Here the error means that C has already let go, which is a success in meaning, yet the server stops on its first closed connection. epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_DEL) returning ENOENT or EBADF after the fd closed, and sqlite3_close returning SQLITE_BUSY, are the real cases.

The owner's bar asks for fault tolerance, and P27 already uses "a stop plus a try_ form".
holes.fix_hint: Give tokens `held.try_end() -> Result[T, (Retained[T], N)]`, which hands the token back on failure, while the plain end stops as designed. Let the contract list the status values that mean C holds nothing, for example `destroys(unwatch, released=[NET_OK, NET_NOT_FOUND])`.

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained
from std.sync import Mutex

class Log:
    samples: Mutex[Array[f32]] = Mutex([])

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `on_sample` was given")
    unsafe fn off_sample(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void, f32), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(any)), destroys(off_sample))
    safe fn on_sample(owns cb: thread_shared fn(f32), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]

fn main():
    log = thread_shared Log()
    tok = Some(on_sample(owns fn(v: f32) thread_shared log: log.samples.lock().push(owns v)))
    with g = log.samples.lock():
        tok = None                 # the token ends while this thread holds the lock
        println(g.len())
holes.what_goes_wrong:
The token's end waits for a callback still running on C's audio thread ([FFI-53]: "unregistering waits until it returns"). That callback waits for `log.samples`, which this thread holds, so both threads wait forever.

Verdict 43 refuses, when compiling, a call that may take a lock this thread holds. The design counts the token's end as a call of `off_sample` and as the end of the state, but not as a wait on the callback's body, so the lock rule never sees this deadlock. The rule spreads threads(any) tokens to every hold.
holes.fix_hint: Count a threads(any) token's end as waiting on every lock its callback may take, worked out from the callback's body as verdict 86 does. Ending the token under one of those locks is then refused with verdict 43's error and help: end `tok` after the `with` block.
