from std.hot import ReloadError

class Inventory:                                # the edit: `gold: int` became `gold: Coins`, and every live inventory gets a map
    items: Array[Item]
    gold: Coins

    static fn migrate_from(owns old: OldInventory) -> Result[Inventory, ReloadError]:
        items = old.items
        items.push(owns Item(name=String("map")))   # refused by [HR-50]
        return Ok(Inventory(items=items, gold=Coins(n=old.gold)))

static mut NEXT_UID: int = 0
fn next_uid() -> int:
    NEXT_UID += 1
    return NEXT_UID

class Enemy:                                    # another edit adds `uid: int = next_uid()`: refused in plan
    hp: int
holes.what_goes_wrong: The design says owns old 'means what it means on any parameter', but [HR-50] takes away the right that owns gives everywhere else (verdict 32, P11's 'a name that owns its value may change it'). A carried list may not be pushed to or popped, and `old.socks.pop()` is refused, though `old` is a bit copy and pop touches only that copy. The refused migration is correct whenever the reload succeeds, as the design's own risk 3 says. The help sends the change 'after the reload', but the language has no place for that (std.hot has only checkpoint and ReloadError). The programmer must add a flag field and code that runs once, or a rebuild loop that costs a copy C's realloc would not make. The default `uid: int = next_uid()`, a natural edit that today's HR-14 runs ('initialised to that default'), becomes a refusal: a program that compiles and reloads today is refused.
holes.fix_hint: Prepare form keeps an undo log instead of refusing. Every store into memory from before the reload (a static, an object, a buffer a taken part brings) records the old bytes. Every end and every buffer it replaces is deferred to reclaim (already in the design). A failed reload replays the log backwards. owns old then means owns, LOG.push and next_uid() work, and nothing changes on failure. Cost: one log entry per such store, in prepare only.

holes.what_goes_wrong: 'Each value of a changed type is rebuilt where it lives' leaves each key in the slot its old two-field hash chose. After the reload, `Pos(x=1, y=2)` hashes three fields, so every lookup misses and `b.tiles[...]` panics with 'key not found' on a board that holds the key. If a migrate_from maps two old keys to one new key (`x: f32` becoming `x: int` by rounding), the rebuilt map would hold the same key twice. Neither case is decided.
holes.fix_hint: A container whose placement depends on its elements' values (a Map's or Set's keys) is rebuilt in prepare by its own insert, with the new type's Hash and Eq, in its iteration order. Two keys that become equal fail the reload with ReloadError.Migration, naming the map and the key.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The roots are 'the frames below a checkpoint, read through the map of their live values that the compiler records at each call of std.hot.checkpoint()'. But `main` is stopped at its call of `serve`, so a map only at checkpoint's own call site misses main's locals. HR-3b's per-call record is what is needed. The wording also does not say the maps read OWN-3's hidden drop flags. After `SESSIONS.push(owns s)` the slot still holds the object's address. A map that treats `s` as live has the walk reach the one-owner Session twice. The design's visited set holds only 'blocks with several owners', so the Session is migrated twice, the second time from a block that has already taken its new layout or moved.
holes.fix_hint: Write the roots as 'each frame below a checkpoint, at the call it is stopped in (HR-3b's record), with the live slots that call's map lists, a slot whose value was handed over on some path read through its drop flag'. Put every block the walk reaches into the visited set, not only shared ones.

holes.what_goes_wrong: A function value's state 'migrates by captured name' and a body change 'applies', but MNG-1 names items, not lambdas, and the rule does not say how an old lambda is matched to a new one. If lambdas are matched by order inside `build`, the live OK button now runs the help body. Both capture one int, so plan sees no change, and pressing OK prints 'help 120' with no error. If they are matched by their text, every body edit removes the old lambda, and HR-7 refuses the reload while a button holds it, so the most common UI edit needs a restart. The design's risk 5 names this but leaves it open.
holes.fix_hint: Put the identity rule in the spec. An old lambda matches a new one in the same enclosing function with the same capture names and words, after a diff of that function's statements. A lambda with live values that matches none, or more than one, refuses the reload, naming it, its line and its count.

from std.mem import Allocator, Layout, System
from std.sync import Atomic

struct Counting:
    live: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

unsafe extend Counting implements Allocator:
    fn allocate(layout: Layout) -> *mut u8:
        this.live.fetch_add(layout.size as int)
        return System().allocate(layout)
    # deallocate and reallocate subtract and delegate to System()

static COUNTING: Counting = Counting()          # ember.toml: [build] global_allocator = "main.COUNTING" (ALC-3)

struct Stats:                                   # the edit adds `misses: int = 0`; J7-16's block must move
    hits: int = 0
holes.what_goes_wrong: [HR-49] gives a moved value 'a new place made the way its old one was: ... the same manager', while the changed [HR-36] takes it 'from the transaction arena', and [HR-50] forbids prepare to change any static or object from before the reload. Here every block comes from COUNTING, user code that changes its counter. Taking the new block from the transaction arena means its later end calls `COUNTING.deallocate`, and so `System().deallocate`, on memory System never gave out: heap corruption. Taking it through `COUNTING.allocate` in prepare changes `live`, which [HR-50] forbids, and a failed reload must call user `deallocate` to undo it. HR-46 settles only managers that may have several instances. A manager with no fields (ALC-1's one instance) or the configured global allocator is left with two contradicting rules.
holes.fix_hint: One rule for every manager. A moved value's new block comes from the manager its old one came from, by that manager's own allocate in prepare, and goes back by its deallocate if the reload fails. These calls are the manager's own changes (ALC-5), which [HR-50] allows as it allows the transaction arena. Only the built-in manager's blocks come from the transaction arena's chunks, and HR-46 stands for managers with several instances.

    sock: Socket

Every `log` Socket prepare opened is then freed without its drop, so each failed reload leaks one file descriptor per live session. While the programmer is iterating on a migration that fails, the server runs out of descriptors. That contradicts the design's 'no outcome ... leaks'. The blanket rule exists only to keep parts taken from `old` alive, and the prepare-form twins already track which places may hold such a part.
holes.fix_hint: On failure, end every value prepare made by its own drop, skipping the parts taken from old (the places the twins already track as holding a taken part), which go back to the old value. Then free the arena.

Read-only check of P09 against owner-bar.md, brief.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, phase1-groups.json (every group's principle), phase2.json J7-15 and J7-16, phase3.json K14 and K48, the J7-15 verdict-159 clash, the HR lead fixes, JOB.md verdicts 32, 55-59, 78-88, 99-105, 114, 145-166, tasks/85/owner-answers.md (A1, A4/ODR-120, A6/ODR-126), and the spec parts p20 (all of Annex B), p08 (OBJ, RC), p07 (OWN, LT-46, DRP), p06 (CLO), p09 (ARN, ALC), p11, p12 (ECS), p15 (STD-11, STD-15), p16 (FFI-36a, FFI-54), p18 (MNG-1). One slip to report: my first directory listing also ran `python -c "print(1)"` while checking which tools exist. It printed 1 and read or changed nothing. Everything else was Read, Grep, and sed or grep through Bash for reading only. I made no edits, ran no compiler and built nothing.

The rule's direction holds: a walk over a live-instance list, zero bytes per value, `owns old`, deferred ends. The ordinary program is unchanged, and the J7-15 and J7-16 answers follow from the rule as written, verdict 159's correction included. Each hole below can be fixed inside option A.

Four high holes:
1. Threads. HR-42a lets other threads enter Ember code during plan, prepare and reclaim. The rule's new writes from the polling thread (prepare's owners, reclaim's ends and drops, allocation in another thread's chunk) are therefore unordered, which clashes with P01 and verdict 101.
2. std's containers. They are written on raw memory and MaybeUninit, and the changed HR-13a gives std no descriptions, so the walk cannot see into Map, Set, SmallArray or the ECS Registry. Every component edit is then either refused or missed. MaybeUninit and union payloads are not refused either.
3. Frame views. A view in a frame below a checkpoint into a removed or unheld part is neither a kept view (HR-51) nor a move (HR-3b), so nothing refuses it.
4. Pruning across reloads. Pruning dyn and fn places by the newest image's facts misses values that older images put there.

The medium holes are mostly additions to the spec text: rehashing maps whose key type changed; roots at every call a frame is stopped in, read with drop flags; a lambda identity rule; one rule for user memory managers that must move a value; ending prepare-made resources on failure; pruning by 'into' rather than 'of'. One of them, HR-50, also needs a change of approach: its refusals take away rights `owns` has everywhere else, and they refuse `id: int = next_id()`, which today's HR-14 accepts. An undo log in prepare form removes those refusals, keeps the failed reload traceless, and costs only prepare.

The lead should give P01, P02, P05, P11 and P15 the clash lines.

design.rule:
A reload moves every value the program can still reach to its new layout, wherever that value lives, and changes nothing else about it. It finds the values by following owners from the program's roots: the statics, the frames below a checkpoint, and what the runtime holds for C and for threads. For each type it reads a description. The compiler emits that description the same way it emits the type's drop. A type whose fields do not say where its values are (std's containers) gives the description in its own code. Nothing is registered per value, and no header grows for reload. While a reload is applied, every other thread is held outside Ember code, and the reload's own code runs on the main thread.

Prepare builds every new value. It also runs the program's own reload code: `migrate_from`, which reads the old value or takes it over with `owns old` as any parameter does, the defaults of added fields, and re-run initialisers. That code sees each value from before the reload as it is at that moment, in its old layout and with its own code. Prepare records every change it makes to anything that already existed, and any end of such a thing waits.

If prepare fails, every recorded change is put back. Every value prepare made is ended by its own drop, and nothing from before the reload is ended. If prepare succeeds, commit publishes the new values and rewrites every owner, link and view. Reclaim then runs with the new code: it ends, each by its own drop, what the old values held that the new ones do not.

A reload is refused before anything changes if it would end or move something a view still points into, run code on a thread a value is bound to, or leave behind a value it cannot see into.
design.spec_text:
Annex B only. It changes [HR-2], [HR-2a], [HR-3], [HR-3b], [HR-11], [HR-12], [HR-12a], [HR-13], [HR-13a], [HR-13b], [HR-14], [HR-15], [HR-15b], [HR-16], [HR-19], [HR-20], [HR-30], [HR-36], [HR-37], [HR-41], [HR-42], [HR-42a], [HR-47] and [BEN-8], and adds [HR-48] to [HR-52]. [OBJ-1] and [COST-3] stand as written in every build. In a process that reloads, "the program" of [OBJ-1]'s weak-count rule means every image loaded in it ([HR-52]).

**Threads**

* `[HR-3]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* **A reload holds every other thread out of Ember code.**
  * A reload is applied only inside `ember_reload_poll()` or at `std.hot.checkpoint()` ([HR-33]). From the start of plan to the end of reclaim the reload generation of [HR-42] is odd. Every way into Ember code waits while it is: an export or a trampoline, a worker taking a job, a thread starting, a join taking its result, and a call into `ember_rt` that reaches Ember memory.
  * Plan starts only when, with the generation odd, no other registered thread is executing Ember code (each depth counter is zero). Otherwise the generation goes back, the poll returns `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT`, and nothing has changed. At a checkpoint the thread's own frames below it stay live ([HR-3b]).
  * The reload's code runs on the polling thread: each `migrate_from`, default, re-run initialiser and `rebuild`, and the `drop`s run by the ends it makes ([HR-50]). When a reload runs any such code, the polling thread must be the main thread ([THR-20], [FFI-33c]). A poll on another thread applies only a reload that runs none. Otherwise it returns `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT`, and `ember_reload_stats()` gives the reason ("this reload runs `Session.migrate_from`, which may reach the main thread's module variables; poll on the main thread").
  * Some values are bound to one thread: a `threads(creator)` value of [FFI-33b], and anything that holds one. An end of such a value that must run on its thread is queued there, as [RC-4] point 2 queues, and runs at that thread's next check point. Code the reload would run on such a value bound to another thread is refused in plan, naming the value and the thread.
  * So no two threads run Ember code during a reload. One-thread state the reload changes (a `shares` count, a module variable) is changed while its own thread is held out, in the order the generation gives, as a lock hands state from one thread to the next. An owner that prepare makes of a `thread_shared` value made on another thread is counted as [RC-4] counts an owner made away from the value's maker.
  * A thread that comes in during a reload waits until reclaim ends: at most plan, prepare, commit and reclaim together, which [HR-32] reports. Compiling and loading happen before, outside the gate.
* `[HR-42]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Making the generation odd opens a reload. Commit writes the new thunk targets and type information. After reclaim, one release store makes the generation even again, and a thread entering Ember code acquires it.
* `[HR-42a]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Entering Ember code is one relaxed increment of the depth counter, one acquire load of the generation and one compare, with no fence on that side. The reload side issues the platform's process-wide barrier (`membarrier` on Linux, `FlushProcessWriteBuffers` on Windows) between making the generation odd and reading the counters. Only an entry that finds the generation odd takes the slow path: it takes back its increment, waits for the generation to change, and enters again. This is in reload builds only; a `release` build has none of it ([HR-27]).
* `[HR-30]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Adds: a reload that runs code of the program is applied only by a poll on the main thread ([HR-3]).

**Finding the values**

* `[HR-48]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A reload finds every value the program can still reach.**
  * **Roots.**
    * Each static that is initialised: its flag is read ([STA-3]). A static not yet initialised is initialised later by the new code ([HR-17]).
    * Each frame below a checkpoint, at the call it is stopped in, read through that call's record ([HR-3b]): the slots that hold owners, links and views at that call. A slot whose value was handed over on some path is read through its hidden flag ([OWN-3]).
    * What the runtime holds that no frame does: the live records of what C keeps ([HR-20]); each thread's start state and each join result not yet taken; each queued job; and each value waiting in its making thread's queue ([RC-4]).
  * **The walk.**
    * From the roots it follows every owner (a one-owner place, `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`), and it reads every link, view and raw pointer it meets.
    * It visits each block once, keeping the set of blocks it has reached.
    * Its order is fixed: the statics in the order they are declared, then the frames from the bottom, then what the runtime holds, and each value's insides in declaration order.
    * It reads each value's description. Usually that is the one the compiler emits for the type as it emits the type's `drop`: per enum variant, a `dyn` value through its type word, a function value's state through its code word. A type of [HR-13a] gives its own.
  * **What it finds.** A value of a changed type wherever it lives:
    * inline in a struct, a tuple, an enum's payload or a list;
    * in a class object;
    * in a block of its own (`owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`);
    * in a function value's state;
    * behind `owns dyn I`, an `AnyError` included;
    * in a generator's frame ([HR-45]);
    * in memory a manager handed out ([HR-46]).
  * **What it visits.** Only a value whose type may hold one of the following, inline, through an owner, or in what an owner holds:
    * a value of a changed type;
    * an owner, link, view or raw pointer whose target may be, or lie inside, a value of a changed type;
    * an owner, link, view or raw pointer whose target may be, or lie inside, a value the reload ends: a removed field's value, a part `migrate_from` may leave in `old`, the old value of a `@reinit_on_reload` static, and everything those own.

    This set is worked out when the reload is built, from the types of every image loaded in the process ([HR-52]).
  * **What it leaves.** A value nothing reaches is never read again, and is left as it is: an ended object's block kept for its `weakref` links ([OBJ-3]), or arena memory that no view points into.
* `[HR-52]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Facts across images.**
  * A reload build is compiled against the running image's manifest ([HR-8]).
  * Every whole-program fact it is compiled with is the union over every image loaded in the process: which class families `weakref` links may reach ([OBJ-1]), which kinds may reach a `dyn` or function place (verdicts 122, 128, 151), and which types may hold which.
  * The runtime keeps each image's descriptions, as it keeps the images ([HR-4]). The walk reads a value's description from the latest image that has the value's type.
  * So a fact never narrows within a process. A value an older image put in a place is still found there, and a header that gained a weak count keeps it until the process restarts.
* `[HR-3b]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Adds: each call's record also lists the frame's slots that hold owners, links and views at that call, with their types. The walk reads them ([HR-48]). These are the stack maps of the owner's ruling A1.
* `[HR-11]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Adds: a type's schema includes its header's shape, that is, whether it has a weak count ([OBJ-1], [HR-52]).
* `[HR-12]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* A reloadable build keeps [OBJ-1]'s header. Nothing is registered for a value Ember keeps; the runtime records only what it hands to C ([HR-20]). A reload finds values as [HR-48] says.
* `[HR-12a]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Every package in a process agrees on whether reload is enabled, and this is enforced at link time (`E9035`). The reason is that the walk reads every package's descriptions.
* `[HR-13]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Value-typed data (structs in arrays, `SoA` columns, ECS storage, arena contents) is found through its container, as every value is ([HR-48]).
* `[HR-13a]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* **A type whose fields do not say where its values are says it in its own code**, just as its `drop` ends those values. A type that keeps values in raw memory or in `MaybeUninit` slots implements `std.hot.Holds`, in unsafe code ([TYP-43]). That covers std's `Array`, `Map`, `Set`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, `RingBuffer`, `Pool` and the ECS's pools, and any of a program's own containers.
  * **`each`** gives each value the type holds, as a place, with its position: a `u64` the type chooses, such as an index, an insertion rank or a handle.
    * The walk calls it with the running image's code.
    * It may only read, which the compiler checks from its body ([EFF-1]).
    * It is the only code of the program that plan runs.
  * **`rebuild`** puts the values back.
    * It is called on the type's new value, whose other fields are carried by name ([HR-14]), with the values `each` gave, migrated, each with its position.
    * It puts each value back at its position, with the new image's code. A `Map` inserts its keys again with the new `Hash` and `Eq`, in insertion order.
    * Prepare calls it whenever a value the type holds is migrated or rewritten.
    * It may fail the reload with `ReloadError.Migration`. Two keys that the reload made equal fail it, naming the map and the key.
  * std's types implement it in every reload build, as every package's descriptions are emitted ([HR-12a]).
* `[HR-13b]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* **What the walk cannot see into is refused, never guessed.** Plan refuses the reload, naming the holder and the type, in three cases:
  * a changed type may sit in a `MaybeUninit`, in a union's payload (`@layout(c, union)`), or in the raw memory of a type that does not implement `std.hot.Holds` (worked out from the types);
  * a raw pointer the walk reads points at or into a value of a changed type, or a value the reload ends, and the walk did not reach that value through an owner;
  * the changed type is used across FFI by value ([HR-14]).

  A raw pointer kept only where the walk cannot read it (in C's memory) stays the `unsafe` code's promise ([HR-15a]).
* `[HR-20]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Adds the following.
  * In a reload build the runtime records each object it hands to C (under a keeping contract, or with `into_raw()`) and each callback state C keeps. These records are roots of the walk ([HR-48]).
  * A record ends in the same step as what it records:
    * the object's end, which tests the kept-by-C mark in its header ([FFI-35a]);
    * a `Retained` token's end;
    * a `once` callback's call.
  * The test is one compare, made only in the end of an object of a class the program may hand to C.

**Migrating**

* `[HR-14]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Rows are added, and "class removed while instances live" becomes the fourth row below:

  | Change | Behaviour |
  |---|---|
  | a type's header gains a weak count | each value is rebuilt with it, at 1 for all its owners; moved where it no longer fits ([HR-15]), refused where it cannot move ([HR-15a], [HR-20], [HR-46]) |
  | a lambda's captures changed | its state migrates by captured name, as a struct's fields do; an added capture is refused while a value of the lambda lives, naming the function and the count |
  | a lambda with live values that no new lambda matches, or that more than one matches | refused, naming it, its line and the count |
  | a type removed while a value of it lives, including one the reload would end | refused, naming the type and the count |
  | an implementation of `I` removed while a value of the type lives behind `dyn I` | refused, naming the type, the interface and the count |

  A lambda is the same lambda across an edit when the new one is in the same function, has the same capture names and words, and is matched in the order the function's statements keep through the edit.
* `[HR-49]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A value keeps everything but its layout.** Migration changes a value's layout and nothing else: not its owners, counts or links, not the thread that made it, and not where its memory came from.
  * A value that keeps its address takes its new bytes at commit.
  * A value that moves ([HR-15]) gets a new block, in prepare, made the way its old one was made:
    * the block comes from the same manager, through that manager's `allocate` (the built-in manager's comes from a memory chunk of the thread that made the value, [OBJ-1]);
    * its header's counts and marks are carried;
    * the manager's own changes in `allocate` are prepare's ([HR-50]), and if the reload fails the block goes back through the manager's `deallocate`.
  * A value made in an instance of a manager that may have several instances stays in that instance ([HR-46]).
  * A value that prepare's code makes is made by the polling thread, as any making is.
* `[HR-15]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* "in live instances and registered containers, in statics, and inside tuples, `owns` blocks and function values' state held by any of these" becomes "wherever the walk of [HR-48] found them, and in what prepare's code made or stored into, which is walked after that code has run ([HR-2a])". A view or link into a part of a value that moves is rewritten to that part's new place: a field by its name, an element by its position. Where the part has no place in the new layout, [HR-51] refuses.
* `[HR-15b]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* Every refusal is decided when compiling or in plan, before prepare runs. Only prepare's own failures come later, and they discard the reload ([HR-41]).
* `[HR-16]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* `static fn migrate_from(old: OldSelf) -> Result[Self, ReloadError]` replaces field-wise migration for its type.
  * `OldSelf` is the previous schema as `Old<Name>`: a struct for a struct or a class, and an enum for an enum.
    * It is visible only in that function.
    * It has no `drop` of its own ([HR-2a], ODR-120).
    * In it, a type that changed has its old schema ([HR-50]).
  * The parameter's word means what it means on every parameter ([FN-1], [OWN-9]).
    * `old: OldSelf` reads the old value.
    * `owns old: OldSelf` takes it over. Its parts are handed into the new value one by one with no word, as `=` hands them ([OWN-11]), and the function may change what `old` alone owns: `return Ok(Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp)))`.
  * A part handed over from a read-only `old` is `E3013`. Its help gives `owns old: OldSession`.
  * Where a changed type's new form is wanted, a part of `old` is migrated at that point, by its type's rows ([HR-14]) or by its own `migrate_from`. From then on it is a value prepare made. Example: `conns.push(owns Conn(sock=s))` for an old-schema `s` from `for s in owns old.socks`.
  * An owner or link that is handed over becomes an owner or link of the migrated target when the reload is applied.
  * `old` ends when the reload is applied, so the result holds no view of `old` or of anything `old` owns. Such a view is `E3063` ([LT-1]), as for any parameter that ends at the return.
  * Prepare runs a type's `migrate_from` before it migrates what that `old` alone owns. Those parts then migrate from whatever state the function left them in.
* `[HR-50]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Preparing a reload: what its code sees, and how a failure is undone.** Prepare's code is each `migrate_from`, each default of an added field ([HR-14]), each initialiser that `@reinit_on_reload` re-runs ([HR-17a]) and each `rebuild` ([HR-13a]), with everything they call and end. It runs for the values in the walk's order. [HR-34] covers all of it: in a default, an initialiser or a `rebuild`, a failed run-time check or an explicit `panic` returns `ReloadError.Migration`. `migrate_from` keeps [HR-35].
  * **What it sees.** A value from before the reload is seen as it is at that moment. A value of a changed type still has its old layout, and is reached with its old schema, whether through `old`, a static or a link.
    * A call on such values runs the running image's code, on that layout. So does a call through a `dyn` or function value from before the reload, and so does a callback that a foreign call runs ([FFI-52]). Every thunk still points at the running image until commit.
    * A call on values that prepare made runs the new image's code.
    * The compiler checks each call by the facts of the image whose code it runs ([HR-44]).
  * **What it may change.** Anything, with two exceptions:
    * The reload itself rebuilds every value from before the reload whose type it changes, so prepare's code reads such a value but does not change it. The one exception is the `old` that a `migrate_from` takes over, together with what that `old` alone owns.
    * Code of the running image is not compiled to record its stores. So code of the running image that prepare's code reaches may change nothing from before the reload. A foreign call whose kept callbacks may change something is refused there, unless its declaration says `@ffi(no_callbacks)`.

    Both are refused when compiling in a `migrate_from`, and in plan for the rest, naming the line: "`players[0]` is a `Player` from before the reload, and this reload rebuilds `Player`, so it does not change while the reload is prepared; change it in `Player.migrate_from`, or after the reload".
  * **Changes are recorded; ends wait.**
    * Every store that prepare's code makes into memory from before the reload is recorded, with the bytes it replaced. That covers a static, an object, a count, and a buffer that a part taken from `old` brings with it.
    * Every end it makes of a value from before the reload waits for reclaim ([HR-2a]). That covers a part taken from `old` and then let go, a value it replaces or removes, and a buffer that a growth gives back.
    * Ending an owner or a link that prepare made subtracts from its count, as anywhere. The count never reaches zero, since every owner from before the reload lives until reclaim.
    * Each count that prepare adds to is checked against its limit there. Reaching the limit is `ReloadError.Migration` ([HR-35]).
  * **Frames.** At a checkpoint, plan refuses (`E9030`) a reload whose prepare code may change what a frame below walks, views or locks ([HR-44]), as it refuses reclaim's ends.
  * **What C would keep is refused.** Handing C anything it keeps is refused when compiling in prepare's code: a `callback(retained)` or `callback(once)` function, an object under a keeping contract, or `into_raw()` ([FFI-52]). What a foreign call does outside Ember memory is C's, and a failed reload cannot take it back. A failure of the call itself is `ReloadError.Foreign` ([HR-39]).
  * **Values prepare made are kept apart.** This applies to a value prepare makes whose end runs code: one with a `drop`, a foreign destructor, or such a value inside it.
    * Such a value stays in what prepare made. It is never stored into memory from before the reload, and never into a container beside such values from before the reload. A container taken from `old` counts as from before.
    * The compiler knows, for every place prepare's code fills, whether it holds a value prepare made or one from before the reload. It knows this the way it knows which names were handed over, with [OWN-3]'s hidden flags where it depends on the path.
    * Such a store is refused when compiling: "`conns` holds sockets taken from `old` (line 9), and line 11 adds one opened here; if the reload failed, that one would have to be closed and the others kept, which one list cannot tell apart; keep the new ones in a list of their own: write `opened.push(owns s)` in place of line 11".
  * **If the reload fails** ([HR-41]), Ember memory is put back as it was before prepare:
    1. Each value prepare made whose end runs code is ended. A value that holds nothing from before the reload is ended by its own `drop`. A value that does hold something from before is ended field by field without its own `drop`, and its parts from before are left as they are, as ODR-120 ends a migrated value's old form. A `migrate_from`'s result is ended this way.
    2. Every recorded store is put back, last first, including the stores made by the ends in step 1.
    3. Every end that was waiting is cancelled. Every block prepare made that is still allocated goes back to its manager, without its value being ended.

    Nothing from before the reload is ended, and every count is as it was. A panic in a `drop` that step 1 runs aborts, as any panic in a `drop` does ([PAN-1]).
* `[HR-51]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A reload ends nothing a view still points into, and loses no view.**
  * Plan refuses a reload, naming the holder, the view and the part, when something points into what reclaim will end. That something may be a kept view, a `sharedref mut` link or a raw pointer that the walk finds, or a view in a frame below a checkpoint (read through its call's record, [HR-48]). What reclaim ends is:
    * a removed field's value, and what it owns;
    * a part of `old` that `migrate_from`'s result does not hold on every path that returns `Ok` (worked out from its body);
    * the old value of a `@reinit_on_reload` static ([HR-47]).
  * A view or link of a whole value is rewritten to the value's new form.
  * A view or link into a part is rewritten to the part's new place ([HR-15]). For a type with `migrate_from`, that place is where its result holds that part of `old` on every path that returns `Ok`, recorded from its body. Where the paths differ, or the part is rebuilt rather than carried, plan refuses.
  * A view into what a carried part owns (a `String`'s text, a list's elements, an object) still points at it, because that memory does not move. A view into elements that a `rebuild` moves is rewritten by their positions ([HR-13a]).
  * A view that prepare's code makes follows the same rules. Where its target is `old` or a removed field, it is refused when compiling ([HR-16]). Otherwise the walk of what prepare made finds it, and it fails the reload.
* `[HR-2]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* A failure in plan or prepare leaves the process running the old image, with Ember memory as it was ([HR-50]) and a report naming the cause. Commit performs only stores of what prepare built (pointers, a value's new bytes over its own block, type and code words), with no allocation, check, callback or other fallible operation. A failure in reclaim is an ordinary panic after the reload has succeeded.
* `[HR-2a]` *(changed in 0.9.16)*
  * **Plan** walks ([HR-48]), reads the schemas and the facts of [HR-44], and makes every refusal ([HR-15b]). It runs no code of the program except `each` ([HR-13a]).
  * **Prepare** builds every new value: each value of a changed type that the walk found, including one that reclaim will end, so reclaim only ever ends values in the new layout. It runs prepare's code ([HR-50]). Then it works out the address map and the rewrites, walking what prepare's code made and stored into ([HR-15]).
  * **Commit** publishes the values, applies the rewrites, patches the type information and repoints the thunks.
  * **Reclaim** runs with the new image's code.
    * It ends, each by its own `drop`, what each old value kept that its new value does not hold: a removed field's value, what `migrate_from` left in `old` or took and let go, and the old value of a `@reinit_on_reload` static.
    * Then it runs the ends that prepare's code deferred, and frees the old blocks.
    * The migrated type's own `drop` never runs, since the value lives on in its new form (ODR-120).
  * At a checkpoint, each end that reclaim makes counts as a call of its `drop` there ([DRP-8]). Plan refuses (`E9030`) an end that may change what a frame below walks, views or locks.
* `[HR-36]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* "The transaction arena" is the set of blocks prepare makes. They are ordinary blocks, taken from where [HR-49] says, and the runtime records each one. Running out is `ReloadError.Allocation`.
* `[HR-37]` *(changed in 0.9.16)* A successful reload keeps them as ordinary blocks. A failed one ends what they hold and gives them back, as [HR-50] says.

Yes. The reload migrates the `Stats` value.

The host calls `ember_reload_poll()` on the main thread between frames, after `game_tick` has returned. Any other thread that tries to enter Ember code while the reload runs waits at the gate ([HR-3]).

The walk ([HR-48]) starts at the static `HUD`, which is initialised. It goes to the `Hud` object, follows the `stats` owner, and reaches the `Stats` block. That value is migrated like every value of the changed type: `hits` is carried by name, and `misses` is set from its default.

If the new 16 bytes do not fit the old block, the value moves to a new block ([HR-49]). The block comes from the same manager, in a chunk of the thread that made it, with its count carried. At commit, `h.stats` and every other owner of the value is rewritten ([HR-15]).

No header grows in any build: a `shares` block stays 8 or 12 bytes and a `thread_shared` one stays 32. Nothing is registered. The export says `threads=main`, which its module variable needs ([FFI-33], `E7012` otherwise).

struct Stats:                                   # the edit while the game runs: add `misses: int = 0`
    hits: int = 0
    misses: int = 0

class Hud:
    stats: shares mut Stats                     # a counted block of its own

static mut HUD: Option[Hud] = None

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `game_tick`
@unsafe(export("game_tick", threads=main))
fn game_tick():                                 # the C host calls this every frame, then ember_reload_poll(), on its main thread
    if HUD exists as ref mut h:
        h.stats.hits += 1
        h.stats.misses += 1                     # new code, reading the new field
    else:
        HUD = Some(Hud(stats=shares mut Stats()))
answers.outcome: It compiles unchanged, and the reload applies. On the next frame `hits` goes on from its old count (120 becomes 121), and `misses` is 1. Release builds are bit-identical (HR-27). Reload builds pay no header bytes and no registration, and a thread entering Ember code during the reload waits at the gate.

answers.answer:
`migrate_from` takes the old session over with `owns old`, the word the language uses for a parameter that takes a value over (verdicts 32 and 147). Each part is then handed into the new value with no word, as a constructor's argument works (verdict 159, [OWN-11]). This applies phase 3's correction to the draft. `Old<Name>` has no `drop` of its own (ODR-120), so its parts are handed over one by one, like any struct's.

What happens to each part:
- The socket and the player owner are carried as they are.
- `old.hp` is read.
- What `old` keeps is ended by its own drop when the reload is applied. Here that is `hp`, an int, so nothing runs.

If the reload fails, for instance because another session's `migrate_from` returns `Err` ([HR-50]):
- The result is ended field by field. `sock` and `target` came from before the reload, so they are left as they are. `Health` has no `drop`, so nothing runs.
- No count changes, and the old session is whole.

With a read-only `old`, `sock=old.sock` is `E3013`, and its help gives `owns old: OldSession`.

If the function wrote `target=shares old.target` instead:
- Prepare adds one owner and records the store.
- Reclaim ends `old.target`, so the count is right after a successful reload.
- A failed reload puts the recorded count back, so there is no double subtract.
answers.code:
from std.hot import ReloadError

struct Socket:                                  # an open connection, one owner
    fd: int
    fn drop():
        println("socket", this.fd, "closed")

struct Health:
    value: int

class Player:
    name: String

class Session:                                  # the edit: `hp: int` became `hp: Health`
    sock: Socket
    target: shares Player
    hp: Health

    static fn migrate_from(owns old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        return Ok(Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp)))

static mut SESSIONS: Array[Session] = []

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `on_connect`
@unsafe(export("on_connect", threads=main))
fn on_connect(fd: int):
    p = shares Player(name=String("ana"))
    SESSIONS.push(owns Session(sock=Socket(fd=fd), target=shares p, hp=Health(value=10)))
answers.outcome: It compiles, and the reload applies. Afterwards the session keeps socket 7 open and the same one owner of the player, with no count changed. Nothing is printed: no "socket 7 closed". A failed reload prints nothing and leaves the old session and every count as they were.

design.prior_art:
**C++.**
- The language has no hot reload. Live++, Recode and Edit and Continue patch function bodies. A layout change needs hand-written pre- and post-patch hooks, nothing finds the live instances, and there is no transaction.
- The strong exception guarantee (copy-and-swap, `std::move_if_noexcept`) is the model for prepare: build the new state beside the old, and drop only the new on failure.

**Rust.**
- None in the language, and hot-lib-reloader requires layouts that do not change.
- `Rc::try_unwrap` returning `Result<T, Rc<T>>` gives the input back on failure, as [HR-50] gives `owns old`'s parts back with no code from the programmer.
- The `gc` and `dumpster` crates have a `Trace` trait that unsafe containers implement by hand, as `std.hot.Holds` is implemented.

**Java.**
- HotSwap swaps bodies only. DCEVM and JRebel carry fields by name, and find the instances with the collector's heap walk, not with a per-object registry.
- `HashMap.writeObject` and `readObject` write the entries and insert them again on reading, because hash codes may differ. That is `Map.rebuild`'s model: a container whose fields do not describe its values gives its own code.

**C# and .NET.**
- Hot Reload and Edit and Continue apply member edits. Changing a field's type or a struct's layout is a "rude edit" that needs a restart.
- The GC suspends threads using `FlushProcessWriteBuffers`, the same asymmetric barrier as the gate's.

**Swift.** None in the language. Injection swaps method bodies only.

**Erlang/OTP.** `code_change(OldVsn, State, Extra)` builds the new state from the old one, and a failure leaves the old state in place.

**Smalltalk.** Class-shape changes migrate every instance by field name.

**Dynamic software updating research.**
- Ginseng (PLDI 2006) wraps every value with a version word, a per-value cost like HR-12's 16 bytes.
- Kitsune (OOPSLA 2012) and Rubah (OOPSLA 2014) traverse the heap from the roots with generated type descriptions, with nothing per object. That is [HR-48]'s design.
- Proteus (POPL 2005) decides when an update is safe from what code still uses a changed type, which is HR-3b's check.

**Stop-the-world and fences.**
- JVM safepoints and .NET GC suspension hold threads out while the heap changes.
- Linux `membarrier` (used by userspace RCU) moves the fence cost from the hot side to the rare side, as [HR-42a] does.

**Undo logs.** Database undo logs (ARIES) and undo-logging software transactional memory (McRT-STM, TinySTM's write-through mode) record each store's old bytes and replay them backwards on abort. That is [HR-50]'s failure path.

**Precise stack maps.** Go's and .NET's GC info are the model for the per-call records of [HR-3b].

**Where each falls short.**
- The managed languages pay for a collector.
- C, C++, Rust and Swift do not migrate data at all.
- Ginseng and today's HR-12 pay on every object.
- Erlang and Smalltalk have no ownership, so they never face hand-over or exact rollback of resources.
design.cost:
**While the program runs, in a reload build.**
- **Bytes per value:** zero. A header that gains a weak count keeps those 4 bytes until the process restarts ([HR-52]). That is OBJ-1's own weak count, not a reload header.
- **Entering Ember code:** one compare more, on the generation the entry already loads, plus a branch that is not taken. There is no fence on entry; the reload side pays a process-wide barrier ([HR-42a]). Today's text has a relaxed increment and an acquire fence, and it races. The gate costs the same and is correct.
- **An object's end,** only for a class the program may hand to C: one test of the kept-by-C mark ([HR-20]).
- **Nothing else:** no count, no list insert or unlink at any make or end, and no container registration. Today's HR-12 costs 16 bytes on every class object plus an insert and an unlink; option B costs 16 to 48 bytes on every block.
- **Release builds:** bit-identical (HR-27).

**Against C.** C has no migration. What a C program pays to carry a struct field, a memcpy, is what `owns old` pays: a bit copy per carried part. A carried owner is not counted.

**At a reload.**
- **The walk:**
  - one visit per value whose type may hold a changed type, or an owner, link, view or raw pointer into one or into what the reload ends;
  - one set entry per block reached;
  - a removed `String` field makes it visit every holder of a `StrView`.
- **Prepare:**
  - one test per store in prepare's code, and one log entry per store into memory from before the reload;
  - one `rebuild` per container whose values change, which means one re-insert per element, as Java's `HashMap` does when it reads an object back;
  - a walk of what prepare made and stored into.
- **Commit:** the same rewrites as HR-15's today.
- **A failed reload:**
  - the ends of made values whose end runs code;
  - one put-back per log entry;
  - one free per block prepare made.
- **Threads:** a thread entering Ember code during plan to reclaim waits that long. Compiling and loading are outside the gate.

**Against today's list.** When the changed type's instances make up most of what the walk visits, the cost is about the same. When a few instances sit in a large graph behind a `dyn` place, the walk visits much more: a million visits for ten values in BEN-8's new fourth edit. HR-1's one-second budget must be re-measured on that edit and on bench/bigpkg.

**Code size, in debug and development reload builds only:**
- descriptions, emitted like drop glue;
- the prepare-form twins of the code prepare reaches;
- `std.hot.Holds` in std's containers.

readability.note:
The ordinary program does not change by one character. The game loop, the shared `Stats`, field-wise migration, and a `migrate_from` whose parts are copied with `=` all read the same.

Only a `migrate_from` that hands on a part that cannot be copied writes more: one word, `owns`, on the parameter, where today no line compiles at all. The constructor takes no word (verdict 159), and `target=old.target` is shorter than today's `shares old.target`. `LOG.push(...)` and a default such as `uid: int = next_uid()` work as written.

The gate, the walk, the recorded stores, the rollback and std's `Holds` are the compiler's, the runtime's and std's work, unseen. A program's own unsafe container writes `Holds` in unsafe code only if it holds a type a reload changes.

The member examples now say `threads=main` with their `# SAFETY:` note. That is what FFI-33 already asks of an export that changes a module variable.

design.compiler_does:
**Descriptions.**
- For every type, in reload builds only, the compiler emits where its owners, links, views and raw pointers sit, per enum variant, the same way it emits drop glue.
- A `dyn` value is described through its method table or type index. A function value's state is described through its code word, which in a reloadable image is a fixed thunk with a manifest entry.
- std's raw-memory containers implement `std.hot.Holds` (`each` and `rebuild`). The compiler checks from the body that `each` only reads.
- Per-call records list each frame's owner, link and view slots, with their drop flags, at every call that may reach `std.hot.checkpoint()` (A1's stack maps).

**Facts.**
- A reload build is compiled against the running image's manifest.
- It works out which types changed, including header shapes ([HR-11]).
- It works out the visit set (types that may hold a changed type, or an owner, link, view or raw pointer that may point at or into one, or into what the reload ends), using the union over every image of the kinds that may reach each `dyn` and function place ([HR-52]).
- It records all of this in the new image's manifest, so the walk skips everything else.

**Lambdas.** The compiler matches each old lambda to a new one: same function, same capture names and words, in statement order through the edit. It records the matches and refuses ambiguous ones that have live values.

**Prepare form.** `migrate_from`, defaults, re-run initialisers and `rebuild`, and every new-image function they may reach, are compiled as twins, the way verdict 88's copies are made. In the twins:
- A call on, or through, a value from before the reload goes to the running image's code. Old-schema reads use the old manifest's offsets.
- A value prepare makes carries the prepare form's type and code words, so a `dyn` or function call on it reaches a twin. Commit rewrites those words to the image's own.
- A store first tests whether its target is memory from before the reload. If it is, the replaced bytes are logged.
- An end of a value from before the reload is moved to the reclaim list.
- A failed run-time check, and an explicit `panic` in a default, an initialiser or a `rebuild`, returns `ReloadError`.
- The compiler tracks, for every place, whether it holds a value prepare made or one from before the reload, the way it tracks hand-overs (hidden flags where it depends on the path). From this it emits each result's rollback glue: end the made parts, leave the parts from before.

**Checks.**
- No change to a value from before the reload whose type changes, except `owns old`'s own.
- Running-image code reached must change nothing, judged by the running image's recorded facts. A C call whose kept callbacks change something is refused unless `@ffi(no_callbacks)`.
- No hand-over to C keeping.
- No code-running made value stored beside or into values from before the reload.
- No result view of `old` (`E3063`).
- A view or link into a part of `old` is rewritten to the place where the result holds that part (recorded); refused where the paths differ.
- At checkpoints, `E9030` for prepare's changes and reclaim's ends, judged by each image's facts.

**The runtime.**
- **The gate.** The generation is made odd, a process-wide barrier is issued, the depth counters are scanned, and everything is backed off if any counter is not zero.
- **Plan** walks from the initialised statics, the frame records and the runtime's roots, in a fixed order, with a set of the blocks reached. It calls `each` for `Holds` types and makes every refusal.
- **Prepare** builds the new values. A moved block comes from its old manager's `allocate`, in its maker's chunk for the built-in manager, and every block prepare makes is recorded. Prepare runs prepare's code with the log, migrates `owns old`'s parts after their `migrate_from` and the leftovers of changed types, calls `rebuild`, and then walks what prepare made and stored into to finish the rewrite list.
- **A failed reload** runs the rollback glue, replays the log backwards, cancels the deferred ends, and gives back the recorded blocks.
- **Commit** applies the stores.
- **Reclaim** ends the leftovers and the deferred ends with the new code, queues thread-bound ends to their threads, frees the old blocks, then makes the generation even and wakes the waiting threads.
- **C-kept records** are added at each hand-over to C and removed by the object's end through its mark.

**What the programmer writes.** Only `owns` on `migrate_from`'s parameter, where a part must be handed on, and `Holds` for a program's own unsafe container of a type a reload changes.
design.misuse:
**Refused when compiling.**
- `sock=old.sock` with a read-only `old`: `E3013`, "`old` only reads the old session, so `old.sock` cannot be handed over; take the session over: `static fn migrate_from(owns old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:`".
- Changing a value from before the reload whose type this reload changes, other than through `owns old`'s own parts: "`players[0]` is a `Player` from before the reload, and this reload rebuilds `Player`, so it does not change while the reload is prepared; change it in `Player.migrate_from`, or after the reload".
- A call that runs running-image code which changes something (`old.counter.bump()`): "`bump` is the running program's code, and what it changes could not be undone if the reload failed; change the new value instead". A C call whose kept callbacks change something: the help gives `@ffi(no_callbacks)` on the declaration, if the function never calls back.
- Handing C anything it keeps in prepare's code (`callback(retained)`, `callback(once)`, a keeping contract, `into_raw()`).
- Storing a value made in prepare whose end runs code into memory from before the reload, or beside such values in one container: "`conns` holds sockets taken from `old` (line 9), and line 11 adds one opened here; if the reload failed, that one would have to be closed and the others kept, which one list cannot tell apart; keep the new ones in a list of their own: write `opened.push(owns s)` in place of line 11".
- A `migrate_from` result viewing `old` or what it owns (`captain=ref old.players[0]`): `E3063`.
- A `migrate_from` that panics: `E2225`, as today.

**Refused in plan.** The old image keeps running, and the report names the holder and the part.
- A kept view, a `sharedref mut` link, a raw pointer, or a frame's view below a checkpoint, pointing into what reclaim would end.
- A view into a part of `old` whose place differs between `Ok` paths, or that is rebuilt rather than carried.
- A changed type in a `MaybeUninit`, a union payload, or a raw-memory type without `Holds`; a raw pointer to a changed value the walk did not reach through an owner.
- A default or re-run initialiser that changes a value of a changed type, or that reaches running-image code which changes anything.
- Prepare's code, or a reclaim end, that may change what a frame below a checkpoint walks, views or locks (`E9030`).
- An object C keeps that must grow or move (HR-20); a header that gains a weak count on such an object.
- A lambda with live values that gained a capture or matches no new lambda one to one; a type removed while a value of it lives; an implementation removed while values sit behind its `dyn`.
- Code the reload would run on a value bound to another thread.

**At the poll.** A reload that runs code of the program, polled on a thread other than the main thread, gets `EMBER_RELOAD_UNSAFE_POINT`, and `ember_reload_stats()` gives the reason.

**Discarded in prepare.** Ember memory is put back as it was, and the old image keeps running. This happens when:
- `migrate_from` returns `Err`;
- a run-time check fails;
- a count reaches its limit;
- a `rebuild` fails (two keys made equal);
- a view prepare made points into what reclaim ends;
- memory runs out.

**After success.** A panic in a leftover's `drop` during reclaim aborts, as any panic in a `drop` does. So does one in a `drop` that a failed reload runs.

**No outcome:**
- leaves an old layout under new code;
- ends a value twice;
- leaks a count or a resource;
- closes a socket the running program still uses;
- lets a thread run beside the reload.
design.verdicts:
All verdicts are kept; none is revisited.

**Owner verdicts.**
- **32** (the parameter's word sets the rights): `old` reads, and `owns old` takes over and may change what it owns, as on every parameter.
- **147** (`owns` on a parameter that takes a value over): kept. The runtime calls `migrate_from`, so there is no call site in the program to write the word at.
- **159** (a constructor's argument takes no word): `Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp))`. This applies phase 3's correction to J7-15.
- **78 and 84** (a part is handed over on its own): `Old<Name>` has no `drop`, so its parts are handed out one by one ([OWN-11]).
- **57** (destroying an object counts as calling its `drop`): reclaim's ends, and prepare's changes too, are checked at a checkpoint against the frames below (`E9030`).
- **58** (`mem.forget` removed; no leaks): a failed reload ends, by its `drop`, each value prepare made whose end runs code. A made value that holds parts from before the reload is ended field by field, as ODR-120 ends an old form, so nothing it does not own is ended and nothing it owns leaks.
- **99** (a loop of owners must be proven freed): relied on. Every live safe value has an owner path to a root.
- **101** (the 32-byte `thread_shared` header): kept in every build. Owners made in prepare are counted per [RC-4], and ends on the wrong thread go through RC-4's queue.
- **114** (a hand-over may move an object): consistent. A reload's move keeps the maker and the counts.
- **122, 128, 151** (pruning by the kinds that reach a place): used by the walk. [HR-52]'s union keeps them true across reloads.
- **137** (what a result views is read from the code): `old` ends at the reload, so a result view of `old` is `E3063`.
- **164 to 166** (one-thread state never reached from another thread): the reload is not a route between threads. The gate holds every other thread out, the reload's code runs on the main thread, and an end bound to another thread runs on that thread. P01 should list the reload as a section that holds every other thread out.

**Owner rulings of 2026-10-19 (tasks/85/owner-answers.md).**
- **ODR-120**, A4 (no user `drop` for an upgraded object): kept, and its reasoning is reused for the rollback.
- **ODR-126**, A6 (search tuples, `Box` contents and closure captures so that reloads succeed instead of being refused): carried to every kind of value, std's containers included.
- **A1** (stack maps at the checkpoint): the per-call records of [HR-3b], read as roots.

**Principles applied.**
- **Principle 7 (correct programs work).** The recorded-store rollback replaces round 0's refusal of any change in prepare. `items.push`, `old.socks.pop()`, `LOG.push` and `uid: int = next_uid()` (which today's HR-14 runs) now work. Refusals remain only where an exact rollback is impossible: running-image code that does not record its stores, C keeping something, and made resources mixed with old ones in one list.
- **Principle 8 (compile time first, then the cheapest run-time check).** Only the gate runs while the program runs: one compare on entry, because compile time cannot know when C threads enter.

**Not a verdict.** HR-12's live-instance list and HR-13's self-registering containers are spec text from the original design, implemented in 0.9.10, never an owner verdict. The rule replaces them. Put it to the owner plainly as option A against option B.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. The reload finds every live value by following owners from the statics, the checkpoint frames and what the runtime holds, with no registration and no header bytes. std's containers say where their values are. While a reload is applied, other threads wait at Ember's door. `migrate_from(owns old)` hands parts on. Prepare may change things, and a failure puts every change back, ends what prepare made and ends nothing that already existed. Reclaim ends the leftovers with the new code.
options_for_owner.code:
class Session:                                  # the edit: `hp: int` became `hp: Health`
    sock: Socket
    target: shares Player
    hp: Health

    static fn migrate_from(owns old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        return Ok(Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp)))

class Hud:
    stats: shares mut Stats                     # Stats gains `misses: int = 0`: nothing to write

class Enemy:                                    # another edit adds `uid: int = next_uid()`: runs per enemy
    hp: int
options_for_owner.outcome: All three reloads apply. Socket 7 stays open, the player keeps one owner, nothing is printed, `hits` is carried, `misses` starts at 0, and each enemy gets a uid in a fixed order. No header grows in any build. If another session's `migrate_from` fails, every session, count and uid is as it was. A C thread that enters Ember code during the reload waits until it ends.

options_for_owner.summary: Phase 2's way of finding values. Every block that lives on its own is registered in the live-instance list, like a class object: 16 bytes more per block in reload builds, 48 for `thread_shared`, and a header added to `owns` blocks and function states. Containers keep registering themselves. Everything else works as in A.
options_for_owner.code:
# the same program as A
# reload builds: every shares, shares mut, thread_shared and owns block carries the 16-byte list link,
# inserted when the block is made and unlinked when it ends; every Array of a reloadable type registers
options_for_owner.outcome: The reloads apply, as in A. Every object and shared block in a reload build is 16 bytes bigger. Every make and end pays the list insert and unlink, and every container pays its registration. Values inline in containers, function states and statics are still found by a walk, so this is two mechanisms.

options_for_owner.summary: Keep today's finding and today's read-only `old`. A reload that changes a type that may sit in a shared block is refused. So is a `migrate_from` that must hand on a part that cannot be copied.

static fn migrate_from(old: OldSession) -> Result[Session, ReloadError]:
        ...
# refused when compiling: "`Session` owns `sock`, a `Socket` that is not `Clone`, which a read-only
#  `old` cannot hand on; restart to change `hp`"
# plan refuses the Stats edit: "`Stats` may live in a shared block (`shares mut Stats()`, line 14),
#  which a reload cannot find; restart to change it"

recommendation.reason: It is one rule for every place a value can live, with no exception by kind: a class, a struct in a shared block, a closure's state, an `AnyError`, an arena value, a queued `thread_shared` value, or an element of std's `Map` or the ECS. It costs nothing per object and one compare on entry, where B costs 16 to 48 bytes and two list operations on every block. It keeps HR-1's promise of preserving all live state, which C breaks with a restart. It reuses `owns` exactly as every parameter does, and the natural migrations compile. Whether the reload applies or fails, no value is left in an old layout, ended twice or leaked, no socket is closed while still in use, and no thread runs beside the reload. It follows the owner's own choice in ODR-126 ('search ... so those reloads succeed instead of being refused'), made general.

owner_short.one_line: Hot reload, in C++ terms. After an edit changes a struct's layout, every live instance must be found and move-constructed into the new layout, all or nothing, while other threads are paused. Today only class objects are found, through a 16-byte intrusive list, so a struct behind a shared_ptr-like `shares` block is missed. And the 'move constructor' `migrate_from` gets only a `const&` of the old object, so a unique_ptr-like socket cannot be moved.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `HUD = Some(Hud(stats=shares mut Stats()))` | a `Stats` in a counted block of its own (8-byte header, then `hits`), owned by the `Hud` |
| 2 | main | each frame, `game_tick` runs `h.stats.hits += 1` | `hits` = 120 |
| 3 | main | the edit adds `misses: int = 0` to `Stats`; the host calls `ember_reload_poll()` | today's reload migrates class objects and registered lists; the `Stats` block is neither, so it keeps its 8-byte layout |
| 4 | main | the new code runs `h.stats.misses += 1` | it reads and writes 8 bytes past the old value, memory the block does not have |
| 5 | main | a `Session` holding socket 7 and one owner of a player changes `hp: int` to `hp: Health`, with `migrate_from` | `old` is read-only: `sock=old.sock` is refused and a `Socket` cannot be copied, so no `migrate_from` compiles |
| 6 | main | reclaim frees the old session | the spec does not say whether old `target` loses its owner (if not, the player never ends) or old `sock` is closed |
owner_short.today: A reload finds only class objects (each with 16 extra header bytes) and registered lists, and it gives `migrate_from` the old value read-only. So a struct in a `shares` block keeps its old layout under new code, and an open socket cannot be carried over.
owner_short.options:
A: find every live value by following owners from the statics, with no extra bytes. Other threads wait at Ember's door during the reload. `migrate_from(owns old)` hands the socket on. A failed reload puts everything back, and the leftovers are ended once the reload is applied.
B: as A, but every shared block is registered like a class object: 16 bytes more per block in reload builds, 48 for `thread_shared`.
C: refuse both. An edit to a type that may sit in a shared block, or one whose `migrate_from` must hand on a part that cannot be copied, needs a restart.
owner_short.recommendation: A: every value is found the same way, at no cost per object. The natural migration compiles. Nothing is lost, leaked or closed twice, whether the reload applies or fails.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. A leftover of a changed type (`old.hp` with `max` added above `value`) is ended by the new `drop` on the old layout, reading `this.note` at the wrong offset.
repairs.answer: [HR-2a]: prepare migrates every value of a changed type the walk finds, leftovers included, so reclaim only ever ends values in the new layout, with the new code. A leftover whose migration is refused fails the reload in plan; one whose migration fails discards it in prepare. A removed field whose type changes in the same edit (`Level.boss: Enemy`), and a taken part let go, are leftovers too. A removed type with a live value, including one the reload would end, is refused: [HR-14]'s class row, made general.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. Pruning skips holders of links into what reclaim ends (`WATCH.target` into a removed `boss`), so [HR-51] cannot refuse it, and neither can [HR-47].
repairs.answer: [HR-48]'s visit set includes every type that may hold an owner, link, view or raw pointer whose target may be, or lie inside, a value the reload ends: a removed field's value, a part `migrate_from` may leave, a `@reinit_on_reload` static's old value, and all they own. `WATCH` is visited and [HR-51] refuses it. [HR-47] now uses the walk. The larger walk is stated in the cost, and [BEN-8] measures it.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. Threads enter Ember code during plan, prepare and reclaim (`mix_audio` pushing to `VOICES`), so they race with the walk, prepare's writes, rollback, reclaim and the allocation in another thread's chunk.
repairs.answer: [HR-3], [HR-42] and [HR-42a] add the entry gate. From plan to the end of reclaim the generation is odd, and every way in waits: an export, a trampoline, a worker taking a job, a thread starting, a join taking its result, and an `ember_rt` call into Ember memory. HR-3's check of the depth counters is the gate's closing step, with a process-wide barrier on the reload side. Entry costs one compare on the word it already loads. The cost is stated: a thread that enters during a reload waits up to the reload's applied time.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. `t = shares old.target`, made and ended in prepare and logged, is subtracted twice when the reload fails, so the player ends under its owner.
repairs.answer: The owner log is gone. [HR-50] records every store prepare's code makes into memory from before the reload, counts included, with the bytes it replaced, and a failure puts them back last first. Ending a prepare-made owner subtracts as anywhere and never reaches zero. The count goes 2, 3, 2, and a failure restores 2. The same holds for a `weakref` and for an owner made for an `owns p: shares Player` parameter.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. A failed reload releases the arena without ending what prepare made: 9,999 dup'd sockets leak, and C's kept callback can point at freed memory. That contradicts verdict 58 and OWN-2, and adopted C objects get a special path.
repairs.answer: [HR-50], step 1: each value prepare made whose end runs code is ended. If it holds nothing from before the reload, its own `drop` ends it. If it does, it is ended field by field without its own `drop`, with the parts from before left as they are (ODR-120's reasoning); a `migrate_from` result is ended this way. Nothing from before the reload is ended. Adopted C objects are ordinary values whose end runs code, so they need no special path. The compiler tracks which places hold which kind and refuses mixing the two kinds in one container. Handing C anything it keeps (a retained or once callback, a keeping contract, `into_raw()`) is refused when compiling in prepare's code.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. The first `weakref Enemy` changes OBJ-1's header (8 to 12 bytes), which the schema does not see, and HR-49 carries a weak count that has no value.
repairs.answer: [HR-11]: the header's shape is part of the schema. A new [HR-14] row: each value is rebuilt with its weak count at 1 for all owners, moved where it no longer fits, and refused where it cannot move. Under [HR-52], 'the program' of OBJ-1's rule is every image loaded, so removing the last `weakref` never shrinks a header in a running process. OBJ-1 and COST-3 stand.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. A `dyn` call in prepare on a value from before the reload (`old.shape.area()` with a changed `Circle`) runs either a new twin on the old layout, or old code checked against new facts, and old kept-callback code can change statics.
repairs.answer: [HR-50], 'What it sees': a call on, or through, a value from before the reload (a `dyn` method, a function value, a callback C runs) runs the running image's code on that value's layout. The thunks are not repointed until commit, so that code is consistent. A call on values prepare made runs the new image's code. Each call is checked by the facts of the image whose code runs. Running-image code does not record its stores, so where it is reached it may change nothing, which is refused when compiling. A C call whose kept callbacks change something is refused unless `@ffi(no_callbacks)`.

- Both members' exports now say `threads=main`, with a `# SAFETY:` note.
