holes.program:
@derive(Copy)
struct Vec2:
    x: float
    y: float

struct Bullet:
    pos: Vec2
    vel: Vec2

struct Gun:
    muzzle: Vec2
    aim: Vec2

    fn fire() -> Bullet:
        return Bullet(pos=this.muzzle, vel=this.aim)   # two Copy parts given to a constructor

    fn muzzle_pos() -> Vec2:
        return this.muzzle                             # a Copy part returned out of `this`, which only reads

fn main():
    g = Gun(muzzle=Vec2(x=0.0, y=1.0), aim=Vec2(x=1.0, y=0.0))
    b = g.fire()
    b.pos = g.muzzle                                   # a field store of a Copy part
    println(b.pos.y, g.muzzle_pos().x)
holes.what_goes_wrong:
Rule 3(a) copies only a Copy value with no parts. Rule 2(b) copies only a whole Copy name. So a part of a Copy struct falls under 'a part goes into a place that owns it only with `owns` or `copy of`, or by `return`. Otherwise the line is refused'.

- `Bullet(pos=this.muzzle, ...)` and `b.pos = g.muzzle` are refused.
- `return this.muzzle` is, by the letter, a hand-over of a part out of a name that only reads (OWN-11's E3013), since the return bullet says nothing about Copy values.
- `owns this.muzzle` is E3013, so every such line needs `copy of`.

This contradicts OWN-7's unchanged first sentence ('duplicated bit for bit by `=` and on use'). C and Rust copy 16 bytes here. It hits every game or math program with Copy vectors (positions, colours, transforms) on its most ordinary lines. The design's claim that nothing ordinary got longer is false.
holes.fix_hint: Add to [OWN-14] 3: a part of a `Copy` type goes into a place that owns it, or out by `return`, as a copy (OWN-7's 'on use'). The `owns`/`copy of` rule for parts covers only parts that are not `Copy`. Rule 5's guard already covers a copy changed by mistake through a name.

    for v in xs.iter_mut():               # iter_mut() is a value: OWN-14 2 makes `v` own its `ref mut int`
        v += 1                            # CTL-1 (sentence kept): E3023, help `for ref mut v in xs:`
    if counts.get_mut("ann") exists as n:
        n += 1                            # GRM-44 today: plain `n` never changes

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Rule 6 and the BRW-14/15 rewrite make 'a name over a value its form took over' an owner that 'may be changed', exempt from BRW-15. A name that owns a `ref mut T` or a `MutSpan` value then writes through it with no `ref mut`.

- `v += 1` changes `xs` with no word, while CTL-1's own example says E3023.
- The design's J4-09 answer says plain `left, right` with `right[i] = ...` is E3023, and its bullet 4 says `ref mut` names a MutSpan's elements. Rule 6 says the opposite.
- Verdict 34: a name that may change something it does not own says `ref mut`.

The same call result also gets two defaults. `r = first_even(ref mut xs)` is a place (VI.2), so `r` only reads. `counts.get_mut(k)` is a value, so `n` would write. This decides common loops over `iter_mut`, `values_mut`, `chunks_mut`, `get_mut` and `split_at`.
holes.fix_hint: Rule 6: owning a view is owning the pointer, not the place. What an owned `ref mut T` names, or an owned MutSpan's elements, is changed only through a name written `ref mut` (verdict 34): `for ref mut v in xs.iter_mut():`, `exists as ref mut n`. Say that `ref mut` before such a name names the view's target, as it names a MutSpan's elements.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Rule 3 requires `name=owns req.name, email=owns req.email`. Verdict 159's own words are 'A constructor's argument takes no word: it works as `=` does'. The owner was shown `Words(names=owns xs)` beside `Words(names=xs)` and refused the word.

The design reads 'as `=` does' through its own `=` rule for parts (a view), and so makes the constructor need the word the verdict removed. Phase 3's verdict-clash resolution for J7-15, now in P09's notes, writes `Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp))`, relying on OWN-11's hand-over of a part into a field. That line is refused under P11.

The design's 'Three rules that are not owner verdicts' list does not name this verdict clash.
holes.fix_hint: Either hand a part over with no word wherever it goes into a place that owns it whole: a constructor's argument, a field store, a literal's element and `return`, Rust's rule, keeping `x = p.name` a view. Or put the literal-reading change of verdict 159 to the owner, quoting it, together with P09's J7-15 line.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
`return req.body` takes no word, but `return Ok(req.body)`, `return Some(u.name)`, `return (p.a, p.b)` and `e.name = p.name` each need `owns`, inside a `return` whose E0109 message says 'return always hands the value over; remove owns'.

`return` takes no word because a part going into a place that owns it can only be moved: a view cannot be stored there, and a silent copy is not allowed (verdict 5). The same reason holds for `Ok(...)`, a field store and a literal's element, so the compiler can infer the move there too.

The design's reason against option E, that `x = p.name` and `e.name = p.name` read alike and do opposite things, already holds for `x = req.body` beside `return req.body`, which it keeps. Error-handling returns and DTO building get longer in ordinary server code.
holes.fix_hint: One rule by the receiving place: a part going into a place that owns it (a field, a constructor's argument, a literal's element, `return`) is handed over with no word. A new name (`=`, headers) views it, and `owns` before a part is written only where the default views (`body = owns req.body`).

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Rule 8 gives only the bare `for` statement the in-place reading. Every adapter and consumer called on the same place takes it over with no word (STD-19: 'An adapter takes the iterator it wraps over (owns this), and so does a consumer', and the object a method is called on is not marked): `take`, `skip_while`, `find`, `any`, `count`.

A comprehension's `for` clause over `toks` desugars to `toks.map(...)` (GRM-27), so it consumes too.

- 'One rule for every loop' (verdict 16) holds for one spelling only.
- The Python reading the design cites (`itertools.islice(it, 1)` leaves `it` usable) breaks on the first adapter.
- No `by_ref` exists, so `for t in toks.take(1):` followed by `for t in toks:` has no spelling.

The `owns this` receiver is also a form that hands a place over with no word, missing from [OWN-14]'s list and against its rule 2. It clashes with P06's 'no word lends it for the call; a callee keeps only what was handed over'.
holes.fix_hint: State rule 8 for every driver of an iterator. A place holding an iterator, given to `for`, a comprehension clause, an adapter or a consumer, is lent and advanced in place (std gives `Iterator` for a `ref mut` iterator, as Rust's `&mut I`). `owns toks` (or `for t in owns toks:`) hands it over. A temporary is taken over as today. Coordinate with P06.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Before a bare view, `copy of` now gives a different type: a String from a StrView, an Array[T] from a Span[T], a T from a `ref T`. TYP-36 still gives StrView a Clone (✓), which the design uses for view fields inside a struct.

In generic code over `T: needs Clone` with T a view, `copy of x` is either T's Clone (another view, no allocation) or the owned type (a type error inside the instance). Either way the same expression means two things for one type, against principle 4 (one word, one meaning, for every type).

The rule also does not say how deep it goes. `copy of` before a `ref StrView`, which is what `keys()` and `iter()` over views yield, gives either the StrView it views or that view's text. So `copy_each()` ('what `copy of` the item would make') over the commonest element types (text views, spans) is undefined, and the library functions written on `Clone` (`to_array`, `fill`, `repeat`) cannot be typed.
holes.fix_hint: Give `copy of` an owned-type function stated once: `copy of x` has type `Owned(T)`, which is T for every non-view, String for StrView, Array[U] for Span[U] and U for `ref U`, one level only. Generic code over `T: needs Clone` gets `Owned(T)` (Rust's ToOwned), and code that must return T reads `x` (T: needs Copy). Write `copy_each`'s item type by it.

I only read files, as the task required. I read:
- owner-bar.md, brief.md and OWNER-DIRECTION.md.
- Every group's principle in phase1-groups.json.
- The 12 member drafts in phase2.json, plus J4-02.
- From phase3.json: clusters K22-K27, K42, K62 and K63; the conflicts J1-09/J3-07, J2-01/J4-02 and J4-09; the J4-09 recommendation change; the J7-15 verdict clash; and the drafts-to-correct list.
- JOB.md, verdicts 1 to 166.
- Spec parts: p03 (GRM-4/5/13/15/27/29/36/41-45 and the grammar), p04 (the Copy marker table, the interfaces, TYP-36, TYP-44), p05 (FN-1/1a/2/2a), p06 (EXP-2/4/5/6/9/10, VI.2, CTL-0..11, CLO-2, CORO-1..14), p07 (VII.1-VII.5, OWN-1..13, BRW-1..22, LT-1/5, SPN-1..5, DRP-1..3), p08 (DSP-4/6), p15 (STD-19), and p16 for CStrView and ObjectPtr.

**Strongest finding (high).** Rule 3's part clause refuses a Copy struct's part going into a field, a constructor or a literal, and by the letter a return out of a read-only `this`. Examples: `Bullet(pos=this.muzzle)`, `b.pos = g.muzzle`, `return this.muzzle`. This contradicts OWN-7's 'on use' and lengthens ordinary game code.

**The medium holes come in three clusters:**
1. Rights. Owned `ref mut` and MutSpan values write with no `ref mut` (CTL-1's `iter_mut` example, the design's own J4-09 answer, verdict 34). Rule 6's 'keeps what it was given' refuses `t = this.base; t += bonus` and verdict 28's `cur = p` walk.
2. The part rule against verdicts. Verdict 159's 'takes no word' at a constructor; P09's J7-15 line; `return Ok(req.body)` needing `owns` while `return req.body` does not. The compiler could infer the move in every one of these. Separately, the general E0109 bullet refuses verdicts 74, 85 and 97's making lines.
3. Generality.
   - Rule 8 reaches only the bare `for`. STD-19's `owns this` adapters, consumers and comprehensions still consume a named iterator, which also clashes with P06.
   - `copy of` before a view changes type, which leaves generic `[T: needs Clone]` code and `copy_each` undefined.
   - Names over temporaries now drop changes silently (verdict 13).

**Cost.** I found no operation costing more than C. The cost table holds, and the only allocation, `copy of` a view, is written on the line.

**What holds.** J1-09, J3-07, J3-09's core, J4-04, J2-10, J5-12, J4-08, J1-10 and J4-09's spelling work as the design says, as does rule 7's life rule, which is better than Rust's scrutinee rule. P05, P10, P12 and P22 fit.

**Fix direction.** Most fixes are one sentence each:
- Copy parts copy on use.
- Owning a view is owning the pointer.
- Rights go by form.
- A part going into an owning place moves with no word.
- `owns` before a new value goes by the place's type.
- Every driver of a named iterator lends it.
- `copy of` gets one stated owned type.

The one owner question to raise plainly is verdict 159 against the part rule.

design.rule:
One rule decides what every name, store and hand-over gets from its source. It covers every form that gives a value a name or a place: `=` with one target or several, `return`, `yield`, a field or element store, a constructor's argument, a literal's element, an argument, `for`, a `match` arm, `exists as`, `is T as`, `with`, `?` and a capture. It covers every kind of source.

(1) **Place or value**, as VI.2 splits them. A place is memory something owns: a local, a part of a place, what a view reaches, a field of a class object, a cast of a place. A value is everything else: a new value, a temporary, a part of a value, a cast of a value.

(2) **A value is taken over** by the form that receives it, with no word, and each name the form binds inside it owns its part. What a link reaches is not a part. So opening a link, from a place or a value alike, names a view of its target. A `shares` part is owned as one more owner, never as the target's only owner.

(3) **For a place, the receiver decides.**
- A name reads the place where it lives. A name given a part of a place is a read-only view, and a header reads a whole place. `=` hands a whole owning name over, as today.
- A place that owns its value and is not a name takes its source over with no word, a part included. These are a field or element store, a constructor's argument, a literal's element, `return` and `yield`.
- A `Copy` value is copied wherever it goes. A name given a `Copy` part that has no parts of its own a name could change holds a copy.
- An argument takes its parameter's word.

(4) **A word before the source means one thing everywhere.**
- `owns` hands a place over where the form would only read it. Before a new value it is written only for a place that owns the value alone, or for an `owns` parameter. Anywhere else it is `E0109`.
- `copy of` copies one level. When the type written for the source is a view or a holder, it copies what that reaches (a `String` from a `StrView`, a `T` from a `ref T`). Otherwise it copies the value itself, a type parameter included. Views and links inside the copy are copied as themselves.
- `ref` views. `ref mut` lets the name change the place; before a changeable view, it lets the name change what that view names.
- A cast keeps its holder word and its memory manager.

(5) **Words before names.** When one line declares several names, each name carries its own word. In `x @ p`, the names in `p` are names for parts of `x`. In a `match` guard, every bound name is a read-only view until the guard holds.

(6) **Rights.**
- A local declared by `=` may always be given another value, and may change what it owns.
- A parameter, a header's name or a pattern's name keeps what it was given, unless it owns it. An owning name may change its value, replace it and hand it on.
- A name holding a changeable view writes through it only when written `ref mut`.
- A change made through an owning header or pattern name, and read by nothing before the name ends, is `E2140`.

(7) **Life.**
- A value a name owns ends with that name's block.
- A value no name owns ends at the end of its statement or header. If something made from it is still used, it ends after the last such use instead.
- It never lives past the end of the block that holds that line. In a loop's body, and for a `while` header, that block is the round.
- A lock is held while any guard of it lives, in a `with` block, a name or a temporary. Taking the lock again while it is held is `E7018`.

(8) **An iterator held in a place is driven where it lives**, by whatever drives it: `for`, a comprehension's clause, an adapter or a consumer. `owns` hands it over.
design.spec_text:
This adds `[OWN-14]` (VII.2) and changes the following, and nothing else (`[BRW-13]` is used as written):
- the rules `[BRW-12]`, `[BRW-14]`, `[BRW-15]`, `[BRW-19]`, `[OWN-3]`, `[OWN-7]`, `[OWN-8]`, `[OWN-9]`, `[OWN-10]`, `[OWN-11]`, `[OWN-13]`, `[GRM-5]`, `[GRM-13]`, `[GRM-15]`, `[GRM-27]`, `[GRM-36]`, `[GRM-38]`, `[GRM-42]`, `[GRM-44]`, `[CTL-1]`, `[CTL-5]`, `[CTL-11]`, `[EXP-4]`, `[DRP-3]`, `[STD-19]`, `[THR-19]`, `[TYP-36]` and `[TYP-44]` (with `[DSP-6]`, which repeats it);
- the VII.1 term "view";
- the grammar's `target` and `primary_pattern`;
- the E0109, E0111, E2116, E2140, E3010, E3023, E3063 and E7018 rows.

* `[OWN-14]` *(new)* **What a name or a place gets from its source.** Every form that gives a value to a name or a place gets it by this one rule. The forms are: `=` with one target or several, `return`, `yield`, a field or element store, a constructor's argument, an element of a tuple or collection literal, an argument (its word is the parameter's, `[FN-1]`, `[FN-2a]`), `for`, a `match` arm's pattern, `exists as`, `is T as`, `with`, `?` and a capture (`[CLO-2]`). No form gives a word a meaning of its own.
  1. **Place or value.** The source is a place or a value (VI.2).
     - A field of a class object is a place, a temporary's included.
     - A cast of a place is that place, typed as its kind.
     - A cast of a value is a value, and so is a part of a struct, tuple or enum value (`f()?.name` is handed over, `[EXP-10]`).
  2. **A value is taken over.** The form that receives a value takes it over, with no word, and every name the form binds inside it owns its part. This covers a loop's item, a pattern's or a destructuring's parts, what `exists as` or `is T as` names, `?`'s payload, and a name given a part of a value (`n = f().name`, where the rest of the value ends with the statement).
     - `while jobs.pop() exists as job:` gives `job` the popped `Job`, and so does `match jobs.pop():` with `Some(job):`, as `j = jobs.pop()` gives `j` the `Option`.
     - What a link reaches is not a part of the value that holds the link (VII.1).
       - Opening a link, from a place or a value alike, names a view of its target, never its owner (`if pick(units) exists as u:`).
       - The form keeps the link value until that view's last use (7), and the view is not used across a call that may end its target (verdict 82).
       - A part that is a `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` owner is owned as that owner: the name is one of the target's owners.
     - A part cannot leave a value whose type has a `drop`, since the `drop` still runs (`E3010`).
       - In a pattern, the name is written `ref`: with `match open_conn():` and `Conn(sock=ref s):`, `s` views the field, and the `Conn` ends after `s`'s last use.
       - Elsewhere, the help names the value first: `c = open_conn()`, then `n = c.name`.
     - `owns` before a value the form already takes over is `E0109`: "`jobs.pop()` makes a new value, which this line already takes over; remove `owns`".
  3. **A place: the receiver decides.**
     - (a) **A name reads its source where it lives.**
       - A name given a part of a place is a read-only view of that part (`[BRW-12]`). This holds for a name given the part by `=` (a new name, or one that already has a value, `[BRW-13]`) and for a name a header or a pattern declares.
       - A header (`for`, `match`, `exists as`, `is T as`, `with`, `?`) reads a whole place where it lives.
       - `=` hands over a whole name that owns its value, as `[OWN-3]` says (`snapshot = items`). A destructuring hands it over part by part (`[GRM-5]`).
     - (b) **A place that owns its value and is not a name takes its source over, with no word.**
       - These places are a field or an element given a value with `=`, a constructor's argument, an element of a literal, and what `return` or `yield` gives.
       - A whole name is handed over (`[OWN-3]`, verdict 159), and so is a part (`[OWN-11]`, verdicts 78 and 148): `User(name=req.name, age=req.age)`, `return Ok(req.body)`, `e.name = p.name`, `pair = (p.name, p.hp)`.
       - A later use of the part is `E3040`: "`req.name` was handed over to the `User` on line 4 and is used on line 6; give it a new value first, or keep a copy: `name=copy of req.name`".
       - A part reached through a name that does not own it is `E3013`: "`p` only reads the caller's person, so `p.name` cannot be handed to the `User`; give it a copy: `name=copy of p.name`".
     - (c) **A `Copy` value is copied** wherever it goes, and its source stays (`[OWN-7]`).
       - So `Particle(pos=this.pos, vel=this.vel)` copies, and so do `b.pos = g.muzzle` and `return this.muzzle` through a `this` that only reads.
       - Some `Copy` types have no parts a name can change: a number, a `bool`, a `char`, a variant with no payload, a `StrView`, a `Span[T]`, a `ref T` and a raw pointer. A name given a part of one of these types holds a copy. The copy reads what a view would read, and leaves the place free to change: after `w = this.rest`, `this.rest = w[i + 1..]` may run while `w` is still used.
     - (d) **An argument takes its parameter's word.** No word lends it, `ref mut` lends it to be changed, and `owns` hands it over (`names.push(owns p.name)`, `[FN-2a]`).
  4. **Words before the source.** Each word means one thing before every source, in every form.
     - **`owns`** hands a place over: a whole name, a part, or a cast of either.
       - It is written where the form would only read the place (`body = owns req.body`, `for x in owns xs:`, `match owns e:`), or where a parameter takes the value over (`circles.push(owns cast s as Circle)`).
       - Where the form already hands the place over (`b = a`, `e.name = p.name`, a constructor's argument, `return`), it is `E0109`.
       - Before a new value, it is written only where the place the value fills owns it alone (`[OWN-10]`: `mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0])`, `left=Some(owns Tree(value=2))`, `e.mesh = owns Mesh(points=[1.0])`), or where an `owns` parameter takes it (`take(owns [1, 2])`, verdict 147).
       - Before any other new value (a header's, a local's `=`, `return`'s), it is `E0109`.
       - A place that may not be left empty is `E3010`, `E3011` or `E3013`, as `[EXP-6]` says. Each help names `mem.take` (`body = mem.take(ref mut req.body)`).
     - **`copy of e`** copies what `e` names, one level, by the type written for `e`.
       - Where that type is a view or a holder, it copies what the type reaches: a `T` from a `ref T` or a `ref mut T`, a `String` from a `StrView`, an `Array[T]` from a `Span[T]` or a `MutSpan[T]`, and what an `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` or `sharedref mut` value holds.
       - Otherwise it copies `e` itself.
       - The copy is made by the copied thing's `Clone` (`[OWN-8]`), which copies the views and links that thing holds as themselves (verdict 79). So `copy of names` of an `Array[StrView]` is an `Array[StrView]`, `copy of names[0]` is a `String`, and `copy of tok` of a `Token` holding a `StrView` views the same text.
       - A type parameter is not a view as written. So in a generic body, `copy of x` with `x: T` is a `T` copied as itself, as a field of type `T` is. The body is checked once with `T` standing for any type (`[TYP-17]`).
     - **`ref`** states the read-only view.
     - **`ref mut`** names the place, so that the name may change it.
       - Before a changeable view (a `ref mut T` or `MutSpan[T]` value, or a name holding one), it names what that view names.
       - Before a part of a value that is not itself a changeable view, it is `E0111`: "`make_pair()` makes a new value, whose parts `a` and `b` already own and may change; remove `ref mut`".
     - **The link words** make links (`[OWN-13]`).
     - **A cast** keeps everything its operand's type says except the kind.
       - `owns cast s as Circle` of an `owns dyn Shape using LevelArena` is an `owns Circle using LevelArena`, and a class object keeps its memory manager.
       - A cast given to a place of another manager is `E2020` (`[TYP-46]`).
  5. **Words before names.** Some lines declare several names without types of their own: a destructuring's targets, a loop's names, a pattern's names and the names after `exists as`. On such a line, each name may carry `ref`, `ref mut` or `copy of`. The word acts on that name's part as it would before the part, under `[GRM-42]`'s comma rule: `ref mut left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)`, `for copy of e in enemies:`, `Some(copy of v):`, `ref k, ref v = entry`.
     - A word before the source of such a line, where it would read as covering several names, is `E0116`: "`ref mut` before the value would cover `left` and `right`; say it on each: `ref mut left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)`".
     - A single target takes its word before the value (`d = ref mut a.as_mut_span()`). `ref mut d = ...` is `E0100`, with that line as its help.
     - In `x @ p`, `x` gets the whole value as its form gives it, and the names inside `p` are names for parts of `x` (3a). So no part has two owners: in `match pair():` with `whole @ (a, b):`, `whole` owns the pair, and `a` and `b` view its parts.
     - In a `match` guard, every name the arm binds is a read-only view of its part. Its own word (an owner's, `copy of` or `ref mut`) takes effect only once the guard holds, so a guard that fails leaves the value for the next arm.
     - A guard that hands over or changes a bound name is `E3013` or `E3023`: "the guard may fail, and the next arm then binds the message again; hand `m` over in the arm: move `consume(owns m)` into its block".
  6. **Rights.**
     - **A local declared by `=`** stands for its own place (`[BRW-13]`).
       - It may be given another value at any time. One that holds a view then views something else (`rest = tail.trim()`, `cur = p`).
       - It may change what it holds when it owns it: a value, a whole name handed over, a part after `owns`, a copy, or `copy of`. The copy `[OWN-7]` guards is the exception.
     - **A parameter, and a name a header or a pattern declares** (a loop's, an arm's, an opened or a kind-test name), keeps what it was given for its scope (`[BRW-14]`), unless it owns it.
       - The names that own are an `owns` parameter, a name over a value its form took over, a name after `owns`, and a `copy of` name.
       - Such an owner may be changed, given another value (the old one ends) and handed on.
       - A copy made by 3c from a place's part does not make the name an owner: `for n in counts: n += 1` is `E3023`, whose help gives `for ref mut n in counts:`.
     - **A name that views** changes nothing (`[BRW-15]`).
     - **A name holding a changeable view** (a `ref mut T` or a `MutSpan[T]`, its own or not) changes what that view names only when it is written `ref mut` (verdict 34): `for ref mut v in xs.iter_mut():`, `if counts.get_mut(k) exists as ref mut n:`, `left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)`. With no word it only reads, and a write is `E3023`, with that line as its help.
     - **A lost change.** A change made through an owning name that a header or a pattern declares, which nothing reads before the name ends, would be lost, and is `E2140` (`[BRW-19]`).
       - Reads include a hand-on, a view taken and a call the name is given to. A `drop` that may read the value counts as a read.
       - The message: "`e.hp -= 10` changes the copy `this.near(x)` made, which ends with this round unread, so the change is lost; to change the world's enemies, walk them: `for ref mut e in this.enemies:`, with `if e.hp > x:` inside".
  7. **Life.**
     - A value a name owns ends with that name's block, or where it is handed on (`[OWN-2]`).
     - A value no name owns ends at the end of the statement or header that made it. While something made from it is still to be used (a view into it, or a name a header opened into it), it lives on to the last use of every such thing, on each path.
     - It never lives past the end of the block that holds that statement or header. For a `while` header, and for every line of a loop's body, that block is the round.
     - A view of it used later is `E3063`: "`best` keeps a view of the copy `l.to_lower()` made in this round (line 6), which ends with the round, and `best` is used on line 9; keep your own text: `best = String(w)`, with `best` declared a `String` before the loop".
     - This is the same for an expression statement and for the header of every `if`, `elif`, `while`, `match` and `for`.
     - A form that holds what it is given for its block keeps it to that block's end: `with` (`[CTL-6]`) and a `for`'s iterable.
     - A guard holds its lock while the guard lives: in a `with` block, in a name or as a temporary. A call that may take that lock meanwhile is `E7018` (`[THR-19]`).
  8. **An iterator in a place is driven where it lives.** An `Iterator` advances through a name that may change it. Whatever drives an iterator held in a place drives it there, with no word.
     - `for names in p:` is `while p.next() exists as names:`.
     - A comprehension's or a generator expression's clause over `p`, and an adapter or a consumer called on `p` (`p.take(1)`, `p.find(...)`, `p.sum()`), work through a `ref mut` view of `p`.
       - The library implements `Iterator` for `ref mut I`, as Rust does for `&mut I`.
       - A method that takes its object over, called on a place whose type's interface is also implemented for `ref mut` of that type, takes that view over instead of the place.
       - So `p` is lent while what was made from it is used (`[BRW-1]`), and keeps its position afterwards.
     - The body may call `p.next()` itself.
     - `p` must be a name that may change it. Otherwise it is `E3023`: "`for` advances `toks`, which only reads the caller's iterator; take it `ref mut toks`".
     - `owns` hands it over: `for t in owns toks:`, `(owns toks).take(2)`.
     - An adapter made over `p` and kept past `p`'s end is `E3063`: "`it.take(2)` advances `it` where it lives, and `it` ends when `first_two` returns; hand it over: `return (owns it).take(2)`".
     - A value (a temporary) is taken over, as 2 says.

The subject's temporaries follow the one life rule (`[OWN-14]` 7). `pop()` gives back a new value, not a view into the guard. So nothing made from the guard is used after the header, and the guard ends at the end of the header, before any arm runs.

If an arm's names viewed the guard, it would live until their last use, never past the block that holds the `match`. A call that takes the lock in the meantime is E7018. `[THR-19]` now covers a guard held as a temporary or in a name, not only inside a `with` block.

from std.sync import Mutex

struct Job:
    id: int

static JOBS: Mutex[Array[Job]] = Mutex([])

fn pending() -> int:
    with g = JOBS.lock():
        return g.len()

fn run_next():
    match JOBS.lock().pop():                # the guard ends here: nothing the arms name points into it
        Some(job):
            println(job.id, pending())      # takes the lock freely
        None:
            pass

fn main():
    with g = JOBS.lock():
        g.push(owns Job(id=1))
    run_next()
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `1 0`.

- With `match JOBS.lock().first():` and `Some(j):`, which views the locked list, the guard lives until `j`'s last use.
- `pending()` after that last use compiles.
- `pending()` before it is E7018 ("`pending()` takes `JOBS`'s lock, and this thread still holds it through the guard line 12 made, which `j` views until line 14; call `pending()` after line 14"). It is refused when compiling, never left to hang.
- `x = JOBS.lock().len() + pending()` is E7018 too, because the guard lives to the end of the statement. The help names the length first.

fn parse_args(line: StrView) -> (String, Array[String], Array[String]):
    toks = line.split_whitespace()
    cmd = String("")
    for t in toks.take(1):                  # the adapter advances `toks` where it lives
        cmd = String(t)
    flags: Array[String] = []
    for t in toks:                          # goes on after the command
        if t == "--":
            break
        flags.push(owns String(t))
    files = [String(t) for t in toks]       # the rest, after `--`
    return (cmd, flags, files)

fn main():
    cmd, flags, files = parse_args("git -v -q -- a.txt b.txt")
    println(cmd, flags, files)
answers.outcome:

        return this.side * this.side

fn keep_circles(owns shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape]) -> Array[owns Circle]:
    circles: Array[owns Circle] = []
    for s in owns shapes:                        # each shape is the loop's own
        if s is Circle:
            circles.push(owns cast s as Circle)  # the same block, now an owns Circle
    return circles

fn main():
    scene: Array[owns dyn Shape] = [owns Circle(r=1.0), owns Square(side=2.0)]
    kept = keep_circles(owns scene)
    println(kept.len())
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `1`.

- The `Square` ends at the end of its round.
- Outside a kind test, a wrong kind stops the program at the cast, before anything is handed over. Inside `if s is Circle:`, the compiler drops the compare.
- Through a read-only `s`, the cast is E3013.
- A plain `c = cast s as Circle` stays a read-only view.
- With `shapes: Array[owns dyn Shape using LevelArena]`, the cast is an `owns Circle using LevelArena`. Pushing it into an `Array[owns Circle]` is E2020, and the list is written `Array[owns Circle using LevelArena]`.

answers.answer:
`return` hands over whatever it is given (verdict 148). A cast of the owner `u` is `u`'s object as a `Player`. So `return cast u as Player` hands the player over with no word.

In a body, `p = owns cast u as Player` does the same, and a plain `p = cast u as Player` is a read-only view. The object keeps its memory manager.

open class Unit:
    name: String

class Player(Unit):
    score: int = 0

fn take_player(owns u: Unit) -> Player:
    return cast u as Player               # hands the player over; stops if `u` is not one

fn main():

    p = take_player(owns u)
    p.score += 10
    println(p.name, p.score)

Compiles. It prints `ann 10`.

- If `u` is not a `Player`, the program stops at the cast with `[TYP-44]`'s message, before anything is handed over.
- The same holds from `owns dyn Shape` to `Circle`.
- A `Player` made `using` an arena stays that arena's after the cast.
- `shares cast s as Circle` on a `shares dyn Shape` is one more owner, as the link words say (P12's question).

answers.answer:
`copy of` copies the thing itself, never a view or a link (verdict 10). It copies one level, by the type written for what follows it:
- Before a `StrView` it gives a `String` of your own, as `String(w)` does.
- Before a `Span[T]` it gives an `Array[T]`, and before a `ref T` a `T`.

What it copies is copied by its `Clone`, which copies the views and links inside it as themselves (verdict 79). So `copy of tok` keeps `text` viewing the source, and `copy of names` is an `Array[StrView]`.

In a generic body, a `T` is copied as itself, since every line there is checked with `T` standing for any type (`[TYP-17]`). So `twice(w)` over `[T: needs Clone]` gives two views.

Every `Copy` type works with `copy of` (verdict 68). E2116 stays for:
- a bare `weakref` (verdict 10);
- a value holding a `ref mut` view or a `MutSpan` among its parts;
- a type with no `Clone`.
answers.code:
@derive(Copy)
struct Token:
    text: StrView
    line: int

fn main():
    src = String("let x = 1")
    tok = Token(text=src.as_str(), line=1)
    t2 = copy of tok                     # a Token whose `text` views the same source
    println(t2.text, t2.line)
    w = src.as_str()
    w2 = copy of w                       # a String of its own
    names: Array[StrView] = [w, "b"]
    n2 = copy of names                   # an Array[StrView]: the views are copied as views
    s = copy of names[0]                 # a String: names[0] is a StrView
    println(n2, s)
    src.clear()
    println(w2, s)
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `let x = 1 1`, then `['let x = 1', 'b'] let x = 1`, then `let x = 1 let x = 1`. `w2` and `s` are text of their own, so `src.clear()` does not touch them.

- `w2 = w` is the free way to get another view. A use of it after `src.clear()` is refused (E3060), and so is a use of `n2`.
- `copy of` before a struct holding a `ref mut` field is E2116 ("no second changing view").

answers.answer: A `StrView` field is a `Copy` value with no parts a name can change. So a no-word read of it is a copy (`[OWN-14]` 3c), and `w` looks at the text, not at the field. Writing `this.rest` changes the field, not the text `w` reads, so verdict 5's promise holds.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `Some('let') Some('x')`.

- `w = words[0]` over a list of views copies the same way, and so does a loop name over it.
- `w = this.buf`, where `buf` is a `MutSpan`, which is not `Copy`, stays a read-only view of the field.
- The compiler's conformance test `LT-22/accept_items_of_a_non_copy_iterator_point_into_what_it_reads` already accepts this pattern.

answers.answer:
OWN-7's reason, that no copy is changed by mistake, holds for every `Copy` value that has parts. So the rule names a struct, a tuple, a fixed array and a variant with a payload alike (`[OWN-14]` 6). Numbers and views have no parts to change, and stay free.

The guard is on names only. A `Copy` value stored in a field, given to a constructor or returned is simply copied (3c).

struct Vec3:
    x: float

fn main():

    p = copy of o
    p.x += 1.0
    origin: [float; 3] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]

    pos[0] += 1.0

- If the source is never used again, the copy may be changed, as for a struct today.

struct Job:
    name: String
    retries: int

fn retry_all(owns jobs: Array[Job]) -> Array[Job]:
    again: Array[Job] = []
    for job in owns jobs:              # `job` owns each Job in turn
        job.retries += 1
        again.push(owns job)
    return again

fn label(owns name: String) -> String:
    if name.len() == 0:
        name = String("unnamed")       # the old empty String ends here
    return name

fn main():

    done = retry_all(owns jobs)

Compiles. It prints `1`, then `unnamed`.

- `kept = job` inside the loop hands `job` over, as `=` does for any owner.
- `for n in counts: n += 1` over a list the function keeps is still E3023, with the help `for ref mut n in counts:`, because that name views.
- `for x in [1, 2, 3]: x += 1`, whose change nothing reads, is E2140: "`x += 1` changes the list's own element, which ends with this round unread; to keep it, use it or collect it".

answers.answer:
Every list of names declared without types takes the same name words (`[OWN-14]` 5, `[GRM-42]`). So `copy of` goes on loop names and pattern names, as it does after `exists as` (verdicts 66 and 67). Each such name is a copy of your own and may be changed.

The copy is one level, by the part's type:
- Over a list of `Enemy`, each copy is an `Enemy`.
- Over a list of views, each copy is what the view views, a `String` for a `StrView` (J2-01).

Parameters keep no copy mode (`[FN-2]`): the copy is written at the call, where it is paid.

struct Enemy:
    name: String
    hp: int

fn preview_hits(enemies: Array[Enemy], dmg: int) -> Array[Enemy]:
    preview: Array[Enemy] = []
    for copy of e in enemies:       # a copy of each enemy, the program's own
        e.hp -= dmg
        preview.push(owns e)
    return preview

fn bump(scores: Map[String, int], name: StrView) -> int:
    match scores.get(name):
        Some(copy of v):
            v += 1                  # the map is untouched
            return v
        None:
            return 0

fn main():
    enemies = [Enemy(name=String("orc"), hp=30)]
    after = preview_hits(enemies, 10)
    println(f"{enemies[0].hp} {after[0].hp}")
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `30 20`.

- `Some(copy of v):` compiles too.
- Each copy is made by the type's `Clone`, and its cost is shown where it is written.
- Under a guard (`Some(copy of v) if v > 3:`), the copy is made only once the guard holds.

answers.answer:
A destructuring's targets are a list of names without types. So each name carries its own word (`[OWN-14]` 5), as loop, pattern and `exists as` names do (`if pair exists as (ref mut a, ref b):`).

`split_at` makes a value, so each name owns its `MutSpan`. A name holding a changeable view writes through it only when written `ref mut` (verdict 34, by what the value is, not by its type). So `ref mut right` may write its half, and plain `left` only reads its own.
answers.outcome:
Compiles. It prints `[1.0, 3.0, 3.0, 5.0]`.

`ref mut left, ref mut right = samples.split_at(mid)` compiles too. `get_pair_mut(i, j)` is opened the same way: `if bodies.get_pair_mut(i, j) exists as (ref mut a, ref mut b):`.

These lines are refused:
- `left, right = ref mut samples.split_at(mid)` is E0116 ("`ref mut` before the value would cover `left` and `right`; say it on each").
- `ref mut left, right` is E0116 by the comma rule.
- Plain `left, right` with `right[i] = ...` is E3023, with this line as the help.

other_cases.case: `n = f().name`: a name given a part of a value.
other_cases.settled:
A part of a struct value is a value, so `n` owns the name, and the rest of the value ends with the statement. `[EXP-10]` (ODR-107) already hands `f()?.name` over the same way.

For a type with a `drop`, it is E3010, and the help names the value first (`r = f()`, then `n = r.name`, a view).

A field of a class object is a place (VI.2). So `n = make_player().name` views it, and the player lives until `n`'s last use, within its block.

other_cases.case: Destructuring: `name, age = parse_line(l)`, `k, v = entry` with `entry` a local `(String, String)`, `a, b = b, a`, `x, y = pos`, `k, v = this.entry`.
other_cases.settled:
- `parse_line(l)` is a value, so each name owns its part.
- `k, v = entry` hands `entry` over part by part, as `=` hands a whole name over (`[OWN-3]`, `[GRM-5]`). `ref k, ref v = entry` keeps `entry` and views both parts. `k, ref v = entry` hands the key over and views the value.
- `this.entry` is a part of a place, so `k` and `v` view it.
- `b, a` builds a tuple value, which takes `b` and `a` in, so the `String` swap works.
- `pos` holds `Copy` numbers, which are copied.
- The spec's own `key, sep, value = line.partition("=")` gives three owned `StrView`s of `line`'s text.

other_cases.case: A part going into a place that owns it: `e.name = p.name`, `User(name=req.name, age=req.age)`, `return Ok(req.body)`, `[p.name, q.name]`, and a typed local `body: String = req.body`.
other_cases.settled:
The field, the constructor's argument, the result and the literal each take the part over with no word (3b, `[OWN-11]`, verdicts 78, 148 and 159). A later use of the part is E3040, with both ways out, and `owns` written there is E0109.

From a name that only reads the value, the line is E3013, with the help `copy of`.

A typed local is still a name, so `body: String = req.body` views the part, as `body = req.body` does.

other_cases.case: `Copy` parts going into places: `Particle(pos=this.pos, vel=this.vel)`, `b.pos = g.muzzle`, `return this.muzzle` through a read-only `this`, `pts = [p.pos, q.pos]`.
other_cases.settled: Each is a copy (3c, OWN-7's "on use"), the source stays, and no word is needed. A name is unchanged: `p = e.pos` is a view of a `Copy` struct part (`[BRW-12]`), so `p.x += 1.0` is E3023, with `copy of` or `ref mut` as the help.

other_cases.case: `yield p.name` and `yield x` in a generator.
other_cases.settled: `yield` gives its value away as `return` does: `yield x` hands a whole `x` over, and `yield p.name` hands the part over. A later use in the generator's body is E3040, decided when compiling. A view of the frame's own locals held across `yield` is still E2221.

other_cases.case: `?` on a value and on a place: `x = f()?`, `x = r?` with `r` a local `Result`, and `this.res?` through a read-only `this`.
other_cases.settled:
- `x = f()?`: `x` owns the payload.
- `x = r?`: `x` views `r`'s payload. On `Err`, the error goes to `return`, which hands it over.
- `x = owns r?` takes the payload.
- `this.res?` is E3013, because the error cannot be handed out of a read-only name.

other_cases.case: `with g = m.lock():`, `with JOBS.lock():` and `with x = this.field:`.
other_cases.settled: A value given to `with` is held to the end of its block, named or not (`[CTL-6]`). It is the explicit way to keep a lock for a block. A place given to `with` is viewed for the block.

other_cases.case: A lock taken again while a guard lives outside a `with` block: `if cache.lock().get(k) exists as v:` with `println(v)` then `refresh()`; `if JOBS.try_lock() exists as g: pending()`; `x = JOBS.lock().len() + pending()`.
other_cases.settled:
- The first compiles: the guard ends after `v`'s last use, so `refresh()` takes the lock. With `refresh()` before `println(v)`, it is E7018.
- `g` owns its guard until the end of the block, so `pending()` there is E7018, with the help "after the `if` block, or `mem.drop(owns g)` first".
- The one-statement form is E7018, with the help "name the length first".

Each is refused when compiling, never left to hang (verdict 43).

- `counts`: E3023, with the help `for ref mut n in counts:`. Python's classic bug stays refused.
- `counts.iter()`: the items are views, so E3023.
- `near(...)`: E2140, with the help `for ref mut e in enemies:` with the test inside. Go's `range` bug is refused.

A name holding a `ref mut T` or a `MutSpan` writes through it only when written `ref mut` (verdict 34), whether or not it owns the view.
- The first is E3023, as `[CTL-1]`'s example says, with `for ref mut v in xs:` as the help.
- The second is E3023, with `exists as ref mut n` as the help.
- The third compiles: `ref mut` before a changeable view names what it names, so `collide(ref mut a, ref mut b)` changes the two bodies.

other_cases.case: Copies over lists of views: `for copy of w in words` with `words: Array[StrView]`, `words.iter().copy_each()`, `m.keys().copy_each()`, and a task's `copy of t`.
other_cases.settled:
- `for copy of w in words`: a loop over the list names its elements, of type `StrView`, so each `w` is a `String` of its own.
- `words.iter()` yields `ref StrView` items, so `copy_each()` removes that one view and gives `StrView`s that no longer point into `words`.
- `m.keys().copy_each()` gives `String`s of their own over `String` keys (verdict 33). Over `StrView` keys it gives views that no longer point into `m`.
- A task's `copy of t` costs one allocation per text, as verdict 93 says.

other_cases.case: Generic code: `[T: needs Clone]` above `fn twice(x: T) -> (T, T): return (copy of x, copy of x)`, called `twice(w)` with `w: StrView`; `xs.fill(v)` over an `Array[StrView]`.

A type parameter is not a view as written, so `copy of x` is a `T`, copied by `T`'s `Clone` as a field of type `T` would be. `twice(w)` gives two views, which E3060 then guards. `fill` writes the same view into each slot.

The generic body is checked once with `T` standing for any type (`[TYP-17]`), so nothing changes at an instance.

other_cases.case: `copy of` before every kind of view and link: `copy of m` (a `MutSpan`), `copy of r` (a `ref mut T`), `copy of this.keep` (a `weakref`), `copy of this.captain` (a `shares`), `copy of this.mesh` (an `owns Mesh`).
other_cases.settled:
- `copy of m` gives an `Array[T]`, and `copy of r` gives a `T`; each needs `Clone`.
- `copy of this.keep` stays E2116 (verdict 10). The help is to open it first, or to write `weakref this.keep` for another link.
- `copy of this.captain` gives a copy of the player (OWN-8).
- `copy of this.mesh` gives a `Mesh`, which an `owns` place takes with `owns copy of this.mesh`.

other_cases.settled:
- `make_shape()` is a value, so `c` owns the `Circle`, and the shape ends before `else` when it is not one.
- `owns s` hands `s` to the test, so `s` is gone in `else` (E3040 if used). To keep the other kinds, test first and cast inside.
- Over a `shares` value, `c` is that owner as its kind, one count, never the only owner. How it is typed is P12's question.

- A list element is E3011, with the help `mem.take`, `mem.replace`, `pop` or `remove`.

These are the `[EXP-6]` refusals, and they are the same for a cast of the place.

other_cases.settled: The match takes the value over, but `sock` cannot leave a value whose `drop` still runs. So the line is E3010, with the help `Conn(sock=ref s)`. With `ref`, `s` views the field, and the `Conn` ends after `s`'s last use, within its block.

other_cases.settled: `take` on a place works through `ref mut it`, and `it` ends when the function returns. So the line is E3063, with the help `return (owns it).take(2)`, which hands the iterator to the adapter. Over a temporary (`return line.split(" ").take(2)`), the adapter takes it over, with no word.

other_cases.settled: On existing names, the word is the one their `=` takes (`[BRW-13]`), written before each name. A single target takes its word before the value: `ref mut d = ...` is E0100, with the help `d = ref mut a.as_mut_span()`. That gives one spelling per form.

other_cases.case: Optional chaining over a place and a temporary: `p?.name` and `f()?.name`.
other_cases.settled: Unchanged: `[EXP-10]` (ODR-107) already states this rule. A place is read where it lives (a `Copy` value copied, any other viewed), and a temporary is taken over.

other_cases.case: `x @ p` over a value: `match pair(): whole @ (a, b):`, and `whole @ (ref mut a, b)`.
other_cases.settled:
`whole` owns the pair, and `a` and `b` are names for its parts, read-only views, so no `String` has two owners.

In the second form, `ref mut a` may change `whole.0`. While `a` is used, `whole` is not read (`[BRW-1]`).

other_cases.case: A guard over owning names: `Some(m) if m.urgent:` then `Some(m):`, `Some(m) if consume(owns m):`, and `Some(m) if bump(ref mut m):`.
other_cases.settled: In the guard, `m` is a read-only view, so the first form reads it, and a failed guard leaves the `Msg` for the next arm, which then owns it. Handing `m` over in a guard is E3013, and changing it there is E3023. Each help moves the work into the arm. This is Rust's rule.

other_cases.case: A link a call made: `if pick(units) exists as u:` where `pick` returns `weakref Unit`.
other_cases.settled: `u` is a view of the `Unit`, never its owner. The link value lives until `u`'s last use, and `u` is not used across a call that may end the unit (verdict 82). `units[0]` stays the unit's only owner.

other_cases.case: A view of a temporary kept across rounds: `if first_word(l.to_lower()) exists as w: best = w`, with `best` declared before the loop and used after it, and `w = l.to_lower().trim()` then `best = w`.
other_cases.settled: Both are E3063. The lowered copy ends with its round, since the bound is the block holding the line, and for a loop's body that is the round. The help: `best = String(w)`, with `best` a `String`. Inside the round, the view may be kept in a name until its last use.

design.prior_art:
**C++** decides what a name gets once, by value category.
- A prvalue initialises the declared object directly; an lvalue is copied unless it is bound to `&`.
- `std::move(x.f)` moves a member out.
- `auto [a, b] = e` copies `e` into a hidden object.
- `std::string_view w = rest;` copies the view, and `std::string(w)` gives text of your own.
- `static_pointer_cast` keeps the control block and its allocator.

Where it falls short:
- A moved-from object stays usable.
- Temporaries end at the end of the full expression, so `m.lock()->len() + other()` deadlocks.
- Lifetime extension differs from form to form: `for (auto& x : f().items())` dangled until C++23's P2718.
- Nothing refuses a dangling view.

**Rust** makes VI.2's place/value split exactly.
- A value is moved into its binding, and a place moves (non-`Copy`) or copies (`Copy`).
- A `Copy` field is copied into a struct literal: `Particle { pos: self.pos }`.
- A part moves out with no word: `User { name: req.name, .. }`, `return Ok(req.body)`. `E0509` refuses moving out of a `Drop` type; this is Ember's E3010.
- Binding modes are set per name: `let (ref a, ref mut b) = pair;`.
- `x @ Some(y)` with a move on both sides is refused unless the inner part is `Copy`.
- A guard sees its bindings as shared borrows until it holds.
- A temporary lives to the end of its statement, and to the end of its block for `let x = &temp()`. Using a view of it past that is an error.
- `impl Iterator for &mut I`, with `by_ref()`, lets an adapter drive a named iterator in place.
- `Clone` copies as itself, while `ToOwned` turns `&str` into `String` and `&[T]` into `Vec<T>`.
- `Box::downcast` keeps the allocation and `Box<T, A>` keeps its allocator.
- `split_at_mut` returns a pair to destructure.

Where Rust falls short:
- Match ergonomics hide binding modes.
- `for x in v` consumes by default.
- `by_ref()` is ceremony.
- There are two copy words.
- A `match` scrutinee's temporaries live through every arm: the classic `match m.lock().unwrap().pop()` deadlock, which Clippy flags as `significant_drop_in_scrutinee`. Rust 2024 only moved `if let` temporaries before `else`.
- A dead store only warns.

**Swift**
- Value types are copied on every binding, with copy-on-write hiding the cost.
- Moves are written per use (`consume x`, SE-0366; `borrowing` and `consuming`, SE-0377).
- A named iterator is resumed with `while let x = it.next()`.
- Exclusivity is partly checked while the program runs.

**Other languages**
- Python: names alias. `for t in it` and `itertools.islice(it, 1)` both advance `it` in place. CPython frees a temporary right after its last use. `pos = origin; pos[0] += 1` changes both lists.
- Go: `for _, v := range xs` silently copies, so `v.hp -= 1` is lost; an unused name is a compile error.
- Zig: `|x|` copies and `|*x|` points, one word per capture.
- C#: a `foreach` variable is read-only (CS1656), and `foreach (ref var x in span)` names the element.
- Mojo: values end at their last use.

**Summary**
- C++ is fast but not safe.
- Rust is safe and fast, but hides binding modes, holds scrutinee temporaries too long and needs `by_ref`.
- Swift copies by default.
- Go and Python copy or alias silently.

The rule takes:
- from Rust: the place/value split, the partial moves into fields and results, the `Copy` copies, the bounded temporary scope, the guard and `@` rules and `Iterator for &mut I`;
- from C++: the prvalue rule;
- from Python: the in-place iterator and loop reading;
- from Zig and Rust: per-name words.

Every word is visible, and nothing runs while the program runs.
design.cost:
Each operation costs what C pays, with two exceptions. An explicit copy costs what C's copy costs, and a cast pays its one compare. Nothing new runs while the program runs, and no header word, field or count is added.

| Operation | Ember | C / C++ / Rust |
|---|---|---|
| A header taking a temporary over (`while jobs.pop() exists as job:`, `match f():`) | Nothing: the name is the temporary's own slot | C: the same local |
| A temporary ending at its last use, within its block or round | Nothing at run time. Drops are placed when compiling, with a one-byte drop flag only where paths differ. A lock is held for less time than to the end of the block. | C++ and Rust hold it to the end of the full statement, or through every `match` arm |
| A part going into a field, a constructor's argument or a result (`User(name=req.name)`, `return Ok(req.body)`) | One move of the part's bytes (24 for a `String`); the existing drop flag only for a hand-over on some paths | Rust's partial move: the same; C: `memcpy` |
| A `Copy` part stored (`Particle(pos=this.pos)`) | A bit copy (16 bytes for a `Vec2`), as `[OWN-7]` already does | C and Rust: the same |
| `owns` before a part on `=` (`body = owns req.body`) | One move | C: the same `memcpy` |
| `owns cast s as Circle`, `return cast u as Player` | One compare of type indices (none inside `if s is Circle:`); no allocation, no copy, same block, same manager | Rust's `downcast`: one `TypeId` compare; C++'s `dynamic_pointer_cast`: an RTTI walk |
| `w = this.rest` (a `Copy` view copied) | A 16-byte copy; the compiler may keep the address where nothing can change it meanwhile | C++'s `string_view` copy: the same |
| `copy of w` (a `String` from a `StrView`), `copy of` a span | One allocation plus a `memcpy`, written on the line | `std::string(w)` and `to_owned()`: the same |
| `copy of` a struct holding views | A field-by-field copy, each view 16 bytes | C++ struct copy: the same |
| `for t in toks`, `toks.take(1)`, a comprehension clause over a named iterator | One `next` call per item, inlined. The adapter holds an 8-byte pointer to the place, which disappears after inlining. | Rust's `by_ref()`: the same; C: a hand-written loop |
| `for copy of e in enemies`, `Some(copy of v)` | One `Clone` per item, written (after the guard, if there is one) | — |
| Words on names, `@`, guard views, rights, E2140, E3063, E7018 | Compile time only | Rust: warnings, or a hang for a re-lock |

readability.ordinary_before:
@derive(Copy)
struct Vec2:
    x: float
    y: float

struct Particle:
    pos: Vec2
    vel: Vec2

struct Emitter:
    pos: Vec2
    vel: Vec2

    fn emit() -> Particle:
        return Particle(pos=this.pos, vel=this.vel)

struct Signup:
    name: String
    email: String

struct User:
    name: String
    email: String

struct Request:
    path: String
    body: String

struct Job:
    name: String
    retries: int

struct Lexer:
    rest: StrView

    fn next_word() -> Option[String]:
        w = this.rest
        if w.find(" ") exists as i:
            word = String(w[..i])          # copied first: `w` views the field, which changes next
            this.rest = w[i + 1..]
            return Some(word)
        word = String(w)
        this.rest = ""
        return Some(word)

fn to_user(owns s: Signup) -> User:
    return User(name=s.name, email=s.email)

fn take_body(owns req: Request) -> String:
    body = mem.take(ref mut req.body)      # leaves an empty String in a request about to end
    println(req.path)
    return body

fn drain(ref mut jobs: Array[Job], ref mut done: Array[Job]):
    while true:
        match owns jobs.pop():
            Some(job):
                done.push(owns job)
                done[done.len() - 1].retries += 1   # `job.retries += 1` is refused: a pattern name changes nothing
            None:
                break

fn split_flags(line: StrView) -> (Array[String], Array[String]):
    flags: Array[String] = []
    files: Array[String] = []
    toks = line.split_whitespace()
    while toks.next() exists as t:         # what `for t in toks:` does is undecided
        if t == "--":
            break
        flags.push(owns String(t))
    while toks.next() exists as t:
        files.push(owns String(t))
    return (flags, files)
readability.note:
The after program is 6 lines shorter and adds no word. The game code (`emit`, a `Copy` part copied into a constructor) and the server code (`to_user`, parts handed into a constructor) read exactly as before.

Every name still has a word on its line, or the plain default, that says what it is:
- `job` owns what `pop()` made.
- `owns req.body` hands the body to a new name.
- `User(name=s.name)` hands the part into a field, as Rust's `User { name: s.name }` does.
- `w` is a view.
- `for t in toks` goes on where the last loop stopped, as in Python.

The lexer returns views with no allocation, where the before program made a `String` per word. The only lines that change for the worse are the rare refused ones: a change to an owning header name that nothing reads (E2140), a view kept past its round (E3063), and a re-lock while a guard lives (E7018). Each comes with the line to write.

design.compiler_does:
The compiler works out all of this from the code. The programmer writes only the words that say a hand-over, a copy or a change.

1. It classifies each source as a place or a value (VI.2). It classifies each receiver as one of: a name, a header, a place that owns its value and is not a name, or a parameter. For every name a form binds, it records whether the name owns its part or views it.
   - Owners get changeable, reassignable names, and drops at the end of their block or where they are handed on, with drop flags only where paths differ (`[OWN-3]`).
   - Viewing names get the `[BRW-1]` promise.
2. For a header over a value, it gives the value's storage to the names. It ends what no name holds at the end of the header, so an `else`, or an arm with no names, drops the value first. In a guard, it checks the bound names as read-only views and applies their words only once the guard holds.
3. It computes the last use of everything made from a temporary with the existing non-lexical liveness (`[LT-5]`). It places the temporary's end right after that last use, on each path, and checks that the end does not pass the end of the block, or the round, that holds the line (E3063).
4. Its set of locks this thread holds now includes every live guard: in a `with` block, in a name, or as a temporary. A call that may take a held lock is checked against that set (verdict 43, E7018).
5. For a part going into an owning place, for `owns` before a part, and for a cast, it tracks the partial hand-over with the `[OWN-11]` machinery: E3040 until the part has a new value, and E3010, E3011 and E3013 where the place may not be left empty. It retypes a cast's block keeping its holder and manager, with no copy. It emits the one type-index compare, and folds it away inside a kind test.
6. It copies a `Copy` value wherever it is stored, given or returned. For a name given a `Copy` part with no parts a name can change, it copies, or it keeps the address where it proves nothing changes the place meanwhile; nobody can observe which. For a `Copy` value with parts given to a name, it applies `[OWN-7]`'s guard using the source's liveness.
7. For `copy of`, it reads the written type of what follows. Before a view or a holder, it calls `Clone` on what that reaches, one level down. Before any other value, a type parameter included, it calls the value's own `Clone`, which copies the views and links inside as themselves.
8. For an iterator in a place, it picks the `ref mut I` implementation for an adapter or consumer called on it. It desugars `for names in p` to `while p.next() exists as names:`, so the existing checks see exactly the `while` form: `p` must be changeable, and an item that points into `p` is ended by the next call.
9. It reads the words on destructuring, pattern and loop names under the comma rule. It refuses a word before a value that would cover several names. It binds the names inside `x @ p` as names for parts of `x`.
10. For each owning name a header or a pattern declares, it runs a dead-change check on the whole value: a change that no later read, hand-on, view, call or `drop` reaches before the name ends is E2140.
design.misuse:
**Refused when compiling, each with a line that compiles:**
- `owns` where the form already takes the value over is E0109, help "remove `owns`". This covers a header's value, `b = a`, `e.name = p.name`, `User(name=owns req.name)`, `return owns x`, and a new value given to a place that does not own it alone.
- `owns` before a place that may not be left empty: a list element is E3011, and a class object's field, or anything reached through a name that does not own it, is E3013. Each help names `mem.take`, `mem.replace` or `copy of` (`body = mem.take(ref mut req.body)`).
- A part handed out of a name that does not own it (`User(name=p.name)` with `p` a plain parameter) is E3013, help `name=copy of p.name`.
- A part taken out of a value whose type has a `drop` is E3010. The help is `ref` in a pattern, or naming the value first.
- `ref mut` before a part of a value that is not itself a changeable view is E0111, help "remove `ref mut`".
- `owns cast s as Circle` through a read-only `s` is E3013. A cast given to a place of another memory manager is E2020.
- A `for`, adapter or consumer that would advance an iterator through a read-only name is E3023, help `ref mut`.
- An adapter over an iterator in a place, kept past that place, is E3063, help `(owns it).take(2)`.
- A word before a destructuring's value is E0116, with the help putting the word on each name. A word before a single target is E0100, help `d = ref mut e`.
- `copy of` before a bare `weakref`, before a value holding a `ref mut` view or a `MutSpan`, or before a type with no `Clone` is E2116.
- Changing a no-word copy of a `Copy` value with parts while its source is still used is E3023.
- Changing or rebinding a name that views is E3023, and so is writing through a name that holds a changeable view without `ref mut`.
- A guard that hands over or changes a bound name is E3013 or E3023, with the help to move the work into the arm.
- A change through an owning header or pattern name that nothing reads is E2140.
- A view of a temporary used past its block or round is E3063.
- A call that may take a lock while a guard of it lives (in a `with` block, a name or a temporary) is E7018.
- Using a name or a part after a hand-over is E3040.

**Stopped at the line while the program runs:** only a cast of the wrong kind, with `[TYP-44]`'s message in the program's own names, before anything is handed over.

**Never undefined behaviour:**
- Every hand-over leaves the giver unusable, checked when compiling.
- No part has two owners.
- No temporary outlives its storage.
- No hidden copy or alias is made.
design.verdicts:
All verdicts are kept, and none is revisited. One needs the owner to confirm its reach: verdict 159.

- **5.** A read-only name still promises that what it reads does not change while it is used. `w = this.rest` reads the text, which still cannot change while `w` is used; only the field moves. There is no silent alias, since a view is read-only and checked. There is no silent copy either: a copy is made only of a `Copy` value, where a copy reads the same as a view.
- **10, 12.** `copy of` copies the thing itself, never a link or a view, one level. A bare `weakref` stays E2116.
- **13.** A change that is silently lost is refused. E2140 now also covers a change through an owning header or pattern name that nothing reads before the name ends.
- **16.** One rule for every loop, and for everything that drives an iterator.
- **25/27, 26.** The spelling is unchanged; a cast of a place is a place.
- **33.** `copy_each()` over `String` keys gives `String`s of their own.
- **34.** It is now stated by what the value is: a name holding a `ref mut T` or a `MutSpan` writes only when written `ref mut`. `[BRW-12]`'s by-type `MutSpan` sentence goes.
- **43.** A lock taken again is refused when compiling, now while any guard of it lives, not only inside `with`.
- **66/67.** `copy of` names, changeable copies of your own, now reach loop and pattern names too.
- **68.** Every `Copy` type works with `copy of` (a `StrView` gives a `String`, a `Span` an `Array`), so E2116 is never given for a `Copy` type.
- **74/85/97.** `owns` on the line that makes a value for a place that owns it alone stays required. E0109 is narrowed so that it never refuses those lines.
- **78.** A part handed over on its own: into a field with no word, as today, and now also into a constructor's argument, a literal and a result.
- **79.** Links inside a copy are copied as links, and by the same rule views as views. A type parameter is copied as itself, as a field of its type is.
- **82.** A name opened from a link is not used across a call that may end its target, whether the link came from a place or from a value.
- **84, 145.** `owns` hands over every type the same way.
- **93.** `copy of t` on a text costs one allocation per text; `ref t` is a view.
- **95.** Nothing changes a list while a loop walks it. An iterator is not a list, and advancing it is the loop's own handle.
- **140.** Unchanged. Only for an interface also implemented for `ref mut T` does a method that takes its object over, called on a place, take a view instead.
- **147/149.** The argument words are unchanged (`names.push(owns p.name)`).
- **148.** `return` takes no word and hands over anything, a part or a cast of a place included. A `Copy` value is copied.
- **150, 158, 160, 161.** Unaffected.
- **159.** A constructor's argument takes no word. A whole name is handed over, as `snapshot = items` is (the verdict's own example), and a number is copied (`Point(x=a)`). A part is handed over too, since a field cannot hold a view and a silent copy is not allowed; `[OWN-11]` and verdict 78 already hand a part into a field this way. The owner was shown whole names only, so its reach for parts goes to him as option E. Phase 3's `Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp))` (P09, J7-15) compiles as written under A.
- **164-166.** Untouched.

Some rules that are not owner verdicts do change. Each must be told to the owner as such:
- `[EXP-4]`: the timing of a header's temporaries, and the new bound by block or round;
- `[DRP-3]`;
- `[CTL-1]`'s three cases;
- `[STD-19]`'s adapters called on a place;
- `[THR-19]`'s "inside a lock's `with` block";
- E2116's view bullet;
- `[OWN-7]`'s "a `Copy` struct";
- E0109's reach;
- the E3023 row.

recommendation.reason:
A is the only option that answers all twelve questions, and the cases nobody asked, with one rule. It follows VI.2's own place/value split, which `[EXP-10]` already applies to optional chaining, and Rust's proven rules for moving parts into fields and results and for copying `Copy` parts.

- C lengthens every loop.
- D refuses a correct re-lock.

owner_short.one_line: This is the C++ question of what `auto x = e`, a range-for's `x`, a structured binding, a `switch` case, a member initialiser and `return` get from `e`. In C++, a temporary (prvalue) is moved in, and a named object (lvalue) is copied, or referred to with `&`. Ember needs that one rule for every form, with `owns` as `std::move`, `copy of` as a written copy, and no silent copy of anything that is not `Copy`.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `while jobs.pop() exists as job:` | `pop()` makes an `Option[Job]` that no name owns yet |
| 2 | main | `job` is opened from it | GRM-44 makes `job` a read-only view, and BRW-12 says a call's new value is the name's own; the spec says both |
| 3 | main | `done.push(owns job)` | undecided: refused (a view hands nothing over), or compiles |
| 4 | main | `match owns JOBS.lock().pop():` | the lock's guard is a temporary of the header: an `if` drops it before its block, but a `match` keeps it through every arm (DRP-3) |
| 5 | main | the arm calls `pending()`, which locks `JOBS` | refused as a lock taken twice under `match`, fine under `if` |
| 6 | main | `User(name=req.name, age=req.age)` | `=` would view `req.name`, while OWN-11 hands a part into a field over: two readings |
| 7 | main | `w = this.rest`, then `this.rest = w[i + 1..]` | `w` is either a copy of the view (fine) or a view of the field (refused); `copy of w` is both allowed (verdict 68) and E2116 |
owner_short.today:
Each form has its own list:
- `=` owns a call's value, `exists as` views it, `for` takes a temporary over, and `match` needs `owns`.
- A header's temporaries end at different times.
- A part going into a constructor has two readings.

`owns` before a part or a cast, `copy of` before a view, words on loop or destructured names, and `for` over a named iterator are each undecided or refused.

- A temporary ends at its last use, within its block.

B: today's defaults, plus only the missing words. Code is longer, and one temporary gets three defaults.
