design.rule: The word before a type says how a value is held, never what the value is. So: (1) every holder word (owns, shares, shares mut, thread_shared, weakref, ref, ref mut, sharedref mut) can be written before every type that can be held that way, an interface (dyn I) and a base class included, and a value converts to an interface or a base class keeping its word (a class object, held alone, converts as `owns` holds, so also to `owns dyn I`); a line is refused only where that word's own rule already says the value cannot be held so. (2) A holder that always holds a live value (an owner or a view) reads as the value it holds wherever that value is wanted: an argument and every conversion the value itself would take, an operand, a field, a method, a loop, an index, either side of `in` and a lookup, printing, `==`, ordering, hashing. It has exactly the rights its word gives, counts nothing, and costs one load. `==` always means the held value's own `==`; a holder hashes as its value wherever what the hash reads cannot change while it is held, which through a sharing word means only what no holder may change (identity, `let` fields, a thread_shared value's plain fields). (3) A holder that may hold nothing (a weakref, like an Option) is opened with `exists as` before anything about its target is read or asked, `is None` included; its Debug shows the link itself. (4) `is` asks whether two operands reach the same value: one address compare, plus a compare of kinds only where two kinds can sit at one address; it reads, opens and counts nothing; `is not` proves only that two values are not one, never that one is not inside the other. (5) A whole value is written only into a place of its own type: a changeable view converted to a base class or an interface changes its value field by field and through its methods, and whatever would put a whole value of another type through it is refused when compiling. (6) `=` on a holder name gives it another holder and says the word, as for `owns` and `weakref` today; a compound assignment through a holder changes the held value, for every held type.
design.spec_text:
Adds [TYP-48]. Changes [TYP-5] (rules 7 and 8, and its sentence on composing), [TYP-13], [TYP-14], [TYP-21], [TYP-36], [TYP-39], [TYP-44], [TYP-45], IV.1's table, IV.9, IV.11 step 1, [OBJ-1], [THR-2], [WK-11], [WK-12], [WK-16], [DSP-4], [EXP-9], [BRW-1], [BRW-17], [SIMD-3], [DSJ-1], [HASH-3], [STD-8], [STD-12], VI.3's `is` row, and the E2150 and E2037 rows. No grammar change: `base_type` (p03 167-171) already admits every holder word before `dyn`.

[TYP-48] (new) **Holders.** `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`, `ref`, `ref mut` and `sharedref mut` are the holder words. Each says how a value is held, never what it is. A class object with no word is held alone, in a block of its own, as `owns` holds a value ([TYP-45]), and is treated so below. Written as part of a function type (`thread_shared fn()`), `thread_shared` is that type's own word ([TYP-45], [CLO-16], verdicts 61 and 94): it says which threads may run the type's functions, and a function value of that type is held as any value is, alone and uncounted. Read as a holder word there it would say something untrue (that the function is counted), so this is stated here with its reason; in both places the word says that any thread may use what follows.

1. **Every holder word before every type it can hold.** Each holder word is written before every type whose values can be held the way it says, an interface (`dyn I`) and a base class included: `weakref dyn Listener`, `thread_shared dyn Sink`, `sharedref mut dyn Damageable`, `shares mut dyn Shape`, `weakref Widget`. A line is refused only where its word's own rule says the value cannot be held so:
   * `owns` written before a class type (`E2114`);
   * a `weakref` of what does not live on its own (`E2119`, [WK-16]; for a `dyn` value judged by every kind it may hold, and for a parameter by what each call passes);
   * a sharing word before a one-owner place (`E2122`);
   * `thread_shared` of what is not `ThreadShared` (`E7015`).
   A value converts to an interface its type implements, and a class object to a base class, keeping its holder word; a value held alone (an `owns T`, or a class object) converts to `owns dyn I` ([TYP-5] rule 8). A changeable view converted so is limited by 5. `Option[H]` is a type for every holder form `H`. Which threads each form may reach is [THR-8] and [THR-9]'s, judged by what it may hold.

2. **A holder that always holds a live value reads as that value.** An owner (`owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, a class object held alone) and a view (`ref`, `ref mut`, `sharedref mut`) are read through, level by level, wherever what they hold is wanted:
   * a field, or a method call;
   * an operand: an operator reads each holder operand through before it chooses its implementation ([TYP-21]);
   * an argument to a plain parameter, a loop's source, an index;
   * a coercion: a holder converts where its held value would ([TYP-5] rules 4, 6 and 8, read-through first), so `title`, a `shares String`, is given to a `StrView` parameter as a `String` is, and `disc`, a `shares Circle`, to a `dyn Shape` parameter as a `Circle` is;
   * either side of `in`, and a lookup: a value of `T`, and any holder that reads through to `T`, finds an element or key held as any holder of `T`, comparing and hashing as `T` does, so the probe makes nothing ([STD-8], [STD-12]): `me in roster` for `me = ref p` and `roster: Array[shares Player]`;
   * printing and formatting, `==`, an ordering and hashing.
   Each owner and view implements `Eq`, `Ord`, `Display`, `Debug` and `Printable` exactly when what it holds does, and each does what the held value's own does. So `scores == others` compares two lists, and a class object's `==` stays identity, as its own is ([TYP-36]).
   It implements `Hash` as what it holds does where what that value's `hash` and `eq` read cannot change while the holder is held, because a map or a set keeps each key where its hash put it ([HASH-1]): always through `owns` and the views (the holder is the only way to the value, or its promise holds the value still, [BRW-1]); through `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared` and `sharedref mut`, whose other holders may change the value at any time ([RC-7], [LT-46]), only where they read nothing a holder may change: a class object's identity ([TYP-36]), a `let` field ([CLS-9a]), a field of a `thread_shared` value that is not an `Atomic`, a lock or `guarded by` ([RC-7]). The compiler reads this from the bodies of `hash` and `eq`, as [HASH-3] reads what they do. Otherwise the holder has no `Hash` (`E2040`: "`shares mut Tile` has no `Hash`: `Tile` hashes `x` and `y`, which another owner may change while the set holds the tile, and a changed key is lost; keep copies in the set: `taken: Set[Tile]` and `taken.insert(copy of t)`, or make `Tile` a class, whose objects hash by identity"). `Ord` stays through every holder: a sort reads the values as they are when it runs and keeps no placement.
   A read through a holder:
   * may do what the holder's word allows: a `shares` or `thread_shared` owner reads; `shares mut`, `ref mut` and `sharedref mut` may also change ([RC-7], [OWN-13]; otherwise `E3023`, or `E7014` for `thread_shared`);
   * is checked by every rule that checks any read or change of that value ([BRW-1], [BRW-18], [RC-5], `guarded by`);
   * counts nothing ([RC-2a], [RC-2b]);
   * never hands the held value over ([OWN-11], `E3013`).
   `copy of` before a holder stays [OWN-8]'s.

3. **A holder that may hold nothing is opened first.** A `weakref` link, like an `Option`, does not read as its target. It is opened with `exists as` before anything about its target is read or asked ([GRM-44]). It has no `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash` or `Display`. Its `Debug` shows the link itself, as a class object's shows the object ([TYP-36]): `weakref Enemy at 0x7f3a…`, or `None` when it holds none; it reads nothing at the target, so a struct holding links keeps [STR-5]'s implicit `Debug`. Reading or asking about its target without opening it (by `==`, `Display`, a kind test, a cast, a method call, or `is None` / `is not None`) is `E2020`: "`cam.target` may be gone; open it: `if cam.target exists as t:`". For `==` the message adds: "to ask whether `cam.target` and `hud.target` name the same enemy, write `cam.target is hud.target`"; for `is None`: "`turret.target` may name an enemy that has ended, which `is None` does not ask; to ask whether it names a live one write `if turret.target exists as t:`, with the other case under `else:`".

4. **`is` asks whether two operands reach the same value.**
   * What each operand reaches: an owner or a view reaches what it holds; a class object is itself; a `weakref` link reaches its target, ended or not; an `Option` reaches what its value reaches. `None`, and a link holding nothing, reach nothing. A link's target keeps its block while the link names it: in the built-in manager's memory by the weak count ([OBJ-3]), and in a memory manager's memory by P02's rule that every link into it ends before the manager gives that memory back. The compare on links relies on that rule.
   * `a is b` is true when both reach the same value. Two links are `is` each other when they name one target or both name none; two `Option`s when both are `None` or both hold values that are `is` each other, so `x is y` and the option test `x is None` never disagree.
   * It compares addresses, never a method table. Where two kinds of value can sit at one address (a struct and its first field, each viewed as a `dyn I`), it also compares which kind each is, read from each view's table, and only when the addresses are equal. Two values of one type that takes no memory are always `is` each other.
   * It reads no value, opens no link and touches no header or count, so it is allowed wherever its operands may be named, in a scoped task too ([WK-11]).
   * `E2150` is an operand with no address of its own to compare: a plain value of a `Copy` type other than a `ref T` ([BRW-8], [BRW-12]), a literal or constructor call written in the line, or a view of several elements (`Span`, `MutSpan`, `StrView`). Message: "`is` asks whether two names reach the same value, and `n` is a number, which `=` copies; compare numbers with `==`: `n == m`".
   * `E2037` is two operands whose types no single value can have: "`boss` is an `Enemy` and `chest` a `Chest`, which are never the same object; remove the test".
   * `x is None` stays the `Option` test, and `x is T` the kind test. On a `weakref` link `is None` and `is not None` are refused (3).
   * **What `is not` proves.** `a is not b` proves that `a` and `b` are not one value, and nothing about their parts. A value stored inside one of them (a field, an element), or owned by it, may be the other, so a change made through a part of `a` (`a.wheel.tag`) is checked against `b` path against path ([BRW-17]). Two paths may lead to one value when one's type may be the other's: one type, a base class and a class derived from it, `dyn I` and a type implementing `I`, two interfaces one type implements. For the memory two views cover (a noalias fact, [SIMD-3]; arguments that may not overlap, [BRW-11]), `is not` proves two views apart only where neither may lie inside the other: both reach whole values in blocks of their own (class objects, the values of `shares` and `thread_shared` owners, `owns` blocks), or both reach values of one type, which never holds itself (`E2200`). Otherwise the program proves them apart with `assert_disjoint(a, b)` ([DSJ-1], two compares), which the refusal's help names.

5. **A whole value is written only into a place of its own type:** the type the place was declared with (a local's, a field's, an element's), not the kind of object a class-typed place holds. A changeable view (`ref mut`, `sharedref mut`, a name opened or tested `ref mut`) converted to a base class or an interface keeps its word, and through it the value is changed field by field and by its methods (`fn damage(ref mut w: Widget)`, called `damage(ref mut hud)`). What would put a whole value through it (`=` on it, `mem.swap`, `mem.replace`, `mem.take`, or a call whose body does one of these to the parameter given it) is refused where the place may be of another type than the view's:
   * through a `dyn` view always, at the write, since no place has the type `dyn I`: "`r` views a `Circle` (line 3) as a `Shape`, so a whole `Square` cannot be put there; change it through its methods, or test its kind first: `if r is Square as ref mut q:` and `q = Square(side=2.0)` under it";
   * through a base-class parameter, at each call that gives it a place of a derived class. What a function writes whole into a view parameter is worked out from its body, through the functions it passes the parameter to, and kept with the function as [BRW-21]'s facts are (in the interface file across a package's edge, [EFF-4]): "`reset` puts a new `Widget` in `w` (its line 2), and `hud` is declared a `Hud`, where a `Widget` cannot stand; to give `hud` a new object write `hud = Hud()` in place of this line, or in `reset` change the widget instead of replacing it: `w.name = String("widget")`";
   * through a kept view (a field, a local, a list's element), at the write, where by following values some line may have made it from a place of a derived class, naming that line.
   The refusal is `E3023`, and nothing is checked while the program runs. Owners, `weakref` links and `ref` views keep their word across a conversion with no such limit: `=` on an owner or a link gives the name another holder in its own place, whose type is the holder's own (6), and a `ref` writes nothing. `ref mut this.child`, for a field `child: Widget` that holds a `Hud`, takes a whole `Widget`.

6. **`=` and compound assignment on a holder.** `=` on a name or place that holds through a holder word gives it another holder, as on any place that owns its value, and the line says the word: `scores = shares mut [1, 2]`, `e.mesh = owns Mesh(points=[1.0])`, `cam.target = weakref boss`. A value of the held type given without it is refused as [OWN-10] (`E2123`) and [WK-16] (`E2020`) refuse it, with both lines: "`hp` is one of several owners of a number (line 1), and `hp + 1` is a new number; to change the number every owner sees write `hp += 1`; for a new number only `hp` owns write `hp = shares mut (hp + 1)`". A view name keeps [BRW-13]'s meaning: `=` writes the place it names. A compound assignment through a holder (`hp += 1`, `pos += Vec2(x=1.0, y=0.0)`) changes the held value, for every held type: by its `…Assign`, or by writing `a op b` into it ([TYP-21]); the holder's word must allow the change (`E3023`, `E7014`). A class object, which is never replaced in its block ([CLS-7]), is changed so only by its `…Assign` (`E2103` otherwise, whose help gives `w = shares mut (w + x)` for a new object).

Edits:
- [TYP-14]: the first sentence becomes: "Every holder that always holds a live value, an owner or a view of any type (`dyn I` included), is read through wherever what it holds is wanted ([TYP-48] 2): a field access, a method call, an operand, an argument to a plain parameter, a coercion, `in` and a lookup, printing, `==`, ordering and hashing." The rest stays.
- [TYP-5] rule 7: "`ref T` from a place (a read-only view of it), and reading through an owner or a view where what it holds is expected ([TYP-14], [TYP-48] 2)".
- [TYP-5] rule 8: "a value to an interface its type implements, and a class object to a base class, keeping its holder word: a value read in place to `dyn I`; a value held alone (an `owns T`, or a class object) to `owns dyn I`; `H T` to `H dyn I` and `H C` to `H B` for every other holder word `H` ([TYP-48] 1); a changeable view so converted takes no whole value of another type ([TYP-48] 5)".
- [TYP-5], the sentence on composing: "Each rule composes with the others only where stated: widening after range erasure, rule 11 after rules 1–4, and rule 7's read-through before rules 4, 6 and 8 (a holder converts where its held value would)." Rule 11 after read-through is P20's composition.
- [TYP-13]: the niche list adds `shares T`, `shares mut T`, `thread_shared T`, `ref mut T`, `sharedref mut T` and the `dyn` form of each, so `Option[shares Player]` is one pointer. The FFI-guarantee sentence is unchanged.
- [TYP-21]: "... with both operands read in place, each holder operand read through first ([TYP-48] 2). `a += b` calls `AddAssign.add_assign` if implemented, else `a = a + b`; where `a` is a holder, both forms change the held value ([TYP-48] 6)."
- [TYP-36]: "A read-only view `ref T` implements `Eq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` as `T` does" becomes: "Every owner and view implements `Eq`, `Ord`, `Display`, `Debug` and `Printable` as what it holds does, and `Hash` where [TYP-48] 2 says: `sorted(m.keys())`; `scores == others`; a `Set[shares Enemy]`, which hashes each enemy by identity. A `weakref` link implements none of them but `Debug`, which shows the link ([TYP-48] 3)." "Two `owns` values compare with `==` when what they hold does; `owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq`" becomes: "a holder of `dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq`: values of two different kinds are never equal, and two of one kind compare their contents." Added: "A class object's identity is its address for `==` and `is`, and for `Hash` a number fixed for its whole life: an object of a class family some `weakref` link may name, which the program hashes by identity, keeps a 32-bit identity number in its header ([OBJ-1]), so a hand-over that moves it to another thread (verdict 114, [THR-2]) leaves its hash as it was."
- [TYP-39]: "An `owns T` and a `Cell[T]` show as the `T` they hold" becomes: "Every owner and view, and a `Cell[T]`, show as the value they hold (an `owns int` holding 5 prints `5`; a `shares mut Array[int]` prints `[10, 20, 30]`); a `weakref` link's `Debug` shows the link ([TYP-48] 3)".
- [TYP-45]: the dyn bullet becomes: "`dyn I` after any holder word (`owns dyn I`, `shares dyn I`, `shares mut dyn I`, `thread_shared dyn I`, `weakref dyn I`, `ref dyn I`, `ref mut dyn I`, `sharedref mut dyn I`): a value of some type implementing `I`, held as the word says ([TYP-48] 1); `dyn I` alone is a parameter's or a local's type ...". The `owns` bullet adds: "`owns` written before a class type is `E2114`; a class object held alone converts to `owns dyn I` ([TYP-5] rule 8)". The function-type bullet adds: "`thread_shared` there is the function type's own word ([TYP-48])".
- IV.1's table: the Shared row adds `thread_shared dyn I`; the Link row adds `weakref dyn I`; the View row adds `ref dyn I`, `ref mut dyn I` and `sharedref mut dyn I`; the Existential row reads "`dyn I` after any holder word".
- IV.9, first bullet: lists the same forms, and says each is one pointer where the value lives in a block with a header (a class object, a shared value), whose type index reaches the table ([OBJ-2]), and a data pointer plus a table pointer otherwise.
- IV.11 step 1: "Strip views, and owners level by level (`owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`); a `weakref` link is opened first."
- [TYP-44], [DSP-4], [EXP-9] (kind tests and casts): "a value of an interface or base-class type, held any way that holds a live value ([TYP-48] 2); a `weakref` link is opened first ([TYP-48] 3)". With this, DSP-4's list gains `shares mut dyn I` and `thread_shared dyn I`.
- [EXP-9], first sentence: "`a is b` tests whether two operands reach the same value ([TYP-48] 4); `a is not b` proves only that they are not one value."
- VI.3's row: "`a is b`, `a is not b` | the same value | owners, links, views of one value, class objects, and `Option`s of these ([TYP-48])".
- E2150 row: "`is` on an operand with no address of its own: a plain value of a `Copy` type (not `ref T`), a literal or constructor call written in the line, a view of several elements; not a kind test | [TYP-48], [EXP-9]".
- E2037 row: adds "or an `is` between operands no single value can be".
- [WK-11]: "`weakref x` makes a link to what `x` names, whatever its type, `dyn I` included ([TYP-48] 1)".
- [WK-12]: adds: "Which header a link's targets may have is worked out by following values. Where one link place may name both a `thread_shared` value and a one-thread one, opening and ending the link first read which header the target has from the header of the memory chunk its block came from ([OBJ-1]), then follow that header's protocol: one address mask, one load and a branch, only at such places; a place that names one kind follows that kind's protocol with no test."
- [WK-16]: adds: "A link made from a parameter, or from `this`, is judged at each call by what the call passes (as verdict 128 follows callers): an argument that does not live on its own is `E2119` at the call, naming the line inside the callee (\"`watch` keeps a link to what `p` names (its line 9), and `pool` is a struct stored in `main`, which no link can follow; give it a block of its own: `pool = shares IntPool(items=[1, 2])`\")."
- [OBJ-1]: (a) after "every shared value of a type some `weakref` link may name", add: "which types a link may name is worked out by following values through every route a value takes (a conversion, a read-through, a parameter, a field, a call): a link made from a value of an interface type may name every type converted to any form of that interface, and one made from a base class every class of its family; a function that makes a link from a parameter or `this` keeps that fact with the function (in the interface file across a package's edge, [EFF-4])". (b) "An object of a class family some `weakref` link may name, which the program hashes by identity, has a 32-bit identity number at offset 12, set from its address when it is made and carried when a hand-over moves it ([THR-2]); where the first field is 8-byte aligned that space was padding." (c) "A `thread_shared` value's block comes from a memory chunk that holds only `thread_shared` blocks, and the chunk's header says so, beside the making thread ([WK-12])."
- [THR-2] (verdict 114's move): adds "the new place keeps the object's identity number ([OBJ-1])".
- [BRW-1]: "unless the compiler proves the two differ (`if t is not a:`, which proves what [TYP-48] 4 says)".
- [BRW-17]: "Two paths may reach the same object when they lead to values of which one's type may be the other's ([TYP-48] 4: one type, a base class and a derived one, `dyn I` and an implementer) and at least one goes through a link or a kept view, unless the compiler knows they differ: types neither of which may be the other, a fresh object, or inside `if a is not b:` for those two paths and not for their parts."
- [SIMD-3]: "(the two have types neither of which may be the other, one is an object made in this function, or the loop is inside `if a is not b:` and neither may lie inside the other, [TYP-48] 4)".
- [DSJ-1]: "compares the two views' address ranges" is stated for any two views: a `ref`, `ref mut` or `sharedref mut` view's range is its type's size, a `dyn` view's is read from its kind's table, and a span's as today.
- [HASH-3]: adds: "A key held through a sharing word is `Hash` only by what no holder may change ([TYP-48] 2), so a key changed through another holder is refused when compiling, not a wrong answer."
- [STD-8]: "for `Array`, `Span`, `MutSpan` and `[T; N]` with `T: needs Eq`, as a linear scan" adds: "and, for elements held as a holder of `U`, `Contains[Q]` for `Q` = `U` and every holder of `U` that reads through ([TYP-48] 2)".
- [STD-12]: adds: "`K`, and every holder of `K` that reads through, is `AsKey[H K]` for every holder `H` of `K` that is `Hash` ([TYP-48] 2), and a `Q: AsKey[K]` is `AsKey[H K]` likewise (a `StrView` finds a `thread_shared String` key)."

answers.answer: Decided by [TYP-48] 2. A `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` owner reads as the value it owns wherever that value is wanted, conversions included. Passed to a plain parameter it is a read-only view of the list, with no count. It prints as the list. `==` is the list's own `==`, contents, because the owner word says who owns the list, not what it is. `is` asks whether two owners own the same list ([TYP-48] 4). Phase 3's K30 second line is added: `cam.target is hud.target` on two `weakref` links (J3-12). A shared list is not a map key by its contents, since another owner may change it ([TYP-48] 2's `Hash` sentence); that line does not touch this program.
answers.code:
fn total(scores: Array[int]) -> int:             # reads a list of scores
    return scores.iter().sum()

class Enemy:
    hp: int = 10

struct Hud:
    target: weakref Enemy = None

class Leaderboard:
    scores: shares mut Array[int]                # shared with the HUD

fn main():
    scores = shares mut [10, 20]
    board = Leaderboard(scores=shares mut scores)
    board.scores.push(owns 30)                   # a method call sees through `shares mut`
    println(total(scores))                       # an argument: the list
    println(scores)                              # printed as the list
    others = shares mut [10, 20, 30]
    println(scores == others)                    # the lists compared
    println(scores is others)                    # two different lists
    println(scores is board.scores)              # one list, two owners
    boss = Enemy()
    cam = Hud(target=weakref boss)
    hud = Hud(target=weakref boss)
    println(cam.target is hud.target)            # the same enemy
answers.outcome: Compiles. Prints `60`, `[10, 20, 30]`, `true`, `false`, `true`, `true`. No count operation is emitted for `total(scores)`, `println(scores)` or `==` ([RC-2a]). Each reads through one pointer load, as C's `*p` does. Each `is` is one pointer compare.

answers.answer: Decided by [TYP-48] 4. `is` takes `weakref` links and compares their targets without opening them. A target that has ended keeps its block while a link names it: by the weak count in the built-in manager's memory ([OBJ-3], verdict 11), and by P02's rule in a memory manager's memory (a link ends before the manager gives its memory back). The rule says it relies on P02, so J3-12 is presented after P02's J5-02. With that, the compare is exact and never confuses two objects. Two links holding nothing are `is` each other. `if cam.target is None:` is refused (E2020, open it), so the language gives one answer to 'is there a live target'. This resolves the EXP-9 / E2150-row contradiction in the row's favour.
answers.code:
class Enemy:
    hp: int = 10

struct Hud:                                    # what the camera or the HUD follows
    target: weakref Enemy = None               # a link that keeps nothing alive

fn same_target(cam: Hud, hud: Hud) -> bool:
    return cam.target is hud.target            # one address compare

fn main():
    boss = Enemy()
    cam = Hud(target=weakref boss)
    hud = Hud(target=weakref boss)
    println(same_target(cam, hud))             # the same enemy
    mem.drop(owns boss)                        # the enemy ends; both links keep its block
    println(same_target(cam, hud))             # still the same (ended) enemy
    hud.target = None
    println(same_target(cam, hud))             # one link now names nothing
answers.outcome: Compiles. Prints `true`, `true`, `false`. Each test is one compare of the two links' pointers: no header load, no atomic, nothing opened. Today's alternative, opening both links and comparing the opened names, answers `false` once the enemy has ended.

answers.answer: Decided by [TYP-48] 1. `weakref dyn Listener` is a type, as every holder word may stand before `dyn I`. `weakref hud` (a `weakref Hud`) converts to `weakref dyn Listener` at the argument, keeping its word (rule 8), as `owns`, `shares` and `shares mut` values already convert. The opened `l` is a read-only `dyn Listener` view ([GRM-44]). The weak count goes where [OBJ-1] puts it: in every type the program converts to any form of `Listener`, found by following values. A list that also holds links to `thread_shared` listeners opens each link by its own target's header ([WK-12]). A bus that owns its listeners holds `Array[owns dyn Listener]`, which a class object now converts to (rule 8). Whether a listener may change itself through the opened link is decided by the existing rules ([BRW-15], and P10's J5-07), not by this one.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints `hud 1`. Each link is one pointer (8 bytes); the table is found through the Hud header's type index ([OBJ-2]). C++'s `weak_ptr<IListener>` is 16 bytes. Opening a link to a one-thread listener on its own thread is one header test with no count change; C++'s `lock()` costs an atomic compare-exchange loop plus an atomic decrement. A listener that has ended is skipped by the `exists as` test.

other_cases.case: `thread_shared dyn Sink`, a log sink that worker threads share: `sink: thread_shared dyn Sink = thread_shared FileSink(path=String("log.txt"))`, then `thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared sink: sink.write("started"))`.
other_cases.settled: Compiles. Conversion 8 keeps `thread_shared`, and `sink.write` dispatches through the header's type index. If any implementation that may reach the call changes its object other than through a lock or an `Atomic`, the call is E7014 ([DSP-5]). FileSink's fields were checked ThreadShared on the line that made it (verdict 165). Its markers are [THR-8]'s, judged by what it may hold (P01).

other_cases.case: `sharedref mut dyn Damageable`: a turret and the HUD both hold a changeable link to whatever they target (an `Enemy` or a `Crate`): `target: sharedref mut dyn Damageable`, `Turret(target=sharedref mut crate)`.
other_cases.settled: Compiles. On one thread both holders may change the target through its methods (verdict 3), and every view into it ends at a reshape made through either holder ([LT-46]). A whole value put through the link is E3023 ([TYP-48] 5): no place has the type `dyn Damageable`. A type holding one never goes to another thread (verdict 164). It is one pointer for a class or shared target, and data plus table for an inline place.

The `mem.swap` case is refused at the call that converts `hud`, since swap writes whole values into its parameters, a fact read from its body. `ref mut this.child` for a field `child: Widget` that holds a `Hud` takes `w = Widget()`: the place's type is `Widget`.

other_cases.settled: E3023 at the write: a `dyn` view's place is always some kind other than `dyn Shape`. The help gives `if r is Square as ref mut q:` and `q = Square(side=2.0)` under it, or changing it through its methods.

A score changed elsewhere after the sort leaves the list out of order, and `binary_search` gives [HASH-3]'s answer, as for any list changed after sorting. design.prior_art:
- **C++.** `operator==` on two `shared_ptr`s compares `get()`, the addresses, and `std::hash<shared_ptr>` hashes the address. Contents need an explicit `*a == *b`, so the meaning of `==` changes when a value moves into a `shared_ptr`. `weak_ptr` has no `==`; ordering is `owner_before`/`owner_less`, and identity equality and hashing arrive only in C++26 (`owner_equal`, `owner_hash`). `weak_ptr<IListener>` is 16 bytes, and `lock()` costs an atomic compare-exchange loop and a later atomic decrement, even on one thread. `Derived&` converts to `Base&` (assignment through it slices), but `Derived*&` to `Base*&` is refused, which is Ember's class-object case, since an Ember class place holds a pointer. Falls short: `==` has two meanings, weak links cost atomics, nothing is checked for aliasing.
- **Rust.** `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` delegate `PartialEq`, `Ord`, `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` to `T`; auto-deref reads through for method calls. Identity is a function, `Rc::ptr_eq`. `Weak` has no `PartialEq`, but has a `Debug` that prints `(Weak)`, so structs holding one still derive `Debug`; `Weak::ptr_eq` compares allocations, and two `Weak::new()` compare equal. `&mut T` is invariant; `&mut T` coerces to `&mut dyn Trait`, and no whole value can be assigned through it (it is unsized), exactly [TYP-48] 5's dyn case. `Rc<K>` is a fine map key because nothing changes `K` through an `Rc`; `Rc<RefCell<K>>` is not `Hash`. `ptr::eq` on wide pointers compares vtables, which can be duplicated (hence `ptr::addr_eq`). Changing through shared owners needs `RefCell`, with run-time borrow flags.
- **Java.** Arrays are covariant, so `Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 1` compiles and throws `ArrayStoreException` at run time: the whole-write hole [TYP-48] 5 refuses when compiling. A `HashMap` whose key object is changed after insertion silently loses the entry. `System.identityHashCode` is kept in the object header because the collector moves objects, the same reason Ember's moved objects keep an identity number.
- **Swift.** `===` is identity for class references; `==` comes from `Equatable`. `weak var` works only on class-bound types, weak references are zeroed through a side table, and every retain/release is atomic.
- **Go.** Interface `==` compares the dynamic type and the value, so it compares the kind as well as the address, like [TYP-48] 4. Go 1.24's `weak.Pointer[T]` values compare equal when made from the same pointer, even after collection. Pointers to distinct zero-size variables 'may or may not be equal'. Garbage collected.
- **Python.** `==` is `__eq__`: contents for lists, identity by default for objects; `is` is identity, and `x is 5` warns since 3.8. Mutable built-ins (`list`, `dict`, `set`) are unhashable, so a key that may change is refused, as [TYP-48] 2 refuses one through a sharing word. `a += b` changes a list in place, seen through every name, while `a = a + b` makes a new list: [TYP-48] 6's split.
- **C.** `restrict` is the programmer's promise, unchecked; comparing a pointer into freed memory is undefined (C11 6.2.4), which is why the `is` compare on links rests on blocks that stay in place (OBJ-3, P02).
- **Ember.** Under the rule Ember takes Rust's contents-`==` and its invariance of whole writes through changeable views, Python's `is` as an operator, its `+=` and its refusal of changeable keys, Go's (address, kind) identity and weak-pointer equality, and Java's header identity hash. It adds compile-time refusal of meaningless `is` tests and of whole writes into narrower places, and single-pointer weak dyn links with no atomics on the owning thread.
design.cost:
- **Holder words before `dyn I` and base classes:** no new field and no new table.
  - One pointer (8 bytes): `weakref dyn I`, `shares dyn I`, `thread_shared dyn I`, `owns dyn I` of a class object, and a `sharedref mut dyn I` of a class object or shared value. The table is found through the header's type index ([OBJ-2]).
  - Two words (data, table): a view of an inline value (`ref dyn I`, `sharedref mut dyn I`), as C++'s `I&` plus the object's vptr.
  - Against C++: `weak_ptr<IListener>` is 16 bytes, so Ember's link is half the size.
- **Opening a `weakref dyn I` on its own thread:** a one-thread target, one header test and no count; a `thread_shared` target, [WK-12]'s test and one plain add. A link place that may name both kinds adds one address mask, one load of the memory chunk's header and a branch, at opening and at the link's end; a place of one kind adds nothing. C++'s `lock()`: an atomic CAS loop, plus an atomic decrement when the `shared_ptr` ends.
- **A call through it:** one table lookup through the type index, cached per value ([DSP-3]), against C++'s vptr load.
- **Read-through** (argument, conversion, operand, field, print, `==`, `Hash`, `Ord`, `in`, lookup, loop, index): one load from the holder's pointer at a fixed offset (8, 12 or 32 bytes of header), no count operation ([RC-2a], [RC-2b]): C's `*p`. A probe against held elements makes no block, where probing with a new `shares` value would cost an allocation, a header and two count operations per lookup.
- **`is`:** one pointer compare, C's `p == q`; for a `weakref`, no header load and no atomic; for two `dyn` views of inline values, one more type-index compare, only when the addresses are equal; for a zero-size type, no instruction.
- **Identity hash of a class object:** for a class family some `weakref` names and the program hashes by identity, one load of a 32-bit number from the header per hash, where C hashes the pointer with no load (Java pays the same header load); 4 bytes at offset 12, free where the first field is 8-byte aligned; one store when the object is made and one when verdict 114's hand-over moves it. Every other class: unchanged.
- **Memory:** nothing else is added to any value. The weak count stays where [OBJ-1] puts it: 4 bytes in each object a link may name. C++'s control block uses 16 bytes or more.
- **Compile time only, zero cost while running:** the whole-write rule ([TYP-48] 5, E3023), the `Hash` condition (E2040), what `is not` proves, E2119 at a call, E2020 for unopened links and `is None` on them, E2123, E2150, E2037, E3023, E7014. A program that needs two nested views proved apart pays `assert_disjoint`'s two compares, where `is not` was one compare and unsound.

readability.note: The after is shorter and adds no word. `weakref dyn Listener` uses two existing words in the order `owns dyn Shape` already uses. `a.target is b.target` replaces a nested opening that also gave the wrong answer once the enemy had ended. Listeners no longer need a common base class. The leaderboard lines `total(scores)`, `println(scores)` and `scores == others` are exactly the lines one writes for a plain list. The repairs add nothing to ordinary code: a whole value through a converted changeable view, a changeable shared key, `is None` on a link and `is not` between nested views are refused where they would corrupt memory or lose a key, each with a line that compiles. Nothing changes in code that holds nothing shared.

design.compiler_does:
1. **Types.** Accepts every holder word before `dyn I` and before a base class, and converts a class object held alone to `owns dyn I`. Converts at every coercion site, keeping the word, and gives a holder every conversion its held value takes (rules 4, 6 and 8 after the read-through). Lays each form out as one pointer when its target lives in a block with a header (the table reached through the type index), and as data plus table otherwise.
2. **Weak counts and header kinds.** Follows values through every route (a conversion, a read-through, a parameter, a field, a call) to find which types a `weakref` may name, and gives those the weak count ([OBJ-1]). Keeps, with each function, the links it makes from a parameter or `this` (in the interface file across a package's edge, [EFF-4]) and checks at each call that the argument lives on its own (E2119 at the call). Finds, for each link place, which headers its targets may have: one kind, a fixed protocol; both kinds, the chunk-header test at opening and at the link's end. Takes `thread_shared` blocks from chunks of their own.
3. **Read-through.** At each operand, argument, conversion, field, method, loop, `in`, lookup, index, print, compare and hash through an owner or a view:
   - inserts the load at the holder's fixed offset;
   - picks the held type's implementation, monomorphised (no table, no count);
   - checks the read or change against the holder's word and every read/change rule (BRW-1, BRW-18, RC-5, E3023, E7014, `guarded by`);
   - compares and hashes a probe against held elements as the held values, making nothing.
4. **Interfaces of holders.** Gives each owner and view `Eq`, `Ord`, `Display`, `Debug` and `Printable` when its held type has them, and `Hash` where the bodies of `hash` and `eq` read only what cannot change while it is held (through a sharing word: identity, `let` fields, a `thread_shared` value's plain fields); otherwise E2040 at the type. Gives a `weakref` a `Debug` that prints the link's type and pointer, reading nothing at the target.
5. **`is`.**
   - Classifies each operand by its type (an address of its own or not) and refuses E2150 or E2037 from the operands' types alone; refuses `is None` on a link (E2020).
   - Emits one pointer compare: no header, no atomics; a type-index compare only for `dyn` views of inline values whose addresses are equal; constant `true` for zero-size types.
   - Uses `a is not b` as a fact about the two heads only; checks a change through a part of `a` against `b` path against path, with two paths possibly one value when one's type may be the other's; gives a range fact (noalias, overlapping arguments) from `is not` only where neither may lie inside the other.
6. **Whole writes.** Works out, for each changeable view parameter, whether the function may write a whole value into it (`=`, `mem.swap`, `mem.replace`, `mem.take`, or passing it to a parameter that may), keeps that with the function as [BRW-21]'s facts are, and refuses (E3023) at a call that gives it a derived class's place, at any whole write through a `dyn` view, and at a whole write through a kept view that, following values, a derived class's place may reach, naming the line that made it.
7. **Holder assignment.** Refuses `=` of a plain value of the held type on a holder name (E2123 or E2020, giving both lines); compiles a compound assignment through a holder as a change of the held value (`…Assign`, or `a op b` written into it), refusing it for a class object without `…Assign` (E2103).
8. **Identity numbers.** For class families some `weakref` names and the program hashes by identity, places a 32-bit identity number at header offset 12, sets it when the object is made, copies it in verdict 114's move, and hashes it.
9. **Unopened links.** Reports E2020 at any read of, or question about, a `weakref`'s target that was not opened first, with the `exists as` line (and, for `==`, the `is` line) to write.
10. **Calls through holder dyn forms.** Works out what each call may change from every implementation that may reach it ([DSP-5]). A `thread_shared dyn I` call whose implementation changes the object directly is refused (E7014), naming that implementation.

Every mistake is refused when compiling. None stops the program, and none is undefined behaviour.

design.verdicts:
Every involved verdict is kept; none is revisited.
- **3:** `sharedref mut dyn I` follows it word for word: on one thread both holders change it (through its methods and fields); on two threads, only under a lock.
- **9, 10, 11:** a `weakref` is still opened with `exists as` before use, now also before `is None`, and `weakref x` still makes another link. Verdict 11's counting of every link is what keeps a target's block in place, so `is` on links is exact (with P02's rule for managers' memory).
- **23:** read-through gives each owner exactly what it could do, and the first owner keeps its rights; the `Hash` condition follows from it (another owner may change the value).
- **27:** `is` keeps its two jobs, "is of this kind" before a type name and "the same object" before a value. The rule spells out, for every holder, what "the same object" already meant, and gives `is` no third job.
- **61, 94:** `thread_shared fn()` stays the function type's word for which threads may run it; [TYP-48] states this with its reason, and verdict 94's spawn line compiles as today.
- **79:** copying is untouched ([OWN-8], [STR-5]).
- **86, 128:** the new facts (whole writes into a view parameter, links made from a parameter) are worked out from bodies and judged by what callers pass, as verdict 86 infers what a function changes and verdict 128 follows callers.
- **101:** the chunk header that already gives the making thread (fix 1) also gives the header kind, so no flag is added to an object.
- **114:** kept as it stands. Its move now also carries the object's identity number, so a set or map handed with the object still finds it; this is a consequence the owner should hear beside verdict 114.
- Also kept as they stand: **103** (no sharing word before a one-owner place), **159, 160** (`Hud(target=weakref boss)` and `bus.listeners.push(weakref hud)` take no word), **164** (a `sharedref mut dyn I` never goes to another thread), **165** (each `thread_shared dyn I` value was checked where it was made), **166** (a scoped task's `is` makes and ends nothing).

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. Owners and views read as their value everywhere, conversions included: `==` compares the value (a class object's stays identity), and a holder hashes as its value where nothing another holder may change is read. `is` asks whether any two holders reach the same value, `weakref` links included, and `is not` proves nothing about parts. Every holder word may stand before `dyn I`; a changeable view converted to a base class or an interface takes no whole value of another type.

println(scores == others)         # true: the two lists are equal
println(scores is others)         # false: two lists
println(cam.target is hud.target) # true: the same enemy
listeners: Array[weakref dyn Listener] = []
reset(ref mut hud)                # E3023: reset would put a Widget where a Hud is

No count operation is emitted, and each `is` is one pointer compare. The holes the breakers found are refused when compiling, each with a line that compiles.

options_for_owner.summary: As A, except that `==` and hashing of two owners compare which value they own, as C++'s `shared_ptr` does.

fn same(a: Array[int], b: Array[int]) -> bool:
    return a == b
println(same(scores, others))      # true: through plain parameters the lists are compared
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles. The same two values compare `false` directly and `true` once passed through a plain parameter, so `==` gives a different answer depending on the route. `==` and `is` mean the same thing on owners. A `Map[shares Key, V]` keys by identity, so a key changed elsewhere is not lost, but a lookup by an equal key made elsewhere misses.

options_for_owner.summary: Keep today's lists. `is` takes only class objects and views. A `weakref` names a class, so listeners share a base class. Owners read through only for method calls.
options_for_owner.outcome: `cam.target is hud.target` is E2150, and the error table is corrected to match. The opened form answers `false` once the enemy has ended. `Array[weakref dyn Listener]` is refused. `println(scores)` and `scores == others` are E2040, and `total(scores)` needs its parameter written as `shares mut Array[int]`. The whole-write and `is not` holes still need [TYP-48] 5 and 4's last bullet, since they exist today for `ref mut` upcasts and `sharedref mut` structs.

recommendation.reason: The word before a type says who holds a value, not what the value is, so the value should read, print, compare and hash the same under every word (Rust's Rc, Python's lists). B makes `==` give two answers for the same values depending on whether they passed through a parameter. `is` already spells 'the same object' (verdict 27), and A only makes it reach every holder, at one address compare. Weak links get the 8-byte, atomic-free `weakref dyn I` that C++ and Swift cannot offer, and listeners need no base class. A's limits refuse only what would corrupt memory or silently lose a key: a whole value of another type through a converted changeable view (Rust's and C++'s rule), a key another holder may change (Rust's and Python's rule), and an `is not` asked to prove more than it can. Each is decided when compiling, with a line that compiles. Nothing is added to code that does nothing unusual; at run time A adds only one header load per identity hash in classes that may move, and one chunk-header test at link places that mix header kinds. Checklist items 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11, 12 and 13.

repairs.answer: For maps and sets: real, answered by [TYP-48] 2's `Hash` sentence, as for safety 3 (E2040 at the type, with copies or a class as the fix). For ordering: `Ord` stays through every holder. A sort or a binary search reads values as they are when it runs and keeps no placement, so a list changed elsewhere after sorting gives [HASH-3]'s answers, as any list changed after sorting does. Std has no container that keeps elements placed by `Ord`, and refusing `roster.sort()` for `Array[shares Score]` would refuse a correct leaderboard.

Std implements [STD-8]'s `Contains` and [STD-12]'s `AsKey` that way, composing with P13's text probes. `me in roster` is true with no block made, and `hits.contains(boss)` likewise. repairs.answer: Real. A link's `Debug` shows the link, as a class object's shows the object: `weakref Enemy at 0x…`, or `None`. It reads nothing at the target and opens nothing, so `Hud` keeps STR-5's implicit `Debug` and `println(hud)` compiles. `Eq` stays refused (`is` instead), and `Display` is not given. repairs.answer: Real. Rule 8 now converts a value held alone to `owns dyn I`: an `owns T`, and a class object, which is held alone in its own block as `owns` holds (one pointer, no count). E2114 refuses only `owns` written before a class type. `bus.owned.push(owns Hud(name=String("hud")))` compiles, the `owns` there being the call's word (verdict 149).

repairs.hole: Engineering 9 (medium): `hp += 1` writes through a holder, but `pos += v` with only `Add` falls back to `pos = pos + v`, and nothing says what `=` on a holder name does, so the two spellings may differ by held type.
repairs.answer: Real. [TYP-48] 6 and [TYP-21] now state both. `=` on a holder name gives it another holder and says the word, as `owns` and `weakref` places already do; `hp = hp + 1` is E2123 with both lines (`hp += 1`; `hp = shares mut (hp + 1)`). A compound assignment through a holder changes the held value for every held type, by its `…Assign` or by writing `a op b` into it, so `pos += Vec2(x=1.0, y=0.0)` moves the position the camera sees. This is Python's split: `+=` changes a shared list in place, while `a = a + b` makes a new one. A class object, never replaced in its block ([CLS-7]), changes that way only by its `…Assign` (E2103 otherwise).

design.open_risks:
1. **P10 overlap (keys).** [TYP-48] 2 now settles which holders are `Hash`. A plain class key whose hand-written content hash reads a field changed through a link (no holder word involved) is still P10's no-change promise; until P10 is answered, [HASH-3]'s wrong answer remains possible there (never undefined behaviour). Present the two together if the owner asks about keys.
2. **P02 dependency.** `is` on links is exact only with P02's rule that a link into a manager's memory ends before the manager gives it back; J3-12 must be asked after J5-02. The chunk-header test of [WK-12] also assumes P02/P03 place `thread_shared` blocks made in a manager where the kind can be read; that needs saying with their answers.
3. **Verdict 114 consequence.** The identity number changes the header of class families that some `weakref` names and that the program hashes by identity (4 bytes, often padding), and adds one load per identity hash in those families. It must be put to the owner beside verdict 114. The alternative is rehashing the handed-over sets and maps in the move: no steady cost, but a hash number a program keeps itself goes wrong, which is why I did not recommend it.
4. **P01 overlap.** The thread markers of `weakref dyn I`, `sharedref mut dyn I` and `thread_shared dyn I`, and of a list mixing link kinds, come from P01's "an erased type by what it may hold".
5. **P11, P13, P18, P20 overlap.** `copy of` and `Clone` through a holder, `owns cast s as Circle` (J2-10), and `for x in owns scores` from a non-sole owner (E3013) are P11's. The probe rule composes with P13's text probes, and must be worded together with them. Whether `runtime` may stand before the new dyn forms is P18's. Rule 11 after read-through is P20's.
6. **Narrowings of today's text, to say plainly to the owner.**
   - EXP-9's "(or two views)" admitted `Span`/`StrView` operands and plain `Copy` views; the rule refuses them (E2150), as the E2150 row already did.
   - BRW-17's "different types", and `if a is not b:` as a proof, are restated ([TYP-48] 4). A program that relied on them for two views where one may lie inside the other (a `sharedref mut` struct and a field of it) is now refused, with `assert_disjoint` as the help. Such programs were unsound, but some may compile today. SIMD-3 gives fewer noalias facts there.
   - [TYP-48] 5 refuses a whole write through a `ref mut` base-class parameter given a derived class's place. Today's rule 8 did not say whether such a call converts; if it did, some programs compile today and would now be refused.
   - [DSJ-1] is stated for any two views, not only spans.
   - IV.11's "one level" of owner becomes "level by level"; the zero-size `is` answer (always true) is new; `=` of a plain value on a `shares` holder, today undecided, is refused.
7. **New inferred facts in interfaces.** "Writes a whole value into this view parameter" and "makes a link from this parameter" join a function's interface facts ([EFF-4]). A change to a `pub` body that adds one is reported as an interface change, as [BRW-10] already does for what a method touches.
8. **TYP-13 niche list.** Widening it (`Option[shares T]` is one pointer) is a layout guarantee. It does not touch the FFI sentence.
9. **J5-13 example.** A listener that changes itself on an event needs `exists as ref mut` through the list. Whether a plain loop name may open a link `ref mut` is P10's J5-07 or BRW-15's, so the example's `on_event` only reads.
10. **Process.** This round was read-only. Through the shell I only listed, searched and printed files (`ls`, `grep`, `sed -n`, `wc`, `cut`); nothing was written, built or run. Round 0's one `json.load` was reported then.
11. **Not checked.** Nothing here was run on a compiler; the task allows reading only.

design.rule:
A String and a StrView holding the same text are the same text, and the language treats them that way in two places.

(1) Storing. A collection written with no type owns the text it holds. This applies to a list as it already does to a set or a map, at any depth (inside a tuple, an Option or a nested collection). An element that is a value, not a literal, keeps its own type and fixes the element type, as numbers already do. Owning text that is written in the program costs nothing. A String made from such text points at it where it lies, with no allocation and no copy, until a change needs room of its own.

(2) Comparing and looking up. Each comparison reads both sides where they are: ==, !=, <, ordering, a match arm's literal, x in c, contains, index_of, binary_search, and every map or set lookup. Text compares with text whichever form each side holds, a list compares with a span of comparable elements, and every container accepts as the thing to look for any value its elements compare with. Nothing is converted, copied or allocated.

The library states (2) as ordinary interface implementations, spelled as Add[StrView] already is: `Eq[Rhs = Self]` and `Ord[Rhs = Self]`, with String implementing `Eq[StrView]`. A program's own types and containers therefore take part by the same rule, with no exception for a type or a construct.
design.spec_text:
CHANGED [TYP-38], second bullet, replaced: "A map literal `{k: v, …}` is a `Map[K, V]` (insertion-ordered, `[STD-11]`); a set literal `{a, …}` is a `Set[T]`. A repeated key keeps its first position and its last value, as Python's `dict` does; `{1, 1}` is `{1}`. With no type written, text that a collection literal holds is a `String`, whatever the kind of collection, since a collection written with no type owns what it holds. This covers a list's, set's or map's element, key or value, at any depth: inside a tuple, an `Option` or a nested collection. So `["ann", "bob"]` is an `Array[String]`, `{"ann": 1}` a `Map[String, int]` and `[("ann", 3)]` an `Array[(String, int)]`. Making these Strings allocates nothing (`[TXT-9]`). An element that is a value, not a literal, keeps its own type and fixes the element type, as `[x, 1]` for `x: i32` is an `Array[i32]`: `[name, "bob"]` for `name: StrView` is an `Array[StrView]`, the literal converting to it. An element type that later uses fix (`[]`, `[TYP-23]`) and that only text literals give is `String`. A collection of views is written with its type (`labels: Array[StrView] = ["a", "b"]`, `[STD-11]`)."

CHANGED [TYP-15], example: "`names: Array[StrView] = ["ann", "bob"]` is a list of views of text written in the program, which may live as long as the program".

CHANGED [TXT-1]: "`String` owns a heap buffer, or holds text written in the program until it is changed (`[TXT-9]`), with the same guarantee." The IV.1 table row "Collection" gains: "(a `String` may hold text written in the program instead, `[TXT-9]`)".

CHANGED [TXT-9], added after its first sentence: "A `String` made from text written in the program holds that text where it lies, with no allocation and no copy. Such text is a literal where a `String` is expected, or the argument of `String(v)` when `v` is a view whose region is static (`[LT-3]`). Its `capacity()` is 0, and dropping it frees nothing. It is an ordinary `String`: it may be changed, handed over and shared, and `copy of` it holds the same text, again allocating nothing. A change that writes its bytes first gives it room of its own (`[TXT-11]`)." The sentence "The allocation happens at the literal and is reported there (`Alloc`)" is deleted. The last sentence becomes: "A `StrView` value never converts implicitly: `String(s)` makes a `String` of your own, which copies `s` unless it is text written in the program."

CHANGED [TXT-5]: "`StrView` → `String` is written `String(s)` and allocates and copies, except for text written in the program (`[TXT-9]`)".

CHANGED [TXT-11], added: "A `String` that holds text written in the program (`[TXT-9]`) has `capacity()` 0. `push`, `push_str`, `insert`, `reserve` and `+=` give it room of its own as growth always does. `remove(i)` does so too, and so carries `Alloc`. `truncate` and `clear` change only its length and never allocate."

CHANGED [PHIL-2]: the item "a string literal in a position that produces a `String` (`[TXT-9]`)" is removed from the allocating forms, and this is added: "a `String` made from text written in the program allocates nothing until a change gives it room of its own, which is container growth (`[TXT-9]`)".

CHANGED, the standard interfaces (IV.8):
  interface Eq[Rhs = Self]:
      fn eq(other: Rhs) -> bool                  # ==, !=
  interface Ord[Rhs = Self]: needs Eq[Rhs]:
      fn cmp(other: Rhs) -> Ordering             # <, <=, >, >=, sort, binary_search; a float's `<` stays IEEE
`T: needs Eq` and `T: needs Ord` mean `Eq[T]` and `Ord[T]`, as `Add` means `Add[T]`. `@derive(Eq)` and `@derive(Ord)` give the `Self` instance.

NEW [TXT-12] One text, owned or viewed: "A `String` and a `StrView` are one text in two holdings, and every comparison reads both where they are. std implements `Eq[StrView]` and `Ord[StrView]` for `String`, and `Eq[String]` and `Ord[String]` for `StrView`, comparing bytes as `StrView`'s own do. It does the same for `Array[T]`, `[T; N]`, `Span[T]` and `MutSpan[T]` with one another, element by element, when `T: needs Eq[U]` (`Ord[U]`). `Option`, `Result`, tuples, `Map` and `Set` compare with their own kind when their parts compare (a `Map` or `Set` as sets of entries, `[STD-16]`). Nothing is converted, copied or allocated. A `String` hashes as its `StrView` does, and a list as its `Span` (`[HASH-1]`). A program's own type takes part the same way, by implementing `Eq[Q]` (`extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:`). An implementation of `Eq[Q]` for `K` and one of `Eq[K]` for `Q` MUST agree, and so MUST `Ord`'s. One that does not gives `[HASH-3]`'s wrong answers, never undefined behaviour."

CHANGED [TYP-21], added: "`a == b` and `a != b` call the `eq` of `Eq[B]`, and `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` the `cmp` of `Ord[B]` (floats keep IEEE, `[TYP-37]`). The instance is the one `[TYP-24]` chooses by `b`'s own type, a text literal counting as a `StrView`. So `cmd == "quit"` for a `String` `cmd` compares the text and makes no `String`."

CHANGED [TYP-24]: "an untyped literal counting as its default type (`int`, `f64`), and a text literal as a `StrView`".

CHANGED [TYP-36]: the `Eq` and `Ord` cells of the `String`, `StrView`, `Array[T]` and `[T; N]` rows add "and with its view or owner, `[TXT-12]`".

CHANGED [HASH-1]: "values equal under `Eq`, of one type or of two (`Eq[Rhs]`), MUST hash equally".

CHANGED [STD-8]: "std implements it for `Set` and `Map` by key, for any `Q: needs AsKey[K]`. For `Array`, `Span`, `MutSpan`, `[T; N]` and every std container that reads as a `Span`, it implements it for every `Q` with `T: needs Eq[Q]`, as a linear scan: `who in names`, for `who: StrView` and `names: Array[String]`, compares each element with the text. ..." The rest is unchanged.

CHANGED [STD-15]: "`index_of(x)` takes any `x: Q` with `T: needs Eq[Q]`, and `binary_search(x)` any `x: Q` with `T: needs Ord[Q]`".

CHANGED [STD-12]: "Lookup methods, `m[k]` and `k in m` accept any `Q: needs AsKey[K]`. `AsKey[K]` holds for every `Q: needs Hash` with `K: needs Eq[Q]` (`[TXT-12]`): `K` itself, `StrView` for `String` and `String` for `StrView`, and `Span[T]` for `Array[T]` and `[T; N]`. Like `ThreadShared`, it is written only in bounds. A hand-written implementation is `E2040`, whose help reads: "`AsKey` follows from `Eq`: write `extend K implements Eq[Q]:`". A lookup hashes `q` and compares it with `K`'s `==`, so it never converts or copies a key. ..." `ToKey` is unchanged, and std implements `ToKey[String]` for `StrView` and `ToKey[Array[T]]` for `Span[T]` when `T: needs Clone`.

CHANGED [CTL-5], added: "A literal pattern matches where `subject == literal` holds, the `==` chosen as for any comparison (`[TYP-21]`). A text pattern against a `String` subject compares the text and makes no `String`."

answers.answer: The list is an Array[String], as the set is a Set[String]: a collection written with no type owns its text, whatever kind of collection it is. Each String points at the program's text, so writing the list costs no allocation per name. Pushing the String read from input compiles. (The draft's `seen.insert(...)` is `seen.add(...)` in STD-16, written with `owns` as verdicts 147 and 149 require.)
answers.code:
fn main():
    names = ["ann", "bob"]              # Array[String]: the program's text, no allocation per name
    seen = {"ann", "bob"}               # Set[String], as today
    newcomer = input()                  # a String the program reads
    seen.add(owns copy of newcomer)
    names.push(owns newcomer)           # a String into a list of Strings
    println(names, seen)
answers.outcome: Compiles. For the input `cid` it prints `['ann', 'bob', 'cid'] {'ann', 'bob', 'cid'}`. Five allocations happen: the list's buffer, the set's table, the copy of `newcomer`, and the growth of the list and of the set. None is made for the four literal names: each is {address of the program's text, length 3, capacity 0}. A program that wants 16-byte views writes `names: Array[StrView] = ["ann", "bob"]`, and then the push is E2020, whose help gives that typed line with `Array[String]`.

answers.answer: A list of Strings is searched with a text view, exactly as a set or map of Strings is. Array[String] implements Contains[StrView] because String implements Eq[StrView]. The literal needle keeps its own type, StrView, because TYP-24 chooses the instance by the needle's own type before any coercion, so no String is made for the test.
answers.outcome: Compiles. For the input `  trudy ` it prints `go away`, then `trudy is banned`. Each test costs one length compare per element and a byte compare where the lengths agree, which is what a C loop of `len == n && memcmp(...) == 0` costs. Nothing is allocated, so both lines are allowed in a `@noalloc` function. `5 in banned` stays E2226, since String has no Eq[int].

other_cases.case: `cmd = input()` then `if cmd == "quit":`, the commonest text test in any program. The spec's own `input() == "m"` (p07 551) is the same. Today Eq's `eq(other: Self)` leaves open whether the literal becomes a String, which would be an allocation per test.
other_cases.settled: String's Eq[StrView] is chosen by the literal's own type (TYP-21, TYP-24). The text is compared and no String is made.

other_cases.case: `match cmd:` with arms `"quit" => ...` and `"help" => ...` on a String subject.
other_cases.settled: A literal pattern matches where `cmd == "quit"` holds (CTL-5), so each arm compares the text and none makes a String. The compiler may test the length first and then the bytes, as a C switch on strings is hand-written.

other_cases.case: `log = []`, then `log.push(owns "start")`, then `log.push(owns line)` with `line: String`.
other_cases.settled: The element type that later uses fix comes only from a text literal at the first push, so it is String (TYP-38), and both pushes fit. The literal's String costs nothing.

other_cases.case: `[name, "bob"]` where `name` is a StrView value, and then where `name` is a String.
other_cases.settled: Values fix the element type, as `[x, 1]` does for numbers. With a StrView `name` the list is an Array[StrView] bounded by `name`'s text (TYP-15). With a String `name` it is an Array[String]. The literal converts either way.

other_cases.case: `index = {name: i for i, name in NAMES.iter().enumerate()}`, where NAMES is a static Array[StrView]. Appendix H (p26 1215) had to add a type annotation, because untyped keys were String and a view does not convert.
other_cases.settled: The comprehension's keys are values of type StrView, so the map is a Map[StrView, int] of static views and compiles with no annotation.

other_cases.case: `row in grid`, where `grid: Array[Array[int]]` and `row: Span[int]`; and `tokens == expected`, where `tokens: Array[StrView]` and `expected: Array[String]`.
other_cases.settled: Array[T] is Eq[Span[U]] and Eq[Array[U]] when T: needs Eq[U] (TXT-12). Both compare element by element, and nothing is copied.

other_cases.case: `cache: Map[Array[u8], Mesh]` looked up with `cache.get(bytes)`, where `bytes: Span[u8]`; and `line in KEYWORDS`, where `KEYWORDS: Set[StrView]` and `line: String`.
other_cases.settled: AsKey[K] holds for every Q: needs Hash with K: needs Eq[Q] (STD-12). Span[u8] looks up Array[u8] keys and String looks up StrView keys, with no key made or copied. A list hashes as its Span and a String as its StrView (HASH-1).

other_cases.case: A program's own `struct Ident: text: String`, with `extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:`, then `"main" in idents` where `idents: Array[Ident]`.
other_cases.settled: This compiles by the same blanket Contains implementation std uses: a program's types follow the rule exactly as String does. A program's own container writes `[Q, T: needs Eq[Q]]` above `fn contains(x: Q) -> bool` and gets the same.

other_cases.case: `names.binary_search(who)` on a sorted Array[String] with `who: StrView`.
other_cases.settled: binary_search takes any Q with T: needs Ord[Q] (STD-15). String's Ord[StrView] orders by bytes, the order the list was sorted in, so no String is made.

other_cases.case: `@noalloc fn status() -> String: return "idle"`, and a struct field default `name: String = "anon"` in a frame loop.
other_cases.settled: A String of text written in the program allocates nothing (TXT-9). The first now compiles under @noalloc (today it is E4001), and the default costs three stores per object.

other_cases.case: `s = String("hello")`, then `s.remove(0)`; and the same inside a @noalloc function that was lent `ref mut s: String`.
other_cases.settled: remove first gives the String room of its own: one allocation and a copy of 5 bytes, once, so it never writes the program's text. remove therefore carries Alloc (TXT-11), and the @noalloc function is E4001, whose help names FixedString[N]. truncate and clear stay allocation-free.

other_cases.case: `xs.iter().find(owns fn(e) => e == who)` over an Array[String] with `who: StrView`. Today E2226's own help line needs `e.as_str() == who` to be sure it compiles.
other_cases.settled: `ref String` implements Eq as String does (TYP-36), so `e == who` compiles as written, and E2226's help line compiles for text.

other_cases.case: String + StrView (P06's J2-04).
other_cases.settled: This stays P06's question. Its option A spells the operator `Add[StrView, Output = String]`, the same right-hand-type spelling as Eq[StrView] here, so the two rules agree whatever P06 decides.

design.prior_art:
C++
- `std::string` compares with `const char*` and `std::string_view` (C++17 and C++20 overloads), so `std::find(v.begin(), v.end(), sv)` and C++23 `std::ranges::contains` take a view.
- Associative containers look up by a view only with an opt-in transparent comparator: `std::set<std::string, std::less<>>` since C++14, and a transparent hash plus equality for the unordered ones since C++20.
- So the default `std::set<std::string>::find("x")` still builds a temporary string. That allocation is exactly J6-13's.
- `std::vector<std::string> v = {"a", "b"}` copies every literal: inline up to 15 bytes in libstdc++, on the heap beyond that, at 32 bytes per element.
- `auto v = {"a", "b"}` is an `initializer_list<const char*>`.

Rust
- String implements `PartialEq<str>` and `PartialEq<&str>`, `Vec<T>` implements `PartialEq<Vec<U>>` where `T: PartialEq<U>`, and HashMap and BTreeMap look up by `Borrow<Q>`. Ember's AsKey plays the role of Borrow.
- But `slice::contains(&T)` and `binary_search` are homogeneous: `v.contains("x")` on a `Vec<String>` is E0308, and the idiom is `v.iter().any(|s| s == "x")`.
- `vec!["a", "b"]` is a `Vec<&str>`, so pushing a String fails and `.to_string()` spreads through code.
- `String::from("x")` always allocates. Free owned literal text needs the opt-in `Cow<'static, str>`.

Swift
- A string literal's default type is String, and `["a", "b"]` is `[String]`.
- A String made from a literal is "immortal": it points at the binary's text, with no allocation and no reference counting, and copies on its first change. Small strings sit inline. This is the model for TXT-9 here.
- But `Array.contains(_:)` needs an Element, so a Substring needle needs `String(sub)` (an allocation) or `contains(where:)`, and `Set<String>.contains` refuses a Substring too.
- `==` between String and Substring works through StringProtocol.

Go, C# and Python
- Each has one immutable, garbage-collected string type, so there is no owned/view split and `slices.Contains` or `in` just work.
- The cost is that text cannot be edited in place without a builder copy, plus the collector.
- .NET 9 added `Dictionary.GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>`, an opt-in view lookup.

Ada and Zig
- Ada.Strings.Unbounded declares `=` and `<` between Unbounded_String and String both ways, written by hand for each pair.
- Zig has no owned string type: `[]const u8` views everywhere, `std.mem.eql`, and StringHashMap keyed by views, with the program managing the memory.

Where each falls short of safe, C-fast and readable
- C++ is fast but opt-in and unsafe (views dangle).
- Rust is safe but homogeneous in list search, and literals into String always allocate.
- Swift has free literals but homogeneous search.
- Go, C# and Python avoid the problem by giving up in-place text and adding a collector.

Ember takes the best of each, always on:
- Rust's `PartialEq<Rhs>` shape, spelled as Ember's own `Add[Rhs]` already is.
- That shape applied to every lookup: contains, index_of, binary_search, map and set lookups, and match. Rust does not do this.
- Swift's free literal String.
- Rust's compile-time view safety.
design.cost:
Costs per operation, against C, worst case first:
- Making a String from text written in the program (a literal where a String is expected, or `String(v)` of a static view) takes three stores: address, length and capacity 0. There is no allocation and no copy. C pays one store for `const char*`. Today Ember pays a malloc and a copy, as C++ std::string past 15 bytes and Rust's `String::from` do.
- An untyped `["ann", "bob"]` costs one allocation for the list's buffer, the same as today's Array[StrView] and as a malloc'd C array. Each element takes 24 bytes: today's StrView takes 16, C's `const char*` 8, and libstdc++'s std::string 32. No element allocates. Untyped map and set literals stop paying one allocation per text key; today they pay it.
- Dropping a String is unchanged. A String with capacity 0 already frees nothing, through the branch every String drop already has (String() and with_capacity(0) allocate nothing).
- The first change to a String of program text costs one allocation and a copy of its length. This is what strdup costs in C, paid once and only by Strings that change. The growth path already exists; when capacity is 0 it copied 0 bytes. remove(i) adds one compare (capacity 0) before its O(n) move.
- `s == "quit"`, `who in names`, `index_of`, a match arm on text, and `Array[String] == Array[StrView]` cost a length compare plus a byte compare per element or arm. That is C's `len == n && memcmp(...) == 0`, with zero allocation. Today's route, where the literal becomes a String, costs an allocation per test.
- binary_search with a view needle costs what it costs with a String.
- Map and Set lookups are unchanged: one hash and one compare.

Where the cost is zero:
- All comparisons and lookups: no run-time check, no conversion, no extra memory.
- Every read of any String.
- Every String drop.
- Compile time: the instance choice is TYP-24's existing rule.

Extra memory beyond C is 8 bytes per String, against a {pointer, length} view, and only where the program keeps owned text. A program that wants 16 bytes writes `Array[StrView]`.

readability.note: The after is shorter and reads as Python. The list needs no type to be added to, and the membership test is `in`, as it already is for a set; the before needs a lambda and an `.as_str()` to be sure `==` compiles. No word, annotation or ceremony is added anywhere. The program is also cheaper than before: the two literal names cost no allocation (before, two), and the test makes no String. The only words left are the ones that state meaning (`owns` at the push, verdicts 147 and 149). The rare program that wants 16-byte views says so with `Array[StrView]`.

design.compiler_does:
1. It types each collection literal written with no type. Elements that are values fix the element type. Where only literals do, text is String at every depth (tuple, Option, nested collection), as numbers are int or f64 today. An element type left open by `[]` and then fixed only by text literals is String.
2. It emits a String made from text written in the program as {address in the read-only image, length, capacity 0}: no allocator call, and no Alloc effect on the line. It does the same for `String(v)` when the region rules (LT-3) prove `v` static. `ember inspect --alloc` stops listing these sites. HR-4 (old images are never unloaded) keeps that text valid across reloads, as it already does for static StrViews.
3. String's library code copies `len` bytes into the first buffer when the capacity is 0; the path exists and copied 0 bytes before. remove(i) tests for capacity 0 before writing. The effect table therefore gives remove Alloc and takes it from literal-String sites.
4. It resolves every ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, `in`, contains, index_of, binary_search, map or set lookup, and literal match arm to the Eq[Q], Ord[Q] or Contains[Q] instance chosen by the needle's own type (TYP-24, a text literal counting as StrView). It monomorphises and inlines the result into a length compare plus memcmp. It may switch text match arms on length, then bytes.
5. It derives AsKey[K] for every Q: needs Hash with K: needs Eq[Q], and the blanket Contains[Q] for every list-like container with T: needs Eq[Q].
6. It gives every refusal a line that compiles. E2226 for a needle that compares with nothing. E2020 at an untyped text list given to a Span[StrView] parameter, with help `names: Array[StrView] = ...` or `Span[String]` on the parameter. E4001 at remove under @noalloc, with help FixedString[N]. E2070 when two instances fit equally, with help `Eq[StrView].eq(a, b)`. E2040 for a hand-written AsKey, with help `extend K implements Eq[Q]:`.
The programmer writes nothing new.
design.misuse:
Every misuse is refused when compiling, with a line that compiles:
- A needle that compares with no element (`5 in names`, a char against Array[String]) is E2226, whose help names the comparison to write.
- A view pushed into an untyped text list (`names.push(owns line.trim())`) is E2020, with help `names.push(owns String(line.trim()))`.
- An untyped text list given to a function taking `Span[StrView]` is E2020 at the call. Its help gives both fixes: write the literal's type, `names: Array[StrView] = ["ann", "bob"]`, or take `Span[String]`.
- `remove(i)` in a @noalloc function on a String it was lent is E4001, naming remove and FixedString[N].
- A comparison that two instances fit equally, both reached by coercion, is E2070, with the `Eq[X].eq(a, b)` form.
- A hand-written AsKey is E2040, with help `extend K implements Eq[Q]:`.

Nothing in safe code can write the program's read-only text, because a String takes room of its own before any byte-writing change. So no crash and no undefined behaviour is possible from the free literal String.

The one case not refused when compiling is a program's own Eq[Q] whose answer disagrees with Q's Eq[K], or whose hash disagrees. It gives HASH-3's wrong answers (a missing key, a false `in`), never undefined behaviour, out-of-bounds access or non-termination. That is today's rule for incoherent Hash and Ord. std's own pairs agree by construction, since both forms compare and hash the same bytes. No run-time check is added anywhere.
design.verdicts:
Every verdict involved is kept; none is revisited.
- 72 ("the loop rule covers lists, maps, sets, strings alike") is kept. This rule carries the same "alike" to literals and lookups.
- 95 (Rust's way for lists and maps while a loop walks them) is kept. Nothing here changes a collection during a walk, and `x in xs` only reads.
- 147 and 149 (owns at the call, push too) are kept. Every push and add in the examples writes `owns`, and `owns copy of` keeps the caller's value.
- 145 and 161 are kept in the spellings used (`owns String(name)`, one call with no brackets).
- 14 ("make the natural way fast; don't add a feature to avoid the work") is followed. Rather than asking programmers to write `Array[StrView]` to avoid allocations, the natural `["ann", "bob"]` is made free.
- 107's spirit (pay nothing the value can do without) is followed by the capacity-0 String.

Rules that are not owner verdicts and do change:
- TXT-9's "the allocation happens at the literal", a spec rule, not a verdict.
- ODR-067 (a lead ruling, not marked as the owner's): AsKey stays the bound's name but becomes derived from Eq[Q] instead of hand-written, so the relation "Q compares with K" has one spelling (checklist 5 and 11).

Rules kept:
- ODR-022 (a lead ruling: an untyped literal is never left open). The element type is decided at the literal; only `[]` stays open, as TYP-23 already allows.
- ODR-055 (equality-based algorithms keep to ==): contains and index_of still use Eq.

Agreement with neighbouring groups:
- P06 (J2-04 A, `Add[StrView, Output = String]`) uses the same right-hand-type spelling.
- P12's read-through for held values agrees with it: `ref`, `owns` and `shares` String compare as String does.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. Text and its view are one text. Any collection written with no type owns its text, and such a String costs nothing while it is the program's own text. Every comparison and lookup takes a String or a view alike (Eq[StrView] on String, as Add[StrView]).
options_for_owner.code:
