names.push(owns newcomer)       # compiles
if who.trim() in banned:         # a view looked for among Strings
    println("go away")
if cmd == "quit":                # the text compared, no String made
    return
options_for_owner.outcome: All compile. Untyped text lists, sets and maps make no allocation per literal, and no String is made for any comparison, lookup or match arm. `names: Array[StrView] = [...]` still gives 16-byte views. `s.remove(i)` on a String of program text takes room of its own first, so remove carries Alloc. A program's own types join by implementing Eq[Q].

options_for_owner.summary: Phase 2's drafts as written. Text in an untyped list is a String made by allocating, as sets and maps do today. A list of Strings is searched with a view (std only).
options_for_owner.code:

names.push(owns newcomer)       # compiles
if who.trim() in banned:         # compiles
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints the same. Every untyped text list now pays one allocation and copy per name where today it pays none, so a read-only keyword table gets slower. Such lists and every literal String are E4001 under @noalloc. A program's own containers cannot search by a view, and `cmd == "quit"` stays undecided.

options_for_owner.summary: Views everywhere. Every untyped collection of text holds views: lists as today, with sets and maps changed to match. Lists are searched with a view.
options_for_owner.code:

names.push(owns newcomer)       # E2020
seen = {"ann"}
seen.add(owns newcomer)         # E2020 now too
options_for_owner.outcome: Zero cost per literal, but the Python-style program is refused for every collection. The help gives `names: Array[String] = [...]`, and those Strings still allocate under today's TXT-9.

options_for_owner.summary: The compiler picks String or StrView for an untyped text list from the function's later uses.
options_for_owner.code:

names.push(owns newcomer)       # this line makes it Array[String]
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles at zero cost when the list is only read. But a line far below changes the literal's type, `names[0]`'s type and which calls accept `names`. This is against ODR-022's 'an untyped literal is never left open'. With A's free String it saves only 8 bytes per element.

options_for_owner.summary: As today. Lists hold views and sets and maps hold Strings. A list of Strings is searched only with a String.
options_for_owner.code:

names.push(owns newcomer)       # E2020

options_for_owner.outcome: The member programs are refused. `"trudy" in banned` and `cmd == "quit"` are undecided: a new String per test, or not.

recommendation.reason:
It is the only option that keeps all three goals together.
- Readability: the Python-style program compiles with no type written, and lists, sets and maps follow one rule.
- Speed: no per-literal allocation (cheaper than today's sets and maps, and than C++ and Rust), and no String made for any comparison, at C's length-plus-memcmp cost.
- Generality: one interface shape that every lookup, every container and a program's own types follow. The spelling is Ember's own (Add[Rhs]), and the compiler does all the work.
B keeps the asymmetry's fix but makes ordinary read-only text lists slower and leaves comparisons undecided. C and E refuse the ordinary program. D hides a type decision in later lines.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: with no type written, should `["ann", "bob"]` be a `vector<string>` (as `{"ann", "bob"}` is already a `set<string>`) whose strings point at the program's text like a `const char*` until changed (Swift does this)? And should `==`, `in` and every lookup on strings take a `string_view` without building a `string`, as a C++ `set<string, less<>>` does?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `names = ["ann", "bob"]` | `Array[StrView]`: two views of the program's text |
| 2 | main | `seen = {"ann", "bob"}` | `Set[String]`: two Strings, two allocations |
| 3 | main | `newcomer = input()` | the String `"cid"` |
| 4 | main | `newcomer.trim() in seen` | `false`: a view looks up a String key fine |
| 5 | main | `newcomer.trim() in banned` (`banned: Array[String]`) | refused, E2226: a list of Strings is searched only with a String |
| 6 | main | `"trudy" in banned` | undecided: a new String made for the test, or not |
| 7 | main | `names.push(owns newcomer)` | refused, E2020: a String into a list of views |
owner_short.today: An untyped list of text holds views while a set or map holds Strings (one allocation each), and a list of Strings can be searched only with a String, so the push and the `in` are refused where the set's lines compile.
owner_short.options:
A: one text, owned or viewed: untyped lists own their text like sets and maps, those Strings cost nothing until changed, and every `==`, `in` and lookup takes a String or a view (recommended).
B: lists own their text, but each literal allocates; lists are searched with a view.
C: views everywhere: lists stay views, and sets and maps become views too; the push is refused.
D: the compiler picks String or StrView from later lines.
E: as today: the push and the `in` are refused.
owner_short.recommendation: A: the Python-style program compiles, no literal or comparison allocates (cheaper than today and than C++ or Rust), and one rule covers every collection, every comparison and a program's own types.

design.open_risks:
1. An existing program that passes an untyped text list to a `Span[StrView]` or `Array[StrView]` parameter becomes E2020. The help gives `names: Array[StrView] = [...]` or a `Span[String]` parameter. The specification itself never does this (grep: Array[StrView] appears only typed, Span[StrView] never), but user code may.
2. remove(i) newly carries Alloc. A @noalloc function that only deletes characters from a lent String is refused and moves to FixedString[N]. This is rare, because such code cannot insert under @noalloc today either.
3. `capacity()` reads 0 for a String holding program text with a length above 0. This is true by TXT-11's definition ("the allocated byte capacity"), but a program that reasons from capacity sees it.
4. AsKey becomes derived from Eq[Q] (it changes ODR-067, a lead ruling). A program's hand-written AsKey becomes E2040 and moves to `Eq[Q]`. Case-insensitive keys were already incoherent under HASH-1.
5. A bare `name = \"ann\"` stays a StrView (LEX-20). The free String would allow making every untyped text literal a String, as Swift does, but that is a separate question for the owner, not widened here.
6. Interplay with other groups:
   - P02: does `using m` reach a String of program text inside an arena-made list? Its text is never in the arena, and its first growth uses the String's manager.
   - P14: the Alloc table loses literal-String sites and gains String.remove.
   - P19: reads Eq as Eq[Rhs = Self], so a `dyn` Eq question is unchanged.
   - P06: J2-04 A's `Add[StrView]` uses the same spelling.
7. If a later rule gives String a writable byte view (an unsafe `as_mut_ptr`), that rule must first give the String room of its own, or unsafe code could write the read-only image.
8. Option A also makes `[v; N]` of a text literal a `[String; N]`, at no allocation and 24 bytes per element. Say this to the owner if it matters.

matrix.guarantee: G1. No read of freed memory: a String holding text written in the program, and every view of it, points only at memory that lives, unchanged, for the whole run.
matrix.how_kept: TXT-9 as changed: such a String is {address in the read-only image, length, capacity 0}. HR-4 never unmaps an image and nothing frees literal text. Dropping it frees nothing. A view of it (s.as_str()) is ended by any reshape of s, as for any String (TXT-8), and s's first change gives it room of its own. This holds only for image text. For String(v) of a static-region view that is not image text it breaks: see hole 1.
matrix.edge_cases: String(v) of a view of a `static mut` String: static region by LT-3, but freed or rewritten when the static changes (hole 1). A `@reinit_on_reload` static's String: HR-47 ends it, and its plan check looks only at view types (hole 1). comptime(e) constant data sits in the image, so it is safe. A StrView value held by a static is always program text by TYP-15, so it is safe. `copy of` shares the triple, which is safe. A String handed to another thread (verdict 114) is safe. HR-2a reclaim frees a migrated String field through the capacity-0 test. An arena-made Array[String] never has its Strings' text in the arena.

static mut TITLE: String = String()

fn main():
    TITLE.push_str("Main menu")        # TITLE has a heap buffer of its own
    saved = String(TITLE.as_str())     # a view of a static item: the static region (LT-3), so no copy, capacity 0

holes.what_goes_wrong: TXT-9 as changed copies nothing for String(v) when v's region is static, and it cites LT-3. LT-3 gives the static region to static items and to views of them, `static mut` included. So `saved` is {address of TITLE's heap buffer, 9, capacity 0}: an owner that no view rule ties to TITLE any more. `TITLE = String("Options")` frees that buffer, and `println(saved)` reads freed memory. Writing `TITLE.clear()` then `TITLE.push_str("aaaaaaaé")` instead rewrites the bytes under `saved`: an owned String changes with no word on its line, and its 9 bytes now end in the first byte of 'é', breaking TXT-1's UTF-8 promise that safe code relies on (UNS-4). A `@reinit_on_reload static MOTD: String` does the same: HR-47 ends the old value, and its plan check looks only for views, so a class field `banner: String` made by `String(MOTD)` is never seen. The design's own justification, HR-4 (images are never unloaded), covers image text only, and HR-4a puts statics outside the image.
holes.fix_hint: Decide the no-copy String by provenance, not by region: only text written in the program, as `from static` already means (LT-45, TYP-15). That is a literal, a bytes literal, comptime constant data, and a StrView value that a static holds (TYP-15 lets a static hold only such views). A view of memory a static owns (its String or Array, mut or not) is copied. Write this in TXT-9 and in compiler_does 2, and drop the LT-3 citation.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule chooses `a == b`'s instance by b's own type (TYP-21, TYP-24) and redefines `T: needs Ord` as Ord[T]. It never says how a view or a holder on either side counts. A loop name over an Array[String] is a `ref String`, so for `x == y` both of String's instances are reached only through a coercion: Eq[String] by reading y through (TYP-5 rule 7), and Eq[StrView] by reading y's String place as a StrView (TXT-8). TYP-24 makes that E2070. `sorted(m.keys())`, the spec's own line (STD-11, TYP-36), sorts `ref String` items, so its bound is Ord[ref String]. TYP-36 gives `ref T` only 'what T does', which is Ord[String] and Ord[StrView], so the line is E2040. Today Eq's `eq(other: Self)` leaves one instance, and both programs compile. Under the rule they are undecided at best. `counts.get(w)` with `w: ref String` raises the same question for AsKey.
holes.fix_hint: State read-through for both operands. Strip an operand's views (ref, ref mut, sharedref mut) and one holder level before TYP-24 chooses, as IV.11 step 1 already does for a receiver; this agrees with P12's 'reads as itself in an operand'. Also: `ref T` implements Eq[ref U] and Ord[ref U], as well as Eq[U] and Ord[U], wherever T implements Eq[U] or Ord[U]. Show `x == y` and `sorted(m.keys())` as must-compile cases.

holes.program:
@derive(Eq, Hash)
struct Ident:
    text: String
    line: int

extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:
    fn eq(other: StrView) -> bool:
        return this.text == other

fn main():
    seen = Set[Ident]()
    seen.add(owns Ident(text=String("main"), line=3))
    idents = [Ident(text=String("main"), line=3)]
    println("main" in idents, "main" in seen)   # true false
holes.what_goes_wrong: AsKey[K] now holds, with no word written, for every hashable Q with K: needs Eq[Q]. A programmer who writes Eq[StrView] only to get `==` also gets set and map lookups by a view, silently. Such a lookup hashes "main" as a StrView, but Ident's derived hash covers text and line, so it probes the wrong bucket. The program prints `true false`, with no refusal and no stop. Before, a lookup by Q needed a hand-written AsKey under STD-12's explicit MUST. Now the obligation (HASH-1 as changed) is invisible at the line that creates it. HASH-3 keeps it free of undefined behaviour, but the owner's bar is 'refused when compiling wherever it can be; never silent'.
holes.fix_hint: Derive AsKey[K] for Q only where the compiler can see that the two forms agree: std's pairs (they hash and compare the same bytes), and a program's type whose Eq[Q] and Hash both go through one declared key view. For example, write `fn key() -> StrView` once and derive Eq[StrView], Hash and AsKey from it. Any other Eq[Q] gives `==` and list `in` only; a set or map lookup by Q is then E2040, with that line as its help. Also extend HASH-3's 'never undefined behaviour' to binary_search, index_of, contains and match under an Eq[Q] or Ord[Q] that disagrees.

holes.what_goes_wrong: STD-8 as changed gives every std container 'that reads as a Span' Contains[Q] for every Q with T: needs Eq[Q], as a linear scan. StrView is a Span[u8] (TXT-1), and a String reads as one (SPN-1). So `b in line` becomes a byte scan: it finds 0xA9 inside 'é' and prints true. STD-8b, which the change keeps, says StrView implements Contains[char] and Contains[StrView] only, so that a character never matches inside another's encoding; under it the line is E2226. Two rules give two answers. The blanket and STD-8b's own Contains[char] may also overlap as TYP-19 judges ('a bound on a type left open never separates'), which would be E2041 inside std.
holes.fix_hint: Word the blanket by the container's item type, not its layout: every std container whose items are T (Iterable with Item = T or ref T) is Contains[Q] for every Q with T: needs Eq[Q]. StrView and String iterate chars, so they keep STD-8b's substring and character tests and get no byte test.

holes.what_goes_wrong: TYP-21 as changed types the right operand by its own type before choosing Eq[B], so the left side no longer gives it a type. Take `tokens == ["go", "north"]`. By TYP-38 an untyped list literal is an Array, and by rule (1) an Array of Strings, so Span[StrView]'s Eq[Array[String]] is chosen. The comparison then allocates a list buffer, which is E4001 under @noalloc. Today Eq[Self] makes the literal a temporary fixed array (TYP-38's Span position), which allocates nothing. `words == []`, `opt == None` and `r == Ok(5)` have no type of their own, and String, Array and Span now have several Eq instances, so each line is E2060 or E2070 where today it compiles. This contradicts the rule's 'Nothing is converted, copied or allocated' and refuses common test lines.
holes.fix_hint: Use the default the interface already declares, Rhs = Self. An operand with no type of its own ([], {}, None, Ok(...) with an open side, or an untyped collection literal) is typed as Self, and another instance is chosen only by an operand that has a type of its own. An untyped list literal that is only read (an operand, or the container of `in`) is a temporary fixed array. Then `tokens == ["go", "north"]` allocates nothing, and neither does `cmd in ["quit", "exit"]`, which allocates today.

holes.what_goes_wrong: remove(i) now allocates when the String holds program text. ALC-4 makes allocation failure a panic, and the effect table files it as Panic(Explicit). So every @nopanic(explicit) function that calls remove is newly E4040, and the design does not say so: it names only E4001 under @noalloc, and its help. Which Strings hold program text is not known where remove is compiled, so both effects land on every remove of every String, including this one, which came from input() and can never allocate there. A contract then refuses a program over an allocation its line never makes, and gives no help that compiles.
holes.fix_hint: State both of remove's effects (Alloc and Panic(Explicit)) in TXT-11 and in P14's effect table. Give E4040 the same help as E4001 (FixedString[N]). Add a @nopanic(explicit) before/after to open risk 2.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule says a list hashes as its Span, and it derives AsKey[[u8; 4]] for Span[u8]. But TYP-36 has no Span or MutSpan row at all: no Eq, no Ord, no Hash. [T; N] hashes 'if all', as a tuple does, and nothing says it feeds the same bytes as its Span. So `routes.get(dst)` is either E2040 (Span[u8] is not Hash), or it compiles and silently returns None for a key that is there: an implementation may hash a Span with its length and a [T; N] without. That is a std pair giving wrong answers, where the design calls std's pairs coherent 'by construction'. The design's own case `cache.get(bytes)` rests on the same missing row.
holes.fix_hint: Add Span[T] and MutSpan[T] rows to TYP-36: Eq, Ord and Hash when T has them. Say in HASH-1 that Array[T], [T; N], Span[T] and MutSpan[T] hash the same element sequence, and String and StrView the same bytes, so every std pair agrees by a written rule.

holes.what_goes_wrong: TXT-12 names its types one by one: String, StrView, Array, [T; N], Span and MutSpan. STD-8 as changed goes by a property instead ('every std container that reads as a Span'). FixedString[N], the type E4001's help sends a @noalloc program to, gets no Eq[StrView], so `name == "escape"` is undecided: E2226, or a String made for the test. A Deque or a RingBuffer is not a Span, so `who in q` stays String-only while the same line on a list compiles. The owner's bar refuses a rule that lists its cases.
holes.fix_hint: State TXT-12 by property. Every type that reads as a StrView (String, FixedString[N]) compares with every other by its bytes. Every container compares, element by element, with every container or view whose items compare. Contains and index_of follow the item type (hole 4's fix). Then Deque, RingBuffer, SmallArray, FixedArray and a program's own containers join with no list.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Until now capacity() >= len() held for every String, and correct code relied on it. A program-text String reports capacity 0 with len 5, so this function, correct before, now stops with a negative count. An assert of the invariant fails the same way. Open risk 3 names the fact, but no rule keeps the invariant.
holes.fix_hint: Make capacity() report max(capacity, len()), 'what it holds without allocating', and keep the 0 as an internal mark. reserve(n) then allocates whenever len() + n is more than the text it holds, which already covers program text. The invariant holds for every String.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The free String is safe only if no operation writes, reallocates or frees its buffer while its capacity is 0, but the rule states this as a list in TXT-11. SPN-1's sentence reads 'An Array[T], a [T; N] or a String converts to Span[T] or StrView ..., and to MutSpan[T] where one is expected'. TYP-5's complete list does not give a String that conversion, but if SPN-1 is followed, `zero(ref mut s)` writes the image: a crash where the image is write-protected, and every merged copy of the literal changed where it is not. HEAP-2's shrink_to_fit is not listed either; one that reallocates to len() would pass an image address to ember_realloc.
holes.fix_hint: State the property in TXT-9: while a String's capacity is 0, no operation writes, reallocates or frees its buffer. Correct SPN-1 to say a String converts to StrView only. Say that shrink_to_fit does nothing at capacity 0.

holes.program:
fn main():
    a = String("ok")
    b = copy of a
    println(a.as_str() is b.as_str())   # true now; false today
holes.what_goes_wrong: Verdict 10 says the copy word copies the thing itself, and EXP-9 says `is` on two views tests 'the same object' by address. A `copy of` a program-text String shares its bytes, so for two owners `is` answers 'the same object'. Two literal Strings of equal text that the compiler merges do the same. A program that uses `is` on text views to skip a self-copy behaves differently than before. This is not unsafe, but `is` no longer means what it says for text.
holes.fix_hint: Either say in EXP-9 that views of text written in the program may be the same object for different owners, or make `is` on StrView an error with help `==`, since text identity has no meaning once text is shared read-only.

fn main():
    names = ["ann", "bob"]
    best = names[0]                    # was a copied StrView; now a view of a String element (BRW-12)
    names.push(owns String("carol"))

safety.notes:
I read owner-bar.md, brief.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, SAFETY-VALIDATION-TASK.md, phase1-groups.json (every group's principle), J3-13 and J6-13 in phase2.json, and phase3.json's K28 and K29 entries and its correction list. In the spec parts I read TXT-1 to TXT-11, STD-7, 8, 8b, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17 and 19, TYP-5, 6, 14, 15, 21, 22, 23, 24, 34, 36, 37 and 45, HASH-1 to 4, IV.8's standard interfaces, LEX-20, PHIL-2, LT-3, LT-45, BRW-12, SPN-1 to 8, STA-1, STA-3, CT-5, HR-2, HR-2a, HR-4, HR-4a, HR-17a, HR-47, HEAP-1, 2 and 8, ALC-4, the effect table, FFI-31b, FFI-54, CTL-1, CTL-5 and EXP-9, and JOB.md verdicts 10, 14, 72, 94, 95 and 145 to 166.

The two halves of the rule stand apart on safety.

(1) The literal String in the read-only image is sound for real program text. Drop frees nothing at capacity 0, every byte-writing change takes room first, there is no safe writable byte view, threads only read the text, and reload keeps images mapped. The one high hole is the condition on String(v). It cites LT-3's static region, which covers views of `static mut` items and of `@reinit_on_reload` statics, so an owner can point into memory that is later freed or rewritten: use after free, and a broken UTF-8 promise. The fix is provenance: text written in the program, as `from static` already means. Low notes on the same half: capacity < len, SPN-1's MutSpan wording and shrink_to_fit, `is` identity, and `best = names[0]` becoming a view.

(2) The Eq[Rhs] scheme causes no undefined behaviour, since HASH-3 holds and E3031 still applies. But it is under-specified at its joints:
- Views and holders on the operands are not read through, so x == y on loop names and the spec's own sorted(m.keys()) are undecided or refused (high).
- An operand with no type of its own loses the Self context, so a list-literal comparison allocates and `== []`, `== None` and `== Ok(5)` become ambiguous (medium).
- AsKey derived from any Eq[Q] silently enables incoherent lookups (medium).
- STD-8's 'reads as a Span' blanket covers StrView, a Span[u8], against STD-8b (medium).
- Span and [T; N] hashing is unwritten (medium).
- TXT-12 lists its types by name (medium).
- remove's new allocation also brings Panic(Explicit), so @nopanic(explicit) changes too (medium; P14).

Cross-group: hole 2's fix should be P12's read-through rule applied to operands. Holes 5 and 6 belong in P14's effect table too. P02 (`using`): a program-text String's growth comes from Global, which is consistent. P06's Add[StrView] and P19's dyn Eq are unaffected. Verdicts 164 to 166 are untouched.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The changed TXT-9 makes `String(v)` free 'when v is a view whose region is static (LT-3)'. LT-3 (p07:611) gives the static region to 'static items and views of them', and a `static mut` is a static item that changes (STA-1, p05:474-480). HR-4a (p20:81) also keeps statics in a runtime table, not in the image. Today `String(v)` always copies, so this prints `untitled - level 1`. Under the rule, `s` is an owner that aliases TITLE's heap buffer. TXT-8's rule that a reshape ends views does not reach `s`, because `s` is not a view. The second push frees the buffer and `println(s)` reads freed memory, in safe code. A `clear()` followed by a `push_str` also silently changes the text of an owned String.
holes.fix_hint: Make 'text written in the program' mean bytes in the read-only image: a literal, or a view the compiler proves comes only from literals and compile-time statics placed in the image (STA-3). Never a view of a `static mut`, of a static built on first access, or of any owner. A view of anything else is copied, as today.

holes.what_goes_wrong: All three compile today: TYP-15's own example says an untyped text list is an `Array[StrView]` of static views (p04:314). Under A the element type is String, which has three effects. (1) `days[i]` is a view of a String the local list owns, so returning it is E3063 (FN-3). (2) A local list cannot be passed where a `Span[StrView]` is wanted, because the strides differ (24 bytes against 16). (3) A view value cannot be stored into the list. Each fix is a written type (`days: Array[StrView] = ...`). So A moves the annotation from J3-13's push program onto the lookup-table, menu and row-parsing programs; it does not remove it. The design's claims ('No word, annotation or ceremony is added anywhere'; risk 1, 'the specification itself never does this') miss this. The owner's bar says such a design is not finished. The options table also undersells D: D keeps these programs compiling as well as the push, not only 8 bytes per element.
holes.fix_hint: State the trade plainly to the owner. The one general way both kinds of program compile untyped is to fix an untyped text list's element type from its uses in the function, as TYP-23 already does for `[]`: String when some use needs an owner, StrView otherwise. This needs ODR-022, a lead ruling made for numbers, to allow it for text, with the reason given. Otherwise list these refusals among A's costs and give each a help line.

fn report(t: Track):

    if t.gains == [0.5, 1.0]:         # f32 list against a literal

holes.what_goes_wrong: TYP-21 as changed picks the instance 'by b's own type'. `None` and `[]` have no own type. Option[String] now has `Eq[Option[String]]` and `Eq[Option[StrView]]` (TXT-12), and `None` fits both. `[0.5, 1.0]` has the own type `Array[f64]`, and f32 has no `Eq[f64]`. Through coercion the literal reaches `Array[f32]`, `[f32; 2]` and `Span[f32]` (TYP-38, p06:91-92), all of which are now instances, so the tie rule makes each line E2070 (TYP-24, p04:563-566). Today each compiles: there is one Eq instance, and the literal is typed from the other side (TYP-23, '1 + x takes x's type'). The help, `Eq[Option[String]].eq(t.name, None)`, is far worse to read. The instance sets are also open-world (TYP-20 lets `Meters`'s package write `extend int implements Eq[Meters]`), so adding a package can break `xs == []` in code that compiled before. Rust has the same failure (E0282).
holes.fix_hint: Let an operand that has no type of its own (`None`, `[]`, `{}`), or a literal whose default type picks no instance, take the other operand's type. TYP-23 already does this for a branch that cannot type itself and for `1 + x`. Because the rule makes a literal String free, a text literal may take String there too at no cost, so the 'counts as StrView' tier is needed only for values.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed STD-12 derives `AsKey[K]` for every `Q: needs Hash` with `K: needs Eq[Q]`, and makes a hand-written AsKey E2040. Writing `Eq[StrView]` for `Ident`, the design's own example of a program taking part, therefore enrols StrView as a lookup key for every `Set[Ident]` and `Map[Ident, V]`, and the program cannot opt out. The lookup hashes the four bytes `main`, but `@derive(Hash)` hashed both `text` and `line`, so the test silently prints nothing. Today the line is refused (E2226). A refusal becomes a silent wrong answer, which the owner's bar excludes ('refused when compiling wherever it can be ... never silent corruption'). The compiler can see this case, because it derived the Hash itself.
holes.fix_hint: Derive AsKey only where both sides hash and compare one projection by construction. std's String/StrView and Array/Span pairs qualify. A program's key type states its projection once (`fn key() -> StrView: return this.text` in an implementation of a key interface), and Eq[Q] in both directions, Hash and AsKey all follow from it, so they cannot disagree. Refuse a derived Hash that hashes more than an Eq[Q] compares.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed TXT-11 gives `remove(i)` the Alloc effect on every String, because a String of program text must take room of its own before its bytes move. This console editor compiles under @noalloc today and becomes E4001, although no caller ever passes program text. The help sends it to FixedString[N]. The rule also states the effect as a list of method names (push, push_str, insert, reserve, +=, remove), which P14's principle forbids ('never by a closed list of names'). PHIL-2's new item calls the allocation 'container growth', and remove is not growth.
holes.fix_hint: Give Alloc to remove only where a String that may hold program text can reach it. Find this as verdict 128 does, by following what callers pass, the way effects are already inferred from bodies (verdict 86). State it as one rule, 'a change that writes a String's bytes gives a String of program text room of its own', and name remove in PHIL-2.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule claims safe code cannot write the read-only image because the listed changes (push, push_str, insert, reserve, +=, remove) take room first. SPN-1 (p07:812-814) says 'An Array[T], a [T; N] or a String converts ... to MutSpan[T] where one is expected', and SPN-8 hands out `as_mut_ptr()`. Neither is on the list. If SPN-1 means what it says, the loop writes into the program's read-only text and the process faults with no message at the line. In unsafe or FFI code (`as_mut_ptr()` given to a C function that fills a String), the person vouching cannot see whether a String holds program text: that fact is now hidden in where the String came from (P04).
holes.fix_hint: One rule: every route that hands out writable access to a String's bytes (a MutSpan conversion, as_mut_ptr, a C buffer parameter) is a change, so it first gives a String of program text room of its own and carries Alloc. Settle SPN-1's String case at the same time: it also breaks TXT-1's UTF-8 guarantee.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed TXT-9 and TXT-11 give a String of program text `capacity()` 0 with `len()` above 0. This breaks the invariant `len() <= capacity()` that Rust, C++ and Swift all keep and that ordinary spare-room arithmetic relies on. Here `spare` is -6, and TXT-11 says a negative run-time count panics, so a correct-looking program stops. Pool and memory accounting code that compares or sums capacity gets negative waste. The design lists this only as risk 3 and calls it 'true by definition'.
holes.fix_hint: Mark program text with a flag bit in the capacity word, as Swift marks immortal strings, and report `capacity()` as at least `len()`. Drop, writes and growth test the flag: the cost is the same one test. `truncate` and `clear` then keep the capacity as TXT-11 says.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule promises (2) for 'every map or set lookup', but STD-16 is left as it was: `entry(k)` and `Set.add(x)` take the key itself. Word counting, the ordinary map program, therefore allocates, copies and frees a String for every word, including every word already counted. C looks up first and calls strdup only on insert. Rust has the same pain, which is why it added `entry_ref`.
holes.fix_hint: `entry(q)` and `Set.add(q)` take any `Q: needs ToKey[K]` and make the key only when the slot is empty, as `m[q] = v` already does (STD-12).

holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed TYP-24 counts a text literal as a StrView when choosing an instance. `config["mode"] = ...` therefore chooses `IndexSet[StrView, V]` (STD-17), whose `to_key()` runs `String(q)` on a parameter whose region is not static, so it allocates and copies. Choosing `IndexSet[String, V]` would cost three stores under the rule's own TXT-9. The Python-style spelling pays an allocation per new key while `insert` pays none, and the literal rule itself picks the slower instance.
holes.fix_hint: Let a text literal take the type that the place keeping it expects (K for ToKey, IndexSet or insert), which costs nothing under TXT-9. Count it as a StrView only where the instance just reads it (Eq, Ord, AsKey, Contains). The fix to H1 (take the other side's type) covers this too.

holes.program:
struct Ident:
    text: String

extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:
    fn eq(other: StrView) -> bool:
        return this.text == other

fn main():
    id = Ident(text=String("main"))
    println(id == "main")             # compiles
    println("main" == id)             # E2226 until a second, hand-kept StrView: Eq[Ident]
holes.what_goes_wrong: TXT-12 makes the programmer write both directions and adds a MUST that they agree, with HASH-3's wrong answers if they do not. The compiler could derive the reverse from the forward one (C++20 rewrites `b == a` as `a == b`). Without that, `==` is not symmetric for a program's own types. In the same way, `binary_search` with `T: needs Ord[Q]` relies on Ord[Q] agreeing with the order `sort` used (Ord[Self]), but the rule states only the K-against-Q and Q-against-K agreement, so a disagreeing Ord[Q] gives unstated wrong answers.
holes.fix_hint: Derive `Q: Eq[K]` (and `Ord[K]` as the reverse) from a written `K: Eq[Q]`, so the two cannot disagree. Writing both is then E2041. State that `Ord[Q]` must agree with `Ord[Self]`, or obtain both from one key projection (see the AsKey fix).

holes.what_goes_wrong: Today this is an `Array[StrView]`: 96 bytes, and its drop frees one buffer. Under A it is an `Array[String]`: 144 bytes and three stores per element. Its drop walks all six elements testing each capacity, because String is not Copy, and `copy of keywords` branches per element where a view list is one memcpy. C keeps a `static const char *` table and does nothing at run time. The design's cost section says 'Dropping a String is unchanged' but leaves out this per-element loop. It rejected B for making 'a read-only keyword table slower', and A makes the same table slower than today, by less.
holes.fix_hint: Put the full cost (size, drop loop, copy) in the owner's options for A against D. Under D, or the use-based typing in the high hole above, a read-only table stays `Array[StrView]` at today's cost.

holes.program:
struct Ident:
    text: String
    hits: Cell[int]

extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:
    fn eq(other: StrView) -> bool:
        this.hits.set(this.hits.get() + 1)
        return this.text == other

fn kind(id: Ident) -> int:
    match id:
        "fn" => return 1
        "struct" => return 2
        _ => return 0
holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed CTL-5 defines a literal pattern as `subject == literal`. Any type with an Eq[StrView] or Eq[int] therefore becomes matchable against literals, and each arm runs the program's own `eq`, which may change state, panic or answer inconsistently. That rules out the switch on length then bytes that the design itself counts on, and the duplicate-arm checks. Rust's structural-match rule exists to prevent this.
holes.fix_hint: A literal pattern matches a subject that reads as the literal's type (String, ref and owns String read as StrView, TXT-8) and compares the bytes or value directly. It never calls a program's eq. This is still one general rule.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Changed STD-8 gives the blanket Contains[Q] to 'every std container that reads as a Span'. That leaves out Deque, RingBuffer and BitSet, although the principle says 'every collection'. The same words take in StrView and String, which are 'a Span[u8]' (TXT-1, IV.4), against STD-8b's 'Contains[char] and Contains[StrView] only'. Under TYP-19, a bound on an open type does not separate two implementations, so the blanket and STD-8b's own instances overlap (E2041 in std), and `u8 in s` becomes undecided.
holes.fix_hint: Name the scope: every std sequence container (Array, FixedArray, SmallArray, Deque, RingBuffer, [T; N], Span, MutSpan) gets Contains[Q] as a linear scan. Text keeps STD-8b's character and substring test, stated as the exception with its reason.

holes.program:
fn same(a: Array[i32], b: Array[i64]) -> bool:
    return a[0] == b[0] and a == b    # a[0] == b[0] compiles (TYP-4); a == b is refused
holes.what_goes_wrong: TXT-12 compares lists 'element by element when T: needs Eq[U]', but whole numbers of different widths compare only through TYP-4's built-in widening, not through an instance. So the elements compare while the lists do not. If std added i32: Eq[i64] to close that gap, HASH-1's equal-hash rule would break, because write_i32 and write_i64 feed different bytes. The rule also does not say that [T; N] and MutSpan hash as their Span, which TXT-12's cross-type equality requires.
holes.fix_hint: Say whether element-wise equality follows TYP-4 (and, if it does, hash whole numbers by value, not width), or that it does not, and why. Add that `[T; N]` and `MutSpan[T]` hash as their `Span`.

holes.program:
@derive(Eq)
struct Tagged[T]:
    value: T

fn main():
    a = Tagged(value=String("x"))
    b: Tagged[StrView] = Tagged(value="x")
    println(Some(String("x")) == Some("x"), a == b)   # the first compiles (TXT-12), the second does not
holes.what_goes_wrong: std's Option, Result and tuples compare across element types when their parts compare, but `@derive(Eq)` gives only the Self instance. A program's own generic wrapper therefore needs a hand-written `extend[T, U] Tagged[T] implements Eq[Tagged[U]]`. The claim that 'a program's own types take part by the same rule' holds only for code written by hand.
holes.fix_hint: Have `@derive(Eq)` and `@derive(Ord)` on a generic type give `Eq[Tagged[U]]` when each field compares, as std's own generic types do.

holes.program:
interface Named: needs Eq[StrView]:
    fn label() -> StrView

fn show(n: dyn Named):
    println(n == "main")
holes.what_goes_wrong: P19's principle names 'an Ord requirement' and 'a Self parameter' as what makes an interface unusable as dyn. Once Eq and Ord take Rhs, `needs Eq[StrView]` has no Self parameter and can be called on any implementer. Read literally, P19 refuses it.
holes.fix_hint: P19's wording should say Eq[Self] and Ord[Self] (an Rhs that is Self); a concrete Rhs stays usable as dyn.

engineering.notes:
Engineering-lens check of P13 option A, read-only. Holes in order of weight:

1. String(v) free for a 'static-region view' is unsafe. LT-3 (tasks/spec-0.9.9/parts/p07-ownership.md:611) gives views of static items, a `static mut` included (p05-declarations.md:470-480), the static region. HR-4a (p20-annex-b.md:81) keeps statics outside the image. The result is a use-after-free in safe code. The condition must be 'bytes in the read-only image'.

2. A does not remove an annotation; it moves it. Programs that compile today because TYP-15 (p04-types.md:314) types an untyped text list as Array[StrView] become refused: returning an element of a local table, passing the local to Span[StrView], storing a view into the list. The readability claim and the dismissal of D are therefore inaccurate.

3. Comparing against an operand with no own type, or a literal whose default type has no instance, becomes E2070 under TYP-24's tie rule (p04-types.md:560-570) once the instance sets are heterogeneous. Examples are `x == None` (ODR-227, p26-appx-h.md:515), `xs == []` and `gains == [0.5, 1.0]` for f32 (TYP-38 lets a list literal be Array, [T;N] or Span, p06-expressions.md:91-92). The sets are open-world, so adding a package can break code elsewhere.

4. Deriving AsKey from Eq[Q] (STD-12, p15-stdlib.md:253-265) turns today's refusal into silent wrong set and map lookups for a program's own @derive(Hash) types.

Medium:
- remove gains Alloc for every String; also a named list against P14's principle.
- Writable routes into a String's bytes (SPN-1, p07-ownership.md:812-814; SPN-8) are not covered.
- capacity() < len() breaks spare-room arithmetic.
- entry/add are not generalised (STD-16, p15-stdlib.md:219-228).
- m["lit"] = v picks IndexSet[StrView] and copies (STD-17).
- The reverse Eq direction and Ord[Q] consistency are left to the programmer.
- An Array[String] read-only table costs more than today's Array[StrView] (size, drop loop, copy).

Low:
- CTL-5 through a program's own eq.
- STD-8 'reads as a Span' scope against STD-8b and Deque.
- Integer widths element by element, and [T;N]/MutSpan hashing.
- @derive(Eq) on generic types.
- P19 wording.

Where the rule holds:
- J6-13's needle lookup, `cmd == "quit"`, binary_search with a view, the P06 and P12 alignment.
- Verdicts 145, 147, 149 and 161 in the spellings used.
- Free literal Strings for plain initialisers.

A general repair for holes 2, 3 and the m["lit"] cost:
- A literal or open operand takes the type the other side or the keeping place expects (TYP-23's existing rule). Literal Strings are free, so this costs nothing.
- An untyped text list is typed from its uses, as [] already is. That needs ODR-022, a lead ruling, to be put to the owner with its reason.

design.rule:
Text written in the program is one text, whether a String or a StrView holds it. The language treats it that way in two places.

(1) Holding. Where no type is written, the function's uses decide how the program's text is held. This covers a variable, and a list, set or map literal at any depth. It works the way uses already decide `[]`'s element type:
- It is a String once a line needs a String there: a String put in, a parameter, method or bound that only a String meets, or a key that a set or map makes from a view of other text.
- It is a StrView where a line needs a view.
- Otherwise it is a StrView, because a view holds the program's text for the program's whole life at no cost.
Lists, sets, maps and variables all follow this one rule. A value that is put in keeps its own type, as numbers do. No program that compiles today changes what it computes; lines that today are refused because the text is a view now compile.

(2) Comparing and looking up. Every comparison reads both sides where they are. This covers ==, !=, the orders, a literal match arm, x in c, contains, index_of, binary_search, every map or set lookup, and every insertion that first looks for its key.
- Text compares with text in any form.
- A list compares with a list in any container, and a set or map with a set or map.
- A container accepts, as the thing to look for, any value its items compare with.
- A literal operand is read where it lies: a list literal is a temporary fixed array, and `None`, `[]` and `Ok(...)` take the other side's type.
Nothing is converted, copied or allocated. An insertion makes its key only when the key is new.

The library states (2) as ordinary implementations, spelled the way `Add[StrView]` already is: `Eq[Rhs = Self]` and `Ord[Rhs = Self]`. One direction is written, and the other follows from it. A program's own types and containers take part by the same rule. A lookup in a set or map by another type also needs `AsKey`, the written promise that both types hash alike.
design.spec_text:
CHANGED [LEX-20]: "A string literal has type `StrView` with the static region: a view of text written in the program. At a site expecting `String` it produces a `String` (`[TXT-9]`). Some sites expect no type: the initialiser of a name declared with no type, or text inside such a literal, at any depth (`name = \"anon\"`, `names = [\"ann\", \"bob\"]`, `pair = (\"ann\", 3)`, `{\"ann\": 1}`). There, the function's uses decide whether the text is held as a `String` or a `StrView` (`[TYP-23]`)."

CHANGED [TYP-23], added after "one still open at the end is `E2060`, highlighting the first use.":
"The same holds for how text written in the program is held where no type is expected at it (`[LEX-20]`). Each place in the declared type where such text sits is a `String` or a `StrView`. A later use fixes it when only one of the two meets that use:
- A value assigned or put in fixes its own type. `names.push(owns line)` gives `String`s for a `String` `line`, and `StrView`s for a view.
- A place, parameter, method or bound that only one meets fixes that one: `draw_menu(names)` for a `Span[StrView]` parameter, `take(owns name)` for an `owns String` parameter, `name.push_str(\"!\")`, `name += \"!\"`, a bound `Copy`.
- A key or element that a set or map makes itself from a view (`counts[w] = 1`, `seen.add(owns w)`, `[STD-12]`) fixes `String` when the view is of text the program did not write, since a collection written with no type keeps such text as its own.
A use that both meet fixes nothing: reading, comparing, printing, iterating, or passing where a `StrView` is expected. Text left open is a `StrView`: all of it is text written in the program, which a view holds for the program's whole life and copies at no cost. Uses that need both are `E2020` at the later one. Its message names the two lines, and its help gives a line that compiles: the declaration with its type (`names: Array[String] = [\"ann\", \"bob\"]`), or the other use changed.
This is not ODR-022's case. A number's type decides where its arithmetic overflows. The two holdings give every line the same text, length, comparison (`[TXT-12]`), hash and printing, so a later use decides only which lines are accepted and what the literal costs (`[TXT-9]`)."

CHANGED [TYP-38]:
* First bullet, added: "As an operand of a comparison or the container of `in`, which only read it (`[TYP-21]`), a list literal is a `Span[T]` of a temporary fixed array of its items, each read where it is (a name is viewed, never handed over), so it allocates nothing (`cmd in [\"quit\", \"exit\"]`, `tokens == [\"go\", \"north\"]`)."
* Second bullet: the sentence "With no context a text key, value or element is a `String`, since a map written with no type owns its text; it holds `StrView` only where the program says so (`labels: Map[StrView, int]`, `[STD-11]`)." is replaced by: "With no type written, the text a list, set or map literal holds is held as the function's uses need (`[TYP-23]`), the same for every kind of collection. `names = [\"ann\", \"bob\"]` and `seen = {\"ann\", \"bob\"}` hold views of the program's text while they are only read. They hold `String`s once a line puts a `String` in (`names.push(owns line)`), or once a set or map makes a key from a view of other text (`counts[w] = 1`)."

CHANGED [TYP-15], example: "`names = [\"ann\", \"bob\"]`, while it is only read, is an `Array[StrView]` of text written in the program (`[TYP-23]`), which may live as long as the program".

CHANGED, the standard interfaces (IV.8):
  interface Eq[Rhs = Self]:
      fn eq(other: Rhs) -> bool                  # ==, !=
  interface Ord[Rhs = Self]: needs Eq[Rhs]:
      fn cmp(other: Rhs) -> Ordering             # <, <=, >, >=, sort, min, max, binary_search; a float's `<` stays IEEE
"`T: needs Eq` and `T: needs Ord` mean `Eq[T]` and `Ord[T]`, as `Add` means `Add[T]`, and `@derive(Eq)` and `@derive(Ord)` give those. An implementation of `Eq[Q]` for `K` also answers `q == k`, called with its operands swapped. One of `Ord[Q]` for `K` answers `q < k`, with its result reversed. This applies wherever an operator, a method or a bound asks it of `Q` (C++20's rewritten comparisons). `Q`'s side is never written by hand; writing it as well is `E2041`, naming both."

NEW [TXT-12] One text, owned or viewed: "A comparison reads text in whichever form each side holds it, and a list in whichever container holds it:
- Every std type that holds text (`String`, `StrView`, `FixedString[N]`) compares with every other by its bytes (`Eq[Q]`, and `Ord[Q]` by bytes).
- Every std list compares element by element, and orders lexicographically, with every std list whose items its own compare with (`T: needs Eq[U]`, `Ord[U]`). A std list is a container whose items keep their positions: `Array[T]`, `[T; N]`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, `Deque[T]`, `SmallArray[T, N]`, `FixedArray[T, N]`, `RingBuffer[T, N]`.
- `Option`, `Result` and tuples compare with their own kind when their parts compare.
- A `Map` or `Set` compares, as sets of entries (`[STD-16]`), with a `Map` or `Set` whose keys find its own (`Q: needs AsKey[K]`, `[STD-12]`) and whose values compare.
Nothing is converted, copied or allocated. Values that a lookup matches hash alike (`[HASH-1]`). A program's own type takes part by implementing `Eq[Q]` or `Ord[Q]` (`extend Ident implements Eq[StrView]:`), from which `q == k` follows (IV.8). It is looked up in a set or map by a `Q` only where `AsKey` is implemented for that `Q` (`[STD-12]`), since a lookup also needs both to hash alike."

CHANGED [TYP-21], added: "`a == b` and `a != b` call the `eq` of `Eq[B]`, and `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` the `cmp` of `Ord[B]` (floats keep IEEE, `[TYP-37]`). Both operands are read where they are, so a comparison never converts, copies or makes a value. Their types are read as follows:
- A view (`ref`, `ref mut`, `sharedref mut`) reads as what it views, as a method's receiver does (IV.11, step 1). A held value reads as `[TYP-36]` says.
- A text literal is text written in the program, a `StrView` (`[LEX-20]`).
- A list literal is a temporary fixed array, read as a `Span` (`[TYP-38]`).
- An untyped number, `None`, `[]`, `{}`, and `Ok(...)` or `Err(...)` with a side left open take their type from the other operand (inside a list literal, from its items), as `1 + x` takes `x`'s type (`[TYP-23]`).
`[TYP-24]` then chooses the instance by the right operand's type. So:
- `cmd == \"quit\"` for a `String` `cmd` compares the text.
- `t.gains == [0.5, 1.0]` for an `Array[f32]` compares with a temporary `[f32; 2]`.
- `words == []`, `t.name == None` and `r == Ok(5)` use the left operand's own instance.
None of these allocates. The same reading holds for `x in c` and its container (`[STD-8]`), for a lookup's argument (`[STD-12]`) and for a literal pattern (`[CTL-5]`)."

CHANGED [TYP-36]:
* The sentence on views becomes: "A read-only view `ref T` meets `Eq[U]`, `Eq[ref U]`, `Ord[U]` and `Ord[ref U]` wherever `T` meets `Eq[U]` or `Ord[U]`, and implements `Hash`, `Display` and `Debug` as `T` does (so `sorted(m.keys())` sorts its `ref String` items)."
* The `Eq` and `Ord` cells of the `StrView`, `String`, `Array[T]`, `[T; N]`, `Option`/`Result`, tuple and `Map`/`Set` rows add "and with the kinds `[TXT-12]` names".
* The `Hash` cell of `[T; N]` becomes "if `T`, as a list (`[HASH-1]`)".
* New rows:
| `Span[T]` | ✓ | ✓ | if `T`, `[TXT-12]` | lexicographic, if `T` | if `T` | empty | if `T: needs Debug` | if `T` |
| `MutSpan[T]` | — | — | if `T`, `[TXT-12]` | lexicographic, if `T` | if `T` | — | if `T: needs Debug` | if `T` |

CHANGED [HASH-1]: "Values equal under `Eq` MUST hash equally, and so MUST a key and a value that finds it (`AsKey`, `[STD-12]`). Every std text type feeds its bytes, and every std list (`[TXT-12]`) its elements in order and then its length, the same way, so std's own pairs agree by this rule."

CHANGED [HASH-3], added: "The same holds for an `Ord[Q]` that a search uses with an order other than the one the list was sorted in (`[STD-15]`), and for an `AsKey` that hashes or compares other than as its key. `contains`, `index_of`, `binary_search`, `match` and every lookup stay in bounds and end, whatever the comparisons return."

CHANGED [STD-8]: "`x in c` requires `c: Contains[typeof(x)]`, read as a comparison reads (`[TYP-21]`). Otherwise it is `E2226`, whose help is `c.iter().any(owns fn(e) => e == x)`. std implements it according to what a container's items are:
- Every std list (`[TXT-12]`) whose items are `T` implements it for every `Q` with `T: needs Eq[Q]`, as a linear scan: `who in names`, for a `StrView` `who` and `names: Array[String]`.
- `Set` and `Map` implement it by key, for every `Q: needs AsKey[K]`.
- Text implements it by characters and substrings (`[STD-8b]`).
- Ranges implement it with two comparisons.
The compiler never synthesises an implementation. A program's own container implements `Contains[Q]` in the same way, under the bound `T: needs Eq[Q]`." STD-8b is unchanged.

CHANGED [STD-15]: "`index_of(x)` takes any `x: Q` with `T: needs Eq[Q]`, and `binary_search(x)` any `x: Q` with `T: needs Ord[Q]`, which MUST order as the list was sorted (`[HASH-3]`)".

CHANGED [STD-12]:
"Lookup methods, `m[k]` and `k in m` accept any `Q: needs AsKey[K]`, read as a comparison reads (`[TYP-21]`). Every `K: needs (Eq, Hash)` is `AsKey[K]` (`is_key` is `==`).
std implements `AsKey` for its own pairs, which agree by `[HASH-1]`'s rule:
- every std text type for every other (`StrView` finds `String` keys, and `String` finds `StrView` keys);
- every std list for every std list whose items find its items (`Span[u8]` finds `Array[u8]` and `[u8; 4]` keys).
A program's own pair is written as it is today (`extend StrView implements AsKey[Ident]:`). An implementation MUST hash and compare as the key it matches would; one that does not gives `[HASH-3]`'s wrong answers, never undefined behaviour.
`interface ToKey[K]: needs AsKey[K]` adds `fn to_key() owns this -> K`, which makes the key from the value it is given (ODR-067). Every key type is `ToKey` of itself (the value becomes the key), and every std text type is `ToKey[String]`.
The operations that put a key in (`m[q] = v`, `insert`, `entry`, `Set.add`) take any `Q: needs ToKey[K]` and make the key only when it is new:
- `m[q] = v` makes it from `copy of q`, which costs nothing for a view.
- The others make it from the value handed over. `counts.entry(owns w).or_default() += 1` with a view `w` makes a `String` only for a new word. `seen.add(owns name)` moves `name` in when it is new and ends it otherwise."

CHANGED [STD-16]:
* "`insert(owns q, owns v) -> Option[V]` and `entry(owns q)` take any `q: Q` with `Q: needs ToKey[K]` and make the key from it only when it is new (`[STD-12]`). An existing key keeps its position and its own key value, and `q` ends." The `entry` example is unchanged.
* For `Set`: "`add(owns q) -> bool` takes any `Q: needs ToKey[T]` and returns whether the element was new; an element already there keeps its position."
* "`m1 == m2` and `s1 == s2` also compare with the kinds `[TXT-12]` names."

CHANGED [STD-17]: "`IndexSet[Q, V]` for every `Q: needs (ToKey[K], Clone)`".

CHANGED [CTL-5], added: "A literal pattern matches where `subject == literal` holds, read as any comparison is (`[TYP-21]`). A text pattern against a `String` subject compares the text and makes no `String`."

CHANGED [TXT-9], added: "A comparison, `x in c` and a lookup only read their operands, so a literal there is never made a `String` (`[TYP-21]`)."

Unchanged: TXT-1, TXT-5, TXT-11, PHIL-2 and TYP-24. Under this rule, a literal where a `String` is held still allocates, and `String(s)` still copies.

answers.answer: The list and the set follow one rule. Each holds the program's text as views while it is only read, and holds Strings once a line puts a String in. Here a String goes into each, so both hold Strings, and the push compiles as the set's add does. A list that is only read stays a list of 16-byte static views, as today. The draft's `seen.insert(...)` is `seen.add(...)` in STD-16, written with `owns` as verdicts 147 and 149 require.

fn main():
    names = ["ann", "bob"]              # the program's text
    seen = {"ann", "bob"}
    newcomer = input()                  # a String the program reads
    seen.add(owns copy of newcomer)     # a String put in: seen holds Strings
    names.push(owns newcomer)           # a String put in: names holds Strings
    println(names, seen)
answers.outcome: Compiles. For the input `cid` it prints `['ann', 'bob', 'cid'] {'ann', 'bob', 'cid'}`. Each of the four literal names becomes a String at its own line, with one allocation each (TXT-9), as the set's names already do today. Option B would make those four free. Without the push, `names` would be an `Array[StrView]` with no allocation per name. A program that needs views and also pushes owned text has to choose one: `names: Array[StrView] = [...]` makes the push E2020, and its help is `names.push(owns String(...))` with the type written as `Array[String]`.

answers.answer: A list of Strings is searched with a text view, exactly as a set or map of Strings is. `Array[String]` implements `Contains[StrView]` because `String` implements `Eq[StrView]`. The literal needle is read as the program's text (TYP-21), so no String is made for the test.
answers.outcome: Compiles. For the input `  trudy ` it prints `go away`, then `trudy is banned`. Each test costs one length compare per element, plus a byte compare where the lengths agree. That is what a C loop of `len == n && memcmp(...) == 0` costs. Nothing is allocated, so `is_banned` may be `@noalloc`. `banned` holds Strings because `is_banned` takes an `Array[String]` (two allocations, TXT-9). If `is_banned` took a `Span[StrView]` instead, `banned` would hold views and allocate nothing per name. `5 in banned` stays E2226, since String has no `Eq[int]`.

design.prior_art:
Typing a literal from later uses
- Rust infers an integer literal's type from later uses (`let x = 5; let y: u8 = x;`), and `Vec::new()`'s element type from a later push. Kotlin's builder inference does the same for `buildList`.
- Ember already does this for `[]` and `None` (TYP-23). A extends it to the holding of text, the one case where the choice changes no computed value.

Comparing owned and viewed text
- C++ compares `std::string` with `string_view` and `const char*`.
- Rust has `String: PartialEq<str>`, `Vec<T>: PartialEq<Vec<U>>`, `VecDeque<T>: PartialEq<Vec<U>>` and `PartialEq<[U; N]>`, and `vec == [\"go\", \"north\"]` compares against an array without allocating.
- But Rust's `slice::contains` and `binary_search` take only an element: `v.contains(\"x\")` on a `Vec<String>` is E0308.
- Swift's `Array.contains` needs an Element, and `Set<String>.contains` refuses a Substring.

Symmetry
- C++20 rewrites `b == a` as `a == b` and makes the reversed `<=>` for you.
- Rust makes you write `PartialEq<A> for B` and `PartialEq<B> for A` by hand, and they can disagree.
- A follows C++20.

Lookups by a view
- Rust's `Borrow<Q>` is a written promise that Hash and Eq agree, as AsKey is.
- C++14/20 transparent comparators and .NET 9's `GetAlternateLookup` are opt-in.

Insertion that makes the key only when it is new
- C++26's heterogeneous `try_emplace`, `insert_or_assign` and set `insert` (P2363).
- hashbrown's `entry_ref`, and Rust's unstable `HashSet::get_or_insert_with`.

Free literal Strings (option B only)
- Swift's immortal strings point at the binary's text until their first change.
- Rust's `Cow<'static, str>` does this, opt-in.

Where each falls short of safe, C-fast and readable
- C++ is fast, but view lookups are opt-in and views can dangle.
- Rust is safe, but list search takes only an element, both directions of `==` are written by hand, and literals put into Strings always allocate.
- Swift has free literals, but its search also takes only an element.
- Go, C# and Python avoid the question with one immutable, garbage-collected string, giving up in-place editing.

Ember takes, always on:
- Rust's `PartialEq<Rhs>` shape, spelled as Ember's own `Add[Rhs]`, carried to every search, lookup, insertion and `match`.
- C++20's single written direction.
- C++26's key made only when it is new.
- Rust's compile-time view safety.
- Holdings decided by the compiler from the function, as Ember already does for `[]`.
design.cost:
Costs per operation against C, worst first:
- A text literal held as a String costs one allocation and a copy, as TXT-9 says today. This happens only where a line in the function needs owned text: the costs of C++ `std::string` past 15 bytes, and of Rust's `String::from`. Option B would make it three stores.
- Text that is only read (a variable, or a list, set or map literal) costs nothing per text. Each element is a 16-byte static view, Copy, and dropping the list frees one buffer. That is today's cost for lists. Read-only set and map literals become cheaper than today, which pays one allocation per text key. C pays 8 bytes per `const char*`.
- `s == \"quit\"`, `who in names`, `index_of`, a text match arm, and `Array[String] == Array[StrView]` each cost a length compare, plus a byte compare per element or arm where lengths agree. That is C's `len == n && memcmp(...) == 0`, with no allocation.
- A list literal used as an operand (`cmd in [\"quit\", \"exit\"]`, `tokens == [\"go\", \"north\"]`) is a temporary fixed array on the stack, with no allocation. Today the `in` form allocates an Array.
- Map and Set lookups by a view are unchanged: one hash and one compare.
- `entry`, `insert` and `Set.add` by a view cost one hash and one compare. They allocate only for a new key, which is C's lookup plus strdup on insert. Today, `entry(owns String(w))` allocates and frees once per word.
- `binary_search` with a view needle costs what it costs with a String.

Where the cost is zero:
- No run-time check, conversion or memory is added anywhere.
- Every String read and every String drop is unchanged.
- Compile time adds one two-valued type variable per untyped text place, solved alongside `[]`'s open types. The comparison instance is chosen by TYP-24's existing rule.

Extra memory beyond C: 8 bytes per element only where a program keeps owned text, as for any owned string in C++ or Rust.

readability.note:
The after is shorter and reads as Python. The list needs no type written to be added to, and the membership test is `in`, as it already is for a set. The before needs a lambda and `.as_str()` to be sure `==` compiles. No word, annotation or ceremony is added anywhere. The only words left are those that state meaning, such as `owns` at the push (verdicts 147 and 149).

The programs that round 1 broke read exactly as they do today, with no type written: lookup tables (`days = [...]`, then `return days[i]`), menus passed to `Span[StrView]`, and row parsers storing views. Their lists only read, or put views in, so they stay views. Every program that compiles today still compiles and computes the same; only lines refused today change, and they now compile.

design.compiler_does:
1. Holdings. Text written in the program may sit where no type is expected: an unannotated declaration's initialiser, or anywhere inside an untyped literal. For each such place the compiler keeps a two-valued type variable (String or StrView), as it keeps `[]`'s element type.
- It fixes the variable from the function's uses. A use that only one value meets fixes it. A key that a set or map makes from a view of text the program did not write fixes String; the compiler knows a view's source from the body, as it does for every view. Otherwise the text is a StrView.
- Two conflicting uses are E2020 at the later one, naming both lines, with a help line that compiles.
- The literal's Alloc follows its holding: a String is TXT-9's allocation. `ember inspect --alloc` lists it, and E4001 names the use that made it a String.

2. Comparisons. For every ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, `in`, lookup argument and literal pattern, it reads the operands as TYP-21 says.
- It reads views through, keeps a text literal as a StrView, and lays a list literal operand out as a fixed array on the stack, its items read in place.
- An untyped number, `None`, `[]`, `{}` or `Ok(...)` takes the other operand's type.
- It then picks the instance by TYP-24. Where only the reverse direction is implemented, it calls that with the operands swapped (and `cmp` reversed).
- It monomorphises and inlines the result into a length compare plus memcmp, and may switch text match arms on length, then bytes.

3. std implements the rest:
- TXT-12's comparisons for its text types, lists, Option, Result, tuples, maps and sets.
- Contains according to what a container's items are, written per container so that no two implementations overlap (TYP-19).
- AsKey for its own pairs, and HASH-1's one way of hashing text and lists.
- ToKey's `to_key` taking its value over, and insert, entry and add making a key only when it is new.

4. Every refusal gives a line that compiles:
- E2226 for a needle that compares with nothing, and for a set or map lookup by a program's type with no AsKey (help: the AsKey implementation, and the hash it must match).
- E2020 for a holding conflict.
- E2041 when both directions of Eq or Ord are written (help: remove the second).
- E2070 when two instances still fit equally (help: the `Eq[X].eq(a, b)` form).

The programmer writes nothing new.
design.misuse:
Every misuse the compiler can see is refused when compiling, with a line that compiles:
- A needle that compares with no element (`5 in names`, a byte in a StrView) is E2226. Its help names the comparison to write, or `as_bytes()`.
- Uses that need both holdings are E2020 at the later use, naming both lines. For example, `names.push(owns s)` with a String `s`, followed by `draw_menu(names)` with a `Span[StrView]` parameter. The help gives the declaration with its type, or the other line changed.
- A set or map lookup of a program's own key type by another type with no AsKey is E2226 (`in`) or E2040 (`get`). The help gives `extend StrView implements AsKey[Ident]:` and says the key's hash must cover only what `is_key` compares.
- Writing both `K: Eq[Q]` and `Q: Eq[K]` (or Ord) is E2041, naming both, so the two directions can never disagree.
- A comparison that two instances fit equally, both reached only by coercion, is E2070, with the `Eq[X].eq(a, b)` form.

What cannot be refused when compiling is a comparison the programmer writes that disagrees with another:
- a hand-written AsKey whose hash or `is_key` disagrees with the key's;
- an `Ord[Q]` that orders otherwise than the order a list was sorted in, used by binary_search.
These give HASH-3's wrong answers: a missing key, a wrong position. They never give undefined behaviour, out-of-bounds access or non-termination. contains, index_of, binary_search, match and every lookup stay in bounds and end, whatever the comparisons return. This is today's rule for a hand-written Hash, Ord or AsKey, unchanged.

Unlike round 1, no Eq written for `==` alone silently signs a program up for hash lookups. std's own pairs agree by HASH-1's written rule.

Option A changes no String's representation and adds no effect. No String ever points at read-only memory, and no String operation newly allocates or panics. No run-time check is added anywhere.
design.verdicts:
Every owner verdict involved is kept; none is revisited.
- 72 ("the loop rule covers lists, maps, sets, strings alike") is kept. This rule carries the same "alike" to holding and to lookups: lists, sets, maps and variables follow one rule.
- 95 (Rust's way for lists and maps while a loop walks one) is kept. `x in xs` and every comparison only read, and nothing here changes a collection during a walk.
- 145, 146, 147, 149 and 161 are kept in every spelling:
  - `owns` before every handed-over argument (`names.push(owns newcomer)`, `seen.add(owns copy of newcomer)`, `counts.entry(owns w)`), where `owns` hands a view over as 145 says;
  - no `owns` before a lookup's argument, which only reads (146);
  - brackets where 161 requires them.
- 14 ("make the natural way fast; don't add a feature to avoid the work") is followed. The natural `[\"ann\", \"bob\"]` costs nothing while it is only read, and the compiler decides the holding; programmers are not asked to write types to avoid allocations.
- 164 to 166 are untouched.

Rules that are not owner verdicts and change:
- ODR-022 (a lead ruling, ADR-040 in docs/DECISIONS.md) is extended, not reversed. Numbers keep it: `total = 0` is int whatever the later uses. The holding of program text joins `[]`'s open types (TYP-23). ODR-022's own reason, that a later use must not change where a number's arithmetic overflows, does not apply: both holdings give every line the same text, length, comparison, hash and printing. The owner should hear this as part of option A.
- TYP-38's "a map written with no type owns its text" (a spec rule) is replaced by one rule for every collection. A set or map still owns text it makes keys from.
- ODR-067 (a lead ruling):
  - AsKey stays hand-written for a program's types; round 1's derivation from Eq[Q] is withdrawn.
  - std's own pairs are stated by property.
  - ToKey's `to_key` takes its value over, so insert, entry and add can make a key only when it is new. Their spellings (`entry(owns k)`, `insert(owns k, owns v)`, `add(owns x)`) are unchanged.

Rules kept:
- ODR-055: contains and index_of keep to `==`.
- TXT-9 and TXT-5: a literal held as a String allocates, and `String(s)` copies.
- TYP-24: unchanged.

Agreement with neighbouring groups:
- P06: J2-04 A's `Add[StrView]` uses the same right-hand-type spelling.
- P12: views are read through here. How a held value (owns, shares) compares stays as TYP-36 says, whatever P12 decides.
- P14: A adds and removes no effect. A literal's Alloc follows its holding, which P14's table should record.
- P19: `Eq[Rhs = Self]` keeps Eq's Self parameter, so its dyn answer is unchanged.
- P07: insert, entry and add stay one function each, with one parameter word.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. Text left untyped is held as the function's uses need, by one rule for variables, lists, sets and maps: views while only read, Strings once a line puts a String in. Every comparison, search, lookup and insertion takes a String or a view alike.
options_for_owner.code:
names = ["ann", "bob"]          # views while only read
names.push(owns newcomer)       # a String put in: names holds Strings
days = ["Mon", "Tue"]
return days[i]                  # only read: static views, as today
if who.trim() in banned:         # a view looked for among Strings
    println("go away")
if cmd == "quit":                # the text compared, no String made
    return
options_for_owner.outcome:
All compile. Every program that compiles today still does, unchanged.
- A variable or collection holding only the program's text is views: 16 bytes, no allocation per text, cheaper than today's sets and maps.
- One that a line puts a String into holds Strings, made as today with one allocation per literal.
- No comparison, `in`, lookup or match arm makes a String. `words == []`, `t.name == None` and `tokens == ["go", "north"]` allocate nothing.
- Insertion by a view (`counts.entry(owns w)`) makes the key only when it is new.
- A program's own types join by implementing `Eq[Q]`. Their set and map lookups by `Q` also need `AsKey`.

options_for_owner.summary: A, plus a String made from the program's text holds that text where it lies until it is changed, as Swift does. This changes String for every program, so it is best asked as its own question after A and P14.
options_for_owner.outcome:
As A, and no literal String ever allocates: field defaults, returns and owned collections included. In exchange:
- Every operation that writes a String's bytes in place (remove, as_mut_ptr, a C buffer) carries Alloc and Panic(Explicit) where a String of program text can reach it. The compiler finds this by following values, as verdict 128 does.
- `capacity()` reports such a String's length.
- Only bytes in the program's read-only image qualify: never a view of any owner, `static mut` included.

options_for_owner.summary: Every collection written with no type owns its text: always Strings (round 1's design, with or without B's free Strings).

draw_menu(items)                # E2020 for a Span[StrView] parameter
options_for_owner.outcome: J3-13 compiles. But lookup tables, menus and row parsers that compile today must write `Array[StrView]`. A read-only keyword table grows from 16 to 24 bytes per element, and its drop must walk every element.

options_for_owner.summary: Phase 2's drafts as written. An untyped text list holds Strings, with an allocation per literal, and a list of Strings is searched with a view (std lists only).
options_for_owner.code:
names = ["ann", "bob"]          # Array[String]: one allocation per name
if who.trim() in banned:         # std lists only
options_for_owner.outcome: The same refusals as C, plus an allocation and a copy for every literal in every untyped text list. `cmd == "quit"` stays undecided (a new String per test, or not), and a program's own containers cannot search by a view.

options_for_owner.summary: As today. Lists hold views and sets and maps hold Strings. A list of Strings is searched only with a String.
options_for_owner.code:

names.push(owns newcomer)       # E2020
