options_for_owner.outcome: The member programs are refused. `"trudy" in banned` and `cmd == "quit"` are undecided: a new String per test, or not.

recommendation.reason:
It is the only option that keeps all three goals and breaks nothing.
- Readability: the Python-style program compiles with no type written, and lists, sets, maps and variables follow one rule. Every program that compiles today compiles unchanged.
- Speed: text that is only read costs nothing per element (sets and maps get cheaper than today). No comparison, search or lookup makes a String, at C's length-plus-memcmp cost. Insertion by a view allocates only for a new key.
- Generality: one interface shape covers every comparison, container and lookup, and a program's own types. The spelling is Ember's own (`Add[Rhs]`), and the compiler decides the holding, as it already decides `[]`'s type.

Against the others:
- B is a real further gain, but it changes every String and P14's effect table, so it deserves its own question.
- C and D refuse lines that compile today.
- E refuses the member programs.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: with no type written, should text in a list, set, map or variable be a `string_view` while the function only reads it, and a `std::string` once a line puts a `std::string` in? Today a list is always views and a set is always strings. And should `==`, `in` and every lookup take a `string_view` against `std::string`s without building one, as C++'s `set<string, less<>>` does?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `names = ["ann", "bob"]` | `Array[StrView]`: two views of the program's text |
| 2 | main | `seen = {"ann", "bob"}` | `Set[String]`: two Strings, two allocations |
| 3 | main | `newcomer = input()` | the String `"cid"` |
| 4 | main | `newcomer.trim() in seen` | `false`: a view looks up a String key fine |
| 5 | main | `newcomer.trim() in banned` (`banned: Array[String]`) | refused, E2226: a list of Strings is searched only with a String |
| 6 | main | `"trudy" in banned` | undecided: a new String made for the test, or not |
| 7 | main | `names.push(owns newcomer)` | refused, E2020: a String into a list of views |
owner_short.today: An untyped list of text holds views, while a set or map holds Strings (one allocation each). A list of Strings can be searched only with a String. So the push and the `in` are refused, where the set's lines compile.
owner_short.options:
A: text with no type written is views while only read and Strings once a line puts a String in, the same for lists, sets, maps and variables; every `==`, `in` and lookup takes a String or a view (recommended).
B: A, plus Strings made from the program's text cost nothing until changed (Swift); a separate question, since it changes every String.
C: every untyped collection always owns Strings; lookup tables and menus that compile today then need a type written.
D: lists always own Strings, with an allocation per literal; lists are searched with a view.
E: as today: the push and the `in` are refused.
owner_short.recommendation: A: the Python-style program compiles, every program that compiles today still does, read-only text costs nothing, and no comparison or lookup makes a String.

repairs.hole: safety/engineering high: a String made from a view of a `static mut` String points into a buffer that is later freed (TXT-9's no-copy decided by region, citing LT-3)
repairs.answer: Closed. The free program-text String is no longer part of this rule. TXT-9 and TXT-5 are unchanged: `String(s)` always copies, and a literal held as a String allocates its own buffer. So no String ever aliases another's buffer. Option B, if the owner takes it, decides by where the text came from, not by region: only bytes in the read-only image qualify (a literal, or a view whose every source is a literal, a `static` StrView or a `from static` field), never a view of any owner (`static`, `static mut` or local).

repairs.hole: safety high: `x == y` with both sides `ref String`, and `sorted(m.keys())`, are refused or undecided (no read-through for operands)
repairs.answer: Closed. TYP-21 reads views through for both operands before the instance is chosen, as IV.11 step 1 does for a receiver, so `x == y` uses `Eq[String]`. TYP-36 says `ref T` meets `Eq[U]`, `Eq[ref U]`, `Ord[U]` and `Ord[ref U]` wherever T meets `Eq[U]` or `Ord[U]`. So `sorted(m.keys())` and `counts.get(w)` with `w: ref String` compile; both are listed among the cases. How held values (owns, shares) compare stays TYP-36's, whatever P12 decides.

repairs.hole: safety medium and engineering high: AsKey derived from Eq[Q] silently signs a type up for hash lookups, and `"main" in seen` prints false
repairs.answer: Closed. AsKey is no longer derived. A program's set or map lookup by another type needs a written `extend StrView implements AsKey[Ident]:`, as under today's ODR-067. That line carries the MUST, and the help names the hash it must match. In the breaker's program, `"main" in seen` becomes E2226 instead of a silent false; `"main" in idents` (a list, compared with Eq) still compiles. std's own pairs agree by HASH-1's written rule (text feeds its bytes, lists their elements and length). HASH-3's never-undefined-behaviour now also covers contains, index_of, binary_search and match. The 'refuse a derived Hash that hashes more than Eq[Q] compares' check is not needed: Eq[Q] alone no longer promises anything about hashing.

repairs.hole: safety medium: STD-8's blanket by layout ('reads as a Span') gives StrView a byte Contains, against STD-8b, and may overlap (E2041)
repairs.answer: Closed. STD-8 now goes by what a container's items are. StrView's and String's items are chars, so `b in line` is E2226, as STD-8b says. std writes each container's implementation for that container (lists by linear scan, Set and Map by AsKey, text by characters and substrings), so there is no blanket over an open type and TYP-19 sees no overlap.

repairs.hole: safety medium: the right operand typed by its own type makes `tokens == ["go", "north"]` allocate under @noalloc, and `words == []`, `opt == None` and `r == Ok(5)` undecided
repairs.answer: Closed by TYP-21's reading of operands, which follows `Rhs = Self`. A list literal operand is a temporary fixed array read as a Span, with no allocation, so the `@noalloc` function compiles; so does `cmd in ["quit", "exit"]`, which allocates today. `None`, `[]`, `{}`, `Ok(...)` with an open side, and untyped numbers take their type from the other operand, as `1 + x` does (TYP-23). So each of the breaker's lines uses the left operand's own instance.

repairs.hole: safety medium: remove's new Alloc also brings Panic(Explicit) (ALC-4), so E4040 under @nopanic(explicit)
repairs.answer: Closed. Under option A, remove gains no effect at all, because no String holds program text in place. Option B states both effects (Alloc and Panic(Explicit)) for every operation that writes a String's bytes in place, gives E4040 the same help as E4001, and decides where they apply by following values (see the remove hole below).

repairs.hole: safety medium: TYP-36 has no Span or MutSpan row, and nothing says [T; N] and Span hash alike, so `routes.get(dst)` may give a wrong answer
repairs.answer: Closed. TYP-36 gains Span[T] and MutSpan[T] rows (Eq, Ord lexicographic and Hash when T has them). HASH-1 says every std list feeds its elements in order and then its length, and every std text type its bytes, the same way. `[T; N]` hashes as a list. So `routes.get(packet[0..4])` finds the `[u8; 4]` key by a written rule.

repairs.hole: safety medium: TXT-12 names its types one by one, leaving out FixedString, Deque, RingBuffer and SmallArray
repairs.answer: Closed. TXT-12 is stated by property: every std type that holds text compares with every other by bytes; every std list (a container whose items keep positions) with every std list whose items compare; Option, Result and tuples with their own kind; sets and maps as sets of entries. The std types are given only as what meets the property, so FixedString, Deque, RingBuffer, SmallArray and FixedArray are covered. A program's own types and containers join by implementing `Eq[Q]` or `Contains[Q]`.

repairs.hole: engineering high: A's always-String lists refuse `return days[i]` (E3063), passing to a `Span[StrView]` parameter (E2020), and storing a view (E2020), all of which compile today
repairs.answer: Closed. The holding is now decided by uses (TYP-23), by one rule for variables, lists, sets and maps. All three programs compile exactly as today: the first only reads, the second's parameter only views meet, and the third puts a view in. J3-13's push still compiles, because a String put in makes the list hold Strings. This extends ODR-022 (a lead ruling) to text holdings, with the reason stated: its overflow argument does not apply, since the holding changes no computed value. The options table now shows C's refusals plainly.

repairs.hole: engineering high: `t.name == None`, `t.gains == [0.5, 1.0]` for f32, and `t.gains == []` become E2070 or E2060, and adding a package can break `xs == []`
repairs.answer: Closed by the same TYP-21 reading. `None` and `[]` take the other operand's type, and the f32 list literal is a temporary `[f32; 2]` whose numbers take f32. Each line uses the left operand's own instance with no coercion, so no tie arises, and a later package's `extend int implements Eq[Meters]` cannot make it ambiguous. The help form `Eq[...].eq(...)` is no longer needed for these lines.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: remove(i) gains Alloc on every String, refusing a @noalloc console editor; stated by a list of names
repairs.answer: Closed. Under option A no String holds program text in place, so remove, as_mut_ptr and every other String operation keep today's effects, and the editor compiles under @noalloc. Option B carries this as its own question, stated as one rule: every operation that writes a String's bytes in place first gives a String of program text room of its own. It carries Alloc and Panic(Explicit) exactly where such a String can reach it, found by following values as verdicts 128 and 129 do, and falling back to the type where values cannot be followed (a pub function's parameter).

repairs.hole: engineering medium: SPN-1's String-to-MutSpan conversion and as_mut_ptr can write the read-only image
repairs.answer: Closed for this rule: under option A no String ever points at read-only memory. Option B covers it with the same rule as remove (every writable route gives room first). Separately, SPN-1's 'a String converts ... to MutSpan[T]' already lets safe code write a String's bytes and break TXT-1's UTF-8 promise. That gap was there before this rule, so it is reported in open risks for the lead, not settled here.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: capacity() 0 with len above 0 breaks len <= capacity
repairs.answer: Closed. Under option A no such String exists: TXT-11's capacity is unchanged. Option B reports `capacity()` as such a String's length, so `len() <= capacity()` holds and spare room is 0. Internally the capacity word stays 0, so drop and growth need no extra test.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: `entry(k)` and `Set.add(x)` take the key itself, so word counting allocates per word
repairs.answer: Closed. `insert`, `entry` and `Set.add` take any `Q: needs ToKey[K]` handed over, and make the key only when it is new (C++26's heterogeneous insertion). `counts.entry(owns w).or_default() += 1` with a view `w` allocates only for a new word: C's lookup plus strdup on insert. ToKey's `to_key` now takes its value over, so a key handed over is moved in with no copy, and a key type that cannot be copied still goes in. The spellings (`entry(owns k)`, `insert(owns k, owns v)`, `add(owns x)`) are unchanged. `m[q] = v` makes its key from `copy of q`, which is free for a view.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: `config["mode"] = "fast"` chooses `IndexSet[StrView]`, whose to_key copies, while `insert` costs nothing
repairs.answer: Not a hole under option A. The claim that `IndexSet[String]` costs three stores relies on round 1's free String. With TXT-9 as it is, the view instance is the cheaper one: it makes the String key only when the key is new (one allocation), while `IndexSet[String, V]` would allocate a String even for a key already there. `insert(owns "scale", ...)` now takes a ToKey value too, so the two forms cost the same. If option B is taken, its design makes a literal that a key-making operation keeps a free String.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: `"main" == id` is refused until a hand-kept reverse implementation exists, and Ord[Q] versus Ord[Self] agreement is unstated
repairs.answer: Closed. A written `K: Eq[Q]` also answers `q == k` with its operands swapped, and `Ord[Q]` answers `q < k` reversed (C++20's rewritten comparisons). Writing both directions is E2041, so they cannot disagree. STD-15 says the `Ord[Q]` that binary_search uses MUST order as the list was sorted. HASH-3 says a disagreeing order gives wrong positions, never undefined behaviour.

repairs.hole: engineering medium: under A a keyword table grows from 96 to 144 bytes, gains a per-element drop walk, and loses a single-memcpy copy
repairs.answer: Closed. A table that is only read stays an `Array[StrView]`: 96 bytes, Copy elements, one buffer freed, copied with one memcpy. That is exactly today's cost. Only a list that a line puts a String into pays String's 24 bytes per element, and that program is refused today.

design.open_risks:
1. ODR-022. The owner should hear that text's holding is decided by the function's uses. Someone reading `names = [\"ann\", \"bob\"]` learns whether it holds views or Strings only from the rest of the function. No line computes differently either way, and each conflict is an error naming both lines. Tools (hover, `ember inspect`) can show the chosen holding.

2. A literal's allocation follows its holding. A push far below makes the literal's line allocate (TXT-9). `ember inspect --alloc` lists it, and E4001 names the use. P14's effect table should record this.

3. `size_of[T]()` and `type_name[T]()` applied to such an element report the holding the uses chose. A program that asks for the type sees it.

4. Option B, free program text, is its own question, best asked after A and P14. Its design, which closes the holes it raised:
- Only bytes in the read-only image qualify: literals, and views whose every source is a literal, a `static` StrView or a `from static` field. Never a view of an owner. HR-4 keeps old images, so the text survives reloads.
- `capacity()` reports the length.
- Every operation that writes a String's bytes in place gives it room first. It carries Alloc and Panic(Explicit) where such a String can reach it, found by following values (verdicts 128 and 129), with E4040 given E4001's help.
- A literal that a key-making operation keeps is made free.
- The cost is one compare in remove and as_mut_ptr.

5. A gap that predates this rule. SPN-1 (p07:812) says a String converts to `MutSpan[T]`. That lets safe code write a String's bytes and break TXT-1's UTF-8 promise (UNS-4). It should go to the lead as its own gap. The likely fix: a String gives only `Span[u8]` and `StrView`, and writable bytes are reached only in unsafe code.

6. A hand-written AsKey or `Ord[Q]` that disagrees gives wrong answers, never undefined behaviour; this is today's model. A key projection would make agreement checkable: write `fn key() -> StrView` once and get Eq[Q], Hash and AsKey from it. That could be a later question if wanted; safety does not need it.

7. Migration:
- A program's own ToKey implementations add `owns this` to `to_key`.
- A program that writes both directions of Eq or Ord gets E2041 and deletes one.
- An untyped set or map literal that is only read becomes views. No program can compute differently because of this.

8. `[v; N]` of a text literal, and text inside tuples and Options inside untyped literals, follow the same rule, each text position fixed on its own.

9. STD-7 barely specifies FixedString[N], Deque, RingBuffer, SmallArray and FixedArray. TXT-12 assumes FixedString holds UTF-8 text and that the others keep their items in positions.

10. Interplay with other groups:
- P12: how holders compare is P12's to decide. Views are read through here.
- P14: no new effects under A.
- P19: `Eq[Rhs = Self]` still has a Self parameter.
- P06: `Add[StrView]` uses the same spelling.
- P07: insert, entry and add stay one function each.

design.spec_text:
**Rules added or changed.**
- New: `[EFF-28]`.
- Changed: the X.1 table (its second column becomes each effect's definition), `[EFF-3]`, `[EFF-9]`, `[EFF-12]`, `[EFF-16]`, `[DET-2]`, `[DET-4]`, `[SIMD-4]`, `[CLO-10]`, `[PHIL-2]`, `[STD-6]` with the module table's `std.core` row, `[ERR-9]`, `[LT-48]` and `[DSJ-6]`.
- Also changed: two `[COST-3]` rows, one new `[COST-6]` row, and the `E4030` and `E4070` rows of XVII.
- Part I takes J1-01's lead-fix wording, now settled: `[PHIL-8]`, I.1, the I.4 row and I.6 name `runtime` and `assert_disjoint`/`check_disjoint` as the alias checks a line asks for.

**X.1 table** *(changed)*. The header becomes `| Effect | Carried by every operation that … (examples) |`.

| Effect | Carried by every operation that … (examples) |
|---|---|
| `Alloc` | takes memory from the heap, directly or through a memory manager that may take more from it. Examples: a value put in a block of its own (a class object; a value made with `owns`, `shares` or `thread_shared`; a function value's state block, `[CLO-10]`; an error turned into an `AnyError`, `[ERR-11]`; the new block of an object handed to another thread, `[THR-2]`), and room taken by a collection, a `String` or a growing arena (growth, `String +`, an allocating literal or f-string). Memory from a region that never grows (a frame, a `FixedArena`, `[ARN-4]`) is not `Alloc`. |
| `Sync` | coordinates with other threads: an atomic read-modify-write stronger than relaxed, a lock, a channel operation, a thread's start or join, making or ending a `thread_shared` owner or a `weakref` link to a `thread_shared` value, and opening such a link |
| `Lock` | takes a lock: a `Mutex` or `RwLock` (`try_lock` included), or a `Lock` held with `with x.lock:` |
| `Block` | may wait for another thread or the world: a blocking lock, `join` and the end of a `with scope` block, `sleep`, a blocking receive or read |
| `Io` | moves data between the program and a file, a socket or the console |
| `Panic(Explicit)` | stops the program where its own words ask for a stop: a line, or the word `runtime` on a value the line uses, that says to stop when something does not hold (`panic`, `assert*` with `assert_disjoint` included, `unwrap`, `expect`, `todo`, `unreachable`, `cast x as T`, a `runtime` value's check, `[LT-48]`); and a heap allocation that fails |
| `RuntimeCheck(k)` | tests while running whether an operation keeps a safety property of kind `k ∈ {Aliasing, Bounds, Stale, Arithmetic}`, where the proofs of `[EFF-15]` leave the test in (`[EFF-9]`) |
| `Unsafe` | is unsafe code: the body contains `unsafe` or the function is `unsafe fn` |
| `FFI` | calls an `extern` function |
| `Nondet` | gives a result, or leaves a value in a place the program reads later, that this specification does not fix as a function of the program's input (`[DET-2]`) |

* `[EFF-28]` *(new)* **An effect is what the operation does.**
  - An operation carries an effect exactly when it does what the effect's row defines, as this specification fixes what the operation does. Its name does not matter, nor whether a row or a rule names it. The operations a row or a rule names are examples of its definition, never the definition.
  - Every fact a definition turns on is fixed by this specification and worked out by the compiler from the code, one answer on every compiler and in every profile (`[PHIL-13]`, `[EFF-15]`). These facts include where a value's memory comes from, whether a result is the same on every machine, and which orders of two threads the program fixes. None is left to an implementation.
  - A rule that adds an operation states the effects it carries, as `[COST-5]` asks for its cost. An effect the rule does not state is still carried.
  - A function's effects are those of everything it runs (`[EFF-1]`, `[EFF-2]`). A contract (X.2) forbids exactly its effects, and a library layer (`[STD-6]`) leaves out exactly its effects: every operation that does what they define, and nothing else.

* `[EFF-3]` *(changed)* An `extern` function carries:
  - `FFI`;
  - the effects its `@ffi(effects=[…])` states, or every effect when none are stated (`[FFI-10]`). Its code cannot be read, so an effect not vouched absent is carried.
  - `Nondet`, unless it is declared `@ffi(deterministic)` (`[DET-8]`).

  What a call of one may change through the callbacks C keeps is `[EFF-26]`'s.

* `[EFF-9]` *(changed)* `RuntimeCheck(k)` enters a function's effect set when a test of kind `k` survives the proofs of `[EFF-15]` in its body. A kind is defined by the property its test keeps:
  - `Aliasing`: whether what a line changes overlaps what another name reads or views. This covers the compare of `assert_disjoint` and `check_disjoint` (`[DSJ-1]`), and the kind compare of a `runtime` value at a line one of its kinds would make overlap (`[LT-48]`).
  - `Bounds`: whether a position or key is inside what it indexes. This covers indices, slices, chunk sizes, a SIMD `load`'s or `store`'s length, a gather's lanes, and `m[k]` for a key the map lacks.
  - `Stale`: whether a target, handle or link is still the one it names. This covers a handle's generation, the header test that opens a `weakref` link, and the weak-count compare of a hand-over with its stop for an object C keeps (`[THR-2]`).
  - `Arithmetic`: whether a number's operation is defined and fits. This covers overflow, an `Atomic`'s `fetch_add`, division by zero, shift amounts, negative integer exponents, and a count compared with its limit before it grows.

  A kind test and a cast answer the program's own question about a kind, which is none of these four; `cast x as T` is `Panic(Explicit)`. A library operation's stop has the kind of what it keeps, however its body raises it.

* `[EFF-12]` *(changed)* `@no_alias_checks` permits `RuntimeCheck(Bounds)`, `(Arithmetic)` and `(Stale)`. It forbids `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` wherever that arises: the compare of `assert_disjoint` or `check_disjoint`, and a `runtime` value's check. A data-oriented inner loop can always do without them: spans the compiler proves apart need no compare, a copy needs none, and a kind known when compiling needs none.
  - `E4030` keeps today's text for `assert_disjoint`.
  - For `runtime`, `E4030` reads: "`mix` is `@no_alias_checks`, and `runtime` on `m` (line 16) compares its kind while running, at `samples.push(owns 0.0)` (line 18); give `m` a kind known when compiling, or remove `@no_alias_checks`".
  - `@static_safe` stays as today.

* `[EFF-16]` *(changed)* `@nopanic(explicit)` forbids `Panic(Explicit)`: the stops the program's words ask for, a `runtime` value's check included, and allocation failure. For `runtime`, `E4040` reads: "`mix` is `@nopanic(explicit)`, and `runtime` on `m` (line 16) may stop the program at `samples.push(owns 0.0)` (line 18); give `m` a kind known when compiling, or remove `@nopanic(explicit)`". A test that only keeps a safety property (bounds, overflow, stale, `check_disjoint`'s compare, a count against its limit) is a `RuntimeCheck` and is allowed under it. The rest of the rule is unchanged.

* `[LT-48]` *(changed; one sentence added)* "Its compare is `RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)` and its stop is `Panic(Explicit)` (`[EFF-9]`), as `assert_disjoint`'s are, at each line where a compare is placed; its reason is `requested_by_type` (`[EFF-11]`). Where every kind that may reach the value is known when compiling, nothing is compared and the word carries neither."

* `[DSJ-6]` *(changed)* `check_disjoint` and `assert_disjoint` are usable in `@noalloc` and `@nosync` code. Each is a run-time alias check (`RuntimeCheck(Aliasing)`, `[EFF-9]`), as a `runtime` value's check is, so inside `@no_alias_checks` each is `E4030` (today's message).

* `[DET-2]` *(changed)* **What `Nondet` is.** An operation is `Nondet` when what it gives back, or what it leaves in a place the program reads later, is not fixed by this specification as a function of the program's input. That happens in two ways, and in no other.
  * **(a) A result left to the platform, the hardware or the moment.**
    - A floating-point result whose bits IEEE 754 does not require. This is every `std.math` function and float method except the operations IEEE 754 requires correctly rounded or exact, and what is built from those alone. The exact operations are `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `sqrt`, `fma`/`mul_add`, conversions, `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `round`, `round_half_away`, `fract`, `abs`, `copysign`, `min` and `max`. Built from them alone: `rsqrt`, `lerp`, `smoothstep`, a vector's `length`, `dot`, `cross` and `normalize`, a matrix product or inverse.
    - So `sin` through `pow`, `cbrt` and `hypot` are `Nondet`, and their `std.math.det` twins are not (`[DET-4]`).
    - The `_approx` operations (`[SIMD-4]`).
    - Floating-point contraction, reassociation, or any `@fastmath` relaxation.
    - The wall clock, the monotonic clock, the system random source, and making a `RandomState`, directly or as a `Map`'s or `Set`'s hasher.
    - Observing a pointer or an object's address as an integer, or hashing one.
    - Reading padding bytes.
    - Any `extern` function not declared `@ffi(deterministic)`.
  * **(b) An order two threads leave open.** This is the case of operations on one place from two threads that may run at the same time, where:
    - at least one of them is a change;
    - the program fixes no order between them;
    - the order can change a value read later.

    The program fixes an order in four ways:
    - a thread's or task's start: it runs after what its starter did before the start;
    - its join: what follows the join runs after it;
    - a blocking receive: it runs after the send of the value it gets;
    - a reduction's combine order (`[THR-21]`, `[PAR-3]`).

    Changes that leave the same values in every order leave nothing open. These are an `Atomic`'s `wrapping_fetch_add` and `wrapping_fetch_sub`, or its `fetch_and`, `fetch_or` or `fetch_xor` used alone, when their results are not used.

    What each thread touches is worked out from its functions (`[EFF-24]`), with the precision `[THR-11]` has for tasks. The threads a function leaves running are part of its summary (`[EFF-4]`). A thread whose handle leaves the function that started it runs until the program ends.

    The line that lets the two run at once carries the effect: the start of the later thread, or the starter's own operation before the earlier thread's join. `E4070` names both starts and the place.
    - `Nondet`: two threads changing what one lock guards; two threads sending on one channel at once; a load of an `Atomic` another thread may change; `try_lock` while another thread may take the lock; `try_recv` while a sender may send.
    - Not `Nondet`: a lock or a channel that one thread uses at a time.
    - Jobs submitted outside a scope count as threads, and a job scope's jobs as its tasks.

  The following are not `Nondet`:
  - iterating a `Map` or `Set` (insertion order, `[STD-11]`);
  - a reduction of scoped tasks or of a `@parallel` loop (`[THR-21]`, `[PAR-5]`).

  Reading uninitialised memory is not `Nondet` but undefined, outside Safe Ember (`[PHIL-10]`; ODR-136).

* `[DET-4]` *(changed)* `std.math.det` provides a twin of every function that `[DET-2]`(a) makes `Nondet`, for `f32` and `f64`, returning the same bits on every supported target. The twins are `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `exp`, `exp2`, the natural logarithm, `log2`, `log10`, `pow`, `cbrt`, `hypot`, and `sqrt`. The natural logarithm's name is P24's question J6-10. The accuracy and conversion sentences stay as today.

* `[SIMD-4]` *(changed; two sentences added)*
  - "`reduce_add`, `reduce_min` and `reduce_max` on float lanes combine the lanes in an order fixed for each target, the same on every machine that runs the binary (`[DET-7]`), so they are not `Nondet`."
  - "The `_approx` operations give the processor's estimate, which differs between processor makers, and are `Nondet` (`[DET-2]`)."

* `[CLO-10]` *(changed)*
  - A function value is two words, `{code, state}`. Its state is what it captured with a word and, when it uses real variables, where they live: the frame of the function that writes it. That is one address, since the variables sit at places in that frame fixed when compiling.
  - A named function, or a lambda that captures nothing and uses no real variable, has no state, allocates nothing, and is `Copy`. A function value with state is not `Copy`, and `=` hands it over.
  - The state is kept in the first of these places that lasts as long as the value. This rule fixes the place on every compiler:
    1. The state word itself, when the state is one word or less (a pointer's size on the target): the frame's address alone, or one word of its own, such as `copy of k` of a `float` on a 64-bit target.
    2. A slot in the frame of the function that writes it, when `[CLO-4]`'s check finds two things: the value ends before that function returns, and no value the same line made is still alive when the line runs again. That means it is kept only in names and places that end before then, and is handed only to calls that keep it no longer. Examples are a handler kept in a local and called in a loop, or a lambda run by scoped tasks.
    3. A block of its own, made with the value, which carries `Alloc` and is listed by `ember inspect --alloc`. Examples are a function value returned, stored where it outlives its writer, given to `thread.spawn`, or made in a loop and kept across rounds.
  - Calling one is one indirect call. The rest of the rule is unchanged: copying the two words out of a list or field, replacing or ending a value, `thread_shared fn()`, and `==`.

* `[PHIL-2]` *(changed)* Two changes:
  - The list's entry "a function value whose state exceeds its inline capacity" becomes "a function value whose state goes in a block of its own (`[CLO-10]`)".
  - The list adds "converting an error into `AnyError` (`[ERR-11]`); a `String` made or grown by `+`". It then ends: "These are examples: every operation that takes memory from the heap carries `Alloc` by the table's definition (`[EFF-28]`), named here or not, and is listed by `ember inspect --alloc`."

* `[STD-6]` *(changed; sentences added after the list of layers)*

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

static INPUT_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut INPUTS: Array[int] guarded by INPUT_LOCK = []

fn receive(player: int):
    with INPUT_LOCK:
        INPUTS.push(owns player)

@deterministic
fn gather_turn() -> Array[int]:
    a = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(1))
    b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(2))   # E4070 here
    a.join()
    b.join()
    with INPUT_LOCK:
        return copy of INPUTS

# what the message gives, which compiles:
@deterministic
fn gather_turn_fixed() -> Array[int]:
    a = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(1))
    a.join()
    b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): receive(2))
    b.join()
    with INPUT_LOCK:
        return copy of INPUTS             # always [1, 2]
answers.outcome:
`gather_turn` is `E4070` at line 14: "`gather_turn` is `@deterministic`, and the threads started on lines 13 and 14 both run `receive`, which pushes to `INPUTS` (line 9) under `INPUT_LOCK`; which gets the lock first decides the list; join the first before starting the second: move line 15 above line 14".

`gather_turn_fixed` compiles and always returns `[1, 2]`.

Not `Nondet`:
- a lock only one thread takes;
- a channel with one sender read by a blocking `recv`;
- an `Atomic` counter changed with `wrapping_fetch_add` and read after the joins.

`Nondet`: `try_lock`, `try_recv`, and an `Atomic` load while another thread may change it.

DET-2(a): a result whose bits IEEE 754 does not require is `Nondet`, whatever its name. This is J6-08's option A, stated as a property, not a list.
- `Nondet`: `cbrt`, `hypot` and the `_approx` operations.
- Not `Nondet`: `sqrt`, `normalize` and `length`.

`std.math.det` gains a twin of each `Nondet` function, so the message always gives a line that compiles.

- `v.rsqrt_approx()` is `E4070`: it is the processor's estimate, which differs between processor makers. The help gives the exact form, a lane-wise `sqrt` and a division.

- `wire` is `E4001` at the push. The function value keeps two words of its own and outlives `wire` in `b.handlers`, so its state is a block. The help offers one word of state (`copy of km` with `km = k * m`) or a type parameter.

Settled by STD-6's property: a type whose values own heap memory belongs to the alloc layer, whichever module declares it. `AnyError`'s error is an `owns dyn Error` in a block of its own (ERR-8), so `AnyError` is alloc's. This is J6-11's option A.

A core-only package names its error types. A core-only `AnyError` (option B) would be a second path for one type.

`-> Result[int]` is refused at that line with the layer's error (`[BLD-11]`): "`Result[int]` fails with `AnyError`, which keeps its error on the heap, and this package uses only `core`; name the error type: `-> Result[int, FrameError]`".

With the error type named, it compiles and allocates nothing. `?` moves the `FrameError` as a C function returns an error code.

other_cases.case: `String +`: `shown = label + "!"` (P06's J2-04 and J6-14)
other_cases.settled: `Alloc`: it takes room from the heap for the new or extended String. Under P06's rvalue refinement, `a + b + c` makes one String and grows it, and is still `Alloc` at that line. `@noalloc` refuses it (E4001), with `format_to` into a `FixedString` as the help. PHIL-2 lists it as an example; the definition already carries it.

other_cases.case: Untyped text list literal `names = ["ann", "bob"]` under P13's J3-13 A
other_cases.settled: If P13 makes it an `Array[String]`, it is `Alloc`: one allocation for the list and one per String. `@noalloc` refuses it with the fixed-array or `StrView` form as help. The rule needs no new PHIL-2 entry: the definition carries whatever P13 fixes.

other_cases.case: A field default made at construction and replaced by init (P15's J3-06)
other_cases.settled: The default expression's effects are the construction's wherever the language's construction rule runs it (EFF-1: "the argument and default expressions it evaluates"). With P15's B, an init that sets the field never runs the default, so that construction gets no `Alloc` from it. P15 must fix this one way; a "may" is not allowed (EFF-28).

other_cases.case: `thread_shared x` making a shared value
other_cases.settled: `Alloc` (a block of its own), and `Sync` for its counts. Unchanged, now by definition.

other_cases.case: Hand-over of an object whose class some `weakref` targets (lead fix J6-03, verdict 114)
other_cases.settled: Every such hand-over carries `Alloc` for the new block, and allocation failure, which is `Panic(Explicit)`. It carries `Alloc` because whether a link exists is known only while running. The weak-count compare and the stop for an object C keeps are `RuntimeCheck(Stale)`. So `@noalloc` and `@nopanic(explicit)` refuse the hand-over (E4001, E4040), naming the class's `weakref` line. A class no `weakref` targets hands over at no cost. The owner should hear this consequence.

other_cases.case: Check points that run queued `thread_shared` drops (P05)
other_cases.settled: A check point carries the effects of every drop it may run, since a drop is a call (EFF-1, DRP-8). A loop whose back edge may run a drop that allocates is `Alloc`. Freeing a block is not `Alloc`. Which points are check points is P05's question; this rule carries the effects.

other_cases.case: `?` into `AnyError` in a `@noalloc` function of a package with alloc
other_cases.settled: `Alloc` on the failure path, and allocation failure, which is `Panic(Explicit)` (ERR-11). `@noalloc` refuses it; a concrete error type moves without allocating. In a core-only package it is refused earlier, by type (STD-6).

other_cases.case: `cast s as Circle`, `unwrap`, `expect`, `todo`
other_cases.settled: Each is `Panic(Explicit)` only: the program's own words ask for a stop. None is a `RuntimeCheck`, since a kind test or a claim about a value keeps none of the four safety properties.

other_cases.case: `xs[i]`, `m[k]` for a missing key, a SIMD `load` too short, a gather lane
other_cases.settled: Each is `RuntimeCheck(Bounds)` only: no word asks for a stop. `@nopanic(explicit)` and `@no_alias_checks` accept them. `m[k]` is Bounds however std's body raises the stop (EFF-9's last sentence), so the answer does not depend on how the library is written.

other_cases.case: Count roll-over compares, an `Atomic`'s checked `fetch_add`
other_cases.settled: `RuntimeCheck(Arithmetic)`: unchanged and allowed under `@nopanic(explicit)`, with COST-6's texts. `wrapping_fetch_add` carries none.

other_cases.case: A stale handle, `if w exists as p:`
other_cases.settled: `RuntimeCheck(Stale)`. The `exists as` test is a branch, not a stop.

other_cases.case: Channels in `@deterministic` code
other_cases.settled: Two threads sending on copies of one `Sender` at once: `Nondet` at the second start, naming the channel. One sender read by a blocking `recv`: not `Nondet`, because the receive is ordered after the send of what it gets. `try_recv` while a sender may send: `Nondet` at the `try_recv`.

other_cases.case: Atomics in `@deterministic` code
other_cases.settled: Two threads `wrapping_fetch_add`ing one `Atomic`, results unused, read after both joins: not `Nondet`. A `load` while another thread may change it, or a used `fetch_add` result: `Nondet`. Two threads using a checked `fetch_add` are `Nondet`, because the place's stop and value may depend on the order; the help names `wrapping_fetch_add` or scoped tasks' reduction.

other_cases.case: `try_lock`
other_cases.settled: `Nondet` exactly while another thread may take the same lock. On a lock only this thread takes it is not, unlike a list entry that names `try_lock` outright.

other_cases.case: Clocks, `RandomState`, address hashing, `Map` iteration, `DefaultHasher`
other_cases.settled: Clocks, the system random source, `RandomState` and address hashing are `Nondet` (DET-2(a)). `Map` and `Set` iteration is not (insertion order). `DefaultHasher`'s fixed seed is not.

other_cases.case: Float reductions: scoped tasks (THR-21), `@parallel` (PAR-3/PAR-5), SIMD `reduce_add`
other_cases.settled: Not `Nondet`: the first two combine in spawn and chunk order. `reduce_add` on float lanes adds in an order SIMD-4 now fixes for each target, which is the same on every machine running the binary (DET-7). Verdict 92's `0.6` stays allowed.

other_cases.case: A `@deterministic` or `@noalloc` function calling through `dyn`, a stored function or a function field
other_cases.settled: It has the effects of every implementation or function that reaches that place (EFF-2, verdict 122). A `dyn Steer` one of whose kinds calls `cbrt` makes the call `Nondet`, and the chain names that kind.

other_cases.case: A C function declared with no `@ffi(effects=…)`
other_cases.settled: It carries every effect (FFI-10; EFF-3 is aligned with it), and `Nondet` unless `@ffi(deterministic)`. A `@noalloc` function calling it is E4001, with the help `@ffi(effects=[...])` in its declaration, an asserted fact listed by `ember tcb`. This is verdict 31's way: a forgotten mark refuses.

other_cases.case: A `thread_shared` value whose `drop` pushes to a guarded log, its last owner ending on any thread
other_cases.settled: The drop's change to the log is an operation of whichever thread ends the value (THR-20, P05's check points). Its order against other threads' changes to the log is not fixed, so DET-2(b) makes the line that lets them run together `Nondet`.

other_cases.case: A class object made and ended inside a `@noalloc` function
other_cases.settled: `Alloc` (CLS-1 puts it in a block). OPT-1's frame placement is an optimisation that verdicts ignore (EFF-15), so the verdict is the same on every compiler. Function values differ because CLO-10 now fixes their placement as a rule of the language.

other_cases.case: Function values given to `thread.spawn` and `scope.spawn`
other_cases.settled: Given to `thread.spawn`, the value may outlive its writer, so a state of more than one word is a block (`Alloc`). Given to `scope.spawn`, it ends before the scope does: a frame slot, or a block if made in a loop and still alive when the line runs again (CLO-10 case 2). A function capturing nothing has no state.

other_cases.case: `runtime` written on a field or a lambda parameter (P18's J1-11)
other_cases.settled: Wherever P18 allows the word, its check carries the same two effects, at the lines where a compare is placed.

other_cases.case: `FixedArena` allocation in `@noalloc` code
other_cases.settled: Not `Alloc`: the memory comes from a region that never grows (ARN-4). Exhaustion is a panic from the library's body; `try_alloc` returns `Option`.

design.prior_art:
**C++**
- No effect system. `noexcept` is enforced while running (`std::terminate`) and never checked when compiling.
- Whether `std::function` holds a lambda without the heap is each library's choice; its small-buffer size differs between libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC. That is CLO-10's "may" exactly.
- A lambda used locally is a stack object, and C++26's `std::function_ref` never allocates. Ember's frame slot gives that without a second type.
- `<cmath>` requires correct rounding only for IEEE's required operations (`sqrt`, `fma`, rounding), so `cbrt` and `sin` differ between glibc, MSVC and Apple's libm.
- Clang 20's function-effect attributes (`[[clang::nonallocating]]`, `[[clang::nonblocking]]`) are the nearest prior art. They are checked when compiling over the callees the compiler can see, and a call it cannot see breaks the promise unless declared. But which operations allocate is the compiler's own list, and the diagnostics are warnings.

**Rust**
- No allocation or panic contract in the language; `#[no_panic]` is a link-time trick.
- `no_std` plus the `alloc` crate are layers by crate: whatever owns heap memory (`Box`, `Vec`, `String`, `Box<dyn Error>`) lives in `alloc`. That is J6-11's answer.
- Closures are stack values; `&mut dyn FnMut` borrows one with no heap, while `Box<dyn Fn>` allocates where it is written.
- The standard library documents `cbrt`, `sin` and the like as of unspecified precision that may vary by platform; `sqrt` and `mul_add` follow IEEE.
- Rayon's float sums depend on how the work is split. Nothing marks a lock race as nondeterministic.

**Swift**
- A non-escaping closure's context goes on the stack and an `@escaping` one is boxed. That is Ember's slot-or-block, but Swift decides it by a word the programmer writes, not by where the value goes.
- Its experimental performance annotations (`@_noAllocation`, `@_noLocks`) are checked on optimised code, so whether a function passes depends on the optimiser. This rule removes exactly that shortfall.

**Ada**
- `pragma Restrictions (No_Allocators, No_Implicit_Heap_Allocations, No_Exceptions)` and the Ravenscar profile are restrictions the language defines, but what allocates implicitly is defined by each implementation, which documents it.
- SPARK infers data flow (`Global`) from bodies, as EFF-24 does.

**Zig**
- Allocation shows in the signature: an allocating function takes an `Allocator`.
- Error unions are integers, so an error never needs a heap. That is closest to naming a concrete error type in a core package.

**Go and C#**
- Neither has an effect system.
- Go randomises map order on purpose, and its specification lets the compiler fuse `x*y + z`, so float results may differ between architectures.
- C#'s `Math.Sin` calls the platform's C library, so lockstep C# engines use fixed-point numbers.

**Where they fall short.** None fixes, as a rule of the language checked when compiling, whether an operation allocates, stops, checks aliasing or depends on the machine or on thread timing. Each leaves it to a list, an annotation or the optimiser. Ember's table of definitions fixes it, and the compiler works the facts out.
design.cost:
Classifying effects and checking contracts cost nothing while running: COST-3's \"Contract and range-type annotations: not observable\". Per operation:

- **`runtime`'s check.** Unchanged: one type-id compare at each guarded line where a kind that may reach the value makes the line unsafe, and none where the kinds are known when compiling. C pays nothing on the same line only because it checks nothing. Added by this rule: zero.
- **DET-2(b), thread orders.** Zero while running. Compile time only, from summaries the compiler already builds for EFF-24 and THR-11.
- **DET-2(a), exact operations.** `sqrt`, `/`, `normalize` and the like keep C's instructions: zero.
- **`det` twins.** A software routine in place of the platform's, paid only where `@deterministic` code calls one. C pays the same when it links a correctly rounded library (CORE-MATH, crlibm). Not measured here.
- **SIMD `reduce_add` in a fixed order.** Zero on a target whose natural instruction sequence is the fixed order. Elsewhere, at most one shuffle per halving step. Not measured.
- **CLO-10, function value state.**
  - Case 1 (the state word): zero time, zero memory, as a C function pointer plus a `void*`.
  - Case 2 (a frame slot): no heap, and stack bytes equal to the state's size, written once at the making line. The same as a C++ lambda object or a C struct passed by address.
  - Case 3 (a block): one allocation and one free per value, only where the value outlives its frame or its loop round. The same as `std::function` past its buffer or Rust's `Box<dyn Fn>`.
  - Against option A, case 2 saves one allocation and one free per call of the enclosing function.
- **`AnyError` in the alloc layer.** Zero. A core package's concrete error moves as a C error code or a returned struct does.
- **Other allocations.** `String +`, literals, `?` into `AnyError` and hand-over blocks keep today's cost rows unchanged; only their classification is stated.

readability.note: The rule adds no word, attribute or annotation, and no program text changes; it fixes what the existing contracts mean. The after is the same program, now accepted the same way on every compiler. The cost falls only on programs that do what a contract forbids: a `runtime` value under `@no_alias_checks`, two threads racing under `@deterministic`, `cbrt` in lockstep code, a heap-holding error in firmware. Each of those gets a refusal whose help line compiles.

design.compiler_does:
1. **Primitives.** Gives each primitive operation the effects its definition meets, as the specification states them where the primitive is defined. A primitive here is a built-in operation or a step the compiler places: a block, a check, a count change, a drop, an extern call.
2. **Inference.** Infers every function's effects from its body and its callees (EFF-1). This runs through function values, dyn and virtual calls (EFF-2, verdict 122), the threads and tasks it starts (EFF-26), and C calls, which carry every effect not vouched absent (FFI-10).
3. **Function value state.** Places each function value's state: the state word, a slot in the writer's frame, or a block. The choice follows where the value goes, using CLO-4's existing check plus whether the making line runs again while an earlier value from that line lives. A block is an `Alloc` site at the making line.
4. **Thread orders.** For each thread, task and job a function starts, works out from its body:
   - the places it touches, at THR-11's precision;
   - the order facts: start, join, blocking receive, a reduction's combine order;
   - which threads are left running, recorded in the summary (EFF-4).

   It then marks `Nondet` at the line that lets two threads touch one place in an open order, at least one of them a change, unless the changes commute.
5. **Floating point.** Classifies float operations by IEEE 754's required set. std's own declarations of C math functions say `@ffi(deterministic)` exactly for those.
6. **Layers.** Applies the layer rule by type (values that own heap memory) and by operation (`Alloc`).
7. **Contracts.** Checks each contract over the whole call graph (EFF-6). A violation names the chain, and for DET-2(b) also both thread starts and the place.
8. **Reports.** Writes each site into the safety side table (EFF-10), read by `ember inspect --alloc`, `--safety` and `--deterministic`.
design.misuse:
Every misuse is refused when compiling, except `runtime`'s own stop, which happens at its line with verdict 157's text. Nothing is silent or undefined.

- **`runtime` under `@no_alias_checks`:** `E4030` at the guarded line, naming the word and its parameter or variable.
- **`runtime` under `@nopanic(explicit)` or `@realtime`:** `E4040`, naming `@realtime` too (EFF-19). The help for both: give the value a kind known when compiling, or remove the attribute.
- **Two threads in an open order under `@deterministic`:** `E4070` at the line that lets them run at once, naming both starts and the place. The help: join the first before starting the second, or use scoped tasks with a reduction. `try_lock`, `try_recv` and an `Atomic` load while another thread may change it get the same code, naming the other thread.
- **Platform math under `@deterministic`:** `E4070` at the call, with `det`'s twin as the help. For `_approx`, the help is the exact lane-wise form.
- **A function value whose state needs a block, under `@noalloc`:** `E4001` at the making line, saying why it needs a block (it outlives its writer, or its loop round). The help: one word of state, or a type parameter `[F: needs fn(...)]`.
- **`AnyError` (`Result[T]`) in a core-only package:** refused at the line that names it. The help gives the concrete error type.
- **A C function with no stated effects called from contract code:** the contract's error. The help gives `@ffi(effects=[...])` for its declaration, an asserted fact listed by `ember tcb`.
- **A forgotten mark refuses, never lets an effect through.** An unstated C effect is carried (verdict 31's way), and `Nondet` stays carried without `@ffi(deterministic)`.
design.verdicts:
- **86, kept.** Every fact is worked out from bodies. The thread-order facts come from the same summaries (EFF-24, THR-11), and no word is added.
- **92 and 105, kept.** A reduction's combine order, spawn order for tasks and chunk order for `@parallel`, is one of DET-2(b)'s order facts, so reductions stay not `Nondet`. Decimal totals may differ from adding one by one but are the same on every run. Whole-number totals still stop where a task's own total overflows.
- **114, kept.** The hand-over's new block carries `Alloc`, its failure carries `Panic(Explicit)`, and its compare and the stop for an object C keeps carry `RuntimeCheck(Stale)`. Nothing changes while running. Lead fix J6-03 is this rule's instance; the owner should hear that `@noalloc` and `@nopanic(explicit)` refuse a hand-over of an object of a `weakref`-targeted class.
- **122, kept.** A call through a stored function carries the effects of the functions that reach that place. CLO-10's placement follows each value the same way, by place.
- **152, 162 and 163, kept.** `runtime` does exactly what they say while running. Only its classification is added. Verdict 152's \"with a word\" is what makes its stop a written one, and its \"I WANT A NEW WORD\" is kept: `runtime` stays its own word, classified like `assert_disjoint` only because it does the same kind of thing.
- **157, kept.** The stop's approved text becomes COST-6's new row word for word. The `E4030` and `E4040` wordings are the lead's (2026-11-01 evening).
- **31, kept and reached further.** An unstated C effect is carried, so a forgotten mark refuses.
- **No verdict is revisited.**

options_for_owner.summary: The rule: every effect is defined by what an operation does, and the compiler works the facts out. `runtime` counts as both effects; `Nondet` covers a result left to the platform and an order two threads leave open; a closure's state sits in its state word, its frame or a block; `AnyError` is in the alloc layer.

recommendation.reason:
Under A, a contract means all of what it says and only that, decided when compiling at no cost while running and with no new word in any program. Every one of the group's seven questions, and every case listed, gets one answer from one definition per effect.

Over B, A accepts correct programs that B's lists refuse: a two-word lambda kept in its own frame, and a lock no other thread takes. And an operation added later cannot fall between lists, as `runtime` did.

C lets a `@deterministic` function return two different answers and lets a `@nopanic(explicit)` function stop: the silent acceptance PHIL-12 calls the worst defect.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: a contract like Clang's `[[clang::nonallocating]]`, but checked as an error when compiling. Does `@noalloc`, `@nopanic(explicit)`, `@no_alias_checks` or `@deterministic` forbid everything that allocates, stops, checks aliasing or depends on timing, or only the operations a list in the spec happens to name?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `gather_turn()`, marked `@deterministic`, starts thread A: `receive(1)` | `INPUTS = []` |
| 2 | main | starts thread B: `receive(2)` before A is joined | `INPUTS = []` |
| 3 | B | gets `INPUT_LOCK` first this run, pushes 2 | `INPUTS = [2]` |
| 4 | A | gets the lock next, pushes 1 | `INPUTS = [2, 1]` |
| 5 | main | joins both and returns a copy | `[2, 1]` this run, `[1, 2]` the next: two answers from one input |
owner_short.options:
A: one definition per effect decides every operation. Here: E4070 at `b = thread.spawn(...)`; `runtime` is refused under both contracts; a two-word local lambda costs no heap.
B: add the missing names to each list. The same refusals today, but a two-word local lambda allocates and is refused, every `try_lock` is Nondet, and the next new operation falls between the lists again.
C: read the lists as written. This program compiles as `@deterministic` and returns [1, 2] or [2, 1], and `runtime` stops a `@nopanic(explicit)` function.
owner_short.recommendation: A: a contract then means all of what it says and only that, checked when compiling at no cost while running, with no new word in any program.

design.open_risks:
1. **DET-2(b) is conservative in two places.** A thread whose `JoinHandle` leaves its function counts as running until the program ends. Two objects of one type the compiler cannot tell apart count as one place, as in THR-11. So some deterministic programs are refused under `@deterministic`; the message names the handle or the two places. Checked `fetch_add` from two threads is refused although it is order-free when every argument is non-negative; the help names `wrapping_fetch_add` or a reduction.
2. **`det` twins are library work.** Eleven functions are new in `std.math.det`, and they are slower than the platform's, paid only in `@deterministic` code. Not measured.
3. **CLO-10's case 2 must be written in CLO-4's exact terms** (\"ends before the writer returns, and before its line runs again\"), so that every compiler agrees. A fixed-capacity list of closures with two-word state, kept across rounds, still allocates one block per value and is refused under `@noalloc`, as Rust's `[Box<dyn Fn>; N]` allocates.
4. **\"One word\" means the target's pointer size.** An escaping `copy of x` of an `f64` sits in the state word on 64-bit targets and needs a block on 32-bit ones, so `@noalloc` acceptance of that line differs by target. PHIL-13 allows this, since it counts the target as an input, and the message must say so.
5. **The layer rule by property may reach other types std lists in core.** One pass over the module table and std/src is needed (iterator adapters holding a function value, `type_name`'s result). The layer ordering is a separate STD-6 question for firmware: `ffi` comes after `alloc`, so a core-only package calling a C HAL needs the whole stack.
6. **SIMD-4's fixed float reduction order must be chosen per target** by the lead, with the target's natural sequence.
7. **This rule only carries effects; other groups' answers fix the facts.** P05 (check points), P13 (J3-13), P15 (J3-06), P06 (String +), P18 (`runtime` placement) and P24 (the name of `det`'s natural logarithm) must each fix their answer, with no \"may\".
8. **EFF-3 now matches FFI-10:** an undeclared C function carries every effect. Contract code calling C must state `@ffi(effects=[…])`. Check XVI.4's Vulkan overlay entries when P04 rewrites that overlay.
9. **Io keeps today's examples.** Whether starting a process is Io follows std's body.

matrix.guarantee: @noalloc code and a core-only package take no memory from the heap at run time
matrix.how_kept: Alloc is defined by what an operation does: it takes heap memory, directly or through a manager that may take more. EFF-1/EFF-2 carry it up from every callee, drop, default, dyn implementation and stored function. CLO-10 fixes where a function value's state lives (state word, frame slot, block). A C function with no stated effects carries every effect. STD-6 puts heap-owning types (AnyError) and Alloc operations in alloc. std's bodies are normative where Part XV is silent (preamble, STD-14).
matrix.edge_cases: A frame slot in a loop or in recursion falls to a block. thread.spawn: block; jobs.submit: JOB-1's 64-byte queue slot (CLASH). FixedArena or `using` a fixed manager: not Alloc. Hand-over of a weakref-targeted object: Alloc (J6-03). `?` into AnyError: Alloc on the failure path. String +. A two-word Copy capture on a 32-bit target. `fn()` as a type in a core package. A push that a capacity test shows cannot grow.
matrix.must_refuse: `@noalloc fn wire(ref mut b: Button, k: float, m: float):` with `b.handlers.push(owns fn() copy of k, copy of m: println(k * m))`: E4001 at the push, because the state outlives `wire` and goes in a block.
matrix.must_compile: `@noalloc fn drag(ref mut ps: Array[Particle], k: float, m: float):` with `slow: fn(ref mut Particle) = fn(ref mut p) copy of k, copy of m: p.vy *= k * m` and `for ref mut p in ps: slow(ref mut p)`: the state sits in a slot of drag's frame.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed or moved memory through a function value's state
matrix.how_kept: CLO-4: a value that uses real variables provably ends before them (E3026). Case 2 applies only when the value ends before its writer returns and before its line runs again. CLO-18 keeps one count across a self-ending call. Ending a value ends its state once.
matrix.edge_cases: A generator's frame moves while suspended (CORO-5/6/9). Case 1's frame address or case 2's slot held across a yield: BROKEN. A handler that ends itself while its state is one word or in a slot: BROKEN, because no count exists to hold. Nested lambdas reach outer frames through a static link via the writer's frame. In recursion each frame has its own slot. A value handed to a callee that ends it needs a drop flag.
matrix.must_refuse: `fn make_counter() -> fn():` with `n = 0` and `return fn(): n += 1`: E3026, since `n` ends when make_counter returns.
matrix.must_compile: `return fn() owns n: n += 1` in make_counter: `n` is the function's own state, one word, kept in the state word.

matrix.guarantee: @nopanic(explicit) has no stop the program's words ask for; one also free of RuntimeCheck has no panic the model knows of (EFF-16)
matrix.how_kept: Panic(Explicit) is defined by property and carried by: panic, assert* (assert_disjoint included), unwrap, expect, todo, unreachable, cast, a runtime value's check (LT-48) and allocation failure. Implicit tests are RuntimeCheck kinds, by what they keep. A library operation's stop counts by what it keeps.
matrix.edge_cases: `runtime` carries the effect only where a compare is placed. FixedArena exhaustion, a full Pool insert, split on an empty separator, range step 0, and a stateful fn converted to extern "C" fn keep none of the four kinds, so three rules give three answers (UNRESOLVED). A hand-over of an object C keeps is a Stale stop, but its allocation failure refuses it anyway.

holes.program:
gen fn wave(k: float, m: float) -> Generator[float]:
    scale: fn(float) -> float = fn(x) copy of k, copy of m => x * k * m   # two words of its own: CLO-10 case 2, a slot in this frame
    for i in 0..3:
        yield scale(i as float)

fn main():
    g = wave(2.0, 3.0)
    println(g.next())        # runs to the first yield; `scale`'s state word holds its slot's address in g's frame
    h = g                    # the suspended frame is handed over and may move (CORO-5, CORO-6)
    println(h.next())        # `scale` reads k and m through the address the frame had before
holes.what_goes_wrong:
`scale` ends before `wave` returns and its line runs once, so the design's case 2 puts its 16 bytes in a slot of the writer's frame, with the state word pointing at that slot. A generator's frame is that writer's frame. It is an ordinary value that moves while suspended: handed over by `=`, or kept in an Array that grows (CORO-5; CORO-6 says the frame may move). After `h = g` the state word points where the frame used to be, so safe code reads moved (freed) stack memory.

The compiler's own placement breaks CORO-9 ("a frame never points into itself in Safe code"). CORO-6's E2221 names only views of the generator's locals, so it does not catch this. Case 1 has the same problem: a lambda that uses the generator's own locals keeps "the frame's address" in its state word across a yield.

Without the written callable type (`scale = fn(x) ...`), CLO-1 keeps the lambda inline and it moves with the frame. The hole is exactly the placement the design adds.
holes.fix_hint: Add to CLO-10's case 2 condition: the value ends before its writer returns or reaches a `yield`. A value alive across a yield goes in a block (case 3). A function value whose state is the frame's address and that is held across a yield is CORO-6's view into the frame (E2221), with a message saying so.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
`owns p` is one word, the Panel's address, so the design's case 1 keeps it in the state word on every compiler. CLO-18 is unchanged and still promises that a body which may end its own state and then uses it "holds one count on it across that call". An inline `owns` word has no count to hold, because a class object with one owner has no owner count, and the design's new COST-3 row drops the count sentence.

`clear()` ends the list element. Ending its state runs Panel's drop and frees `title`, and the body then reads `p.title` through its copied word: a use after free in safe code. This holds if E3022 does not refuse the handler, and CLO-18 says such handlers exist.

Today's "may" lets a compiler choose a counted block here; the design forbids that choice. A case-2 slot ended by the same call has the same problem.
holes.fix_hint: In CLO-10: a function value whose body may end its own state and use it afterwards (CLO-18, known from its summary) keeps its state in a counted block (case 3), whatever its size. Alternatively, the call takes the state out of its place for the call's length. Put COST-3's count sentence back.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
`turn_size` starts no thread, and its summary leaves none running. Effects are worked out per function from its body and callees (EFF-1), and DET-2(b)'s line rule puts the open order on main's line, "the starter's own operation before the earlier thread's join". So `turn_size` passes @deterministic, although its result is not fixed by the program's input, which is DET-2's own definition of Nondet.

The design's example "a load of an Atomic another thread may change" points the other way for `@deterministic fn score() -> int: return SCORE.load()`, and which answer holds is never said.

Moving J6-07's two spawns into main lets its own example through. The usual lockstep layout, with network threads started once and the simulation reading their inputs, gets no protection. A callback C runs on another thread (threads(any)) and an export with threads=any have no Ember start line at all.
holes.fix_hint: Keep effect sets per function. Record in each summary the shared places the function touches under a lock or atomically. DET-1 then checks every call of a @deterministic function: a call made while a thread that may change one of those places runs in an open order is E4070 at the call, naming the function, the thread's start (or the C callback's registration) and the place. Treat a callback C may run on another thread as a thread started at its registration.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

static TOTAL_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut TOTAL: int guarded by TOTAL_LOCK = 0

fn add(n: int):
    with TOTAL_LOCK:
        TOTAL += n

@deterministic
fn add_both() -> int:
    a = thread.spawn(owns fn(): add(1))
    b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): add(2))   # Nondet here, or not?
    a.join()
    b.join()
    with TOTAL_LOCK:
        return TOTAL
holes.what_goes_wrong:
DET-2(b) says changes that leave the same values in every order leave nothing open, then says "These are" and gives a closed set of Atomic operations. EFF-28 says the operations a rule names are only examples of its definition.

Here both orders give TOTAL + 3, unless the checked `+=` overflows, and that depends on TOTAL's earlier value and on the order. In general it cannot be decided whether two changes commute, or whether "the order can change a value read later". So one compiler proves it and accepts `add_both`, another refuses it, against EFF-28's "one answer on every compiler" and EFF-15. Two threads calling `fetch_max` on one Atomic commute too, but are outside the set.
holes.fix_hint: State in DET-2(b) that the commuting set is fixed by the language: the listed Atomic operations, with fetch_max/fetch_min if wanted. State in EFF-28 that where a rule fixes a fact by an exhaustive set, that set is the fact's definition. Any other change to one place by two threads in an open order is Nondet, whatever it does, and 'read later' means any later read of the place.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Three rules give three answers:
- EFF-1 carries std's `panic` up to the caller: Panic(Explicit), E4040.
- The design's EFF-9 gives a library stop "the kind of what it keeps". A capacity or a caller's precondition keeps none of the four kinds, though a FixedArena's cursor could be read as "a count compared with its limit before it grows" (Arithmetic).
- EFF-16 and PHIL-11 put "exhaustion outside Alloc" outside the model, with no effect at all.

So whether `emit`, the usual `@noalloc @nopanic(explicit)` arena loop, and `fields` compile is undecided. Under the third reading, EFF-16's promise (free of RuntimeCheck means no panic the model knows of) is false for `split`. The same goes for a full `Pool.insert` (HND-3), `range` with step 0, and CLO-3's conversion of a stateful function value to `extern "C" fn`.
holes.fix_hint: Give every library stop one effect by one rule. Either a caller's precondition or a fixed capacity running out is Panic(Explicit) (the library's words), with the try_ form as the help (P27). Or add a fifth RuntimeCheck kind, Capacity, and say so in EFF-16. Align PHIL-11's 'exhaustion outside Alloc' with the choice.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
The design defines RuntimeCheck(Aliasing) by a property: "tests while running whether what a line changes overlaps what another name reads or views". EFF-28 adds that no name decides it.

Three tests check exactly that: `if i != j:`, get_pair_mut's "differ" test (BRW-5), and `if a is not b:` (SIMD-3's alias proof, THR-18's E7018 help). check_disjoint does the same (DSJ-1: "In its Ok branch ... as inside if i != j:"), and it is refused.

So one of two things follows:
- `hit` and `hit_pair` are E4030, and BRW-5's E3022 message gives a line that does not compile in @no_alias_checks code. Verdict 98's way out is then closed in the very inner loops it serves.
- A program's own branch is not a check, and then check_disjoint's refusal has no reason left.

The property does not draw the line between them.
holes.fix_hint: Define RuntimeCheck(k) as a test that can stop the program, or one the compiler places, never the program's own branch on a value it computed (if, match, exists as on an Option or Result). Then say whether check_disjoint, which only returns a Result, stays refused under @no_alias_checks. That is an owner question, because it changes DSJ-6. Also name get_pair_mut and `is not` explicitly.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
Today Lock means the named lock types, and channel operations are Sync, so `report` compiles. The design makes Lock "takes a lock" by property, with the names only examples. THR-15 says a channel has "the channel's lock", so `try_send` takes a lock and is E4042. @realtime includes @nolock, so real-time audio code could no longer post to a channel.

The heap allocator's internal lock, stdout's lock, and an allocator that "may wait" (Block) are platform choices. So @nolock and @noblock verdicts on `push` or `println` depend on the implementation, which EFF-28 says nothing may.
holes.fix_hint: Define Lock as taking a lock the program can name (a Mutex, an RwLock, a Lock, a guarded field's lock), and Block as waiting on something the program's words wait for. State each std operation's Lock and Block effects in its declaration (std/**/*.em), never by an internal mechanism.

import std.thread

@deterministic
fn announce():
    a = thread.spawn(owns fn(): println("red team ready"))
    b = thread.spawn(owns fn(): println("blue team ready"))
    a.join()
    b.join()
holes.what_goes_wrong: DET-2(b) counts an order only where it "can change a value read later". No later line reads the console, or a file the program never reads back, so `announce` passes @deterministic and prints its two lines in either order. X.3 names golden-image tests ("two runs ... compute the same bits") as the contract's reason, and the spec never says whether output order counts as a result.
holes.fix_hint: Count what the program writes out (console, file, socket) as a place read later: two threads writing to one stream in an open order are Nondet, at the line DET-2(b) names. Or say in DET-6 that @deterministic does not cover output order, so the owner can choose.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design's CLO-10 puts this 16-byte state in a block, because it outlives its writer (case 3). That is Alloc, so the function is E4001. JOB-1, which the design leaves unchanged, keeps a job's captured state of up to 64 bytes inline in its queue slot with no Alloc, so the function compiles. Two rules give two verdicts, and the design's list of changed rules does not include JOB-1.
holes.fix_hint: Make one rule. Either list the job queue slot as a fourth place in CLO-10, for state up to 64 bytes and with no Alloc (a place that lasts as long as the job), or rewrite JOB-1 to follow CLO-10's three places.
