recommendation.reason:
Under A, a contract means all of what it says and only that. It is decided when compiling, at no cost while running, with no new word in any program. Every one of the group's seven questions, and every case listed, gets one answer from one definition per effect, the same on every compiler.

Over B, A accepts correct programs that B's lists refuse: a two-word lambda kept in its own frame, a job's state in its slot, and a lock no other thread takes. A also catches what B's lists miss: a simulation read while a network thread writes its inputs, and two threads printing. And an operation added later cannot fall between lists, as `runtime` did.

C lets a `@deterministic` function return two different answers and lets a `@nopanic(explicit)` function stop: the silent acceptance PHIL-12 calls the worst defect.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: a contract like Clang's `[[clang::nonallocating]]`, but checked as an error when compiling. Does `@noalloc`, `@nopanic(explicit)`, `@no_alias_checks` or `@deterministic` forbid everything that allocates, stops, checks aliasing or depends on timing, or only the operations a list in the spec happens to name?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `gather_turn()`, marked `@deterministic`, starts thread A: `receive(1)` | `INPUTS = []` |
| 2 | main | starts thread B: `receive(2)`, before A is joined | `INPUTS = []` |
| 3 | B | gets `INPUT_LOCK` first this run, pushes 2 | `INPUTS = [2]` |
| 4 | A | gets the lock next, pushes 1 | `INPUTS = [2, 1]` |
| 5 | main | joins both and returns a copy | `[2, 1]` this run, `[1, 2]` the next: two answers from one input |
owner_short.options:
A: one definition per effect decides every operation. Here that is E4070 at `b = thread.spawn(...)`. A `@deterministic` function called while a network thread writes its inputs is refused at that call, `runtime` is refused under both contracts, and a two-word local lambda costs no heap.
B: add the missing names to each list. That gives the same refusals today, but a two-word local lambda allocates and is refused, every `try_lock` is Nondet, and the next new operation falls between the lists again.
C: read the lists as written. Then this program compiles as `@deterministic` and returns [1, 2] or [2, 1], and `runtime` stops a `@nopanic(explicit)` function.
owner_short.recommendation: A: a contract then means all of what it says and only that. It is checked when compiling, at no cost while running, with no new word in any program.

repairs.hole: Safety 1 (high), the same as Engineering 2 (high): a function value's state is put in a slot of a generator's frame (case 2), or the frame's address in its state word (case 1). It is held across a `yield`, and the frame moves (`h = g`), so `wave` and `drag_steps` read freed memory.
repairs.answer:
Real. The fix is in CLO-10 and CORO-6:
- CLO-10's case 2 now requires, in a generator, that the value not be alive across a `yield`, since the frame may move while suspended. Such a value goes to a block (case 4), so its state stays where it is when the frame moves.
- A function value that uses the generator's own variables borrows them, and so is CORO-6's view into the frame: held across a `yield` it is `E2221`, with `copy of` as the help.

`wave`'s `scale` copies `k` and `m`, so it compiles with one block per generator call and `h.next()` gives 6.0. `drag_steps`'s `slow` is the same. Under `@noalloc`, the help is to leave the callable type off, which keeps the lambda in the frame itself (CLO-1). CORO-9 holds: no frame points into itself.

repairs.hole: Safety 2 (high): `on_click owns p` is one word, so it was kept in the state word. The handler clears its own list, which ends its state and the Panel, and then reads `p.title`. CLO-18's "one count" had nothing to count, and COST-3 had lost the count sentence.
repairs.answer:
Real. CLO-10 now says that a function value whose body may end its own state and use it afterwards keeps that state in a block with one count. This holds whatever its size and wherever it goes, so a frame slot ended by the same call is covered too. Each call holds one count. Its summary says whether the body may end its state, so the compiler knows.

COST-3's count sentence is back. In `click`, the Panel lives until the call ends, `println(p.title)` prints "hp", and the Panel is dropped after the call.

repairs.hole: Safety 3 (high): `turn_size` starts no thread, so it passed `@deterministic`, while `main`'s network thread pushes to `INPUTS` as it reads. The breaker also asked about an Atomic load, a C callback with `threads(any)`, and an export with `threads=any`.
repairs.answer:
Real. A `@deterministic` function's promise now holds where it is called (DET-1). Summaries record the places a function touches and the threads it leaves running. A line that lets another thread change one of those places in an open order is `E4070`, whatever the caller's contracts.

`println(turn_size())` in `main` is therefore `E4070`, naming the thread's start and `INPUTS`, with the help to join first.
- The Atomic load is answered the same way: `Nondet` exactly where another thread may change the Atomic in an open order at that point.
- A callback C may run on another thread is a thread started at its registration.
- An export with `threads=any` is a thread running from start-up.

repairs.hole: Safety 4 (medium): DET-2(b) said "These are" and gave a closed set of commuting changes, while EFF-28 said named operations are only examples. Whether `add_both`'s locked `TOTAL += n` commutes was left to each compiler's proof.

Safety 5 (medium): a library's stop had three answers: EFF-1's Panic(Explicit), round 1's "the kind of what it keeps", and EFF-16's "exhaustion outside Alloc" with no effect. The examples were a full FixedArena, `split` on an empty separator, a full Pool, `range` with step 0, and CLO-3's conversion.
repairs.answer:
Real. There is now one rule.
- A stop the words of the running code ask for is `Panic(Explicit)`, in a library as in the program (EFF-1).
- `RuntimeCheck(k)` is only the language's run-time checks, a complete list in EFF-9.
- So a full FixedArena, a full Pool, a full callback table, `split("")` and the `extern "C" fn` conversion are `Panic(Explicit)`, with their `try_` forms as the help (P27). `emit` and `fields` are `E4040`.
- `range`'s zero step is the trip count's division check, `RuntimeCheck(Arithmetic)`, removed for a constant step (STD-26).
- EFF-16's escape clause now names only the stack running out, a hardware fault and foreign code, so its promise holds for `split`.
- Round 1's last sentence of EFF-9 is removed.

repairs.hole: Safety 6 (medium), the same as Engineering 8 (medium): defining RuntimeCheck(Aliasing) by a property catches `if i != j:`, get_pair_mut's test and `if a is not b:`. That makes `hit`, `hit_pair` and `bounce` `E4030` and breaks verdict 98's way out, or else leaves check_disjoint's refusal with no reason.
repairs.answer:
Real. RuntimeCheck(Aliasing) is now the language's alias checks, a complete set: the address-range compare of `check_disjoint` and `assert_disjoint`, and `runtime`'s kind compare. A compare that code writes itself and branches on is a branch, in the program or in std's body: `if i != j:`, `j` from `i + 1..`, `is not`, get_pair_mut's index test, `swap`'s `i == j`.

`check_disjoint` stays a check because its compare is one of the language's tests, made on two views' addresses, which no safe code can compute. This matches today's Stale: `pool.get(h)` and `if w exists as p:` give the program an Option to branch on, and still carry Stale.

So DSJ-6 holds as today and no owner question is needed. `hit`, `hit_pair` and `bounce` compile under `@no_alias_checks`. `swap` carries Bounds where its indices are not proved, never Aliasing, so today's verdict is unchanged.

repairs.hole: Safety 7 (medium): with Lock defined by a property, `try_send` takes "the channel's lock" and becomes `E4042` under `@nolock`. The heap's and stdout's internal locks, and an allocator that may wait, made verdicts depend on the platform.
repairs.answer:
Real.
- Lock is again an exact set: taking a `Mutex` or an `RwLock` (`try_lock` included), or a `Lock` with `with x.lock:`.
- Sync is today's exact set.
- Block is "may wait, as this specification says the operation does".
- EFF-28 adds: a std operation carries the effects of what this specification says it does, and how std or a platform builds it adds none. That covers the heap's lock, the console's lock and a channel's queue.

`report` compiles under `@nolock` as today, and `push` and `println` get no Lock or Block. Open risk 12 records the constraint this puts on std's channel (THR-15).

repairs.hole: Safety 8 (medium), the same as Engineering 13 (medium): DET-2(b) counted only "a value read later", so two threads printing, writing a replay log or sending lockstep packets in either order passed `@deterministic` (`announce`).
repairs.answer:
Real. DET-2(b) now counts the world outside the program as one place, which every Io operation reads and changes. DET-6 says that what the program writes, and in what order, is a result.

`announce` is `E4070` at the later start (line 6): "... both print to the console, in an order the program does not fix; join the first before starting the second: move line 7 above line 6". "Read later" is gone: an open order of changes that are not order-free is Nondet whatever is read afterwards.

repairs.hole: Safety 9 (medium), the same as Engineering 3 (medium): CLO-10's case 3 put a 16-byte job state in a block (Alloc), while JOB-1 keeps up to 64 bytes inline in the queue slot. `queue_product` and `queue_gain` got two verdicts.
repairs.answer:
Real. CLO-10 gains a third place before the block: room its holder keeps for the state. It applies where the value is made (or becomes a function value) as the argument of a call that takes it over into room of its own, and the state fits there. A job's 64-byte queue slot is std's one such room, and the job system keeps the state word pointing at it.

JOB-1 is rewritten in CLO-10's terms. Both functions compile under `@noalloc`, as JOB-1 says today, and a state over 64 bytes is a block.

repairs.hole: Safety 10 (medium): the STD-6 sentence "a type whose values own heap memory is alloc's" makes every callable type alloc's, so a core-only package could name no `fn()`. And core's `Result` names AnyError (alloc) as its default.
repairs.answer:
Real. The type sentence now covers only a type every value of which owns a heap block, which is `AnyError`. A callable type, `dyn I` and `Option[T]` stay core. What a core-only package cannot run is a line that carries Alloc.

A default type argument belongs to the package that writes the type, so core's `Result` uses nothing of alloc. `board_hal`'s `make_irq` compiles.

repairs.hole: Safety 11 (medium): a `thread_shared` value's drop, queued to main, runs at a check point inside `frames_until_freed`'s loop, at a moment set by timing. Both operations are main's, so DET-2(b) found nothing.
repairs.answer:
Real. DET-2(b) now gives an operation to the thread that decides when it runs. A drop run at a check point for an owner another thread ended belongs to that thread.

So `frames_until_freed`'s reads of `FREED` meet `h`'s possible drop in an open order. Main's call `frames_until_freed(1000)` is `E4070` by the call-site rule, naming `h`'s start and `FREED`. The same holds where the drop runs on `h` itself (RC-4 point 4). Where P05 puts check points does not change it.

repairs.answer:
Real. Case 1 now holds only for state the body never gives a new value and never ends: the frame's address, or one word it only reads. It may still change what the word points at.

State the function changes goes to a slot or a block, so the state word always points where the change lands. CLO-10 also says a call passes the state word. `make_counter`'s `bump` outlives its writer, so it is a block, and `hud.on_frame()` prints 1 and then 2.

repairs.hole: Engineering 4 (medium): frame placement became a language rule for function values only, while `Probe()` (a class object) still allocates and is refused under `@noalloc`.
repairs.answer:
Partly real. The reason was missing, and CLO-10 now states it (principle 6). A function value's state has no header, no identity and no address a program can see, so where it lives changes only its cost. A class object is its block (CLS-1): its header, `is`, and the address its Debug prints.

The language's spelling for a value with no block is a `struct`. With `struct Probe`, `count_hits` compiles under `@noalloc` with nothing on the heap. Making class objects frame-placed by rule changes what CLS-1 says a class object is. That is P03's storage question, put to the owner in open risk 6, not ruled here.

Real. That sentence is removed, and layers stay lists of modules with one property: core has no heap. A core-only package runs no line that carries Alloc, and `AnyError` (every value a heap block) is alloc's. FFI, Sync and Io map to no layer.

EFF-28 also says the C library behind std.math adds no effect. So `imu_driver`'s `pitch` compiles, std.math stays core, and `println` stays io.

Real. The sentence is removed. std's `m[k]` stop and a program's own `Ring.at` are both `Panic(Explicit)`: a library's words after its own test, one rule for every library (EFF-9). The language's checks are reached the same way by any code, by running a checked operation.

`newest` is `E4040` twice, at `m[7]` and at `r.at(0)`. The help is `m.get(7)` and a `get` form of `Ring`.

repairs.answer:
Real in part. It is now one rule, by who raises the stop.
- A capacity the program sized (a FixedArena, a Pool, a callback table) and the heap are a library's stop: `Panic(Explicit)`, each with its `try_` form, which is P27's rule.
- A count's limit is a check the language places at every owner-making line, on a width the program never chose. It stays `RuntimeCheck(Arithmetic)` (verdict 59, EFF-16), with the reason written (principle 6).

Real. The order-free set now includes a checked add or subtract that moves the place one way by RNG-4's facts, where a constant or an unsigned type gives the sign. In each case the results must be unused and every read come after the joins.

`count_positive` compiles, and so do workers storing `true` into one flag. The overflow check stays.

repairs.answer:
Real. Each is now a written rule:
- A loop that joins each round's handle on every path, and leaves only at its end, joins every handle in the list.
- "Read later" is gone. An open order of changes that are not order-free is Nondet whatever is read afterwards. For order-free changes, every read of the place must come after all of them.
- With one sending thread, the k-th receive gets the k-th send. With two senders in an open order, the sends themselves leave the queue open.

`run_workers` is `E4070` at its spawn line, since its pushes are an open order. The help gives scoped tasks, whose pushes combine in spawn order.

repairs.answer: Real. The order fact is now a property: B is ordered after A when the language starts or continues B only after A has finished. The operations that have it are listed as today's, with `submit_after` among them, and a rule that adds one says so (EFF-28). `load_then_link` compiles and returns [1, 2].

A method's twin is a function that takes the receiver first (`det.slerp(a, b, t)`). std writes each such method once, over its scalar functions, so a method and its twin are the same code built on std.math's scalars and on det's.

`turn` compiles with `det.slerp`. The spelling of each twin is P24's question.

design.open_risks:
1. **DET-2(b) is conservative in four places.**
   - Two objects of one type the compiler cannot tell apart count as one place, as in THR-11.
   - A thread whose handle is not joined on every path counts as running until the end.
   - The world outside the program is one place, so two threads writing two different files are refused: the compiler cannot tell that two paths name two files.
   - A checked add whose operands' sign RNG-4's facts do not show (a plain `int` parameter) leaves its order open.

   Each message names the place and gives the help: join first, use scoped tasks' reductions, or do the Io on one thread.
2. **An order-free checked add that overflows** stops in every order, but which thread's line the stop names may differ between runs. The owner should hear it.
3. **The call-site rule.** A `@deterministic` function's promise is checked where it is called, so `E4070` can appear in a caller with no contract. This is what lockstep code needs: a network thread beside the simulation. It is the one place a contract refuses a line outside its own function, as E7013 does for a lock a callee needs held. The owner should hear it.
4. **Library stops are Panic(Explicit):** `m[k]`, `normalize`, `inverse`, `split`, and a full FixedArena or Pool.
   - `@nopanic(explicit)` and `@realtime` code needs a `try_` or `get` form for each.
   - std must give every capacity stop a `try_` form (P27; `try_alloc_array` is new).
   - A caller's-bug stop such as `split` has no twin today (STD-14). That is library work, with no language change.
   - If the owner wants a full FixedArena allowed under `@nopanic(explicit)`, that is a fifth check kind and a question of its own.
5. **`dyn` effects, one line for the owner.** Should EFF-2's `dyn` and `virtual` calls carry the effects of the kinds that reach the place, as verdict 122 does for stored functions and 151 for views? Not ruled here.
6. **Class objects in the frame (P03's storage question).** Should a class object that the compiler proves ends in its writer's frame, unlinked, unshared and never handed over, be made there by rule, so that `@noalloc` accepts it? Function values get the rule here because nothing about them is observable.
7. **`det` twins are library work.** About twenty functions and the derived types' methods that call them are new, and they are slower than the platform's, paid only in `@deterministic` code. Not measured.
8. **"One word" means the target's pointer size.** An escaping `copy of x` of an `f64` sits in the state word on 64-bit targets and needs a block on 32-bit ones, so `@noalloc` acceptance of that line differs by target. PHIL-13 allows this, since it counts the target as an input, and the message must say so.
9. **SIMD-4's fixed float reduction order** must be chosen per target by the lead, using the target's natural sequence.
10. **This rule only carries effects; other groups' answers fix the facts.** P05 (check points), P13 (J3-13), P15 (J3-06), P06 (`String +`), P18 (`runtime` placement), P24 (`det`'s names) and P27 (`try_` forms, the callback table) must each fix their answer, with no "may".
11. **EFF-3 now matches FFI-10:** an undeclared C function carries every effect, so contract code calling C must state `@ffi(effects=[…])`. Check XVI.4's Vulkan overlay entries when P04 rewrites that overlay.
12. **std's channel.** THR-15 promises that `try_send` and `try_recv` never block, and says the receiver drains \"under the channel's lock\". Under EFF-28 that lock adds no Lock or Block. So std must build `try_send` and `try_recv` so they never wait on it (a lock-free queue, or an internal try that reports the queue busy), or THR-15's promise is false. The lead should confirm this against the std implementation.
13. **CLO-10's third place exists only in std (the job slot).** A program's own holder cannot keep inline room for a function's state in Safe code. If the owner wants that, it is a later type, like SmallArray's inline room.
14. **Generators.** A function value with more than one word of its own state, kept across a `yield`, costs one block per generator call. Written without its callable type, it stays in the frame at no cost (CLO-1), and the `E4001` message says so.

design.rule:
A value is built by one builder, which gives each field exactly one value. Every type has one init: the `fn init` it writes, or else the one made from its fields (or, for a derived class that writes none, its base's). Every line that builds the type calls that same init: `Name(…)`, `Self(…)` and `super.init(…)`. A derive the type asks for (`Clone`, `Copy`, `Default`, `Deserialize`), zero-filling and a reload's migration by name build the value field by field instead, and run no written init.

Each field gets the first of three values: what the builder gives it; else the field's written default; else, only for a builder that has no line of the program to take the value from (a derive, a reload's added field), its type's `Default`. An init never falls back to a type's `Default`. A field left with none of the three is refused when compiling.

A default is evaluated only where it is the value. That means at most once per construction, at the first line of `init` that needs the field before setting it, and never when `init` has already set it. Which line that is follows from init's own lines alone.

The init made from fields can be called wherever every one of its fields may be written.
design.spec_text:
New subsection V.3a, Construction: rules [CON-1] to [CON-4], cited from Parts V, IX, XIV and Annex B. Changes [STR-1], [STR-2], [STR-6], [CLS-2], [CLS-3], [CLS-10], [DRV-1] (one sentence added), [SER-2] and XIV.2's missing-field sentence (p14 116-117). Keeps [CLS-4], [CLS-11], [MOD-7], [HR-14], [FFI-26], [FFI-39b] and [ARN-11] as written; they become instances of the rules below.

* `[CON-1]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A type has one init.** A struct's or class's init is the `fn init(…)` it writes. A struct or class with no base that writes none has the **init made from its fields**: `Name(field0, field1, …)`, taking positional or named arguments in field order, where a field with a default may be omitted. A derived class that writes none has its base's init (`[CLS-10]`). That one init is what every line that builds the type calls: `Name(…)`, `Self(…)` in its `static fn`s, and a derived `init`'s `super.init(…)`. Over a base that writes no `init`, `super.init(id=id)` calls the init made from the base's fields; over a C++ base it calls the constructor `[FFI-39b]` selects. Its arguments take the words `[FN-2a]` gives a constructor's arguments: none, working as `=` does (verdict 159), and `owns` on the line that makes a value for an `owns` field (`[OWN-10]`).

* `[CON-2]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Each field gets one value.** It is the first of the following:
  1. the value its builder gives it;
  2. the field's written default;
  3. only for a builder the program writes no line for, a stated fallback: the field type's `Default` for a derived `Default`, for a field a derived `Deserialize` may find missing, and for a field a reload adds (`[HR-14]`); for an `@export_table`, the module's function of the field's name (`[FFI-26]`).

  An init has no third step. A field without a default that an init leaves unset is `E2100`, and an omitted argument for one in the init made from fields is refused as a missing argument, so a forgotten field is never filled in silently. A field that a derive can give none of the three is `E2080` at the derive, naming the field; for a reload, `[HR-14]` refuses it in plan.

  The builders are a type's init, and the following, which build field by field and run no written `init`: the derives a type asks for (`Clone`, `Copy`, `Default`, `Deserialize`, `[DRV-1]`), zero-filling (`alloc_zeroed`, `[ARN-11]`, which gives every field a value, so no default runs) and a reload's migration by name (`[HR-14]`). `migrate_from` builds through `Self(…)`, the init.

* `[CON-3]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A default runs only where it is the value.** A field's default is evaluated only in a construction that gives the field no other value, and then once. It is evaluated just before the first line of `init` that needs the field while the field is unset. These lines need fields:
  * a read or change of the field or of any part of it (giving the whole field a value is not a need);
  * a call of a method of `this`, any other use of `this` as a whole (`[CLS-2]`'s list), or `super.init(…)`: every field the type itself declares;
  * a `return` or the end of `init`: every field.

  Defaults needed at one line are made in field order. A field that `init` sets on every path before it is needed never evaluates its default. A field it sets on some paths evaluates the default only on the others, tracked with the hidden flag of `[OWN-3]`. The init made from fields evaluates the defaults of the omitted fields after its arguments, in field order. Which line needs a field follows from `init`'s own lines only, never from another function's body (`[MOD-9]`).

  So with `buf: Array[u8] = Array.with_capacity(4096)` and an `init` whose first line is `this.buf = Array.with_capacity(size)`, no 4 KB list is ever made. With `id: int = next_id()`, `next_id()` runs only in a construction that does not set `id`. `init` may read a defaulted field it has not set: the default is made there. A construction's effects (`Alloc`, `@noalloc`, Part X) are those of its `init` and of the defaults it may make.

* `[CON-4]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Who may build it.** A written init is visible as its own mark says (`[MOD-2]`; std writes `pub fn init()`). The init made from fields sets every field, so it is visible where every one of them may be written:
  * `pub` when every field is `pub`;
  * `pub(package)` when every field is `pub` or `pub(package)`;
  * otherwise only in its module: a private field, or a `pub(read)` or `pub(package, read)` field, which only its module writes (`[MOD-7]`).

  A type with no fields is built wherever it is visible. A derived class's inherited init is visible as its base's is. A call where the init is not visible is `E1052`, naming the field that narrows it and that field's visibility.

Changed texts:
* `[STR-1]`: "It is `pub` iff every field is `pub`" becomes "It is visible as `[CON-4]` says". "A declared `fn init(…)` replaces it" gains "(`[CON-1]`)".
* `[STR-2]`: "it is evaluated at each construction that omits the field, in field order" becomes "it is evaluated only in a construction that gives the field no other value, where `[CON-3]` says".
* `[STR-6]` and `[CLS-2]`: "Before any `init` body runs, every field default of the class and of its bases is evaluated and stored. Every field without a default MUST then be set…" becomes "Each field's default is evaluated by the init of the type that declares it, where `[CON-3]` says. Every field without a default MUST be set…" (the rest unchanged).
* `[CLS-3]`: "…gets a memberwise constructor as a struct does" gains "; it is the class's init (`[CON-1]`), and a derived class's `super.init(…)` calls it".
* `[CLS-10]` gains "(over a base with no written `init`, the init made from its fields: `Panel(id=3)`)".
* XIV.2 (p14 116-117): "A field missing from the data takes its type's `Default` under `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=N)`" becomes: "A field missing from the data under `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=N)`, and a `@ser(skip)` field, which is never in the data, takes its written default, else its type's `Default` (`[CON-2]`). A skipped field with neither is `E2080` at the derive ("`captain` is skipped, so reading a `Crew` back needs a value for it: give it a default, or remove `@ser(skip)`")."
* `[SER-2]`: "a missing field without `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=…)` is an error" becomes "…without `@ser(default)`, `@ser(since=…)` or `@ser(skip)` is an error".
* `[DRV-1]` gains, after the table: "A derive builds its value field by field and runs no written `init` (`[CON-2]`), as the implicit `Clone` of `[STR-5]` does."

answers.answer: [CON-1]: a base with no written init has the init made from its fields, and that is its init for every caller, so `super.init(id=id)` calls it. Its arguments work as any constructor's (verdict 159: no word). An omitted field takes its default inside that init ([CON-3]). The same holds through [CLS-10]: a derived class with no init whose base wrote none gets the base's made init (`Panel(id=3)`). No new path is added: `Widget(id=7)` and `super.init(id=7)` call the same function.
answers.code:
open class Widget:                      # a UI base class with no `init` of its own
    id: int
    visible: bool = true

class Button(Widget):
    width: int                          # no default, so Button writes `init`

    fn init(id: int, width: int):
        this.width = width              # own field first ([CLS-11])
        super.init(id=id)               # Widget's init made from its fields; `visible` keeps its default

class Panel(Widget):
    pass

fn main():
    b = Button(7, 120)
    p = Panel(id=3)                     # [CLS-10]: Widget's made init
    println(b.id, b.visible, b.width)
    println(p.id, p.visible)
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints `7 true 120`, then `3 true`. `super.init(7)`, positional, works too, as does `super.init(id=id, visible=false)`. `super.init()` is refused as a call missing `id`. Calling `super.init` twice or not at all is still refused by [CLS-4].

answers.answer: [CON-3]: a field's default runs only in a construction that gives the field no other value, once, just before the first line of `init` that needs the field while it is unset. The same rule holds for structs and classes, so [CLS-2]'s 'every default before the body' goes. `data` is set before anything needs it, so its 4 KB default never runs. `pos` is read by `println(this.pos)` before `init` sets it, so its 0 is made just before that line. If `init` set `data` only on some paths, the default would run only on the other paths. The compiler places it there from init's own lines, with [OWN-3]'s hidden flag where the paths join. A class is changed too: with `id: int = next_id()` and an `init` that sets `id`, `next_id()` is not called. This is C++'s initialiser-list behaviour, here without an initialiser list.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints `0` twice. `Buffer(64)` allocates once, 64 bytes, and nothing is freed unused. `Ticket(5)` calls no `next_id()`, and `Ticket(-1)` calls it once, so no id number is skipped. Under `@noalloc` the `Buffer` init above is still refused, because `Array.with_capacity(size)` allocates. An init that sets `data` from caller-given storage on every path compiles under `@noalloc`, because the allocating default never runs.

answers.answer: [CON-4]: the init made from fields sets every field, so it is visible wherever every field may be written. That is the narrowest write visibility among the fields: here `pub` and `pub(package)`, so `pub(package)`. This is MOD-7's own reasoning ('construction is a write') carried through MOD-2's three levels. A `pub(read)` or `pub(package, read)` field still makes the constructor module-private, as MOD-7 says.
answers.code:
# net/packet.em
pub struct Packet:                     # a packet the network layer builds
    pub kind: u8
    pub(package) seq: u32              # seen only inside the `net` package

# net/send.em, a module of the same package
from net.packet import Packet

pub fn first() -> Packet:
    return Packet(kind=1, seq=7)       # the made init is pub(package): allowed here

# app/main.em, in a package depending on `net`
from net.packet import Packet

fn main():
    p = Packet(kind=1, seq=7)          # outside `net`
answers.outcome: `net/send.em` compiles. `app/main.em` is `E1052`: the constructor of `Packet` is visible only inside `net` because its field `seq` is `pub(package)` (packet.em line 4). The help says that to let other packages build a `Packet`, `net` must write a `pub fn init` or a `pub static fn` in `Packet`. No builder function is needed inside the package.

answers.answer: [CON-2]: a derived `Deserialize` is a builder the program writes no line for. A field it gets no value for from the data takes the field's written default, else its type's `Default`. This is DRV-1's `Default` row and HR-14's added-field rows, the same ladder. A `@ser(skip)` field is never in the data, so it always takes that fallback. One with neither a default nor a `Default` type is refused when compiling at the derive (E2080), never at run time. The same ladder fixes `@ser(default)` and `@ser(since=N)`: the written default now comes before the type's `Default`.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints `3 0`. `path_cache` is `{}`, its written default, and `frames_drawn` is 0, `int`'s `Default`. A skipped `captain: shares Player` with no default is `E2080` at `@derive(Deserialize)`: "`captain` is skipped, so reading a `SaveGame` back needs a value for it: give it a default, or remove `@ser(skip)`".

other_cases.case: `@ser(since=2) hp: int = 100`, and a version-1 save that has no `hp`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]: the written default comes first, so `hp` is 100, as [HR-14] gives a reloaded field added with a default. Today's XIV.2 text gives `int`'s Default, 0. This changes the outcome of ODR-159, a ruling made under the delegation, so it needs the owner's yes.

other_cases.case: `@derive(Default)` on a class whose written `init(name: String)` pushes `weakref this` into a roster.
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]: the derive builds field by field (each declared default, else the type's Default, as DRV-1 already says) and runs no written init, as the implicit Clone already does. The object is not put in the roster. A field with neither a default nor a `Default` type is E2080.

other_cases.case: A derived class `class Button(Widget):` with `clicks: int = 0` and `label: String`, whose `init` sets `label` and calls `super.init(id=1)`, while the base init calls a virtual method that reads `clicks`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-3]: `super.init(…)` needs every field the class itself declares, so `clicks`'s 0 is made just before it and the virtual method reads 0. CLS-11's promise holds: every field has a value when any method runs.

other_cases.case: `let id: int = next_id()`, and an `init` that writes `this.id = given`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-3]: the field gets one value, `given`, and `next_id()` is not called. CLS-9's 'set only in init' holds with no double assignment.

other_cases.case: `@noalloc fn init` on a struct with `buf: Array[u8] = Array.with_capacity(4096)`, where every path sets `buf` from a `FixedArena`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-3]: the default never runs, so the construction has no Alloc from it and the init compiles. If one path leaves `buf` unset, the default's Alloc counts and E4001 names the default's line.

other_cases.case: `init` writes `this.renderer = r`, then `this.assets = this.load_assets()`, then `this.cache = build()`, with `cache: Map[String, int] = {}`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-3]: a method call on `this` needs every field the type declares, so `cache`'s `{}` is made before `load_assets()` and is then replaced. This is decided from init's own lines, never from `load_assets`'s body ([MOD-9]). Setting `cache` before the call gives one value. E2100 still checks the fields without a default that `load_assets` reads ([CLS-2]).

other_cases.case: `super.init(id=id)` followed by `this.visible = false` in a derived init.
other_cases.settled: [CON-1] and [CON-3]: the base's made init gives `visible` its default `true`, and the derived init then changes it, an ordinary change after the base part is built. `super.init(id=id, visible=false)` gives it one value.

other_cases.case: A reload adds `armor: int = 5`, `name: String` and `target: shares Player` (no default).
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]'s ladder, as [HR-14] already states: 5, then `""`, then the reload is refused in plan, naming `target`.

other_cases.case: An `@export_table` field written with no default.
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]: the builder's stated fallback is the module's function of the field's name ([FFI-26], unchanged). A field naming no function is E1010.

other_cases.case: `alloc_zeroed` of a `@derive(Zeroable)` struct with `hp: int = 100`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]: zero-filling gives every field a value, zero bytes, so no default runs and `hp` is 0, as [ARN-11] promises. `alloc_array` calls `T.default()`, which for a derived Default is the ladder.

other_cases.case: Enum values: `Shape.Circle(1.0)`, and a derived `Default` whose `@default` variant has a payload.
other_cases.settled: Variant fields have no defaults in the grammar, so every builder gives each one a value. A derived Default gives each payload field its type's Default, else E2080 naming the field.

other_cases.case: `Self(v)` in `NonZero.new`, and `Self(…)` in a `static fn` of a type with a written init.
other_cases.settled: [CON-1]: `Self(…)` calls the type's one init. For NonZero that is the private made init, visible in its module ([CON-4], STD-4's 'no NonZero holds 0'); for the second type it is the written init.

other_cases.case: A derived Ember class with no init, over a C++ base that has no default constructor.
other_cases.settled: [CON-1]: 'its base's init' is the constructor [FFI-39b] selects, so E5058 holds as written, and ODR-219's order is unchanged.

other_cases.case: `pub struct Config:` with `pub name: String` and a private `cache: Map[String, int] = {}`.
other_cases.settled: [CON-4]: the made init sets `cache` too, so it is module-private; another module gets E1052 naming `cache`. An invariant between a public and a private field cannot be broken from outside.

other_cases.case: A panic in `init` before a defaulted field is needed.
other_cases.settled: [CON-3]: the default never runs. The fields already set end as they do today; an unset field is never ended.

other_cases.case: `migrate_from` building the new value.
other_cases.settled: [CON-2]: it builds through `Self(…)`, the type's init, so P09's J7-15 line `Session(sock=old.sock, target=old.target, hp=Health(value=old.hp))` follows [CON-1] and verdict 159.

design.prior_art:
**C++.**
* A default member initialiser (`int sent = 0;`) is used only when the constructor's mem-initialiser list does not name the member.
* An assignment in the constructor body comes after the default has run, so it is paid twice; avoiding that needs a second syntax (the initialiser list), and the cost depends on where the line is written.
* An aggregate, which gets the compiler-made constructor `T{…}`, may have no private members. That is the two-case visibility rule.
* C++17 aggregates with bases, and `using Base::Base` for inherited constructors.

**Rust.**
* There are no constructors. A struct literal needs every field visible at the use (E0451), the narrowest-visibility rule.
* `..Default::default()` builds a whole default value first (every default evaluated), then moves the given fields in.
* serde's `#[serde(skip)]` takes `Default::default()` or `default = "path"`, and a missing field is an error otherwise. Rust has no declared field default for it to consult first.

**Swift.**
* A struct's memberwise init has the minimum access level of its stored properties, capped at internal, and properties with defaults become optional parameters. Writing an init in the type's body removes the memberwise init.
* Class two-phase init (own properties before `super.init`) is Ember's CLS-11.
* Default property values are stored as part of initialisation, so an init that reassigns one pays twice.
* Codable: a property left out of `CodingKeys` must have a default value or synthesis fails, which is Ember's E2080 for a skipped field.

**Java, C#, Kotlin.** Field initialisers always run: Java's after `super()`, C#'s before the base constructor. A constructor that reassigns pays twice.

**Ada.** A record component's default expression is evaluated only for components an aggregate or object declaration does not give (`others => <>`). A private type cannot be aggregated outside its package.

**Zig.** Default field values fill only the fields a struct literal omits. `std.json` fills a missing field with its default value and errors when there is none.

**Go.** A literal with unexported fields cannot be written outside the package. An omitted field silently gets its zero value: the silent fill Ember refuses for an init.

**Python dataclasses.** `default_factory` runs only when the argument is omitted, and a subclass's generated `__init__` appends its fields after the base's.

**Where they fall short of safe, as fast as C, and readable:**
* C++ needs a separate syntax to avoid paying twice.
* Swift, Java, C#, Kotlin and Rust's `..Default::default()` always pay for the default.
* Go fills forgotten fields silently.
* serde ignores the field's own default.

**What Ember takes:** C++'s 'a default only where the constructor gives none', with no list to write because the compiler reads init's lines (as it already does for E2100); Swift's and Rust's narrowest-field visibility; Swift Codable's 'a skipped field needs a value'; and serde's Default fallback, placed after the field's own default.
design.cost:
**[CON-1]**: zero. `Name(…)`, `Self(…)` and `super.init(…)` are direct calls of one known function, inlined like C's struct initialisation. Nothing is stored in the object.

**[CON-3]**:
* Zero at run time whenever `init` sets a field on every path or on none (decided when compiling). Against today's class rule it saves one full evaluation of the default plus its drop for every field `init` sets: in J3-06, one 4,096-byte allocation and one free per `Buffer(64)`.
* When `init` sets a defaulted field on some paths only, the cost is one bit (OWN-3's hidden flag) in a register or stack slot while `init` runs, plus one test where the paths join. That is the same branch a C programmer writes as the `else` of the `if`. It adds zero bytes to the object, and the optimiser removes the test when the default has no effect to order.
* A default with no effect at the end of init costs the store C pays.

**[CON-2]**: compile time only. It decides which fallback each derive emits: per missing or skipped field, either the default's expression or one `T.default()` call, exactly what C code filling a missing field writes. An init gets no hidden fill.

**[CON-4]**: compile time only.

**Memory**: no word, flag or header byte is added to any value; the flags live only during init.

readability.ordinary_before:

    port: int
    buf: Array[u8] = Array.with_capacity(4096)
    sent: int = 0

    fn init(port: int, size: int):
        this.port = port
        this.buf = Array.with_capacity(size)   # today: the 4 KB default was made first and is freed here

# J3-05 today: to be sure `super.init(id=id)` compiles, Widget writes an init by hand
open class Widget:
    id: int
    visible: bool = true

    fn init(id: int, visible: bool = true):
        this.id = id
        this.visible = visible
readability.ordinary_after:
# the same program, character for character
class Conn:
    port: int
    buf: Array[u8] = Array.with_capacity(4096)
    sent: int = 0

    fn init(port: int, size: int):
        this.port = port
        this.buf = Array.with_capacity(size)   # the 4 KB default never runs; `sent`'s 0 is stored at the end of init

# J3-05 under the rule: no init to write

    visible: bool = true
readability.note:
No new word, attribute or line appears in any program.
* `Conn`, the overview's `Emitter` and Part V's `Script`/`Door` read exactly as before and do less work.
* J3-05 drops a three-line init a base needed only so `super.init` had something to call.
* J3-18 drops the `pub(package) static fn new` builder that the two-case rule forced.
* J3-06 and J6-15 are unchanged in text and now have one meaning.

The one change a reader of the rules meets: for a class, a default runs where `init` first needs the field, not before its first line. For pure defaults (`0`, `[]`, `true`, `Vec3.ZERO`, every default in the spec's examples) nothing observable changes. A default with an effect (`id: int = next_id()`) now runs only when `init` does not set the field. That is what STR-2 already says ('evaluated at each construction that omits the field') and what the field line means: the value when nothing else gives one (checklist 1, 15).

The line that runs it is read from init's own lines, never from another body, so MOD-9's 'a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does' holds.

design.compiler_does:
1. **Finding the init.** For each struct and class the compiler takes the written `init`, else the init made from fields (no base), else the base's init (CLS-10, a C++ base's by FFI-39b). It resolves `Name(…)`, `Self(…)` and `super.init(…)` to that function, and checks their arguments as the calls they are.

2. **Placing defaults.** The definite-assignment pass that init already gets for E2100 and E2102 now also places defaults. For each field at each point of init it knows whether the field is set, unset, or set on some paths.
   * At each need point named in CON-3 (a read or change of the field or a part of it; a method call on `this`, `this` used as a whole, or `super.init(…)`, which need the type's own fields; a `return` or the end, which need all fields) it inserts the evaluation of each still-unset default, in field order.
   * Where a field is set on some paths, it reuses OWN-3's hidden drop flag. The flag decides at the need whether to make the default, and at a later assignment whether the old value is dropped or this is the first store.
   * On a panicking path, a default not yet made is never made.
   * The made init evaluates the omitted fields' defaults after its arguments.
   * Only init's own lines are read, never a called method's body (MOD-9).

3. **Effects.** The effects of a construction (Alloc, Panic, `@noalloc`, `@nopanic`) are init's own effects plus those of the defaults it may make on some path.

4. **Visibility.** The made init's visibility is the narrowest write visibility of its fields (MOD-2 levels, with MOD-7's read-only fields as module-private). E1052 names the narrowing field.

5. **Derives.** Clone, Copy, Default and Deserialize are built field by field without running a written init. For each field the derive can lack a value for (every field for Default; for Deserialize, the skip, default and since fields), it emits the field's default expression, else a `T.default()` call. It gives E2080 naming the field when neither exists. Deserialize's generated code reads the declared default before std's `or_default`. The expansion that `ember inspect --expand` prints shows that field-by-field build (wording is the lead's).

6. **Unchanged checks.** CLS-11, E2101, E2102, E5058, HR-14's rows and FFI-26 are checked as today.
design.misuse:
Every mistake is refused when compiling; nothing here can read an unset field at run time.

* **A forgotten field.** A field without a default that init leaves unset on some path, or reads first, is E2100, with the line to write (as today). An omitted argument for such a field in the made init is refused as a missing argument, never filled with a type's Default.
* **A skipped or always-missing field with no value.** For example a `@ser(skip)` `captain: shares Player` with no default and no `Default` type: E2080 at the `@derive`, naming the field. The help: "give it a default, or remove `@ser(skip)`".
* **A constructor called outside its visibility.** A made init called where some field cannot be written is E1052, naming that field and its visibility. The help: "write a `pub fn init(…)` (or `pub(package)`) in `Packet`, or a `pub static fn`".
* **Wrong `super.init(…)` calls.** Arguments that name no parameter of the base's init, or miss a required one, are the ordinary call errors. A derived init that calls `super.init` twice or never is still CLS-4's error, and a read of an inherited field before it is still E2102.
* **Defaults wasted on purpose by an ordinary assignment.** Setting a field after a method call that needed it (CON-3), or after `super.init`, is no error, just the program's own second assignment. No warning is proposed, since the program says what it does.
* **No undefined behaviour.** No path reads an unset field: the flag of a field set on some paths is tested before any need, and a field is never dropped before its first store.
design.verdicts:
* **74, 85, 97 (`owns` on the making line for an `owns` field): kept.** `super.init(mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0]))` over a memberwise base writes `owns` as `Entity(mesh=owns Mesh(…))` does. A field default for an `owns` field is a making line too (`mesh: owns Mesh = owns Mesh(points=[])`).
* **159 (a constructor's argument takes no word, as `=`): kept.** `super.init(id=id)` over a made init is a constructor call, so its arguments take no word. A written init's own call words stay P06's J1-07; under every J1-07 option this group's lines are unchanged (phase 3's K32 note).
* **86 and 137 (the compiler works facts out by reading the code): followed.** Where a default runs is read from init's lines by the definite-assignment pass E2100 already runs, with nothing written.
* **MOD-9 (a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does): kept.** The need points are init's own lines only. A method called from init counts as needing every field, whatever its body does, so where a default runs never depends on another function's body. This was the phase-3 note for J3-06.
* **5 and JOB.md's 'the compiler does not silently decide what the programmer did not say': kept.** A type's `Default` fills a field only for builders the program asked to fill: derives with skip, default or since, a derived Default, and HR-14's reload rows. An init never falls back to one.

**Revisited (not owner verdicts):**
* CLS-2's 'every default before any init body'. It is a lead rule (Parts V, VIII, Annex H show no JOB.md verdict).
* XIV.2's 'its type's Default' for `@ser(default)` and `@ser(since=N)`, ODR-159, ruled under the delegation.

Both change what programs do: a default with an effect no longer runs when init sets the field, and on load a written default wins over the type's Default. So both go to the owner as part of this ODR, said plainly. The evidence: one rule with no class/struct split; no wasted 4 KB allocation; `next_id()` skips no numbers; the same ladder HR-14 already uses for reload.

recommendation.reason: One rule settles all four questions and the cases nobody asked about (super.init over a made base, struct and class defaults, pub(package) constructors, skipped and versioned fields, derived Default, reload, @export_table, zero-fill, enums) with no exception by type or construct. It costs nothing over C, is cheaper than today's class rule, and needs no new word: the compiler reads init's lines as it already does for E2100. Its one change for existing programs, a default with an effect no longer running when init sets the field, is what STR-2 and the field line already say. B and C pay twice for a default (C only on some paths). D, E and F each make the programmer write lines or a second rule that A makes unnecessary.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: a default member initialiser (`int sent = 0;`) runs only when the constructor's initialiser list doesn't set the member, and the compiler-made aggregate constructor exists only when every member is public. Ember has no initialiser list, so it must say when a field's `= default` runs, what `super.init` calls when the base wrote no `init`, who may call the compiler-made constructor, and what a `@ser(skip)` field holds after loading.

owner_short.today: A class makes every field default before `init` runs, even one that `init` immediately replaces. Four things are not decided: what a struct's `init` does with a default, what `super.init` calls when the base wrote no `init`, whether a `pub(package)` field's constructor works inside the package, and what a `@ser(skip)` field holds.
owner_short.options:
A (recommended): one init per type, which `super.init` also calls; a default runs only where nothing else gave the field a value; the made constructor is as visible as its narrowest field; a skipped field takes its default, else its type's Default.
B: as A, but every default still runs before `init` (today's class rule, for structs too), so the 4 KB list is made and thrown away.
C: as A, but defaults run before `init` except for fields it always sets first, so a field set on only some paths pays twice.
D: as A, but a base with a field that has no default must write `init` before anything can derive from it.
E: as A, but a `@ser(skip)` field must write its default.
F: as A, but the made constructor is either `pub` or private to its module, so `pub(package)` fields need a hand-written builder.
owner_short.recommendation: A: it is C++'s initialiser-list behaviour without the list. It costs nothing over C, adds no word, and answers the four questions with one rule. Its one visible change is that a default with a side effect (`id: int = next_id()`) no longer runs when `init` sets the field.

design.open_risks:
1. **Derives bypass a written init.** Derived Default and Deserialize build field by field and run no written init, as the implicit Clone already does. A class whose init registers itself or establishes an invariant is therefore not registered and not checked when built by those derives. Memory safety holds for safe fields, but unsafe code that trusts an init-made invariant (`len <= cap`) is the vouching author's duty (P04). The real alternative for the owner: refuse `@derive(Default)` and `@derive(Deserialize)` on a type that writes an init, with the help 'write `deserialize` yourself'. DRV-1's 'the generated code is ordinary Ember' needs a printed form for a field-by-field build on such a type. Clone already needs one, so this is a lead wording task.

2. **Default order for classes changes.** Defaults now run at init's first need, often its end, instead of before its first line. A program whose default's side effect must precede init's first statement sees a new order. No spec or std example depends on it (checked: Emitter, Script/Door, CLS-2's load_assets example, std/src/collections.em and ecs.em's inits). A test that logs from a default would change.

3. **Load results change.** A written default now wins over the type's Default for `@ser(default)` and `@ser(since=N)` (ODR-159 was delegated). A save format relying on `hp: int = 100` loading as 0 would load as 100.

4. **Absence stays strict.** A field with a written default but no `@ser(default)`, `@ser(since)` or `@ser(skip)` that is missing from the data stays an error, as serde and Swift Codable behave. Zig's std.json instead lets a written default permit absence; the owner may prefer that.

5. **Kept as is, a possible separate question.** A derived class with no init over a base with a written init still needs a default for every field it declares (E2101). A made init for derived classes covering the base's init parameters plus their own fields (Python dataclass style) is a separate question. It would need rules for C++ bases' overload sets (P07) and for name clashes.

6. **Derive visibility.** A derived Deserialize on a `pub` type with private fields lets any reader of its data build it, as serde does; this rule does not change that. Whether derived implementations follow CON-4's narrowest-field visibility is not asked here.

7. **Shared flag machinery.** The hidden flag for fields set on some paths reuses OWN-3's drop-flag machinery. The compiler must keep 'first store' and 'replace (drop the old)' apart on those paths, which is the drop-flag logic already needed for conditional hand-overs.

# package ui, file ui/widget.em
pub open class Widget:
    pub name: String

    pub fn init(n: StrView):
        this.layout()                  # Widget's own layout reads nothing, so E2100 passes when `ui` is compiled
        this.name = String(n)

    pub virtual fn layout():
        pass

# package app (depends on ui), file app/main.em
from ui.widget import Widget

class Label(Widget):
    width: int = 0

    fn init(n: StrView):
        super.init(n)                  # [CLS-11]: own fields first (width's 0 is made here, [CON-3]), then the base

    override fn layout():
        this.width = len(this.name)    # reads `name`, which Widget.init sets only after it calls layout()

fn main():
    l = Label("ok")
holes.what_goes_wrong: Widget.init calls layout(), which dispatches to Label.layout, which reads `name`: a String that was never set, so its pointer and length are whatever bytes the block held. That is undefined behaviour (a garbage read, then a free of a garbage pointer when the object ends). `ui` was checked without Label, so CLS-2's E2100, which reads the bodies of the methods init calls ('every override the program has', DSP-5), saw only Widget.layout. `app`'s checks of Label.init (its own field set, super.init called once) and of Label.layout (an inherited field read after construction) find nothing. Nothing in CON-3, CLS-11, MOD-9 or EFF-4 records across the package edge that Widget.init calls layout() while `name` is unset. CON-3 covers only fields with a default (they are made before every method call); a field without one depends on reading bodies, and the base package cannot read a dependant's override. So CLS-11's 'when any method runs, even a virtual method called from a base init, every field of the object holds a value' and the design's 'No path reads an unset field' are both false here. A base init that calls a virtual on_create or layout is common in UI and game frameworks: it is the C++/Java trap of calling a virtual method from a constructor.
holes.fix_hint: Record in the package's interface file, for each init, which fields are still unset at each call that may reach an override (EFF-4 and MOD-9 already keep worked-out facts there). Check every override against it: E2100 at the override's read ("`Widget.init` (ui/widget.em line 5) calls `layout()` before it sets `name`, and this override reads `name`"). This keeps the compiler doing the work and accepts every correct base. A simpler but stricter alternative, decided from init's own lines: a call in init that may reach an override (a virtual method, or an interface or dyn method on `this`) needs every field of the type set, as CON-3 already says for defaults.

fn main():

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2 builds a derived Default field by field and runs no written init. It says nothing about a base part, or about fields the derive's module may not write. Dialog.default() fills Window's private `handle` with 0, and Window.init never runs. When `d` ends, Window's drop calls win_destroy(0), so the fact `ui` vouched for in its `# SAFETY` note is broken by a one-line safe attribute in another package (P04: safe code relies only on what is checked or vouched). The same happens with @derive(Deserialize) on Dialog, which sets `handle` to any number in the data, and with @derive(Clone), which copies the handle so that two objects destroy it (STR-5's 'a type that declares drop is not implicitly Clone' reads as Dialog's own drop only). CON-4 makes Window's made init visible only in ui/window.em, because `handle` is private, yet a derive writes that field from a dependant. So the design's 'an invariant between a public and a private field cannot be broken from outside' fails.
holes.fix_hint: A derive is a builder and keeps the builders' rules. It builds field by field only the fields its module may write (CON-4). A derived class's base part is built through the base's one init (`super.init()` with no arguments, here Window.init). Where the base's init needs arguments, or the base has a field the derive cannot write, the derive is E2080 naming the base, with the help to write `static fn default() -> Dialog: return Dialog()` by hand. Clone of a type with a drop anywhere among its bases follows STR-5.

holes.program:
from std.ser import json

static CURVE: Array[f32] = make_curve()   # 101 gain values, index 0 to 100

@derive(Serialize, Deserialize)
pub struct Volume:
    level: int                            # private; init keeps it in 0..=100

    pub fn init(level: int):
        assert(level >= 0 and level <= 100, "volume out of range")
        this.level = level

    pub fn gain() -> f32:
        unsafe:                           # SAFETY: init keeps level in 0..=100, and CURVE has 101 entries
            return CURVE.get_unchecked(this.level)

fn main() -> Result[void]:
    v = json.from_str[Volume]("{\"level\": 5000}")?   # [CON-2]: field by field, no init, so the assert never runs
    println(v.gain())                     # reads CURVE[5000], past the end
    return Ok(())
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2 and the new DRV-1 sentence make a derived Deserialize run no written init. `json.from_str[Volume]` therefore returns a Volume with level 5000, which `Volume(5000)` would have stopped at its assert. gain() then reads past the end of CURVE under a `# SAFETY` note that holds for every value init can make. SER-2 promises 'Deserialising never produces an invalid value'. P15's own principle says that reading back from saved data goes through the type's one init. ARN-11 makes the same kind of field-by-field build (zero-fill) an unsafe marker precisely because 'only its author can vouch for its invariants', yet Deserialize and Default get neither a mark nor a refusal. Without unsafe code the same hole gives a silent wrong value (a validated port of 0, a percentage of 500) that stops far from the load, if at all. The same applies to @derive(Default) on a type whose init acquires what its drop releases: a File-like struct's Default descriptor 0 is closed by its drop, which closes standard input. A range type fixes only a one-field case like this one; an invariant across fields has no such escape.
holes.fix_hint: On a type that writes `init`, a derive that builds a value builds it through that init. Deserialize reads the fields and calls `Self(level=…)`, matching init's parameters by name; a skipped or missing field is omitted, so init's own defaults and checks run, and a failed assert stops the program at the load. Default calls `Self()`. Where init's parameters are not the fields, the derive is E2080, with the help: 'Volume writes init, which a derived Deserialize would skip; write `static fn deserialize` yourself, building with `Volume(...)`'. A type with only the made init keeps the field-by-field build, which is the same thing.

holes.program:
from std.sync import Lock
import std.thread

class Log:
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    lines: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

    fn init():
        this.lines = [String("start")]   # [THR-18]: init sets a guarded field without the lock

    fn push(s: StrView):
        with this.lock:
            this.lines.push(owns String(s))

    fn restart():
        this.init()                       # nothing refuses an ordinary call of `init`

fn main():
    log = Log()
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): log.push("a"))   # the task changes log.lines under its lock
        log.restart()                            # init's lock-free store to lines, at the same time
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1 names the lines that build a value (`Name(...)`, `Self(...)`, `super.init(...)`) but refuses no other call of init, while an explicit `x.drop()` is E3070 (shape O7). init's stores are first stores (CON-3: every flag starts unset). So `log.restart()` on a live object does three things. It overwrites `lines` without ending the old list, so its Strings are never freed (OWN-2: 'nothing ends an owner without running it'). At init's end it makes `lock`'s default and stores a new Lock over the live one. It writes the guarded `lines` without the lock while the scoped task pushes under the lock: a data race. THR-18 allows that lock-free write only because, during construction, nobody else can see the object. On a class with `let id: int = next_id()`, it also gives a `let` field a new value after construction (CLS-9a, P10). Python programmers reset an object with `self.__init__()`, so this is a natural thing to write.
holes.fix_hint: Only a builder calls init: `Name(...)`, `Self(...)`, and `super.init(...)` as the one call in a derived init. Any other call (`this.init(...)`, `x.init(...)`) is refused, as `x.drop()` is, with the help: "to start again, build a new one: `log = Log()`, or write a method that sets the fields: `fn restart():`".

holes.what_goes_wrong: Today CLS-2 makes `name` before init's body, and the walk is fine. Under CON-3, `next_name()` runs just before `println(this.name)`, inside the walk of NAMES, and pushes to NAMES. The rule says where the default runs and that its effects (Alloc, Panic) count for the construction. It does not say that the placed call counts at that line for the walk, lock and task rules (E3020, E7018, THR-11), and the design's compiler steps never mention them. EFF-1 counts 'the default expressions it evaluates' for a construction, which today runs them before the body. If the placed call is not counted, the push can move NAMES's buffer while the loop reads it: a read of freed memory. If it is counted, a program that compiles today is refused at a line that calls nothing, with no message saying that a default is made there. The same holds with `with IDS_LOCK:` in init over `id: int = next_id()` where next_id takes IDS_LOCK (a wait for ever, or E7018 at `println(this.id)`), and inside `with scope = thread.scope():` where a task reads the static the default changes (a race, or E7007).
holes.fix_hint: Add to CON-3: a default made at a line counts as a call written at that line for every rule that looks at calls (effects, walks, locks, tasks, views), as EFF-1 counts a call's default arguments. A refusal it causes names both lines: 'line 14 reads `name`, so its default `next_name()` (line 8) is made there, and that changes `NAMES`, which this loop walks; give `name` a value above line 12, or read it after the loop'.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CLS-2, which the design keeps, lets init call a method 'once every field that method's body reads is set'. `reset` reads no field: it stores `inbox`, and a store ends the old value first (OWN-5). Called from init, `inbox` was never set, so the store ends garbage: undefined behaviour. CON-3's 'giving the whole field a value is not a need' is right for init's own lines, where the compiler knows the store is a first store. A method's body, though, is compiled once and always ends the old value. The rule also does not say whether E2100 counts reset's store as setting `inbox`. If it does, this program compiles and frees a garbage pointer. If it does not, `this.inbox = []` must be written above the call, and the call is still undefined behaviour whenever init sets the field after it.
holes.fix_hint: In CON-3 and CLS-2: a call of a method of `this` in init needs every field its body reads, changes or gives a value (a store ends the old value), so each such field is set or defaulted before the call, or it is E2100 naming the method's store line. Only init's own lines set a field, never a method it calls (MOD-9).

holes.program:
@derive(Default)
struct Config:
    name: String
    retries: int = 3

    fn init(text: StrView):
        this = Config.default()          # [FN-4] lets a struct's method give `this` a whole value
        this.name = String(text)
holes.what_goes_wrong: FN-4 lets a struct method give `this` a whole new value, and nothing excludes init. CON-3 lists `this = v` neither as a need nor as a store of every field. Read as an ordinary assignment, OWN-5 ends the old `this` first, which ends `name`, an unset String: undefined behaviour. Read as a need of every field, `name` has no default and the line is E2100, while `retries`'s 3 is made only to be thrown away. The rule decides neither reading.
holes.fix_hint: In CON-3: in init, `this = v` gives every field a value. It is a first store for each unset field and a replace (the old value ended) for each set one, using the same flags; it is not a need. Alternatively, refuse `this = ...` in init, with the help to set the fields.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2 has a reload's migration by name use the written default for an added field, and has migrate_from build through `Self(...)`, the init. So a default's or an init's panics (unwrap, assert, allocation failure) run during prepare, once for each live Enemy. HR-34 says prepare cannot panic, and HR-35 refuses an explicit panic only in migrate_from's own body. A panic here aborts the running program (PAN-1) instead of refusing the reload.
holes.fix_hint: Hold a default or init that a reload runs to HR-35: an explicit panic it may reach refuses the reload in plan, naming the default's line, and its run-time checks return ReloadError.Migration.

holes.what_goes_wrong: In `debug`, the assert reads `id`, so `next_id()` runs there and its value is then replaced. In `release`, the assert is removed and init sets `id` before any need, so `next_id()` never runs. Every later id differs between the two profiles, yet debug_assert's rule says it MUST NOT change a program's result, and W2016 does not fire because its argument calls no function. 'Which line needs a field follows from init's own lines alone' does not say whether a line the profile removes counts.
holes.fix_hint: Need points are init's lines as written, in every profile: a debug_assert that reads a field makes that field's default in release too. Alternatively, W2016 counts a default its argument would make.

safety.notes:
Read: owner-bar.md, brief.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, P15 in phase1-groups.json (and the other groups' principles), J3-05/J3-06/J3-18/J6-15 in phase2.json, K32/K33/K49/K66 and the critic's J3-06 B note in phase3.json, JOB.md 150-166, and the spec parts p05 (MOD, FN, STR, CLS), p07 (OWN-2..13), p09 (ARN, ALC), p10 (EFF-1, 24, 25), p11 (THR-3, 17..20), p13/p06 (PAN-1), p14 (XIV.2, DRV-1, SER-1/2), p16, p17 (shape O7: `x.drop()` is E3070), p20 (HR-14..16, 34..36) and p21 (FFI-39, 39b). No verdict clash was found: 74/85/97 and 159 are kept, 164-166 are untouched.

Where the rule is sound: CON-3's lazy defaults with OWN-3 flags never read an unset defaulted field, because every need list (a field read or change, any method call or use of `this` as a whole, super.init, return or the end) comes before any use, and PAN-1's abort-only panics mean a half-built object is never ended. CON-4's narrowest-field visibility is sound for the made init. The CON-2 ladder is well-founded, and an init never fills a field silently.

The holes are at the rule's edges:
(1) init's callers are not limited to builders: `x.init()` races with tasks through THR-18's init exemption, loses drops and changes `let` fields.
(2) A compiler-placed default is not said to count, at its line, for the walk, lock and task checks.
(3) Derives that build field by field bypass the one init. Across a package edge this lets a dependant break a library's vouched drop (high). Within a module it breaks SER-2's 'never produces an invalid value' and P15's own principle that reading back saved data goes through the type's one init. ARN-11 already treats a field-by-field build as needing the author's vouch.
(4) Fields without a default still rely on E2100 reading bodies, which fails for a base init's virtual call to a dependant's override, and for a helper method that stores an unset field. `this = v` in a struct init is undecided.

Minor points, not holes:
- The J3-06 other case 'every path sets buf from a FixedArena' cannot be written, because ALC-1 makes a field's type name its manager, so a Global `Array.with_capacity(4096)` default is E2020 on a `using FixedArena` field. Caller-given storage through `owns body: Array[u8]` works and shows the same point.
- The design's 'fields already set end as they do today' after a panic is moot: PAN-1 aborts and nothing ends.
- A need inside a loop body costs a flag test on every round, not 'one test where the paths join' (cost, not safety).

Every fix proposed reuses an existing spelling or rule (E3070's shape, EFF-1, EFF-4's interface file, CON-4's visibility, HR-35) and adds no word to ordinary programs.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-3 counts any call of a method of `this` as needing every field the type declares. So `{}` is built before `load_assets()` and freed one line later, and `next_id()` runs even though init sets `id` on every path. That makes CON-3's own sentence false: "With `id: int = next_id()`, `next_id()` runs only in a construction that does not set `id`". The headline "a default is evaluated only where it is the value" is false here too, and J3-06's promise that no id number is skipped breaks. For the same call, E2100 ([CLS-2], the owner's row 7, then verdict 86) asks only for the fields `load_assets`'s body reads. Delete `= {}` and `= next_id()` and this init compiles and makes one map. So a default the init never uses makes the init slower and changes what it does. This is CLS-2's own example pattern (set one field, call a helper, set the rest), so the ordinary class init pays twice, which is what the rule set out to remove. The only way out is to reorder lines, and nothing on the page tells the reader to.
holes.fix_hint: Answer "which fields does this call need to hold a value?" once, the way E2100 already does: a method call needs the fields its body reads (verdicts 86 and 137, "read the code"). A default is then made only where a read needs it. That moves an effectful default when a far body changes, and MOD-9's last sentence (lead text, not a verdict) forbids that, so the owner decides: (a) body reads decide for every default, and MOD-9's sentence is narrowed to what compiles; (b) keep CON-3, correct its promise to "runs unless init's own lines set the field before any need", and add a warning naming the line to move above the call.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The type says twice how a fresh value looks: its `init` (step 1) and `@derive(Default)`. CON-2 lets the derive build field by field and skip init, so `mem.take` leaves a `Pacer` with `step` 0 that no line of `Pacer` makes, and `100 // c.pacer.step` panics. The same holds for `@derive(Deserialize)` over a validating init: with `fn init(v: int): assert v <= 100`, `json.from_str` gives a value of 900. That breaks SER-2's "deserialising never produces an invalid value", and unsafe code trusting the init's invariant becomes reachable from input data (P04). This is the one exception to the rule's own headline, "every line that builds the type calls that same init". `Pacer.default()` and `json.from_str[T]` are lines the program writes, and the compiler silently picks a meaning per route (checklist 5 and 15).
holes.fix_hint: On a type that writes `init`: a derived `Default` calls `Self()` when init takes no arguments, and is E2080 otherwise ("`Pacer` writes `init`, so a derived `Default` would skip it: write `fn default() -> Self: return Self(...)`"). A derived `Deserialize` is E2080 unless init's parameters are exactly its fields, in which case it reads them and calls init. Clone, Copy, zero-fill (vouched, ARN-11) and migration start from a value an init already made, so they stay field by field. Put it to the owner beside the design's open risk 1.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2 and the DRV-1 sentence it adds say Clone and Default build the value field by field and run no written init. `Badge`'s base part is a C++ object. It has no Ember fields, it must be made by a C++ constructor (and get its vtable through FFI-39's trampoline), its copy constructor may be user-written or deleted, and here it has no default constructor. Field by field is undefined for it. FFI-39b and E5058 cover only `super.init(...)` and a derived class with no init, so nothing refuses these derives. A derive over a C++ base is left to the compiler's choice or to undefined behaviour. The same holds for `@derive(Deserialize)`.
holes.fix_hint: Add to CON-2: over a C++ base, a derive builds the base part with the C++ constructor of its kind (the copy constructor for Clone, the default constructor for Default). Where C++ has none or deletes it, the derive is E2080 naming the base. `Deserialize` over a C++ base is E2080. Check this with P07, which owns how C++ constructors are chosen.

class Label:
