    fn init(text: String):                # only reads its argument
        this.text = copy of text

fn main():
    caption = String("smoke")
    sign = Label(caption)
    println(caption)
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1's text says "That one init is what every line that builds the type calls ... Its arguments take the words [FN-2a] gives a constructor's arguments: none, working as `=` does (verdict 159)". The paragraph's subject is the one init, written or made, and the sentence also follows the C++ constructor of FFI-39b. Read that way, `Label(caption)` hands `caption` over and `println(caption)` is E3040, though `Label`'s first line says it only reads (FN-2: "A parameter with no word reads"). That silently decides P06's open J1-07 as its option (c), the one phase 2 shows to be wrong. It also gives C++ constructor arguments a hand-over C++ never asked for. The design's verdicts section says J1-07 stays P06's, but the spec text it proposes decides it.
holes.fix_hint: Scope the sentence to the made init: "The init made from fields takes its arguments as [FN-2a] gives a constructor's arguments (none, as `=`, verdict 159; `owns` on a making line for an `owns` field). A written init's and a C++ constructor's call words are [FN-2a]'s for their first lines (P06, J1-07)."

holes.program:
open class Widget:
    id: int
    visible: bool = true

class Button(Widget):
    width: int

    fn init(id: int, width: int):         # three lines that only pass fields through
        this.width = width
        super.init(id=id)

fn main():
    b = Button(id=7, width=120)
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1 gives the init made from fields only to a type "with no base". A derived class with no init gets its base's made init, which cannot set the derived class's own fields. So any field without a default forces E2101 and a hand-written init that only copies parameters into fields. The design's own J3-05 answer shows this boilerplate. UI and game hierarchies (Widget/Button, Entity/Enemy) meet it in the ordinary program. C++17 aggregates with bases (`Button{{7}, 120}`) and Python dataclasses build these with no constructor written. "With no base" is a construct-specific limit inside a rule that is otherwise general. The design itself leaves this as open risk 5.
holes.fix_hint: Give the init made from fields to every type whose chain writes no init: base fields first, then its own, each defaulted one omissible, named arguments always allowed. Fields cannot be overridden (CLS-4), so names never clash. A base with a written init, or a C++ base, keeps CLS-10 and E2101 as today. Show it to the owner as a line of J3-05.

holes.program:
# net/packet.em
pub struct Packet:
    pub kind: u8
    pub(package) seq: u32

fn resend(p: Packet) -> Packet:
    return Packet(kind=p.kind, seq=p.seq + 1)

# net/compat.em, another module of `net` ([IFC-1] allows `extend Packet:` here)
from net.packet import Packet

static mut SENT: int = 0

extend Packet:
    pub fn init(kind: u8, seq: u32):
        this.kind = kind
        this.seq = seq
        SENT += 1
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1 says a type's init is "the `fn init(...)` it writes", and IFC-1 lets any module of the package write `extend Packet:` with methods. Nothing says whether an init in an extend block counts. If it counts, a module elsewhere in the build silently replaces what `Packet(kind=..., seq=...)` in packet.em calls, so that line now counts SENT, and the type's init depends on which modules are built. If it does not count, the type has two inits. Either way the "one init" guarantee and CON-4's visibility rule rest on an undecided case. A Swift programmer writes exactly this, since Swift keeps the memberwise init when the custom one is in an extension.
holes.fix_hint: In CON-1: an `init` is written only in the type's own body. `fn init` in an `extend` block is refused with the help to move it into the type, as `init` and `drop` are each type's own (CLS-4).

holes.program:
# game/enemy.em
@derive(Default)
pub struct Enemy:
    pub hp: int
    pub pos: Vec2
    cooldown: f32 = 0.0                  # the module's own bookkeeping

# game/spawner.em
from game.enemy import Enemy

fn spawn(p: Vec2) -> Enemy:
    return Enemy(hp=5, pos=p)            # E1052 under [CON-4]: `cooldown` is private

fn spawn2(p: Vec2) -> Enemy:
    e = Enemy.default()                  # compiles, and builds the same value
    e.hp = 5
    e.pos = p
    return e
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-4 makes the made init module-private because `cooldown` is private, though the call never names `cooldown` and it takes its author's default. The stated reason ("an invariant between a public and a private field cannot be broken from outside") protects nothing here. Any module may write the pub fields after construction, and `spawn2` builds the identical value through the derived Default. The cost falls on an ordinary game program: to be built from a sibling module, `Enemy` needs a hand-written `pub fn init` that repeats every pub field as a parameter and an assignment.
holes.fix_hint: Decide per call: a call may name a field only where that field may be written (E1052 naming it), and an omitted field takes its own default. The made init is then refused only where a field without a default cannot be written, so a private field with no default still seals the type. A defaulted pub(read) field then follows the same rule (MOD-7's "construction is a write" applies to the fields written). This is the owner's choice beside J3-18.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2's ladder says each field gets the first of: what the builder gives, else its written default. A derived Deserialize that finds no `fullscreen` gives it no value, so the ladder says `false`. The changed SER-2 says a missing field without `@ser(default)`, `@ser(since=...)` or `@ser(skip)` is an error. The rule's two texts decide this program differently. The design means the error (open risk 4), but CON-2 does not say so.
holes.fix_hint: In CON-2 add: "for a derived Deserialize, a field missing from the data counts as given no value only under @ser(default), @ser(since=N) or @ser(skip); otherwise it is SER-2's error". Or, the owner's choice: a written default permits absence (Zig, Kotlin), and `@ser(default)` is needed only to fall back to the type's Default.

holes.program:
struct Level:
    names: Array[String] using LevelArena = []     # which LevelArena instance does `[]` use?

@derive(Default)
struct Room:
    tiles: Array[u8] using LevelArena              # Default fallback: Array.default() names no instance

fn load(current: LevelArena):
    l = Level() using current
holes.what_goes_wrong: ALC-1 says the line that makes a value of a `using A` type names the instance. A field default cannot name the construction's instance. Under CON-3 it is evaluated inside init, where `current` is not in scope, and CON-2's third step (the type's Default) has no instance either. CON-2 does not say whether such a default or fallback is refused, takes Global (a kind mismatch ALC-1 checks), or takes the making line's instance.
holes.fix_hint: A written default or a Default fallback for a field whose manager type has several instances must name one (a static instance), or it is refused, E2080 at a derive. Agree the wording with P02, which owns `using`.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new STR-6/CLS-2 sentence reads "Each field's default is evaluated by the init of the type that declares it". Door declares `angle` but has no init: by CON-1 its init is Script's, and Script's init does not declare `angle`. CLS-10's kept sentence ("evaluates Door's field defaults and then runs Script.init(entity)") says otherwise, so the changed text contradicts a rule it keeps.
holes.fix_hint: Write: "by the init that builds the part of the object declaring it: the type's own init, the init made from its fields, or, for a derived class with no init, just before its base's init runs ([CLS-10])".

holes.program:
# net/packet.em
pub struct Packet:
    pub kind: u8
    pub(package) seq: u32
    flags: u8 = 0

# app/main.em
from net.packet import Packet

fn main():
    p = Packet(kind=1, seq=7)
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-4 says E1052 names "the field that narrows it and that field's visibility". Here two fields narrow it (`seq` to the package, `flags` to its module). A message naming one sends the programmer to fix `seq`, recompile and meet `flags`. Verdict 134 says a diagnostic that stands for several places names all of them.
holes.fix_hint: E1052 for the made init names every field that narrows it, each with its visibility and line.

holes.program:
struct Histogram:
    total: int = 0
    buckets: Array[int] = [0, 0, 0, 0]

    fn init(samples: Span[int]):
        for s in samples:
            this.total += s              # unset only on the first round: a flag test every round
            this.buckets[s % 4] += 1
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-3 places a default "just before the first line of init that needs the field while the field is unset". When that line is in a loop the field enters unset, the field is unset on the first round only, so the compiler emits OWN-3's flag and a test on every round, here two per sample. C writes the two stores before the loop. The optimiser can hoist only when the default has no effect to order, and the cost section counts "one test where the paths join", not one per iteration.
holes.fix_hint: A need inside a loop that the field enters unset on every path counts as a need at the loop's entry, decided from init's lines. The flag stays only for fields set on some paths before the loop.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-2 closes the list of builders: "The builders are a type's init, and the following ..." (derives, zero-fill, migration). A by-value C result, a C out-parameter, `ffi.adopt` (P08), a read through a raw pointer and `mem.zeroed` also make values of Ember types. The rule says nothing of them, so "a value is built by one builder" is untrue as stated. That is the closed-list shape P14's principle warns against.
holes.fix_hint: One sentence in place of the list's closure: every other source of a value (C, `ffi.adopt`, raw reads, `mem.zeroed`) gives every field a value itself, and no default and no init runs. What it gives is vouched where `unsafe` is written (P04, P08).

holes.program:
struct Rgb:
    r: u8
    g: u8
    b: u8

    fn init(hex: StrView):
        this.r = parse_byte(hex[0..2])
        this.g = parse_byte(hex[2..4])
        this.b = parse_byte(hex[4..6])

    static fn black() -> Rgb:
        return Self(r=0, g=0, b=0)        # refused: the one init takes `hex`
holes.what_goes_wrong: Under CON-1, a type that writes an init whose parameters are not its fields can never be built from its fields, not even inside its own body. `black()` must write `Self("000000")` and parse at run time, a cost C does not pay. Otherwise the author must restructure the type. The one-init rule is a deliberate choice, but the program meets a refusal whose message today would only say the arguments are wrong.
holes.fix_hint: Keep one init, and have the refused call's help give the idiom: "keep `Rgb`'s init made from its fields and move the parsing into `static fn parse(hex: StrView) -> Rgb`" (wording is the lead's).

holes.program:
struct Enemy:
    hp: int = 100
    pos: Vec2

fn main():
    e = Enemy(Vec2(1.0, 2.0))          # `hp` or `pos`?
holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1 restates STR-1: "positional or named arguments in field order, where a field with a default may be omitted". With a defaulted field before a required one (common in game structs), a positional call either fills `hp` (and is then missing `pos`) or skips `hp`. Neither rule says which, and FN rules state no order for defaulted parameters either. Under the J3-05 fix, base fields with defaults come before derived ones, so this case grows.
holes.fix_hint: Positional arguments fill fields in order and never skip one. A field after an omitted defaulted one is given by name, so the call above is refused with `Enemy(pos=Vec2(1.0, 2.0))` as its help.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CON-1 makes the made init one function, and CON-3 gives a construction "the effects of its init and of the defaults it may make". Read as the function's effects, `Frame(pixels=storage)` carries the omitted-or-not default's Alloc, and the @noalloc function is refused (E4001). The same effect would reach EFF-24's change facts for a default like `id = next_id()`. Read per call, it compiles. The design's compiler steps lean to per call, but the spec text does not say it, and P14's principle (an effect is carried by exactly the operations that do it) needs it said.
holes.fix_hint: Write in CON-3: "a call of the init made from fields has the effects of the defaults of the fields that call omits".

engineering.notes:
The rule holds up as a whole. CON-1 to CON-4 add no word, the spec's examples read the same, CON-1, CON-2 and CON-4 cost nothing at run time, and CON-3 removes the 4 KB waste for every field init sets before a method call. It agrees with verdicts 159, 74, 85 and 97 for the made init, and it keeps E2100, E2101, E2102, CLS-11, HR-14, FFI-26 and ARN-11.

Six medium holes make it broken:
1. A method call in init forces every default. A default that is then replaced is built and freed, and `next_id()` runs and its number is lost. That contradicts CON-3's own Ticket sentence, and E2100 answers the same call by reading the method's body (owner row 7, verdicts 86 and 137).
2. Derives (Default, Deserialize) silently bypass a written init, so `mem.take` or `json.from_str` give values the init never makes, against SER-2's "never invalid".
3. Derives over a C++ base have no defined field-by-field build.
4. CON-1's "Its arguments take ... none" is unscoped. As written it decides P06's open J1-07 (its option c) and C++ constructor arguments.
5. A derived class over a made base still writes a pass-through init (J3-05's own Button). C++17 aggregates and Python dataclasses avoid that.
6. `fn init` in an `extend` block (IFC-1) is undecided, and the one-init guarantee rests on it.

The lows are wording or rare corners: private defaulted fields narrowing the made init although Default gives the same value, CON-2's ladder against SER-2's strictness, `using` fields with defaults (P02), CLS-10's Door against the new STR-6/CLS-2 sentence, E1052 naming one field (verdict 134), loop flag tests, the closed builder list (P08), a non-field init blocking Self(fields), positional made-init calls with a defaulted field before a required one, and per-call effects of the made init (P14).

Where a fix changes what programs do (holes 1, 2, 5 and 7), it is the owner's question, not a lead fix. Hole 1's option (a) narrows MOD-9's last sentence, which is lead text in 0.9.15, not a verdict.

design.rule:
A value is built by one builder, which gives each field exactly one value. Every type has one init, written in its own body. A type none of whose chain writes one has the init made from its fields, its bases' fields first. A derived class that writes none, over a chain that does, has its base's init. Every fresh value is built by calling that init: `Name(…)`, `Self(…)`, `super.init(…)`, and every builder the compiler writes (a derived `Default` or `Deserialize`, an export table). Nothing else calls it. Copying a value an init made (`Clone`, `Copy`, a reload's carry by name) copies each part by its own type's rule, and a base part by the base's own `Clone`. Zero-filling skips init only where the type's author vouched for it (`@derive(Zeroable)`).

Each field gets the first of two values: what the builder gives it; else the field's written default. A builder with no line of the program to take an argument from gives that argument the parameter's default, else the written default of the field it names, else its stated fallback (its type's `Default`). With none of these it is refused when compiling. An init never falls back to a type's `Default`.

A default is evaluated only where init's own lines need the field before giving it a value, and then once. It counts there as a call written at that line. A method that init calls never gives a field its first value. Every field that the bodies the call may run use must already hold one. Where those bodies include overrides another package may write, that means every field.

The made init can be called wherever every field it sets may be written.
design.spec_text:
New subsection V.3a, Construction: rules [CON-1] to [CON-5], cited from Parts V, VII, IX, XIV, XVI and Annex B.

It changes:
* [STR-1], [STR-2], [STR-6];
* [CLS-2], [CLS-3], [CLS-10], [CLS-11];
* [FN-4], [IFC-1], [DRP-1] (with `E3070`);
* [DRV-1] (its Default, Clone and Deserialize rows and the sentence after the table), [SER-2], and XIV.2's missing-field sentence (p14 116-117).

It keeps [CLS-4], [MOD-7], [MOD-9], [HR-14], [FFI-26], [FFI-39b] and [ARN-11] as written. They become instances of the rules below.

* `[CON-1]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A type has one init, and only a builder calls it.**
  * A struct's or class's init is the `fn init(…)` written in its own body. `init` and `drop` are each type's own (`[CLS-4]`), so one written in an `extend` block is refused: "`init` is written in `Packet`'s own body; move it to net/packet.em, or build here with a `static fn` that calls `Packet(…)`".
  * A type that writes no init, none of whose bases writes one, has the **init made from its fields**. `Name(…)` takes every field, its bases' fields first, in the order they are laid out (`[CLS-4]`), as positional or named arguments. A field with a default may be omitted. Fields are never overridden, so the names never clash: `Button(id=7, width=120)` for `class Button(Widget):` with `width: int` over `Widget`'s `id: int` and `visible: bool = true`.
  * A derived class that writes no init, over a base whose chain writes one, has its base's init (`[CLS-10]`). Over a C++ base it has the constructor that `[FFI-39b]` selects.
  * The init is called only by a line that builds a fresh value: `Name(…)`; `Self(…)` in the type's `static fn`s; a derived `init`'s one `super.init(…)` (`[CLS-4]`); and the builders the compiler writes (`[CON-2]`). Over a base whose init is made, `super.init(id=id)` calls that made init.
  * Any other use of `init` is refused, as `x.drop()` is (`E3070`). That covers `this.init(…)`, `x.init(…)`, and `init` taken as a function value: "`init` builds a new `Log`; it does not run again on one that exists. To start again, build a new one: `log = Log()`, or write a method that sets the fields: `fn restart():`".
  * The made init's arguments take the words `[FN-2a]` gives a constructor's arguments: none, working as `=` does (verdict 159), and `owns` on the line that makes a value for an `owns` field (`[OWN-10]`). The words at a call of a written init or of a C++ constructor are `[FN-2a]`'s to decide (P06, J1-07); this rule does not decide them.

* `[CON-2]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Each field gets one value, and every fresh value passes through the init.**
  * **One value per field.** A field of a fresh value gets the first of two values:
    1. the value its builder gives it;
    2. its written default.

    An init has no third step. A field without a default that `init` leaves unset is `E2100`. An omitted argument for such a field in the made init is a missing argument. So a forgotten field is never filled in silently.
  * **Every builder of a fresh value calls the type's one init.** Besides the lines the program writes, the compiler writes the following builders, as ordinary Ember in the type's own module, which `ember inspect --expand` prints:
    * a derived `Default`: `Self(…)`;
    * a derived `Deserialize`: the fields are read from the data, then `Self(…)` is called, with each parameter given the field of its name. Each parameter names a field of the type, and each field the derive reads from the data is a parameter. The fields it reads are every field not marked `@ser(skip)`, its bases' fields included. The made init's parameters are its fields, so this always holds for it. Otherwise the derive is `E2080`, naming the parameter or the field:
      * "`Volume.init` takes `scale`, which is no field of `Volume`, so reading a `Volume` back has no value for it: write `static fn deserialize` yourself, building with `Volume(…)`";
      * "`gain` is written to the data, but `Volume.init` does not take it, so reading it back would lose it: mark it `@ser(skip)`, or give `init` a `gain` parameter";
    * an `@export_table` constant (`[FFI-26]`): `Name(…)`.
  * **Arguments such a builder has no value for.** These are every argument of a derived `Default`, and, for a derived `Deserialize`, a parameter whose field is `@ser(skip)`, or is `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=N)` and is missing from the data. Each takes the first of:
    1. the parameter's own default (the argument is left out);
    2. the written default of the field the parameter names;
    3. the builder's stated fallback: its type's `Default` for a derive, and the module's function of that name for an export table.

    For the made init, the first two are the same thing: the field's written default. An argument with none of the three is `E2080` at the derive, naming it: "`captain` is skipped, so reading a `Crew` back needs a value for it: give it a default, or remove `@ser(skip)`".
  * **The generated call is checked as the call it is.** If the init is not visible in the type's module, or does not accept the arguments, the derive is `E2080`, naming the field that narrows the init or the parameter.
  * So init's own checks run for every fresh value. `json.from_str[Volume]` over `{"level": 5000}` stops at init's `assert`, as `Volume(5000)` does. `mem.take` of a `Pacer` field leaves what `Pacer()` makes. `Dialog.default()` for `class Dialog(Window):` runs `Window.init()`.
  * **Copying builds no fresh value, and runs no init.**
    * A derived `Clone` or `Copy` copies a value an init made, each field as `[STR-5]` says. A class's base part is copied by the base's own derived `Clone`. So a derive over a base that is not `Clone`, or whose `clone` is written by hand (it makes a whole object, not the part), is `E2080` naming the base: "`Dialog`'s `Window` part cannot be copied: `Window` (ui/window.em line 10) is not `Clone`".
    * A reload carries a live value to its new layout by name (`[HR-14]`). An added field takes its written default, else its type's `Default`; with neither, the reload is refused in plan.
    * Zero-filling (`alloc_zeroed`, `mem.zeroed`) skips init only for a type whose author declared `@derive(Zeroable)`. That is the `unsafe` marker by which the author vouches that all-zero bytes are a valid value (`[ARN-11]`), so no default runs.
  * `migrate_from` builds through `Self(…)`.

* `[CON-3]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **A default runs only where it is the value.** A field's default is evaluated only in a construction that gives the field no other value, and then once. It runs just before the first line of `init` that needs the field while the field is unset. Which lines need a field follows from init's own lines, never from another function's body (`[MOD-9]`):
  * a read or change of the field, or of any part of it. Giving the whole field a value is not a need. Nor is `this = v` in a struct's `init` (`[FN-4]`): it gives every field a value, a first store for each field not yet set and a replace for each one that is set, ending its old value first (`[OWN-5]`);
  * a call that may run a method of `this`, any other use of `this` as a whole (`[CLS-2]`'s list), and `super.init(…)`: these need every field the type itself declares;
  * a `return`, or the end of `init`: these need every field.

  Where several defaults are needed at one line, they are made in field order. A field that `init` sets on every path before any need never evaluates its default. A field it sets on some paths evaluates the default only on the other paths, tracked by `[OWN-3]`'s hidden flag. The made init evaluates the omitted fields' defaults after its arguments, in field order. A panic before a need makes no default.

  **A default made at a line counts as a call written at that line**, for every rule that looks at calls, as `[EFF-1]` counts a call's default arguments and `[DRP-8]` counts a drop:
  * effects and contracts (`Alloc`, `@noalloc`, Part X);
  * summaries (`[EFF-24]`);
  * a walk (`E3020`);
  * a held lock (`E7018`);
  * a task's use (`[THR-11]`);
  * a view.

  A refusal it causes names both lines: "line 14 reads `name`, so its default `next_name()` (line 8) is made there, and `next_name` adds to `NAMES` (its line 4), which this loop walks (line 12); give `name` its value above line 12: `this.name = next_name()`".

  Examples:
  * With `buf: Array[u8] = Array.with_capacity(4096)` and an `init` whose first line is `this.buf = Array.with_capacity(size)`, no 4 KB list is ever made.
  * With `id: int = next_id()`, `next_id()` runs only in a construction whose `init` needs `id` before giving it a value. A line `this.assets = this.load_assets()` above `this.id = given` is such a need, since a method of `this` may read any field. Write `this.id = given` above it, and `next_id()` never runs.

* `[CON-4]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **Who may build it.**
  * A written init is visible as its own mark says (`[MOD-2]`; std writes `pub fn init()`).
  * The init made from fields sets every field, its bases' fields included, so it is visible where every one of those fields may be written:
    * `pub` when every field is `pub`;
    * `pub(package)` when every field is `pub` or `pub(package)`;
    * otherwise only in its module. That is the case for a private field, and for a `pub(read)` or `pub(package, read)` field, which only its module writes (`[MOD-7]`).
  * A type with no fields is built wherever it is visible. A derived class's inherited init is visible as its base's is.
  * A call where the init is not visible is `E1052`, naming the field that narrows it and that field's visibility.
  * A derive is written on its type's own declaration and builds through the init in that type's module. So a derived `Deserialize` lets whoever has the data build the type. That is the author's request, and init's checks still run.

* `[CON-5]` *(new in 0.9.16)* **What a call in init needs.**
  * Before a call in `init` that may run a method body on `this`, every field that body uses MUST hold a value. A field is used when the body reads it, changes it, or gives it a value (giving a value ends the old one, `[OWN-5]`). The fields are worked out from the body and from what it calls (`[EFF-24]`).
  * Only init's own lines give a field its first value; a method that `init` calls never does. A field with a default holds a value at such a call (`[CON-3]`). A field without one is `E2100`: "`init` calls `reset()` (line 7), which gives `inbox` a value (its line 11), ending the one it holds, and `inbox` is set only on line 8; give it its value first: write `this.inbox = []` above line 7".
  * The bodies that a call of a `virtual` or `abstract` method may run are its overrides.
    * For a method that only its own package may override, these are the overrides the program has (`[DSP-5]`).
    * For a method that another package may override (some `pub` class that is `open` or `abstract` has it), they include bodies that cannot be read when this package is compiled. So the call needs every field set, just as no promise to another package rests on code the compiler cannot read (`[MOD-9]`, `[IFC-6]`): "`Widget` is `pub open`, so another package may replace `layout`, and its version may read any field; `name` is set only on line 7: set every field first: move line 6 below line 7".
  * The same holds for inherited fields before `super.init(…)` (`E2102`, `[CLS-11]`).
  * So when any method runs during construction, even a virtual method called from a base `init`, every field it uses holds a value.

Changed texts:
* `[STR-1]`: "It is `pub` iff every field is `pub`" becomes "It is visible as `[CON-4]` says". "A declared `fn init(…)` replaces it" gains "(`[CON-1]`)".
* `[STR-2]`: "it is evaluated at each construction that omits the field, in field order" becomes "it is evaluated only in a construction that gives the field no other value, where `[CON-3]` says".
* `[STR-6]` and `[CLS-2]`:
  * "Before any `init` body runs, every field default of the class and of its bases is evaluated and stored. Every field without a default MUST then be set…" becomes "Each field's default is evaluated by the init of the type that declares it, where `[CON-3]` says. Every field without a default MUST be set…".
  * In `[CLS-2]`, "once every field that method's body reads is set" becomes "once every field the bodies it may run use is set (`[CON-5]`): a field they read, change or give a value". The examples stay.
* `[CLS-3]` becomes: "A class whose chain writes no `init` has the init made from its fields, its bases' first (`[CON-1]`); a derived class's `super.init(…)` over it calls it."
* `[CLS-10]` becomes: "A derived class with no `init`, over a base whose chain writes one, gets its base's init. `Door(entity)` makes `Door`'s field defaults, then runs `Script.init(entity)`, as an `init` whose one line is `super.init(entity)` would (`[CON-3]`). Such a class with a field that has no default MUST declare an `init` (`E2101`). Over a base whose chain writes none, it has the init made from every field (`[CON-1]`)."
* `[CLS-11]`: its last sentence becomes "So when any method runs, even a `virtual` method called from a base `init`, every field it uses holds a value (`[CON-5]`)."
* `[FN-4]`: "A struct's method may give `this` a whole new value" gains "(in `init`, `[CON-3]` says what that sets)".
* `[IFC-1]` gains: "it adds methods, never `init` or `drop` (`[CON-1]`)".
* `[DRP-1]`: "Calling it explicitly is `E3070`" becomes "Calling it explicitly, or calling `init` other than to build (`[CON-1]`), is `E3070`". The codes table row becomes "`drop`, or `init` outside a line that builds, cannot be called explicitly".

For a type whose init is made from its fields, that is each field's declared default, else its type's `Default`, as before. For an enum, it is the variant marked `@default`, each payload field taking its type's `Default`."

  * `Serialize`, `Deserialize`: "§XIV.4; `Deserialize` builds through the init (`[CON-2]`)".
  * The sentence after the table becomes: "A derive that builds a fresh value (`Default`, `Deserialize`) calls the type's one init; `Clone` and `Copy` copy a value an init made (`[CON-2]`)."
* `[SER-2]` becomes: "Deserialising never produces an invalid value. A range-typed field is checked (`[RNG-10a]`). An unknown enum tag is an error. A missing field without `@ser(default)` or `@ser(since=…)` is an error. The value is built by the type's init, so init's checks run (`[CON-2]`)."

answers.answer: [CON-1]: a base with no written init has the init made from its fields, and that is its init for every caller. So `super.init(id=id)` calls it. Its arguments work as any constructor's do (verdict 159: no word), and an omitted field takes its default inside that init ([CON-3]). A derived class that also writes no init gets the init made from every field of the chain, its base's first, so `Button(id=7, width=120)` needs no hand-written init (the round-1 repair of hole 11; C++17 aggregates with bases and Python dataclasses do the same). No new path is added: `Widget(id=7)` and `super.init(id=7)` call the same function.
answers.code:
open class Widget:                      # a UI base class with no `init` of its own
    id: int
    visible: bool = true

class Button(Widget):                   # writes no init either
    width: int

class Slider(Widget):
    max: int

    fn init(id: int, max: int):
        this.max = max if max > 0 else 1   # own field first ([CLS-11])
        super.init(id=id)                  # Widget's init made from its fields; `visible` keeps its default

fn main():
    b = Button(id=7, width=120)         # the init made from Widget's and Button's fields
    s = Slider(8, 0)
    println(b.id, b.visible, b.width)
    println(s.id, s.visible, s.max)
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints `7 true 120`, then `8 true 1`.
* `Button(7, true, 120)`, with positional arguments in field order (base fields first), works too. `Button(7, 120)` is refused: 120 is not a `bool`, so the help names the arguments.
* `super.init(id=id, visible=false)` gives `visible` one value. `super.init()` is refused as a call missing `id`.
* Calling `super.init` twice or not at all is still refused by [CLS-4].

answers.answer:
[CON-3]: a field's default runs only in a construction that gives the field no other value, and then once, just before the first line of `init` that needs the field while it is unset.

Which lines need a field follows from init's own lines:
* a read or change of the field;
* a call of a method of `this`, or another use of `this` as a whole;
* `super.init`;
* a `return` or the end of init.

The same rule holds for structs and classes, so [CLS-2]'s 'every default before the body' goes.
* `data` is set before anything needs it, so its 4 KB default never runs.
* `pos` is read by `println(this.pos)` before `init` sets it, so its 0 is made just before that line.
* A field set on some paths makes its default only on the other paths ([OWN-3]'s hidden flag).
* A default made at a line counts there as a call for every rule: effects, walks, locks, tasks.
* With `id: int = next_id()`, `next_id()` runs only when init needs `id` before giving it a value. A call of a method of `this` above `this.id = given` is such a need, so set `id` first.

This is C++'s initialiser-list behaviour, without an initialiser list.
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints `0` twice.
* `Buffer(64)` allocates once, 64 bytes, and nothing is freed unused.
* `Ticket(5)` calls no `next_id()`, and `Ticket(-1)` calls it once, so no id number is skipped.
* Under `@noalloc`, the `Buffer` init above is still refused, because `Array.with_capacity(size)` allocates. An init that sets `data` from storage the caller gives, on every path, compiles under `@noalloc`, because the allocating default never runs.
* Had `Ticket.init` called `this.log_created()` above `this.id = given`, `next_id()` would run at that call, since a method of `this` may read `id`.

answers.answer: [CON-4]: the init made from fields sets every field, its bases' fields included, so it is visible wherever every one of those fields may be written. That is the narrowest write visibility among the fields; here, with a `pub` field and a `pub(package)` field, it is `pub(package)`. This is [MOD-7]'s own reasoning ('construction is a write') carried through [MOD-2]'s three levels. A `pub(read)` or `pub(package, read)` field still makes the constructor private to its module, as [MOD-7] says.

# net/packet.em
pub struct Packet:                     # a packet the network layer builds
    pub kind: u8
    pub(package) seq: u32              # seen only inside the `net` package

# net/send.em, a module of the same package
from net.packet import Packet

pub fn first() -> Packet:
    return Packet(kind=1, seq=7)       # the made init is pub(package): allowed here

# app/main.em, in a package depending on `net`

fn main():

No builder function is needed inside the package.

design.prior_art:
**C++**
* A default member initialiser is used only when the constructor's mem-initialiser list does not name the member. An assignment in the body pays twice.
* `T{}` value-initialisation runs the default constructor.
* An aggregate may have no private members; C++17 aggregates may have bases (`Button{{7}, 120}`).
* A derived class's implicit copy constructor calls the base's copy constructor, and is deleted if that one is deleted or inaccessible.
* A virtual call made during a base constructor runs the base's own version, never the override: safe, but surprising.
* A constructor is never called on a live object outside placement new.

**Swift**
* A memberwise init has the minimum access level of the stored properties.
* Writing an init in the type's body removes the memberwise init; one written in an extension keeps it.
* Two-phase init: an initializer cannot call an instance method, read a property, or use `self` as a value until every stored property of its class has a value. That is [CON-5]'s rule for a `pub open` class, which Swift applies to every class.
* `self.init` may be called only inside another initializer.
* Codable: a property left out of `CodingKeys` must have a default value.

**Java, C#, Kotlin**
* A constructor's virtual call reaches the override. Java's override sees zeroed fields: no undefined behaviour, but a wrong value. Kotlin warns 'calling non-final function in constructor'.
* kotlinx.serialization builds through the constructor and runs its `init` blocks, so a deserialised object passes the class's checks. That is [CON-2]'s Deserialize.
* System.Text.Json deserialises through a parameterised constructor, matching parameters to properties by name. That is [CON-2]'s parameter-to-field rule.
* Jackson does the same with `@JsonCreator`.

**Rust**
* A struct literal needs every field visible at the use (E0451).
* `#[derive(Default)]` builds each field from its own `Default` and bypasses `new()`.
* serde builds field by field and bypasses validation unless `#[serde(try_from = …)]` routes it through a checked constructor; `#[serde(skip)]` takes `Default` or `default = "path"`.

**Python**
* Dataclass inheritance puts the base's fields first in the generated `__init__`, and `default_factory` runs only when the argument is omitted.
* `pickle` bypasses `__init__`, a known source of objects their class never made.
* `self.__init__()` re-runs a constructor on a live object.

**Ada, Zig, Go**
* Ada evaluates a component default only for components an aggregate leaves out.
* Zig fills only omitted fields, and `std.json` uses the field's default.
* Go fills forgotten fields silently with zero values.

**Where they fall short of safe, as fast as C, and readable**
* C++ needs a second syntax to avoid paying twice.
* Swift, Java, C#, Kotlin and Rust's `..Default::default()` always pay for the default.
* Rust, serde and pickle let a derive build what the type's own constructor refuses.
* Java and C# reach an override before the base is set up.
* Go fills fields silently.

**What Ember takes**
* C++'s 'a default only where the constructor gives none', with no list to write.
* Swift's and Rust's narrowest-field visibility.
* Swift's two-phase rule, only where the override cannot be read.
* Kotlin's and System.Text.Json's 'deserialising runs the constructor', matched by name.
* C++'s derived copy delegating to the base's.
* Python dataclasses' base-first made init.
* Swift Codable's 'a skipped field needs a value', with serde's `Default` fallback after the field's own default.
design.cost:
**[CON-1]**
* Zero. `Name(…)`, `Self(…)` and `super.init(…)` are direct calls of one known function, inlined like C's struct initialisation. Nothing is stored in the object.
* The refusals (`E3070`, an init in `extend`) are compile time only.

**[CON-2]**
* For a type whose init is made from its fields, a derived `Default` or `Deserialize` emits the same stores as today's field-by-field build.
* For a type with a written init, it costs that init's own work: one direct call, inlined. That is exactly what the author made every value of the type pay, as C++'s `T{}` and kotlinx.serialization pay.
* `Deserialize` reads each field into a stack local, in the data's order, then passes them to the init. After inlining, those are the same moves as storing the fields. No heap is used. Matching parameters to fields happens when compiling.
* Clone, Copy, zero-fill and reload carry cost what they cost today.

**[CON-3]**
* Zero at run time when `init` sets a field on every path, or on none; this is decided when compiling.
* Against today's class rule, it saves one full evaluation of the default plus its drop for every field `init` sets before any need. In J3-06 that is one 4,096-byte allocation and one free per `Buffer(64)`.
* Where `init` sets a defaulted field on some paths only, the cost is one bit (OWN-3's hidden flag) in a register or stack slot while `init` runs, plus one test where the paths join: the branch a C programmer writes as the `else`. The object gains zero bytes.
* Where a method call of `this` comes before the line that sets a defaulted field, the default is made at the call and then replaced. That is what C++, Swift and Java pay for every defaulted field. A default whose only effect is its allocation is then an allocation and free pair that the optimiser may remove (LLVM removes unused malloc/free pairs), while `@noalloc` still counts it.
* Counting a placed default as a call costs compile time only.

**[CON-4], [CON-5]**: compile time only. CON-5 reads the summaries E2100 already reads.

**Memory**: no word, flag or header byte is added to any value; the flags live only while `init` runs.

readability.note:
No new word, attribute or line appears in any program.
* `Conn`, the overview's `Emitter`, Part V's `Script`/`Door` and every `@derive(Default)` struct read exactly as before. They do less work, or the same.
* The UI hierarchy drops two inits, eleven lines, that existed only to pass fields through.
* J3-18 drops the `pub(package) static fn new` builder that the two-case rule forced.
* J3-06 and J6-15 are unchanged in text and now have one meaning.

The changes a reader of the rules meets:
* A class's default runs where `init` first needs the field, not before its first line.
* `@derive(Default)` and `Deserialize` run the type's own `init`, so a value read back passes the same checks as one built by hand.
* `this.init()` is refused, with the line to write instead.
* A `pub open` class sets its fields before it calls a method a subclass may replace.

For pure defaults (`0`, `[]`, `true`, `Vec3.ZERO`, every default in the spec's examples), nothing observable changes. Each refusal names the line to move or write. Where a default runs is read from init's own lines, never from another body, so MOD-9's 'a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does' holds.

design.compiler_does:
1. **Finding the init.**
   * For each struct and class, the compiler takes the `fn init` written in its body. An `init` or `drop` in an `extend` block is refused.
   * Otherwise, when no class in its chain writes one, it takes the init made from every field, the bases' fields first.
   * Otherwise it takes the base's init ([CLS-10]); over a C++ base, the constructor [FFI-39b] selects.
   * `Name(…)`, `Self(…)`, `super.init(…)` and the derive builders resolve to that function and are checked as the calls they are.
   * Any other naming of `init` (`x.init(…)`, `this.init(…)`, a function value) is refused by the check that refuses `x.drop()` (`E3070`).

2. **Placing defaults.** The definite-assignment pass that init already gets for E2100 and E2102 also places defaults.
   * At each need point named in [CON-3], it inserts the evaluation of each still-unset default, in field order. The need points are: a read or change of the field; a call that may run a method of `this`, another use of `this` as a whole, or `super.init(…)`, which need the type's own fields; and a `return` or the end, which need all fields.
   * In a struct's init, `this = v` is a store of every field: a first store, or a replace, by the flags.
   * Where a field is set on some paths, OWN-3's hidden flag decides at the need whether to make the default, and at a later store whether the old value is ended first.
   * A default not yet made at a panic is never made.
   * The made init evaluates the omitted fields' defaults after its arguments.
   * Only init's own lines are read for placing defaults.

3. **Calls in init ([CON-5]).**
   * At each call that may run a method body on `this`, every field the summary reads, changes or gives a value must be set. A method's store never counts as a first store.
   * For a virtual or abstract method that another package may override (some `pub` `open` or `abstract` class has it), every field must be set.
   * Before `super.init(…)` the same holds for inherited fields.
   * The messages are E2100 or E2102, naming the method's line and the line to move.

4. **Defaults as calls.** Each inserted default evaluation is a call at its need line for effects and contracts, summaries, walks, locks, tasks and views. Each message about it names the default's line and the need line.

5. **Visibility.** The made init's visibility is the narrowest write visibility of its fields, its bases' included. [MOD-7]'s read-only fields count as module-private. `E1052` names the field that narrows it.

6. **Derives.**
   * `Default` emits `Self(…)`, each argument from the ladder: the parameter's default, else the written default of the field it names, else its type's `Default`.
   * `Deserialize` reads each field into a stack local, then emits `Self(…)`. It checks that each parameter names a field and that each field it reads is a parameter.
   * `@export_table` emits `Name(…)` with the module's functions.
   * Each generated call is type-checked as written; `E2080` names what fails.
   * `Clone` and `Copy` copy field by field per [STR-5], a class's base part through the base's derived `Clone`, else `E2080`.
   * Zeroable and `alloc_zeroed` are unchanged.
   * `ember inspect --expand` prints the `Self(…)` code.

7. **Unchanged checks.** [CLS-11]'s order; `E2101`, now only over a chain with a written init or a C++ base; `E5058`; HR-14's rows; FFI-26's fallback.
design.misuse:
Every mistake is refused when compiling, or, for data read at run time, stops the program at a line with init's own message. Nothing here reads an unset field, frees garbage or races.

* **A forgotten field.** A field without a default that init leaves unset, or reads first, is E2100, with the line to write. An omitted argument for such a field in the made init is a missing argument, never filled with a type's `Default`.
* **A helper that sets a field from init.** A method called in init that reads, changes or gives a value to an unset field is E2100. The message names the method's line and gives the line to write above the call. The idiom that compiles is to return the value: `this.assets = this.load_assets()`.
* **A `pub open` base calling a hook too early.** An init that calls a method another package may override before every field is set is E2100 in the base's own package, with the line to move. A dependant's override never meets an unset field.
* **Calling init on a live object.** `this.init()`, `x.init(…)`, or `init` as a value is E3070, as `x.drop()` is. The help gives `log = Log()` or `fn restart():`.
* **An init in an `extend` block.** It is refused, with the help to move it, or to write a `static fn` there that calls `Name(…)`.
* **A default whose effect clashes where it is made.** A walk, a held lock or a running task at the need line is refused (E3020, E7018, E7007). The message names the default's line and the need line, and gives the line that sets the field earlier.
* **A skipped or always-missing field with no value.** It is E2080 at the `@derive`, naming the field.
* **A derive that cannot go through the init or copy a part.** E2080 names the parameter, the field or the base, and the help says what to write (`static fn deserialize`, `@ser(skip)`, a parameter, or `clone` by hand).
* **Bad data for a validating init.** `json.from_str` stops at init's `assert`, with init's message, as the same call written by hand would. A range-typed field gives a recoverable `SerError` instead ([SER-2]).
* **A constructor called outside its visibility.** It is E1052, naming the field and its visibility.
* **Wrong `super.init(…)` calls.** These are the ordinary call errors. A derived init that calls `super.init` twice or never is still [CLS-4]'s error.
* **Defaults wasted by the program's own order.** A defaulted field set after a method call of `this` is no error: the program says what it does.
design.verdicts:
**Kept and followed**
* **74, 85, 97 (`owns` on the making line for an `owns` field): kept.** `super.init(mesh=owns Mesh(points=[0.0]))` over a made base writes `owns` exactly as `Entity(mesh=owns Mesh(…))` does. The derive-generated `Self(…)` follows the same words.
* **159 (a constructor's argument takes no word, as `=`): kept, scoped to the made init.** [CON-1] states verdict 159 for the init made from fields only. A written init's and a C++ constructor's call words stay [FN-2a]'s and P06's (J1-07), so `Label(caption)` is not decided here (round-1 repair of hole 10).
* **86 and 137 (the compiler works facts out by reading the code): followed.** [CON-5] reads each called method's summary, stores included, to decide whether a call in init compiles, as E2100 does today.
* **PHIL's and MOD-9's 'a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does': kept.** Where a default runs is read from init's lines only. Body facts only refuse or accept a call (E2100), which is what that sentence allows.
* **108 and 113 (a `pub` promise is written or self-contained; only a private generic may leave its needs to the compiler): followed.** An init of a `pub open` class does not rely on override bodies another package will write ([CON-5]), just as a `pub` generic writes its bounds ([IFC-6]).
* **5 and JOB.md's 'the compiler does not silently decide what the programmer did not say': kept.** An init never falls back to a type's `Default`. A derive fills only by its stated ladder, on the programmer's `@derive` or `@ser` request.

**Revisited (lead rules, not owner verdicts), each of which changes what programs do**
* CLS-2's 'every default before any init body' (Parts V and VIII; Annex H shows no JOB.md verdict).
* XIV.2's 'its type's Default' for `@ser(default)` and `@ser(since=N)` (ODR-159, ruled under the delegation).
* DRV-1's Default row and the field-by-field Deserialize, for types that write an init: they now go through the init.
* CLS-3, CLS-10 and E2101: the made init now covers a chain with no written init.
* CLS-11's sentence 'every field of the object holds a value', which was not true.
* A new refusal: a `pub open` init that calls an overridable method before every field is set.

All of these go to the owner as part of this ODR, said plainly. The evidence:
* one rule with no class/struct split;
* no wasted 4 KB allocation;
* a validating init that loading data cannot bypass;
* no derive writing another package's private field;
* the same ladder HR-14 already uses for a reload.

options_for_owner.summary:
The rule.
* One init per type, which every builder calls, the derived `Default` and `Deserialize` included; `this.init()` is refused.
* A default runs only where init's own lines first need the field, and counts as a call there.
* A call in init needs the fields its method uses; for a method another package may override, every field.
* The made constructor covers a chain with no written init, and is as visible as its narrowest field.
* A skipped field takes its default, else its type's `Default`.
