recommendation.reason:
One rule settles the four questions and every way a value is built, with no exception by type or construct: written and made inits, derived classes, derives, data, reload, export tables, zero-fill and enums.

It costs nothing over C, is cheaper than today's class rule, and adds no word. It also closes the holes the review found:
* a derive or a load cannot build what the init refuses;
* init cannot re-run on a live object;
* a placed default is checked where it runs;
* a helper's store cannot end garbage;
* an override never meets an unset field.

Against the other options:
* B and C pay twice for a default.
* D makes the author write `default` and `deserialize` by hand for every type with an init.
* E accepts the trap and refuses the ordinary dependant, where nobody can fix it.
* F lets a far edit change when an effect runs.
* G and H bring the pass-through inits back.
* I and J add a second rule or a builder function.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: a default member initialiser runs only when the constructor doesn't set the member, `T{}` runs the constructor, and a constructor is never called on a live object. Ember has no initialiser list, so it must say five things: when a field's `= default` runs; what `super.init` calls when the base wrote no `init`; who may call the made constructor; whether `@derive(Default)` and `Deserialize` run your `init`; and what a `@ser(skip)` field holds after loading.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `box = TextBox(7, 64)` calls `TextBox.init` | nothing built yet |
| 2 | main | today ([CLS-2]): `buf`'s default `Array.with_capacity(4096)` runs before the body | a 4,096-byte list is allocated |
| 3 | main | `this.buf = Array.with_capacity(size)` | 64 bytes allocated; the 4,096-byte list is freed, never used |
| 4 | main | `super.init(id=id)`, but `Widget` wrote no `init` | the spec does not say what this calls |
| 5 | main | today: `json.from_str[Volume]("{\"level\": 5000}")` | a `Volume` with `level` 5000, built field by field; `Volume.init`'s assert never runs |
| 2' | main | under the rule: `buf` is set before anything needs it | its default never runs: no 4 KB list |
| 4' | main | under the rule: `super.init(id=id)` calls `Widget`'s constructor made from its fields | `id` 7, `visible` true (its default) |
| 5' | main | under the rule: the derived `Deserialize` reads `level`, then calls `Volume(level=5000)` | init's assert stops the program at the load, as `Volume(5000)` would |
owner_short.options:
* A (recommended): one init per type, which every builder calls, derives included; a default runs only where nothing else gave the field a value; the made constructor needs no pass-through inits and is as visible as its narrowest field; a skipped field takes its default, else its type's Default.
* B: as A, but every default still runs before `init`, so the 4 KB list is made and thrown away.
* C: as A, but only fields always set first skip their default.
* D: as A, but a type that writes `init` cannot derive `Default` or `Deserialize`.
* E: as A, but a `pub open` base may call an overridable method early, and each override elsewhere is checked against it.
* F: as A, but where a default runs follows the bodies of the methods `init` calls.
* G: as A, but a derived class with its own fields writes an `init`.
* H: as A, but a base with a field that has no default must write `init`.
* I: as A, but a `@ser(skip)` field must write its default.
* J: as A, but `pub(package)` fields need a hand-written builder.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. A base init calls a virtual method before setting a field, and an override in another package reads that field (`Widget.init` calls `layout()` before `name`; `Label.layout` reads `name`). CLS-11's and the design's 'no unset field is read' were false.

Safety, high. `@derive(Default)` (and `Deserialize`, `Clone`) on `class Dialog(Window)` in another package builds `Window`'s private `handle` field by field and skips `Window.init`, so `Window`'s drop destroys handle 0.
repairs.answer:
[CON-2]: every builder of a fresh value calls the type's one init. `Dialog.default()` is `Dialog()`, which runs `Window.init()` ([CLS-10]), so `handle` comes from `win_create()`.
* A derived `Clone` copies a class's base part only through the base's own derived `Clone`. `Window` is not `Clone`, so `@derive(Clone)` on `Dialog` is E2080 naming `Window`.
* `@derive(Deserialize)` on `Dialog` is E2080: `title` is read from the data, but `Dialog`'s init does not take it.

No derive writes a field its module may not write.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium. A derived `Deserialize` skips a validating init: `Volume` with level 5000 makes `gain()` read past `CURVE` under its `# SAFETY` note, against SER-2.
repairs.answer:
[CON-2]: `Deserialize` reads the fields, then calls `Self(…)`, each parameter taking the field of its name. So `Volume.init`'s assert stops the program at the load, as `Volume(5000)` does. SER-2 now says the value passes the init.

Where init's parameters are not the fields it reads, the derive is E2080, with the help to write `static fn deserialize`. A recoverable check is a range-typed field ([RNG-10a]).

`Default` likewise calls `Self(…)`, so an init that acquires what its drop releases always runs.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. `this.init()` or `x.init(…)` re-runs init on a live object: it leaks the old list, replaces a live `Lock`, writes a guarded field without its lock while a task holds it, and gives a `let` field a second value.
repairs.answer: [CON-1]: only a line that builds a fresh value calls init: `Name(…)`, `Self(…)`, the one `super.init(…)` in a derived init, and the compiler's builders. Every other use (`this.init(…)`, `x.init(…)`, `init` as a function value) is refused, as `x.drop()` is (E3070, DRP-1 widened). The help: `log = Log()`, or a method that sets the fields, `fn restart():`.

repairs.hole: Safety, high. A default placed at its need line runs inside a walk of `NAMES` (or a held lock, or a scope with tasks) without the walk, lock or task rules counting it.
repairs.answer:
[CON-3]: a default made at a line counts as a call written at that line for every rule that looks at calls (effects and contracts, summaries, walks, locks, tasks, views), as EFF-1 counts a call's default arguments and DRP-8 a drop. The `NAMES` program is E3020, naming both lines, with the help `this.name = next_name()` above the loop, which compiles.

That program compiled under the old class rule, because its default ran before the walk. The change is part of the class-default question the owner is asked, and it is stated in open risk 2.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium. `reset()`, called from init, stores `this.inbox = []`, which ends an `inbox` that was never set.
repairs.answer: [CON-5]: a call in init needs every field its body uses: each field it reads, changes or gives a value, since giving a value ends the old one (OWN-5). This is worked out from the summary E2100 already reads. Only init's own lines give a field its first value. `this.reset()` is E2100, naming reset's line 11, with the help `this.inbox = []` above line 7.

repairs.hole: Safety, medium. `this = v` in a struct's init is decided neither as a need nor as a store.
repairs.answer:
[CON-3]: in a struct's init, `this = v` gives every field a value. Each field not yet set gets its first store, and each set field is replaced, its old value ended first, by the same flags. It is not a need, so no default runs.

It is not refused: FN-4 allows `this = v` in every struct method, and refusing it in init would be an exception for one method. `this = Self(…)` or a derived builder of the same type inside its own init calls init again, which is ordinary recursion (FN-7); open risk 9 states it.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium. A method call of `this` needs every field, so a default that init sets after the call is made and thrown away (`{}` and `next_id()` in `Level`), and CON-3's promise about `next_id()` was false.
repairs.answer:
The promise was false as worded, and it is reworded in [CON-3]: `next_id()` runs only in a construction whose init needs `id` before giving it a value. A method call of `this` above `this.id = given` is such a need; write `this.id = given` above it and `next_id()` never runs. J3-06's answer says the same.

Placement stays decided from init's own lines:
* PHIL, MOD-9, EFF-25 and BLD-14 each say that a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does. Body placement would let a far edit of `load_assets` start or stop `next_id()`.
* It is never worse than C++, Swift or Java, which always pay.
* A default whose only effect is its allocation, replaced unread, is an allocation and free pair the optimiser may remove, while `@noalloc` still counts it.

E2100 uses body facts only to accept or refuse a call, which those rules allow. Body placement is owner option F, with this evidence.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium. `Pacer.default()` gives `step` 0, which no line of `Pacer` makes; Deserialize over a validating init; derives over a C++ base are undefined.
repairs.answer:
[CON-2]: a derived `Default` is `Self(…)`, so `Pacer.default()` is `Pacer()`, with `step` 1.

Over a C++ base, a derive's `Self(…)` runs the class's own init, whose `super.init(…)` runs the C++ constructor (FFI-39b). `Badge.default()` is `Badge(label="")`: `label`'s parameter has no default, so it takes the field's written default `""`, and init then calls `Widget(0)`. `Deserialize` reads `label` and calls the same init.

A `Clone` over a C++ base copies the base part only by the base's `Clone`. Whether a C++ class with a copy constructor is `Clone` is P07's question; until then the derive is E2080 naming the base.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium. CON-1's sentence on call words covered every init, written ones and C++ constructors included, and so decided P06's J1-07 as option (c).
repairs.answer: [CON-1] now states verdict 159's words for the init made from fields only. The words at a call of a written init or a C++ constructor are left to FN-2a (P06, J1-07), so `Label(caption)` is not decided here, and nothing in this design depends on J1-07's answer.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium. Only a type with no base had an init made from its fields, so every derived class with a field that has no default needed a pass-through init (`Button(Widget)`).
repairs.answer:
[CON-1]: a type none of whose chain writes an init has the init made from every field, its bases' fields first, in layout order. A defaulted field may be omitted, and named arguments are always allowed. Fields are never overridden (CLS-4), so the names never clash. `Button(id=7, width=120)` needs no init.

A chain with a written init, or a C++ base, keeps CLS-10 and E2101, because that init must run and its parameters are not fields. Visibility counts the bases' fields ([CON-4]). This closes round 0's open risk 5; owner option G keeps the old limit.

repairs.hole: Engineering, medium. A `fn init` written in an `extend` block in another module of the package was undecided: either it silently replaces what `Packet(…)` calls, or the type has two inits.
repairs.answer: [CON-1]: an init is written only in the type's own body. One in an `extend` block is refused, with the help to move it there, or to write a `static fn` in the `extend` block that builds with `Packet(…)` (Ember's spelling of Swift's extension inits). `drop` follows the same rule, because CLS-4 names `init` and `drop` together as each type's own (one rule for both, checklist 16).

design.open_risks:
1. **Bad data stops the program.** A derived `Deserialize` runs init, so an `assert` in init stops the program when the data breaks it, with init's message, never a silent wrong value. A recoverable check needs a range-typed field ([SER-2] gives a `SerError`) or a written `deserialize`. The owner may want init's failure turned into a `SerError`, but that needs a fallible init, which the language does not have.

2. **Default order for classes changes.** A default now runs at init's first need, often its end, instead of before its first line. A default whose effect clashes with a walk, lock or task at its need line is now refused (E3020, E7018, E7007), with a line that compiles. No spec or std example depends on the old order (checked: Emitter, Script/Door, CLS-2's load_assets example, std/src/collections.em and ecs.em's inits). A test that logs from a default would change.

3. **Load results change.** A written default now wins over the type's `Default` for `@ser(default)` and `@ser(since=N)` (ODR-159 was delegated), so `hp: int = 100` loads as 100, not 0.

4. **Absence stays strict.** A field with a written default but no `@ser(default)`, `@ser(since)` or `@ser(skip)` that is missing from the data is still an error, as in serde and Swift Codable. Zig's `std.json` lets a written default permit absence; the owner may prefer that.

5. **Making a class `pub open` can refuse its init.** An init that calls an overridable method before setting every field, which compiled while the class was private, becomes E2100, as making a generic `pub` makes it write its bounds. Owner option E accepts such bases instead.

6. **Derived `Default` fills an init parameter silently.** A parameter of a written init that has no default and names no field takes its type's `Default` in a derived `Default`. If init asserts against that value, `T.default()` stops the program. The stricter alternative is E2080 there, asking for a parameter default.

7. **Other derives that read a base part.** Serialize, Debug and other derives that read a base part declared in another module may need to delegate to the base's own implementation, as `Clone` now does. That is not asked here.

8. **Class objects and `Default`.** TYP's interface table gives class objects no `Default` ("—"). Whether `@derive(Default)` applies to a class is that table's question; the rule holds either way.

9. **`this = v` in a struct init can recurse.** Where `v` is built by a builder of the same type (`Self(…)`, the derived `T.default()`), init is called again, and does so unconditionally (FN-7 permits recursion). The useful forms are `this = copy of proto` and a value handed in.

10. **Reload skips the new init's checks.** A reload's added field takes its written default without the new init's checks ([HR-14]). That is P09's to decide with `migrate_from`.

11. **Shared flag machinery.** The hidden flag for fields set on some paths reuses OWN-3's drop-flag machinery. The compiler must keep 'first store' and 'replace (end the old value first)' apart on those paths, and for `this = v`.

design.rule:
Parallel code means what the same code means run one by one. The parts of a piece of parallel work are the tasks of a `with scope` block, the jobs of a `with jobs.scope()` block, the chunks of a `@parallel` loop, and each stretch of the starting code between two starts. Their one-by-one order is the order the code would run in if every task ran at the line that starts it and the loop ran its rounds in turn. Each place a part changes, other than its own locals, is one of three things, and the compiler works out which from the line itself and the functions the part calls; nothing is declared.

(1) An element only that part touches. This is an element of any list that keeps its elements at positions (`Array`, `[T; N]`, `MutSpan`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, an `SoA` column), or anything inside such an element, at an index the compiler proves differs between parts. In a loop that index is `i + k` with one `k`. It can also be the round's own `ref mut` element, or the counter `j` of the range loop that starts each task. The list is reached by one path, and its length does not change.

(2) A reduction. The place is changed in every part only by combining a value into it with one associative operation: `total += x`, `hp -= d`, `n *= k`, `|=`, `&=`, `^=`, `best = max(best, x)`, `min`, `and`/`or`, `push`, `extend`, set `add`, `counts[k] += 1`, `counts.entry(owns k).or_default() += 1`, `hist[b] += 1`, or a program's own operator that the compiler reads to combine each field this way (Vec3's `+`). Nothing in the parts reads the place. Each part keeps its own total of the place's type. The total starts empty, so its first change is taken as it is, and for `-=` it adds up what is taken away. Every step is checked as the place's own operations are (verdict 105). Once every part has ended, the totals are combined into the place in one-by-one order. So whole numbers, lists, text, sets and maps come out exactly as one by one (unless a part's own total overflows, which stops there). Decimals differ only by rounding, and the result is the same on every run (verdict 92).

(3) An `Atomic`, a lock, a guarded field or a channel, ordered by itself.

Anything else is refused when compiling, and the message gives the line to write: a plain assignment, a read of a place another part changes, two operations on one place, or an operation whose result depends on the grouping (`/=`, a `Mat4` `*`, saturating `+`). `@parallel(reduce=...)` goes. Remove `@parallel` or the scope, and the program is the same one, run on one thread.
design.spec_text:
Rules changed: [THR-21] (rewritten as the one rule), [THR-11], [THR-13], [THR-17], [PAR-1], [PAR-2], [PAR-3], [PAR-4], [PAR-5], [SIMD-5], [DET-2], [LT-46], COST-3's row "Scoped tasks and their reductions", the glossary's "reduction", and the E7010 and E7016 rows. Removed: `@parallel(reduce=...)`. Unchanged: the E7007 and E7011 rows, [PAR-2a] and [PAR-2b]; the lead fixes J7-12 (repeated types in view_mut) and J7-20 (`?` in a @parallel body) are assumed.

[THR-21] (changed) **What parallel parts change.** The *parts* of a piece of parallel work are the tasks of a `with scope` block ([THR-11]), the jobs of a `with jobs.scope()` block ([JOB-2]), the chunks of a `@parallel` loop ([PAR-1]), and each stretch of the code that starts them, between one start and the next. Their **one-by-one order** is the order their code would run in if every task or job ran at the line that starts it and the loop ran its rounds in turn. Every place a part changes, other than its own locals, is one of the three below. The compiler works out which from the part's body and every function it may run ([EFF-24]); a change made in a function a part calls counts as the part's.

1. **An element only this part touches.** This is an element of a list that keeps its elements at positions (an `Array`, `[T; N]`, `MutSpan`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, or an `SoA` column), or anything inside one. Its path indexes one level by an index the compiler proves differs between any two parts, and every access to that level in the parts, reads included, has the same form. In a `@parallel` loop over a range the form is `i + k` for one constant `k` ([PAR-2]). In a `@parallel` walk it is the element the loop's `ref mut` name is on. For a task it is the element `ref mut t` gives it from the loop that starts it ([THR-17]), or `j + k` (one `k`), where `j` is the counter of a range loop each of whose rounds starts at most one such task, given with `copy of j`. The list is reached by one path only: no other name, and no link the compiler cannot tell apart from it ([SIMD-3]); no `Cell`, no raw pointer. No part changes the list's length.

2. **A reduction.** Every change the parts make to the place combines a value into it with one operation, the same in every part. The forms are:
   * `P op= e` or `P = P op e`;
   * `P = max(P, e)` or `P = min(P, e)`, with `P` on the same side in every part;
   * `P.push(owns e)`, `P.extend(e)`, `P.add(e)`;
   * any of these on an element or entry: `hist[b] += 1`, `m[k] op= e`, `m.entry(owns k).or_default() op= e`.

   The parts read the place nowhere else, `e` included. The operation must give the one-by-one result in any grouping:
   * `+`, `*`, `|`, `&`, `^` and `-` on whole numbers, under `@overflow(panic)` or `@overflow(wrap)`, but not `@overflow(saturate)`, whose results depend on the grouping;
   * `+`, `-` and `*` on decimals;
   * `max` and `min` of any `Ord` type, exactly (floats by `cmp`, [TYP-37]);
   * `and` and `or` where `e` changes nothing;
   * appending to a list or a `String`, and adding to a set or a map's entries;
   * a program's own operator whose body the compiler reads to combine each field by one of these (`Vec3`'s `+`), checked per instance in generic code.

   The place may be a local, a field (a field reached through two `sharedref mut` links to one object included, verdict 77), a module variable ([THR-20]), or an element, entry or object a part works out while it runs.

   Each part keeps its own **total** for the place. It has the place's type and is empty at the start: the part's first change is taken as it is, and each later one is combined into it. For `-=` the total adds up what is taken away. Every operation on a total is checked as the place's own are ([TYP-8]): a part whose own total overflows stops the program there, even where one by one would not (verdict 105).

   Once every part that changes the place has ended, the totals are combined into the place in one-by-one order, each step checked the same way; for `-=`, each total is taken off the place. A `@parallel` loop's parts have ended at the end of the loop. Tasks and jobs have ended at their joins: `h.join()`, or the end of the `with` block (verdict 104). A key a part adds to a map or set is added then, in that order. Nothing reads the place before that (`E7007`: "tasks add their parts to `total`, which is known only once the `with` block (lines 11 to 14) ends; read it after the block: remove line 14 and write `println(total)` above line 15").

   So a whole-number total is the one-by-one total whenever no part's own total overflows, and a list, a `String`, a set or a map gets its elements in one-by-one order. A decimal total may differ from the one-by-one total by rounding, and is the same on every run of one binary (verdict 92). A total goes to the place's thread at the end, so its type is `Send` ([THR-8]); everything a part may make already is ([THR-2], verdict 166).

3. **A place its own operations order:** an `Atomic`, a `Mutex`, an `RwLock`, a channel end, or a `guarded by` field under its lock ([THR-3], [THR-18]). What parts do through it happens in the threads' order ([DET-2]).

Anything else is refused when compiling: `E7007` in a task or job, `E7010` in a `@parallel` loop. The message names the place and the lines, and gives a line that compiles:
* a plain assignment (`best = x`, verdict 77);
* a read of a place another part changes. For `if best < x: best = x` the message gives "write `best = max(best, x)`"; for `if stats.total < 10: stats.total += x` it gives a lock ([THR-11]);
* two operations on one place, `boss.hp += heal` in one part and `boss.hp -= dmg` in another. The message: "`hp` is changed with `+=` on line 6 and with `-=` on line 7 by tasks whose totals cannot be put together in one order; write `boss.hp += -dmg` on line 7". That is for a signed place; for an unsigned one it gives a lock;
* an operation the compiler does not find gives one result in any grouping (`/=`, `Mat4`'s `*`, saturating `+`): "write each task's result into its own element, `parts[j] = ...`, and combine them after the block".

An unscoped thread (`thread.spawn`) or a job submitted outside a scope is not a part. Nothing waits for it before the place is read again, so it has no reductions, and it changes what other threads reach only in the third way.

[THR-11] (changed), its sentence on clashes: "... two of them changing one place, or one reading a place another changes, is `E7007`, other than as [THR-21] allows: an element only one task touches, a reduction, or an `Atomic` or a lock."

[THR-13] (changed), its second item: "a place parts change by a reduction, or an element only one part touches: each part has its own total or its own element, and the end combines the totals in one-by-one order ([THR-21]);"

[THR-17] (changed), after the `ref t` sentence: "`ref mut t` lets a scoped task change the element `t` is on in that round, from a loop that walks with `ref mut`. No other task reaches that element, and the walked collection keeps its length until the end of the `with scope` block ([THR-21] point 1)."

[PAR-1] (changed): "A `@parallel` loop splits into chunks a range (`for i in 0..n:`), or a walk by element of a collection that keeps its elements at positions: `for ref mut p in players:` over an `Array`, `[T; N]`, `MutSpan`, `Deque`, `SmallArray` or `SoA`, and `for k, ref mut v in counts:` over a `Map`'s entries. It runs its body over each chunk on the job system (§XI.5). Over anything else it is `E7016` ..."

[PAR-2] (changed): "**Iterations MUST be independent.** The body MUST NOT contain `break`, `return`, `?`, `yield`, or a `continue` naming an outer loop, and each place it changes from outside is one [THR-21] allows. In a loop over a range, for each list `P` whose elements the body writes, the compiler collects every index expression through which `P` is accessed in the body, **reads included**. The loop is accepted only if: (a) each has the form `i + k` for a constant `k`; (b) all of them share **one** `k`; and (c) `P` is a list ([THR-21] point 1) that the body reaches by one path (not through a link it cannot tell apart from another path, [SIMD-3]; not a `Cell` or a raw pointer), and the body does not change its length. A loop walked by element hands each chunk its own elements through the loop's `ref mut` name, and its list holds each element once (... `Array[shares mut Player]` is refused). Otherwise it is `E7010`, whose message gives the lines that make the loop compile. Where an `Atomic`, `chunks_mut`, or a reduction's line (`best = max(best, x)`) makes the loop compile, the message gives that line."

[PAR-3] (changed): "**Reductions in a loop.** A `@parallel` loop's chunks are [THR-21]'s parts, and its reductions are found from the body as a task's are: `total += masses[i]`, `count += 1` and `best = max(best, x)` need no declaration. Each chunk combines its rounds left to right. Where the chunk is vectorised ([SIMD-5]), it keeps one partial total per vector lane instead (the lane count is fixed when compiling) and adds them in lane order at the chunk's end; a whole-number total is split into lanes only where [SIMD-7] proves that no partial total overflows in any grouping. Chunk totals are combined in chunk order. The grouping depends only on the trip count, `chunk` and the binary. So a decimal total may differ from the one-by-one total by rounding and is the same on every run (verdict 92), and whether a whole-number total stops does not depend on the machine (verdict 105). `@parallel(reduce=...)` is gone (`E0104`: 'the compiler finds the loop's totals in its body; write `@parallel` (line 4)')."

[PAR-4] (changed): "... and not `Alloc`: its chunk descriptors, each chunk's totals among them, live in the calling frame ... A total that is a collection, or one total per element or key a chunk works out while it runs (`hist[b] += 1`, `m[k] += 1`), allocates one per chunk (`Alloc`), and holds at most the smaller of the list's length and `chunk` entries."

[PAR-5] (changed): "... computes the same bits whatever the worker count and scheduling, and is not `Nondet` ([DET-2]), apart from what its body does through an `Atomic` or under a lock, whose order is the threads'."

[SIMD-5] (changed), its last clause: "... and every floating-point reduction is made in a `@parallel` loop ([PAR-3]), or the function is `@fastmath`."

[DET-2] (changed): "A reduction of a scope's tasks or jobs, or of a `@parallel` loop's chunks, combined in one-by-one order, is not `Nondet` either ([THR-21], [PAR-5])."

[LT-46] (changed): "... on two threads it is changed only under a lock, through `Atomic`, or by a reduction from scoped tasks or a `@parallel` loop ([THR-21])."

COST-3 row: "Parallel parts and their reductions | guaranteed present | one private total per part (a task, a job, a chunk), kept in a register, the task's record or the chunk's descriptor, and one combine per part at the end, as C's per-thread counter; no atomic per change. A type with no start value the compiler knows tests one flag per change. A collection total, or one total per element or key chosen while running, is one private collection per part (`Alloc`), each element moved once at the end, with at most the smaller of the list's length and `chunk` totals per chunk ([THR-21])."

Glossary: "**reduction** | a combining change (`total += e`, `best = max(best, e)`, `push`) made to one place by a scope's tasks or a `@parallel` loop's chunks: each keeps a private total, and the totals are combined at the end in one-by-one order ([THR-21])".

E7010 row: "a parallel loop changes a place other than as [THR-21] allows". E7016 row: "a `@parallel` loop over something it cannot split into chunks: neither a range nor a walk by element of a collection that keeps its elements at positions".

answers.answer: Point 1 settles it: an element only one round touches may belong to any list that keeps its elements at positions (`Array`, `[T; N]`, `MutSpan`, `Deque`, `SmallArray`, an `SoA` column). The element is written at `i + k` with one `k`, the list is reached by one path, and the body does not change its length. `pixels` is an `Array` reached through the `ref mut` parameter, every access is `pixels[i]`, and the body neither pushes nor removes, so each round writes only its own pixel. `pixels[i]` of the `Array` is the very element a `MutSpan` of it would name, so no conversion line is asked for.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 0.2. `pixels.push(owns 1.0)` in the body is E7010: it changes the list's length while other rounds write it. `pixels[i] = pixels[i + 1]` is E7011 (two offsets, PAR-2a).

answers.answer: The rule's parts settle it. A @parallel loop's chunks are parts, as a scope's tasks are. So `total += masses[i]` and `count += 1` are reductions found from the line, decimals and whole numbers alike, combined in chunk order (PAR-5 unchanged). `@parallel(reduce=...)` goes, since it only repeated what the line says (E0104 where written). An `Atomic`, or a guarded field under its lock, may be changed in the body (point 3), so E7010's own advice now compiles. SIMD-5's permission to regroup a decimal total is the `@parallel` word itself: it says the rounds run in groups, and verdict 92 accepted that for tasks. A loop that is not `@parallel` keeps one-by-one order unless the function is `@fastmath`, as in C without `-ffast-math`. Nothing is lost: `reduce=` only ever stood on `@parallel` loops.
answers.code:
fn total_mass(masses: Span[float]) -> float:    # a physics step: the mass of every body
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    @parallel
    for i in 0..masses.len():
        total += masses[i]          # a decimal total: a reduction, as in a task
        count += 1                  # a whole-number total: a reduction
    println(count)
    return total

fn main():
    println(total_mass([1.0, 2.0, 3.5]))
answers.outcome: Compiles. Prints 3, then 6.5, the same on every run of one binary on any machine. Written with `@parallel(reduce=[total: +, count: +])`, it is E0104: 'the compiler finds the loop's totals in its body; write `@parallel` (line 4)'. A decimal total may differ from one by one by rounding; here it does not, since 1.0 + 2.0 + 3.5 is exact.

answers.answer: Point 2 settles it: `P = max(P, e)` and `P = min(P, e)` are reductions as `P += e` is, in tasks and @parallel loops alike. Max and min of any Ord type give the one-by-one result in any grouping, exactly (floats by `cmp`, TYP-37). `best` stands only as max's argument, and no task reads it anywhere else. Each task's total starts empty and keeps the largest length it saw. At the end of the block, `best` becomes the max of itself and each total, in spawn order. No `max=` operator is added; the line people already write is the spelling.
answers.code:
import std.thread

fn longest(lines: Array[String]) -> int:      # the longest line of a text file, split across tasks
    best = 0
    with scope = thread.scope():
        for t in lines:
            scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: best = max(best, t.len()))   # a max reduction
    return best

fn main():
    println(longest([String("ember"), String("is fast"), String("c")]))
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 7. In a task, `best = max(best, t.len()) + 1` or `if best < 3:` is E7007: it reads `best`, which is known only after the block. The message gives `best = max(best, t.len())`. The same line compiles in a `@parallel` loop.

answers.answer: Point 2's totals settle it. Each task's total has the place's type and starts empty (its first change is taken as it is). For `-=` it adds up what the task takes away. At the end of the block the totals are taken off `hp` in spawn order, each step checked as `hp -= d` is. So verdict 105's promise (the one-by-one result whenever no task's own total overflows) holds for every operator and every whole-number type. A place gets one operation from all its parts: two different operations on one place have no order-free way to be combined, so they are refused when compiling.
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints 7 every time: the task totals are 1 and 2, then 10 - 1 = 9 and 9 - 2 = 7. A task whose own amount taken passes 255 stops there ('integer overflow in `-=`'), as verdict 105 decided. `boss.hp += d` in one task beside `boss.hp *= 2` in another is E7007, naming both lines. With `hp: int`, `+=` beside `-=` is E7007 too, and the help is `boss.hp += -d`.

other_cases.case: A histogram in a parallel loop: `@parallel` over `for i in 0..pixels.len():` with `hist[pixels[i] as int] += 1`, `hist` a list of 256 counts reached through `ref mut`.
other_cases.settled: A reduction into an element the round works out (point 2). Each chunk keeps one count per bin it touches (at most min(256, chunk)), and the counts are added into `hist` in chunk order: exactly the counts one by one gives. It is `Alloc` (PAR-4). `hist[b] = 1` in the body is E7010 (a plain assignment).

other_cases.case: Collecting in order: `@parallel` loop with `if keep(xs[i]): picked.push(owns i)`.
other_cases.settled: A push reduction. Each chunk keeps its own list, and the lists are appended in chunk order, so `picked` holds the indices in increasing order, as one by one. `picked.insert(0, i)` is E7010 (not an append).

other_cases.case: Word count with a map in tasks: `scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: for w in t.split_whitespace(): counts.entry(owns String(w)).or_default() += 1)`.
other_cases.settled: A keyed reduction. Each task keeps its own counts per word; at the end the words are added to `counts` and their counts summed, in spawn order, so the map's insertion order is the one-by-one order. With `counts[w] += 1` in every task instead (the key must exist, STD-16), no part adds keys, so the check reads `counts` as it was before the block and stops at the line, as one by one would. Mixing the two forms on one map is two operations: E7007.

other_cases.case: Summing forces and composing transforms: `net += bodies[i].force` (`Vec3`) and `xform *= locals[i]` (`Mat4`) in a `@parallel` loop.
other_cases.settled: `Vec3`'s `+` adds x, y and z by decimal `+`, which the compiler reads from its body, so `net` is a reduction (rounding as for decimals). `Mat4`'s `*` is not field by field, so the compiler cannot show it gives one result in any grouping: E7010, 'write each round's matrix into `parts[i]` and multiply them after the loop'.

other_cases.case: Overflow modes: `h ^= hash(xs[i])` or `h += k` in a function marked `@overflow(wrap)`, and `total += x` in one marked `@overflow(saturate)`.
other_cases.settled: Wrapping arithmetic gives one result in any grouping, so wrapped totals are reductions: exact, and they never stop. Saturating `+` depends on the grouping: with i8, [100], [100, -100] gives 100, but one by one gives 27 (100, then 127 saturated, then 27). So it is E7010/E7007, with a lock or per-part results as the help.

other_cases.case: A running maximum written as `if score > best: best = score` (or `if score > best: best = score; at = i` for the index of the best).
other_cases.settled: It reads `best` in the round, so E7010/E7007. The help gives `best = max(best, score)`, and for the index `best = max(best, (score, i))`: a tuple's Ord, where ties go to the larger index. The line people already write for a maximum is the one spelling.

other_cases.case: A prefix sum: `run += xs[i]` then `out[i] = run` in a `@parallel` loop.
other_cases.settled: `run` is read in the round, so E7010: 'each round needs the total of the rounds before it, so they cannot run apart; remove `@parallel` (line 3)'. It is a scan, not a reduction.

other_cases.case: An Atomic or a lock in a `@parallel` body: `hits.fetch_add(1)`, or `with log.lock: log.lines.push(owns s)`.
other_cases.settled: Point 3: compiles, in loops as in tasks (E7010's own advice is now true). PAR-5's same-bits claim does not cover what is done through them: the order is the threads' (DET-2; which line carries Nondet is P14's J6-07).

other_cases.case: A reduction made inside a method: tasks call `stats.add(x)`, whose body is `this.total += x`.
other_cases.settled: A change in a called function counts as the part's. `stats.total` is a reduction, and the call is compiled against a copy of `add` that adds into the task's total (one more copy of its code, as BRW-11). If `add` also reads `this.total`, it is E7007, naming `add` and its line.

other_cases.case: Tasks filling their own slots: `for j in 0..4: scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of j: part[j] = sum_part(j))`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1: two rounds of one range loop give `j` different values, the proof BRW-5 asks for, so each task writes its own element. `part[0] = ...` from two tasks is E7007. So is two tasks started in one round both writing `part[j]`.

other_cases.case: A task that changes the element it is given: `for ref mut slot in results: scope.spawn(owns fn() ref mut slot: slot = render(slot.job))`.
other_cases.settled: Point 1 with THR-17's `ref mut t`. The loop hands each element to one task, and `results` keeps its length until the scope ends, so it compiles. It is the changing companion of verdict 93's `ref t`. `for t in results:` (a read-only walk) with `ref mut t` is refused: the walk only reads.

other_cases.case: The starting code takes a share itself: inside the block, after starting tasks for `parts[1..]`, it does `total += sum(parts[0])`.
other_cases.settled: That stretch of the starting code is a part of its own, last in one-by-one order, and its total is added after the tasks'. A `println(total)` in the same place is E7007 until the tasks are joined.

other_cases.case: Joining early (verdict 104): tasks `h1` and `h2` both add to `total`; the code does `h1.join()`, then `println(total)`.
other_cases.settled: E7007: `h2` still adds to `total`. After `h2.join()` inside the block, `println(total)` compiles. The totals are combined at the last of the joins, in spawn order, so the order never depends on which join came first.

other_cases.case: Nested lists: `grid[i][j] = v` inside `for j` in a `@parallel` loop over `i`, and an in-place transpose `grid[j][i] = grid[i][j]`.
other_cases.settled: The first is the round's own row (level 1 at `i`), so it compiles. In the transpose, level 2 is written at `i` but read at `j` by another round: E7010.

other_cases.case: A one-thread `@simd(assert)` loop with a decimal total and no `@parallel`.
other_cases.settled: E4020 (SIMD-5): 'a decimal total in a loop that is not `@parallel` keeps one-by-one order; write `@parallel` above it, or `@fastmath` on the function'. This is C's rule without `-ffast-math`, and the same as today, where the permission came only from `@parallel(reduce=...)`.

other_cases.case: "Found any" from tasks: `if x == target: found = true`, and `found = found or x == target`.
other_cases.settled: The first is a plain assignment, E7007 (verdict 77); its help gives the second. The second is an `or` reduction, since its right side changes nothing: an exact result, the same as one by one.

other_cases.case: Text from tasks: `log += line` with `log: String`, and a generic sum `total += x` in a task with `x: T`, written `[T: needs Add[T, Output = T]]` above the function.
other_cases.settled: Appending text is a reduction; the text comes out in spawn order. The generic one is decided per instance: an `int` or `Vec3` instance compiles, while an instance whose `add` the compiler cannot show gives one result in any grouping is E7007 at the line that makes the instance.

other_cases.case: A `thread.spawn` thread or a job submitted outside a scope doing `total += x`.
other_cases.settled: Not a part: nothing waits for it before `total` is read again, so it has no reductions (THR-21's last sentence, verdict 77). It uses an `Atomic` or a lock; this is unchanged.

other_cases.case: A parallel walk of a map's values: `@parallel` over `for k, ref mut v in counts: v *= 2`.
other_cases.settled: PAR-1: a map keeps its entries at positions in insertion order, so the walk is cut into chunks, each changing its own entries. Adding or removing a key in the body is E7010 (it changes the map's length).

other_cases.case: A narrow total that overflows inside one part: `[[-100], [100, 100]]` summed into an `i8` by two tasks.
other_cases.settled: The second task's own total overflows at 100 + 100 and the program stops there (verdict 105). Unchanged.

design.prior_art:
How each language handles the general problem, and where it falls short of safe, as fast as C, and readable:

C / OpenMP: `#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum)` gives each thread a private copy started at the operator's identity (0 for `+`, 1 for `*`, all ones for `&`; min/max since 3.1). Array sections (`reduction(+:hist[:256])`, 4.5) and user reductions (`declare reduction` with an initializer and a combiner) exist. Falls short: the reduction must be declared, and a shared write that isn't declared is a data race, undefined behaviour. The combine order is unspecified, so a float total changes with the thread count and from run to run. A user combiner's associativity is never checked. The `-` reduction identifier confused people enough that OpenMP 5.2 deprecated it, which is J7-08's question.

C++17: `std::reduce(std::execution::par, b, e, init, op)` requires an associative and commutative `op`, unchecked: a wrong `op` gives a silently wrong result. `std::for_each(par, ...)` writing shared state is undefined behaviour. Float results are not deterministic.

Rust / Rayon: safe. A `par_iter().for_each(|x| total += x)` is refused by the borrow checker (the closure is `Fn + Sync`). The program is rewritten as `par_iter().map(..).sum()` or `fold(|| 0, ..).reduce(|| 0, ..)`, with identity closures written by hand and associativity unchecked. Rayon's adaptive splitting makes float sums differ from run to run. `std::thread::scope` cannot share `&mut total` between threads (needs an Atomic or a Mutex). `par_iter_mut()` and `par_chunks_mut()` work on a `Vec` directly, with no conversion, as J7-11 A does. Falls short on readability: the serial loop must be rewritten into a different shape.

Swift: Swift 6 strict concurrency refuses changing a captured `var` from a `@Sendable` closure (`concurrentPerform`, `TaskGroup`). A TaskGroup's results arrive in completion order, so a non-commutative combine is not deterministic. There are no reductions; you use actors or locks.

Go: goroutines with `sync.Mutex`, `sync/atomic` or channels by hand; races are found only by the run-time `-race` detector.

C#: `Parallel.For(0, n, () => 0, (i, s, local) => local + a[i], local => Interlocked.Add(ref total, local))`: the start value and the combine are written by hand, the combine order is not deterministic, and races are not checked.

Ada 2022: `parallel for` loops with compile-time conflict checks (`Conflict_Check_Policy`, `Global` aspects), and `'Reduce` / `'Parallel_Reduce` with an explicit initial value and reducer. Safe, but declared.

Chapel: `forall i in 1..n with (+ reduce sum) do sum += a[i];`. A reduce intent starts each task's shadow copy at the operator's identity; writing an outer variable without an intent is a compile error. Declared.

Fortran 2023: `do concurrent (...) reduce(+:s)`; declared.

Cilk++ / OpenCilk reducer hyperobjects (Frigo, Halpern, Leiserson, Lewin-Berlin, SPAA 2009): each strand gets a view started at the identity, and views are merged in the program's serial order, so any associative operation, even a non-commutative one such as list append, gives exactly the serial result. This is the semantics Ember's one-by-one order copies. But the reducer is a declared type (`cilk::reducer<op_add<int>>`, OpenCilk's `int cilk_reducer(zero, add) sum;`).

Halide `rfactor` (Suriana, Adams, Kamil, CGO 2017): proves an update's associativity by matching its body against known associative patterns, field by field for tuples. This is what Ember does for a program's own operator (Vec3's `+`).

Zig: nothing in the language.

Ember's rule takes:
* Cilk's serial-order merge (exact for every associative operation, deterministic);
* Chapel's and OpenMP's identity start, generalised to "empty", so no type needs a stated identity;
* Halide's body-reading associativity proof;
* Rust's compile-time refusal of every other shared write.

No language above infers the reduction from the ordinary `+=` / `max(...)` line in both tasks and loops. Ember does: the declaration is the line itself, and deleting `@parallel` or the scope leaves the serial program (Cilk's 'serial elision' property).
design.cost:
Per change in a part: one operation on the part's own total, held in a register or in the task's or chunk's slot. That is the instruction C's per-thread local counter costs, with no atomic read-modify-write per change. A whole-number total's overflow check is TYP-8's, the same as any `+=` in serial Ember (C pays none in either); parallelism adds nothing.

Start value: zero cost where the operation has a value that gives every value back unchanged. The compiler uses it: 0 for whole-number `+`, `-` (what is taken), `|` and `^`; -0.0 for decimal `+` (not +0.0, which turns -0.0 into +0.0); 1 for `*`; all ones for `&`; the lowest value for `max` and the highest for `min`; an empty list, text, set or map. A type with no such value the compiler knows (a program's own Ord type under `max`) costs one flag test per change, a branch taken once, or none where the compiler peels the part's first change.

Per part: one total of the place's size, stored in the chunk's descriptor in the calling frame or in the task's record, with no allocation for numbers and structs. One combine per part at the end, in order. OpenMP combines once per thread; Ember combines once per task or chunk, for a deterministic result. A 1,000,000-round loop at `chunk=4096` has 245 chunks, so 245 combines beside its 1,000,000 adds (0.02%).

Own-element writes: a store, as in C. Bounds checks are removed by OPT-2's entry test as today. Zero added.

Collection totals (`push`, `extend`, set `add`, a map entry, an element or key chosen while running): one private collection per part, allocated as the pushes themselves would allocate (`Alloc`), and each element moved once more at the end. C's per-thread vectors and their concatenation cost the same. A per-element total keeps at most the smaller of the list's length and `chunk` totals per chunk, so the end does at most one combine per round. A 256-bin histogram of 1,000,000 pixels does 245 x 256 = 62,720 adds at the end beside the 1,000,000 increments; C's per-thread histograms on 8 threads do 8 x 256 = 2,048. That extra is what a deterministic result costs.

A decimal total in a `@parallel` loop may vectorise with one partial total per lane, as C does with `#pragma omp simd reduction(+:total)` or `-ffast-math`, but the same bits on every run of one binary.

Removing `@parallel(reduce=...)`: zero. All the refusals: zero (compile time). Compile time: the classification runs on EFF-24's summaries. A function a part calls that adds into a total is compiled once more against the part's total (one more copy of its code, as BRW-11), with nothing added while running.

readability.note: The after is 9 lines shorter. It has no declaration, no conversion line, no lock and no helper function, and every line in it is the line the one-thread version has. Delete `@parallel` or the scope and it is the same program on one thread, with the same result (decimals by rounding). The only new thing a reader meets is a refusal, and only in code that would race or depend on order. Each such refusal gives the one line to write (`best = max(best, x)`, `hp += -d`, a lock).

design.compiler_does:
1. Finds the parts: for each `with scope` / `with jobs.scope()` block, each task or job and each stretch of the starting code between starts; for each `@parallel` loop, its chunks (boundaries from the trip count and `chunk` only, PAR-5). It orders them one by one (spawn or submit order, chunk order; a task started inside a task comes right after the stretch that starts it).

2. From EFF-24's summaries, reading through every function a part may run, collects each place a part reads and changes, and the operation of each change. The summaries record, for each changed place, whether every change is one combining operation, so this holds across calls and packages (BRW-10's interface file).

3. Sorts each changed place:
   (1) Own element: a list that keeps positions, indexed at one level by `i + k` (loops), by the loop's `ref mut` element, or by `j + k` for a range loop's round counter (tasks), every access at that level in the same form. One path, no link it cannot tell apart (SIMD-3), no length change.
   (2) Reduction: one operation across all parts, the place unread elsewhere. The operation must be associative: whole-number `+ - * | & ^` under panic or wrap, decimal `+ - *`, `max`/`min` of an Ord type, `and`/`or` with a right side that changes nothing, appends, set adds and keyed entries, or a program's own operator whose body combines each field by one of these, checked per instance.
   (3) Atomic, lock, guarded field, channel.
   Otherwise it refuses: E7007 or E7010, naming the place and both lines and giving a line that compiles.

4. For each reduction, gives every part a private total of the place's type: registers in a chunk, the task's record for a task. It uses the identity where one exists bit-exactly (the -0.0 start for decimal `+` included); otherwise it peels the first change or keeps a one-bit 'empty' flag. It rewrites the part's changes to target the total, compiling a called function that changes the place against a copy that writes the total.

5. Inserts the combine: at the loop's end, or at the last join of the tasks changing the place. It runs in one-by-one order, every step checked as the place's own operations are; `-=` totals are taken off. It refuses any read of the place before that point (E7007).

6. In a `@parallel` loop it may keep one partial total per vector lane for a decimal total (SIMD-5 now reads `@parallel` as the permission), and for a whole-number total only where SIMD-7 proves no partial overflows.

7. Refuses `@parallel(reduce=...)` with E0104 and the line `@parallel`.
design.verdicts:
All the involved verdicts are kept; none is revisited.

16 ('one rule for every loop'): applied. Tasks and `@parallel` loops share THR-21, which is the reason `reduce=` goes.

14 (make the natural way work rather than add a feature): `total += x` is the spelling, and `reduce=` was a feature that only repeated it.

77: kept, and stated for loops too. A field added to from several tasks is a reduction, through two `sharedref mut` links as well. A plain assignment (`a.target.hp = 5`) and a read-then-change still need a lock, and a `thread.spawn` thread has no reductions.

92: kept, and now true in `@parallel` loops too (PAR-3 already allowed declared decimal totals). One wording point to say to the owner plainly: 'may differ in the last digit' becomes 'may differ by rounding'. Regrouping can change more than the last digit: [1.0, 1e16, -1e16] gives 0.0 one by one and 1.0 split as [1.0], [1e16, -1e16]. This states the fact he accepted exactly; it changes nothing he decided (still allowed, still the same on every run).

93: `copy of t` and `ref t` kept. `ref mut t` is added beside them for a task that changes the element it is on: the same 'as long as there is no clash' reasoning, but a newly accepted form, so it is part of option A for the owner to see.

98: kept. Two parts' elements count as apart only when the compiler proves their indices differ (`i + k`, two rounds of one range loop); nothing is compared while running.

104: kept. The totals are combined at the last join of the tasks that change the place, so the parent may read it after those joins, inside the block.

105: kept, and read for every operator. Each part's total has the place's type and stops on overflow, and the combine's steps are checked. For `-=` the part's total is what it takes away: that is how verdict 105's own example (`hp -= 1`, `hp -= 2` leave 7) comes out 7, and how a `u8` place works at all.

100 (clashes of work run at once refused when compiling) and 3 / LT-46 (`sharedref mut` on two threads only under a lock, an Atomic or a reduction): kept.

166 (a task makes no shares owner): relied on, since it makes every total Send.

61 and 94 (`thread.spawn` takes a `thread_shared fn()`, `scope.spawn` a plain one): unchanged.

options_for_owner.summary: One rule for scoped tasks and @parallel loops. The compiler finds own elements of any list (an Array included) and reductions from the line itself (`total += x`, `hp -= d`, `best = max(best, x)`, `push`, `counts[k] += 1`, a Vec3 `+`). Each part's total starts empty, and `-=` adds up what is taken. The totals are combined in one-by-one order. One operation per place. `@parallel(reduce=...)` goes; Atomics and locks are allowed in loops too.
options_for_owner.outcome: All compile. `grade` gives the one-by-one pixels and count, and the largest pixel, the same on every run. `longest` prints 7, and the boss prints 7. `@parallel(reduce=...)` is E0104. In parts, `best = x`, `if best < x:`, and `+=` beside `-=` on one place are E7007/E7010, each with the line to write.

options_for_owner.summary: As A, but a @parallel loop declares every total, whole numbers too, in `@parallel(reduce=[...])`; scoped tasks keep finding theirs from the line (J7-10 B).
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles with the list; without it, E7010. In a loop each total is written twice (in the list and in its line), and in a task once, so the same line means two things depending on where it stands (checklist 5, verdict 16). Start values, `-=`, max and Array elements are as in A.

options_for_owner.summary: Today's text read narrowly: a task's total starts at 0 of the place's type; max and min only through a loop's `reduce=`, so tasks take a lock; only a MutSpan's or SoA column's elements may be written; loops declare decimal totals.
options_for_owner.outcome: The boss program stops in its first task ('integer overflow in `-=`'), though one by one gives 7. `longest` needs a Mutex and one lock per task. `brighten` written on the Array itself is E7010 until the `as_mut_span()` line is added. Loops still declare decimal totals.

options_for_owner.summary: As A, plus `+=` and `-=` on one signed place accepted as one total of the net change.
options_for_owner.code:
class Boss:
    hp: int = 10
# ...
            scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of d: boss.hp -= d)    # d = 1
            scope.spawn(owns fn(): boss.hp += 5)
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints 14 (net changes -1 and +5, added in spawn order). With `hp: u8` the same two lines are still E7007: a net change below zero has no `u8` value. The same lines compile or not by the field's type, an exception by type (principle 4), which is why A refuses both and gives `boss.hp += -d` for a signed place.

recommendation.reason: It is the one rule the principle asks for: the same line means the same thing in a scoped task and in a `@parallel` loop (verdict 16), with nothing declared (verdict 14). Every listed reduction can be written in the words people already write: `max(best, x)`, `hp -= d` on a u8, an Array's own elements. The result is the one-by-one result: exact for whole numbers, lists, text, sets and maps whenever no part's own total overflows (verdict 105), and decimals only by rounding, the same on every run (verdict 92). It is decided when compiling, and as fast as C's per-thread counters, with no atomic per change. B says each loop total twice and splits one line's meaning by place. C refuses correct programs (the u8 boss stops at 0 - 1, a max needs a lock, an Array needs a conversion line). D adds an exception by type.

owner_short.one_line: What OpenMP's `#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:total)` does, and what a `std::thread` pool writing `results[j]` does, but with no pragma: in a scoped task or a `@parallel` loop, `total += x`, `best = max(best, x)`, `hp -= d` and `pixels[i] *= gain` give the result the same code gives on one thread, and the compiler reads that off the line itself.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `boss.hp` is a `u8` (like `uint8_t`) and is 10; two tasks start, one with `d = 1` and one with `d = 2`; `boss.hp -= d` is a reduction | `hp` = 10 |
| 2 | task 1 | its `-= 1` goes into its own private total, not into `hp`; the spec says the total has `hp`'s type but not what it starts at | total 1 = 0 - 1? a `u8` cannot hold -1: the program stops |
| 3 | task 2 | the same with `-= 2` | total 2 = 0 - 2? it stops too |
| 4 | main | at the end of `with scope` the totals are put into `hp` 'in spawn order', by an operation the spec does not name | one by one: 10 - 1 - 2 = 7 |
| 5 | (the rule) | each total starts empty and adds up what its task takes away; at the end they are taken off `hp` in spawn order | totals 1 and 2; 10 - 1 = 9, 9 - 2 = 7 |
owner_short.today: Today tasks find `total += x` themselves, but a `@parallel` loop must declare its totals in `reduce=` (and whole-number totals get two answers). A task's total has no start value, so `-=` on a `u8` may stop at once. `max` and `min` are on the list, but no line spelling them compiles in a task. A loop may write a MutSpan's elements and maybe not an Array's.
owner_short.options:
A: one rule for tasks and loops. The compiler finds own elements (an Array's too) and reductions from the line; totals start empty, `-=` adds up what is taken, and they are combined in one-by-one order; one operation per place; `reduce=` goes.
B: as A, but each `@parallel` loop also lists its totals in `@parallel(reduce=[...])`, which tasks don't.
C: today read narrowly. A total starts at 0 (the u8 boss stops at 0 - 1), max in a task needs a lock, and an Array needs an `as_mut_span()` line.
D: as A, plus `+=` and `-=` together on a signed field (but still not on a u8: an exception by type).
owner_short.recommendation: A: the parallel program is the one-thread program plus one word, and it gives the same result. It is decided when compiling and as fast as C's per-thread counters, with nothing declared and no exception.

design.open_risks:
1. Verdict 92's words: the rule says 'may differ by rounding', not 'in the last digit', because regrouping can change more ([1.0, 1e16, -1e16]). Tell the owner plainly that this states his verdict's fact exactly and changes nothing he decided.

2. `ref mut t` for a scoped task's loop element is a newly accepted form. The capture word itself also touches P11's name-word table; confirm the spelling with P11's designer.

3. Mixed `+=`/`-=` on one place is refused (option D is the alternative). Under verdict 105 ('for now'), a wider-type total would remove both this and the 'stops where one by one would not' cases; if the owner revisits 105, D's exception disappears.

4. A program's own operator is a reduction only when the compiler proves it combines field by field (Halide-style). An associative but not field-by-field operator (`Mat4 *`) is refused, an understandable limitation with a one-line fix. No vouching word is offered: a wrong vouch would give silently wrong results, which the owner's bar forbids.

5. Per-chunk totals for elements or keys chosen while running (histograms) cost up to one more combine per round (62,720 against C's 2,048 adds for a 256-bin, 1,000,000-pixel image on 8 threads). This is computed, not measured: measure it against C's per-thread histograms before the cost row is final. The bound depends on totals holding at most min(length, chunk) entries.

6. PAR-1's walk over a Map's entries assumes the map keeps its entries in one array in insertion order. STD-11 implies this but does not state it; verify before writing.

7. The 'one-by-one order' for a task started inside a task (Cilk's serial order) is defined, but the spec never says whether a task may start tasks in its scope. If it may, each spawning stretch needs its own total (Cilk's mechanism). State that rule, or refuse it, first.

8. PAR-5 now excludes what a body does through an Atomic or under a lock. Which line carries Nondet is P14's J6-07; keep the two rules consistent. Output (`println`) from parts appears in the threads' order. That is DET-2's 'thread completion order', not a place this rule covers.

9. Collection totals make a `@parallel` loop `Alloc` (PAR-4), so `@noalloc` refuses such a loop. P14's Alloc rows must list it (as for J3-13).

10. A one-thread, deterministic, vectorised decimal sum still has no spelling except `@parallel` (as today, where it was `@parallel(reduce=...)`). If wanted, std's `sum()` could be given a fixed lane grouping; that is a stdlib question, not this rule's.

11. Writes through raw pointers in unsafe code inside parts stay refused, as PAR-2(c) does today. P04's vouching principle may want a path (`assume_disjoint`-like) for them; it is not designed here.

12. E7007 versus E7010, and every message's words, are the lead's.

13. J7-20 (`?` in a @parallel body) and J7-12 (repeated types in view_mut) are lead fixes this text assumes.

14. The compiler must record in a function's summary whether each change is one combining operation, so a reduction made through a call holds across packages. This is an addition to EFF-24's interface file (BRW-10).

matrix.guarantee: No data race on any place a part changes
matrix.how_kept: Every place a part changes is one of three kinds: (1) an element proved apart (i + k, the walk's ref mut element, j + k); (2) a reduction into a private total, combined on the starting thread after every part has ended; (3) an Atomic, a lock, a guarded field or a channel. Anything else is E7007/E7010.
matrix.edge_cases: Element interiors that cross a link (a sharedref mut field, a shares mut element): H2. A lock the starting code holds around a @parallel loop: H3. j + k from two loops, from a nested loop, or with the parent touching the same round's element: H5. Paths that may reach one object: H14. Reductions through a function value or a dyn call: H13.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed or moved memory
matrix.how_kept: No part changes a written list's length. Collection reductions go to private totals. The combine runs after every part has ended. Each total lives in the frame or the task record until the combine.
matrix.edge_cases: reserve, shrink_to_fit or sort on the list: they move or reorder the buffer without changing the length. They are refused only because the list itself is not one of the three kinds; the text names only length. A total made in an arena (H11). Task records freed at h.join() before the last join: the totals must outlive them.

matrix.guarantee: No double end, no raced owner or link count
matrix.how_kept: Old PAR-2 said a chunk 'follows the rules of a scoped task (THR-11, THR-2)', and verdict 166 says a task neither makes nor ends a shares owner. The design's PAR-2 rewrite drops that clause (H1), yet its Send argument for totals still relies on it.
matrix.edge_cases: push(shares x) as a reduction. An own-element write whose old value holds a shares owner. A range loop over Array[shares mut T] (the walk form keeps its 'each element once' clause, the range form has none).

matrix.guarantee: No undefined behaviour (overflow, memory managers)
matrix.how_kept: Totals have the place's type and its checked operations (TYP-8, verdict 105). Wrap is two's complement. Saturate is refused. Raw-pointer writes and Cells are refused.
matrix.edge_cases: + under panic in one part beside wrapping + in another, through an @overflow(wrap) method: the combine has no stated policy (H10). Totals 'of the place's type' for an Array using Arena grow from a one-thread arena on several threads (H11).

matrix.how_kept: Each total's step is checked. A missing map key is checked against the map as it was before the block (no part adds keys). Combine overflow names the block's end line. A part's own overflow is accepted by verdict 105.
matrix.edge_cases: and/or whose right side may panic, evaluated where one by one would short-circuit (H7). A ? exit from the block: the combine is not stated to run (H9). hist[b] must be bounds-checked at the change, not at the combine.

matrix.guarantee: The same result on every run of one binary (verdict 92, PAR-5)
matrix.how_kept: Chunk boundaries come from the trip count and chunk only. Tasks are combined in spawn order. The lane count is fixed when compiling. Atomics, locks and output are excluded and run in the threads' order.
matrix.edge_cases: Whether a chunk is vectorised decides the float grouping, so @simd or the profile changes the bits (H21). Output from parts. The rule's first sentence ('means what the same code means run one by one') overclaims for output and point 3.

matrix.guarantee: The one-by-one result: exact for whole numbers and collections
matrix.how_kept: Totals start empty (the identity, or the first change peeled). -= adds up what is taken away. Totals are combined in one-by-one order. The place is not read in the parts.
matrix.edge_cases: A reduction call whose result is used (Set.add, a fixed-capacity push) reads the place against the private total (H8). Reads through another link to one object (H14). Parent stretches are dynamic in number and each needs its own total for push and String append.
matrix.must_refuse: scope.spawn(owns fn() ref t: if seen.add(owns copy of t): unique += 1)   # E7007: reads seen

matrix.guarantee: No wait for ever (verdict 43, THR-19)
matrix.how_kept: THR-19 refuses a join, or the end of a with scope block, inside a lock its tasks take. Nothing covers a @parallel loop, now that point 3 lets its body take locks (H3).
matrix.edge_cases: A @parallel loop inside with log.lock: whose body calls log.push (which takes the lock) or uses log.lines directly. PAR-4's 'the calling thread runs the chunk itself' mixes threads that hold the lock and threads that do not.

matrix.guarantee: Correct programs accepted; every message gives a line that compiles and means the same
matrix.how_kept: Reductions are found from the ordinary lines. Messages give max(...), a lock, or per-part elements.
matrix.edge_cases: A whole place that only one part changes is refused (H4). += in one task beside -= in another is refused though exact (H6). The ref mut capture clashes with CLO-2's E0120 (H12). The max help changes float meaning (H18).
matrix.must_refuse:
scope.spawn(owns fn(): a.sort())
scope.spawn(owns fn(): a.sort())        # E7007: two tasks change a
matrix.must_compile:
scope.spawn(owns fn(): a.sort())
scope.spawn(owns fn(): b.sort())

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design's PAR-2 replaces the old clause 'what it uses from outside follows the rules of a scoped task ([THR-11], [THR-2])' with 'each place it changes from outside is one [THR-21] allows'. THR-21 governs places only. Nothing now says a chunk obeys verdict 166 (it neither makes nor ends a shares owner), and THR-2's weakref sentence reaches chunks only as 'any function that may run on another thread'. So `seen.push(shares enemies[i])` passes as a push reduction. Two job threads each add 1 to the one enemy's owner count with plain, non-atomic adds; one add is lost. The count ends one below the real number of owners, and the enemy is freed while an owner still points at it: a read of freed memory, then a double end. The same path lets `slots[i] = None` on an Array[Option[shares Enemy]] end shared owners on workers. The design's own Send argument for totals ('everything a part may make already is', THR-2, verdict 166) depends on the very clause it drops.
holes.fix_hint: Keep the clause in PAR-2: 'and what it uses from outside follows the rules of a scoped task ([THR-11], [THR-2], verdict 166): a chunk neither makes nor ends a `shares` owner, and makes, ends or opens a `weakref` link only to a `thread_shared` target' (E7015). In THR-21's parts sentence, add that every part, a chunk or job included, follows [THR-11]'s rules for what it may make and end.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 1 accepts 'an element ... or anything inside one', and moves the link exclusion onto the list's own path only ('The list is reached by one path only ... no Cell, no raw pointer'). Old PAR-2(c) excluded every place 'reached through a link (shares, shares mut, sharedref mut, thread_shared)'. Read as a field path, `turrets[i].target.hp` is inside element i, so the plain assignment is accepted as an own-element write. Both turrets link one boss, so two job threads write boss.hp at once: a data race in safe code, undefined behaviour in the generated C. A shares mut element range loop (`players[i].hp = 0` on Array[shares mut Player]) has the same race. The walk form keeps its 'each element once' clause, but the range form and the new `ref mut t` task form have none.
holes.fix_hint: Point 1: 'anything inside one: reached from it through its fields, its elements and its `owns` parts only. A place reached through a link (`shares`, `shares mut`, `sharedref mut`, `weakref`, `thread_shared`), a `Cell` or a raw pointer is not inside it.' Say the same in PAR-2's walk sentence and in THR-17's `ref mut t`. Such a write stays a reduction where it combines (`turrets[i].target.hp -= 1`, keyed by object) and is otherwise E7010/E7007, with a lock as the help.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 3 now lets a @parallel body use a guarded field 'under its lock', and THR-18 lets a direct call 'enter past' a lock this thread holds when the name is the same. Lexically the body is inside `with log.lock:`, so E7013 passes and `log.push` enters past the lock. But PAR-1 runs the chunks on job workers that do not hold it. Several workers push to `log.lines` at once: a data race on the list, whose growth frees a buffer another worker is still writing (a read of freed memory). If the compiler instead takes the lock in each chunk, the workers wait for a lock the calling thread holds while it waits for them: a hang. Verdict 43 refuses that when compiling, but THR-19's E7018 list names a join and the end of a with scope block, never a @parallel loop. PAR-4's 'the calling thread runs the chunk itself' makes some chunks hold the lock and others not.
holes.fix_hint: Add: 'A part (a task, a job, a chunk) holds none of the locks of the code that starts it. In a `@parallel` body a guarded field is used, and a call enters past a lock, only inside the body's own `with x.lock:`.' Extend THR-19: 'a `@parallel` loop inside the `with` block of a lock its body may take, directly or through a call, is E7018 ("move the loop below the `with log.lock:` block; `push` takes the lock in each round")'.
