holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-5 places a heap-owning comptime(e) result once, as constant data, and gives every evaluation of the expression a read-only view of it. Only statics get the 'no Mutex, RwLock, Cell, Atomic' test; comptime(e) results get none, and P17 keeps CT-5 as it is. A Cell is not ThreadShared, but both tasks reach the same Cell through the constant. E7007 sees no change, because a Cell's set is not a change of a place. So two threads write one Cell in safe code, which breaks THR-13's data-race guarantee. If the constant is in read-only memory, the store is a memory fault with no message. If it is writable, record keeps state from call to call like a hidden static mut, and within one build an evaluation that calls record changes what a later evaluation reads. The same goes for an object's counts in such a result: `w = weakref p` for `p = comptime(make_player())` writes the weak count in the header, from any thread. That is P03's J6-06, but for comptime results rather than statics.
holes.fix_hint: Decide placement from the value the evaluator holds, by walking it, once for comptime(e), const and static alike. Any place built on UnsafeCell (Cell, Mutex, RwLock, Atomic, Once, a channel's state), and any count a link or owner word changes, keeps the value out of shared constant data. For comptime(e) or a const that is E6010, naming the field and the line that made it, with help that compiles: `hits = copy of comptime(make_hits())` for Cell-only contents, or calling the function at run time. A static is built at first access, as CT-5 already does for a Mutex. Agree the counts half with P03.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Under P17, making a thread_shared owner and an atomic both run at compile time, since CT-1's Sync gate goes. So HOOK is built while compiling. CT-5's static test reads the declared type, and `thread_shared fn()` has no Mutex, Atomic or Cell field on its path, so HOOK goes to read-only memory with its state and the Counter. Calling HOOK() is not a change of its holder: CLO-18 covers only a function's own state, and the Counter is shared, not owned alone. So it compiles. At run time fetch_add writes read-only memory and the program dies with a memory fault, not a message at the line. Copying HOOK adds an owner, which writes the Counter's count too. `static R: owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu()`, with an Atomic field in Gpu and a read-only draw that adds to it, fails the same way. P17 opens this, because these values could not be made at compile time before.
holes.fix_hint: The same walk as the comptime(e) hole: the evaluator sees the function value's state and the dyn's concrete value. A static whose walked value holds any UnsafeCell-based place or count is built at first access. CT-6's 'a static whose value is fixed when compiling' follows the same walk, so `comptime(HOOK())` is E6005 and does not change the evaluator's copy.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Every CT-8 check passes: the write lands inside a live block, aligned, and writes a valid u8. CT-2's 'memory the evaluation did not make' covers only integer-made pointers and pointers from C. CT-8 has no obligation for a pointer made from a view: nothing forbids writing through a pointer made from a read-only view (a literal's, a file's text, a Span, a ref) or writing constant data (a literal, a const's or static's value). CT-8's 'keeps its word' bullet covers only views made from a pointer, so a write to a place while a safe-made read-only view reads it passes too. CT-9 places a file's bytes once for every reader, so the write silently changes the text main prints. The result also depends on which evaluation runs first. At run time the same shout writes read-only memory. This is the commonest unsafe mistake, and the rule's claim that UB becomes a compile error fails on it.
holes.fix_hint: CT-8 adds: a pointer carries the word of the view it was made from, and each place records the views that read it. Then each of these is E6011 at the line, naming the view: a write through a pointer made from a read-only view; any write to constant data (literals, read_file and read_bytes text, a const's or static's value); and a write to a place while a read-only view of it, made in safe or unsafe code, is in use. This is UNS-4's 'used as its word allows' checked for every view, not just pointer-made ones.

holes.what_goes_wrong: UNS-4 says 'A raw pointer made from a view is not used after the view's last use, nor after what it points into is reshaped or ended, nor after a hand-over of its object to another thread'. The view as_mut_ptr was given ends with that call (SPN-8), so every write in the loop comes after it. An evaluator that checks UNS-4 as written stops with E6011 at the write, which contradicts the design's own outcome for J6-04. An evaluator that does not check it leaves UNS-4's last sentence unchecked, including use after a hand-over that may move the object. CT-8 covers only 'a view made from a pointer'. The aliasing model the evaluator checks ('of Miri's Tree Borrows class') is not written anywhere. So whether `t[0]` read between two writes through p is E6011 differs between two conforming evaluators, and a false E6011 in a static leaves no way out.
holes.fix_hint: Write a raw pointer's permission into UNS-4 and CT-8 in plain words. A pointer made from a view may be used, with that view's word, until the place is next used through another name, reshaped, ended, or handed to another thread. CT-8 checks exactly that, and nothing stricter. Since it changes UNS-4 of a cut hardening, it is the owner's question; show the CRC loop and the `t[0]`-between-writes case.

holes.program:
fn name_view() -> StrView:
    s = String("player")
    # SAFETY: wrong: the view outlives s
    unsafe:
        v = mem.transmute[(*u8, usize), StrView]((s.as_ptr(), s.len()))
    return v                                  # s ends here, and v views its freed buffer

const NAME: StrView = comptime(name_view())
holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-8 checks views 'in use', and v is not used after s ends. The end-of-evaluation walk looks only for leaked blocks and raw pointers. 'A view is placed with what it views' then places a block the evaluation ended: either its old bytes are revived as constant data, so a UB function passes and differs from its run-time result, or the outcome is unstated. Likewise, two owners of one block made with ptr.read() and both kept in the result are never ended during the evaluation, so 'nothing is ended twice' never runs, and an invalid value is placed.
holes.fix_hint: The placement walk checks every view, owner and link in the value. Each points at a block live at the end and lies within it. Each owned block is reached by exactly one owner, or by as many as its count says. Otherwise E6011, naming the field, the line that made the value and the line that ended the block.

holes.program:
static TABLE: [int; 4] = [1, 2, 3, 4]

fn table_addr() -> [u8; 8]:
    out: [u8; 8] = [0; 8]
    q: *int = TABLE.as_ptr()
    # SAFETY: reads q's own 8 bytes
    unsafe:
        b = ((ref q) as *(*int)) as *u8
        for i in 0..8:
            out[i] = b.add(i).read()
    return out

const ADDR: [u8; 8] = comptime(table_addr())

fn main():
    # SAFETY: ADDR holds TABLE's address
    unsafe:
        p = mem.transmute[[u8; 8], *int](ADDR)
        println(p.read())
holes.what_goes_wrong: Each byte read is initialised, so 'a read finds bytes that hold a value' passes. There is no `as usize`, so DET-2's statically visible address observation is absent. The result's type holds no raw pointer, so the result check passes. ADDR then holds bytes of the evaluator's own pointer representation. The run-time program makes a pointer from them and reads unrelated memory, where without comptime it prints 1. So compile-time evaluation turns a correct program into undefined behaviour. Ordering two pointers into different blocks (p < q, sorting pointers), or comparing a block pointer with an integer-made one, also answers with addresses the evaluator does not have.
holes.fix_hint: Give each byte its provenance. Reading a pointer's bytes at any other type (a byte read, transmute, copy_nonoverlapping into bytes, MaybeUninit) is 'an address seen as an integer', E6010 where it is read. The placement walk checks provenance, not field types. Ordering pointers into two blocks, or comparing one for equality with an integer-made pointer or with one past another block's end, is the same observation.

holes.program:
@derive(Copy)
struct Slot:
    p: *mut int

# SAFETY: wrong: the two tasks below write through one pointer
unsafe extend Slot implements Send:
    pass

fn bump(s: Slot):
    # SAFETY: wrong: another task may write through s.p at the same time
    unsafe:
        s.p.write(s.p.read() + 1)

fn count_twice() -> int:
    t: [int; 1] = [0]
    s = Slot(p=t.as_mut_ptr())
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of s: bump(s))
        scope.spawn(owns fn() copy of s: bump(s))
    return t[0]

const N: int = comptime(count_twice())
holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-10 runs the tasks one after the other, so N is 2 in every build. No step carries Nondet, because plain writes through a raw pointer are in no list. CT-8's list leaves out UNS-4's 'Send and ThreadShared are respected'. At run time count_twice is a data race and may give 1. So CT-10's 'no other order could give another value' is false, and a race, the UB the rule most needs to catch, passes silently.
holes.fix_hint: The evaluator keeps a happens-before clock per thread and per byte, as Miri's race detector does. Two accesses to one byte from threads nothing orders, one of them a write that is not atomic, are E6011 at the second, naming both lines and the unsafe extend that vouched for Send.

holes.what_goes_wrong: ORDER is [0, 1] in every build, while arrival() called at run time gives [0, 1] or [1, 0]. CT-10 says such steps are Nondet and refused, but DET-2 does not list a contested lock, a receive from a channel two threads send on, a try_ operation, or an atomic read while another thread writes. That is P14's open K54, and the design admits it in open risk 5. If P14 classes every contested lock as Nondet, a lock-guarded counter, whose value is the same either way, is refused instead. A spin-wait (`while not ready.load(): pass`, with ready set by a later task) never 'waits', so it runs to CT-3's step limit and stops with E6001 and no line.
holes.fix_hint: CT-10 states its own test, not DET-2's list, using the clocks from the race fix. A step is refused (E6010, naming both lines) when another runnable thread that nothing orders could change its outcome: a lock acquired by both, a channel both send on, a try_ operation, an atomic place one reads and the other writes. A reduction spelled as THR-21 says is not refused, and the message offers it. A spin-wait is then refused at its atomic read.

holes.program:
static mut SCALE: int = 2
static LIMIT: int = SCALE * 100            # today: 200, placed while compiling

fn worker():
    println(LIMIT)                         # the first access may be here, on another thread

fn main():
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn(): worker())
    SCALE = 3
    h.join()
holes.what_goes_wrong: Reading SCALE is now refused at compile time, so LIMIT is built at its first access. That may happen on the worker, reading SCALE while main writes it: a static mut reached from another thread (THR-20), which is a data race unless E7012 counts LIMIT's lazy initialiser at every read of LIMIT. No rule says it does. If it does, a program that compiles today stops compiling at a distance. LIMIT, a static that 'never changes', is 200 or 300 depending on timing. A @deterministic function reading it passes DET-1 though its result varies, because DET-2 lists no 'time of first access'.
holes.fix_hint: Either refuse it, as CT-6 refuses comptime(FRAME): a static whose initialiser reaches a static mut is E6005, help `fn limit() -> int: return SCALE * 100` or `static mut LIMIT`. Or state that each read of a lazily built static carries its initialiser's reads and effects (EFF-1), so E7012, E7007 and DET-1 judge it where it is read. It changes what compiles today, so it is the owner's question.

holes.program:
from std.arena import FixedArena

fn pack() -> int:
    frame = FixedArena.with_capacity(64)
    a = [1, 2] using frame
    b = [3, 4] using frame
    # SAFETY: wrong: a has 2 entries
    unsafe:
        a.as_mut_ptr().add(2).write(99)    # lands in b's entries, inside frame's one buffer
    return b[0]

const FIRST: int = comptime(pack())
holes.what_goes_wrong: There are two readings. If the evaluator runs FixedArena's own allocate, a and b are carved from one buffer block. Then CT-8's 'inside the live block the pointer was made from' passes, and FIRST is 99: an overflow into a neighbour that is never caught. If allocation for `using` is 'served by the evaluator's own heap' (CT-1), the overflow is caught, but the manager's own code does not run. Then a full FixedArena never fails, its counters read differently, and a program's own Allocator behaves differently at compile time. Either way one half of the rule fails: UB is caught, or the function means the same.
holes.fix_hint: Run the manager's own code. Each pointer `allocate` returns starts a block of its own, inside the manager's memory, with the Layout's size and alignment. That block ends at `deallocate`, at a reset, or when the manager ends, and CT-8's checks apply to it. The Allocator interface is the language's own boundary, so this holds for every manager, a program's own included.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-3 bounds an evaluation's steps and heap. It does not bound the size of a file comptime reads, the depth of calls, or the checker's own tables (CT-8's per-byte maps and view tags). So the compiler can run out of memory or stack and stop with no line. A package entry that is not a regular file (a pipe) makes the read wait for ever. Two instances reading one file at different moments of one build may see different bytes, although CT-9 says they are placed once.
holes.fix_hint: CT-3's limits also count a file's bytes (a size in `[comptime]`, E6001 naming the path), the call depth (E6001 at the call, with the chain) and the checker's tables. read_file and read_bytes accept only regular files (E6012). Each input is read once per build, and every reader gets that one copy.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-8 checks alignment against 'the live block', but the rule gives a file's bytes no alignment. If the evaluator's block is 8-aligned, MAGIC compiles, while magic() run at run time reads bytes placed at alignment 1, as a bytes literal needs: a misaligned read. The compile-time check says nothing about the run-time placement.
holes.fix_hint: State the alignment read_file, read_bytes and bytes literals are placed with (1, or a stated larger one), and give the evaluator's block exactly that, so the check and the image agree.

interface Shader:
    const PATH: StrView

[S: needs Shader]
pub fn source() -> StrView:
    return comptime.read_file(S.PATH)

# the game, another package

extend Sky implements Shader:

fn main():

The game's shader is not there (E6012), or a file of engine's with the same name is read silently. The design gives this generic form as the fix for E6005 but does not say which package's root applies when the path comes from another package's const.
holes.fix_hint: Resolve a path that a const gives against the package that wrote the const (where the text of the path is written), and record it as that package's input. A path written at the call stays the calling package's.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design refuses 'a raw pointer into the evaluator's memory' in a result, but does not say whether a literal's bytes, a file's text or a static's placed value count as that memory. C writes `static const char *p = "help";` as one relocation and no start-up code. Here it is either E6010, refusing a correct table such as getopt's or an extension's method table, or left undecided. Taking an Ember function's address for an `extern "C" fn` table at compile time is likewise not stated.
holes.fix_hint: A pointer into constant data the image holds (a literal, a file's text, a static's placed value, a function's entry) is placed as that data's address, a relocation. Only a pointer into memory the evaluation made and ends is refused.

from std.sync import Mutex

static CACHE: Mutex[Map[int, int]] = Mutex({})

fn fib(n: int) -> int:
    with g = CACHE.lock():
        if g.get(n) exists as v:
            return v
    r = n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)
    with g = CACHE.lock():
        g.insert(n, r)
    return r

const F20: int = comptime(fib(20))
holes.what_goes_wrong: options_for_owner B's outcome says B refuses 'a function with a private Mutex cache', implying A runs it. But the design's CT-2 refuses 'a static whose memory a safe operation may write', which is exactly CACHE. So under A, F20 is E6010 at the first lock too. The owner would be shown a benefit the rule does not give.
holes.fix_hint: Remove 'a function with a private Mutex cache' from B's comparison, or say that A refuses it too, and why: the cache's value while compiling is not its value when the program runs.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design's CT-5 addition and its 'using arena' case say a value made in a manager is placed as constant data and drops the instance word. But comptime(e) may not name the run-time local arena (E6005). An arena made inside the evaluation ends before the value, which TYP-46 refuses (E3063). A static arena is state that changes (ALC-5), so it is refused. A one-instance manager keeps no word anyway. So the clause decides no program that compiles, and the owner is told one does. If a path were found, `copy of` such a constant would have to allocate from an instance its type names and the value no longer records, which is undecided.
holes.fix_hint: Drop the clause and the case, or state the one program it is for. If one exists, say which instance `copy of` and growth use.

A view given where an owned TypeDesc is expected is a type mismatch, or an implicit copy, and nothing states which. So the spec's own static example stops being decided. read_file has TXT-9 for this. reflect has nothing.
holes.fix_hint: Say that inside what compile time evaluates (a static's initialiser, a const) reflect[T]() gives the description as a value, and in run-time code a read-only view. Or give reflect the literal-to-owned conversion read_file has.

safety.notes:
The rule's core is sound for safe code: run what is reached, refuse what is reached, read_file as a literal, E6010 at the line with the chain. Of the 15 holes, three are high, and all three come from two causes.

(1) Placement is decided by declared type, or not at all. Constant data is reached by every call and every thread with no Send check, so a Cell in a comptime(e) result races in safe code. A thread_shared fn or dyn hiding an Atomic gets placed in read-only memory, and P17 newly allows such values because the Sync gate goes.

(2) CT-8 checks views made from pointers but not pointers made from views. So writes through read-only views, and writes into constant data (a file's text placed once for every reader), pass silently.

Both fixes are one general rule each: walk the actual value, and give every pointer its view's word. The counts half of (1) is P03's J6-06 for statics; agree one placement rule with P03.

The medium holes (UNS-4's last sentence against the CRC example; placement-walk liveness; byte provenance; unsafe races; CT-10's dependence on DET-2's list; a static mut read moving a static to first access; memory-manager sub-blocks) are each one stated check the evaluator can make.

Checked and not a hole:
- A raw-pointer container in a static: STA-1 requires ThreadShared, which raw pointers never are, so only static mut can hold one, and that is built at run time.
- std's Array, String and Map are compiler-known, so there is no special path.
- Library updates breaking a const elsewhere are consistent with verdict 86 and EFF-4, and are the design's open risk 6.

No owner verdict is contradicted. Hole 9 (static reading static mut) and hole 4 (the pointer-permission wording in UNS-4) change what the language does, so they go to the owner.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design's STA-3 moves any static whose initialiser reaches a static mut to first access, and its settled case says START_FRAME 'reads FRAME's value at that moment'. Three things go wrong. (1) The meaning of a program that compiles today changes silently: today's text places START_FRAME as 0, and the design's open risk 4 claims such programs 'stop compiling', but this one compiles with another value. Even on one thread, `FRAME = 7` then `println(START_FRAME)` prints 7. (2) The value depends on when the static is first read, which brings back the initialisation-order problem STA-2 says Ember does not have. (3) The first read here runs the initialiser on the spawned thread, which reads FRAME while main writes it. THR-20's E7012 counts functions that read a static mut by name, through calls, and through drops. Nothing in the spec counts a static's first-access initialiser as run by the accessing function, so nothing refuses this. The result is a data race in safe code.
holes.fix_hint: Treat a static's initialiser like comptime(e) for state that changes. Reaching a static mut, or a static whose memory a safe operation may write, is E6005/E6010 with the fix (`static mut START_FRAME` set in main, or a function). Fall back to first access only for 'the world outside the program'. Also state that an access to a static built at first access counts as running its initialiser: its effects, its summary and THR-20.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Making a thread_shared owner carries Sync, so today's gate never builds this at compile time. The rule drops the gate, so CFG is now computed while compiling. CT-5 places it in read-only memory, because there is no Mutex, RwLock, Cell, Atomic or guarded field on the path. `thread_shared CFG` then adds to the count in OBJ-1's 32-byte header, which sits in read-only memory, so the program faults. The header's 'home' count also belongs to the making thread (RC-4), here the evaluator, which is no run-time thread. Two more cases have the same cause. A `weakref` link made at run time to a class object in a static changes the object's weak count in constant data. A comptime(e) result that holds a Cell, Atomic or Mutex is a read-only view of constant data (CT-5), and `cell.set(1)` writes through it. The design says compile time runs 'a lock, an atomic or a Cell of a value the evaluation made', but never says where such values may then live.
holes.fix_hint: Make one property-based rule in CT-5. Constant data holds only values that no operation changes through a read-only name: no Cell, UnsafeCell, Atomic, lock or guarded field, and no counted object (making an owner or a weakref link changes its count). A static whose value holds one is built at first access (CT-5's second bullet, widened). A const or comptime(e) that holds one is E6010, naming the field. 'Immortal' headers would also work, but they cost a test on every count change, which C does not pay.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Today this compiles: spawning carries Sync, so the static is built at first access. Under the rule, the evaluator runs start_logger, and the parent returns tx. The logger thread then waits in `for line in rx`, and the evaluation ends with every thread waiting. CT-10 calls that E6010 'at the line that waits'. STA-3 falls back to first access only 'if the evaluation reaches an operation that [CT-2] refuses', and CT-10's two E6010s are not such operations, so read literally the build fails. A static whose value holds a raw pointer has the same gap: `static mut FREE_LIST: *mut Node = make_free_list()` gets 'E6010 at the line that made the pointer', which compiles today through the Unsafe gate. A static logger or worker pool is a common program in servers and games.
holes.fix_hint: In STA-3, say that every E6010 an initialiser's evaluation reaches makes the static be built at first access instead, whichever rule gives it: a CT-2 operation, a CT-10 thread case, or a raw pointer in the value. Then nothing the abandoned evaluation did remains.

holes.program:
import math.det

fn build_noise() -> Array[float]:
    t: Array[float] = []
    for i in 0..4_000_000:
        v = 0.0
        for o in 0..32:
            v += det.sin(i as float * 0.001 * (o + 1) as float) / (o + 1) as float
        t.push(owns v)
    println("noise table built")
    return t

static NOISE: Array[float] = build_noise()
holes.what_goes_wrong: Today the println (Io) makes the gate build NOISE at first access, and the program compiles. Under the rule, the evaluator runs the loops first and passes CT-3's 10^8 steps before it reaches the println. The design's STA-3 makes a passed limit E6001, so the build fails. Procedural tables built at start-up, often with @parallel and a log line, are ordinary in games, and they become compile errors that depend on the manifest's step limit. Every clean build also spends up to the limit on an evaluation it throws away.
holes.fix_hint: When a static's initialiser passes CT-3's limit, build the static at first access, with a warning naming the static, the limit and the `[comptime]` setting. Keep E6001 for a const, comptime(e), an array length and a comptime: block. Cache the abandoned result with its inputs (CT-4).

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rewritten STA-3 says when a static is built at first access, but not that an access to such a static carries its initialiser's effects (Alloc, Io, Panic) and summary, plus Block for the once-wait. EFF-6 checks contracts over 'the whole reachable call graph', and THR-20 checks which threads reach a static mut. Neither one sees the initialiser. So `mix` can be accepted as @realtime and still allocate, read a file and block on the realtime thread. The design now decides the fallback by what the evaluator reaches, so effect and contract verdicts also have to be computed after evaluation. The design does not say that either.
holes.fix_hint: Add to STA-3: every access to a static that is built at first access counts as a call of its initialiser, for effects (Block included), summaries, contracts and the thread rules. Effects are worked out after the evaluator has decided each static's placement.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-2 refuses 'an address seen as an integer', and CT-8 checks bounds and liveness, but neither says what comparing or subtracting raw pointers does. If a compare counts as seeing the address, this C idiom over one block is refused for no reason. If a compare is answered from the evaluator's own blocks, then `a < b` for two blocks, or a one-past-the-end pointer compared with the start of another block (true at run time in C when the blocks touch), gets an answer the compiled program may not give. That breaks the rule's one-value promise without an error.
holes.fix_hint: Say in CT-2/CT-8 that compare and difference of pointers into one block, and equality with null, run. A compare whose answer could differ between runs (an order across blocks, one past the end against another block) is Nondet and is refused where reached, as Rust's const eval does with its guaranteed_eq.

holes.program:
static mut RX_BUF: [u8; 256] = [0; 256]

const RX_PTR: *mut u8 = RX_BUF.as_mut_ptr()      # C: uint8_t *const rx_ptr = rx_buf;

@derive(Copy)
struct DmaDesc:
    addr: *mut u8
    len: u32

static mut RX_DESC: DmaDesc = DmaDesc(addr=RX_BUF.as_mut_ptr(), len=256)
holes.what_goes_wrong: RX_PTR is refused twice over. RX_BUF is a static mut ('state that changes'), and the value holds 'a raw pointer into the evaluator's memory'. Yet the address is fixed at link time and nothing reads RX_BUF's value. RX_DESC moves to first access, so every access pays a once-check (a load and a branch), even from an interrupt handler. C and Rust place both with a relocation. ODR-145 refused a pointer into 'the evaluator's heap'. The rule says 'the evaluator's memory', which also covers statics, and it lists ODR-145 as 'kept', so a lead ruling is silently widened. Embedded descriptor and vector tables need exactly this.
holes.fix_hint: Naming a static's place (its address) is not reading its value. A raw pointer to a static, or into one, is a link-time address and is placed as such. Keep ODR-145's refusal for blocks of the evaluator's heap and for the evaluation's own locals.

@layout(c)
struct Entry:
    kind: u8                 # three bytes of padding follow
    id: u32

fn swap_entries(ref mut a: Entry, ref mut b: Entry):
    tmp = MaybeUninit[Entry].uninit()
    # SAFETY: a, b and tmp are three different places of 8 bytes each
    unsafe:
        pa = ref_to_ptr(ref mut a) as *mut u8
        pb = ref_to_ptr(ref mut b) as *mut u8
        pt = ref_to_ptr(ref mut tmp) as *mut u8
        mem.copy_nonoverlapping(pa, pt, 8)
        mem.copy_nonoverlapping(pb, pa, 8)
        mem.copy_nonoverlapping(pt, pb, 8)

fn sorted_pair() -> [Entry; 2]:
    t = [Entry(kind=2, id=20), Entry(kind=1, id=10)]
    swap_entries(ref mut t[0], ref mut t[1])
    return t

const TABLE: [Entry; 2] = comptime(sorted_pair())
holes.what_goes_wrong: CT-8 says 'a read finds bytes that hold a value', and DET-2 makes reading padding Nondet, so the first byte copy of the padding is E6011 or E6010. Yet the program never looks at padding. A memcpy of a padded struct, or a generic swap, rotate or sort written with copy_nonoverlapping over T, is ordinary unsafe code. CT-8 also checks validity at 'a value made by a write', so building a value byte by byte through `*mut u8` can be refused at an intermediate state that is never read.
holes.fix_hint: Use Miri's model. An untyped byte copy carries each byte's state, a value or none. Only a read at a type of a byte that holds no value is broken (Nondet or E6011), and a type's validity is checked where a value is read or used at its type, not at each raw write.

fn demo() -> int:
    slot = MaybeUninit[int].uninit()
    # SAFETY: slot is written before it is read
    unsafe:
        p = ref_to_ptr(ref mut slot) as *int
        r = ref mut slot.write(owns 5)        # a ref mut view of the int
        seen = p.read()                       # another name reads r's place while r is used
        r += 1
        return seen + r

const D: int = comptime(demo())
holes.what_goes_wrong: UNS-4 and verdict 2 ('ref mut keeps others from reading and changing') make a ref mut name the only name of its place while it is used. CT-8 checks only that 'no other name changes the place of a ref mut view', so `p.read()` passes. The evaluator gives 11. The compiled function may assume nothing else reads r's place, and may give 12. So the const and a run-time call disagree, and there is no E6011. CT-8 also leaves out two more UNS-4 obligations: a raw pointer made from a view is not used after the view's last use, and Send and ThreadShared are respected across CT-10's threads. The checks are also on 'each operation of unsafe code', but the conflicting use may be in safe code.
holes.fix_hint: Make CT-8 check every obligation of UNS-4 word for word: reads as well as writes against a live ref mut view, a pointer from a view not used after that view's last use, and Send and ThreadShared across the evaluation's threads. Track every access, safe ones included.

const SHADER_NAMES: [StrView; 3] = ["sky.wgsl", "water.wgsl", "terrain.wgsl"]

fn load_shaders() -> Array[StrView]:
    out: Array[StrView] = []
    for name in SHADER_NAMES:
        out.push(owns comptime.read_file(f"shaders/{name}"))    # E6005: `name` is a loop variable
    return out

static SHADERS: Array[StrView] = load_shaders()
holes.what_goes_wrong: Every step here runs while compiling, and the path is known when it is reached. But CT-9 decides read_file's argument by where it is written, and a loop variable is a run-time local (E6005). The programmer must write one read_file line per file (50 assets, 50 lines), or one type per file with a `const PATH`. Zig (`inline for` with @embedFile) and D (`static foreach` with import) handle this as written. It is also the one place where the design decides by position and not by 'each operation the evaluation reaches' (its own CT-1).
holes.fix_hint: In an evaluation, read_file reads the path the evaluation holds when it reaches the call, recorded as a build input as before. In code that runs while the program runs, a path not known when compiling is E6005, reported where run-time code reaches the call, with the chain. The message also offers passing the text instead of the name.

pub interface Shader:
    const PATH: StrView

[S: needs Shader]

The build reads engine/shaders/sky.wgsl: E6012 when it is missing, or another package's file of the same name. It never reads game's file. This is the form the design's own E6005 message gives as the fix, and it is the usual shape of an engine (a generic loader) and a game (its assets).
holes.fix_hint: Resolve a path against the package whose source wrote the path's text: the literal's package, so for a type's const, the package of the instance's type. Keep each path confined to that package, so a library's own literal still cannot read the builder's files.

struct Point:
    x: float
    y: float

static D: TypeDesc = reflect[Point]()        # the example in Part XIV.2's ODR-158 paragraph
holes.what_goes_wrong: Under CT-9, reflect[Point]() is 'a comptime(…) of its own' and 'gives one value at both'. CT-5 gives a heap-owning comptime(e) as a read-only view of constant data 'with no copy'. Part XIV.2's ODR-158 paragraph (kept except its last clause) says a description 'owns its text (String), so it is no view and lives in a static', and writes this very line. So either the line is a silent copy into an owned static (verdict 5), or it is an error asking for `copy of`. In that case the spec's own example breaks, and compile-time code that edits a description (`d = reflect[T]()` then `d.fields.push(...)`) needs `copy of` too.
holes.fix_hint: Settle it in the rule. Either reflect[T]() is a read-only view everywhere (remove the 'no view, lives in a static' sentence and its example, and say compile-time edits take `copy of`), or it stays an owned value inside an evaluation and is a view only in run-time code, said in those words.

holes.what_goes_wrong: After the RFL-1 change, two spellings give the same description at run time with different requirements. type_info[T]() needs @reflect and `needs Reflect` (E2040 without it); reflect[T]() needs neither. A pub generic's written needs (verdict 108) then no longer say whether it reads descriptions. Checklist 5 and 11 (one idea, one spelling) and 16 (a ruling that replaces a spelling reaches every place) make this part of the ruling. The design leaves it as a knock-on for the owner.
holes.fix_hint: Decide it in this rule. Either the static `type_info[T]()` goes (reflect[T]() is the spelling, and @reflect only enables `h.type_info()` on class objects), or reflect[T]() outside an evaluation stays E6010 (ODR-158's clause kept), with read_file and size_of covered by CT-9 alone.

data = fs.read("models/ship.bin")                     # std's bytes form
text = fs.read_to_string("notes.txt")                 # std's text form
