owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: `auto frame = scene.renderer->draw(scratch); scratch.push_back(1); use(frame);` dangles when the `std::unique_ptr<Renderer>` member is the subclass whose `draw` returns `scratch` itself. Ember refuses this, and your word `runtime` turns the refusal into a `typeid` compare at the `push_back`. The question: may that word go on a class member, a static, a lambda's parameter and `this`, and before a `shared_ptr`, a `weak_ptr` or a `vector<unique_ptr<...>>`, with the same meaning it has on a parameter and a local?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `r` is made a `Gpu` or a `Software` from what the player typed, and `scene = Scene(renderer=r)` keeps it in the field `renderer` | `scene.renderer` is a `Software`, known only while running |
| 2 | main | `render` runs `frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)` | a `Software` gives back the buffer it was handed, so `frame` points into `this.scratch` |
| 3 | main | `this.scratch.push(owns 1)` | the list may move to a bigger block, leaving `frame` pointing at freed memory |
| 4 | main | `println(frame)` | would read freed memory (in C++, a span into a vector after `push_back`). So Ember refuses step 3 when compiling (`E3021`), and its help offers `runtime` only "on the parameter or the variable": the field cannot carry it |
owner_short.today: `runtime` may go only on a function's parameter (verdict 152) or a local variable (verdict 163), before a `dyn` or class type. A field, a static, a lambda's parameter, `this`, and the word before `shares mut A`, `weakref A` or `Array[owns dyn I]` are undecided, so `render` gets its check only through an extra local in every method.
owner_short.options:
A: `runtime` on every declaration that writes a type (field, static, enum field, lambda parameter, as on parameters and variables) and `runtime this`; before the whole type; covers every dyn or class value inside it; the compiler follows it to every line.
B: fields and lambda parameters only, with the word only before an outermost dyn or class type; `Array[owns dyn I]` and `this` cannot carry it.
C: no word on fields; each method declares a local to carry it (J1-11 b).
D: A, plus the word before names declared without a type (`for runtime e in level.spawn_wave(n):`).
E: no word; the compiler checks wherever it would otherwise refuse (Swift's way; reverses verdict 152).
owner_short.recommendation: A: one word in one place with one meaning on every declaration. Its only cost is one compare at the lines that would otherwise be refused, and your verdicts 152, 162 and 163 keep their programs.

design.open_risks:
1. K58 (P14) decides what kind of effect the check is under `@no_alias_checks` and `@nopanic(explicit)`. This rule names it LT-48's check and leaves the effect to K58.
2. How precisely kinds are followed into fields and lists decides how many lines get a check, not what the word means. LT-1 says 'followed through its names and calls'; `tasks/96/redesign/compiler-0.9.15/dyn-per-kind-design.md` leaves fields and lists as open question 2. If kinds are not followed into a field, every kind of the interface counts as reaching it.
3. Point 4's kept-kind sentence repairs LT-48's wording for verdict 163's variables as well as for fields. It should reach the owner inside this question, because it says what a program does when a name is given another value. 163's own program is unchanged.
4. `runtime this` and `owns runtime this` are a slot nobody asked for. The alternative, a local viewing `this`, does not compile for a method that changes its object.
5. A field's word reaches lines in other functions and packages, so a stop can come at a line whose function has no word of its own; the word sits in the field's declaration, beside its type. If the owner wants the word visible in every function, B or C is the narrower reading.
6. Covering values at any depth extends verdict 162's line to the values inside a class or struct. This is said plainly in the options.
7. The new refusals (nothing to check, a parameter of a function with no body, the word inside a type) need error codes, which are the lead's.
8. The built compiler's limits are implementation gaps, not part of this rule: a class override's kind cannot be told from the table, and lambdas are resolved only from their own locals.
9. The 'before' program and verdict 152's line rest on J5-08's resolution: a bare `dyn I` local views a temporary.

matrix.how_kept: The compare reads only words that never change. A struct's kind is the dyn table's word. holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 4 keeps the kind only "where the name may be given another value before a guarded line (a variable, a field, a `static mut`, a `ref mut` parameter)", and §X.4 prices the kept word on that same list. Everywhere else the guard reads the kind from the value at the guard. That list leaves out a loop name, which gets a new value every round. With layers `[Pass, Flat]`, round 2's guard reads `l` = Flat, although `prev` came from round 1's Pass. The push passes and may move `buf` to a bigger block, and `println(v)` reads the freed block. The list also leaves out an `owns` parameter, or an owned loop or pattern name, that is handed over or ended. In `run`, the guard at the push reads the type index in the header of a `B` that `mem.drop` already freed: the check itself reads freed memory, and if the block was reused its answer is garbage. The same happens when an index on the path changes between the call and the guard (`v = layers[i].paint(buf)`, `i += 1`).
holes.fix_hint: State the condition, not a list of declaration sorts. The kind is kept (one word) wherever, between the start of the danger and the guard, the path from the declaration may reach a different value or none at all: a name or place given another value (a loop name each round included), a value handed over or ended (an `owns` parameter, an owned loop or pattern name), an index or key that changes, an element replaced, removed or moved. The guard reads the live value's kind only where the compiler proves that the path still reaches the same live value. Change §X.4's row to match.

holes.program:
fn compose(layers: runtime Array[owns dyn Layer], ref mut buf: Array[u8]):
    views: Array[Span[u8]] = []
    for l in layers:
        views.push(owns l.paint(buf))   # each round begins a danger
    buf.push(owns 0)                    # guarded: which round's kind?
    println(views)

# Flat and Pass as above; `layers` built from input as [Pass, Flat]
holes.what_goes_wrong: The danger began at a different call in every round, and every round's view is still alive at the guard. Point 4 says "the kind the value had at the line that began the danger", and §X.4 and point 8 promise "one word in a register or the frame". One word kept per call line holds only the last round's kind. Here that is a Flat, so the push passes, `buf` may move, and `println(views)` reads round 1's view into the freed block. The rule never says what is kept when the number of live views from different starts is not known when compiling: a list or map of views, or an Option carried across rounds.
holes.fix_hint: Tie the kept fact to the holder of the views, not to the call line. For each local holder, keep one bit, set at every start whose kind makes a later line unsafe and cleared when the holder is emptied or given a new value. The guard tests the bit (still one word, in the frame), and the stop names the first round that set it. Where the holder is not a local of the function (a field, a returned value), the line stays E3021.

fn frame(ref mut r: runtime owns dyn Renderer, scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
    r = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)
    f = r.draw(scratch)
    r = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)   # guarded: passes after a Software's draw

fn main():

    scratch: Array[u8] = [0]

    scratch.push(owns 1)          # guarded by `r`'s word: compares `r`'s kind at the call

Point 4 checks "the kind the value had at the line that began the danger (the call that gave the view)". In `main` that call is `frame(...)`. With inputs `soft`, then `gpu`, `r` is a Gpu before the call and after it, but the draw inside `frame` was a Software, so `f` views `scratch`. `main` compares a Gpu, the push passes, `scratch` moves, and `println(f)` reads freed memory. Neither moment the caller can see (before or after the call) gives the kind of the draw inside the callee. The same happens with `static mut ACTIVE` toggled inside the callee, and when the callee picks which element of a covered list makes the view (`layers[this.top]`).
holes.fix_hint: A guard compares only a kind its own function reads at the start of the danger. A caller may use an argument's kind at the call only when the callee's summary is decided by that argument's kind and the callee neither changes it (it is passed read-only and reached by no field or static the callee changes) nor chooses among several covered values. Otherwise the caller's line stays E3021, with the help "make the call that gives the view here: `f = r.draw(scratch)`", which compiles.

struct Logged implements Renderer:
    inner: owns dyn Renderer
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        println("draw")
        return this.inner.draw(scratch)

fn main():
    s = input()
    inner: owns dyn Renderer = owns Software(unused=0) if s == "soft" else owns Gpu(pixels=[0])
    r: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Logged(inner=inner) if s != "plain" else owns Gpu(pixels=[0])
    scratch: Array[u8] = [0]
    frame = r.draw(scratch)
    scratch.push(owns 1)          # stops for input `gpu`: a Logged wrapping a Gpu
    println(frame)
holes.what_goes_wrong: The guard compares only the outer kind. Because a Software may reach `Logged.inner` somewhere in the program, `Logged` counts as a kind that makes the push unsafe. So for input `gpu`, a correct program (a Logged around a Gpu, whose frame views the Gpu's pixels) stops at the push, with verdict 157's message "`r` is a `Logged`, whose `draw` gives back the buffer it was handed", which is false. Wrappers and composites are common (logging, caching or profiling renderers, UI containers, server middleware), and a recursive composite (a Layer holding Layers) cannot be decided by "one type-id compare" at all.
holes.fix_hint: Where a kind's danger is decided by a value it holds and reaches by a fixed path (`this.inner`), let the guard follow that value's kind too: one compare per level, and a loop for a kind that holds its own interface. The stop names the chain ("`r` is a `Logged` whose `inner` is a `Software`"). Where the path is not fixed, the stop's message says "may give back", and §X.4 states the cost per level.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule says the word lets lines "do what one kind of that value would make unsafe". But its mechanism, cost and help speak only of E3021 ("The word only turns an E3021 into a check"). A refusal that holds for one kind only and carries another code stays refused with the word written, and its help never mentions `runtime`. Here that is E3063 for the returned view of a local. The same holds for E3020 (a Yours's list walked by `for x in p.rows(xs):` while `xs.push(owns x)`), for E3060 (a view put in through `ref mut` by one kind, `[LT-47]`), and for a kind-dependent `drop` effect (P05). One word then has two reaches, and the correct Mine program cannot be written.
holes.fix_hint: Let the word turn every refusal that holds only for some of the kinds reaching a covered value into a guard at the refused line, with the same compare: E3020 at the change, E3060 at the use, E3063 at the return or at the owner's end, where the stop names the exit line. Otherwise, say plainly that the word covers only E3021, and give those codes a help that compiles.

safety.notes:
The safety lens finds three high holes and three medium holes. All of them are in the run-time half of the rule, point 4 ('which kind is checked') and the cost it promises. None is in the placement half. The placement itself (after the colon, before the whole type, on every declaration that writes a type, plus `runtime this`) keeps every guarantee for the cases the design lists, and its refusals (nothing to check, inside a type, a bodiless function, the wrong place) are sound.

The three high holes share one cause. Point 4 ties the kept kind to 'the call that gave the view' and to a list of declaration sorts, and §X.4 prices it as one word. Safety needs the kind of the value each live view came from, at the moment it was made, read by the function that holds the guard.
(1) The list leaves out loop names, owns parameters and owned names that are handed over or ended, and changing indices. The `owns a: runtime A` case makes the guard itself read a freed header.
(2) Views from many rounds in one holder need a bit per holder, not a word per call line.
(3) A view returned by a callee that changes or chooses the covered value cannot be checked in the caller, so the caller's line must stay E3021.

The medium holes:
(4) A wrapper or composite kind is stopped with an untrue message.
(5) Kind-dependent E3063, E3020 and E3060 refusals are not turned into checks, against the rule's own statement of what the word means.
(6) The deny-list form is sound only in a closed world, and nothing says when the set of kinds is closed across packages (EFF-4). HR-44 covers a reload if adding a kind behind a dyn counts as a changed fact.

The data-race claim holds: OBJ-1 keeps the type index at its own offset, apart from the atomic counts. Static mut access is confined by THR-20.

Not raised as holes, for the lead or for other lenses:
- the stop message says '`this.renderer` is a `Software`' after the field already holds a Gpu ('was ... at line N' reads true; message wording is the lead's);
- a field's word makes a line stop in a function (`tick`, or another package) that writes no word of its own (design risk 5, a readability and verdict-152 question for the engineering lens);
- the effect the check carries under @nopanic(explicit) and @no_alias_checks is P14's (K58).

Verdicts 152, 157, 162 and 163 keep their programs under every fix proposed here. Each fix sharpens point 4 or §X.4. None changes where the word is written.

    views: Array[Span[u8]] = []
    for l in layers:
        views.push(owns l.paint(buf))   # the danger begins once per round, each with that round's kind
    buf.push(owns 0)                    # unsafe if ANY round's layer was an Overlay
    println(views)

fn main():
    first: owns dyn Layer = owns Overlay(unused=0) if input() == "o" else owns Sprite(pixels=[1])
    layers: Array[owns dyn Layer] = []
    layers.push(owns first)
    layers.push(owns Sprite(pixels=[2]))
    buf: Array[u8] = [9]
    draw_all(layers, ref mut buf)

# second form: the danger begins inside a callee that gives the field another value

    renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer
    scratch: Array[u8] = []
    fn redraw() -> Span[u8]:
        this.renderer = owns Software(unused=0) if input() == "s" else owns Gpu(pixels=[0])
        f = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)
        this.renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[1])   # guarded in redraw: stops if the draw's kind was a Gpu
        return f
    fn render():
        frame = this.redraw()
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)            # the field holds a Gpu here on every run
        println(frame)

In draw_all the danger begins at every round, with a different kind each time, and the loop name is given another value each round. Typed `o`, round 1 is an Overlay (views[0] points into buf) and round 2 a Sprite. The one kept word holds Sprite at `buf.push(owns 0)`, so the compare passes, the push may move buf, and `println(views)` reads freed memory. The rule names no kind to check when two lines began the danger, and its stated cost (one word) cannot hold one kind per round. In render, the kind that began the danger is the one at redraw's own draw, which render cannot see. Before the call the field holds whatever init gave; after it, always a Gpu. Comparing either one lets `frame`, which points into scratch when `s` was typed, dangle. Point 4's list of names that 'may be given another value' (variable, field, static mut, ref mut parameter) also leaves out loop names and list elements.

Where the danger begins inside a callee that may give the value another kind before returning, refuse the caller's line (E3021, naming the callee's line), or return the flag. For a field, the spec never says which kinds count as reaching it. Under a per-field set, this program is refused at the push. Under a per-type set, or with a second Scene somewhere else, it compiles and stops for certain at run time. If each `scene.render()` call is followed (as parameters are, per call), the call with the Software is refused even when a Gpu Scene exists. So whether a program compiles depends on precision that the specification leaves open. Open risk 2 says this precision decides 'how many lines get a check, not what the word means'. It also decides compile-or-run, which is the owner's (verdict 152).
holes.fix_hint: Write into LT-1 how kinds are followed, with EFF-2's model for function values (verdicts 122, 128): each field of each type apart from every other, a list's elements with the place that holds it, a parameter with every argument given to it. 'Known when compiling' is then a rule. Correct open risk 2, and put the compile-or-run consequence in the question.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule's one meaning is 'may do what one kind of that value would make unsafe', yet its mechanism (compiler_does 3) handles only lines that 'would be E3021'. DSP-5 gives a dyn call the effects of every implementation the program has, not those of the kinds that reach the value. So whether `runtime` turns replay's walk refusal (E3020, decided by one kind's effects) into a check is undecided, a case nobody has asked about. Function values are refused with the reason 'a function value's result is decided by its type (LT-7)'. That is true for views and untrue for effects, which EFF-2 and verdicts 122 and 128 decide by what reaches the place, just as kinds decide a dyn call. One code-word compare would check `w` as one type-id compare checks `s`. The exclusion is a special case resting on half a reason.
holes.fix_hint: Either state that runtime covers only dangers decided by where a kind's result points (E3021), give the reason, and have E3020's message say so; or make it cover every danger that one kind or one function decides. That means following kinds for effects per place, as EFF-2 follows function values, and accepting runtime on a function type checked by a code-word compare. Put the choice to the owner.

engineering.notes:
P18 checked through the engineering lens; I only read files, nothing was run. The ordinary program is unchanged and the field form is shorter, so readability holds. Two high holes, both in the check's mechanism rather than in where the word goes:
(1) Point 4 keeps one kind. The danger can begin many times (a loop collecting views) or inside a callee that gives the field another kind before returning. The kept word then lets a dangling view through. A kept flag per guarded line fixes it (one OR at each line that begins the danger), or a refusal for the callee case.
(2) The guard is a list of bad kinds built from the bodies one build can see. Across a package edge (EFF-4, BLD-14 interface files) a downstream kind passes it. A per-method bit in each kind's own table is one load and one test whatever the number of kinds, fails safe across packages, and also removes the k-compares cost. The design widens the word to pub fields but does not raise dyn-per-kind-design.md open question 8.
Six medium holes:
- The guarded-line wording does not reach the push line, so read literally the rule refuses its own examples.
- `runtime this` is option D's before-name form, which the design rejects everywhere else; `owns runtime this` uses the word order it refuses for types; and the premise that a local cannot carry the word for `this` holds only when `this` changes while the local is used.
- How precisely kinds are followed into fields decides whether a program compiles (verdict 152 'a'), not only how many checks there are.
- The spec_text says a callee is checked 'under its own declarations', yet the field word guards tick and render, which wrote no word. Against verdict 152's placement, and disclosed only as a risk.
- A private field reached through a pub getter is undecided (verdict 108).
- Whether runtime covers dangers decided by one kind's effects (E3020) is unsaid; the refusal on function values rests on a reason that holds for views only (EFF-2, verdicts 122 and 128).
Low: inferable types written only to carry the word; struct vs non-open class refusal; GRM-41, BLD-14, nameless variant fields and const missing from the change list; the 'nothing in any object' cost claim. Verdicts 157, 162 and 163 hold as the design says. P12 (holder forms) and P14/K58 (effect kind) are deferred correctly, but K58's option (a) ('the runtime word is refused') cannot be applied to a word written on another declaration's field. design.rule:
`runtime` is a word of a declaration, and it means the same thing wherever it is written. Without it, the compiler refuses a line that would be unsafe for only some of the kinds that may reach a value the declaration covers. With it, the program checks that line while it runs instead. The line stops exactly where the compile-time check would refuse it if it had known this run's kinds, and nowhere else.

Where it goes. One rule covers every declaration:
- If the declaration writes a type, or could write one, the word goes right after the `:` and before the whole type. That covers a parameter of any function with a body (lambdas included), a variable, a field of a struct, class or enum variant, and a static.
- If the declaration cannot write a type, the word goes directly before the name, after the name's own words. That covers:
  - a loop's or a pattern's name;
  - a name opened with `exists as` or `is ... as`;
  - a `with` name and a capture;
  - a method's `this`: `fn layout() runtime this:`, and `owns runtime this` for a method that takes its object over.

What it covers: every `dyn` value and every value of an `open` or `abstract` class that the declared value holds, at any depth. It also covers every name, view and capture taken from it, in code that can name the declaration.

How it is checked. The compiler does all of this:
- Each kind keeps an answer in its own table for each method that gives back a view: which of the call's arguments (`this` included) the view may point into. The package that compiles the kind writes this answer. A kind that passes the call on to a value it holds has that value's answer.
- At a call through a covered value, the program reads the answer once, from the value the call runs on. It keeps it as one word with the name the view goes into.
- The refused line is the one that changes, walks, uses or ends what the view may point into while the view is still used. That line tests the kept words and stops if one is set, and the stop names the kind. The line never reads the value again.
- The compiler finds which kinds may reach a value the same way it follows function values (`[EFF-2]`): each field on its own, a list together with the place that holds it, and each call of a function on its own. If every kind known when compiling makes the line safe, or every one makes it unsafe, the word changes nothing.

Limits:
- A function's lines are guarded only by declarations those lines can name: the function's own declarations, and the fields and statics the lines name. A caller's word never reaches the lines of a function it calls.
- A view returned by a call carries the kept answer only where the caller can read that answer at its own call.
- The word is never part of a type.
- It checks only where a view points. What a call through `dyn` may change is the same for every kind (`[DSP-5]`), so there is nothing there for it to check.
design.spec_text:
This changes:
- `[LT-48]` (rewritten) and one sentence of `[LT-1]`;
- the grammar (`field_decl`, `variant_field`, `static_decl`, `lambda_param`, `opened_name`, `with_item`, `capture`, the name forms of `primary_pattern`, `fn_takes`, and the notes on `param` and `var_decl`);
- `[LEX-15]` (its `runtime` entry), and one sentence each in `[GRM-3]` and `[GRM-41]`;
- `[BLD-14]` (one sentence, and a new item 8) and `[HR-44]` (one sentence);
- the `runtime` row of §X.4, the help of the `E3021` row, and the references of the `E3020`, `E3060` and `E3063` rows;
- J1-01's lead-fix sentence, and Annex H.

`[LT-48]` *(new in 0.9.15)* *(changed in 0.9.15_Hardened_12)* **`runtime`: a value's kind checked while the program runs.**

`runtime` on a declaration lets a line run that would otherwise be refused when compiling only because some of the kinds that may reach a value the declaration covers make it unsafe (`[LT-1]`). The line is checked while the program runs, and it stops the program when, in this run, the kind that gave the view makes it unsafe. It stops where the compile-time check would refuse it if that check had known this run's kinds (including the kinds of the values a kind passes the call on to), and nowhere else. The word means this on every declaration it is written on.

1. *Where it is written.*
   - On a declaration that writes or can write its type, right after the `:` and before the whole type, holder words included:
     - a parameter of a function, method, local function or lambda that has a body (`fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker):`, `fn(p: runtime dyn Picker):`);
     - a variable (`renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)`);
     - a field of a struct, a class or an enum variant (`renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer`, `Filled(item: runtime owns dyn Item)`; a nameless variant field puts it before its type, `Filled(runtime owns dyn Item)`);
     - a `static` or `static mut` (`static mut ACTIVE: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0])`).
   - On a declaration that cannot write a type, directly before its name and after its name words:
     - a loop's or a pattern's name (`for runtime e in level.spawn_wave(n):`, `for ref mut runtime e in wave:`, `Event.Spawn(runtime e):`);
     - a name opened with `exists as` or `is ... as` (`if level.find(id) exists as runtime e:`);
     - a `with` name (`with runtime r = make_renderer():`);
     - a capture (`fn() owns runtime p:`);
     - a method's object, in the place where `[GRM-41]` puts its words: `fn layout() runtime this:`, and `fn finish() owns runtime this:` for a method that takes its object over.

2. *What it covers.*
   - Every `dyn` value and every value of an `open` or `abstract` class that the declared value holds, at any depth: the value itself, a list's elements, an `Option`'s contents, a link's target, and a field of a struct it holds. Examples: `p: runtime dyn Picker`, `a: runtime shares mut Unit`, `target: runtime weakref Unit`, `layers: runtime Array[owns dyn Layer]`, `tool: runtime Option[owns dyn Tool]`.
   - Every name, view and capture taken from such a value: a local, a loop's, a pattern's or an opened name, a capture, an owner it was handed to.
   - A view a call gives is taken from the declaration it points into (`[LT-22]`). Inside the declaration's package, that is decided by what the called function's code shows. Across a package's edge, it holds only where the function's first line names the declaration with `from` (`[BLD-14]`).
   - So a `pub fn active() -> ref dyn Renderer` in another package, which gives a view of a private field, carries no word. Its caller declares one: `r: runtime dyn Renderer = scene.active()`.

3. *Whose lines it guards.* It guards code that can name the declaration:
   - for a parameter, a variable, an untyped name or `this`: its function, after the declaration, the lambdas in it included (verdict 163);
   - for a field or a static: every function that names it, in every package its visibility reaches.

   A function's lines are guarded only by declarations they can name: the function's own declarations, and the fields and statics its lines name. A caller's word does not reach a function it calls: `show(p)` with `fn show(p: dyn Picker):` is `E3021` in `show`, with the help `fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker):`. A field's word, on the other hand, guards every line that names the field, including lines in a function that wrote no word of its own: `fn tick(ref mut scene: Scene):` doing `f = scene.renderer.draw(scene.scratch)`, `scene.scratch.push(owns 2)`, `println(f)`.

4. *Which lines.* A line is guarded when the compile-time check would refuse it only because of one thing: a view that a call through a covered value gave may point into what the line touches, and whether it does depends on that value's kind. The cases:
   - a change, reshape, hand-over or end of what the view may point into while the view is used (`E3021`): `this.scratch.push(owns 1)` after `frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)`, or `mem.drop(owns a)` after `r = a.first(xs)`;
   - a change of a list that a generator the call gave walks (`E3020`);
   - a use of a view put in through `ref mut` after the argument it may point into changed (`E3060`, `[LT-47]`);
   - a `return` of the view, or the end of what it points into while it lives on (`E3063`): `return p.pick(tmp)`.

   The guarded line does not have to name the covered value.

5. *How it is checked.*
   - **The answer.** For each method that gives a view (a result, a view put in through `ref mut`, a generator), a kind's table holds one word: which of the call's arguments, `this` included, that view may point into. The package that compiles the kind works this out from the method's code (`[LT-22]`) and writes it there.
   - **A kind that passes the call on.** Example: `Logged.draw` doing `return this.inner.draw(scratch)`. Such a kind has the answer of the value it passes the call on to, read at the same call, level by level. That holds as long as the value is reached from the object or an argument through fields, `Option` contents and list elements, and the method changes nothing on that way before it calls. Otherwise, its answer is that the view may point into every argument such a value may give back, and its stop says "may give back".
   - **Reading and keeping it.** At the call, the program reads the answer once, from the value the call runs on. It keeps the answer with each name the view goes into, as one word that is either empty or names the kind. The word is:
     - set when the view is put in the name (a list or an `Option` keeps every view put in it since it was last given a whole new value);
     - copied when the view is copied;
     - replaced when the name is given a whole new value;
     - set and cleared exactly where the compile-time check would add and end the loan.
   - **The guarded line** tests the kept words of the names that still hold such a view, and stops if one names a kind. It never reads the covered value again.
   - Examples:
     - `frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)`, then `this.renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0])`, then `this.scratch.push(owns 1)`, then `println(frame)`. If the renderer was a `Software` at the draw, the push stops, whatever the field holds by then. If it was a `Gpu` at the draw, the reassignment stops, because it ends the pixels `frame` looks at.
     - `for l in layers:` doing `views.push(owns l.paint(buf))`, then, after the loop, `buf.push(owns 0)` and `println(views)`. The push stops if any round's layer gave back `buf`, and names the first such round.
     - `prev = Some(l.paint(buf))` at the end of each round, and `buf.push(owns 0)` at the start of the next. The push stops when the previous round's layer gave back `buf`, whatever this round's layer is.
     - `r = a.first(xs)`, `mem.drop(owns a)`, `xs.push(owns 2)`, `println(r)`. An `A` stops at the drop. A `B` passes the drop and stops at the push, without reading the freed `a`.

6. *A view a call gives.* A function's result, or a view it puts in through `ref mut`, carries a kept answer to its caller only where the caller can read that answer at its call. That is the case when the function gives back views it was given, or what a call through one of its arguments (or through a value in it: a field, an `Option`'s contents, each element of a list) gives, and the function changes nothing on that way before the call.
   - Then the caller copies the kept words of those arguments, or reads those values' answers at its own call. Example: `fn via(p: dyn Picker, xs: Array[int]) -> Span[int]: return p.pick(xs)`, called as `r = via(p, xs)` with `p: runtime dyn Picker`.
   - Otherwise, the view may point into whatever any kind there may give back, exactly as without the word. That is `E3021` at the caller's line, with the help "make the call that gives the view in this function, or pass in the value whose kind decides it". Examples: a function that gives its `ref mut` parameter another value before drawing, that sets a `static mut` first, or that picks which element of a list draws by data of its own.

7. *Which kinds may reach a value, and what the word changes.* The kinds that may reach a value (`[LT-1]`) are followed the way `[EFF-2]` follows function values:
   - each field of each type on its own, apart from every other;
   - a list's elements together with the place that holds the list;
   - a local with the values that may be in it at the line;
   - a parameter for each call on its own, just as a generic is checked for each type it is given. Verdict 151's `show(Mine(items=[9]))` and `show(Yours(items=[9]))` are two separate checks.

   Where code that another package compiles may put a value there (a `pub` function's parameter, a `pub` field, what another package's function gives back), any kind may reach it. Then:
   - Where no kind that may reach the value makes the line unsafe, the line compiles with no check, with or without the word.
   - Where every one of them makes it unsafe, and all of them are known when compiling, the line is refused, with or without the word. For example, `show(Yours(items=[9]))` is refused at `xs.push(owns 3)` (verdict 152).
   - In every other case the line is refused without the word, and checked with it.
   - A call from another package that gives a `pub` function's parameter a kind known when compiling, where that kind's answer makes one of the function's guarded lines stop, is refused at the call, naming that line. The package's interface file records each guarded line, with the argument and method that decide it (`[BLD-14]`).

   A line that compiles without the word compiles in the same way with it.

8. *What it does not check.* It checks only what depends on where a view points.
   - What a call through a `dyn` or `virtual` method may change, read or end is that of every implementation the program has, whatever the kind (`[DSP-5]`, `[EFF-2]`). So a refusal that comes from what a call may change (for example `E3020` for a call that may change the list a loop walks) never depends on the kind. It is refused as it would be without the word, and its message offers no `runtime`.
   - A function value's view is decided by its type (`[LT-7]`), and what it changes by every function the program puts in its place (`[EFF-2]`). So no line depends on which function a place holds, and the word has nothing to check on a function value.

9. *It is not part of a type* (`[GRM-3]`).
   - `fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker)` is a `fn(dyn Picker)`.
   - A value is given to the name exactly as it would be without the word.
   - An implementation or override may write the word or leave it out, whatever its interface or base class says.
   - Layout, construction and hot reload are unchanged.

10. *Where it is refused* (`E0104`; the codes are the lead's). Each message gives the line to write.
    - On a type that holds no `dyn` value, no value of an `open` or `abstract` class and no type parameter, so has nothing to check: `count: runtime int`, `g: runtime Gadget` with `class Gadget` not open, a `const`, or `f: runtime fn(Span[int]) -> Span[int]` (with point 8's reason). Message: "remove `runtime`".
    - On a parameter of a function with no body. Help: "write it on the parameter of the implementation that needs it".
    - Inside a type (`Array[runtime owns dyn Shape]`, `fn(runtime dyn Picker)`). Help: "write `shapes: runtime Array[owns dyn Shape]`".
    - Before the name of a declaration that can write its type, or after a type's first word (`runtime p: dyn Picker`, `runtime x = e`, `fn(runtime p):`, `owns runtime dyn Renderer`). Help: "write `p: runtime dyn Picker`"; for a variable or a lambda parameter written without a type, the help gives the line with its type written.
    - On a name whose every value already comes from a covered declaration, the word is said twice. A warning names the declaration that already says it.

11. *Its stop and its help.*
    - The stop happens at the guarded line, and names the line, the view and the path. For a parameter: "panic at main.em:17:5: `xs` changes while `r` looks at it: `p` is a `Yours`, whose `pick` gives back the list it was handed". For a field: "`this.renderer` is a `Software`". For a kind that passes the call on, the chain: "`r` is a `Logged`, whose `inner` is a `Software`".
    - When a refusal from point 4 comes from a kind known only while running, its help names the declaration of the name the call runs on:
      - `fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker):` for `p`;
      - `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer` for `this.renderer`;
      - `fn layout() runtime this:` for `this`;
      - `for runtime e in level.spawn_wave(n):` for a loop over a new value.
    - Where the call runs on what another call gives, the help names a variable to hold it: `r: runtime dyn Renderer = scene.active()`.

12. *Its cost* is the one given in §X.4.

`[LT-1]`: after "followed through its names and calls", add "(which kinds may reach a value: `[LT-48]` point 7)".

Grammar (Part III):
```
param         := [param_word] IDENT ":" ["runtime"] type ["..."] ["=" expression]   -- `runtime` ([LT-48]): before a type that holds a `dyn`, open or abstract class, or type-parameter value
var_decl      := IDENT ":" ["runtime"] type ["=" expr_list]                         -- the same
field_decl    := ["let"] IDENT ":" ["runtime"] type ["from" (IDENT | "static")] ["guarded" "by" IDENT] ["=" expression] NEWLINE
variant_field := {attribute} [IDENT ":"] ["runtime"] type
static_decl   := "static" ["mut"] IDENT ":" ["runtime"] type ["guarded" "by" IDENT] "=" expression NEWLINE
lambda_param  := [param_word] IDENT [":" ["runtime"] type]
fn_takes      := "owns" ["runtime"] "this" | "runtime" "this" | capture_list
capture       := capture_word ["runtime"] (IDENT | "this")
opened_name   := [name_word] ["runtime"] IDENT | "(" opened_name {"," opened_name} [","] ")"
with_item     := [["runtime"] IDENT "="] expression
primary_pattern := ... | ["ref" ["mut"]] ["runtime"] IDENT | ...                    -- replaces `IDENT` and `"ref" ["mut"] IDENT`
```

`[LEX-15]`: the entry "`runtime` after the `:` of a parameter or a variable and directly before a type" becomes: "`runtime` directly before the type of a declaration that writes one (after its `:`, or first in a nameless variant field), and directly before the name of a loop's, a pattern's, an opened or a `with` name, a capture, or `this`, after their name words (`[LT-48]`)".

`[GRM-3]`, add: "`runtime` is a word of a declaration, not of a type (`[LT-48]`). No type contains it, including a function type's parameter and a type argument."

`[GRM-41]`: "`owns this`, for a method that takes its object over" becomes "`owns this`, `runtime this` or `owns runtime this`, for a method's object (`[LT-48]`)".

`[BLD-14]`, add after its first sentence: "The one fact that a line reads while the program runs is a kind's answer for `runtime` (`[LT-48]`): which of a method's arguments the view it gives may point into. The package that compiles the kind works it out from the method's code and writes it in the kind's table, and it decides, in any package, whether a guarded line stops." Add as item 8: "for a function whose view may point into an argument depending on a kind: which argument and which method decide it; and for a `pub` function, each line `[LT-48]` guards, with the argument and the method that decide it."

`[HR-44]`, add: "This includes which kinds may reach a value, where a line was compiled with no check because none of them made it unsafe (`[LT-48]`). A reload that lets a new kind reach such a value is refused, unless the reload rebuilds that code. A kind's `runtime` answer is read while the program runs, so changing a kind's method changes its answer with no refusal."

§X.4, the row "A `runtime` declaration's check | guaranteed present | only where a line is unsafe for some of the kinds that may reach a covered value and not others (`[LT-48]`). At the call that gives the view: one load of the kind's answer from the table the call already reads, and one store of the kept word; one more load and test for each level where a kind passes the call on; one load per element where a caller reads the answers for a callee that passes on a call through each element of a list. At the guarded line: one test of each kept word the line depends on, and a branch that is never taken. Memory: one word for each name that may hold such a view, in a register or the frame (the generator's frame across a `yield`), and one word of static data per view-giving method in each kind's table; nothing in any object. None where the kinds known when compiling decide the line."

`E3021` row, help: "`runtime` on the declaration of the name the call runs on: its parameter, variable, loop or pattern name, the field or static it names, or `this`; or a variable to hold what a call gives". The `E3020`, `E3060` and `E3063` rows add `[LT-48]` to their references.

J1-01's lead fix: "a value marked `runtime`" becomes "a value reached through a declaration marked `runtime`".

Annex H: "Verdict N: `runtime` goes on every declaration: after the `:` where a type is written, and before the name where none can be, `this` included. It covers every `dyn` and class value inside the declared value, and it is checked through the kind's answer, read at the call that gives the view and kept with the view (`[LT-48]`, `[LT-1]`, the grammar, `[LEX-15]`, `[GRM-3]`, `[GRM-41]`, `[BLD-14]`, `[HR-44]`, §X.4, `E3021`)."

answers.answer:
A field may say `runtime`. It is a declaration that writes a type, so the word goes right after its colon. It guards every line that names the field: the class's own methods (`this.renderer`) and any other code that can name the field (`scene.renderer` in `tick`), which writes no word of its own.

At the draw, the program reads the renderer's answer and keeps it with `frame`. The push then tests that kept word. Construction, the field's type, and every line that is safe for both kinds are unchanged.
answers.code:
interface Renderer:
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]

struct Gpu implements Renderer:
    pixels: Array[u8]
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return this.pixels.as_span()       # a view of its own pixels

struct Software implements Renderer:
    unused: int
    fn draw(scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]:
        return scratch.as_span()           # a view of the buffer it was handed

class Scene:
    renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer    # which kind is known only while running
    scratch: Array[u8] = []

    fn render():
        frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)   # the answer is read here, kept with `frame`
        this.scratch.push(owns 1)          # tests `frame`'s kept word
        println(frame)

fn tick(ref mut scene: Scene):
    f = scene.renderer.draw(scene.scratch)
    scene.scratch.push(owns 2)             # names the field: guarded by its word
    println(f)

fn main():
    r: owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)
    scene = Scene(renderer=r)
    scene.render()
    tick(ref mut scene)
answers.outcome:
Compiles.
- Typed `gpu`: both `render` and `tick` print their frames.
- Typed anything else: the program stops at line 20 with "panic at main.em:20:9: `this.scratch` changes while `frame` looks at it: `this.renderer` is a `Software`, whose `draw` gives back the buffer it was handed". `tick`'s push is checked the same way, with no word written in `tick`.
- Without the word: `E3021` at line 20, with the help "write `runtime` on the field: `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer`".

answers.answer:
A lambda's typed parameter takes the word right after its colon, because a lambda with a body is a function with a body. The word guards the lambda's lines and does not change the lambda's type.

A lambda parameter can always write its type, just as a variable can (verdict 163's spelling). So a parameter written without a type writes its type to carry the word, and `fn(runtime p):` is refused with the typed line as its help.
answers.code:
interface Picker:
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]

struct Mine implements Picker:
    items: Array[int]
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return this.items

struct Yours implements Picker:
    items: Array[int]
    fn pick(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return other

fn main():
    xs = [1, 2]
    check = fn(p: runtime dyn Picker):    # a lambda's parameter
        r = p.pick(xs)
        xs.push(owns 3)
        println(r)
    p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])
    check(p)
answers.outcome:
Compiles. `check` is a `fn(dyn Picker)`.
- Typed `m`: prints `[9]`.
- Typed anything else: stops at `xs.push(owns 3)` with "`xs` changes while `r` looks at it: `p` is a `Yours`, whose `pick` gives back the list it was handed".
- Written as `fn(p):`, the push is `E3021`, with the help "write the parameter's type with `runtime`: `fn(p: runtime dyn Picker):`". `fn(runtime p):` is refused with the same line.

answers.answer: The word stands before the whole type, holder words included, on every holder form P12 allows before a `dyn` or class type: `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`, `ref`, `ref mut`, `sharedref mut`. It also stands before any type that holds one of these, at any depth. Verdict 163's `runtime owns dyn Renderer` is the model.
answers.code:
open class Unit:
    let items: Array[int] = [7]
    virtual fn first(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return this.items

class Archer(Unit):
    override fn first(other: Array[int]) -> Span[int]:
        return other

fn main():
    u: Unit = Unit() if input() == "u" else Archer()
    a: runtime shares mut Unit = shares mut u     # before the whole type
    xs = [1]
    r = a.first(xs)
    xs.push(owns 2)
    println(r)
answers.outcome:
Compiles.
- Typed `u`: prints `[7]`.
- Typed anything else: stops at `xs.push(owns 2)` with "`xs` changes while `r` looks at it: `a` is an `Archer`, whose `first` gives back the list it was handed".
- `a: shares mut runtime Unit` is refused, with the help `a: runtime shares mut Unit`.
- The same holds for `target: runtime weakref Unit` opened with `exists as` (the opened name is taken from it), and for `units: runtime Array[shares mut Unit]`.

other_cases.case: A static: `static mut ACTIVE: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0])`, changed by a settings function, and `fn frame(ref mut scratch: Array[u8]):` doing `f = ACTIVE.draw(scratch)`, `scratch.push(owns 1)`, `println(f)`.
other_cases.settled: Allowed, because a static writes a type. Every line that names `ACTIVE` is covered, so `frame` compiles. `ACTIVE`'s answer is read at the draw and kept with `f`, and the push stops if `ACTIVE` was a `Software` at that moment, whatever the settings function sets later. Without the word: `E3021`, with the help `static mut ACTIVE: runtime owns dyn Renderer = ...`.

other_cases.case: The name is given another kind between the call and the guarded line: `frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)`, then `this.renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0])`, then `this.scratch.push(owns 1)`, then `println(frame)`.
other_cases.settled:
The answer is read at the draw and kept with `frame`.
- A `Software` at the draw: the reassignment passes, and the push stops, even though the field now holds a `Gpu`.
- A `Gpu` at the draw: the reassignment stops, because it ends the pixels `frame` looks at.
Neither line reads the field's kind again. The same holds for a variable (verdict 163), a `static mut` and a `ref mut` parameter.

other_cases.case: Views kept across rounds in an `Option`: `fn compose(layers: runtime Array[owns dyn Layer], ref mut buf: Array[u8]):` with `prev: Option[Span[u8]] = None`. For each `l in layers`, it does `buf.push(owns 0)`, `if prev exists as v: println(v)`, then `prev = Some(l.paint(buf))`. The layers are `[Pass, Flat]`, and `Pass.paint` gives back `buf`.
other_cases.settled: Round 1's `Pass` answer (it points into `buf`) is kept with `prev`. Round 2's push tests `prev`'s word and stops, with "`buf` changes while `prev` looks at it: a `Pass` from `layers` gave back the buffer it was handed (round 1)". The guard never reads `l`, which is a `Flat` by then. When `prev` is given round 2's view, its word is replaced, so a `Flat` round never stops the next one.

other_cases.case: Views kept across rounds in a list: `for l in layers:` doing `views.push(owns l.paint(buf))`, then `buf.push(owns 0)` and `println(views)` after the loop. The first layer is an `Overlay` (it gives back `buf`), the second a `Sprite`.
other_cases.settled: Each round's answer is added to `views`'s word, which keeps the first kind that set it. The push stops and names the `Overlay` of round 1. The word is replaced only when `views` is given a whole new value: emptying the list does not clear it, just as emptying it does not end the loan when compiling.

other_cases.case: An owned value ended between the call and the guard: `fn run(owns a: runtime A, ref mut xs: Array[int]):` doing `r = a.first(xs)`, `mem.drop(owns a)`, `xs.push(owns 2)`, `println(r)`, with verdict 162's `A` and `B`.
other_cases.settled:
At the call, `a`'s answer is kept with `r`: an `A`'s `first` points into `a`, and a `B`'s points into `xs`.
- An `A` stops at the drop, which would end what `r` looks at.
- A `B` passes the drop, `a` is freed, and the push stops on `r`'s kept word. The freed header is never read.
The same holds for an owned loop or pattern name that is handed over.

other_cases.case: The index on the path changes: `v = layers[i].paint(buf)`, `i += 1`, `buf.push(owns 0)`, `println(v)`.
other_cases.settled: The answer is read from `layers[i]` at the call and kept with `v`, so changing `i` changes nothing at the push. Replacing, removing or moving that element while `v` looks into it is itself a guarded line, which stops for a kind whose view points into the element.

other_cases.case: A wrapper: `struct Logged implements Renderer` holds `inner: owns dyn Renderer`, and its `draw` prints, then does `return this.inner.draw(scratch)`. `r` is chosen from input: a `Logged` around a `Gpu`, a `Logged` around a `Software`, or a plain `Gpu`. Then `frame = r.draw(scratch)`, `scratch.push(owns 1)`, `println(frame)`.
other_cases.settled:
`Logged.draw` passes the call on to `this.inner` and changes nothing on the way, so a `Logged` has its inner's answer, read at the same call.
- A `Logged` around a `Gpu` prints its frame.
- A `Logged` around a `Software` stops, with "... `r` is a `Logged`, whose `inner` is a `Software`, whose `draw` gives back the buffer it was handed".
A kind that holds its own interface (a `Group` of layers giving its first child's view) is followed level by level, one load and one test per level. Ownership has no loops (`[WK-1]`), so the walk always ends. A method that gives its `inner` another value before drawing, or picks the child by data it computes, has the answer 'may point into the buffer', and its stop says 'may give back'.

other_cases.case: Two callees. First: `fn via(p: dyn Picker, xs: Array[int]) -> Span[int]: return p.pick(xs)`, called as `r = via(p, xs)` in `main` with `p: runtime dyn Picker`. Second: `fn frame(ref mut r: runtime owns dyn Renderer, scratch: Array[u8]) -> Span[u8]` gives `r` a kind chosen from input, draws, gives `r` another kind, and returns the frame. `main` then does `f = frame(ref mut r, scratch)`, `scratch.push(owns 1)`, `println(f)`.
other_cases.settled:
`via` passes the call on to its argument `p` and changes nothing on the way. So `main` reads `p`'s answer at its call to `via`, and `main`'s push is checked.

`frame` gives `r` another value before its draw, so `main` cannot read the kind that drew. `f` may point into `scratch`, and in every run in which `frame` returns it does, because a `Gpu` draw stops at `frame`'s second reassignment. So `main`'s push is `E3021`, as it should be. The same applies to a callee that sets a `static mut` before drawing, or that picks which element of a list draws by data of its own (the `Scene.redraw` and `render` pair included). The help: make the call that gives the view in this function, or pass in the value whose kind decides it.

other_cases.case: Two packages. `engine` has a `pub class Scene` with `pub renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer`, and its `render` draws, then pushes; `engine` itself knows only `Gpu`. `game` adds `Software` and `Raster`, which give back the buffer, and builds against `engine`'s interface file.
other_cases.settled:
Another package may put a value in a `pub` field, so `engine`, compiled alone, places the check at `render`'s push.
- `game`'s `Raster` carries its own answer in its table, written when `game` compiles it, so the push stops for a `Raster`. A `Gpu` prints.
- Nothing depends on which kinds `engine` saw, and `engine`'s code does not change when `game` adds kinds.
- A `game` call that gives an `engine` `pub` function's `runtime` parameter a kind known when compiling, whose answer makes a guarded line stop, is refused at `game`'s line, which names `engine`'s line. This is verdict 152 across the package edge.

other_cases.case: A private field reached through a `pub` function: `engine` has `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer` (private) and `pub fn active() -> ref dyn Renderer: return this.renderer`. `game` does `f = scene.active().draw(scene.scratch)`, `scene.scratch.push(owns 1)`, `println(f)`.
other_cases.settled: `game` cannot name the private field, and `active`'s first line shows no word, so `game`'s line is `E3021`. Its help: hold the view in a variable with the word, `r: runtime dyn Renderer = scene.active()`, then draw through `r`. That compiles, and then `game`'s own declaration says the line may stop. Inside `engine`, `this.active().draw(this.scratch)` is covered, because `engine` can name the field.

other_cases.case: A returned view of a local: `fn longest(p: runtime dyn Picker) -> Span[int]:` with `tmp = [4, 5, 6]` and `return p.pick(tmp)`.
other_cases.settled: Covered (`E3063`). `p`'s answer is kept with the result. The `return` stops when the result points into `tmp`, which ends there: "`tmp` ends at this `return` while the returned view looks at it: `p` is a `Yours`, whose `pick` gives back the list it was handed". A `Mine` returns its own items. Callers see the result pointing into `p` only.

other_cases.case: Two walks. First: `interface Rows: fn rows(xs: Array[int]) -> Generator[int]`, where one kind walks its own list and another walks `xs`; then `for x in p.rows(xs): xs.push(owns x)` with `p: runtime dyn Rows`. Second: `fn replay(s: runtime dyn Sink):` doing `for line in LOG: s.write(line)`, where `Memory.write` pushes to `LOG`.
other_cases.settled:
The first is checked. Which list the generator walks is where its view points, so `p`'s answer is kept with the walk, and the push stops for the kind that walks `xs`.

The second is refused (`E3020`), with or without the word. What `s.write` may change is what every implementation may change (`[DSP-5]`), whichever kind `s` is, so no kind makes the loop safe. Its message offers no `runtime`.

other_cases.case: A function value: `w: runtime fn(String) = memory_write if input() == "m" else println`.
other_cases.settled: Refused with "remove `runtime`". A function value's view is decided by its type (`[LT-7]`), and what it changes by every function the program puts in its place (`[EFF-2]`). So no line depends on which function `w` holds, and there is nothing to check.

other_cases.case: Held and opened forms: `tool: runtime Option[owns dyn Tool] = None`, then `if this.tool exists as t:` doing `r = t.apply(this.buf)`, `this.buf.push(owns 0)`, `println(r)`. The same with `target: runtime weakref Unit`, a `Map`'s values, a tuple's elements, and an enum variant field `Filled(item: runtime owns dyn Item)` opened by `match`.
other_cases.settled: Covered: `t` and `item` are taken from the marked declarations. A nameless variant field puts the word before its type: `Filled(runtime owns dyn Item)`.

other_cases.case: A capture: `p: runtime dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])`, then a lambda `report = fn():` whose body does `r = p.pick(xs)`, `xs.push(owns 3)`, `println(r)`.
other_cases.settled: Covered: the lambda reaches `p` through a capture taken from it (verdict 163). A capture of an unmarked value may carry the word itself (`fn() owns runtime q:`). The answer is kept when the lambda's own call runs, so a lambda that runs later is safe too.

other_cases.case: A method whose line depends on its own object's kind: `open class Widget` has `let label: Array[int] = [1]` and `virtual fn measure(buf: Array[int]) -> Span[int]: return this.label`, and `class Wide(Widget)` gives back `buf` instead. `fn layout():` does `buf = [0]`, `m = this.measure(buf)`, `buf.push(owns 9)`, `println(m)`.
other_cases.settled:
`this` writes no type, so the word goes before it, in the place where `[GRM-41]` puts the object's words: `fn layout() runtime this:`. A method that takes its object over writes `owns runtime this`: the name's words, then `runtime`, then the name, as in `for ref mut runtime e`.
- A `Widget` prints `[1]`.
- A `Wide` stops at the push.
A variable `me: runtime Widget = this` would also compile, but would exist only to carry the word. Without the word: `E3021`, with the help `fn layout() runtime this:`.

other_cases.case: A new value handed straight to a loop: `for e in level.spawn_wave(n):` doing `h = e.hitbox(scratch)`, `scratch.push(owns 0)`, `println(h)`.
other_cases.settled: No declaration holds the list, so the loop's name carries the word: `for runtime e in level.spawn_wave(n):`. Without it: `E3021`, with that line as the help. A loop over a marked declaration (`for e in wave:` with `wave: runtime Array[owns dyn Enemy]`) needs no word. Writing it there anyway is said twice, and a warning names `wave`'s line.

other_cases.case: A function with no body: an interface method with no default body, an `extern` function, or an `abstract` method, written with `fn paint(r: runtime dyn Renderer)`.
other_cases.settled: Refused: a function with no body has no lines to check. The help says to write the word on the parameter of the implementation that needs it. An implementation or override may write the word or leave it out, and an interface's default body may carry it.

other_cases.case: The wrong place, or nothing to check: `Array[runtime owns dyn Shape]`, `fn(runtime dyn Picker)`, `runtime p: dyn Picker`, `runtime x = e`, `owns runtime dyn Renderer`, `count: runtime int`, `g: runtime Gadget` (with `class Gadget` not open).
other_cases.settled: Each is refused with the line to write: `shapes: runtime Array[owns dyn Shape]`; `fn(p: runtime dyn Picker): ...` on the stored function; `p: runtime dyn Picker`; `x: runtime T = e`; `runtime owns dyn Renderer`; and "remove `runtime`" for `int` and for a class that is not open, since a `Gadget` is always a `Gadget`. A type parameter (`item: runtime T`) is accepted; an instance whose `T` holds no kind checks nothing.

other_cases.case: Several declarations on one path, or two values in one danger: `fn tick(scene: runtime Scene)` together with the field `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer`; or `r = a.pick(b.pick(xs))`.
other_cases.settled: There is one test per kept word the line depends on, however many declarations cover the value. In `r = a.pick(b.pick(xs))`, both answers are read at their calls. The inner view is passed to the outer call as an argument, so if the outer answer points into that argument, it carries the inner word on. If either value is covered by no declaration, the line stays `E3021`, and the message names it.

other_cases.case: A `thread_shared dyn` value, or a static, read on another thread under the word.
other_cases.settled: A kind's answer is written once in its table and never changes, so reading it needs no lock on any thread. The kept word lives in the reading thread's frame.

other_cases.case: A hot reload adds a kind that reaches a value whose function the reload does not rebuild, where that function was compiled with no check because the kinds it knew were all safe.
other_cases.settled: Refused (`E9030`, `[HR-44]`): restart, or rebuild that code. A reload that changes a kind's method changes the kind's answer in its table. Guards read the answer while running, so that change needs no refusal.

other_cases.case: A `pub` field read in another package: `scene.renderer.draw(buf)` in a game's own module.
other_cases.settled: Covered, because the word is part of the field's written declaration, which a `pub` interface shows. The other package's line may stop, as the library's declaration says it may.

design.prior_art:
C++: nothing ties a check to a declaration, and nothing tracks whether a virtual call's result aliases an argument. A `std::span` or an iterator into a `std::vector` after `push_back` is undefined behaviour. A programmer can write `typeid(*r) == typeid(Software)` or a `dynamic_cast` at each use, and a forgotten one fails silently. Per-type data does live in the vtable and its `type_info`, which is where Ember puts a kind's answer.

Rust: borrows are decided by signatures. A `dyn Trait` call's result is tied to the lifetimes the trait method declares, for every implementation, so the Picker program is refused for every kind unless the trait is rewritten. Rust's vtables carry per-type facts (size, alignment, drop), the same place Ember's answer goes. Its run-time route is `RefCell`, a type that can go anywhere a type can: a flag word in every value, a read-modify-write at every borrow, and longer code at every use.

Swift: exclusivity is enforced statically where it can be. Elsewhere (class properties, globals, escaping captures; in release builds too, since Swift 5) the runtime records each access in a per-thread access set, a cost on every such access. Its one declaration word, `@exclusivity(unchecked)`, governs every access through a stored property or a global: the same per-declaration placement as here, used to switch checks off.

Ada: run-time accessibility checks. An access parameter carries its accessibility level as an implicit extra word, passed along with the value and compared where the value is stored. That is the nearest prior art to Ember's kept word: a fact read where the value arises, carried with it, and tested at the dangerous line. Ada also has `pragma Suppress (Check, On => Entity)`, which attaches a check decision to a named object, type or subprogram and governs every use of it.

Zig: `@setRuntimeSafety` applies to a block scope, not to a value.

C# and Go: a garbage collector keeps a view's target alive. Go's slices alias silently after `append`. C# refuses `Span<T>` in class fields when compiling.

Where each falls short:
- C++, and Zig with safety off, are unsafe.
- Rust's run-time route costs memory in every value and work at every access.
- Swift's checks cost every unproven access.
- Ada's accessibility word is about lifetimes, not kinds.

Ember takes Ada's and Swift's per-declaration placement, Rust's generality (anywhere a value is held, at any depth), the vtable as the home for a per-type fact, and the owner's visible word (verdict 152). It pays only at the calls and lines that would otherwise be refused.
design.cost:
At each call through a covered value whose view a guarded line depends on:
- One load of the kind's answer. The answer sits in the kind's table beside the method's slot, which the call already loads, so it is on the same cache line. Then one AND, and one store of the kept word, usually into a register.
- For a kind that passes the call on, one more load and test per level.
- Where a caller reads the answers for a callee that passes a call on through each element of a list, one load per element.

At each guarded line:
- One test of each kept word the line depends on (usually one), and a branch that is never taken.
- Together with the call: about three instructions per dangerous view.

Memory:
- One word for each name that may hold such a view, in a register or the stack frame. A generator's frame holds it across a `yield`.
- One word of static data per view-giving method in each kind's table, in every program.
- Nothing in any object, and nothing per value.

Where the cost is zero:
- Any line the word does not guard.
- Any line where the kinds known when compiling decide it.
- Any program that compiles without the word, apart from the static table word.
- No compare against a list of kinds: the number of kinds, and which package made them, do not change the cost.

Against the other languages:
- C pays nothing at the line, and has the bug: a span into a vector after `push_back` is undefined behaviour.
- C++ with a hand-written `typeid` pays one compare at each use the programmer remembers.
- Rust's `RefCell` costs a flag word in every value, plus a read-modify-write at the start and end of every borrow.
- Swift's run-time exclusivity costs a call into the runtime at every access it cannot prove.
- Ada's accessibility check costs one hidden word per access parameter, as Ember's kept word does.

Compile time:
- LT-1's per-kind check, as today.
- One answer word per view-giving method for each kind compiled.
- Following kept words where views flow, which is the same walk as the loans of the borrow check.

readability.note:
The ordinary program pays nothing. A game loop, a server handler or a parser with no line whose safety depends on a kind known only while running has no word, before or after, and compiles to the same code.

The rare program (a renderer chosen at startup, a wave of enemies) writes the word once: at the field, or on the loop's name. Before, it needed a variable in every method and every loop only to carry the word. The after is shorter by one line per use, and the word sits where the declaration says what the value is.

The 'before' is the only spelling that compiles today. It rests on the J5-08 reading that a bare `dyn` local may view a value.

design.compiler_does:
1. It reads `runtime` in its two places:
   - right after the `:` of every declaration that writes a type (parameters of functions with bodies, lambdas included; variables; fields of structs, classes and enum variants; statics);
   - directly before the name of a declaration that cannot write a type (loop, pattern, opened and `with` names, captures, `this`).
   It refuses the word in every other place, and wherever nothing in the type has a kind. Each refusal gives the line to write, and the word said twice gets a warning.
2. For every kind it compiles, it writes into the kind's table, beside each method that gives a view, the method's answer: which of the call's arguments (`this` included) that view may point into, worked out from the method's code (LT-22). For a method that passes the call on along an unchanged way of fields, `Option` contents and list elements, it writes instead a small function that reads that value's answer, level by level. Otherwise it writes 'may'.
3. It runs LT-1's per-kind check, following kinds per LT-48 point 7: each field of each type on its own, a list with its place, a local by the values that may be in it at the line, a parameter for each call on its own. A place another package can fill may hold any kind.
4. Where a line would be refused (E3020, E3021, E3060, E3063) only for some of the kinds, and the call that gives the view runs on a value covered by a declaration the line's code can name:
   - It makes that call read the answer and keep it with each name the view goes into.
   - It carries the kept words wherever the loans go: names, lists, `Option`s, structs, copies, the result of a callee that passes the call on, and a view put in through `ref mut`.
   - It places a test at each point where the line is lowered: a `defer`'s body at each exit; a generator's frame keeps the word across `yield`s.
5. Otherwise it reports the refusal. The help names the declaration of the name the call runs on, or a variable to hold what a call gives. It never names a field the line cannot name.
6. It records in the interface file each `pub` function's guarded lines and the arguments and methods that decide them, and each function's view that a kind decides (BLD-14, item 8). It refuses at the call a call from another package that gives a known kind which would stop one of those lines.
7. It emits the stop with verdict 157's message, naming the path (for a wrapper, the chain).
8. It leaves alone the declared type, the function's type, construction, layout, hot reload (apart from HR-44's check of added kinds) and every other line.
design.verdicts:
All verdicts involved keep their programs and outcomes. What changes is the text of LT-48's mechanism.

- 151: the per-kind check when compiling is unchanged. Which kinds reach a value is now written down (LT-48 point 7). For a parameter it is per call, which 151's two calls need.
- 152: the word on the parameter, its program (`fn show(p: runtime dyn Picker):`, `p: dyn Picker = Mine(items=[9]) if input() == "m" else Yours(items=[9])`, `show(p)`) and both outcomes stay. A visible `Yours` is refused when compiling, with or without the word; across a package's edge it is refused at the call. A caller's word never reaches the lines of a function it calls.
  Said plainly: a field's or a static's word guards lines in functions that wrote no word of their own (`tick`). Option D is the reading in which every stopping line's own function says it.
- 157: both messages stay. For a field the stop names the path, and for a wrapper the chain. `E3021`'s help names the declaration to mark; its wording is the lead's.
- 162: kept. The word also covers class values held inside a type (a list, an `Option`, a link, a struct's field), which 162 did not show. Said plainly, this extends the verdict; it does not change its program.
- 163: kept, written in Ember as `renderer: runtime owns dyn Renderer = owns Gpu(pixels=[0]) if input() == "gpu" else owns Software(unused=0)` (TYP-45). Its reason, 'No function is needed only to carry the word', is why fields, statics, lambda parameters, untyped names and `this` take the word themselves rather than through a variable. Its LT-48 text, 'checks the kind at the line that would be unsafe', is replaced by 'reads the kind's answer at the call that gives the view and keeps it'. Read literally, the old text lets a variable given another value in between, or a loop's next round, through. 163's own program and outcome are unchanged.
- Principle 2 / 108 (a library's promise is written out): the word on a `pub` declaration is written. A view given out of a private field reaches another package only through a written `from`.
- 122, 128, 129: their model for following function values is used for kinds, except that a parameter is followed per call, which 151 and 152 need.
- 141: function values stay decided by their type, and `runtime` is refused on them, now with the full reason (LT-7 and EFF-2).
- 147, 149, 159, 160, 161 are followed in every example.
- 164 to 166 are not touched.

Nothing is reversed.

recommendation.reason: One word with one meaning on every declaration. It sits where the declaration says what the value is: with the type where one is written, before the name where none can be. `this` is an instance of that rule, not a special case. Nothing is exempted for missing syntax (checklist 12), and no variable exists only to carry the word (verdict 163's reason). The compiler does the rest: it reads each kind's own answer at the call, keeps it with the view, and tests it at the line. That is sound for a loop's rounds, reassigned or ended values, wrappers, and kinds from other packages. The cost is about three instructions per dangerous call and line, and nothing in any object or in any ordinary program. Verdicts 152, 157, 162 and 163 keep their programs. B needs a variable only to carry the word, C cannot cover a list of interface values, D needs a variable in every method, and E reverses verdict 152.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: `auto frame = renderer->draw(scratch); scratch.push_back(1); use(frame);` dangles when the `unique_ptr<Renderer>` member holds the subclass whose `draw` returns `scratch` itself. Ember refuses this, and your word `runtime` turns the refusal into a check at the `push_back`. Two things need deciding. First, may the word go on a class member, a static, a lambda's parameter, a loop's name and `this`, and before a `shared_ptr`, a `weak_ptr` or a `vector<unique_ptr<...>>`, with the same meaning it has on a parameter and a variable? Second, the check must read the kind at the `draw` and keep the answer, because the spec's 'check the kind at the push' lets a loop's next round, or a variable given another value, through.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `r` is made a `Gpu` or a `Software` from what the player typed, and `scene = Scene(renderer=r)` keeps it in the field `renderer` | `scene.renderer` is a `Software`, known only while running |
| 2 | `render` runs `frame = this.renderer.draw(this.scratch)` | a `Software` gives back the buffer it was handed, so `frame` points into `this.scratch` |
| 3 | `this.scratch.push(owns 1)` | the list may move to a bigger block, leaving `frame` pointing at freed memory |
| 4 | `println(frame)` | would read freed memory (in C++, a span into a vector after `push_back`). So Ember refuses step 3 when compiling (`E3021`), and its help offers `runtime` only "on the parameter or the variable": the field cannot carry it |
owner_short.today:
`runtime` may go only on a function's parameter (verdict 152) or a local variable (verdict 163), before a `dyn` or class type. A field, a static, a lambda's parameter, a loop's name, `this`, and the word before `shares mut A` or `Array[owns dyn I]` are undecided, so `render` gets its check only through an extra variable in every method.

The spec also says the kind is checked 'at the line that would be unsafe'. For a variable given another value in between, or a loop whose views from earlier rounds are still used, that reads the wrong kind and lets a dangling view through.
owner_short.options:
A: the word on every declaration: after the colon where a type is written (field, static, enum field, lambda parameter, as on parameters and variables), and before the name where none can be (a loop's or pattern's name, `exists as`, a capture, `this`). It covers every dyn or class value inside the declared value.
B: only where a type is written. A loop over a new value and a method's own object each get a variable only to carry the word (`me: runtime Widget = this`).
C: fields and typed lambda parameters only, before an outermost dyn or class type. A list of interface values cannot carry it.
D: no word on fields. Each method, and each outside function, declares a variable to carry it (J1-11 b).
E: no word. The compiler checks wherever it would otherwise refuse (Swift's way; this reverses verdict 152).
A to D all share the repaired check: the kind is read at the `draw`, and the answer is kept with the view and tested at the push.
owner_short.recommendation: A: one word, one meaning, on every declaration, and no variable only to carry it (your reason in 163). It costs about three instructions at the dangerous call and line, and nothing anywhere else. Your verdicts 152, 157, 162 and 163 keep their programs and outcomes.

repairs.answer:
Point 4 is gone, and no list of declaration sorts remains. The kind's answer is read once, at the call, from the value the call runs on, which is live there. It is kept with the name the view goes into. The guarded line tests only that kept word and never reads the value again.
- `compose` stops at round 2's push because of round 1's `Pass`.
- `run` stops at the drop for an `A`, and at the push for a `B` without reading the freed `a`.
- Changing `i` changes nothing.
§X.4's row no longer has a condition on reassignment.

repairs.hole: Safety: a danger begun at a different call in every round, with every round's view still alive. One kept word per call line holds only the last round's kind, and a list, map or Option of views is not handled.
repairs.answer:
The kept word belongs to the name that holds the view, not to the call line.
- It is set at every call that puts a view in the name; a list or an `Option` keeps every view put in it.
- It is replaced when the name is given a whole new value.
- It follows exactly the compile-time loan, so emptying a list does not clear it, just as emptying does not end the loan when compiling.
`draw_all` with `[Overlay, Sprite]` stops at the push and names round 1, and a `Flat` round never stops the next one. It is still one word per name, in a register or the frame. A view that leaves the function is covered by LT-48 point 6.

repairs.hole: Safety: the danger begins inside a callee (`frame` reassigns `r`, draws, reassigns). The caller compares `r`'s kind before or after the call, and neither gives the kind that drew. The same holds for a `static mut` toggled in the callee, or a callee choosing the element.
repairs.answer: LT-48 point 6: a view a call gives carries an answer to the caller only where the caller can read it at its call, meaning the callee passes on a call through an argument (or a value in it) and changes nothing on that way. `frame` gives `r` another value before drawing, so `main`'s push is `E3021`. That is right: in every run where `frame` returns, `f` views `scratch`, because the `Gpu` path stops at `frame`'s second reassignment. A toggled static, or an element chosen by the callee's own data, is `E3021` too, with the help to make the call here or pass the value in. `via` (a plain pass-on) works. The caller never compares an argument's kind.

repairs.answer:
LT-48 point 5: a kind whose method passes the call on to a value it holds, along a way it does not change, has that value's answer, read at the same call, level by level. The compiler puts a small function for it in the kind's table.
- A `Logged` around a `Gpu` prints.
- A `Logged` around a `Software` stops, naming the chain.
- A `Group` of layers is followed level by level; ownership has no loops (WK-1), so the walk ends.
Where the way is changed or chosen by data, the answer is 'may', and the stop says 'may give back'. This is exactly what the compile-time check would say knowing the run's kinds. The cost is one load and one test per level (§X.4).
