- OWNER-DIRECTION.md principles and checklist; owner-bar.md; brief.md; phase1 P20 and the other groups' principles; phase2 J2-05; phase3 K41

Nothing was edited or run.

design.rule:
A place of type `Option[T]` takes every value that a place of type `T` takes at that same site. It does to the value exactly what the `T` place does there, then holds the result as `Some`.
- Where the `T` place takes the value (`=` from a whole name, `return`, a field, a constructor's argument, an `owns` argument, an element, a default), the `Option` holds the value taken.
- Where the `T` place reads or views the value in place (a plain parameter, a name bound to a part), the `Option` is a read-only `Some` over the caller's own value. Nothing is handed over, copied or ended.

What the `T` place refuses, the `Option[T]` place refuses with the same error.

Every conversion goes in at most three steps, in one order for every rule: read through views and owners (and erase a range), then at most one other conversion, then the wrap.

The wrap applies only where a value is given:
- never to a `ref mut` argument, which is the caller's own place and must already be an `Option[T]`;
- never to an operator's operand, whose type comes from the other operand.

The wrap is one level only. An existing `Option` is never wrapped again and never converted inside.

The branches of a conditional or `match` expression, and the elements of a tuple being written, are sites of their own. So `return w if ok else None` and `return (n, line)` convert.

A view held inside an `Option` is an address, as it is in a written `Some(...)`.

In generic code, the wrap is decided once, where the body is checked.
design.spec_text:
This changes:
- [TYP-5] (p04-types.md 71-73, the sites; 89-91, rule 11; 100-102, the closing paragraph);
- [TYP-23] (p04-types.md 839-841);
- [BRW-8] (p07-ownership.md 403-416), one sentence added;
- [BRW-16] (p07-ownership.md 421-430), one sentence added.

Nothing else changes. The `Option[owns T]` case of [OWN-10] (p07-ownership.md 104-116) and `E2123` stand as written: under rule 11 they are simply what the `T` place asks for.

[TYP-5] opening, replaced:
  At a coercion site (assignment or initialisation, argument, return, field initialiser, collection element, default value, an element of a tuple being written, and a branch of a conditional expression or an arm of a `match` expression given to one of these), and only there, a value converts implicitly by exactly these rules. A branch or an arm converts on its own, to the type the site expects. An element of a tuple being written is taken as a constructor's argument is (`[OWN-9]`) and converts to its element's type.
  A `ref mut` or `const ref mut` argument, and a place given to a `ref mut` name, is not a value but the caller's place. It is given as it is: a place of the expected type, reached through views and owners as `[TYP-14]` reads them. It converts by no rule except rule 6's `ref mut` form, which makes a new span over its elements (`[FN-1a]`). So both of these are `E2020`:
  - `clear_slot(ref mut hp)` for `fn clear_slot(ref mut slot: Option[int])` and `hp: int`, with the message "`clear_slot` may set its slot to `None`, and `hp` is an `int`, which cannot hold `None`; declare `hp: Option[int] = 10`";
  - `ref mut s`, where `s` is an `owns Sword`, for a parameter `ref mut w: owns dyn Weapon` (the callee could put an `Axe` in a `Sword`'s place).

[TYP-5] rule 11, replaced:
  11. a value given to an `Option[T]` place, as `Some` of it, when `T` is not itself an `Option` and the value neither is nor reads as an `Option` (`[TYP-14]`). The value converts to `T` by the steps below, with that site's words. The place then does to it exactly what a `T` place does at that site:
  - Where a `T` place takes the value (`=` from a whole name, `return`, a field, a constructor's argument, an `owns` argument, an element, a default), the `Option` holds the value taken.
  - Where a `T` place reads or views the value in place (a plain parameter, `[FN-1]`; a name bound to a part, `[BRW-12]`), the `Option` is a read-only `Some` over that same value. Nothing is handed over, copied or ended, and an operation through it (a lock taken, `[BRW-15]`) reaches that value.
  What a `T` place refuses, an `Option[T]` place refuses with the same error and the same fix. An untyped literal takes `T`. Examples:
  - `return v` in a function returning `Option[T]`;
  - `f(5)` for a parameter `x: Option[int] = None`;
  - `load("a", cfg)` for `fn load(name: StrView, opts: Option[LoadOptions] = None)`: `opts` reads `cfg` in place as `Some`, and `cfg` is still the caller's;
  - `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)` for `weapon: Option[owns dyn Weapon]` (rule 8; without `owns` it is `E2123`, as for an `owns dyn Weapon` place);
  - `s.on_hit = log_hit` for `on_hit: Option[OnHit]` (rule 10);
  - `cap: Option[u64] = n` after `n = 5` (rule 12);
  - `return this.cause` in `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` for `cause: owns dyn Error` (read through the owner, then a `ref` of the place).
  A value of type `Never` converts to the `Option` itself (rule 9).
  One level only: nothing is wrapped twice, and no `Option` is put inside a `Some` unless `Some(...)` is written. So `x: Option[Option[int]] = 5`, and `x: Option[Option[int]] = o` for `o: Option[int]`, are `E2020`, whose help writes `Some(...)`.
  The wrap does not apply to an operand of an operator (`[TYP-21]`), `in` included. An operand's type comes from the other operand, not from a place the program declared, and with `None < Some` a wrapped `cap < n` would be true when no cap is set. So `p.cap < n` and `hp == 5` for an `Option` are `E2020`. The help either opens the `Option` (`if p.cap exists as c:` and, inside it, `if c < n:`) or writes `Some(...)` (`hp == Some(5)`). `hp is None` and `hp == None` are unchanged.
  The wrap holds a view as a written `Some(...)` holds it: as an address (`[BRW-17]`, `[BRW-16]`).
  Whether a type is an `Option` is read where the code is checked. In a generic body a type parameter is not one, so `slot = v` for `slot: Option[T]` and `v: T` is `Some(v)` in every instance, `T = Option[int]` included (`[TYP-17]`).
  A type argument still to be inferred is inferred from the value as for a parameter of type `T`: `first(5)` for `fn first[T](x: Option[T])` takes `T = int` (`[TYP-18]`).

[TYP-5] closing paragraph, replaced:
  A value converts in at most three steps, in this order:
  1. It is read through a view or an owner (rule 7's reading through, only as far as the next step needs), and its range is erased (rule 3).
  2. At most one of rules 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7's `ref` of a place, 8, 10 and 12 applies.
  3. Rule 11's wrap applies.
  Rule 9 is a step on its own. So `y: i64 = r` for `r: ref i32` reads, then widens. `v: StrView = r` for `r: ref String` reads, then views. A range value converts by rule 12 once its range is erased, and `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)` is rule 8, then the wrap. No other chain converts.
  An existing value of a holder type (an `Option`, a `Result`, a tuple, a collection) converts as a whole only by a rule that names it (rules 5 and 6), never by converting what it holds:
  - `found: Option[owns Sword]` given to `weapon: Option[owns dyn Weapon]` is `E2020`, whose help gives `s.weapon = found.map(owns fn(owns w) => w)`;
  - `cam.focus = find_boss()` for `focus: Option[Enemy]` and `-> Option[Boss]` is `E2020`, help `cam.focus = find_boss().map(owns fn(owns b) => b)`;
  - `show_label(p?.name)` for `label: Option[StrView]`, where `p?.name` is an `Option[ref String]`, is `E2020`, help `show_label((p?.name).map(owns fn(owns n) => n))`.
  A tuple, list, map or set that is being written converts element by element, each element a site.
  There is no implicit `Ok`. A `Result[T, E]` place could take a value as `Ok` or as `Err` (`Result[int, int]` is a `Result`, `[ERR-1]`), so the line writes which. The argument of `Ok(...)`, `Err(...)` and `Some(...)` converts to its type by these rules, as any argument does. `Some(...)` is a constructor: its argument is taken as `=` takes it (`[OWN-9]`), so `load("a", Some(cfg))` hands `cfg` to the new `Option`.
  Nothing converts implicitly to or from `bool` or `char`.

[TYP-23], the sentence "a branch of a conditional expression that cannot type itself (`None`, `[]`) takes the other branch's type." replaced by:
  The type a site expects reaches each branch of a conditional expression, each arm of a `match` expression and each element of a tuple being written, and each converts on its own (`[TYP-5]`): `return w if w > limit else None` in a function returning `Option[int]`; `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4) if lvl > 3 else None`. With no type expected, a branch that cannot type itself (`None`, `[]`) takes the other branch's type, and a `None` branch makes the expression an `Option` of it, as `x = None` then `x = v` does: `x = w if w > limit else None` gives `x` the type `Option[int]`.

[TYP-23], one sentence added after "A lambda with unannotated parameters and no expected callable type is `E2061`.":
  An `Option[F]` place gives a lambda the expected callable type `F` (`[TYP-5]` rule 11): `b.on_click = fn() => println("start")` for `on_click: Option[Handler]`.

[BRW-8], one sentence added after "it is an ABI decision and cannot be observed.":
  A plain parameter of an `Option` type that is passed by address, and every read-only view of an `Option` (a `ref Option[T]`, a plain `this`, a local that views one), is the address of its payload, null for `None`: the layout of `Option[ref T]` (`[TYP-13]`). So:
  - a `T` read in place is given as `Some` of itself, by its own address (`[TYP-5]` rule 11);
  - an `Option` place is given by its payload's address;
  - `None` is given as null;
  - `as_ref()` on such a view is the view itself.

[BRW-16], one sentence added after "A list reached through a link ... gives addresses, `[BRW-17]`.":
  A view held inside a value (an `Option`, a struct, a tuple) is not a name for the element. It is a kept view, an address (`[BRW-17]`), whether the line writes `Some(...)` or `[TYP-5]` rule 11 wraps it. After `pick: Option[ref Enemy] = enemies[0]` for a struct `Enemy`, `enemies.push(...)` ends `pick`, as it ends `pick = enemies.get(0)` (`E3060`). The plain `boss = enemies[0]` stays a position.

answers.code:
interface Weapon:
    fn damage() -> int

struct Sword implements Weapon:
    edge: int
    fn damage() -> int:
        return this.edge * 2

type OnHit = fn(int)

fn log_hit(dmg: int):
    println("hit for", dmg)

struct Slot:
    weapon: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = None
    on_hit: Option[OnHit] = None

fn main():
    s = Slot()
    s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)     # rule 8, then Some
    s.on_hit = log_hit                 # rule 10, then Some
    n = 5
    cap: Option[u64] = n               # rule 12, then Some
    if s.weapon exists as w:
        if s.on_hit exists as f:
            f(w.damage())
    println(cap)
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints `hit for 8`, then `Some(5)`. Variations:
- `s.weapon = Sword(edge=4)` (no `owns`) is `E2123` with help `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)`, as for a plain `owns dyn Weapon` field.
- `cap: Option[u64] = x` for a parameter `x: int` is `E2020`, as `y: u64 = x` is.
- `if cap < n:` is `E2020`, with help `if cap exists as c:` then `if c < n:`.
- The explicit `Some(...)` lines still compile.

other_cases.case: An optional settings parameter given a named value: `fn load(name: StrView, opts: Option[LoadOptions] = None)` with `struct LoadOptions` holding `path: String`. `main` calls `load("a", cfg)`, then `load("b", cfg)`, then `println(cfg.path)`. The same with `fn plot(xs: Span[float], labels: Option[Array[String]] = None)` called `plot(xs, labels=names)`, then `println(names)`.
The same call written `load("a", Some(cfg))`.
other_cases.settled: `Some(...)` is a constructor, and its argument is taken as `=` takes it (verdict 159). So `cfg` goes into the new `Option`, and `println(cfg.path)` afterwards is `E3040`. The help says that `Some(cfg)` makes an `Option` of its own, and that to lend `cfg` for the call you write `load("a", cfg)`.

other_cases.case: A field or part read in place: `greet(name=p.name)` for `fn greet(name: Option[String] = None)` and a class object `p`; `label: Option[String] = p.name`; `s.label = p.name` for a field `label: Option[String]`.

A `ref mut` argument for an `Option` parameter: `fn disarm(ref mut slot: Option[owns dyn Weapon]): slot = None` called `disarm(ref mut w)` for `w: owns dyn Weapon`; `clear_slot(ref mut hp)` for `hp: int`; an `Option[MutSpan[int]]` parameter given `ref mut buf`.
other_cases.settled: `E2020` in each case. A `ref mut` argument is the caller's own place, and here it cannot hold `None`. The help declares the place as an `Option` (`w: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = owns Sword(edge=4)`, `hp: Option[int] = 10`). Nothing is put in a temporary, and no change is lost (verdict 13). The same sentence refuses `ref mut s` for `s: owns Sword` given to `ref mut w: owns dyn Weapon`, a hole that exists today.

other_cases.case: An optional view of a list element: `pick: Option[ref Enemy] = enemies[0]` for a struct `Enemy`, then `enemies.push(owns Enemy(hp=9))`, then `if pick exists as e: println(e.hp)`.
other_cases.settled: `E3060` at the use. A view inside an `Option` is an address ([BRW-17]), as in a written `Some(enemies[0])` and in `enemies.get(0)`, and the push may move the buffer. The plain `boss = enemies[0]` stays a position that survives the push ([BRW-16]). The `Option[ref Enemy]` keeps the plain-pointer layout [TYP-13] promises.

other_cases.case: A tuple with an optional part: `fn count_field(line: StrView) -> (Option[int], StrView)` with `return (n, line)` and `return (None, line)`.
other_cases.settled: Both compile. Each element of a tuple being written is a site of its element's type, so `n` is wrapped and `None` takes `Option[int]`. An existing tuple `t: (int, StrView)` returned whole is `E2020` (a holder is not converted inside), with help `return (t.0, t.1)`.

other_cases.case: Conditional and `match` expressions: `return w if w > limit else None` in a function returning `Option[int]`; `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4) if lvl > 3 else None`; `return match kind: "sword" => owns Sword(edge=4), _ => None` for `-> Option[owns dyn Weapon]`; `x = w if w > limit else None` with no type written.
other_cases.settled: All compile. Each branch and arm is a site of the expected type and converts on its own (rule 8, then the wrap; `None` as it is). With nothing expected, the `None` branch makes `x` an `Option[int]`, as `x = None` then `x = w` does ([TYP-23]).

other_cases.case: Operators on an `Option`: `p.cap < n`, `p.cap < 5`, `used > p.cap` and `hp == 5` for `cap: Option[u64]`, `hp: Option[int]`.
other_cases.settled:
`E2020`, since an operand is not wrapped. Today `p.cap < 5` reads as `p.cap < Some(5)`, which is true when no cap is set (`None < Some`); that is Swift's `nil < 5`, which SE-0121 removed. The help:
- for an order: `if p.cap exists as c:` and inside it `if c < n:`;
- for `==`: `hp == Some(5)`.
`hp is None`, `hp == None` (ODR-227) and `hp == Some(5)` compile.

other_cases.case: An error's cause: `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]: return this.cause` for a field `cause: owns dyn Error`.
other_cases.settled: Accepted as `Some` of a read-only view of the cause: read through the owner, a `ref` of the place, then the wrap, exactly as `-> ref dyn Error` takes it. Today the line must be `return Some(this.cause)`.

other_cases.case: An optional callback filled with a lambda: `b.on_click = fn() => println("start")` for `on_click: Option[Handler]`, or `fn(d) => println(d)` for `Option[fn(int)]`.
other_cases.settled: Accepted. The lambda's parameters are typed from `Handler` / `fn(int)`, as for a plain callback field (the [TYP-23] sentence). It captures and outlives exactly as in a plain field (`E3026` if it would outlive a real variable it uses).

other_cases.case: A list literal and a view of a row: `fn defaults() -> Option[Array[int]]: return [1, 2]` (and `return []`); `fn row(i: int) -> Option[Span[f32]]: return this.rows[i]`.
other_cases.settled: Accepted by rule 5 or rule 6, then the wrap. The literal allocates exactly as the plain one does (`Alloc`, and `E4001` in `@noalloc`). The span has the region the plain `Span` result has, its source read from the body (verdict 137).

other_cases.case: Read-through chains: `best: Option[i64] = r` for `r: ref i32`; `v: Option[StrView] = r` for `r: ref String`; `m2: Option[Mesh] = m` for `m: owns Mesh`.
other_cases.settled: Each reads through first, then converts once, then wraps, as the plain place does (`y: i64 = r` and `v: StrView = r` now compile too). `m2` does whatever `y: Mesh = m` does (P11's question). If that is a view, the read-only view layout represents it. If it is a hand-over, the hand-over is wrapped. No further edit is needed either way.

other_cases.case: An `Option` of another type: `s.weapon = found` for `found: Option[owns Sword]`; `cam.focus = find_boss()` with `-> Option[Boss]` and `focus: Option[Enemy]`; `show_label(p?.name)` for `label: Option[StrView]`.
Generic code: `fn put[T](ref mut slot: Option[T], owns v: T): slot = v`, then `put[Option[int]](ref mut s, owns None)`.
other_cases.settled: The body is checked once, with `T` a parameter, which is not an `Option`. So `slot = v` is `Some(v)` in every instance, and with `T = Option[int]` the slot holds `Some(None)` ([TYP-17]). `slot = v` writes a value into the place `slot` names, so it is a site; the `ref mut` rule concerns the argument `ref mut s`, which is an exact `Option[Option[int]]` place.

other_cases.case: Two levels: `x: Option[Option[int]] = 5`, and `= o` for `o: Option[int]`.
other_cases.settled: `E2020`; the help writes `Some(Some(5))` / `Some(o)`. `x: Option[Option[int]] = Some(5)` compiles (the written `Some`'s argument is wrapped), and gives `Some(Some(5))`.

other_cases.case: Result's success side: `return out` in a function returning `Result[Map[String, int], E]`; `return Ok(owns Sword(edge=4))` for `-> Result[owns dyn Weapon, E]`.
other_cases.settled: There is no implicit `Ok`, so `return out` stays `E2020`. The argument of `Ok(...)` is an ordinary argument of type `T`, so the second line compiles, as today.

other_cases.case: List elements, constructor arguments and defaults: `[owns Sword(edge=1), None]` for `Array[Option[owns dyn Weapon]]`; `Slot(weapon=owns Sword(edge=4))`; `spawn("orc", weapon=owns Axe(edge=3))` for `owns weapon: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = None`.
other_cases.settled: All are accepted, each with its own site's words: the making-line `owns` (verdicts 85/97), a constructor's argument works as `=` (verdict 159), and an `owns` parameter's argument says `owns` (verdict 147). One `owns` serves both.

other_cases.case: A value that never completes, `x: Option[int] = panic("no config")`; an optional thread function, `on_done: Option[thread_shared fn()] = worker`; inference, `x = None` then `x = owns Sword(edge=1)`.
other_cases.settled: `Never` converts to the `Option` itself. `worker` is accepted where a plain `thread_shared fn()` place takes it and refused (`E7015`) otherwise; verdicts 164 to 166 are untouched. `x` is `Option[owns Sword]`, so a later `owns Axe` is `E2020`, with help `x: Option[owns dyn Weapon] = None`.

design.prior_art:
C++17 `std::optional<T>`
- The converting constructor `optional(U&&)` is implicit whenever `U` converts to `T`. So `std::optional<std::unique_ptr<Weapon>> w = std::make_unique<Sword>(4);` compiles: the wrap follows every conversion, which is this rule.
- The trap this design avoids: passing `cfg` to `const std::optional<LoadOptions>&` silently copies `cfg` into a temporary `optional`, a deep copy C never pays. The C idiom is `const LoadOptions*`, with NULL for none. That is exactly what Ember's reading `Option` parameter becomes: the caller's own address.
- C++ also follows lossy conversions (`optional<int> o = 3.9` stores 3), and it converts `optional<U>` to `optional<T>`.

Rust
- No implicit `Some`. The expected type flows into `Some(...)`'s argument, so the composition exists, paid for with `Some(...)` on every line.
- Rust separates `&Option<T>` from `Option<&T>` and converts with `.as_ref()`. Ember gives a read-only view of an `Option` the layout of `Option<&T>` itself, so the two are one, and `as_ref()` is free.
- `Option<Box<Sword>>` does not coerce to `Option<Box<dyn Weapon>>`; it needs `.map(...)`, as option A's help does.

Swift
- Injection composes with upcasts, existentials and function conversions, and is decided where generic code is checked (`func wrap<T>(_ v: T) -> T?` with `T = Int?` gives `.some(v)`), which is this rule's generic clause.
- `Optional<U>` to `Optional<T>` lifting is option C.
- The promotion inside operators made `nil < 5` true, and SE-0121 removed the optional comparison operators. This design refuses the wrap at every operand.

C#
- Lifted conversions S to T? and S? to T? (options A and C, value types only).
- The lifted relational operators return false when one side is null, a third meaning of `<` that Ember does not add.

Kotlin
- `T` is a subtype of `T?`, so upcasts compose and `Base?` takes a `Derived?` (C).
- `<` on `Int?` is refused, as here.

Zig
- `T` coerces to `?T` through any coercion of the child type (A).
- It does the same for `E!T`, which hides the success path. Ember keeps `Ok` written because `Result[int, int]` would be ambiguous.

The pattern: the languages that read best define the wrap by the payload's own conversions and keep it out of operators. C++ shows the two costs to avoid: lossy conversions and a hidden copy at a reading parameter.

readability.note:
The after is shorter and adds no new word.
- An optional field is filled the way a plain field is, and the `owns` that says who keeps the icon stays on the line (verdicts 85/97).
- An optional argument is given the way a plain one is. `show(b, tip)` lends `tip` for the call, as it would to a plain `String` parameter, so `tip` is printed afterwards. The before needed `Some(copy of tip)`, a deep copy, because a written `Some(tip)` takes `tip` (verdict 159).
- The before still compiles, so no existing program changes, except the lines that compare an `Option` with a plain value through an operator (`hp == 5`, `cap < 5`). Those become `E2020`, and the fix line is `hp == Some(5)` or the `exists as` form.
- The rare lines are two levels, converting an existing `Option` of one type into another, and a `ref mut` given a non-`Option` place. Only these need `Some(...)`, `.map(...)` or another declaration, and their messages give that line.

design.compiler_does:
At each coercion site whose expected type is `Option[T]`, the compiler works in this order.
0. It reads the site's kind.
   - A `ref mut` or `const ref mut` argument, or a place given to a `ref mut` name, is matched as a place of the exact type, through views and owners. The only exception is rule 6's `ref mut` span. Otherwise it is `E2020`, whose help declares the caller's place as the `Option`.
   - An operator's operand is never wrapped: `E2020`, whose help writes `Some(...)` or opens the `Option`.
   - A branch, an arm and an element of a tuple being written are each checked as their own site.
1. If the value is `None`, has type `Never`, or is or reads as an `Option` ([TYP-14]), it is matched against `Option[T]` as it is: an exact match, or `E2020`. The help names `Some(...)` for two levels, or `.map(owns fn(owns w) => w)` for another `Option` type.
2. Otherwise, if `T` is itself an `Option`, the result is `E2020` with `Some(...)`.
3. Otherwise it runs the ordinary check against `T` at the same site, with that site's rules: the making-line `owns` of [OWN-10], the call word of [FN-2a], a view's region, the expected callable type for a lambda, and the known-numbers rule of [STD-19]. The conversion goes in the fixed order: read through, then one conversion, then the wrap. Any refusal is reported in terms of the `Option` place.
4. It builds the `Some`.
   - Where the site takes the value, the converted value is stored as `Some`. No code is needed for a niche type; otherwise one tag store.
   - Where the site reads in place, it passes or holds the address of the value: the caller's own value, or the view value a conversion made, which owns nothing and is never dropped. `None` is given as null.

Every read-only view of an `Option` uses one layout, the payload's address or null ([BRW-8], the layout of `Option[ref T]`). So a plain `Option` parameter, a plain `this` of `Option`'s methods, a `ref Option[T]`, a generic instance at `T = Option[X]` and a `dyn` entry all agree. Making such a view from an `Option` place is a tag (or null) test and a select. A zero-sized payload is given any non-null aligned address. A `Copy` `Option` no larger than two pointers still goes by value, in registers ([BRW-8]).

In a generic body the check runs once, with `T` a type parameter, which is not an `Option`.

A function value put into an `Option` place is followed as in a plain function place (verdicts 122, 128 and 129). A wrapped view keeps its source and region (verdict 137) and is an address for [BRW-17]'s ending rules.

The programmer writes nothing new, and the program gains no code.
design.misuse:
Everything is refused when compiling; nothing is checked while running.
- A value the `T` place refuses is refused in the `Option[T]` place, with the same error and the same fix line. `s.weapon = Sword(edge=4)` is `E2123`; `cap: Option[u64] = x` for a parameter `x: int` is `E2020`.
- Nothing is handed over without a word. A plain `Option` parameter reads the caller's value in place, so `load("a", cfg)` leaves `cfg` usable, and `load("a", owns cfg)` stays refused (verdict 146). The read-only `Some` is the caller's own value, never a bit copy, so a lock taken through it is the caller's lock, and nothing is ended twice.
- No change is lost or put in a place that cannot hold it. A `ref mut` argument must already be an `Option` place. `disarm(ref mut w)` for an `owns dyn Weapon` and `clear_slot(ref mut hp)` for an `int` are `E2020`, and so is a `ref mut` upcast or interface conversion of any place.
- No surprising comparison. `cap < n` with `cap: Option[u64]` is `E2020`, never `None < Some(5)`.
- An `Option` never slips into another `Some`, and an `Option` of one type is never converted into another. So a `None` never quietly becomes a `Some`, and nothing is converted hidden inside a container.
- A wrapped view of a list element is an address: a push that may move the buffer ends it (`E3060`), so it never reads freed memory.
- A wrapped view that would outlive what it views is `E3063`, and a wrapped lambda that would outlive a variable it uses is `E3026`. A wrapped function that may not run on another thread is `E7015` at an `Option[thread_shared fn()]` place.
- A generic interface implemented for both `T` and `Option[T]` may meet `E2070` at an argument that reaches both through conversions, as it can today for rules 1 to 4. The help writes `I[A].m(...)`; the compiler never picks one silently.
- There is no undefined behaviour. Every wrap either stores what the written `Some(...)` stores, or passes the address of a live value that does not change while it is read ([BRW-1]).
design.verdicts:
- 85/97 kept: the line that makes a value for an `owns` place inside an `Option` says `owns` (`s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)`), and `E2123` stays without it.
- 5 kept, and now held at reading sites too: a plain `Option` parameter given a `T` reads the caller's value in place. It makes no silent copy (C++'s temporary `optional`) and no silent alias (a bit copy that would carry its own lock).
- 13 applied: a `ref mut` argument whose place cannot hold what the callee may write is refused, so no change lands in a temporary.
- 146 kept: `load("a", owns cfg)` stays an error, and `load("a", cfg)` now has a meaning, a loan.
- 150 kept: a function from a variable given to an `Option` parameter that reads is lent, as for a plain one.
- 158 kept: the `map` help writes `owns fn(...)`.
- 159 kept: a constructor's argument works as `=`, so the written `Some(cfg)` takes `cfg`, and the help says so.
- 147 kept: an `owns` parameter's argument says `owns`.
- 9 kept: `Some(...)` stays for making a value where no `Option` place is expected, and in a `match` arm.
- 122/128/129 and 137 kept.
- 164 to 166 untouched.

No verdict is revisited. One existing behaviour changes, and it is no verdict's: an operator no longer wraps its operand. `hp == 5` and `cap < 5` for an `Option` compile today through rule 11 at the operator's argument, and become `E2020`, fixed by `hp == Some(5)`.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. An `Option[T]` place takes whatever a `T` place takes there, after any one of the other conversions. It does what the `T` place does (a plain parameter lends, `=` hands over) and holds it as `Some`. A `ref mut` argument must already be an `Option`. An operator never wraps. Branches and tuple elements convert on their own. One level, and an existing `Option` is never converted inside.
options_for_owner.code:
s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)            # owns dyn Weapon, then Some
s.on_hit = log_hit                        # OnHit, then Some
cap: Option[u64] = n                      # after n = 5
b.on_click = fn() => println("start")     # lambda typed by Handler
load("a", cfg)                            # opts reads cfg in place
println(cfg.path)                         # cfg is still main's
s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4) if lvl > 3 else None
if cap < n:                               # E2020: open it first
found: Option[owns Sword] = owns Sword(edge=1)
s.weapon = found                          # E2020
s.weapon = found.map(owns fn(owns w) => w)   # compiles
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints `hit for 8`, then `Some(5)` and the config's path. `if cap < n:` is refused with the help `if cap exists as c:` then `if c < n:`. `s.weapon = found` is refused with the `map` line as its help. `Some(...)` written by hand still compiles.

options_for_owner.summary: As today: `Some` follows only widening, range erasure and the string conversions (rules 1 to 4). After any other conversion, the line writes `Some(...)`. The site rules of A (a plain parameter lends, `ref mut` needs an `Option` place, no wrap at operators, branches convert) are needed here too, since they answer `load("a", cfg)` with no conversion at all.
options_for_owner.code:
s.weapon = Some(owns Sword(edge=4))
s.on_hit = Some(log_hit)
cap: Option[u64] = Some(n)
b.on_click = Some(fn() => println("start"))
options_for_owner.outcome: The unwrapped lines are `E2020`, and an unannotated lambda into an `Option` of a function is `E2061`. With `Some(...)` written, the program compiles and prints the same. Readers must know which four conversions may come before the wrap.

options_for_owner.summary: A, and an existing holder whose type names each value it holds (an `Option`, either side of a `Result`, a tuple) also converts part by part, when each part converts. `None` stays `None`. Each part converts once, never with the wrap. A collection never converts this way, since that would mean a new buffer and a pass over every element.
options_for_owner.code:
found: Option[owns Sword] = owns Sword(edge=1)
s.weapon = found                 # Some(sword) becomes Some(weapon), None stays None
cam.focus = find_boss()          # Option[Boss] into Option[Enemy]
show_label(p?.name)              # Option[ref String] into Option[StrView]
return parse_sword(text)         # Result[owns Sword, E] into Result[owns dyn Weapon, E]
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles, with one step per part: a tag test and the part's own conversion (a table pointer, an upcast, a pointer and a length). `Array[owns Sword]` into `Array[owns dyn Weapon]` and `Option[int]` into `Option[Option[int]]` stay `E2020`. It needs one more decision: whether a program's own enum whose payloads are its type parameters (`enum Either[A, B]: Left(A), Right(B)`) converts the same way, as the property says.

options_for_owner.summary: No implicit `Some` at all (Rust's way): every line writes the wrap.
options_for_owner.code:
s.weapon = Some(owns Sword(edge=4))
cap: Option[u64] = Some(n)
return Some(v)                           # `return v` in an Option function is E2020
load("a", Some(copy of cfg))             # Some(cfg) would take cfg
f(Some(5))                               # for x: Option[int] = None
options_for_owner.outcome: Consistent, but every `Option` line in every program gets longer, and an optional argument the callee only reads costs a deep copy or a change to the function's type. Lines that compile today (`return v`, `f(5)`) stop compiling.

recommendation.reason:
`x: T = v` and `x: Option[T] = v` then take the same values and do the same thing to them: a loan where the plain place lends, a hand-over where it hands over. There is no list to learn and nothing is paid at run time beyond C's `const T*`.

- B keeps a closed list that refuses correct lines (checklist 2 and 7).
- D makes every program longer, and makes optional arguments cost a copy (readability, speed).
- C is safe, O(1), and reads better on `cam.focus = find_boss()`. But it is a second rule, a holder converting through what it holds, and it needs a decision of its own on how far it reaches (the program's own enums). A answers this question completely, its help lines compile, and choosing C later changes no line of A.

The one-level limit and the refusal at operators prevent the surprises other languages hit (`nil < 5`, `Int??`).

owner_short.one_line: In C++, `std::optional<std::unique_ptr<Weapon>> weapon = std::make_unique<Sword>(4);` compiles, because `optional` takes anything that converts to its `T`. In Ember, the same line into an `Option[owns dyn Weapon]` field is refused unless it is written `Some(...)`. And when a plain value is given to an optional parameter, the spec does not say whether the value is lent or taken.

| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `w: owns dyn Weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)` | compiles: the Sword becomes a Weapon (rule 8) |
| 2 | main | `s.weapon = owns Sword(edge=4)`, where the field is `Option[owns dyn Weapon]` | refused today (E2020): `Some` may follow only widening, range erasure and string conversions |
| 3 | main | `s.on_hit = log_hit`, where the field is `Option[OnHit]` | refused today, for the same reason |
| 4 | main | `n = 5`, then `cap: Option[u64] = n` | refused today, though `y: u64 = n` compiles |
| 5 | main | `load("a", cfg)` for `opts: Option[LoadOptions] = None`, then `println(cfg.path)` | undecided today: "as `Some(value)`" would take `cfg` with no word at the call, so line 2 would be E3040 |
| 6 | main | under A, lines 2 to 5 as written | compile; prints `hit for 8`, `Some(5)`, then the path; `cfg` was only lent |
owner_short.today: An `Option` place takes a plain value as `Some` only after widening, range erasure or a string conversion. After any other conversion (to an interface, a function type, a list, a view, a known number), the line must write `Some(...)`. What happens to a value that a plain `Option` parameter only reads is not said. Today, too, `cap < 5` compares as `cap < Some(5)`, which is true when there is no cap.
owner_short.options:
A: an `Option[T]` place takes whatever a `T` place takes, and does what the `T` place does (a plain parameter lends, `=` hands over), as `Some` of it. An operator never wraps (`cap < n` is refused; write `if cap exists as c:`). One level only.
B: as today: write `Some(...)` after an interface, function, list, view or known-number conversion.
C: A, and also convert an existing `Option`, `Result` or tuple part by part (`Option[Boss]` into `Option[Enemy]`), never a list.
D: no implicit `Some` anywhere (Rust): `return Some(v)`, `f(Some(5))`, `load("a", Some(copy of cfg))`.
owner_short.recommendation: A: a plain place and an optional place then take the same values and do the same with them, with no list to learn and no run-time cost beyond C's `const T*`. C is safe and reads better for `Option[Boss]` into `Option[Enemy]`, but it is a rule of its own, with its own reach to decide.

design.open_risks:
1. TYP-24 ties. A generic interface implemented for both `T` and `Option[T]` can meet `E2070` at an argument that reaches both through conversions. It is a refusal with a fix line, as today for rules 1 to 4. If a real program meets it, the lead may rank "without the wrap" first, as Swift scores injection.
2. `is` between two read-only views of `Option`s. With the payload-address layout, two views of two different empty `Option`s are both null. `ref o1 is ref o2` then answers "the same", although they are not the same object. This is rare, and it is P12's question (what `is` asks of holders and views). It is listed so the lead decides it there rather than by accident.
3. Option C's reach, if chosen: the program's own enums whose payloads are its type parameters, and a tuple whose parts convert differently (one part handed over, another viewed, which hands over that part alone, as [OWN-11]).
4. Positions inside an `Option` (`pick` surviving a push) would need [BRW-16] to carry a position into an `Option` name, `enemies.get(0)` included. That is BRW-16's own question; this design keeps the address, which is what a written `Some(...)` and `get` give today.
5. The three-step order adds chains that do not involve `Option`: read-through, then any conversion; range erasure, then rule 12. A chain whose first step would hand an owner over from behind a view (read through `ref owns Sword`, then `owns dyn Weapon`) is refused (`E3013`), never done silently. Verify on the compiler that no existing test changes meaning.
6. Existing programs that compare an `Option` with a plain value through an operator (`hp == 5`, `cap < 5`) stop compiling. The fix-it writes `Some(5)`, or opens the `Option` for an order. The migration note should list it.
7. Every `map` help relies on the expected type reaching a generic call's result ([TYP-23]) to pick `U`, and on `(p?.name)` ending the chain. Verify both on the compiler before the messages ship.
8. P11: whatever `y: Mesh = m`, or `n = p.name` then `n = String(...)`, comes to mean for a plain name, the `Option` name follows it. The payload-address view layout represents a viewing `Option`, and the written `Some` represents a taking one, so no further edit is needed.
9. Function values are not in [TYP-13]'s niche list, so `Option[OnHit]` may be a tag larger than C's null function pointer. That is [TYP-13]'s question (P14's J3-15); the written `Some(log_hit)` pays the same.
10. No implicit `Ok`. If it is ever raised, `Result[int, int]` must be answered first.
11. `E2123`'s help today gives `left=Some(owns Tree(value=2))`. Under A the shorter `left=owns Tree(value=2)` also compiles; which one the help shows is the lead's wording.

design.rule: A pack fills any list it is written in: type arguments, a tuple, a function type's parameters, a variant's fields, a call's arguments, a list. The list it gives is exactly the list written by hand for that many members. With one member it is a list of one: `(int,)`, `fn(int)`, `View[Position]`, `f(a)`. With none it is that list's own way of writing none: `()` (which is `void`), `fn()`, no type arguments (`Event`), `f()`. A tuple keeps its brackets at every size, so a tuple of one is `(int,)`, written with its comma as Python and Rust write it, and never `int`. A tuple's elements are a pack: `for v in t:` walks them and `t...` passes them on. An element written with `...` is written out once per member of the packs it names. A pack that nothing gives any types holds none, as a parameter that is left out takes its default. Everything happens when compiling, and nothing runs for any of it.
design.spec_text:
Rules changed: [TYP-27], [TYP-47] (three paragraphs added), the [TYP-36] table's `void` row, [TYP-39] (one clause), the grammar of III.3 and III.5 (list items), [STD] `zip` (p15 34), [ECS-4] (the count). Unchanged and now agreeing: [GRM-29], [GRM-38], [TYP-19], [TYP-26].

[TYP-27] (changed) `()` is the value of type `void`; `Ok(())` is the success value of `Result[void, E]`. A function with no `->` returns `void`. A tuple type has any number of elements. Written as a type, `()` is `void`, the tuple of none. A tuple of one is written with its comma, `(T,)`, as its value is (`(e,)`, `e,`; [GRM-38], [GRM-29]). `(A, B)` has two, and so on. A tuple of one is never its element: `(int,)` and `int` are two types. `(T,)` is laid out as `T` is, and `void` takes no memory (ODR-071's `()` kept).

[TYP-47] (added after "...anywhere else either is `E0100`.")
**A pack fills every list it is written in.** An element written with `...` after it stands for one element per member of the packs it names, in order, with the element's other parts repeated in each. This holds in any list of types (type arguments, a tuple type, a function type's parameters, a variant's fields) and in any list of values (a call's arguments, a tuple, a list, an `expr_list`). With `[Cs...]` as `Position, Velocity`: `(ref mut Storage[Cs]...)` is `(ref mut Storage[Position], ref mut Storage[Velocity])`, and `fn(Cs...)` is `fn(Position, Velocity)`. With `its` of type `(Is...)`, `(its.next()?...)` is `(its.0.next()?, its.1.next()?)`, evaluated left to right and ending as the tuple written by hand ends. Written out, a list is exactly the same list written by hand, for every number of members:
- With one member: `(Ts...)` is `(int,)`, `fn(Ts...)` is `fn(int)` and `View[Cs...]` is `View[Position]`.
- With none: `(Ts...)` is `()`, which is `void`; `fn(Ts...)` is `fn()`; `Event[Ts...]` is `Event`; `f(values...)` is `f()`; `Msg.Data(values...)` and the pattern `Data(xs...)` are `Msg.Data` and `Data`.
Nothing else changes with the number. Round brackets around a list that holds an element with `...` make a tuple whatever its number, with no comma needed; so do `(values...)` and `return values...`. A list that takes a fixed number of items cannot hold such an element in a generic body, where the number is not known (`E2020`). Examples are `Array[T]`'s one type, a function's fixed parameters and a pattern of named parts. The packs one element names are walked together and must have one number, known when compiling; in a generic body that means packs of one type pack (`E2020` otherwise).
**How a pack gets its types.** A pack is given its types in brackets (`Event[int, StrView]`), or they are worked out from a call's arguments and from the type the place wants, as for any type parameter. A pack that nothing gives any types holds none, as a parameter that is left out takes its default: `Event()` and `on_click: Event` are an event of no values, and `zip()` is a zip of none.
**A tuple's elements are a pack.** `t...` passes a tuple's elements on wherever values are listed (`log(row.cells...)`). `for v in t:` walks them as it walks a pack's values: the body is written out once per element, each `v` of its element's type. `for a, b in (this, other)...:` walks two tuples of one pack side by side. `t.len()` is the number of elements, known when compiling. A tuple type's elements are a pack of types in the same way (`type Physics = (Position, Velocity)`, then `reg.view[Physics...]()`). A place keeps a pack's values as a tuple of the pack, `cells: (Ts...)`, made with `(values...)`. In a generic body, a value of a pack's tuple is used as any tuple of any size is: with `...`, `for`, `len()` and the interfaces its pack's needs give. `.k` and fixed patterns reach only the elements written before the first `...`. Each instance is made for its exact types ([MONO-1]), and nothing runs for a pack, a written-out list or a walk.

Grammar (III.3, III.5): `type "..."` may stand for a type in `tuple_type`, `fn_type_param`, `generic_arg` (in place of `IDENT "..."`) and `variant_field`. `expression "..."` may stand for an expression in `tuple_lit`, `list_lit`, `expr_list` and `arg` (in place of `IDENT "..."`). A `tuple_type` or `tuple_lit` whose items include one needs no comma. A variant's field list written out of a pack may be empty, and the variant then carries nothing.

[TYP-36] table: the `void` row becomes the tuples' row, since `void` is the tuple of none: Clone, Copy, Eq, Ord, Hash, Default `()`, Display `()`, Debug `()`. The tuple implementations written once over a pack in std (`extend[Ts...: needs Eq] (Ts...) implements Eq:`) cover it.
[TYP-39] (added) A tuple of one prints with its comma, `(7,)`, and `()` prints `()`, as Python's do.
[STD] (p15 34) `zip(a, b, ...)` takes any number of iterables ([TYP-47]). Each item is a tuple of one item from each iterable, `(x,)` from one, as Python's. It stops at the shortest, and with none it gives nothing.
[ECS-4] A view takes one component type or more, with no upper limit (`[C, Cs...]` above `fn view()`). A view walks its smallest pool, so `reg.view()` names none and is `E2060`, whose message gives `reg.view[Position]()`. `.exclude[...]`, `all_of` and `any_of` take any number, none included (`all_of()` is true, `any_of()` is false).

answers.answer: Decided as option B, with no new spelling. `Row[int]`'s `cells: (Ts...)` is `(int,)`, the tuple of one that the grammar's `tuple_type`, [GRM-29] and [GRM-38] already spell; [TYP-27]'s 'two or more' is the only sentence that changes. `Row[]`'s `cells` is `()`, which is `void`. `fn(Ts...)` is `fn(int, StrView)` for `Event[int, StrView]`. A struct, class or enum may take a pack and write it in any list. In Row's generic body, `for c in this.cells:` walks the cells at every size.
answers.code:
[Ts...]
struct Row:                                    # one parsed CSV row, one cell per column type
    cells: (Ts...)                             # a tuple of the pack's types, at every size

[Ts...]
class Event:                                   # a game event handing several values to each handler
    handlers: Array[fn(Ts...)] = []            # Event[int, StrView]: fn(int, StrView)

    fn fire(values: Ts...):
        for h in this.handlers:
            h(values...)

fn on_hit(dmg: int, who: StrView):
    println(who, "takes", dmg)

fn main():
    hit = Event[int, StrView]()
    hit.handlers.push(owns on_hit)
    hit.fire(5, "orc")                         # prints: orc takes 5
    pair = Row[int, StrView](cells=(7, "ann"))  # cells: (int, StrView)
    one = Row[int](cells=(7,))                 # cells: (int,), a tuple of one, as Python writes it
    println(pair.cells.1, one.cells)           # prints: ann (7,)
    println(one.cells.0 + 1)                   # prints: 8
answers.outcome: Compiles and prints `orc takes 5`, `ann (7,)`, `8`. As the finding wrote it, `Row[int](cells=7)` is E2020: "`cells` is a tuple of one, `(int,)`, and `7` is an `int`; write `cells=(7,)`".

other_cases.case: `fn(Ts...)` with no types: an event with no payload, `clicked = Event()` or `on_click: Event`, handlers `fn()`, `clicked.fire()`.
other_cases.settled: The pack holds none (nothing gives it types, as a left-out default), `fn(Ts...)` is `fn()`, `fire(values: Ts...)` takes no values and `h(values...)` is `h()`. It compiles. `Event[]` is not a form (E0100, help `Event()`): none is written by leaving the types out, so there is one spelling.

other_cases.case: `View[Cs...]` with one component: `for e, p in reg.view[Position]():`.
other_cases.settled: `View[Position]`; each item is `(Entity, ref Position)`, a pair, so there is no tuple of one anywhere, as verdict 115 asked. The library writes `[C, Cs...]`, because a view walks its smallest pool. `reg.view()` is E2060 with help `reg.view[Position]()`. `exclude`, `all_of` and `any_of` take none too.

other_cases.case: `zip` of one iterator, of none, of two.
other_cases.settled: `zip(xs)` gives `(x,)` items, as Python's zip does. `zip()` gives nothing; the library writes it with `this.iters.len() == 0`, known when compiling. `for x, y in zip(xs, ys):` is unchanged. Zip's `next` is `return Some((this.iters.next()?...))`, so the library function can be written by the rules (no hidden path).

other_cases.case: A tuple's interfaces written once for every size (verdict 115's use).
other_cases.settled: `extend[Ts...: needs Eq] (Ts...) implements Eq:` with `for a, b in (this, other)...: if a != b: return false`, then `return true`. It covers `()`, `(T,)`, pairs and up, with no '2 to 12' cap and no separate implementation for `void`. The compiler stops answering void's interfaces by name (D-463). `void` gains Display `()`. Display of `(7,)` prints `(7,)` (TYP-39).

other_cases.case: A pack of one tuple type against a pack of two: `Row[(int, int)]` and `Row[int, int]`.
other_cases.settled: `cells` is `((int, int),)` and `(int, int)`: two types, as the declarations say. Row's `for c in this.cells:` walks one member and two. Under option A both would be `(int, int)` and walk differently: this case is the evidence against A.

other_cases.case: One-type expansion in a field: `pools: (ref mut Storage[Cs]...)`.
other_cases.settled: With `Position, Velocity` it is `(ref mut Storage[Position], ref mut Storage[Velocity])`. With `Position` alone it is `(ref mut Storage[Position],)`. With none it is `()`. Each pool reference follows the view rules of its word.

other_cases.case: An enum variant over a pack: `[Ts...]` above `enum Msg:` with `Data(Ts...)` and `Quit`.
other_cases.settled: `Msg[int, StrView].Data(5, "orc")`; with one type, `Data(int)`. With none, `Data` carries nothing and is made `Msg.Data` and matched `Data`, as a variant written by hand with no fields is. The generic body's `Msg.Data(values...)` and pattern `Data(xs...)` are written out to exactly that.

other_cases.case: A pack put in a list of fixed length in a generic body: `xs: Array[Ts...]`, `pair(values...)` for `fn pair(a: int, b: int)`, `a, b = this.cells`, `this.cells.0`.
other_cases.settled: Each is E2020 at the generic declaration, once and never per instance (TYP-17's check-once): "`Array` takes one type, and `Ts` may hold any number"; "`cells` holds one value per type of `Ts`, which may be none; walk them with `for c in this.cells:`". `(A, Ts...)` may use `.0`, which is known to be there.

other_cases.case: Keeping a pack's values for later: `pending: Array[(Ts...)]` with `this.pending.push((values...))`, and `-> (Ts...)` results.
other_cases.settled: `(values...)` is the tuple of the values at every count: `(5,)` for `Event[int]` and `()` for `Event`. A function returning `(Ts...)` returns `void` at none. `Result[(Ts...), E]` at none is `Result[void, E]`, which succeeds with `Ok(())`.

other_cases.case: GRM-29's `x = 7,` and GRM-38's `(7,)` in ordinary code, which today have no type (TYP-27 refuses it).
other_cases.settled: `(int,)`; `println(x)` prints `(7,)`, as Python does. `(int)` is not a type (the grammar has no parenthesised type). Its E0100 help gives `(int,)` for a tuple of one and `int` for the type. The parser stops reading `(A)` as a tuple of one (an implementation fix).

other_cases.case: Naming a list of types once: `type Physics = (Position, Velocity)` and `reg.view[Physics...]()`; spreading a concrete tuple: `println(row.cells...)`.
other_cases.settled: A tuple type's elements are a pack of types and a tuple value's a pack of values, so `reg.view[Position, Velocity]()` and `println(7, ann)` are what they write out to. In a generic body, `T...` for a plain `T` is E2020, because `T` is not known to be a tuple.

other_cases.case: Packs walked together with a tuple of another number: `log((origin, values)...)` in a generic body, `origin: (float, float)`.
other_cases.settled: E2020: "`origin` has 2 elements and `values` any number; the parts of one `...` are walked together". It is refused and never zipped silently. In concrete code, tuples of one known number are walked together, as the `...` says.

design.prior_art:
C++: a pack fills every list: template arguments, function parameters, braced lists and base classes. `std::tuple<Ts...>` is the same at every size because a tuple is a library class: `std::tuple<int>` is not `int`, and `std::tuple<>` is an empty type. Pattern expansion (`Storage<Cs>&...`, `f(g(args)...)`) writes one element per member. A trailing pack that nothing deduces is empty ([temp.arg.explicit]), which Ember's 'none when nothing gives it types' takes. Where C++ falls short: a template is checked only when instantiated, so mistakes show in instances. Walking a tuple takes `std::get<I>`, `index_sequence`, `std::apply` or fold expressions. `std::tuple<>` still takes a byte, and none of it is memory safe.
Rust: no variadic generics; tuple implementations come from macros up to 12, the cap verdict 115 named. It has `(T,)`, and `()` is both the unit type and the empty tuple. That is the uniform tuple this rule takes. `Fn(A)` is `Fn<(A,)>` underneath, which is why Rust needs a tuple of one.
Swift (SE-0393, SE-0398, SE-0399, SE-0408): packs on functions and on types, checked once as Ember's are. Swift has no tuple of one, so a tuple of a one-element pack is that element. That is option A, and it is the size at which a generic tuple stops being a tuple. SE-0408's `for (l, r) in repeat (each a, each b)` walks two packs together, the model for `for a, b in (this, other)...:`. Unspecialised Swift generic code passes pack metadata at run time.
Zig: tuples of any size, `.{x}` and `.{}` included. `inline for` over a tuple and `@call` with an argument tuple are the models for `for v in t:` and `t...`; Zig is duck-typed, with errors at instantiation.
Python: `(7,)` and `()`; PEP 646's `tuple[*Ts]` is the same at every size; `zip(xs)` yields `(x,)`; `f(*t)` spreads.
C#: `ValueTuple<T1>` and the empty `ValueTuple` exist as types, though the literal syntax starts at two; no variadic generics (`Func` overloads up to 16).
Go: no tuples and no type packs; `...T` is one type in a slice.
Ada: nothing comparable.
Each one either caps the number of types (Rust, C#), collapses one type into the type itself (Swift), checks only at instantiation (C++, Zig) or is unsafe (C's `...`). The rule takes C++'s list filling and Python's and Rust's tuple of one, and checks once as Swift does.
design.cost:
Zero at run time, in time and memory, for every part of the rule.
- `(T,)` is laid out as `T`: a one-field struct in C's layout ([TYP-11]) has the same size, alignment and passing as T.
- `()` is `void`: 0 bytes by IV.2. The C backend today gives a `void` struct member one byte (ADR-062), so a `(Ts...)` field with no types costs a byte plus padding in C output until that is fixed. That is an implementation matter the rule does not need.
- A written-out list is the list written by hand, so `h(values...)` costs what `h(a, b)` costs in C.
- `for v in t:` is the body written once per element: no counter, no branch, no table.
- `t...` passes the elements as separate arguments, as C passes each.
- `(its.next()?...)` is the hand-written tuple.
- Each set of types is its own instance, as for every generic ([MONO-1]); verdict 115 accepted that code size.
Against C: C has no typed variadics. Its typed equivalent is a hand-written function per number of arguments (the same machine code), and `va_list` is unchecked, walks a pointer per argument and is unsafe. Against C++: the same code as `std::tuple` and pack expansion, without `std::tuple<>`'s byte. Against Swift: no pack metadata is ever read at run time.

readability.note: Identical, character for character: the rule adds no word, annotation or line to any program. A game loop, a server handler or a parser that names no pack is untouched. The only text any program gains is the comma of a one-type pack's tuple written by hand, `Row[int](cells=(7,))`, which is Python's own spelling of a tuple of one. That line is rare: views, events, zip of two or more and println never produce a tuple of one. Generic library code becomes writable and shorter: one tuple Display for every size instead of 12 macro copies or a `[A, B, Ts...]` workaround.

design.compiler_does:
The compiler does the following, and the programmer writes none of it:
- It parses `type ...` and `expression ...` as list items.
- It checks each generic body once, with every pack standing for any number of any types. A pack's tuple offers `len()`, `for`, `...` and the interfaces its pack's needs give, and `.k` only before the first `...`.
- It refuses, at the generic declaration and never at an instance (E2020), a pack in a list of fixed length, and packs walked together that may differ in number.
- At each instance it writes every list out per member, with C++'s substitution. With no members it gives that list's own none: `()` (which is `void`), `fn()`, no type arguments, no call arguments, a variant with no fields.
- It infers a pack from the call's arguments and the wanted type, and gives it none when nothing gives it types.
- It unrolls `for` over a tuple or a pack into the body once per element.
- It evaluates an expanded value element left to right, ending what was made if a `?` returns part-way, exactly as for the tuple written by hand.
- It lays out `(T,)` as `T` and `()` as zero bytes.
- It stops answering `void`'s interfaces by name (D-463), because std's tuple implementations written once over `(Ts...)` cover `()`.
- Implementation fix: the parser stops reading `(A)` as a tuple of one; today `(A)` and `(A,)` both make `Tuple([A])`.
design.misuse:
Every mistake is refused when compiling, with a line that compiles; nothing is checked at run time and nothing is undefined.
- `Row[int](cells=7)` is E2020: "`cells` is a tuple of one, `(int,)`; write `cells=(7,)`".
- `(int)` as a type is E0100: "a tuple of one is `(int,)`; the type itself is `int`".
- `this.cells.0` or `a, b = this.cells` in a generic body is E2020, giving `for c in this.cells:`.
- `Array[Ts...]`, or `values...` given to a function of fixed parameters, in a generic body is E2020 ("`Array` takes one type, and `Ts` may hold any number").
- Packs of different numbers walked together (`(origin, values)...`) are E2020.
- `log(values)` without the dots is E0100, giving `log(values...)` or the tuple `(values...)`.
- `x...` for a value that is neither a pack nor a tuple is E0100.
- `Event[]` is E0100, giving `Event()`.
- `reg.view()` is E2060 (a view lists one component or more), giving `reg.view[Position]()`.
- An empty pack's `fn()` handler given an `fn(int)` is the ordinary E2020 type mismatch, so a forgotten type list is never silent.
design.verdicts:
115 kept. A function or type takes any number of types; this rule is what makes that hold at one and at none (a struct, class or enum with `[Ts...]`, `fn(Ts...)`, `(Ts...)`). A view keeps no tuple: `reg.view[Position]()` walks `(Entity, ref Position)` items, so `(A,)` never appears where the owner objected to it.
116 kept. C++'s dots, extended as C++ extends them: pattern expansion `ref mut Storage[Cs]...` and `(its.next()?...)`. An empty pack is written by leaving its types out, C++'s deduced-empty pack, as Ember leaves out a parameter with a default.
117 kept. `println()` passes no values.
ODR-071 is a delegated ruling that the owner accepted on 2026-10-21 together with 88 others. Its answer, the type `()` is `void`, is kept and strengthened: `void` is the tuple of none, so the tuple implementations cover it. Its clause 'a tuple type has two or more elements' is revisited, on this evidence:
(1) The specification already contradicts it. GRM-29 ('or of one expression followed by a comma, is a tuple'), GRM-38 ('`(e,)` a tuple') and the grammar's `tuple_type` (`"(" type "," ")"`) all make a tuple of one, so the change removes a contradiction and adds no spelling.
(2) ODR-071 answered D-355, which asked what the type `()` is. A tuple of one was never asked.
(3) Without a tuple of one, a pack of one type has no tuple. If it collapses to the type instead, `Row[(int, int)]` and `Row[int, int]` get one field type that the same loop walks once and twice.
Also supported by verdict 84 and principle 4 (one rule, no exception by type, here by size), verdict 29 ('one rule with no exception') and principle 10 (Python's `(7,)` and `zip(xs)`).

options_for_owner.summary: One type collapses to the type itself, and none is `void` (Swift's way, phase 2's recommendation). A tuple has two or more elements, so [GRM-29]'s `7,` and [GRM-38]'s `(7,)` must stop being tuples. The library writes tuple interfaces from two up (`[A, B, Ts...]` above `extend (A, B, Ts...)`) and `void`'s separately.
options_for_owner.code:
one = Row[int](cells=7)          # cells is an int
println(one.cells + 1)           # 8
r2 = Row[(int, int)](cells=(1, 2))
r3 = Row[int, int](cells=(1, 2))   # same field type as r2
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints 8. But `r2.cells` and `r3.cells` are both `(int, int)`, while Row's `for c in this.cells: println(c)` prints `(1, 2)` for r2 and `1`, `2` for r3: one type with two behaviours. `zip(xs)` gives `x`, unlike Python's `(x,)`. Three grammar and lexical rules change.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. A pack fills every list as written by hand. A tuple of one is `(int,)`, the spelling [GRM-29], [GRM-38] and the grammar already have; only [TYP-27]'s 'two or more' changes. `()` stays `void`, the tuple of none. Tuple interfaces are written once for every size.
options_for_owner.code:
one = Row[int](cells=(7,))       # a tuple of one, as Python writes it
println(one.cells.0 + 1)         # 8
println(one.cells)               # (7,)
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles and prints `8` and `(7,)`. `Row[int](cells=7)` is E2020, giving `cells=(7,)`. `Row[(int, int)]` and `Row[int, int]` are two field types. `zip(xs)` gives `(x,)`, as Python's does. It costs nothing at run time, since `(int,)` is laid out as `int`.

options_for_owner.summary: B, plus a 13th conversion in [TYP-5]: a `T` becomes `(T,)` where a tuple of one is wanted, beside rule 11's `T` to `Some(T)`.
options_for_owner.code:
one = Row[int](cells=7)          # 7 becomes (7,)
println(one.cells.0 + 1)         # 8
options_for_owner.outcome: Compiles. But the line reads as if `cells` were an `int`, and `one.cells + 1` is then E2020. One value gets two spellings (`7` and `(7,)`), and `((1, 2),)` from `(1, 2)` comes with it. The conversion composes with P20's question about Option conversions. Rare programs gain a shortcut and every reader gains a rule.

recommendation.reason: It is the general rule: one meaning of a tuple at every size, with no exception for one. A tuple of one is spelled the way the language already spells it (GRM-29, GRM-38, the grammar). It removes the spec's present contradiction and a special path for `void`'s interfaces, and lets the library's own zip, View and tuple interfaces be written by the rules. It costs nothing at run time. A collapsing tuple (A) makes one type behave two ways, and a conversion (C) makes a line misstate a field's type; B adds no word to any ordinary program.

owner_short.one_line: In C++, `std::tuple<Ts...>` with one type is `std::tuple<int>`, a type of its own and not `int`. Ember's `(Ts...)` has no type for one type, because TYP-27 says a tuple has two or more elements.

owner_short.today: Undecided and contradictory: TYP-27 says a tuple type has two or more elements, while GRM-29 and GRM-38 already make `7,` and `(7,)` tuples, so `Row[int]`'s field has no type.
owner_short.options:
A: one type is the type itself, as in Swift. You write `cells=7`, but `Row[(int, int)]` and `Row[int, int]` get one field type that the same loop walks once and twice.
B: a tuple of one is `(int,)`, as Python and Rust write it and as GRM-38 already spells it. You write `cells=(7,)`; `()` stays void.
C: B, plus `7` converting to `(7,)` where a tuple of one is wanted.
owner_short.recommendation: B: no new spelling, no exception for one, one tuple at every size, zero cost (`(int,)` is laid out as `int`). Only a program that names a one-type pack's tuple writes the comma, as Python does.

design.open_risks:
- The value side goes beyond what J2-07 asked: tuples as packs, `t...`, `for v in t:`, `(its.next()?...)` and `for a, b in (this, other)...:`. It is needed so that std's zip, View and tuple interfaces can be written by the rules (no hidden path), but the owner has not seen these spellings. Present them with the rule, or as its second line.
- `for a, b in (this, other)...:` names each member's place in turn. What words those names get is P11's binding table, which must agree.
- `void` gains Display (`f\"{()}\"` prints `()`), a visible change to TYP-36's table.
- ECS-4's 'any number of component types' becomes 'one or more' for `view` (a view walks its smallest pool). That is a library rule change.
- In concrete code, tuples of one known number named in one `...` element are walked together. A tuple meant whole inside such an element cannot be written there; generic code refuses the mix (E2020), but concrete code accepts it when the numbers agree.
- No rest pattern (`first, rest... = t`) and no computed index (C++'s `get<I>`) in generic code; walks cover the library's uses (YAGNI).
- The C backend emits a byte for a `void` member (ADR-062) although IV.2 gives `void` size 0.
- The parser reads `(A)` as a tuple of one today. Both are implementation fixes.
- Option C would add a TYP-5 conversion that composes with P20's question; keep the two apart.
- The Swift claim (a tuple of a one-element pack becomes the element) is from SE-0393 as I recall it; check the wording before quoting it to the owner.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed memory (no dangling view)
matrix.how_kept: A written-out list is the list written by hand, so every element goes through the view rules as written by hand. A tuple of a pack that holds a view is a view type (TYP-34) and lives no longer than what it views (TYP-15, E3063). A class field holding one says `from` (E2118). `t...` and `values...` pass the elements in place, read-only, for the call.
matrix.edge_cases: Pack members that are views (`Row[StrView]`, `Event[ref mut Player]`). `(values...)` built from read-only names: for members that are not Copy it must be refused, never a silent copy or a kept view. `pending: Array[(Ts...)]` in a class instantiated with `StrView`. zip items viewing their lists. `for v in t:` while `t` is reassigned between rounds (hole 6).

matrix.guarantee: No double end
matrix.how_kept: `owns values: Ts...` takes each value over once. A written-out list ends what it made as the hand-written list does, `(its.next()?...)` included (EXP-1, EXP-4). `owns t...` hands each element over once (EXP-6, part by part). Concrete code is checked after writing out, so a repeated hand-over is E3040.

Leaving a walk over `owns` elements part-way (hole 6). `Event[owns Mesh]` with each handler taking the value (hole 3). A `?` part-way through `(its.next()?...)`, which is stated.
