design.rule:
Where a piece of text stands decides what it is. A rule about raw text never takes away a form the grammar offers at that place. Raw-text rules are: how characters are cut into tokens, what a line's first token makes of the line, and which words are reserved. The rule has three facets.

(1) Lines. Whether text begins a line, and what begins it, is decided on logical lines, at a place where an item, a member, a statement or a match arm begins. Each is read as what may begin there. An arm begins a pattern, so `["go", dir]:` is an arm whose pattern is a list. A physical line inside brackets, inside a triple-quoted string or after a `\` begins nothing. How near two lines are (a `[T]` line directly above its declaration, a safety note immediately before its block) is counted in physical lines, so a blank or comment line between them counts (verdict 154). A statement never begins with `[` (verdict 155, written into the statement grammar), so every `[` line where a declaration may begin is read one way.

(2) Tokens. The lexer reads the longest token. Where the grammar does not take that token at its place but takes a shorter one made of its first characters, the shorter one is read. So `t.0.1` is `(t.0).1`, and `**c_char` in a type is a pointer to a pointer. Where the grammar does take the longest token, it stands, so `r?.name` stays optional chaining.

(3) Names. A word is reserved so that it keeps its meaning where it may have one. After `.` and `?.` only a name or an element number can stand, so every word there is a member name (`event.type`, `b.owned`), as `a.not()` already is. Anywhere else a reserved word used as a name is an error (verdict 156). `r#word` is the name `word` for every word the lexer gives another meaning: the 52 keywords, `async`/`await`/`macro`, `owned`, `self`, a contextual word, and `_`. It never has the word's meaning.

List patterns get the meaning the language already gives their parts. Element names are pattern names: views, with `ref mut` and `owns` working as everywhere. `..rest` is the slice `xs[i..j]` of the remaining elements. A list pattern matches exactly what a `Span[T]` parameter accepts. Four facts every pattern needs are written down with them:
- A match views its scrutinee until an arm is chosen. Inside a guard every name is a read-only view, and nothing is handed over until the guard is true.
- The arms are exhaustive when every value is matched. For lists this means every length up to rustc's bound, each length checked as a tuple.
- A `for` loop's pattern, or a comprehension's, must match every element.
- `x @ p` names one place twice, under the view rules.
design.spec_text:
Adds [LEX-27] and [GRM-47]. Changes:
- the `identifier` and `raw_ident` productions;
- [LEX-10] and the comment table's `#!` line, [LEX-13], [LEX-14], [LEX-15], [LEX-18], [LEX-19];
- the statement production, [GRM-13], [GRM-40], the postfix production with [EXP-10], and the list-pattern production;
- [CTL-1], [CTL-5], [GRM-27];
- the keyword row of the FFI name table (p16 194).

II.4 `identifier := XID_Start XID_Continue* | "_" XID_Continue+` (Unicode; NFC-normalised). `raw_ident := "r#" word`, where `word := (XID_Start | "_") XID_Continue*`: any word, a keyword or a lone `_` included.

[LEX-10] (changed) There are no block comments. A line that begins with `#!`, where a line may begin ([LEX-27] 1), is a directive ([GRM-37]) and never a comment. Before the first import or item it applies; after it, it is `E0104`. Inside brackets or a string, a `#!` begins nothing: it is a comment, or text. The comment table's line becomes `#! language "0.9.15"  (a directive; only before the imports, [GRM-37])`.

[LEX-13] (changed) A lone `_` is the discard pattern and never names a variable. `r#_` is the name `_` ([LEX-27] 3). A name may begin with `_` (`_unused`, a C field `__pad0`).

[LEX-27] (new in 0.9.15_Hardened_12) **Where text stands decides what it is.** A rule about raw text never takes away a form the grammar offers where the text stands. Such rules are:
- how characters are cut into tokens ([LEX-21]);
- what a line's first token makes of the line ([GRM-37], [GRM-40], [LEX-10], [LEX-23]);
- which words are reserved ([LEX-14], [LEX-15]).

1. *Lines.*
   - Whether text begins a line, and what begins it, is decided on logical lines ([LEX-5] to [LEX-7]), at a place where one of these begins: an item (of a file, an overlay or an `extern` block); a member (of a type, an enum, an interface or an `extend` block); a statement; or an arm of a `match`. Each is read as what may begin there.
   - A physical line begins nothing when it is inside brackets, inside a triple-quoted string, or joined to the line before by `\`. So `grid = [`, followed by `[1, 0],` and `[0, 1],`, is one statement, and a `[package]` line inside `"""…"""` is text.
   - Among a `match`'s arms, at their indentation, a line begins a pattern, so `["go", dir]:` is an arm whose pattern is a list ([GRM-47]). A type-parameter line stands only where a declaration may begin, and only there does [GRM-40] look at the next line.
   - How near two lines are is counted in physical lines. This covers [GRM-40]'s "directly above" and "the line after it", and [LEX-23]'s "the line immediately before". A blank line or a comment line between them counts:
     - `[T]`, then a comment line, then `fn first(xs: Array[T]) -> T:` is `E0100` (verdict 154);
     - a `# SAFETY:` line with a blank line under it is no safety note.
     A rule that skips blank lines says so ([LEX-11]).
2. *Tokens.* The lexer reads the longest token ([LEX-21]). Where the grammar does not take that token where it stands, but takes a shorter one made of its first characters, the shorter one is read, and then the characters after it.
   - Directly after `.` or `?.`, a run of digits is an element number: a whole decimal number with no fraction, exponent or suffix. `edges[0].0.1` is `(edges[0].0).1`; `t.0.1e5` is `E0100`.
   - In a type, `**` is two `*`: `names: **c_char` is a pointer to a pointer, C's `const char *const *`.
   - Where the grammar takes the longest token, it stands. `r?.name` is optional chaining ([EXP-10]), and handing the error back first is written `(r?).name`. `r#note` is a raw identifier.
3. *Names.* A word is reserved so that it keeps its meaning where it may have one.
   - Directly after `.` or `?.`, wherever they stand (an expression, a type's path, a pattern's path, an import's module path), only a name or an element number can follow. No word there can have another meaning, so every word there is a member name, read as written: `event.type`, `b.owned`, `lib.in`, `a.not()`.
   - Everywhere else a reserved word is that word, and one used as a name is [LEX-14]'s `E0005` or [LEX-15]'s `E1010`. A member whose name is a reserved word is declared, and named outside a `.`, with `r#`: `r#type: int`, `Event(r#type=1)`, `from lib import r#in`.
   - `r#word` is the name `word`, for every word: a keyword of the table, a word reserved for a future version, `owned`, `self`, a contextual keyword where it would be one, and `_`. It never has the word's meaning:
     - `r#self` is a name like any other; a method's object is `this` ([GRM-41]);
     - `r#owned` among a C contract's words is an unknown word.
   - For a word with no other meaning where it stands, `r#` changes nothing: `r#count` is `count`, and `event.r#type` is `event.type`. So a program keeps its meaning when a word joins or leaves the reserved set.

[LEX-14] (changed) "A raw identifier `r#name` uses a keyword as a name (for imported C fields such as `type`)" becomes "A raw identifier `r#name` is the name `name`, for every word ([LEX-27] 3). After `.` and `?.` every word is a member name, so an imported C field `type` is read as `event.type`." The rest stands: E0005 with the help `r#type` (verdict 156), for `type = 3`, `yield = 1`, a field `class: int` and a parameter `in: int`.

[LEX-15] (changed)
- "using one as a name is `E0005`" becomes "the bare word used as a name is `E0005` (`r#async` is a name)".
- "any use is `E1010`" becomes "any use of the bare word is `E1010`, except after `.` and `?.`, where every word is a member name ([LEX-27] 3). `r#owned` and `r#self` are names, never these words."
- "and after `.` and `?.`, so `Not` can have its method `not` (`a.not()` is `~a`, ODR-040) and `AnyError` its method `is[E]()`" becomes "so `Not` can have its method `not` and `AnyError` its method `is[E]()`. Each is called after `.`, as every member is ([LEX-27] 3): `a.not()` is `~a` (ODR-040)."

[LEX-18] (changed) Append: "Directly after `.` or `?.`, digits are an element number, never a float ([LEX-27] 2): `t.0.1` is `(t.0).1`."

[LEX-19] (changed) Append: "The expression in a hole is read as it would be anywhere else ([LEX-27]):
- a `"` in it begins a string (`f"{scores["ann"]}"`);
- digits after `.` are an element number (`f"{pair.0.1}"`);
- a `:` that the expression's grammar takes is its own (a lambda's `:`, after its brackets or result type);
- the first other `:` at bracket depth zero begins the format spec (`f"{ratio:.2f}"`)."

III.4 `simple_stmt := var_decl | assignment | expr_list | "pass"` gains the note `-- never begins with "[" ([GRM-40], verdict 155)`.

[GRM-40] (changed)
- "and so is every line that begins with `[` anywhere else, one that begins with a list included (`[10, 20].len()` on a line of its own; `n = [10, 20].len()` is the way)" becomes: "and so is every other logical line that begins with `[` where an item, a member or a statement begins ([LEX-27] 1). A simple statement never begins with `[` (the statement production). So every `[` line where a declaration may begin is read one way, as type parameters, and one that stands where none may gets this one message. `[10, 20].len()` on a line of its own is `E0100`, and `n = [10, 20].len()` is the way (verdict 155)."
- "A line that begins with `[` is a type-parameter line when the line after it begins …" gains "where a declaration may begin, and never among a `match`'s arms, where a line begins a pattern. The line after it is the next physical line ([LEX-27] 1)."
- The examples of verdicts 154 and 155 stand word for word. Each of these is `E0100`:
  - a comment line between `[T]` and its `fn`;
  - `[T: needs Add]` above an `enum` (one `E0100`);
  - `[10, 20].len()` on a line of its own.

III.5 postfix: `| "." member_name | "." INT | "?." member_name | "?." INT | "?"`, with `member_name := IDENT | raw_ident | KEYWORD` (every word, [LEX-27] 3). A path segment after `.` and an import's module path take `member_name` the same way. [EXP-10] gains: "`a?.0` takes element 0 of the tuple inside, as `.0` does."

III.6 patterns: replace `| "[" [pattern {"," pattern}] ["," ".." [IDENT]] "]"` with `| "[" [list_item {"," list_item} [","]] "]"`, where `list_item := pattern | ".." [["ref" ["mut"]] IDENT]`.

[GRM-13] (changed) Append, for every pattern:
- *Guards.* A `match` views its scrutinee from the `match` line until an arm is chosen, its guards included (VII.4: a tested place is a view). A guard that changes the scrutinee, or a part a name views, is refused by [BRW-1] (`E3021` at the change).
  - Inside a guard every name of its arm is a read-only view of its part. This includes a `ref mut` name, a rest name (a `Span[T]`) and a name under `match owns`. Nothing is changed or handed over through one (`E3023`, `E3013`).
  - Under `match owns e:` nothing is handed over until an arm is chosen. When the arm's guard is true, or it has none, `e` is handed over to that arm and each of its names takes its part. A guard that is false leaves `e` as it was, for the next arm.
- *Parts no name takes.* Under `match owns e:`, the parts of `e` that no name of the chosen arm takes end by their own drop, in their order, when the arm's block begins. Such parts are those matched by `_`, by a literal or by `..` without a name, and a variant's fields left out.
- *`@`.* `x @ p` names the whole value `x`, and its parts by `p`'s names. These are names of one place, under [BRW-1]: a `ref mut` among them is the only name while it is used.
  - Under `match owns`, the whole goes to `x`, and `p` is matched against `x`'s value without taking it over. So `p`'s names are views of `x`'s parts, by this rule's first sentence.
  - Example: `all @ [first, ..]:` gives `all` the list and `first` a read-only view of its element 0.

[CTL-5] (changed) A `match` tests arms top to bottom. The first arm that matches, and whose guard (if it has one) is true, runs. A guard is evaluated after its arm's pattern matches, with its names as [GRM-13] gives them inside a guard. The arms MUST be exhaustive: every value the scrutinee may have is matched by some arm without a guard. A literal covers only its own value, and `_` or a name covers every value. A match that misses a value is `E2090`, naming each value not matched; for a list, see [GRM-47]. An arm no value reaches is `W2091`.

[CTL-1] (changed) Append: "A loop's names are a pattern that every element matches, exhaustive as a `match` with that one arm is ([CTL-5]). One that may not match is `E2090`: a list pattern over a list that may have another length, `Some(x)`, a literal. Its help gives `for row in rows:` then `if [x, y] = row:`. Over `Span[[float; 2]]`, `for [x, y] in pts:` compiles." [GRM-27] gains the same for a comprehension's `for` clause: `[w for [w, _] in rows]` over `Array[Array[float]]` is `E2090`.

[GRM-47] (new) **List patterns.**
- *What it matches.* A list pattern matches a value whose type converts to `Span[T]` where one is expected ([SPN-1]), so exactly the values a `Span[T]` parameter accepts. Today these are an `Array[T]`, a `[T; N]`, a `Span[T]` and a `MutSpan[T]`, or a view of one.
  - Text converts to a `StrView`, not to a `Span`. A list pattern over text, a `Set` or a `Map` is `E2020`, whose help gives the words (`match line.split(" ").collect():`) or the bytes (`s.as_bytes()`).
  - The pattern matches when the value has as many elements as it has element patterns (at least as many, with a `..`), and each element matches the pattern in its place. The length is tested first.
  - A literal compares as `==` does: `"quit"` against a `StrView` or `String` element compares the text.
- *The rest.* One `..` stands for any number of elements, none included, at its place: `[first, ..]`, `[.., last]`, `[first, .., last]`, `[..]`.
  - A second `..` is `E0100`. So is `..` before a literal: `[..5]` is refused, because a range pattern gives both ends (`0..5`).
  - `..rest` names those elements as `xs[i..j]` names them, as a read-only `Span[T]`. `..ref mut rest` names them as a `MutSpan[T]` that may change them.
- *Names.* Every name in a list pattern is a pattern name, with the words and meanings of [GRM-13] and [GRM-42]. A plain name is a read-only view of its element (a number is copied), and `ref mut` lets it change the element. The comma rule `E0116` holds: write `[ref mut first, ..ref rest]`.
- *Under `match owns xs:`*, the arm takes over only what `xs` owns ([GRM-13]).
  - Over an `Array[T]` or a `[T; N]`, each element name owns its element.
  - A named rest owns its elements as a value of the source's kind. From a `[T; N]` it is a `[T; M]`. From an `Array[T]` it is an `Array[T]` that keeps the list's block, its elements moved to the block's front, with no allocation.
  - The elements no name takes end when the arm's block begins ([GRM-13]). The block is freed then, unless a named rest keeps it.
  - A `Span` or `MutSpan` owns no elements. `owns` hands over the view, and the names are views, as without it.
- *Exhaustiveness* ([CTL-5]). Let `L` be the larger of two numbers:
  - one more than the most elements of an arm without `..` (counted as 0 elements when there is no such arm);
  - the most elements before a `..` in any arm, plus the most after a `..` in any arm.
  Each length below `L` is checked on its own, with the arms that accept it read as tuple patterns of that length. All lengths from `L` up are checked as one: the first and last elements as positions of a tuple, and the elements between them matched by every arm with `..`.
  - A `[T; N]` has the one length `N`. One whose `N` is a `const` parameter is checked for every length, as a span is.
  - Over a `Span[bool]`, the arms `[]`, `[false, ..]` and `[.., true]` miss `[true, .., false]`.
  - Over a `Span[StrView]`, the arms `[]`, `["quit"]`, `["go", dir]` and `[_, _, _, ..]` miss a list of one word other than `"quit"`, and a list of two words whose first is not `"go"`. `E2090` names each.

FFI name table (p16 194): "an identifier that is an Ember keyword | a raw identifier `r#type` ([LEX-14])" becomes "an identifier that is an Ember keyword, a reserved word, or `_` | the same name: as written after `.` (`event.type`, `b.owned`), and with `r#` where it is named elsewhere (`from lib import r#in`, `Event(r#type=1)`, `rename r#_ as tr`; [LEX-27] 3)".

answers.code:
enum Command:
    Quit
    Go(String)
    Say(int)                             # how many words follow "say"
    Unknown

fn parse_cmd(words: Span[StrView]) -> Command:
    match words:
        ["quit"]:                         # exactly one word, "quit"
            return Command.Quit
        ["go", dir]:                       # two words; `dir` views the second
            return Command.Go(String(dir))
        ["say", ..rest]:                  # `rest` views the words after "say"
            return Command.Say(rest.len())
        _:
            return Command.Unknown

fn main():
    line = "go north"
    words = line.split(" ").collect()
    println(parse_cmd(words))            # Command.Go("north")

answers.answer: Facet 3 decides it. After `.` only a member name can stand, so `owned` there is the field's name. `b.owned` reads the C field, as `a.not()` already calls a method. `r#owned` is the same name, for the places where the bare word would be the reserved word, such as a keyword argument: `buf.buffer(data=p, len=n, r#owned=true)`. LEX-15's E1010 and E0005 stay for the bare word anywhere else.
answers.outcome:
It compiles and reads the C field. The emitted C is `b.owned`, so the cost is zero, and `b.r#owned` means the same.

The bare word keeps its errors where it could be the word:
- `owned` as a name or a word elsewhere is E1010, "write `owns`";
- `async` alone is E0005, naming the reservation.

`r#owned` written as a C contract word is an unknown contract word (the word is `owns`), so verdict 102 holds. `r#self` and a C field read as `b.self` are never a method's object, so verdict 2 holds.

Under option A, which keeps verdict 156's words at the dot, the line is `b.r#owned`, and `b.owned` is E1010 with that help.

answers.answer: Facet 2 decides it. Directly after `.`, the grammar takes only a name or an element number, never a float. So the digits are read as a whole number, and `edges[0].0.1` is `(edges[0].0).1`. The same holds after `?.`.
answers.outcome:
It compiles and prints 5. The access is a constant offset folded into the load, as C's `edges[0].a.y` is, so it costs nothing at run time.

Refused forms: `t.0.1e5`, `t.0x1` and `t.1i32` are E0100, because an element number is plain digits.

other_cases.case:
A matrix literal written across lines:
`grid = [`
`    [1, 0, 0],`
`    [0, 1, 0],`
`]`
other_cases.settled: Facet 1: the lines inside the brackets begin nothing (LEX-6), so this is one statement and compiles. This is what the compiler does today.

other_cases.case: A triple-quoted string holding TOML or INI text: `cfg = """` / `[package]` / `name = "game"` / `"""`
other_cases.settled: Facet 1: inside a string a line is text, so this compiles and the string holds `[package]`.

other_cases.case: A line joined by `\`: `total = \` with `[1, 2, 3].len()` on the next line
other_cases.settled: Facet 1: the second line continues the statement (LEX-7), so this compiles. The formatter never writes `\`.

other_cases.case: A match expression's arms: `n = match pair:` with arms `[a, b] => a + b` and `_ => 0`
other_cases.settled: Same as a statement match: a list-pattern arm, by GRM-47. It compiles, and `_` makes it exhaustive.

other_cases.case: An arm whose block begins with a local function: `["go", dir]:`, then `fn step(d: StrView): ...` indented under it
other_cases.settled: Facet 1: GRM-40's look at the next line is made only where a declaration may begin, never at the arms' indentation. So the line is an arm. Inside its block, a `[T]` line above a local `fn` is a type-parameter line as anywhere else.

All are E0100:
- the first because nearness is counted in physical lines (verdict 154);
- the others because no simple statement begins with `[`, and an enum takes its brackets after its name (verdict 155).

The help gives `xs = [1, 2, 3]` and then the call. J1-04's lead fix to LEX-11 stands.

other_cases.case: A safety note, a blank line, then `unsafe:`
other_cases.settled: LEX-23's "immediately before" counts physical lines (LEX-27 1), so the comment is no safety note. The block gets the missing-note diagnostic it gets today. LEX-23 is unchanged.

other_cases.case: Ranges against the rest, `..` against `..rest`: `[0..5, ..rest]`, `[..5]`, `[x, ..=5]`, and `xs[..n]` in an expression
other_cases.settled:
In a list pattern, a `..` followed by a name, `ref`, `,` or `]` is the rest, and `literal .. literal` is a range pattern.
- `[0..5, ..rest]` is one element in 0..5, then the rest.
- `[..5]` and `[x, ..=5]` are E0100, because a range pattern gives both ends.
- In an expression, `xs[..n]` is still a RangeTo slice.

other_cases.case: A pointer to a pointer in an extern declaration: `fn lib_names(count: c_int, names: **c_char)`
other_cases.settled: Facet 2: in a type the grammar takes `*` and never the power operator, so `**` is two pointers (C's `const char *const *`). The compiler refuses it today, so writers must put a space, `* *c_char`. `a ** b` is still power.

other_cases.case: Optional chaining against `?` then `.`: `r?.name` and `r?.0` where `r` is a `Result`; `opt?.0` where `opt` is an Option of a tuple
other_cases.settled:
Facet 2: the grammar takes `?.` there, so it stands.
- `r?.name` on a Result is E2020, and its help gives `(r?).name`. A spelling never changes meaning with the type.
- `opt?.0` is optional chaining to element 0.

other_cases.case: f-string holes: `f"{pair.0.1}"`, `f"{ratio:.2f}"`, `f"{scores["ann"]}"`, `f"{fn(x): x}"`
C names that begin with `_` (`st.__pad0`, `hdr._reserved`, `_mm_add_ps`), and a Python-style local `_unused`
other_cases.settled: The `identifier` production takes a leading `_` (Rust's and Python's rule; the compiler's is_ident_start already does). These are plain names. A lone `_` stays the discard, and `r#_` names C's `_`.

other_cases.case: `r#` on a word with no other meaning (`r#count`), and on a word that later leaves the reserved set (as `open`, `from` and `union` did)
other_cases.settled: `r#count` is `count`. A program keeps its meaning across versions in both directions, with no diagnostic.

other_cases.case: `r#self` and `r#owned` written to get around the reserved words: `r#self.hp` in a method, and `@ffi(param(w, r#owned, one))`
other_cases.settled:
A raw identifier never has the word's meaning:
- `r#self.hp` is an unknown name unless one is declared, since the object is `this`;
- `r#owned` among contract words is an unknown contract word.

Verdicts 2 and 102 hold.

other_cases.case: A comment written directly after a name `r` with no space: `x = r#note`
other_cases.settled: Facet 2: the grammar takes the longer token, a raw identifier. So `x` gets the name `note`, or its error if no `note` exists. The formatter writes `x = r  # note`.

other_cases.case: Element access chains and number tails: `m.0.1.2`, `t.0..t.1`, `1.0.max(x)`, `t.0.max(x)`
other_cases.settled:
- `m.0.1.2` is `((m.0).1).2`.
- `t.0..t.1` is a range between two elements.
- `1.0.max(x)` is a float method call, since the `1.0` does not follow a dot.
- `t.0.max(x)` calls a method on an element.

other_cases.case: A list pattern over text (`match line:` with the arm `["a"]:`), and over a fixed array (`match rgb:` with `rgb: [u8; 3]` and the single arm `[r, g, b]:`)
other_cases.settled:
Over text it is E2020: text converts to a StrView, not a Span, and has no positional elements. The help gives the words or the bytes.

Over `[u8; 3]`, the one arm is exhaustive, since its only length is 3.

other_cases.case: `match owns args:` with `args = ["build", "fast", "quiet"]`, the arm `[cmd, ..rest] if cmd == "run": run(owns rest)`, then the arm `[cmd, ..rest]: println(...)`
other_cases.settled: In the guard, `cmd` and `rest` are read-only views, and nothing moves. The guard is false, so the list is as it was. Arm 2 then takes `cmd` ("build") and `rest` (an `Array[String]` keeping the block, its two elements moved to the front once) and prints `unknown command build with 2 arguments`. Nothing is ended twice.

other_cases.case: A guard that changes the scrutinee: `match xs:` with the arms `[_, _, ..] if take_all(ref mut xs):`, `[_, _, c]: println(c)` and `_:`
other_cases.settled: Refused when compiling. The match views `xs` until an arm is chosen, its guards included, so `take_all(ref mut xs)` is E3021 at the call (BRW-1), as rustc's fake borrows refuse it. No name can point into a freed block.

Under `owns`, `all` owns the list and `first` is a read-only view of its element 0. Returning `first` where a `String` is wanted is refused, and the help gives `[first, ..rest]:`. Element 0 is never owned twice.

In the second program, `first = 9` changes what `all` reads while `all` is still used, so it is E3021 at that line (BRW-1).

other_cases.case: `for [x, y] in rows:` and `[w for [w, _] in rows]`, with `rows: Span[Array[float]]`; and `for [x, y] in pts:` with `pts: Span[[float; 2]]`
other_cases.settled:
Over `Array[float]` rows, the pattern may not match, so both are E2090. The help gives `for row in rows:`, then `if [x, y] = row:`, and nothing reads past a row's end. Over `[float; 2]` the pattern has one length and matches every element, so it compiles.

`for Some(x) in opts:` is E2090 too.

other_cases.case: `match flags:` over a `Span[bool]` with the arms `[]`, `[false, ..]` and `[.., true]`
other_cases.settled: L = max(0 + 1, 1 + 1) = 2. Lengths 0 and 1 are matched. Lengths 2 and up are checked as `[first, .., last]`, and `[true, .., false]` is missed, so the match is E2090 naming it. Without the bound, a two-element list would fall off the end.

other_cases.case: `match owns jobs:` with `jobs: Array[Job]`, the arms `[first, ..]: return Some(first)` and `[]: return None`
other_cases.settled: `first` takes element 0. When the arm's block begins, the other jobs end by their drop, in order, and the block is freed. Nothing leaks and nothing is ended twice.

other_cases.case: `match hits:` with `hits: SmallArray[int, 4]`; likewise a `FixedArray[T, N]`, an `ArenaArray[T]` or a program's own contiguous type
other_cases.settled: A list pattern matches exactly what a `Span[T]` parameter accepts, so today it is E2020, as `fn f(xs: Span[int])` given a `SmallArray` is a type error. The rule holds no list of types of its own, so if SPN-1 is widened (open risk 3), these match as lists with no edit.

other_cases.case: A const-generic array: `[T, const N: usize]` above `fn head(xs: [T; N])`, then `match xs:` with the arms `[a, ..]` and `[]`
other_cases.settled: N is not known in the generic body, so the arms are checked for every length, as a span's are. The `[a, ..]` and `[]` arms are exhaustive. `[a, b, c]` alone is E2090, naming `[]` and the other lengths.

design.prior_art:
C++11 (N1757, "Right angle brackets"). C++03 lexed `>>` in `vector<vector<int>>` as a shift and refused the line. C++11 made the parser read it as two `>` where a template argument list ends. That is facet 2: the longest token yields to the place. C++ has no raw identifiers, so a C header with a field named `class` cannot be used from C++. Xlib's `Visual` struct renames it by hand: `#if defined(__cplusplus) int c_class; #else int class; #endif`.

ECMAScript:
- An ExpressionStatement is specified with a lookahead restriction: it may not begin with `{`, `function`, `class` or `let [`. A line beginning with `{` is a block, by the grammar, not by a text rule. Verdict 155 is written that way: a simple statement never begins with `[`.
- ES5 (2009) made every IdentifierName a property name after `.`, reserved words included: `obj.class`, `promise.catch()`, `module.default`. That is facet 3's dot half.

Swift. SE-0071 (Swift 3) allows most keywords after `.` without backticks, for the same reason. `t.0.1` reads as nested element access. There are no array patterns in `switch`.

Python:
- PEP 634/636 sequence patterns are the J1-05 program itself: the tutorial's `match command.split(): case ["go", direction]:`.
- PEP 701 (3.12) re-lexes f-string holes with the full expression grammar.
- Python refuses `obj.class` even after a dot (`class_` is the habit), which is the cost facet 3 removes.

Rust:
- `r#ident` (Rust 1.30) was added so that `async` and `await` could become keywords while old names kept compiling. It cannot reach `self`, `super`, `crate` or `_`, so bindgen renames a C field `self` to `self_`.
- Rust 1.46 accepts `t.0.0` by splitting the float token after `.`. The parser also splits `&&` in `&&T`.
- Guards: since 1.39 (bind-by-move pattern guards), a guard sees shared references to the arm's bindings, and the moves happen only after it succeeds. Issue 27282 (a guard that changes the scrutinee, so an arm reads freed memory) was closed by NLL's "fake borrows" of the scrutinee during guards. GRM-13's Guards facet is both.
- Slice exhaustiveness (rustc_pattern_analysis) splits lengths at max(longest fixed length + 1, longest prefix + longest suffix) and reports `[true, .., false]`. GRM-47 states that bound.
- A refutable pattern in a `for` is refused (E0005, "refutable pattern in `for` loop binding"). CTL-1 does the same.
- `x @ Some(y)` (bindings after `@`, 1.56) is checked by the borrow rules. Rust refuses a by-move `x` with a borrowed part; Ember makes the part a view of `x`, which accepts the correct program.
- A `Vec` cannot be matched as a slice directly (write `v.as_slice()`), and `rest @ ..` reads worse than `..rest`.

C#. `@class` reaches any keyword, but it is needed even after `.`. C# 11 list patterns `[1, .. var rest]` match any countable, indexable type.

Zig. `@"any name"` reaches every C name.

Go. Keywords are never names. cgo reaches a C field `type` as `x._type`, a special case.

Ember's own precedent:
- LEX-15 already reads `not` and `is` as member names after `.` and `?.`, and facet 3 generalises it.
- The owner's standing rule of 2026-09-08 (`from` made contextual: "If you run into a from-like issue again, use the same strategy") says the same.
- The lead's ruling N47 reads keywords by position.
- The parser already reads list patterns in arms, splits `t.0.1`, accepts `r#owned`, and lets identifiers begin with `_`.

Where each falls short of safe, as fast as C, and readable:
- C++ cannot reach C names at all.
- Rust cannot reach `self` and cannot match a Vec.
- Swift cannot match lists.
- Python is slow and refuses `obj.class`.
- C# needs `@` after a dot.
- Go and bindgen rename by special cases.

The rule takes Python's readability, Rust's guard and exhaustiveness rules, C++11's and Rust's token splitting, ECMAScript's statement restriction and member names, and C#'s reach for `r#`, with C's machine code.
design.cost:
Everything is decided while compiling; nothing is checked while running.

Per operation, against C:
- **A list-pattern arm** is one length compare plus one compare per literal element. Several arms share one switch on the length. That is what C's hand-written `if (n == 2 && strcmp(w[0], "go") == 0)` runs.
- **An element name** is a pointer into the span (8 bytes), or a copied number.
- **A rest name** is a Span: a pointer and a length, 16 bytes, as C passes `w + 1, n - 1`.
- **No allocation and no copy.** `..ref mut rest` costs the same.
- **A guard** reads through the same pointers the arm uses, which adds nothing. Under `match owns`, the hand-overs come after the guard instead of before it: the same moves, never more. A false guard costs no move at all.
- **Under `match owns xs:`**:
  - a named rest of an `Array[T]` that follows other elements moves the remaining elements to the block's front once: one memmove of their bytes and no allocation, what `xs.drain(0..k)` pays;
  - a rest that comes first (`[..init, last]`) moves nothing;
  - the elements no name takes end once each, as their drops would anyway, and the block is freed once.
- **`t.0.1`** is a constant offset folded into the address: zero.
- **`**c_char`** is a type: zero.
- **A raw identifier or a member word after `.`** is a name, and the C emitted uses the C name: zero.

Compile time:
- the lexer remembers one previous token;
- the parser splits a token where the grammar refuses the whole, as rustc and every C++11 compiler do;
- exhaustiveness checks L + 1 length classes, each as a tuple pattern, as rustc does;
- a `for` pattern gets one one-arm check;
- the scrutinee's view through guards is one more live range for the existing view checker.

Memory: none beyond the views the program names.

readability.note:
The after is four lines shorter and adds no word.
- `parse_cmd` reads as Python's own `case ["go", direction]:`, and the shape of each arm says what it matches. The before hides the shape in nested `if`s and repeats `return Command.Unknown`.
- `event.type` reads as the C header and every SDL tutorial write it.

A program that uses none of these forms (a game loop, a server handler) is unchanged character for character. The rules that make list patterns safe (guards, exhaustiveness, `for` patterns, `@`) add no word: a refused program gets a help line that compiles.

design.compiler_does:
**Lexer.**
- It remembers the token before. After `.` or `?.` it reads digits as a whole decimal number. Today the parser's float split does this after `.` only (body.rs, the `eat_tuple_index_pair` branch); moving it into the lexer also covers `?.`.
- `r#` followed by any word, a keyword or `_` included, is a raw identifier (already).
- An identifier may begin with `_` (is_ident_start, lib.rs 1100, already).
- A `#!` that begins a line where a line may begin is a directive token wherever it stands. One after the first import or item is E0104.

**Parser.**
- After `.` and `?.`, any word is a member name. `expect_member_name` (lib.rs 427) takes `not` and `is` today; it takes every keyword token. Path segments and import module paths after `.` do the same.
- A simple statement that begins with `[` is refused with GRM-40's one message. Type-parameter lines are recognised only where a declaration may begin, never in the arm loop (parse_match_tail, body.rs 683, already). "Directly above" and "the line after" count physical lines, so a comment or blank line between them is seen.
- Where the token in hand is not taken but a token made of its first characters is, the parser splits it. This is new for `**` in a type.
- `?.` takes an element number.
- List patterns (body.rs, the `LBracket` pattern branch) gain `ref` or `ref mut` before the rest name. A second `..` is refused; today it silently replaces the first.

**Checker.**
- It types a list pattern against the scrutinee's span type, from SPN-1's conversion. Each element name gets its element's type and words (GRM-13, GRM-42). The rest name gets a `Span[T]` or a `MutSpan[T]`, or under `match owns` an owned `[T; M]` or `Array[T]`.
- It keeps the scrutinee viewed from the `match` line until an arm is chosen, its guards included, as rustc's fake borrows do. It types every name inside a guard as a read-only view, and places the hand-overs after the guard.
- Exhaustiveness: it splits list lengths at L = max(longest arm without `..` + 1, most before a `..` + most after), and checks each class as tuple patterns, as rustc does. Arms with guards count for no value. E2090 names each missing value, and W2091 marks an arm no value reaches.
- It checks a `for` target or a comprehension clause as a one-arm match.
- `x @ p` gives two names of one place, under BRW-1. Under `match owns`, `p`'s names are views of `x`'s parts.
- On a Result, `r?.name` is E2020 with the help `(r?).name`.

**Code generation.**
- A switch or compare on the length, then the literal compares, then pointer offsets into the span: the code C writes by hand.
- Under `match owns`, once the arm is chosen: the element moves, the rest's one memmove, then the drops of the elements no name takes, in order, then the arm's block.

**Messages** are the lead's, and each gives the line to write in the program's own names.

The programmer writes nothing new.

1. **The arm half narrows verdict 155's literal words** and must be put to the owner as such (phase 3's clash). Show him `["go", dir]:` beside the enum and `[10, 20].len()` cases he ruled on.

3. **SPN-1's list of what converts to a Span is closed.** `SmallArray[T, N]`, `FixedArray[T, N]`, `ArenaArray[T]` and a program's own contiguous type hold their elements in one run, yet cannot be passed where a `Span[T]` is expected, so they cannot be matched as lists either. design.rule: Ending a value means giving back. On every way out of its scope (the end of the block, `return`, `?`, `break`, `continue`), and when it is overwritten, cleared, handed to `mem.drop` or left in a dropped generator, a value ends by its type's `drop`. Every standard type's `drop` does the same three things. (1) It gives back everything the value still holds: memory, a lock, a file, a swapchain image, a count, C's hold. (2) It keeps what the value's calls have already done (bytes written, changes made under a lock, tasks started, commands recorded). It throws away work that only a call taking the value over makes real (a frame's submission at `end_frame`, a transaction's `commit`), and leaves what that work would have changed as it was before. (3) It cannot fail and never stops the program; any step of it that can fail is also a call returning a `Result`, which the program makes first if it must hear of the failure. A value that gives back to something in the program is made by a method of that thing, so it points into it (LT-1, inferred, no word) and never outlives it. A call that finishes a value (`end_frame`) takes the pending work out of it, so the drop that runs at that call's end finds nothing left to do. There is one way to end a value, and its `drop` always runs. For J7-19: a `?` before `end_frame` abandons the frame. Nothing is shown, the image goes back to the device, the recording is discarded, the frame's memory is freed, and the next frame works as usual.

answers.answer: The rule decides it: an early exit by `?` ends `frame` by its drop, and a Frame that ends without end_frame is abandoned (GPU-2 under DRP-9 rule 2). The frame's submission and its shown image were pending until `end_frame(owns frame)`, a call that takes the frame over. So the drop discards the recording, gives the swapchain image back unshown and frees the frame's memory. Every resource the frame recorded keeps the contents and access state it had before the frame, and the device is ready for the next begin_frame. The error goes back to the caller as the program says. Nothing stops the program and nothing undefined happens. The program is written with `match owns` because whether a name opened by `exists as` from a temporary may be handed over is P11's question; the outcome is the same in either spelling.
answers.code:
from std.gpu import Device, Frame, GpuError, TextureDesc, TextureHandle

fn draw_sky(ref mut frame: Frame, sky: TextureHandle):
    pass                                             # records the sky pass

fn render(ref mut dev: dyn Device, desc: TextureDesc) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    started = dev.begin_frame()                      # acquires a swapchain image, opens a recording
    match owns started:
        Some(frame):
            sky = dev.create_texture(desc)?          # on an error, `?` returns: `frame` ends here, abandoned
            draw_sky(ref mut frame, sky)
            dev.end_frame(owns frame)                # submits and shows; the frame's drop then finds no work
        None:
            pass                                     # a minimised window: no frame this time
    return Ok(())
answers.outcome: Compiles, as it does today. When create_texture fails, render returns that error, and frame ends at the `?` line by its drop, which runs dev.abandon_frame. The recording is discarded, swapchain image goes back unshown, the frame's arena is freed and nothing it recorded is in flight. The window keeps the last frame shown, and the next dev.begin_frame() works as usual. When create_texture succeeds, end_frame submits and shows the frame; the frame ends at the end of end_frame, and its drop finds the work already taken and does nothing.

other_cases.case: A command list left in the middle of a render pass, with the frame going on: `with cmd = frame.command_list():` then `cmd.begin_render_pass(...)`, a `continue` in a loop over meshes before `cmd.end_render_pass()`, then `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` later.
other_cases.settled: GPU-13 under DRP-9 rule 2. The list's end puts its recorded draws into the frame and records end_render_pass for the open pass, so the recording is valid. Draws recorded before the exit are shown when the frame is ended; abandoning the frame instead would discard them.

other_cases.case: `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` while a command list of that frame is still used (`cmd = frame.command_list()`, then end_frame, then `cmd.draw(...)`).
other_cases.settled: Refused when compiling. The list is a view of the frame (it is the result of the frame's method, LT-1), and a frame is not handed over while a view of it is used. No command can be added to a frame already submitted.

other_cases.case: A Frame kept past its device: a `Renderer` that stores `this.pending = dev.begin_frame()` and outlives the `ref mut dev` parameter, or a function returning a Frame made from a device it does not return.
other_cases.settled: Refused when compiling (E3063). The Frame holds a kept sharedref mut link to its device, so it lives no longer than the device. The program can still use the device while the frame lives, so `dev.create_texture` during a frame stays allowed. No run-time count.

other_cases.case: A frame skipped on purpose on an ordinary path: `if scene.is_empty(): mem.drop(owns frame)`, or a `continue`/`return Ok(())` out of the frame's branch.
other_cases.settled: Abandoned, as for `?` (DRP-9: every end that is not end_frame). The window keeps the last frame and the next begin_frame works. `mem.drop(owns frame)` is the existing spelling for ending a value now. A forgotten end_frame on a normal path also abandons the frame, so nothing is shown; it is not refused (that is option E).

other_cases.case: A frame's holder overwritten or cleared: `this.pending = dev.begin_frame()` while a frame is held there, or a discarded `dev.begin_frame()` as a statement.
other_cases.settled: The old frame, or the temporary at the end of its statement (DRP-3), is abandoned (OWN-5, DRP-9). By DRP-8, ending it counts as a call of its drop, which changes the device, so doing it inside a walk of what abandon_frame changes is refused, as `enemies.clear()` inside `for line in LOG:` is.

other_cases.case: A generator that holds a frame across a `yield` and is dropped while suspended.
other_cases.settled: CORO-7 drops the locals live at the suspension point, so the frame is abandoned (DRP-9's list of ends). Frame is not @must_drop: no safety guarantee rests on its drop, because the tie to its device is checked when compiling.

other_cases.case: `device.destroy(h)` called during a frame that is then abandoned, and a buffer written through `Ring.current(frame)` in it.
other_cases.settled: GPU-2 under DRP-9 rule 2. The handle is invalid at once (GPU-6), and physical destruction waits only for the frames already submitted, since the abandoned frame never ran. The ring slot is not in flight because of the abandoned frame, so the next frame may write it with no GPU-4 panic.

other_cases.case: A panic, or process.exit, while a frame (or a lock guard, a file, a scope) lives.
other_cases.settled: No scope is left: the process ends with no drop run (PAN-1, STD-24), and the operating system and driver take back the device, files and memory. This is unchanged and now stated in DRP-9.

other_cases.case: File and Socket ending on an early `?` (`f = File.create(path)?` then `f.write(data)?` failing).
other_cases.settled: DRP-9 rules 1 to 3. The handle is closed on every exit; bytes a write reported written are with the operating system. A close error is not reported, as with an ignored fclose in C. A library Socket follows the same rules: closed, and bytes `send` accepted are left to the OS to send.

other_cases.case: A BufWriter whose final write fails when it is dropped (a full disk), on a path that returns Ok.
other_cases.settled: STD-22 under DRP-9 rule 3. The drop tries to write its bytes; that failure is lost, the wrapped file is still closed, and the program goes on. A program that must know writes `w.flush()?` before the end. This is unchanged in behaviour, now stated (Rust and C++ do the same).

other_cases.case: Lock guards, Scope and JobScope, ScopedArena, JoinHandle and Retained callback tokens ending on `?`.
other_cases.settled: These are DRP-9's instances, unchanged. A guard unlocks and changes made under it stay (DRP-6). A scope joins its tasks, which run to their end (THR-5, JOB-2). A scoped arena releases its memory after the values made in it, which cannot outlive it (ARN-6, E3063). A JoinHandle detaches. A Retained token unregisters its callback once, staying alive while that callback runs (FFI-23, verdict 62; P08's).

other_cases.case: A library transaction type: `struct Transaction` with `conn: sharedref mut Connection`, `open: bool = true`, `fn commit() owns this -> Result[void, DbError]:` whose body is `this.conn.exec("COMMIT")?` then `this.open = false`, and `fn drop():` whose body is `if this.open: this.conn.exec("ROLLBACK").ok()`.
other_cases.settled: DRP-9 rule 2 and its finishing-call sentence, with no new word. A `?` before commit rolls the work back. A COMMIT that fails leaves `open` true, so the drop rolls back. A successful commit marks the work taken, so the drop does nothing. The drop always runs, and there is no `forget` or `discard self`. The conn link ties the transaction to its connection (E3063).

other_cases.case: GPU buffers and textures created before an early exit (handles are Copy, GPU-1).
other_cases.settled: A handle names an object and the device holds it, so DRP-9 rule 1 applies to the device. The object stays until `device.destroy(h)` or the device's end, which destroys every object still live (GPU-6 as changed), and debug reports each as leaked (GPU-7). A mapping, a view of a buffer's memory, ends by DRP-6 (a view type ends whatever in it needs ending): it is unmapped, and the writes made through it stay (rule 2).

design.prior_art:
C++: destructors run on every scope exit (return, exceptions). std::lock_guard unlocks. fstream closes and swallows a failed flush. std::thread's destructor calls std::terminate if the thread was not joined (option B; C++20's jthread replaced it with joining). libpqxx's transaction aborts in its destructor unless committed (option A). Where it falls short: nothing ties a frame or command buffer to its device, so destroying the device first is a use-after-free that only the Vulkan validation layer reports, at run time; and a destructor's failure is either swallowed or terminates the program.

Rust: Drop runs on every exit, `?` included. Types are affine, not linear, so a type cannot require its finishing call. wgpu discards a SurfaceTexture dropped without present() and a CommandEncoder dropped without finish(), and a RenderPass ends its pass when dropped: that is A, and GPU-13's closing of an open pass. rusqlite and sqlx roll back a Transaction dropped without commit (A); rusqlite also offers DropBehavior::Panic (B). BufWriter flushes on drop and ignores the error, which is the limit DRP-9 rule 3 states. Ties are made with a written lifetime (RenderPass<'a>, which wgpu now lets a program forget) or with Arc counts (wgpu inside, vulkano's Arc<Device> everywhere): an atomic count per object, which Ember's inferred link avoids.

Swift: deinit runs on every exit. ~Copyable types (SE-0390) end through `consuming` methods that write `discard self` to skip deinit, which is a second way to end a value and a new word. Ember's `mem.take` pattern does the same without either. Swift has no must-consume types.

Ada: controlled types' Finalize runs on every exit, exceptions and aborts included (A's coverage).

C#: using/IDisposable. TransactionScope.Dispose without Complete() rolls back (A). Dispose may throw.

Go and Zig: cleanup is written by hand. Go writes `defer tx.Rollback()`, which a later Commit turns into a no-op; Zig writes `errdefer` for the error path only. Forgetting either leaks.

Python: `with` lets __exit__ see the exception and choose commit or rollback (sqlite3). That is a hidden path that depends on how the block exits; Ember's explicit `?` does not need it.

Vale and Austral: linear types and higher RAII refuse a value that is not finished by its consuming call (option D). That refuses `?` while a frame lives.

Ember's design takes three things from these. From C++ and Rust: a drop on every exit. From Rust, C# and wgpu: rolling back, by default, work that waits for a finishing call. And, at no run-time cost, a tie to the provider that is inferred from the call that made the value (LT-1, verdict 140) and checked when compiling, which none of them has.
design.cost:
Ending on every exit: the compiler places the same cleanup calls C writes by hand on each error path (`goto cleanup`). Where a value is handed over on only some paths, it costs one hidden flag byte and one test (OWN-3), the same as C's `if (frame) abandon(frame)` in a cleanup label, and nothing where the path is known.

The tie (DRP-9, GPU-2, GPU-13): checked when compiling. At run time it is one pointer in the Frame to its device, which a C frame struct holds anyway (`frame->device`): zero extra time and memory. A command list's tie to its frame costs nothing.

Abandoning a frame: discarding command buffers that were never submitted (a pool reset the next frame does anyway), giving the image back (one driver call, or keeping it for the next begin_frame), and resetting the frame arena (one pointer store). That is what a C renderer's error path does, and nothing per draw.

A finishing call taking the work out: one store per part. The drop's test of whether work is still in it is one compare per frame end. It is folded away when the call is known (static dispatch); through `dyn Device` it stays one compare per frame against C's zero (about a nanosecond per 16 ms frame). Memory: at most one flag per frame.

Command list closing an open pass: one end_render_pass record, only when a pass was left open (C must record it too, or its command buffer is invalid).

BufWriter, File, lock guards, scopes, arena scopes, JoinHandle and callback tokens: unchanged from today, equal to C's fflush, fclose, unlock and join at the same points.

from std.gpu import Device, GpuError

fn run(ref mut dev: dyn Device, ref mut game: Game) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    while game.running:
        game.update(1.0 / 60.0)
        started = dev.begin_frame()
        match owns started:
            Some(frame):
                minimap = dev.create_texture(game.minimap_desc())?   # on an error the frame is abandoned; the next frame works
                draw_world(ref mut frame, game)
                draw_minimap(ref mut frame, minimap)
                dev.end_frame(owns frame)
                dev.destroy(minimap)                                 # freed once the GPU has finished this frame
            None:

    return Ok(())
readability.note: The two programs are identical, character for character apart from the comment. The rule adds no word, no annotation and no line; the same `?` goes from undecided to stated. The only line a program might add is `mem.drop(owns frame)`, to skip a frame on purpose, and that spelling already exists. The library code does not get longer either: a finishing call uses the existing `mem.take`, not a new `discard` word.

design.compiler_does:
- Places each value's end on every exit of its block: falling off the end, `return`, `?`, `break`, `continue`, and a `with` block's exit. It also places it on an overwrite, at the end of a temporary's statement, and in a dropped suspended generator. All of this is as today (CTL-8, DRP-2, DRP-3, CORO-7). Where a value is handed over on only some paths, it keeps one hidden flag (OWN-3).
- Infers the ties with no word: the results of `dev.begin_frame()` and `frame.command_list()` point into their objects, as every method's result does (LT-1, verdict 140). It refuses keeping a Frame past its device or a CommandList past its frame (E3063), and refuses `end_frame(owns frame)` while a list of that frame is still used. Because the Frame's link is a kept `sharedref mut` one (LT-4, LT-46), the device stays usable during the frame.
- Counts each end as a call of the drop (DRP-8). The Frame's drop changes the device through abandon_frame, so a frame ended inside a walk of what abandon_frame changes, or under a lock it needs, is refused like any other call.
- Folds away the drop's test of whether work is still in the value when the finishing call is known (static dispatch, inlined). Through `dyn Device` the test stays, one compare.
- Applies verdict 164: a type holding a `sharedref mut` link is neither Send nor ThreadShared, so a Frame stays on its thread; scoped tasks reach it through the caller's variable.
- Nothing is written by the programmer.
design.misuse:
- Calling end_frame for a frame that never began, or twice: refused when compiling (GPU-2, unchanged).
- Keeping a Frame where it would outlive its device, or a CommandList past its frame: refused when compiling (E3063). The message names the device and the line, and gives a fix that compiles, for example "end the frame in this function: `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` above line 12, or keep the device with it".
- `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` while a command list of that frame is still used: refused when compiling, the help being to move the call below the list's last use.
- `frame.drop()`: E3070 (DRP-1).
- A value made in `frame.arena()` kept past the frame: E3063 (GPU-3, unchanged).
- Ending a frame inside a walk of what its drop changes: refused (DRP-8, E3020).
- Sending a Frame to another thread: refused (verdict 164, E7015).
- Forgetting end_frame on a normal path is not refused (option E would refuse it). The frame is abandoned: nothing is shown, and the program, device and memory stay sound, so the mistake is visible on the first run and never undefined.
- A panic inside a frame stops the program at its line with its message (PAN-1); no drop runs, and the OS and driver take the device back.
- A program's own drop that panics aborts with its message (DRP-4).
- Writing a resource that was used only in an abandoned frame is allowed, because it is not in flight. A resource in a frame that was submitted still stops with GPU-4's message.
design.verdicts:
No verdict is revisited.

- **56, kept.** A value counts as ended before its drop runs. The Frame's drop lends its own object to abandon_frame by `ref mut`, as a drop uses its object (DRP-5 forbids only making an owner of it), and no weakref reaches a half-ended frame.
- **57, kept and relied on.** Ending a Frame counts as a call of its drop (DRP-8), and every rule sees the changes that drop makes to the device through abandon_frame.
- **58, kept.** A finishing call takes the pending work out with mem.take. Nothing ends a value without its drop, and no forget or `discard self` comes back.
- **69, kept.** Frame's drop writes no `changes` word.
- **140, used.** "A method gives a result that points into its object, as every method does" gives the frame-to-device and list-to-frame ties with no word.
- **164, applied.** A Frame, holding a `sharedref mut` link, is neither Send nor ThreadShared; scoped tasks still reach it through the caller's variable.
- **THR-6 (ODR-054), unchanged.** No safety guarantee rests on a Frame's drop, since the tie is checked when compiling. So Frame is not @must_drop, and the library still applies @must_drop to Scope and JobScope only.
- **The rule also matches verdict 11 and principle 7.** The correct `?` program is made to work, not refused (D is rejected for that). It matches principle 8: the tie is decided when compiling, and the abandonment is the cheapest run-time act, the one C does.

options_for_owner.summary: One rule for every value's end (DRP-9): give back what it holds, keep what is done, discard work that waits for a finishing call. A Frame ended without end_frame is abandoned.
options_for_owner.code:
fn render(ref mut dev: dyn Device, desc: TextureDesc) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    started = dev.begin_frame()
    match owns started:
        Some(frame):
            sky = dev.create_texture(desc)?      # an error: `frame` ends here and is abandoned
            draw_sky(ref mut frame, sky)
            dev.end_frame(owns frame)
        None:
            pass
    return Ok(())

The image goes back to the device, the recording is discarded and the frame's memory is freed. The next begin_frame works as usual. Keeping a Frame past its device is refused when compiling (E3063). It costs what C's cleanup path costs.

options_for_owner.summary: Refused when compiling unless every path hands the frame to end_frame (or mem.drop): a linear type, as in Vale and Austral.

    match owns started:
        Some(frame):
            match dev.create_texture(desc):
                Ok(sky):
                    draw_sky(ref mut frame, sky)
                    dev.end_frame(owns frame)
                Err(e):
                    mem.drop(owns frame)         # every path must end it in writing
                    return Err(e)
        None:

options_for_owner.outcome: The program in A compiles and behaves as under A. The `return Ok(())` line is refused: "`frame` ends on line 6 without `dev.end_frame(owns frame)`, so this frame is never shown; show it with `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` above line 6, or skip it with `mem.drop(owns frame)`". A forgotten end_frame is caught when compiling. The cost is a new attribute word, and an end rule that depends on how a path exits (`?` against `return`), which the language has nowhere else. It can be added to A later without changing A.

recommendation.reason: It is how every resource in Ember already ends (a guard unlocks, a scope joins, a scoped arena frees, a token unregisters), stated once as one law and extended to work that waits for a finishing call. The `?` program works unchanged; nothing is undefined, nothing half-done is shown or committed, and the device is ready for the next frame. The programmer writes nothing: the tie to the device is inferred from the method that made the frame and checked when compiling, and it costs what C's cleanup path costs. B turns a handled error into a crash. C shows half a frame (and would commit half a transaction) and loses the submit's failure. D refuses the correct program and makes every frame longer. E catches a forgotten end_frame when compiling, but needs a new word and an end rule that depends on how the path exits, for a mistake that is visible on the first run and harmless. Checklist 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 11 and 13.

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: what a frame guard's destructor does when an early return (Ember's `?`) leaves `render()` between `begin_frame()` and `end_frame()`. It could submit, call `std::terminate`, or roll back the way an uncommitted transaction's destructor does.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | `started = dev.begin_frame()` | a `Frame`: swapchain image 2 acquired, a recording open, its arena empty |
| 2 | main | `match owns started:` takes `Some(frame):` | `frame` owns that `Frame` |
| 3 | main | `sky = dev.create_texture(desc)?` fails (out of GPU memory, say) | an `Err(GpuError)` |
| 4 | main | the `?` returns that error from `render` | `frame` ends on that line with no `end_frame`, so its `drop` runs |
| 5 | main | today: `Frame` has no stated `drop`; GPU-2 covers only a frame never begun or ended twice | image 2 still acquired? recording still open? next `begin_frame` works, hangs or fails? undecided |
| 6 | main | under A: the drop abandons the frame | recording discarded, image 2 back to the device unshown, arena freed; the window keeps the last frame; the next `begin_frame` works |
owner_short.today: Undecided: a `?` between begin_frame and end_frame leaves the acquired swapchain image and the open recording in no stated state, because Frame has no drop and GPU-2 only refuses a frame never begun or ended twice.
owner_short.options:
A: the frame's end rolls it back (recording dropped, image back unshown, memory freed, next frame fine), by one rule for every resource's end, with no new word.
B: the frame's end stops the program ("a Frame ended without end_frame"), like C++'s std::thread destructor calling std::terminate.
C: the frame's end submits and shows what was recorded, as end_frame does: a half-drawn frame on an error, and a failed submit goes unreported.
D: refused when compiling unless every path calls end_frame or mem.drop: no `?` while a frame lives.
E: A, plus a library mark (`@ends_by(end_frame)`) so that a frame left any way but by an error is refused when compiling.
owner_short.recommendation: A: the `?` program works unchanged. Nothing is shown half-drawn and nothing is undefined. It is the rule every Ember resource already follows (a guard unlocks, a scope joins), it costs what C's cleanup costs, and the programmer writes no word.

design.open_risks:
1. **How a Device implementer is told about an abandoned frame.** The spec text adds `fn abandon_frame(ref mut frame: Frame)` to the Device interface so that host renderers know what to do. A program could also call it directly. Annex D still has to settle whether the hook is hidden from programs and how an implementer's end_frame takes the work out of a std type with private fields; the effect on the device is fixed either way.
2. **end_frame returns nothing.** A failed submit or present (device lost, out-of-date swapchain) has no stated result. Rule 3's pattern (a step that can fail is a call returning `Result`) points to `end_frame(owns frame) -> Result[void, GpuError]`. That is an API change outside this group's principle, so it should be its own question.
3. **A BufWriter's write at drop time can fail silently.** The failure is lost, as in Rust and C++; a program learns of it only by calling `w.flush()?` first. A check when compiling that a writer ends by its drop on a path returning Ok would need the compiler to know the buffer is empty after flush() (tracking a library's state) or a new word. Not designed here; it could be its own question.
4. **A Frame cannot move to another thread.** Because it holds a `sharedref mut` link, it is neither Send nor ThreadShared (verdict 164). Scoped tasks still record through the caller's frame, but a design that moves frames between threads would need another kind of link, and the spec has none today.
5. **The examples use `match owns started:`.** J7-19's `if dev.begin_frame() exists as frame:` followed by `owns frame` depends on whether a name opened from a temporary may be handed over, which is P11's question. This rule's outcome is the same in either spelling.
6. **Textures created before an early exit stay alive.** GPU handles are Copy names (GPU-1), so such a texture stays until destroy or the device's end, which this rule makes destroy it; debug reports it (GPU-7). An owning handle type whose end calls destroy would bring it under rule 1. That would be a library addition and is not decided here.
7. **Option E can still be added later.** It would sit on top of A without changing A, if the owner wants a forgotten end_frame refused when compiling.

matrix.guarantee: No read of freed memory
matrix.how_kept: A Frame holds a kept `sharedref mut` link to the device that began it, inferred from the method that made it (LT-1 rule 1, LT-45), so it lives no longer than the device (E3063), and DRP-7 has its drop (which reaches the device) run while the device is valid. matrix.how_kept: Verdict 164: a Frame, holding a `sharedref mut` link, is neither Send nor ThreadShared, so it never goes to another thread; a CommandList is a view of the frame. from std.gpu import Device, Frame, GpuError

fn render(ref mut dev: dyn Device, scene: Scene) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    started = dev.begin_frame()
    match owns started:
        Some(frame):
            if scene.is_empty():
                dev.abandon_frame(ref mut frame)   # skip this frame, through the method Annex D now lists
                return Ok(())                      # `frame` ends here: its drop runs abandon_frame again
            draw_world(ref mut frame, scene)
            dev.end_frame(owns frame)
        None:
            pass
    return Ok(())
holes.what_goes_wrong: It compiles. The spec text adds `fn abandon_frame(ref mut frame: Frame)` to `interface Device`, and nothing stops a program calling it. The frame is abandoned twice: its image goes back twice, its recording is discarded twice, its arena is freed twice. If `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` follows the call instead of the `return`, a frame whose image was already given back is submitted and shown. GPU-2's 'a frame is either submitted or abandoned, once' also depends on every implementer's end_frame taking the work out of std's Frame, which open risk 1 admits has no defined way to reach Frame's private fields. Without that, every frame's drop at end_frame's end abandons a frame that was already submitted. For a Vulkan host renderer, releasing an image twice, or presenting one that was not acquired, is invalid use and undefined in the driver.
holes.fix_hint: Do not add a hook. Make the pending work a value the Frame owns, given by the implementer at begin_frame (`work: Option[owns dyn FrameWork]`, or the device's own type), whose own drop abandons it. end_frame takes it with `mem.take(ref mut frame.work)` and submits it. 'Submitted or abandoned, once' then follows from one owner (OWN-1), not from implementer discipline. A program that ends the work early abandons it exactly once. This is DRP-9's own finishing-call sentence, with no special path.

fn render_windows(ref mut main_view: dyn Device, ref mut tool_view: dyn Device, world: World) -> Result[void, GpuError]:

    match owns started:
        Some(frame):

holes.fix_hint: Either make the finishing call the frame's own, `frame.present() owns this`, reaching its device through the link it already holds, as a Transaction's commit does. Or keep `dev.end_frame(owns frame)` and state in GPU-2 that a frame begun by another device stops the program at the line, with one pointer compare against the frame's link: "`tool_view.end_frame` was given the frame `main_view` began on line 3; end it with `main_view.end_frame(owns frame)`".

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design's case for an overwritten holder says the old frame is abandoned and the device then works as usual. But OWN-5 evaluates the new value before it drops the old one, so begin_frame runs while the old frame still holds its swapchain image and open recording. GPU-2 does not say what begin_frame does while a frame of the same device is open. A Vulkan host acquires a second image. Once more images are held than imageCount minus minImageCount, an acquire without a timeout is invalid use and in practice waits for ever: a hang with no message, not a stop at a line. The same happens for two begin_frame calls in a row, and for a suspended generator kept in a struct with a frame held across its `yield` (legal, because Frame is not @must_drop). THR-6's reason for leaving Frame off @must_drop ('no safety guarantee rests on its drop') holds only if begin_frame copes with an open frame.

fn draw_meshes(ref mut frame: Frame, ref mut instances: Ring[BufferHandle, 3], meshes: Array[Mesh]):

        cmd.begin_render_pass(RenderPassBegin(target=None))
        for m in meshes:

So inside the list's block, `instances.current(frame)` and `frame.arena()` are refused, though a renderer's inner loop does exactly this: per-draw data from the frame's ring or arena while recording. Two lists of one frame at once are refused too, so one list per scoped task cannot be written. That is how engines record in parallel (Vulkan secondary command buffers, D3D12 command lists). If the link is a `sharedref mut` one instead, the read compiles, but by verdict 164 no scoped task may record through it. GPU-13 says neither kind.

Yet this program is sound: fields end in reverse declaration order (DRP-2), so `pending` is abandoned while `dev` still lives. The program has to keep the device outside the renderer and pass a link around.

That is a rule for every self-contained holder, not an exception for Frame. Or a Frame whose end does not reach into the device: each frame carries a generation as handles do (GPU-1), the device reclaims a frame ended unsubmitted at its next begin_frame, and a stale frame stops at its use. If it is None, as for a minimised window, the game runs on silently showing nothing; nothing stops at a line and the caller is never told. The design leaves this as open risk 2, but under its own rule 3 the type the rule is about breaks the rule.
holes.fix_hint: `fn end_frame(owns frame: Frame) -> Result[void, GpuError]` and `fn begin_frame() -> Result[Option[Frame], GpuError]` (an error for a lost device, None only for a frame skipped by design), following rule 3's own pattern, as create_texture already does. This is an API change, so it should go to the owner as its own line beside this question.

fn save(path: StrView, world: World) -> Result[void, io.Error]:

safety.notes:
What holds: for the program J7-19 is about (one device, one frame, a `?` before end_frame), design A keeps every guarantee. The frame is abandoned once, values made in its arena and its command list end before it, nothing is shown half-drawn, and nothing undefined happens. Lock guards, scopes, ScopedArena, JoinHandle, Retained tokens, File and the Transaction pattern are faithful instances of rules already in the spec. I found no clash with verdicts 56, 57, 58, 69, 140 or 164, and none with THR-6/ODR-054.

Where it breaks: the holes are in the frame-specific spec text, not in the general law.
- High: `abandon_frame` is a public Device method, so a frame can be ended twice, and 'taking the work out' has no defined mechanism for std's Frame.
- High: the finishing call is a device method that accepts another device's frame.
- Medium: begin_frame with a frame of the same device still open is undecided, and OWN-5's order produces that state in the design's own overwrite case.
- Medium: the command list's view kind is unstated; read as exclusive (as written), it refuses ordinary per-draw ring and arena use and all parallel recording.
- Medium: tying Frame to its device makes Frame a view type, which refuses a class that owns both its device and its pending frame.
- Medium: rule 3 loses two failures silently, a failed present (end_frame returns nothing) and a BufWriter's last write; the owner's bar says never silent.

A possibly better design for the lead to weigh: pending work as an owned value (fixes hole 1 with no hook), plus handle-style generations for frames (no view tie, so holes 2, 3 and 5 go away at one compare per use). I did not develop it further.

Depends on other groups: P11 (`exists as` from a temporary, which is why the examples use `match owns`), P12 (`sharedref mut` on a dyn value), P01 (a frame's drop as a route to another thread), P02 (the frame arena freed at abandon), P05 (compiler-placed ends counted as calls).

holes.program:
from std.gpu import Device, Frame, GpuError

fn run(ref mut dev: dyn Device, ref mut game: Game) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    while game.running:
        started = dev.begin_frame()
        match owns started:
            Some(frame):
                if game.paused:
                    mem.drop(owns frame)        # the frame's drop changes the device through its link (DRP-8: abandon_frame)
                    continue                    # `dev`, a ref mut name, is used again on line 5
                draw_world(ref mut frame, game)
                dev.end_frame(owns frame)
            None:
                pass
    return Ok(())
holes.what_goes_wrong: BRW-1 (p07 255-258) says that while a ref mut name is still used its place is changed only through it, and another name, 'a link of the same type included', is E3022. The frame's sharedref mut link changes the device at mem.drop (and wherever recording reaches the device through the link, which can include J7-19's own draw_sky) while `dev` is still used, so BRW-1 refuses what DRP-9 and GPU-2 say compiles. The only sentence that lets a ref mut name and a link made from it coexist is LT-4's, written for memory managers. The design adds a second per-type sentence in GPU-2 ('while the program goes on using the device') and a general one in DRP-9, a destruction rule the view checker does not read. So the spec gives two answers, and the tie is a special case for each type that needs it.
holes.fix_hint: State it once where views are ruled (LT-46 and BRW-1): a sharedref mut link made from a name, whether an owner or a ref mut name, makes that name one of the link's holders. BRW-1's aloneness then holds against every other name. LT-4 and GPU-2 cite that sentence instead of each stating it. This changes BRW-1, so it is an owner question.

holes.program:
from std.gpu import Device, Frame

class Renderer:
    dev: owns dyn Device
    frame: Option[Frame] = None

    fn begin():
        this.frame = this.dev.begin_frame()

    fn finish():
        match owns mem.take(ref mut this.frame):
            Some(f):
                this.dev.end_frame(owns f)
            None:
                pass
holes.what_goes_wrong: This compiles today, because Frame holds no link. Under the rule a Frame holds a sharedref mut link into `this.dev`, so `frame` becomes a view field of a class. LT-45 then requires `from <let field>` (E2118), and a `let` field's object is never changed through it (CLS-9a, E2104), so `this.dev.begin_frame()` is refused. No spelling compiles. A Renderer that begins a frame in one method and ends it in another is the common engine shape, and in C++ (`struct Renderer { Device dev; Frame* frame; }`) it is correct and safe as long as the frame field ends first. The design's own E3063 help, 'or keep the device with it', is therefore a line that does not compile (checklist 9).
holes.fix_hint: Let a class field holding a sharedref mut link say `from <field>` for an `owns` field (its block never moves) without `let`. A sharedref mut link already tolerates changes and ends at a reshape (BRW-17), so replacing `this.dev` ends the frame (E3060 at its later use), and DRP-2's reverse field order abandons the frame before the device ends. This is the general rule for kept sharedref mut fields, not a GPU case. It changes LT-45, so it is an owner question; the E3063 help must then give that line.

holes.program:
# std.gpu, as the rule needs Frame to be declared
struct Frame:
    device: sharedref mut dyn Device     # the tie DRP-9 and GPU-2 rely on
    # ... image, recording, arena
holes.what_goes_wrong: Frame is one std type for every Device, so its link has to be type-erased, `sharedref mut dyn Device`. TYP-45 (p04 413-415) and IV.9 (p04 781-783) give `dyn I` only as a parameter, as `ref dyn I`, or as `owns`/`shares`/`shares mut dyn I`. `sharedref mut dyn I` is exactly P12's open form (its other_places). Unless P12 adds it, the tie cannot be written in Ember, and std would need a hidden form programs cannot write, which is a special path (checklist 13). A program's own provider-tied type behind an interface (`sharedref mut dyn Connection`) hits the same gap.
holes.fix_hint: Present P23 after P12, and say that the tie depends on P12's principle ('every holder word applies to every type that can be held that way, an interface value included'), which gives `sharedref mut dyn I`. Do not let std use a form that is not in TYP-45.

holes.program:
fn render(ref mut dev: dyn Device, ref mut game: Game) -> Result[void, GpuError]:
    started = dev.begin_frame()
    match owns started:
        Some(frame):
            dev.abandon_frame(ref mut frame)     # the hook the design adds to interface Device
            draw_world(ref mut frame, game)      # records into a frame whose image was given back
            dev.end_frame(owns frame)            # submits and presents what?
        None:
            pass
    return Ok(())
holes.what_goes_wrong: The spec text puts `fn abandon_frame(ref mut frame: Frame)` in the public `interface Device`, and open risk 1 admits it is not hidden. A program can then abandon a frame and go on to record into it and end_frame it, or let its drop abandon it a second time. Nothing defines either. GPU-2's 'a frame is either submitted or abandoned, once' is then false. The hook is also a second spelling of 'skip this frame' beside `mem.drop(owns frame)` (P24, checklist 11), and an explicit call of what a drop does, which DRP-1 forbids for drop itself (E3070).
holes.fix_hint: Keep the implementer's hooks off anything a program holds: put them on an implementer-only interface that std's Frame and std's end_frame call (for example `interface DeviceBackend`, with `dyn Device` the std face that has no abandon method). A program skips a frame only by ending it (mem.drop or any exit).

holes.what_goes_wrong: DRP-9's finishing-call sentence makes once-ness depend on each Device implementer's end_frame taking the pending work out of a Frame. The work is read by Frame's drop, a different type written by a different author. If one implementer forgets, the frame's drop at end_frame's end runs abandon_frame after the submit: the image is presented and also given back, and the recording and arena the submitted work uses are freed. Frame's fields are std's and private, so an implementer outside std has no mem.take to call at all. Whatever std exposes for it (`frame.take_work()`) a program can call too, ending a frame whose image is never given back, and the next begin_frame then waits. Rule 3 ('never stops the program') also rests on implementer code, since a panicking abandon_frame aborts (DRP-4).
holes.fix_hint: Put the protocol in the one type whose drop tests it. std's Frame keeps a private pending flag. end_frame is std code (a method std defines for dyn Device, or `frame.end(ref mut dev) owns this`) that calls the implementer's submit hook and clears the flag. The implementer writes only a submit hook and an abandon hook, sees the frame's parts and never the flag, and std's drop calls the abandon hook only while pending. The general wording: a finishing call is a method of the value's own type, as Transaction.commit is.
