engineering.notes:
I only read files; nothing was edited, built or run. Sources: owner-bar.md, brief.md, OWNER-DIRECTION.md, phase1-groups.json (P24, plus the principles of P01-P28), phase2.json (J1-13, J6-10, and J2-11 and J6-08 for context), phase3.json (K65, K73 and the closing note), JOB.md (verdicts 48, 49, 109-113, 130, 133, 164-166), decisions.md section 7 (the lead's 'dyn and some keep +'), and spec parts p01, p03, p04, p05, p06, p10, p12, p13, p14, p15, p16, p17a, p26 and p27.

Most serious: read word for word, rule 3 ('a form or a name that gives a program nothing another does not ... is refused', binding every program) refuses STD-19's stated-identical shortcuts (xs.enumerate() is xs.iter().enumerate()), verdict 48/49's type aliases, and list order and repeats. It cannot be decided for a program's own names. Rule 3 should bind the specification and std, as rule 2 does.

Rules 2 and 4 contradict each other on free-function/method pairs: ln vs sqrt are the same shape. pow has three meanings for an integer, which TYP-21 contradicts; the design calls this settled.

The 'line always exists' promise for E4070 fails for STD-28's trigonometric operations (Quat.from_axis_angle, slerp, perspective_rh), for a float ** and for SIMD _approx calls.

Option D was turned down on a misreading of PHIL-16. TYP-9 already makes float modes lexical, and @fp(allow_fma) already gives different last bits for the same line in two functions. The owner should see the real trade-off: a contract that also chooses an implementation.

dyn (A, B) to dyn A is refused by TYP-5 and TYP-40 as written.

Under J2-11 B the cast makes the programmer write a pointee type that can only be the inferred one, and the FOLLOWS line decides P07's owner question ahead of P07.

What holds up: the dyn/some spelling itself (zero cost, no + ambiguity, consistent with verdicts 109-112, asked as the owner's question); det.ln with det complete under DET-2; fma for mul_add; the cost claims.

Process (not a language hole): option A of J6-10 bundles five language changes (the ln name, det's completeness, removing det.sqrt, integers replacing ODR-046, fma for mul_add). The owner's practice is one question at a time, so each should be its own line.

design.rule:
One idea, one spelling. This specification spells each idea of the language and of its standard library one way, wherever the idea is written or offered.
(1) A list of interfaces that one type has is one interface bare, or two or more in round brackets separated by commas. This holds after `needs`, `dyn` and `some` alike: `[T: needs (Shape, Debug)]` beside `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`. The list names the interfaces of one type, markers included. After `dyn`, that type is the type of each value held. Neither the order of the items nor an item that another item brings changes the list, and one canonical form names it in every compiler.
(2) An operation of the library keeps one name in every module, type and call form that offers it, and one name in one module or type is one operation. Two forms are one operation when they give the same result for every argument both accept; each form keeps its own parameters. A version under a stated property says the property once (by its module, by a word joined to its name, or by the attribute that sets it), and it stands beside its plain operation. A module of such versions offers one for each operation whose result the property changes, under that operation's name, and no other.
(3) A second spelling is a form of the specification, or a name of its library, that can be written wherever another is, and the other wherever it is, with the same result. The specification keeps one of the two: the one that writes only what the compiler cannot work out, and among those the main spelling. The other is refused, and the message gives the kept line. The following are not second spellings: call forms of one operation, compositions, versions under a property, forms that differ, a form that accepts strictly less, and anything a program names or orders itself.
design.spec_text:
ADDED `[PHIL-17]` (Part I.3, new in Hardened_12) **One idea, one spelling.** This specification spells each idea of the language and of its standard library one way. The spelling is the same wherever the idea is written or offered: a construct in every position of the grammar, an operation in every module, type and call form.
  1. **A list of interfaces** that one type has is one interface bare, or two or more in round brackets separated by commas. It follows `needs` (`[TYP-17]`). It follows `dyn` and `some` directly, because those words already say what the list is for: `[T: needs (Shape, Debug)]`, `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, `-> some (Iterator[Item = int], Clone)`.
     * It names the interfaces of one type, markers included. After `needs` that type is the parameter's type, after `some` the one type the function returns, and after `dyn` the type of each value held. What a `dyn` value itself has is stated in §IV.9.
     * Neither its order nor an item that another item brings changes it. It has one canonical form, by which every compiler names it and lays it out (`[TYP-17]`, `[MNG-6]`).
  2. **An operation of the standard library** keeps one name in every module, type and call form that offers it. The call forms are a free function, a method, an operator together with its interface's method, and a method called on an `Iterable`, which reads it as `iter()` would (`[STD-19]`). One name in one module or type is one operation.
     * Two forms are one operation when they give the same result for every argument both accept. Each form keeps its own parameters, and one may accept more. `math.ln(9)` takes an integer, although no integer has an `ln` method, because a `std.math` function is its method called on its argument's `Real` (`math.sqrt(x)` is `x.to_real().sqrt()`, `[STD-27]`).
     * A version that differs from an operation by a stated property says the property once. It does so by the module that offers it (`std.math.det`), by a word joined to the operation's name (`wrapping_add`, `try_insert`, `rsqrt_approx`), or by the attribute that sets the property for a function or module (`@overflow(wrap)`, `@deterministic`). The operation itself stands beside the version under the plain name (`v.rsqrt()` beside `v.rsqrt_approx()`).
     * A module of such versions offers one version for each operation of the module it stands beside whose result the property changes. Each version has that operation's name, parameters and answer type, and the module offers nothing else.
  3. **A second spelling** is a form of this specification, or a name of its library, that can be written wherever another is, and the other wherever it is, with the same result. The specification keeps one of the two: the one that writes only what the compiler cannot work out, and among those the language's main spelling (an older or local spelling goes). A removed form is `E0100` and a removed name is `E2072`. The message gives the line in the one spelling, and that line compiles (`[DIA-25]`). These are not second spellings:
     * the call forms of one operation (rule 2): `len(xs)` and `xs.len()`, `enumerate(xs)` and `xs.enumerate()`, `a + b` and `Add.add` (which is also a function value);
     * a composition: `xs.iter().enumerate()`;
     * a version under a property beside its operation: `det.ln(p)` beside `ln(p)`, `wrapping_add` beside `+`;
     * forms that accept or give something different, where the specification states the difference: `len(s)` refuses text, while `s.len()` counts its bytes (`[STD-26]`); `import math` finds a package's own `math` first (`[MOD-3]`);
     * a form that accepts strictly less than another form. Removing it is a separate decision, and its reason is written;
     * anything a program names or orders itself: its functions, a `type` alias (`type Drawable = owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, verdicts 48 and 49), `import ... as`, and the order of a list.

CHANGED Grammar III.2 (p03 71-72):
  `needs := type | "(" type "," type {"," type} [","] ")"   -- one bare, two or more in round brackets ([TYP-17], [PHIL-17])`
  The line `bound_list := type {"+" type} -- after dyn and some only` is removed.
CHANGED Grammar III.3 (p03 171): `| "dyn" needs | "some" needs | "[" type ";" expression "]"`.

CHANGED `[TYP-17]`:
  * After "... and a `where` clause", add: "; and directly after `dyn` and `some` (`owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, `-> some (Iterator[Item = int], Clone)`, `[PHIL-17]`). In each of these places, round brackets are the list and never a tuple type, because a tuple type is not an interface."
  * Add: "A list names the interfaces one type has. A type has the list when it implements each interface in it (`[TYP-40]`); the list itself is never implemented. Its order does not matter. An item that another item brings (a parent, `[IFC-3]`, or the same interface with fewer bindings) may be written or left out: `dyn (Debug, Shape)` is `dyn (Shape, Debug)`, and `needs (Ord, Eq)` is `needs Ord`. An interface written twice is `E0100`, and its message gives the list with the interface once. Two different bindings of one associated type (`some (Iterator[Item = int], Iterator[Item = String])`) are `E2040`, because a type states each associated type once (`[IFC-4]`). An item that is not an interface is `E2020`, as it is after `needs`."
  * The `E0100` sentence becomes: "A bound without `needs`, interfaces joined with `+` after `needs`, `dyn` or `some`, and one interface in brackets are `E0100`. The message gives the line in the one spelling: `[T: Add + Copy]` gives `[T: needs (Add, Copy)]`, `owns dyn Shape + Debug` gives `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, and `[T: needs (Copy)]` gives `[T: needs Copy]`."

CHANGED §IV.9 (first bullet), sentences added: "`dyn (I, J)` is a value of some type that has every interface listed (`[PHIL-17]`). It is what `dyn K` is for an interface `K` declared `interface K: needs (I, J):` with nothing of its own, except that every such type qualifies without naming `K`. Each interface listed is usable as `dyn` (`[TYP-22]`); a marker is, because it has no methods.
  * The value has the listed interfaces' methods and their parents' methods (`[IFC-3]`). It can be copied with `copy of` when its list brings `Clone`. `Copy` brings `Clone`, and the copy goes into a new block, never bitwise (`[TYP-22]`). It compares with `==` when its list brings `Eq` (`[TYP-36]`).
  * A listed marker is a fact about each value held. `owns dyn (Handler, Send)` holds only values whose types are `Send`, and it is itself `Send`, as an `owns` value of a `Send` type is. `shares dyn (Handler, Send)` is not `Send`, because no `shares` value is (`[TYP-43]`). When no marker is listed, the marker table says what an interface value is.
  * A `dyn` value is never `Copy` and never `Sized`, whatever its list says. So a method marked `where Self: needs Sized` cannot be called on one (`E2040`, as on `dyn Shape`).
  * It is laid out as `dyn I` is, with one table pointer for each listed interface that has methods. A class object is one pointer, and each table is reached through its type index (`[OBJ-2]`, `[DSP-3]`). Any other value is a data pointer followed by those table pointers, in the list's canonical order (`[MNG-6]`). Each pointer points to the table `dyn I` uses for that type and interface. That table holds the parents' methods, and one pointer to each parent's table for the same type."

CHANGED `[TYP-5]` rule 8: "a value to an interface, or a list of interfaces, that its type has, keeping the word that says who owns it (as today: in place to `dyn I`, `owns T` to `owns dyn I`, `shares T` to `shares dyn I`, `shares mut T` to `shares mut dyn I`). A value of an interface type converts to another interface type when its own list has or brings every interface that type lists. It keeps its word, or is read in place as a view: `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)` to `owns dyn Shape`, `dyn (A, B, C)` to `dyn (C, A)`, `dyn Error` to `dyn Display` (`[IFC-3]`). The conversion keeps the table pointers wanted with no load, and reaches a parent's table with one load. A class object converts to a base class (upcast)."

CHANGED `[TYP-32]`: "`some I` or `some (I, J)` in a return type means one concrete type, chosen by the function body, that has every interface listed, markers included".

CHANGED `[MNG-6]`, after "... `thread_shared fn()`)", add: "; an interface list as `(a, b)`. Each item is written by its spelling here, with its associated-type bindings after its arguments, sorted by name (`Iterator[Item = int]`). The items are sorted by the bytes of their spellings, each appears once, and an item that another item brings is left out (`[TYP-17]`). So `dyn (Debug, Shape)` and `dyn (Shape, Debug)` have one spelling. A value of a list type holds its table pointers in this order (§IV.9), and a shared body (`[MONO-6]`) takes one table per item, in this order".

CHANGED `[STD-20]` (one name in one type is one operation, `[PHIL-17]` rule 2):
  * The entry "`pow(e)` (`x ** e` under the default panic policy)" is removed. An integer's `pow` is `Pow`'s method, and that method is the operator (`[TYP-21]`): `a.pow(2)` is `a ** 2` under the lexical policy (`[TYP-8]`), as `3.add(4)` is `3 + 4`. Its forms with a fixed contract are `checked_pow`, `wrapping_pow`, `saturating_pow` and `overflowing_pow`.
  * "an overflowing `pow` or `next_power_of_two`" becomes "an overflowing `next_power_of_two`".

CHANGED `[DET-4]` (replaces ODR-046; option D, recommended):
  * "**Deterministic maths.** Code marked `@deterministic` computes each `std.math` function whose platform result is `Nondet` (`[DET-2]`) with Ember's own implementation. This covers every call form: `ln(p)`, `math.ln(p)`, `p.ln()`, and a float `**` (`d ** 0.5` is `pow`, `[TYP-30]`)."
  * "The choice is lexical, as `[TYP-8]`'s overflow policy and `[TYP-9]`'s float mode are. A lambda takes the choice of the function it is written in, and instantiation, inlining and calls keep each function's own choice. So a helper that is not `@deterministic` keeps the platform's implementation, and a call to it from deterministic code is `E4070` (`[DET-3]`). The help writes `@deterministic` above the helper (`fn wobble(t: f64) -> f64:`, line 12) or on its module (`[DET-8]`)."
  * "`std.math.det` offers the same functions for one call anywhere, as `wrapping_add` offers one wrapping addition outside `@overflow(wrap)`. They have `std.math`'s names, parameters and answer types (`[STD-21]`, `[STD-27]`: any number type; an integer's answer is an `f64`, and an `f16`'s and an `f32`'s answer is an `f32`), and det offers nothing else (`[PHIL-17]`)."
  * "These are the functions that `[DET-2]` makes `Nondet`: `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `sinh`, `cosh`, `tanh`, `exp`, `exp2`, `ln`, `log2`, `log10`, `pow`, and any further function `[DET-2]` names (`cbrt` and `hypot` if it names them)."
  * "Ember's own implementation gives the same bits on every supported target. An `f32`'s result is its `f64` result rounded once. Every NaN it returns, whatever its arguments, is `NAN`: positive, quiet, with payload zero (`0x7FF8000000000000` for an `f64`, `0x7FC00000` for an `f32`). Each function states its accuracy bound: within one unit in the last place for `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `exp`, `ln` and `pow`, `atan2` within 1.3, and the rest as measured when built."
  * "`det.sqrt(x)` is `E2072`, and its help is `math.sqrt(x)`. `sqrt` is correctly rounded by IEEE 754, so it is not `Nondet`: one binary gives the same bits on every machine (`[DET-7]`). `det.log(x)` is `E2072`, and its help is `det.ln(x)`."
  * Option A differs only in the first two bullets. It makes no lexical choice: in `@deterministic` code, a `Nondet` call of a `std.math` function, a float method or a float `**` is `E4070`, and the help gives det's call (`ln(p)` and `p.ln()` give `det.ln(p)`, and `d ** 0.5` gives `det.pow(d, 0.5)`).

CHANGED `[CT-4]`: "A transcendental function runs at compile time when it is Ember's own: `std.math.det`'s, or any such function in `@deterministic` code (`[DET-4]`). It gives the same result it gives at run time. The platform library's function does not run at compile time, and the evaluator never puts Ember's own in its place (ODR-056)."

CHANGED `[STD-28]`: "The operations that use `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `acos` or another function that `[DET-2]` makes `Nondet` are `Quat.from_axis_angle`, `from_rotation_x`/`y`/`z` (on `Quat` and `Mat4`), `slerp`, `Mat2`/`Mat3.from_angle` and `perspective_rh`. They use Ember's own implementation of those functions (`[DET-4]`) in every program, so none of them is `Nondet`."

CHANGED `[STD-3]`, `[STD-20]`, `[STD-27]`, `[STD-28]`:
  * The fused multiply-add has one name, `fma`. The free function `math.fma(a, b, c)` takes what `[STD-21]`'s functions take: any number type, answering in `T.Real` (`math.fma(2, 3, 1)` is `7.0`). The float method is `a.fma(b, c)` and the float vectors' method is `v.fma(a, b)`. This is how `std.simd` (`[SIMD-4]`) and `@fp(allow_fma)` already spell it.
  * `a.mul_add(b, c)` is `E2072`, and its help is `a.fma(b, c)`. STD-27's list of C names reads "`fma` its `fma`".

CHANGED `[SIMD-4]`: "approximations named `_approx` (`rsqrt_approx`, `rcp_approx`) stand beside the float vectors' exact lane-wise `sqrt`, `rsqrt` (`1.0 / sqrt(x)`) and `rcp` (`1.0 / x`), each lane rounded as those operations are (`[PHIL-17]`)."

CHANGED (wording, the lead's):
  * `[ERR-3]`: "`Error` is the interface of error types, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`, with `fn source() -> Option[ref dyn Error]` ...".
  * `[EFF-18]`: "have `Sync`, `Lock` and `Block`; `try_lock` has `Sync` and `Lock`; a blocking read has `Io` and `Block`".
  * E0100's row: "a bound written without `needs`, or interfaces joined with `+` after `needs`, `dyn` or `some` (the message gives the line with brackets)".

NOT DECIDED HERE: P07's J2-11 (`ref_to_ptr` beside the safe cast).

Appendix H: ODR-046's row is marked "replaced by `[DET-4]`, Hardened_12". ODR-084's row gains "(an integer's `pow` is the operator, `[TYP-21]`, Hardened_12)".

answers.answer:
PHIL-17 rule 1 decides this, and it is the owner's question. Verdict 109 gave a list of what a type must have one spelling: round brackets and commas. Under the rule, that spelling also holds directly after `dyn` and `some`, and `+` is the second spelling, which goes. `dyn` and `some` already say what the list is for, so no `needs` follows them. Side by side: `[T: needs (Shape, Debug)]` and `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`.

The rule also says what the type is:
* It is a value of some type that has both interfaces.
* It is the same type whatever the order of the items.
* It can be passed where one of its interfaces is wanted (`dyn Shape`), with no load.
* It is laid out as `dyn I` is, with one table pointer for each interface.

The owner was never asked about `dyn` and `some`, so the lead does not widen verdict 109 to them; it goes to him.
answers.outcome:
Compiles and prints `Square(side=2.0) has area 4.0`.
* `owns dyn Shape + Debug` is E0100: "a list of interfaces goes in round brackets, as after `needs`: write `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`".
* `owns dyn (Debug, Shape)` is the same type.
* `owns dyn (Shape, Shape)` and `owns dyn (Shape)` are E0100, each with `owns dyn Shape` as help.
* Each element is three words: the square's data pointer, then Debug's and Shape's table pointers in the canonical order.
* `area_of(s)` passes the data pointer and Shape's table pointer, with no load.
* A program with one interface after `dyn` is unchanged, at two words.

answers.answer:
PHIL-17 rule 2 decides the name. The natural logarithm is one operation, so it is `ln` in every module that offers it, and `det.log` goes.

std.math.det offers exactly the std.math functions whose platform result differs between machines. That is DET-2's list, so log2, log10, asin and the rest join it. They keep std.math's names, parameters and answer types, integers included (ODR-038 replaces ODR-046). `det.sqrt` goes. Every NaN these functions return is `NAN`, so their bits match on every target.

How deterministic code says it is the owner's choice. The recommendation is D. `@deterministic` already says it once, so inside such a function std.math's own calls (`ln(p)`, `p.ln()`, `p ** 0.5`) are computed by Ember's implementation. The choice is lexical, as `@overflow(wrap)` makes `+` wrap. `det.ln` stays for one call elsewhere, as `wrapping_add` does. Option A writes `det.ln` at every call in deterministic code instead.
answers.outcome:
Compiles.
* `gain_db` and `gain_db_lockstep` have one body; the second gives the same bits on every machine.
* `SINE` is computed at compile time (CT-4).
* `det.log(p)` is E2072: "the natural logarithm is `ln`, as in `std.math`: write `det.ln(p)`". `det.sqrt(x)` is E2072 with the help `math.sqrt(x)`.
* Suppose `gain_db_lockstep` calls a helper without the attribute, `fn wobble(t: f64) -> f64: return t.sin()`. That call is E4070, and its help writes `@deterministic` above `fn wobble`.
* Under option A, `ln(power)` in `gain_db_lockstep` is E4070 with the help `det.ln(power)`.

other_cases.case: `where` clauses, interface parents, `extend` lines, associated types (`where T: needs (Eq, Hash)`, `interface Error: needs (Debug, Display):`, `extend[T: needs Display]`, `type Iter: needs Iterator[Item = Item]`)
other_cases.settled: These already use the one spelling (verdicts 109 to 112, TYP-17). Nothing changes. The canonical form (order, implied items) now holds in these places too.

other_cases.case: `struct Square implements Shape, Debug:`, a list after `implements`
other_cases.settled: This is not a bound. It is a list of separate claims, each implemented on its own (each could be its own `extend Square implements Debug:`), so it keeps its commas without brackets. Swift draws the same line (`some P & Q` against `struct S: P, Q`), and so does Java (`<T extends A & B>` against `implements A, B`).

other_cases.case: Order, repeats, implied items: `owns dyn (Debug, Shape)` given where `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)` is expected; `dyn (Shape, Shape)`; `dyn (Error, Display)`
other_cases.settled:
* Order: the same type. MNG-6 sorts the items by their canonical spellings, so every compiler and every package lays the value out alike.
* An exact repeat is E0100, with the list written once as help.
* An item another item brings may be written or left out, and the list means the same: `dyn (Error, Display)` is `dyn Error`.

other_cases.case: Two bindings of one associated type: `some (Iterator[Item = int], Iterator[Item = String])`; and two instances of a generic interface: `dyn (Add[i32], Add[f64])`
other_cases.settled: The first is E2040. A type implements an interface once and states each associated type once (IFC-4, E2041), so no type has both. The second is allowed: these are two interfaces with different arguments, which one type may implement (TYP-24).

other_cases.case: Passing `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)` where `dyn Shape` is wanted; `dyn (A, B, C)` to `dyn (C, A)`; `dyn Error` to `dyn Display`
other_cases.settled:
TYP-5 rule 8 covers all three, keeping the value's word.
* To any part of the list: the value keeps the table pointers wanted, with no load.
* To a parent: one load, through the pointer each interface's table holds (Rust 1.86's upcast).
* A class object stays one pointer, and its tables are reached through its type index.

other_cases.case: A marker in the list: `jobs: Array[owns dyn (Handler, Send)]`, `dyn (Shape, Copy)`, `dyn (Shape, Sized)`
other_cases.settled:
After `dyn`, a marker is a fact about each value held. It adds no word to the value.
* `owns dyn (Handler, Send)` is Send, so it can be sent. `shares dyn (Handler, Send)` is not, because a `shares` value never is.
* `Copy` brings `Clone`, so `copy of` works on `owns dyn (Shape, Copy)`. The copy goes into a new block; it is never Copy itself.
* `Sized` is true of every value held. The dyn value stays unsized, so a `where Self: needs Sized` method is E2040 on it, as on `dyn Shape`.
* With no marker listed, P01's line in the marker table decides.

other_cases.case: `some (Iterator[Item = int], Clone)` and `some (Iterator[Item = int], Send)`
other_cases.settled: After `some`, every listed interface, markers included, holds of the one concrete type. The caller may write `copy of` on the result, or send it.

other_cases.case: `owns dyn (Shape, Debug) using LevelArena`; today `owns dyn Shape + Debug using LevelArena`
other_cases.settled: With brackets, `using` applies to the whole type, as GRM-3 says. Today `bound_list := type {"+" type}` reads `Debug using LevelArena` as one item. The rule removes that parse hazard.

other_cases.case: `+` after a type inside an expression (`x as T + 1`); round brackets after `dyn` read as a tuple
other_cases.settled: After the rule, `+` never appears inside a type, so a `+` after a type is always the operator. There is no case like Rust's E0178. Round brackets after `needs`, `dyn` or `some` are always the list, because a tuple type is never an interface.

other_cases.case: One interface in brackets: `[T: needs (Copy)]`, `owns dyn (Shape)`
other_cases.settled: This is a second spelling of the bare form. It is E0100, with `[T: needs Copy]` or `owns dyn Shape` as help. It carries out verdict 109's own words, "one need has no brackets".

other_cases.case: MONO-6 shared bodies for `[T: needs (Shape, Debug)]`
other_cases.settled: A shared body takes one table per item, in MNG-6's canonical order. Separately compiled packages therefore agree on which table holds `area`.

other_cases.case: The det module's names against std.math: exp, pow, sin, cos, tan, atan2; and log2, log10, exp2, asin, acos, atan, sinh, cosh, tanh, cbrt, hypot
other_cases.settled: The first six already share std.math's names. Each of the rest gets Ember's own implementation under its std.math name when DET-2 (P14's J6-08) makes it Nondet. det's list therefore follows DET-2, never a hand-kept list. The implementations are built from the same FreeBSD msun source as det.em today.

other_cases.case: A NaN from det: `det.sin(f64.INF)`; and a NaN from arithmetic or from an exact function: `f64.INF - f64.INF`, `math.sqrt(-1.0)`
other_cases.settled:
* Every NaN Ember's functions return is `NAN` (0x7FF8000000000000), so sorting their results gives the same order on x86-64 and AArch64. det.em's `x - x` returns become `NAN`, at no cost.
* NaNs from arithmetic and exact functions fall under DET-7, which promises the same bits for one binary on every machine.
* Making NaN canonical across instruction sets (WebAssembly's deterministic profile) would be a widening of DET-7, and that is P14's question.

other_cases.case: Method forms and `**` in deterministic code: `v.x.sin()`, `p.ln()`, `d ** 1.5`
other_cases.settled:
* Under D: Ember's own implementation, since the lexical choice covers every call form.
* Under A: E4070, whose help gives `det.sin(v.x)`, `det.ln(p)` or `det.pow(d, 1.5)`.
* Either way the line the message gives always exists and compiles.

other_cases.case: std.math's types' operations in lockstep code: `Quat.from_rotation_y(yaw) * facing`, `slerp`, `Mat4.perspective_rh`
other_cases.settled: They compute sin, cos, tan and acos with Ember's own implementation in every program (STD-28), so they are never Nondet. They compile in `@deterministic` code as written. A program builds its own compound maths the same way, so std uses no path a program cannot use. The cost is in the cost line, not measured here.

other_cases.case: A helper or function value without the attribute, called from `@deterministic` code
other_cases.settled: Under D, a helper keeps its own choice (TYP-8: "calling never replaces a declaration's policy"). Its call is E4070, naming the chain, and the help writes `@deterministic` above the helper. A function value made in ordinary code is E4070 by DET-3. A lambda written inside the deterministic function takes its choice (TYP-9). Nothing is compiled twice.

other_cases.case: SIMD estimates: `v.rsqrt_approx()` in `@deterministic` code
other_cases.settled: Rule 2 puts a version named by a joined word beside its plain operation, so std.simd's float vectors gain the exact `sqrt`, `rsqrt` and `rcp`. If P14's J6-08 makes `_approx` Nondet, E4070's help is `v.rsqrt()`.

other_cases.case: `det.sqrt(x)` (exists today)
other_cases.settled: det offers only the functions whose result the guarantee changes (rule 2). `sqrt` is correctly rounded under IEEE 754, and DET-7's one binary gives it the same bits on every machine. So `det.sqrt` is E2072, with `math.sqrt(x)` as help.

other_cases.case: `math.fma(a, b, c)` beside the float method `a.mul_add(b, c)` and `Vec3.mul_add`, where std.simd and `@fp(allow_fma)` say `fma`
other_cases.settled: Rule 2: one operation keeps one name in every call form. STD-3 now says `math.fma` takes any number type, as STD-21's functions do. The method becomes `a.fma(b, c)`, and `mul_add` is E2072 with that help. `fma` is also C's, C++'s, Java's and Python 3.13's name. Cost: zero.

other_cases.case: Integer `pow`: `a.pow(2)` under `#! module overflow(saturate)`; and `math.pow(2, 10)` beside `2.pow(10)`
other_cases.settled:
* An integer's `pow` is Pow's method, which is the operator (TYP-21). So `a.pow(2)` is `a ** 2`, 127 under saturate, as `3.add(4)` is `3 + 4`. STD-20's second `pow` goes, and the fixed contracts keep their joined words (`checked_pow`, ...).
* `math.pow(2, 10)` is the method called on the arguments' Real (STD-27): `1024.0`, as Python's `math.pow` gives.
* `2.pow(10)` is `2 ** 10`: `1024`, as Python's `pow` gives.
* This is one operation, and each form says which type computes it.

other_cases.case: Affix families: `checked_add`, `wrapping_add`, `saturating_add`, `overflowing_add`, `try_lock`, `try_insert`, `rsqrt_approx`
other_cases.settled: These already have rule 2's shape: the base name is kept, and the property is said once, by the word joined to it, beside the plain operation. Nothing changes except `v.rsqrt()`, which joins std.simd.

other_cases.case: Forms that stay: `len(xs)` and `xs.len()`; `math.sqrt(9)` and `x.sqrt()`; `enumerate(xs)`, `xs.enumerate()` and `xs.iter().enumerate()`; `a + b` and `Add.add`; `import math` and `import std.math`
other_cases.settled:
* Rule 2: call forms of one operation. `math.sqrt` also takes integers.
* Rule 3: `xs.iter().enumerate()` is a composition, not a form of the operation.
* `len(s)` refuses text (STD-26), and `import math` finds a package's own `math` first (MOD-3). Both differences are stated.
* None of these is refused.

other_cases.case: A program's own names: `type Handler = fn()`, `type Drawable = owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, `from std.math import ln as natural_log`, a wrapper `fn area() -> f64: return this.size()`
other_cases.settled: Rule 3 binds the specification's forms and its library's names only. What a program names or orders itself is its own (verdicts 48 and 49). The compiler never judges whether two of a program's functions are one idea.

other_cases.case: P07's J2-11: `ref_to_ptr(x)` and `ref_to_ptr(ref mut x)` beside the safe cast `ref x as *T`
other_cases.settled: Not decided here. Under rule 3's mutual test, `ref_to_ptr` is strictly narrower than the cast (it has no form for `ref mut T` to `*T`), so it is not a second spelling, and removing it needs its own reason. Rule 3's choice criterion (keep the spelling that writes only what the compiler cannot work out) also counts against the cast as written, because it repeats the pointee type the compiler knows. P07 weighs both.

other_cases.case: Stale prose spellings: ERR-3's "Error is `Display + Debug`"; EFF-18's "`Sync + Lock + Block`"; Appendix H's ODR rows (`K: Eq + Hash`, `Send + Sync`)
other_cases.settled: ERR-3 is rewritten in verdict 110's spelling, and EFF-18 as "`Sync`, `Lock` and `Block`". This is wording, the lead's. Appendix H is a history of rulings and is kept as written.

design.prior_art:
Lists of interfaces:
* C++: constraints have one spelling (`requires Shape<T> && Debug<T>`). There is no value type for "an object that is both"; you need a combined abstract base. An object that derives from two abstract bases holds one vtable pointer per base, and a pointer to it as the second base is adjusted by a constant.
* Rust uses `+` in all three positions (`T: A + B`, `dyn A + B`, `impl A + B`). `dyn A + B` with two non-auto traits is refused (E0225), so users declare a supertrait with a blanket impl. `&dyn A + Send` is the ambiguous-`+` error E0178. Rust 1.86 (trait upcasting) puts a pointer to each supertrait's vtable in the subtrait's vtable, so a conversion to a supertrait is one load. A conversion to a part of a list cannot be written, because the list type does not exist.
* Swift uses `&` in all three positions (`T: P & Q`, `some P & Q`, `any P & Q`), with commas only for conformance (`struct S: P, Q`), which is this rule's boundary. `any P & Q` carries one witness-table pointer per protocol, the layout adopted here: any conversion to fewer protocols drops pointers.
* Go: an anonymous composed interface (`interface{ Shape; fmt.Stringer }`). A conversion between interface types looks up the method table (itab) while running, with a cache.
* Java (`<T extends A & A>`) and C# (CS0405) refuse a constraint written twice, and both accept an implied one, as here.
* Ember's version shares verdict 109's spelling with `needs` (no new punctuation) and has no `+` ambiguity. It allows any number of interfaces, unlike Rust. Every conversion to a part of the list or to a parent is decided and costs at most one load, where Go looks up tables while running.

Deterministic maths and twin modules:
* Java's Math and StrictMath: StrictMath (fdlibm) mirrors Math name for name, so code moves by changing the class name.
* Go's math package and Zig's std.math are one software implementation for every program, the same bits everywhere.
* Box2D v3.1 replaced the C library's sine and cosine in its rotations with its own, for cross-platform determinism. That is STD-28's choice here.
* WebAssembly's deterministic profile (Wasm 3.0) makes NaN results canonical. Ember's own functions do this; for arithmetic it is P14's question.
* x86-64 makes its default NaN negative (0xFFF8000000000000) and AArch64 positive (0x7FF8000000000000). That is why det's `x - x` returns had to go.
* A lexical mode that changes what an operation computes is Ember's own pattern: TYP-8's overflow policy (`+` wraps under `@overflow(wrap)`, beside `wrapping_add` for one call) and TYP-9's `@fp(allow_fma)`. Option D applies the same pattern to `@deterministic`.
* Rust's `libm` crate uses C's names (`log`) while std uses `ln`, the same mismatch det has today.
* Natural logarithm: C, C++, Python, Java, C#, Go and Swift call it `log`, Rust calls it `ln`, and ISO 80000-2 writes ln. Ember's std.math chose `ln` beside `log2` and `log10`.
* Fused multiply-add: `fma` in C99, C++11, Java 9, Python 3.13, GLSL and Go (`math.FMA`); `mul_add` is Rust's alone.
* Python: `pow(2, 10)` is `1024` and `math.pow(2, 10)` is `1024.0`, the split STD-27 gives `2.pow(10)` and `math.pow(2, 10)`.

Inside Ember: STD-13 already refuses a second name (`append` gives `push`), and verdicts 130 and 133 removed `-> unsafe` everywhere. PHIL-17 states the shape those rules share.
design.cost:
Zero while running for every spelling change, in time and memory.
* A list value that is not a class object, such as `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`, is a data pointer followed by one table pointer per listed interface with methods, in the canonical order. For two interfaces that is three words, one more than `owns dyn Shape`. A C struct holding a `void*` and two function-pointer tables is the same three words. C++ pays the same word per interface inside every object (one vtable pointer per base).
* A class object stays one pointer (OBJ-2).
* A call is one load of the method and one indirect call, the cost of `dyn I` and of a C function-pointer table.
* Converting to any part of the list keeps the pointers wanted: no load. Converting to a parent (`dyn Error` to `dyn Display`) is one load, as in Rust 1.86.
* The tables are `dyn I`'s own, made when compiling. Each interface's table gains one word per parent (static memory). There is no table per list, so nothing grows with the number of lists a program writes, and no table per part of a list, which would be 2^n of them.
* A listed marker (`Send`) adds no word.
* Ember's own maths functions cost what the same msun algorithm costs in C (FreeBSD's libm). That cost is paid only inside deterministic code and in std.math's rotations, slerp and projections, which every program uses. It is not measured here (read-only) and must be measured before the cut, as det.em is today.
* Returning `NAN` costs nothing on the normal path, because the NaN branches already exist.
* `det.ln` for `det.log`, `fma` for `mul_add`, and `pow` as the operator: zero.
* The exact simd `rsqrt` and `rcp`: a lane-wise square root and divide, paid only where written.
* Memory: nothing added, except the parent pointers in static tables and the word per further interface in a list value.
* While compiling: the parser loses a production (`bound_list`), and the type checker sorts each list once.

readability.note: The same list reads the same way in both places it appears. The deterministic function is now the ordinary one with its attribute: shorter, one rounding instead of three, and one import fewer. The `dyn` line is one character longer (`(Shape, Debug)` against `Shape + Debug`), and only when a value names two interfaces, which is rare. A program with one interface after `dyn` and no deterministic code is unchanged, character for character. No new word or annotation appears anywhere. Under option A the last line would be `return 10.0 * det.log10(power)` with `import math.det`.

design.compiler_does:
* The parser reads `dyn` and `some` followed by the same list production as `needs`. Round brackets in these places are the list, never a tuple.
  * On a `+` after a list item it stops with E0100 and gives the bracketed line.
  * On `Array[owns dyn Shape, Debug]` it gives `Array[owns dyn (Shape, Debug)]`.
* The type checker reduces every list to its canonical form: items by their MNG-6 spellings, sorted, with implied items left out. The same list in any order is therefore one type in every compiler.
  * It refuses an item written twice (E0100), two bindings of one associated type (E2040), an item that is not an interface (E2020), and an item not usable as dyn after `dyn` (E2050).
* It checks a conversion from `dyn L` to `dyn M` by seeing that every item of M is in L or is a parent of one. It emits no instruction for the first case and one load for a parent.
* It lays a list value out as the data pointer and then each item's own `dyn I` table pointer, in canonical order. A class object stays one pointer.
* It gives a `dyn` value the listed methods, `copy of` and `==` as TYP-22 and TYP-36 say, and Send or ThreadShared as listed under the holder word's rule. A `dyn` value is never Copy or Sized.
* Under option D, inside `@deterministic` code it resolves each Nondet std.math function, in every call form and as a float `**`, to Ember's own implementation, lexically.
  * Lambdas take the enclosing function's choice. Calls keep each function's own.
  * A call to a helper that is not deterministic is E4070, naming the chain, and the help writes `@deterministic` above the helper. That line compiles.
* The standard library carries std.math's names and generic parameters into det, so `det.ln(9)` resolves as `math.ln(9)` does.
* A removed name (`det.log`, `det.sqrt`, `mul_add`) gets E2072 with the one spelling.
* An integer's `x.pow(e)` resolves to Pow's method, the operator, under the lexical policy.
* Nothing the compiler works out from a body changes what a line does (PHIL-16). `@deterministic` is written, as `@overflow(wrap)` is. The programmer writes only what a value must have, and the compiler supplies the canonical order, the tables, the implementation and the line to write.
design.misuse:
Each of these is refused when compiling, with a line that compiles. None reaches run time.
* `owns dyn Shape + Debug` and `-> some Iterator[Item = int] + Clone`: E0100, with `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)` and `-> some (Iterator[Item = int], Clone)`.
* `[T: needs Shape + Debug]`: E0100, as today.
* `owns dyn needs (Shape, Debug)`: E0100, "after `dyn` the list follows directly: `owns dyn (Shape, Debug)`".
* `owns dyn (Shape)`, `[T: needs (Copy)]` and `owns dyn (Shape, Shape)`: E0100, with the bare form or the list written once.
* `Array[owns dyn Shape, Debug]`: refused (two type arguments, one a bare interface), with the help `Array[owns dyn (Shape, Debug)]`.
* `owns dyn ()`, `owns dyn (Shape, int)` and `some (Iterator[Item = int], Iterator[Item = String])`: refused (an empty list, an item that is not an interface, two bindings no type can have).
* `s.scaled(2.0)` with `where Self: needs Sized`, on `dyn (Shape, Sized)`: E2040, as on `dyn Shape`. The listed `Sized` speaks of the values held, never of the dyn value.
* Putting a value whose type is not Send into `owns dyn (Handler, Send)`: refused at the conversion, naming the field that is not Send.
* `det.log(x)`: E2072, help `det.ln(x)`. `det.sqrt(x)`: E2072, help `math.sqrt(x)`. `a.mul_add(b, c)`: E2072, help `a.fma(b, c)`.
* A helper without the attribute, called from `@deterministic` code: E4070, naming the call and the chain, with the help `@deterministic` above the helper (under option A: help `det.ln(x)` at each call).
* `v.rsqrt_approx()` in `@deterministic` code, if J6-08 makes it Nondet: E4070, help `v.rsqrt()`.
* A forgotten attribute or a forgotten `det.` therefore always ends in a refusal, never in silently machine-dependent results (checklist 8). Ember's own functions return `NAN` for every NaN, so sorting or printing a NaN they made does not differ between targets.
design.verdicts:
* Verdict 109 (what a type parameter needs: `needs`, several in round brackets): kept. The rule carries its spelling to `dyn` and `some`, a place never put to the owner, so this goes to him as his question rather than being applied as a widening. Its own words, "one need has no brackets", are carried too (`needs (Copy)` is refused). The refusal of an exact repeat, the conversion rule and the layout come with it, and the owner hears them.
* Verdicts 110, 111 and 112 (interface parents, extend, associated types): kept; these places already use the one spelling.
* Verdicts 48 and 49 (long things named once with `type`): kept, and now stated. A `type` alias is a program's own name and never a second spelling (rule 3).
* Verdict 133 (a verdict that replaces a spelling reaches every place): kept. PHIL-17 states its lesson generally.
* Verdicts 164 to 166 (P01): untouched. IV.9's Send sentence says what a listed marker does and leaves an unlisted one to P01's line in the marker table.
* No owner verdict is reversed.
* Lead rulings, which are not verdicts:
  * ODR-046 (det takes only f32/f64): replaced. det takes what std.math takes (ODR-038, which the owner ruled).
  * ODR-056 (the evaluator never puts det's sin in place of the platform's): kept. Under D the attribute, written in the source, makes the choice, never the evaluator.
  * ODR-084 (lexical overflow policy; integer methods keep fixed contracts): narrowed for `pow` only. STD-20 had a second `pow` on every integer beside Pow's, which TYP-21 says is the operator. One name in one type is one operation, so `pow` is the operator, and the fixed forms keep their joined words. This changes `a.pow(2)` under wrap or saturate, so the owner hears it.
  * ODR-084 and ODR-090 (lexical modes): their model is reused by option D.
  * ODR-075 (`ref_to_ptr` kept): P07's J2-11, not decided here.
  * STD-13 (no second name for Python's method names): kept; it already has this rule's shape.

Compiles, as A does, with nothing written at the calls. Inside `@deterministic` code, every Nondet std.math function, its method form and a float `**` are Ember's own; outside it they are the platform's.

Its real cost:

recommendation.reason:
The list half is the same in A, C and D. A list of interfaces is `(A, B)` after `needs` in every place verdicts 109 to 112 reached; `+` after `dyn` and `some` survives only because nobody asked. The rule also decides what the type is (any order, any part of it, one load at most) at C's memory cost.

For deterministic maths, D is A with the marking said once. `@deterministic` already tells the compiler which maths to use, so writing `det.` on every call says the same thing twice (principle 3), and it refuses method calls the compiler knows how to fix (principle 7). D uses only the lexical model Ember already has for `@overflow` and `@fp(allow_fma)`, and it adds no word.

B keeps two spellings with no reason, and C renames the main module to match a corner. Every change is a rename, a grammar line or a lexical choice, costing nothing while running except the word per further interface in a list value. The ordinary program is unchanged.

owner_short.one_line: One thing, two spellings. A type that is both Shape and Debug is written `needs (Shape, Debug)` on a type parameter (C++'s `requires Shape<T> && Debug<T>`) but `dyn Shape + Debug` on a value. C's `log` is `ln` in std.math but `log` in std.math.det, which deterministic code must write at every call.

owner_short.today: After `needs`, two interfaces are written `(Shape, Debug)`, and `+` is an error. After `dyn` or `some`, they must be written `Shape + Debug`. std.math's natural log is `ln`, but det's is `log`, and det lacks log2, log10, asin and the rest.
