design.prior_art:
**C.** `bool` and `char` are integers. `(int)b` and `(char)n` wrap silently, and `(_Bool)x` is `x != 0`, even for a float. A float-to-int conversion out of range is undefined behaviour, and any int converts to an enum unchecked. A constant that does not fit gets only a warning.

**C++.** The same, and `enum class` needs `static_cast` in both directions. `static_cast<Dir>(9)` is undefined behaviour when 9 is outside the values of an enumeration without a fixed underlying type (C++17). Whether `char` is signed depends on the target.

**Rust.** `as` takes bool, char and fieldless enums to every integer (low bits), and only `u8` into `char`. It refuses bool or char to a float, although `f32::from(bool)` exists. Nothing converts into bool by `as`, and an enum is reached only through `match`, `TryFrom` or a crate (num_enum). `char::from_u32` takes only a `u32`, and `TryFrom` is written per pair, so from an `i64` the program first writes `u32::try_from(n)`. In `300 as u8` the literal takes the cast's type, so the deny-by-default `overflowing_literals` lint refuses it. Float to int saturates (since 1.45). Value ranges serve LLVM's optimiser only, never typing: the alphabet is `(b'a' + i as u8) as char`, which cuts `i` silently.

**Swift.** There is no `Int(Bool)` (`b ? 1 : 0`). `Unicode.Scalar(UInt32)` and `init?(rawValue:)` return optionals even where the value is visibly valid, and `Int(Double)` traps while running.

**C#.** `(int)'a'` and `(char)65` are allowed (unchecked truncation). `(int)true` is a compile error. `(Dir)9` silently makes an enum value no member has.

**Go.** `rune` is `int32`, so `rune(0xD800)` is a character that is not one. There is no bool-to-int conversion. A constant conversion that does not fit (`uint8(300)`) is a compile error.

**Zig.** `@intFromBool`, `@intFromEnum`, `@enumFromInt` and `@intCast` are checked while running in the safe modes, and are undefined behaviour in ReleaseFast. A comptime-known value is checked when compiling.

**Ada.** `Boolean`, `Character` and enumerations are discrete types. `T'Pos(x)` gives the number and `T'Val(n)` the value; a number that is not one raises Constraint_Error, a check the compiler removes when a subtype's range proves it. No conversion exists between two enumeration types.

**LLVM and GCC.** Value-range analysis (LLVM's ConstantRange, GCC's VRP) follows each operation's range using its wrap flags (nsw/nuw), wrapped ranges included, and narrows ranges in the arms of comparisons and switches. RNG-4's policy-aware operators and arm facts are what these already compute, made part of the language so that every implementation reaches one verdict.

**Ember** takes Ada's model: coded types meet the numbers, never each other, and proof removes the check. It is spelled with Rust's `as` and keeps TYP-6's lossy number rules. Like Zig and Ada it proves when compiling, but where the proof fails it refuses with a one-line help instead of checking while running. Its one checked conversion is spelled as the range types already spell it, `T.checked(x)`. The result is C's machine code, with no undefined behaviour and no run-time check behind the program's back.
design.cost:
Per operation, against C:

* **bool to an integer:** one zero-extending move (`movzx`), which is what C's `(int)b` compiles to. Nothing at all into u8 or i8.
* **bool to a float:** `movzx` and `cvtsi2ss`, as C's `(float)b`.
* **char to an integer:** a char is a 32-bit code. Widening is a zero-extension (free on x86-64) and narrowing takes the low bits (free), as C's casts of a `char32_t` do.
* **char or enum to a float:** one convert, as in C.
* **Enum to a number:** its representation's integer cast, zero or one instruction.
* **A number into bool, char, an enum or a range type, proved by the compiler:** zero cost. Only the integer move or narrowing, the same code as C's unchecked cast, with no run-time check.
* **Where the proof fails:** nothing is added behind the program's back; the line is refused. The conversion the programmer then writes costs what Rust's `TryFrom` costs. `n != 0` is one `test`/`setne`. `bool.checked(b)` is one unsigned compare. `char.checked(n)` from any integer is two or three compares (0 to 0x10FFFF, outside D800 to DFFF). `Dir.checked(n)` is one unsigned compare for contiguous codes, or a table for sparse ones. `int.checked(v)` from a float is a truncation, an equality compare and two range compares. Each returns a `Result[T, RangeError]` and emits no check where the compiler knows it cannot fail.
* **Range targets:** RNG-10's existing cost: zero when known, `checked` or `clamped` otherwise.

Memory: zero everywhere. No representation changes and no header.

Compile time: the facts are those the compiler already computes for RNG-4's check removal and STD-19's counts, now one set per expression. Each set is an interval or a few: a char's two, a wrap's two, an or-pattern's as written. Each operator is one interval computation; for `&`, `|` and `^` the standard bound algorithms are used (Hacker's Delight 4-3). Each comparison or pattern is one cut. The work is linear in the function's size.

Zero cost against C everywhere, except the checked forms a program chooses.

readability.note: Every line is shorter and has no new word. `as` reads as it does in Rust, C#, Go and C. The alphabet and the ASCII fold lose their `.unwrap()` and their run-time checks, because the compiler can see the values are letters. A program that does nothing unusual changes in nothing else. The only new refusals are lines that could make an invalid bool, char, enum or range value, which are undecided today, and lines under `@overflow(wrap)` that the mathematical reading let through with a silently cut number. Each refusal's help is one call that compiles for every source type: `T.checked(x)`, or `n != 0` for a bool.

design.compiler_does:
1. It gives each scalar type its kind: number types (integers and floats, and range or newtype types over them) or coded types (bool, char, unit-only enums). It gives each value its number.
2. It keeps one set of numbers for each value (RNG-4), as intervals with few pieces. Literals and constants are exact. Names set once carry their value's set, and loop counters their range. An operator takes its operands' bounds, computes its least and greatest result and applies the line's overflow policy (kept under panic only where it fits, clamped, or wrapped into at most two pieces). `as` maps each piece. Comparisons and patterns cut the set in the arms where nothing changes the name. A type the target decides starts as its values on every target. TYP-4, TYP-5 rule 12, TYP-6 rules 3 and 4, RNG-3, RNG-10, STD-19's counts and the check removal all read this one set.
3. For `x as T` it picks the rule by T's kind. A plain number target takes any scalar's number by the four existing rules (a zero- or sign-extension, a truncation, or a cvt instruction), the same code C emits. A range or coded target needs the source's set to lie inside the target's values: the range; or the codes, on every target (for a char, 0 to 0x10FFFF less 0xD800 to 0xDFFF; for an enum, its discriminants; for a `@non_exhaustive` enum, its representation's range). It then emits the plain move with no check.
4. Otherwise it reports E2020 (coded) or E2215/E2211 (range) at the `as`. The message names the value and says why in one line ("`n` may be any `int`, and only 0 and 1 are `bool`s"). It gives the line to write, shaped to the context: `n != 0`, `bool.checked(n)`, `char.checked(code)`, `Dir.checked(n)`, `Op.checked(word).ok()` where an Option is expected, `t != 0.0`, or `'1' if flag else '0'`.
5. `T.checked(x)` compiles, for each source and target pair, to the compares that test the exact number, and to none where the set proves the conversion.
6. The operand of `as` gets no expected type: a literal there is `int` or `float` unless it has a suffix.
7. N4's scalar-mismatch help gives the exact `as` for a bool or char operand (`count += visible as int`). E5013's help gives `flag as c_int` for a bool passed through C's `...` (verdict 123).
8. P3's help for Python's `int(c)` on a char gives `c as int - '0' as int` for a digit, since Python's `int` parses, and `c as int` for `ord(c)`. This is wording, the lead's.
9. `as` carries no effect (no Alloc, Panic or RuntimeCheck; that is P14's matter) and means the same at compile time (P17's matter). In a generic body it exists only on concrete scalar types (TYP-17, unchanged).
design.misuse:
Refused when compiling, each with a line that compiles for every source type:

* `n as bool` for an `n` that may be other than 0 or 1: E2020, help `n != 0` or `bool.checked(n)`.
* `code as char` for a `code` the compiler cannot see is a code, of any whole-number type: help `char.checked(code)`. That gives Err for a surrogate or a number past U+10FFFF, and nothing in the help's route cuts the number first.
* `n as Dir`: help `Dir.checked(n)`.
* `t as bool` and `t as char` for a float: help `t != 0.0` and `char.checked(t)`.
* `flag as char` and `d as Mode`: help `'1' if flag else '0'` and `Mode.checked(d as int)`.
* `x as Percent` out of range or unknown, and `limit as Percent` for a known 300: E2215 (E2211 for a constant), help `Percent.checked(x)` or `Percent.clamped(x)`. The number is never cut into range.
* `((i as u8) - 1) as Dir` under `@overflow(wrap)`: E2020, because 255 is no `Dir`.
* `ch as char` for a `c_char`: E2020 on every target, help `ch as u8 as char`.
* `s as StrView` and `nz as u32`: E2020. The help says no word is needed at a coercion site, and gives `nz.get()`.
* `count += visible`: TYP-5, help `visible as int`.

Never undefined behaviour: no `as` can make a bool other than 0 or 1, a surrogate char, an enum value no variant has, or a range value outside its range, under any overflow policy or on any target. TYP-2, TYP-3 and RNG-9 stay reachable only in `unsafe`. Nothing stops at run time because of `as`.

The one silent change kept is the one Ember already makes for every integer: narrowing into a plain integer type keeps the low bits (`'€' as u8` is 0xAC, as `8364 as u8` is, and `300 as u8` is 44, as `limit as u8` is). `u8.checked(c)` is the checked form; option D refuses the char case instead.
design.verdicts:
No verdict from 1 to 166 decides a cast.

Kept:
* Verdicts 84 and 145, "one rule for every type": a bool and a char convert by the same integer rule as every whole number, with no special treatment of either.
* Principle 7 and verdicts 11, 93 and 114, "correct programs are made to work": the alphabet, the ASCII fold, the bit test and the direction rotation compile instead of needing a checked call.
* Principle 8 and verdict 98, "decided when compiling": `as` gains no run-time check, unlike Swift's and Zig's.
* Verdict 73 and checklist 9: every help names a call that compiles for every source type, since `T.checked` takes any scalar `as` takes.
* Verdict 123: E5013's help `flag as c_int` now compiles.
* Checklist 11 and verdict 133: one idea, one spelling. Range types already spell the checked conversion `T.checked(x) -> Result[T, RangeError]`; it reaches every place, and `T.try_from`, `char.from_u32` and `Mode.from_repr` go (TYP-6, ENM-3, the FFI-8 row, the FFI-31b help).
* The owner's design G8-4 D (TYP-42, 'only as a count ... converts to and from the other integers'): kept unchanged, and TYP-6 cites it with its reason. The first design withdrew its float exclusion as 'the lead's list'; that was wrong, since G8-4 D is the owner's decision. This design does not reopen it (see open risks).
* TYP-8's "these policies do not change ... casts": kept. `as` does the same under every policy; only the facts before it follow the policy, as the arithmetic itself does.
* TYP-5's "Nothing converts implicitly to or from bool or char": a code is written with `as` (principle 2).
* TYP-6's own `char → u32` and `u8 → char`: kept, as instances of rules 1 and 4.

Changed, and part of option A, said plainly:
* The owner's rulings of 2026-10-06 (the known-numbers rule, TYP-5 rule 12) move word for word into RNG-4, which becomes the one list every rule reads. The list widens with the arms of comparisons and matches, `min`/`max`/`clamp` (RNG-4's own already), `as`, the bitwise operators, and policy-aware arithmetic. Lines refused today then compile: `y: u8 = 97 + i` inside `if 0 <= i < 26:`, and range constructions from names set once. Inside an `if` that bounds a range, `enumerate` may number in `int` instead of `i128`. Under `@overflow(wrap)` or `saturate`, a line that the mathematical reading let through with a silently cut number is refused. EFF-15 calls adding proofs a language revision that makes more programs satisfy a contract, never fewer.

repairs.answer: RNG-4 now states all three. Item 8: where a condition has held or failed, each local or parameter it compares, and that nothing there changes, is among the values of its type for which the comparison came out that way. A coded value compares by its value, so `c <= 'z'` keeps `c` at most 122. Item 9: a match arm's pattern (literal, or-pattern, range pattern, variant) gives the matched name its numbers, and a later arm gets those no earlier unguarded arm took. Item 5: every integer operator, `&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<` and `>>` included, gives the numbers from its least to its greatest result. So `(c as int - 32) as char` in the fold, `b as Op` under `0 | 1 | 2`, and `((flags >> i) & 1) as bool` all compile, each with one verdict everywhere (EFF-15).

design.open_risks:
1. **The one fact list widens three rules.** Moving STD-19's list into RNG-4 and adding comparison and match arms, `as`, the bitwise operators and the overflow policy changes which programs compile. TYP-5 rule 12 accepts `y: u8 = 97 + i` inside `if 0 <= i < 26:`. RNG-10 accepts range constructions from names set once and from `as`. Inside an `if` that bounds a range, `enumerate` may number in `int` instead of `i128`. Under `@overflow(wrap)` or `saturate`, a line that the mathematical reading let through with a silently cut number is refused. This is part of option A and goes to the owner with the owner's 2026-10-06 rulings named.
2. **One checked conversion, `T.checked(x)`.** It replaces `T.try_from`, `char.from_u32` and `Mode.from_repr` (checklist 11, verdict 133), and gives a Result where two of them gave an Option (`.ok()` gives the Option). `checked` is chosen over `try_from` because the range types already use it most and it pairs with `clamped`. If the owner prefers another name, every place follows that name instead. If the owner keeps the old names, each must at least take any whole number exactly, or the helps do not compile.
3. **Floats for 256-bit counts.** TYP-42's exclusion is kept as the owner's G8-4 D. The general integer-to-float rule would let `done as float / total as float` compile. That is its own question for the owner, together with any float route for the counts.
4. **Per-target C aliases beyond `as`.** Rule 4 and every fact read are now the same on every target. But identity and widening through a transparent alias (`b: u8 = ch` compiles where c_char is u8; `x: c_long = 3_000_000_000` compiles where c_long is i64) were target-dependent before this rule. The general fix, checking a line as each type the alias may be, is FFI-8's question for the lead to route.
5. **Cutting a char's code.** `c as u8` keeps the low byte, which is a silent wrong byte for text past Latin-1, as every integer narrowing is. Option D is the alternative.
6. **A constant cut by `as`.** `300 as u8` is 44, as `limit as u8` is (rule 1, with no context from the target). Rust and Go refuse a constant that does not fit. A warning would be the lead's.
7. **Wording.** The E2020 and E2215 messages, the shaping of each help to its context (`Op.checked(word).ok()` where an Option is expected), P3's help for `int(c)`, FFI-31b's text and the Appendix E rows are the lead's wording.

design.rule: A layout decides only where a value's parts are stored, never what an expression means. A layout can come from an attribute (`@layout(c)`, `@packed`, `@align`, `@repr`, `@gpu_layout`, `@soa(flatten)`), from the columns `SoA[T]` keeps, or from a C header's bit-fields. Every expression that reads, writes, names, views, copies, compares, matches, walks, calls a method on or passes a value or a part of one keeps the type, the meaning, the rights and the checks it has with the type laid out plainly. It compiles, or is refused, exactly as it would then. The compiler reaches each part where it is stored. A read gathers the parts, a write scatters them, and a part is reached on its own. A view of data kept in another layout (a field split into columns, one field of every element, an unaligned packed field, a padded GPU field, a bit-field) stays a view of the same type, and nothing is copied. Each function given such a view, and each type holding one, is compiled again for that layout, as a generic is compiled for its types and as verdict 88's copy is made. Two cases are decided while the program runs. The first is views of two layouts meeting in one place. The second is a call whose function is chosen while running (a function value, or a `dyn`, interface or virtual method). In both, the compiler compiles every possibility and picks one by a compare, made before a loop rather than inside it. Only an operation that asks where data lives sees the layout. `size_of`, `align_of`, `offset_of` and `@simd(assert)` report it. A raw pointer must be a real address of a plainly laid-out value, so one into split or unaligned data is refused when compiling. C code, which Ember does not compile, is given one value as an exact copy at one address, written back after the call. C is refused a view of many elements, because it would read them in a row. Two layout statements that cannot both hold are refused at the declaration. Two bit-fields in one word stay two places, and writes to them from two threads at once are made atomic. A union is outside the rule, because it declares that its fields are one place.
design.spec_text:
ADDED, in IX.5 Layout:

* `[LAY-3]` *(new)* **A layout decides where data lives, never what an expression means.** A *layout* is where a type's parts are stored. It can be chosen by an attribute of `[LAY-2]`, by `@gpu_layout` (Annex D) or by `@soa(flatten)` (`[SOA-1]`). It can be the columns `SoA[T]` and `ArenaSoA[T]` keep each field in (`[SOA-1]`). It can be the bits a C header gives a bit-field (`[FFI-8]`). A type's *plain layout* is the one `[TYP-11]` gives it on its own. Some expressions read, write, name, view, copy, compare, match or walk a value or a part of one, or call a method on it, or pass it. Each such expression has the type, the meaning, the rights and the checks it has in the plain layout, and is accepted or refused exactly as it would be there. The only exception is an expression that asks where the data lives (point 5). The compiler reaches each part where the layout keeps it:
  1. **Values and parts.** Reading a value gathers its parts, and writing it scatters them. A part (`ps[i].pos.x`, `h.len`, `s.mode`) is read and written on its own. Each costs the loads and stores C would write by hand for the same layout.
  2. **Views.** Data can be kept in another layout: a field split into columns; one field of every element of a list, with the other fields between them; an unaligned field of a `@packed` type; a field `@gpu_layout` pads; a bit-field. A view of such data is a view of the same type as in the plain layout: `ref T`, `ref mut T`, `Span[T]`, `MutSpan[T]`, a plain name of a part, a loop's name, an `SoA` element. Nothing is copied. A function given such a view, and a type holding one, is compiled again for that layout, as an instance (`[MONO-1]`). The copy is named (`[MNG-6]`) and deduplicated like an instance. `ember inspect` lists it with the call that needs it. It counts toward `[MONO-3]`'s ceiling and is never shared (`[MONO-6]`). It computes what its lines say, as `[MONO-10]`'s copy does. Calls whose views are all in the plain layout use the plain body.
  3. **Views of two layouts in one place.** Views of different layouts can meet in one place: an `if` and its `else`, a list's elements, a field, a function's results. The place then keeps which layout its view has, in one word. Code that uses it runs the copy for that layout after one compare. When the place does not change in a loop, the compare is made once, before the loop.
  4. **Callees chosen while running.** A call can go through a function value, or through an interface, `dyn` or virtual method, with a view in another layout. It then reaches the copy of whichever function is there. The compiler compiles that copy of every function the program can put there (`[BRW-21]`, `[EFF-1]`). The call picks it by comparing the value's code word, or its method table, with each of those functions. That is at most one compare per function, or a search when there are many. When the callee does not change in a loop, this is done once, before the loop.
  5. **What asks where data lives.** These operations see the layout and get its answer:
     * `size_of`, `align_of` and `offset_of` give the numbers of the type's own layout. `@soa(flatten)` changes only how an `SoA` keeps a field.
     * `@simd(assert)`'s vectorisable form (`[SIMD-5]`) sees the layout: a column is read at unit stride, and one field of every element of a plain list is not.
     * A raw pointer (`ref x as *T`, `ref_to_ptr`) is the address of a `T` in its plain layout. Some data has no such address: an unaligned field of a `@packed` type, a field split into columns, a bit-field. A raw pointer to such data is `E2170`. Its message names the layout and gives the line that compiles: a pointer to one column's element, or to a copy of your own.
     * A C or C++ function's code is not compiled by Ember. When such a function is given one value kept in another layout, it gets a copy in the plain layout, at an address in the caller's frame. The copy is written back when the call has returned and nothing the call returned from that argument is still used (`[BRW-2]`). The copy is exact. While the call runs and its results are used, no other name reaches the place (`[BRW-21]`, `[BRW-22]`, `[FFI-52]`). C can reach the place only through a pointer that `unsafe` code gave it, and that code vouches for it (`[UNS-11]`). An address C keeps after the call (`retained`, `[FFI-11]`) must be an address in the plain layout, so such data there is `E2170`.
     * A C or C++ function reads several elements in a row. Giving it a view of several elements kept in another layout is refused (a new code). The message names the layout and gives the lines that copy the elements into a list of your own and write them back after the call. A whole column is never copied unseen.
  6. **Layouts that cannot hold.** Two layout statements that cannot both hold are refused where they are declared, never at an expression. Two cases are `E0104` (ODR-138, ODR-157):
     * `@packed` beside `@align(N)`;
     * a `@packed` type holding a field whose type states its alignment because its operations need it: an `@align` type, a SIMD vector, an `Atomic`, `Mutex` or `RwLock`.
  7. **Parts the machine cannot write apart.** Bit-fields that share a word are different places, as different fields are (`[BRW-4]`). Two threads may write parts of one word at once: scoped tasks (`[THR-11]`), or a `@parallel` loop (`[PAR-2]`). Where the compiler finds such writes, it compiles each one as a relaxed atomic compare-and-swap of the word, so neither thread loses the other's bits. Being relaxed, it carries no `Sync` effect. Every other write is a plain read-modify-write, as in C.

  `@layout(c, union)` is not a layout in this sense. It declares that its fields are one place, so what reading one gives depends on which field was written last. Its fields are read and viewed only in `unsafe` (`[FFI-8]`).

CHANGED:
* `[LAY-2]`, the `@packed` bullet becomes: "no padding; an unaligned field is read and written by byte copies, and a view of it is a view in that layout (`[LAY-3]`); a raw pointer to one is `E2170`". This replaces "taking a reference to one is `E2170`". The ODR-138 paragraph adds `Atomic`, `Mutex` and `RwLock` beside SIMD vectors.
* `[SOA-1]`: "A field marked `@soa(flatten)` whose type has its parts at fixed places (a struct, a tuple, a fixed array) is kept as one column per part (`ps.pos.x`). A part marked `@soa(flatten)` in its own type is split again, at any depth. On a field of another type the attribute is `E0104`: an enum, whose parts depend on its variant; a class object; a view; a SIMD vector, which is one machine value. `@soa(flatten)` decides only how `SoA[T]` and `ArenaSoA[T]` keep the field. `T` on its own, or in any other container, keeps its plain layout."
* `[SOA-2]`: "`ps.f` names field `f` of every element: a view of those values, a `MutSpan[F]`. This holds for every field, flattened or not; a flattened field's view keeps its columns' layout (`[LAY-3]`). `ps.f.g` names part `g` of every element's `f`, at any depth, as a `MutSpan[G]`. When `f` is flattened this is a column of its own. Otherwise it is every element's `g`, with the rest of `f` between them." The rest of SOA-2 is unchanged.
* `[SOA-6]`, after "no `T` is assembled": "For a flattened field `f`, `ps[i].f` is one place made of `f`'s columns at index `i`. Reading it gathers an `F`, writing it scatters one, and each of its parts is a place in its own column. A proxy is a view of element `i` in the `SoA`'s layout. An `SoARef[T]` is given, read, compared and called on wherever a `ref T` is, and an `SoAMut[T]` wherever a `ref mut T` is. `T`'s methods run on it (`[LAY-3]`)."
* `[TYP-5]` rule 6: "`Array[T]`, `[T; N]`, `SoA[T]` and `ArenaSoA[T]` to `Span[T]` (a read-only view) or, given with `ref mut`, to `MutSpan[T]` ...". An `SoA`'s span is in its columns' layout (`[LAY-3]`).
* `[FFI-8]`, the bit-field row becomes: "An integer bit-field narrower than its declared type is a field of a range type the importer generates over that type, as it generates `<Parent>_anon<N>`. For `unsigned mode : 3` this is `type Flags_mode = c_uint in 0 ..= 7`; signed widths start from -2^(w-1). A `_Bool` bit-field is a `bool` field. Such a field is read and written as any field (`f.mode = 3`, under `[RNG-3]`): a constant out of range is `E2211`, and another value is written through `.checked(v)` or `.clamped(v)`. A view of it is in its bits' layout (`[LAY-3]`)." This replaces "`get_<f>`/`set_<f>` methods; not addressable".
* `[HR-14]`, a new row: "a layout changed (`@soa(flatten)`, `@packed`, `@align`, `@gpu_layout`) | carried over by name, as a reorder: each value is moved to the new layout and what points into it is rewritten (`[HR-15]`); a type used across FFI by value is refused (the row above)". `[HR-9a]` adds: a reload replaces every layout copy of a changed function.
* `[MNG-6]`, at the end: "and, for `[LAY-3]`'s copy, the layout of each view parameter that is not plain, after the arguments".
* The code table: `E2170` becomes "a raw pointer, or an address C keeps, to data a layout keeps with no address in its type's plain layout". One new code is added: "a view of several elements kept in another layout given to a C or C++ function" (its number is the lead's).

answers.answer: `ps.pos` is what SOA-2 says it is for every field: a `MutSpan[Vec3]` of every particle's `pos`, here kept in three columns. `integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)` compiles. `integrate` is compiled a second time for that layout (LAY-3 point 2), and in that copy `pos[i] += vel[i] * dt` updates the three columns at `i`. No array of `Vec3` is made. `ps[0].pos` is one place made of the three columns: reading it gathers a `Vec3`, and `ps[0].pos = Vec3.ZERO` writes all three. `ps.pos.x` stays the x column (a `MutSpan[f32]`).
answers.code:
from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: Vec3                     # kept as three f32 columns: ps.pos.x, ps.pos.y, ps.pos.z
    vel: Vec3                     # one Vec3 column

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(1024)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)   # compiles: integrate's copy for pos's three columns
    ps[0].pos = Vec3.ZERO                       # one place of three columns: writes all three
    println(ps.pos.x[0])
answers.outcome: It compiles. After the call `ps.pos.x[0]` is 0.016 and `ps.pos.y[0]` and `ps.pos.z[0]` are 0.0. `ps[0].pos = Vec3.ZERO` writes 0.0 into all three, and the program prints `0.0`. The copy of `integrate` runs the loop a C programmer writes over three float arrays: unit stride, vectorisable (SIMD-5), and accepted under `@parallel` (PAR-2 (c)). The only cost is one more copy of `integrate`'s code.

other_cases.case: `ps.pos.x` where `pos` is not flattened: the attribute is removed from J7-13's program.
other_cases.settled: It still compiles. It is a `MutSpan[f32]` of every element's x, read at a 12-byte stride inside the Vec3 column, and a function given it gets its strided copy. Adding or removing `@soa(flatten)` changes no line's meaning. Only `@simd(assert)` over it changes its answer: it reports the non-unit stride (E4020), because it asks where the data lives.

other_cases.case: Nested and odd flatten. `struct Transform:` has `@soa(flatten) pos: Vec3` and `rot: Quat`; `struct Body:` has `@soa(flatten) xf: Transform` and `mass: f32`, in `SoA[Body]`. Separately, `@soa(flatten)` on an `int`, an enum, a `[f32; 4]` or an `f32x8` field.
other_cases.settled: `bs.xf` is kept as columns `xf.pos.x`, `xf.pos.y`, `xf.pos.z` and `xf.rot`, split at every depth that is marked. `bs.xf`, `bs.xf.pos`, `bs.xf.pos.x` and `bs[i].xf = t` mean what they mean unflattened. A `[f32; 4]` or a tuple splits into one column per element. An int has no parts, so it is E0104 under ATT-6, which never accepts an attribute only to ignore it. An enum, class object, view or SIMD vector field is E0104 with its reason: "an enum's payload depends on its variant, so it has no fixed parts to keep in columns; remove `@soa(flatten)` (line 3)". `Transform` in an `Array` keeps its plain layout.

other_cases.case: SoA elements given to functions and methods: `ps[i].speed()`, `update(ref mut ps[i], dt)` for `fn update(ref mut p: Particle, dt: f32)`, and `for ref mut p in ps: p.step(dt)`.
other_cases.settled: All compile. A proxy is a view of a Particle in the SoA's layout, and `speed`, `update` and `step` each get a copy for that layout that reads and writes the columns at `i`. Nothing is gathered unless the body reads the whole value. SOA-6's proxy rules hold unchanged: while used, an `SoAMut` is the only name of its element, and a reshape ends it.

other_cases.case: After `Array[Particle]` becomes `SoA[Particle]`, `total_mass(ps)` for `fn total_mass(ps: Span[Particle]) -> f32`.
other_cases.settled: It compiles, through TYP-5 rule 6 widened. The span is in the SoA's layout, and inside `total_mass`'s copy `ps[i].mass` reads the mass column. So the one-word change Part XII promises really is one word.

other_cases.case: `@packed struct Header:` with `tag: u8` and `seq: u32`. `bump(ref mut h.seq)` for `fn bump(ref mut n: u32)`. Also a method called on an unaligned inner struct, `h.inner.check()`.
other_cases.settled: Both compile; the first is E2170 today. `bump` gets a copy that reads and writes `n` with unaligned loads and stores, the same as C's packed access, and `check` gets one for its unaligned `this`. A raw pointer, `ref h.seq as *u32`, stays E2170 because every `*u32` must be 4-byte aligned.

other_cases.case: C functions given SoA data. `c_nudge(ref mut ps[0].pos)`, where C has `void c_nudge(Vec3*)`. `c_integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.len())`, where C has `void c_integrate(Vec3*, size_t)`.
other_cases.settled: `c_nudge` compiles. The three columns are gathered into one Vec3 in the caller's frame, C gets its address, and the columns are written back after the call. The copy is exact because the call check (BRW-21, FFI-52) lets nothing else reach the place meanwhile. Nothing is allocated, and this is what C's own code pays. `c_integrate` is refused: "`c_integrate` is a C function and reads `pos` as `Vec3`s in a row, but `ps.pos` keeps them in three columns (`@soa(flatten)`, line 4); give it a list of your own and write it back: `tmp = ps.pos.iter().copy_each().to_array()`, `c_integrate(ref mut tmp.as_mut_span(), tmp.len())`, then `for i in 0..tmp.len(): ps[i].pos = tmp[i]`".

other_cases.case: A raw pointer into split data in `unsafe`: `p = ref ps[0].pos as *Vec3`. Also a C function declared as keeping the address (`retained`).
other_cases.settled: Both are E2170 at the line: "`ps[0].pos` is kept in three columns (`@soa(flatten)`, line 4), so no address holds one `Vec3` of it; point at one column's element: `ref ps[0].pos.x as *f32`, or at a copy of your own: `v = copy of ps[0].pos`, then `ref v as *Vec3`". A pointer to one column's element is a real `*f32` and is accepted.

other_cases.case: A callee chosen while running. `for s in systems: s.run(ref mut ps.pos)` with `systems: Array[owns dyn System]`. `this.on_tick(ref mut ps.pos)` with a field `on_tick: fn(ref mut MutSpan[Vec3])`.
other_cases.settled: Both compile. Each System kind's `run`, and each function the program can put in `on_tick` (BRW-21, verdicts 122 and 129), gets the copy for three columns. The call compares the method table or code word with each of them and calls that copy directly. The data is not copied. The cost is at most one compare per candidate per call, made once before a loop when `s` or `on_tick` does not change in it.

other_cases.case: Views of two layouts in one place. `if use_soa: d = ref mut ps.pos` and `else: d = ref mut plain_positions.as_mut_span()`, then `integrate(ref mut d, vel, dt)`. Also a list `Array[MutSpan[Vec3]]` holding both kinds.
other_cases.settled: It compiles. `d` keeps which layout it holds, in one word, and the call runs `integrate`'s plain copy or its column copy after one compare. A list holding both kinds keeps that word per element, and a loop over the list compares once per element. C has no such place: it would write two loops.

other_cases.case: C bit-fields. The header has `struct Flags { unsigned ready : 1; unsigned mode : 3; }`. The program writes `f.mode = 5`, `f.mode = 9`, `f.mode += 1` and `f.mode = x`. Two scoped tasks run at once, one setting `f.ready` and the other `f.mode`.
other_cases.settled: `mode` becomes a field of a range type the importer generates, `Flags_mode = c_uint in 0 ..= 7`. `f.mode = 5` compiles. `f.mode = 9` is E2211. `f.mode += 1` checks as range operators do (RNG-5a1). `f.mode = x` needs `Flags_mode.checked(x)` or `.clamped(x)`, which is RNG-3's existing spelling. `ready` is the range type `c_uint in 0 ..= 1`; only a `_Bool` bit-field would be a `bool`. The two tasks compile, and each write is a relaxed compare-and-swap of the shared word, so neither bit is lost. In C this is a data race on one memory location (C11). The `get_`/`set_` methods go.

other_cases.case: A `@gpu_layout(std140)` uniform block where std140 pads a field's own parts: `weights: [f32; 4]` with each element 16 bytes apart, and `normal_matrix: Mat3` stored as three 16-byte columns.
other_cases.settled: Each field reads, writes and is viewed as its own type. `u.weights[2] = 0.5` writes one element. `sum(u.weights)` for `fn sum(xs: Span[f32])` uses `sum`'s 16-byte-stride copy. `u.normal_matrix = m` scatters the 3x3 into the padded columns. The struct's bytes are what the GPU reads, and `offset_of` and `size_of` give the std140 numbers.

other_cases.case: `@packed struct Slot:` with `tag: u8` and `count: Atomic[u32]`; also a `@packed` struct with an `f32x8` field.
other_cases.settled: E0104 at the declaration, which generalises ODR-138 and ODR-157: "an `Atomic[u32]` needs 4-byte alignment for its instructions, and `@packed` (line 1) gives `count` none; remove `@packed`, or keep the count outside the packed struct". Nothing is ever refused at an expression for this.

other_cases.case: `@layout(c, union) struct Bits:` with `i: u32` and `f: f32`.
other_cases.settled: Outside LAY-3, by its own declaration: its fields are one place, so writing `b.i` changes what `b.f` reads. Reading or viewing a field stays `unsafe` only (FFI-8), as today.

other_cases.case: Hot reload: an edit adds `@soa(flatten)` to `Particle.pos` while 100,000 particles live in an SoA.
other_cases.settled: Covered by HR-14's new row: the values are carried over by name, as a reorder is. The SoA moves each `pos` into the three new columns through its container (HR-13). Kept views of the old column are rewritten (HR-15), and every layout copy of every function is replaced. A type used across FFI by value is refused, as today.

other_cases.case: SIMD and parallel loops over a split column: `f32x8.load(ps.pos.x[i..i + 8])`, and `@parallel` over `for i in 0..ps.len(): ps.pos[i] += ps.vel[i] * dt`.
other_cases.settled: The x column is contiguous and 64-byte aligned (SOA-7), so the first is an aligned vector load. The `@parallel` loop is accepted: under PAR-2 (c) the pos columns are SoA columns written at offset 0, and each chunk updates three columns. If `pos` were not flattened, a `load` of the strided x view would give the same lanes by a gather, at the cost of the layout.

design.prior_art:
C has no SoA layout. `&s.packed_field` gives a misaligned pointer, which is undefined on strict-alignment targets; GCC 9 added -Waddress-of-packed-member to warn about it. `&s.bitfield` is a constraint violation. Adjacent bit-fields are one memory location (C11 3.14), so two threads writing different bit-fields of one word race. SoA is written by hand: three float arrays and one function per layout.

C++ has all of C's rules. On top of them, a non-const reference cannot bind to a bit-field, while a `const&` silently binds to a temporary copy that stops seeing changes. That is the silent copy Ember refuses (verdict 5). C++23's `std::mdspan` puts the layout in the type (`layout_right`, `layout_left`, `layout_stride`). It is fast and general, but a function that should take two layouts must be a template, and the layout shows in every signature.

Rust makes a reference to a packed field a hard error (E0793). The programmer copies the field out (`{ h.seq }`) or uses `addr_of!` with `read_unaligned`. Rust has no SoA in the language. The `soa_derive` crate generates `ParticleVec` with its own `ParticleRef`/`ParticleRefMut` (nested fields through `#[nested_soa]`). So a function written for `&mut [Vec3]` does not take a column of a nested field: the layout changes the types, which is option C.

Swift defines `inout` as copy-in copy-out (call by value-result), done by reference when the argument has an address. Computed properties pass through it, and the Law of Exclusivity (SE-0176) makes the copy unobservable. That is exactly right for one value. For a whole column it would be a real copy, and Swift has no packed or SoA layouts.

Ada's representation clauses and `pragma Pack` change representation, not meaning. A component that is not addressable is passed to an `in out` parameter by copy, and `'Access` needs an `aliased` component. A conversion between types with different representation clauses performs the change of representation (RM 13.6). Ada is the closest in principle, but it copies values where this rule compiles copies of the code instead.

Fortran passes a strided array section to an assumed-shape dummy through a descriptor, so the stride is read at run time, which is harder to vectorise. It passes one to an explicit-shape dummy by copy-in/copy-out through a temporary (gfortran -Warray-temporaries). Compiling the callee once per layout avoids both costs.

Zig's `std.MultiArrayList(T)` gives `items(.pos)` as a slice for top-level fields only; `get(i)` gathers and `set(i, v)` scatters. A pointer to a packed-struct field has its own bit-offset pointer type (`*align(1:3:1) u8`), which does not coerce to `*u8`.

C# refuses a property passed by `ref` (CS0206). Go refuses `m[k].f = v` for a struct held in a map, because map elements are not addressable. That is storage changing what an expression may do, which this rule forbids. ISPC's `soa<N>` keeps `a[i].x` the same in both layouts, which is the aim here.

What Ember takes from these:
- Ada's principle: representation never changes meaning.
- Swift's argument that exclusivity makes a copy unobservable, used only at the C boundary.
- mdspan's compile-time layouts, without a template in every signature. The compiler makes the copies per layout, as it already does for generics and for verdict 88.
- None of Fortran's run-time descriptors or temporaries.
design.cost:
Each operation is compared with C written by hand for the same layout.
- **Reading or writing a whole value:** the gather or scatter is the loads or stores C writes. A Vec3 in three columns takes 3 loads or 3 stores; a part takes one. It is zero over C.
- **Inside a copy for a split column:** the loop is the three-float-array loop, unit stride and vectorisable. Over a plain Vec3 column it is better than C's: stride 4 per part instead of a stride-12 interleave.
- **A view in another layout:** it holds what finds each part. A Vec3 split into three takes a base per column plus the length, 4 words against 2 for a plain span. That is what C passes by hand: three pointers and n.
- **A packed field:** unaligned loads and stores. That is one instruction on x86-64 and ARM64, and byte copies on strict-alignment targets, as C's packed access is.
- **A strided view:** one load per element at the stride, as C's `p[i].x`.
- **A bit-field:** a read is load, shift, mask; a write is load, mask, or, store. Both are C's.
- **A call with such a view:** a direct call to the copy, with zero run-time cost. In memory, it costs one more copy of the function's code per layout it is given, plus compile time. That is zero when no line gives such a view.
- **Views of two layouts in one place:** one word in the place and one compare per use, hoisted before loops, so zero inside them. C has no such place; it writes two loops.
- **A callee chosen while running, given such a view:** at most one compare per function that can be there, before the call and hoisted out of loops. C cannot make this call at all; it would have to gather into a temporary array.
- **A C function given one such value:** a gather into a slot of the caller's frame and a scatter back. That is what C's own code pays to call a `Vec3*` function on SoA data, and it allocates nothing.
- **A C function given a whole column:** refused. The program writes the copy it pays for, visibly: an allocation and 2n element copies.
- **Two threads writing bit-fields of one word:** a relaxed compare-and-swap per such write, a few nanoseconds uncontended. In C this is a data race, undefined behaviour. Every other write is zero over C.
- **A program with no layout attribute and no SoA:** zero. There is no new code, no new check and no new word.

from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: Vec3
    vel: Vec3

# today: to be sure it compiles, the function is written against the three columns
fn integrate(ref mut x: MutSpan[f32], ref mut y: MutSpan[f32], ref mut z: MutSpan[f32], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..x.len():
        x[i] += vel[i].x * dt
        y[i] += vel[i].y * dt
        z[i] += vel[i].z * dt

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(1024)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    integrate(ref mut ps.pos.x, ref mut ps.pos.y, ref mut ps.pos.z, ps.vel, 0.016)
    ps[0].pos.x = 0.0
    ps[0].pos.y = 0.0
    ps[0].pos.z = 0.0

# and for a packed header (E2170 today):
#     seq = copy of h.seq
#     bump(ref mut seq)

readability.ordinary_after:
from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: Vec3
    vel: Vec3

fn integrate(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], dt: f32):
    for i in 0..pos.len():
        pos[i] += vel[i] * dt

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(1024)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, 0.016)

# and for a packed header:

readability.note: The after is Part XII's own example plus the one attribute line the programmer chose. It is 5 lines shorter than the before, and no column name appears in it. Adding or removing `@soa(flatten)` changes no other line. The packed case goes from three lines to one. A program with no layout attribute is unchanged: the rule adds no word, annotation or check to it. Everything the rule needs is done by the compiler: which layout a view has, the copies, and the compares.

design.compiler_does:
The compiler does the following:
1. It knows each type's layout in each place the type is kept: an SoA's columns (flattened parts at every depth), a packed type's offsets, `@gpu_layout`'s padding and strides, and a C bit-field's word, shift and width.
2. It lowers each read to the loads of the parts it needs: a whole value is gathered, a part is read on its own. It lowers each write to the stores, scattered.
3. For every view, it works out the layout of the data the view points at. It does this by following where the view was made and every place it goes: a local, a parameter, a field, a list element, a result. It already follows functions into places this way (verdicts 122, 128, 129).
4. It compiles again, for that layout, each function given a view in another layout and each type holding one. Each copy is an instance named by MNG-6, deduplicated across packages as MONO-1 says, and listed by `ember inspect` with the call that needs it. This repeats down the calls: a copy's own calls get copies. Inside a copy, a split `pos[i] += d` becomes per-column updates, which SIMD-5 and PAR-2 then read as columns.
5. Where views of several layouts meet in one place, it stores which layout the place holds and makes one version of the code per layout. The test is hoisted before loops.
6. For a call through a function value, or a `dyn`, interface or virtual method, with such a view, it compiles the copy of every function the program can put there (BRW-21). The call picks its copy by comparing the code word or method table. The compare is hoisted out of loops where the callee does not change.
7. At a C or C++ call, it gathers one value into a frame slot in the plain layout and scatters it back after the call and the last use of anything C returned from it. It refuses a many-element view in another layout, and any raw pointer or kept address to data that has no plain address.
8. It refuses, at the declaration, layouts that cannot hold.
9. It uses the scoped-task and `@parallel` analyses to find writes from two threads to parts of one word, and compiles those writes as relaxed compare-and-swaps.
10. At a reload, it moves values to a changed layout by name and replaces every layout copy of a changed function.

The programmer writes nothing for any of it.
design.misuse:
These mistakes are refused when compiling, each with a line that compiles:
- **A raw pointer to data with no address in its plain layout:** E2170. For split data: "`ps[0].pos` is kept in three columns (`@soa(flatten)`, line 4), so no address holds one `Vec3` of it; point at one column's element: `ref ps[0].pos.x as *f32`, or at a copy of your own: `v = copy of ps[0].pos`, then `ref v as *Vec3`". For packed data: "a `*u32` must be 4-byte aligned, and `h.seq` is at byte 1 of a `@packed` struct (line 1); point at a copy of your own: `seq = copy of h.seq`, then `ref seq as *u32`, and write it back with `h.seq = seq`".
- **An address C keeps (`retained`) to such data:** E2170, with the same advice.
- **A many-element view in another layout given to C or C++:** the new code, whose message gives the three lines that copy the elements into a list and write them back.
- **Layouts that cannot hold** (packed beside, or holding, a type that states its alignment): E0104 at the declaration, naming the field and both lines.
- **`@soa(flatten)` on a field with no fixed parts:** E0104, with its reason.
- **A bit-field constant out of range:** E2211. Another value needs `.checked(v)` or `.clamped(v)` (RNG-3), and is E2020 with that line as help.

Nothing reaches undefined behaviour:
- No aligned access is made at an unaligned address: every access to an unaligned part is compiled unaligned.
- No pointer of a plain layout ever points into split data.
- No copy of Ember data is read stale. None is made between Ember functions, and the one at a C call is exact because of the call check.
- Bit-field writes from two threads cannot lose each other's bits.

No new run-time stop is added. The compares of points 3 and 4 choose which code runs; they check nothing.
design.verdicts:
P26 lists no owner verdict, and none is revisited. The rule keeps and uses these:

- **88:** the compiler makes a copy of the function for a call ("as fast as C either way; the cost is one more copy of the function"). The rule's copies per layout are the same kind of copy (MONO-10, MNG-6).
- **14:** make the natural way fast instead of adding a feature to avoid the work. This is the reason not to add a `SoASpan` type or require a per-column rewrite.
- **84 and 34:** one word, one rule, for every type; the rule extends this to every layout.
- **1 and 34:** `ref mut` at the call, and on a `MutSpan` name. Unchanged: `integrate(ref mut ps.pos, ps.vel, dt)`.
- **5:** no silent copy. No copy is made between Ember functions. The one copy, at a C call, is exact and unobservable, because nothing else reaches the place during the call. It is still a copy, and the owner should hear this plainly (see open_risks).
- **122, 128, 129, with BRW-21:** the compiler knows every function a function value or `dyn` call can reach. That is what lets point 4 compile each copy instead of refusing.
- **98 and 100:** nothing is checked while running. The compares of points 3 and 4 choose code; they are not checks.
- **115:** no limit. Flatten works at any depth, with any number of columns.
- **Principles 6 and 7:** correct programs are made to work, not refused. The exceptions (raw pointers, a column given to C, unions) exist only where the general rule would be untrue, and each says why.

Delegation rulings:
- **ODR-138 and ODR-157** are kept and generalised to Atomic, Mutex and RwLock, as types that state their alignment.
- **ODR-140** (E2170's wording) is overtaken: E2170 moves from "a reference to a packed field" to "a raw pointer to data with no plain address". It is a lead ruling, not an owner verdict, but the owner should know that E2170 changes.
- **ODR-116** (MutSpan to Span) holds in every layout.
- **ODR-062** (PAR-2b reads through inline-header calls) holds for each copy.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule: a layout changes only where data lives. Each function given a view of split, strided, packed or bit data is compiled again for that layout, and nothing is copied. C gets an exact copy of one value and is refused a whole column. A raw pointer into such data is refused.

recommendation.reason: A is the only option that keeps Part XII's promise that a layout is a one-word change. It costs nothing at run time over hand-written C for the same layout; the only price is one more copy of a function's code per layout it is given, the price verdict 88 already accepted. It refuses nothing that compiles without the attribute, except operations that ask where data lives: a raw pointer, a C function reading a column in a row, and `@simd(assert)`'s stride. It also settles, under one rule, the cases the spec leaves open today: methods and `ref mut T` parameters on SoA elements, `ps.pos.x` without flatten, nested flatten, packed views (E2170), C bit-fields, std140-padded fields, `dyn` and function-value calls, and reloads. B and C make the attribute change what programs compile, and C adds a type for one attribute (verdict 14's lesson). D is slower than C, allocates, and copies silently.

| step | thread | what happens | the value |

| 1 | main | `ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))` | `@soa(flatten)` keeps `pos` as three `f32` columns: `ps.pos.x = [0.0]`, `ps.pos.y = [0.0]`, `ps.pos.z = [0.0]`; `ps.vel = [(1, 0, 0)]` |

owner_short.today: SOA-2 says `ps.pos` is a `MutSpan[Vec3]` column and SOA-6 that `ps[0].pos` is a place in it. But `@soa(flatten)` leaves `pos` with three `f32` columns and no `Vec3` column, so neither line has a meaning. `@packed` refuses any reference to an unaligned field (E2170) for the same kind of reason.
owner_short.options:
A: the attribute changes only where data lives. `integrate` is compiled a second time for three columns, and `ps[0].pos = v` writes three columns. Nothing is copied, and it runs as fast as hand-written C. C code gets an exact copy of one value, and is refused a whole column.
B: `ps.pos` of a flattened field is refused, and you rewrite `integrate` to take `ps.pos.x`, `ps.pos.y` and `ps.pos.z`.
C: `ps.pos` gets a new type, `SoASpan[Vec3]`, which functions taking `MutSpan[Vec3]` refuse, so you write them twice.
D: `ps.pos` is copied into a hidden list for the call and written back. It compiles, but it allocates and copies every particle twice per call.
owner_short.recommendation: A: adding `@soa(flatten)` stays a one-word change, and the compiler writes the three-column loop that C programmers write by hand. Nothing that compiles without the attribute is refused, except an operation that asks where data lives: a raw pointer, or C reading a column in a row.

design.open_risks:
1. **Code size and compile time.** The layout copies add code and compile time. The number is bounded: a type has finitely many layouts, fixed by its own fields, and strides are constants. MONO-3 counts them. They should be measured on a real particle or ECS program before the rule is built (principle 8, "measured").
2. **The compares of points 3 and 4.** These must be measured against a plain indirect call. A function value called inside a loop with a callee that changes every iteration pays them on every call. For dyn methods, a method-table entry per layout (completed at link time) would remove the compare; that is an implementation choice to measure.
3. **Separate compilation.** Copies of another package's non-generic functions need those functions' bodies, as MONO-10's copies already do. Check that BLD-2 and CG-C-3b carry every body a copy can need.
4. **Reload.** A kept view whose layout an edit changes can change size (one base per column), so its holder migrates too. Check that HR-15 covers a view stored in a list of views.
5. **Verdict 5.** The copy at a C call is exact and unobservable, but it is a copy. The owner may prefer a refusal with the three-line rewrite (`v = copy of ps[0].pos`, `c_nudge(ref mut v)`, `ps[0].pos = v`). Present it to him plainly.
6. **Rules this changes.** E2170's meaning moves (ODR-140 was a delegation ruling). FFI-8's bit-field row changes what the importer writes for every C header with bit-fields: the get_/set_ methods disappear and range types appear. The owner may take the bit-field part as a separate question.
7. **Programs newly accepted.** TYP-5 rule 6 (SoA to Span) and SOA-6 (proxies used as `ref T`) widen which programs compile. P24 may ask whether `SoARef[T]` and `SoAMut[T]` stay types a programmer writes, beside `ref T`.
8. **Other groups' answers.**
   - P07's answer on the raw-pointer spelling (`ref_to_ptr` against `ref x as *T`) decides the line E2170's message gives.
   - P14 may reclassify the effect of a relaxed compare-and-swap.
   - P10's read-only-promise question does not touch this rule, because no copy is made between Ember functions.

from std.math import Vec3

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: Vec3
    vel: Vec3

struct Batch:
    xs: Span[Vec3]               # a view field (LT-18)
    dt: f32

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(16)
    plain: Array[Vec3] = [Vec3.ZERO]
    jobs: Array[Batch] = []
    jobs.push(owns Batch(xs=plain.as_span(), dt=0.016))   # a plain span: 2 words
    jobs.push(owns Batch(xs=ps.pos, dt=0.016))            # three columns: 4 words, plus point 3's layout word
    println(size_of[Batch]())
holes.what_goes_wrong: IX.5 makes `size_of[Batch]()` one compile-time number, and point 5 says it gives "the type's own layout", 24 bytes. The second Batch holds 4 words plus the layout word, so `jobs` needs elements of at least 48 bytes. Unsafe code that lays out T's by `size_of[T]()` writes past its slots. That includes a user's pool, std's own Array if it is written in Ember, and a byte copy in `transmute`. The design leaves open which size a layout copy of `Batch` reports. Either answer overflows a buffer that code of the other copy allocated. A value type now also carries a hidden word, which PHIL-9 says no value type does.
holes.fix_hint: Give each view type one representation and size for the whole program, whatever layout it holds: for example, a non-plain view as a pointer to its source's own column table plus start and length, packed into the plain span's words. Then size_of, offset_of, Array slots and unsafe code agree in every copy, and PHIL-9 holds. Otherwise state that size_of[T] is the widest copy's size everywhere and amend PHIL-9 openly.

# vec.h: typedef struct { float x, y, z; } Vec3;  const float* vec3_x(const Vec3* v);   (returns &v->x)
# overlay: @ffi(no_callbacks) fn vec3_x(v: borrowed one) -> borrowed one from(v)
import c "vec.h" with (overlay = "overlays/vec.em") as m

struct Particle:
    @soa(flatten)
    pos: m.Vec3
    vel: m.Vec3

fn first_x(ps: SoA[Particle]) -> ref f32:
    return m.vec3_x(ps[0].pos)        # from(v): typed as a view into ps

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(4)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=m.Vec3(x=1.0, y=2.0, z=3.0), vel=m.Vec3(x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0)))
    x = first_x(ps)
    println(x)
holes.what_goes_wrong: Under point 5, `ps[0].pos` is gathered into a slot in `first_x`'s frame, and C returns the address of the slot's x. FFI-11's `from(v)` types the result as a view of the argument's place, which is part of `ps`, so LT-1 lets it leave `first_x`. The design writes the slot back when "nothing the call returned ... is still used", but that last use is in `main`, after the frame is gone. `println(x)` reads a dead stack slot. Without `@soa(flatten)` the same program is correct.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a result C returns from a gathered argument is a view of the frame slot, not of the place. It may not outlive the calling function: refuse that at the return, with `v = copy of ps[0].pos` and the call on `v` as the fix. The slot is written back on every path out, a `?` included.

# slots.h: typedef struct { _Atomic uint32_t hits; uint32_t id; } Slot;  void slot_log(const Slot* s);
# overlay: @ffi(no_callbacks) fn slot_log(s: borrowed one)
import c "slots.h" with (overlay = "overlays/slots.em") as sl
import std.thread
from std.sync import Atomic

fn count_hits(ss: SoA[sl.Slot]):
    for _ in 0..100_000:
        ss[0].hits.fetch_add(1)          # an Atomic changes through a plain name (verdict 3)

fn main():
    ss = SoA[sl.Slot].with_capacity(4)  # FFI-8: hits is an Atomic[u32] column
    ss.push(owns sl.Slot(hits=Atomic(0), id=1))
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): count_hits(ss))
        sl.slot_log(ss[0])               # point 5: gathered into a frame slot, then written back
    println(ss[0].hits.load())
holes.what_goes_wrong: The design calls the C copy exact because "no other name reaches the place", but a read-only argument is not exclusive. Verdict 3 and BRW-1 let the task `fetch_add` through a plain name during the call. The gather is a plain read of an Atomic that another thread is changing. The unconditional write-back then stores the stale `hits` over the task's increments: a plain store racing atomic read-modify-writes, undefined in C11, and the count printed falls short of 100000. Two tasks that each call `slot_log(ss[0])` race the same way with no Atomic at all, because both write back to the same columns. This also bears on open risk 5: the copy is observable.
holes.fix_hint: Write back only a `ref mut` argument, which BRW-1 makes exclusive. A read-only argument is gathered and never stored. A value holding an Atomic, Mutex, RwLock or Cell part is never gathered for C: refuse it, with the lines that give C a plain copy of the fields it reads.

from std.sync import Atomic

struct Counter:
    hits: Atomic[u32]

@packed
struct Slot:
    tag: u8
    c: Counter          # at byte 1; Counter itself states no alignment

fn main():
    s = Slot(tag=1, c=Counter(hits=Atomic(0)))
    s.c.hits.fetch_add(1)    # E2170 today; under LAY-3, a view of an unaligned Counter with a layout copy
    println(s.c.hits.load())
holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 6 refuses only a field whose own type is an @align type, a SIMD vector, an Atomic, a Mutex or an RwLock. Counter holds one a level down, so the declaration is accepted, and the narrowed E2170 no longer refuses the view. `fetch_add`'s copy for byte 1 is an atomic instruction at an unaligned address. That is undefined in C (`__atomic` on a misaligned object), an alignment fault on ARM64, and a split lock on x86-64 (which can trap). Done with byte copies instead, it is not atomic, and another thread's increments are lost. The same goes for `@packed struct Tagged[T]: tag: u8; v: T` with T = Atomic[u32], which a check at the declaration cannot see, against point 6's "never at an expression".
holes.fix_hint: Make "needs its alignment" a property of a type that holds, at any depth (a field, a tuple, a fixed array, an enum payload, an Option), an Atomic, Mutex, RwLock, SIMD vector or @align type. A @packed type holding one is E0104 at its declaration. A generic @packed type is checked at each instance's line, and the message names the declaration.

holes.what_goes_wrong: BRW-22 compiles both `ref mut` parameters with noalias (C's restrict, LLVM's noalias), but both are read-modify-writes of one storage word: two restrict pointers to one object, both written, which is undefined in C. The C or LLVM compiler may load the word for `m` before the store for `r` and then store it back, so the program prints `0 5`. That is a lost write on one thread. Point 7 handles only two threads.
holes.fix_hint: In BRW-22, add that views of bit-fields that may share a storage word are different places but one memory location. They are never given noalias against each other, and their copy reaches the word through one pointer.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Under the new FFI-8 row, `prio` and `done` are fields of the generated range types `Task_prio` and `Task_done`. RNG-10b says "A range type may not appear in a foreign signature, directly or inside an aggregate or behind a pointer (E5054)", so `task_run`'s import is refused. So is every C function that takes a struct with a bit-field: Vulkan's VkAccelerationStructureInstanceKHR, and Win32 and Linux UAPI structs. RNG-8 also requires `checked` or `clamped` for a range value arriving from C, so a struct C returns by value has no spelling that is allowed. The design changes neither rule.
holes.fix_hint: Amend RNG-10b and RNG-8 in the same change: an importer-generated bit-field range type crosses C as its bits, because C cannot store a value outside its width. It is never E5054 and needs no `checked` on arrival. Say so in FFI-8's row.

import c "flags.h" as fl          # struct Flags { unsigned ready : 1; unsigned mode : 3; };
import std.thread

fn main():
    f = fl.Flags(ready=0, mode=0)
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): f.mode = 5)          # the word's only writer: a plain read-modify-write (point 7)
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): println(f.ready))    # reads another place in the same word
holes.what_goes_wrong: THR-11 allows this, because the two tasks touch different places, and point 7 makes a write atomic only when two threads write. Task 1's plain load and store of the word and task 2's plain load of it touch one C11 memory location, from two threads, one of them writing. That is a data race, undefined in the C the backend emits. Even with two writers, each writer's own reads of its bit-field are plain loads racing the other's compare-and-swap. "The word" is also undefined for a `#pragma pack` struct whose bits sit at an odd byte or straddle an aligned unit. There an aligned compare-and-swap covers a neighbouring field, or the next element of an array, that another task writes plainly.
holes.fix_hint: Point 7: when a task may write part of a word that another task reaches (reads or writes) before the join, make every access to that word in both tasks atomic: relaxed loads and compare-and-swap writes. Define the word as the aligned unit inside the struct's own bytes. Under such sharing, refuse a bit-field that straddles an aligned unit or sits in a packed struct, with a lock as the fix.

holes.what_goes_wrong: LAY-3 defines a type's plain layout as "the one [TYP-11] gives it on its own". TYP-11 is C's natural layout, not the @packed layout that Packet's declaration states. Read as written, `send` gets an 8-byte copy with `len` at offset 4 and reads `len` from bytes 1 to 4, which is garbage. By the same words, `ref u as *U` for a `@gpu_layout(std140) struct U` (every uniform upload) would be E2170, and a packed header passed by pointer to C would never be in its plain layout. A written declaration must mean only what it says (checklist 15).
holes.fix_hint: Define the plain layout as the layout the type's own declaration gives it: TYP-11 together with its own LAY-2 and @gpu_layout attributes. "Kept in another layout" then means a part that its container places differently from its own type's plain layout.

@layout(c, union)
struct Bits:
    i: u32
    f: f32

struct Sample:
    @soa(flatten)
    v: Bits                  # changed SOA-1: a struct, so one column per field
    t: f32

fn main():

        println(ss[0].v.f)
holes.what_goes_wrong: It prints 0.0 instead of 1.0. The changed SOA-1 accepts flatten on any struct, and a union is a struct. Today's SOA-1 also gives `SoA[Bits]` itself one column per field. Either way the union's fields stop being one place, which is what its declaration states and what its unsafe code vouches on. With a union `{p: *u8, bits: usize}` written through `bits`, reading `p` reads an unwritten column: a garbage pointer. The design keeps unions outside the rule, but nothing keeps them out of an SoA.
holes.fix_hint: In SOA-1, keep a `@layout(c, union)` struct as one column, both as an SoA's element and as a field. `@soa(flatten)` on a union field is E0104, with the reason "its fields are one place".

But the changed SOA-6 keeps "a proxy ... finds element i again at each use, so adding to ps keeps it", and the design says "SOA-6's proxy rules hold unchanged". The design does not say what happens when a method table matches none of the compares. Either a plain body is called with a column view and reads three bases as a pointer and a length, or the call falls off the chain. PHIL-13 requires the reload build to accept the same program.

static mut PS: SoA[Particle] = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(0)
static mut JOBS: Array[Batch] = []

fn setup():

# package physics (a dependency):
pub fn upload(xs: Span[Vec3]):
    # SAFETY: xs is xs.len() Vec3s in a row (SPN-8)
    unsafe:
        gl.buffer_data(xs.as_ptr() as *u8, xs.len() * 12)

# the program, with pos flattened:
physics.upload(ps.pos)
holes.what_goes_wrong: Once `as_ptr()` on a non-plain view is refused (first hole), the refusal arises in `upload`'s layout copy, on a line in physics that the programmer cannot edit. The same holds for the new C code and for E4020 in a callee's @simd(assert) loop. The design does not say where these are reported, whether they name the chain, or that the fact is recorded in physics's interface file (EFF-4), as BRW-10's facts are. As written, a body edit in physics breaks callers with no change to its interface. It also does not say that std's own view methods (sort_by, iter, a bulk copy) work in every layout. If any of them is written with a raw pointer or a C memcpy, common lines on `ps.pos` are refused deep inside std.

Record "needs its plain layout for parameter p" in the interface file. Specify that std's view methods have a body for every layout.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The cost section says a view "holds what finds each part ... a base per column", so this Span[f32] carries 256 bases (2 KB) on every call. open_risks says "strides are constants", which is untrue here: the distance between columns is the SoA's capacity rounded up to 64 bytes (SOA-7), known only while running. C indexes `w[j * cap + i]` with one run-time spacing.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a view of a part split into N columns of one type holds the first column's base and one spacing, read from the SoA, rather than N bases. State that cost, and drop "strides are constants".

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design settles this as "checks as range operators do (RNG-5a1)", but RNG-5a1 generates no compound assignment, so the line is E2214 with the fix-it `f.mode = fl.Flags_mode.clamped(f.mode + 1)`. Every `+=` and `|=` on a C bit-field, common in code over C headers, becomes that longer line. The outcome has to be said, not left to "as range operators do".
holes.fix_hint: Say plainly that it is E2214 and give the fix-it. Or have the importer generate checked compound forms for its bit-field range types, and say which.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-8 row maps only integer and _Bool bit-fields, and it removes `get_<f>`/`set_<f>`. An enum bit-field, which C++, C23 and GCC's C allow, then has no mapping at all.

safety.notes:
Overall: the core of option A survives the safety lens. Layout copies of functions, gather and scatter of parts, E2170 narrowed to raw pointers, and the refusal of a whole column given to C hold up for SoA columns, @packed fields, std140 padding, nested flatten, and dyn or function-value calls without a reload. The holes sit where a view's representation leaks out:
- SPN-8's safe `as_ptr()`, which breaks IX.4's own `parse` example on a strided span.
- `size_of` and PHIL-9 for types that hold a view.
- BRW-22's noalias on two bit-field views of one word.
- The C copy: a `from(v)` result outliving the frame, and write-back racing the sharing verdict 3 allows. This also answers open risk 5: the copy is observable.
- Bit-fields: RNG-10b's E5054 refuses every C signature carrying one, and point 7 misses the case of one writer and one reader.
- Point 6's list of types that need their alignment is closed, not transitive.

Smaller gaps:
- The definition of "plain layout" points at TYP-11 alone.
- Unions are not kept out of an SoA.
- SOA-6's "adding keeps it" conflicts with BRW-21.
- Compare-chain dispatch conflicts with HR-9a under reload.
- HR-15 cannot rewrite a view that changes size.
- Refusals that arise inside a dependency's copy have no reporting site.

None of the holes needs an owner verdict reversed. I found no conflict with verdicts 164 to 166. ODR-140's meaning of E2170 changes, as the design itself says.

holes.program:
import std.thread
import c "flags.h"          # struct Flags { unsigned ready : 1; unsigned mode : 3; };

fn main():
    f = Flags(ready=0, mode=0)
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): f.mode = 5)          # one writer: point 7 makes this a plain load/mask/or/store of the word
        scope.spawn(owns fn(): println(f.ready))     # a plain load of the same word
holes.what_goes_wrong: BRW-4 and point 7 make `ready` and `mode` two places, so THR-11 accepts the tasks: no place is read by one task and changed by another. Point 7 makes only write/write pairs atomic. Here only one thread writes, so its write is a plain read-modify-write. The other task's read is a plain load of the same C11 memory location (C11 3.14 and 5.1.2.4: adjacent bit-fields are one location). That is a data race, which is undefined behaviour in the C the C backend emits. On the LLVM backend the racing load returns undef, so `f.ready` may print anything. The write/write case has the same flaw: each task's later plain read of its own bit-field races with the other task's CAS. The rule as written allows undefined behaviour, and the old get_/set_ methods did not: they took the whole struct.
holes.fix_hint: In point 7, cover every access, not only writes. Any access to a word that another thread may write at the same time is atomic: a read is a relaxed load (a plain mov on x86-64 and ARM64, so it costs nothing), and a write is a relaxed RMW of that unit. Every other access stays plain.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-8 row makes every C struct that has a bit-field hold a range-typed field (`mode: Flags_mode`). RNG-10b says a range type may not appear in a foreign signature, directly, inside an aggregate or behind a pointer (E5054). So `apply(f)`, and every C function taking or returning such a struct, is refused. RNG-8 also says a value from C becomes a range value only through `checked`/`clamped`, so `current()` cannot return a `Flags`. Real headers do this all the time: VkAccelerationStructureInstanceKHR (`instanceCustomIndex:24`, `mask:8`, and more), Win32's DCB, and device register structs. The design's CHANGED list amends neither rule.
holes.fix_hint: State the exception where it is true (principle 6). Inside an imported C aggregate, a bit-field's generated range type covers every value its bits can hold, so every bit pattern is valid. It crosses as its bits, and RNG-10b and RNG-8 exempt it. Put both amendments in the CHANGED list.

from std.math import Vec3

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("p points at n floats in a row")
    unsafe fn upload_floats(p: *f32, n: usize)

fn upload(xs: Span[f32]):
    unsafe:
        # SAFETY: a Span's elements are in a row, xs.len() of them
        upload_floats(xs.as_ptr(), xs.len() as usize)

struct Particle:
    pos: Vec3
    vel: Vec3

fn main():
    ps = SoA[Particle].with_capacity(1024)
    ps.push(owns Particle(pos=Vec3.ZERO, vel=Vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)))
    upload(ps.pos.x)       # pos not flattened: every element's x, 12 bytes apart
holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 5 lists `ref x as *T` and `ref_to_ptr` as the raw-pointer routes. It misses `as_ptr()`/`as_mut_ptr()`, which SPN-8 makes safe to call. So in `upload`'s copy for a 12-byte stride, either `as_ptr()` returns the base of x and C reads y and z as x values (for a column view of a flattened Vec3, it reads past the x column), or it is refused inside `upload`, at a line in a function that compiles for every other caller. The `# SAFETY` note was true of every Span when it was written, and a line far away makes it false. The same happens to any callee, std's span functions included, that uses a raw pointer, a C call on a span or `@simd(assert)`. The rule's promise ('compiles, or is refused, exactly as it would then'; 'adding @soa(flatten) changes no other line') then fails, and the spec does not say where the refusal lands. A pub function's acceptance of a layout comes to depend on its body, which goes against verdict 108's 'a library's promise does not depend on reading its body', and a body change silently breaks dependents.
holes.fix_hint: (1) Under point 5, list by property every operation that needs elements at one address each, in a row: as_ptr, as_mut_ptr, `ref x as *T`, ref_to_ptr, a C call given a span, and @simd(assert). (2) Record in each function's BCK-8 summary, in the interface file (EFF-4, BRW-10), which view parameters it needs in a row. Refuse at the caller's line, naming the chain, with the copy-of rewrite. (3) Give library code a compile-time question about a view's layout, folded per copy, so std keeps a memcpy path for plain views and an element path for others (checklist 12).

holes.what_goes_wrong: Without flatten, the C result points into `ps`, so `-> ref f32 from ps` is right and the program compiles. With flatten, point 5 gives C a copy in `first_x`'s frame, and the result points into that copy. The copy is written back when 'nothing the call returned from that argument is still used', which is after `first_x` has returned and its frame is gone. If the checker reads the result as pointing into `ps` (LT-1's from(v)), the caller holds a dangling view. If it refuses, the layout has changed what compiles, and the spec states neither.
holes.fix_hint: Say that a result a C call returns from a copied argument points into the caller's frame slot. BCK-4 then checks it as such: E3063 when it is kept past the function, with a message naming the layout and giving `ref ps[0].pos.x` or a copy of your own. The write-back happens at the earlier of the result's last use and the end of the function.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Point 7 and the cost statement say a bit-field write is 'load, mask, or, store' of 'the word', and never say what the word is. Taken as the declared type's width (4 bytes for `unsigned`), writing `cells[i].dirty` reads and writes bytes 1 to 4: element i+1's kind and dirty byte, and element i+2's kind. PAR-2 accepts the loop because the elements are distinct, so chunks running at once lose each other's writes, and the last element's write runs 3 bytes past the list. The same happens with two tasks, one writing `c.kind` and one `c.dirty`, which C11 makes separate memory locations. This is the 2012 Linux btrfs bug, where GCC on IA64 wrote a bit-field with a 64-bit RMW and clobbered an adjacent spinlock.
holes.fix_hint: Define the unit: a bit-field read or write touches only the bytes that hold its bits (C11's memory location), never the declared type's width or a neighbouring member or element. Point 7's atomic form works on that same unit.

@packed
struct Header:
    tag: u8
    seq: u32

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("p points at one Header")
    unsafe fn send_header(p: *Header)

fn send(h: ref Header):
    unsafe:
        # SAFETY: h is a whole Header for the call
        send_header(ref h as *Header)
holes.what_goes_wrong: LAY-3 defines 'a type's plain layout' as 'the one [TYP-11] gives it on its own'. Header's real layout is the packed one its own attribute gives it, not TYP-11's. Read literally, every Header value is 'kept in another layout': `ref h as *Header` is E2170 although a `*Header` (alignment 1) points exactly at it, and every function taking `ref Header` gets a 'copy'. The same goes for `ref u as *Uniforms` of a @gpu_layout(std140) block uploaded to the GPU, and for any @align(N) type. This also contradicts point 5, where size_of gives 'the type's own layout'.
holes.fix_hint: Define the plain layout as the one the type's own declaration gives it: TYP-11's, or the type's own @packed, @align, @gpu_layout or @repr. A layout in LAY-3's sense is one a holder imposes on a part: an SoA, a packed or GPU holder, or a bit-field.

    pos: Vec3
    mass: f32

fn first(ps: ref SoA[Particle]) -> Option[ref Particle] from ps:
