holes.what_goes_wrong: A borrowed callback takes a slot for the length of its call, and the slot comes back with the next generation (FFI-21, FFI-53). On a 32-bit target, 65,536 slots of 65,536 generations allow about 4.29 billion registrations in the program's life; the design states this. After that, every C call given a capturing function stops, although at most one callback was ever live. At 100,000 ray queries a second that is about 12 hours, so a 32-bit game or simulator dies in normal use. The design leaves the question of reuse for later (open risk 2).
holes.fix_hint: Let only kept callbacks (retained, once) use up numbers that are never reused. A borrowed slot is marked running only during its call, so a stale call after the return already fails on the idle mark. Its generation may therefore wrap. A stale number could then reach only a live callback of the same type during a later call, which needs C to break its vouched borrowed contract, and the type compare keeps that memory-safe. State the ceiling that remains for kept callbacks on 32-bit.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CAP-1 says the stop names "the form that hands the failure back, where one exists". CAP-2 promises both forms for "every" standard-library operation that can run out, but then gives a closed list ("These are:") with only alloc and try_alloc for arenas. alloc_array, alloc_zeroed and alloc_uninit also run out of a FixedArena, and FixedArena is "the arena for @noalloc code" (ARN-4). With P14's Panic(Explicit), this @realtime function is refused, and the message has no line to give that compiles (checklist 9). Without Panic(Explicit), a realtime path stops with no way to handle a full arena. The same gap covers Registry.emplace (its component storage), Deque.push_back, collect and building a String. try_reserve covers some of these; nothing covers the arena ones.
holes.fix_hint: Write CAP-2 as the property: every standard-library operation that can run out of room, and whose result is not a Result, has a twin named try_ plus its name. Give the list as examples only, and add try_alloc_array, try_alloc_zeroed and try_alloc_uninit (each -> Result[MutSpan[T], CapacityError]) and try_reserve on a Registry's storage. Add a conformance check that every plain form's stop text names a twin that exists.

holes.what_goes_wrong: A C registration's reporting form is chosen by the result its declaration writes. An overlay entry's result is contract words, never an Ember type (GRM-35), so a registering function imported from a header has no reporting form. The program must write a second hand declaration of the same symbol with link_name (open risk 7), outside the overlay that is meant to describe the header. That is an exemption made only because the syntax is missing (checklist 12, ODR 13). It is also a second convention for one event: the standard library gives the try_ twin by name (CAP-2), and C gives it by a declared result type.
holes.fix_hint: Use one convention. The compiler already makes the wrapper for every registering function, so it gives each one both names: `on_click`, which stops, and `try_on_click`, which returns Result[token, CapacityError[F]]. That follows CAP-2's naming rule exactly, so the name is not hidden. A hand declaration and an overlay then need nothing new, and no symbol is declared twice. If the owner prefers the declared result, add an overlay spelling for it rather than exempting overlays.

holes.what_goes_wrong: When the allocator has run out of memory, try_reserve returns Err(CapacityError.Full). `?` into the default error type then allocates the AnyError's block (ERR-11, and COST-3's row for it), which also fails. So the program stops with "out of memory" at the `?` line instead of returning the Err it asked for. With try_push, the block must also hold T's bytes. No function with the default Result can pass an out-of-memory failure up, which is the case the twins exist for. CAP-1 lists AnyError as an error that "says the room ran out" without accounting for this.
holes.fix_hint: Make converting a CapacityError into AnyError need no memory. The AnyError holds the payload-free CapacityError, a zero-sized error that needs no block, and the value is ended at the `?` line (the same fix as hole 2). State in ERR-11 that this conversion allocates nothing.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The design classifies a bounded send as not running out, "because its receiver makes room". Here the receiver is on the sending thread and has been given to no other thread or task, so nothing makes room. The program hangs at line 6 with no message, whereas a full FixedArray in the same place stops and names its 10. PHIL-11 lists deadlock as possible. But verdict 43 refused the comparable case of a lock taken twice because it can be decided, and this case can be decided cheaply on the full-queue path.
holes.fix_hint: A blocking send that finds the queue full, while the channel's receiver is held by the sending thread and lent to no live scoped task, stops at the line: "the queue of `tx` is full (10) and its receiver `rx` is on this thread, so this send would wait for ever; receive first, or use `tx.try_send(owns i)`". The receiver's thread is stored at the hand-over places, which are known when compiling (RC-4 point 4), and the test runs only on the full path.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CAP-4 says "a limit the compiler can count against is refused when compiling". Whether the second loop compiles then depends on how far a compiler counts, and EFF-15 and PHIL-13 forbid that: every implementation must reach the same verdict. CAP-4 also calls the first loop's proof a range fact (RNG-4), which EFF-15 applies to verdicts, and then says "neither removal changes a verdict". RNG-4 tracks numeric expressions, not a container's length. So whether @nopanic(explicit) accepts the first loop is undecided.
holes.fix_hint: Make the compile-time refusals a closed list: the four CAP-4 names (a literal past N, the type index, nesting depth, the compile-time budget). For the room check, either add a stated length fact to EFF-15's list of proofs (a fixed container made or cleared empty, then pushes in a counted loop), so every compiler accepts the first loop under @nopanic(explicit). Or say it is an implementation's own removal that never changes a verdict, and drop the reference to RNG-4.

At 1,000,000 a second that is about 15 slots a second, held for ever: hundreds of MB a year at 16 to 32 bytes a slot, and no limit names this growth. The stated "2^48 slots" cannot exist in a table that never moves: 2^48 slots of 16 bytes is 4 PiB, past a 47-bit user address space. So the real limit is the memory the table can reserve. And CAP-4's sentence "a check whose limit is more than the target's memory can hold is removed", read as written, would drop the 64-bit full-table test.

The number is then still never a user-space address, as FFI-53 wants, and a slot retires only once per 2^31 uses. State the 64-bit table's limit as the memory it can get (its growth is ALC-4's stop, or the Result form's Err). Keep CAP-4's removal off tables (hole 1).

Many C libraries read NULL as "no user data" and never call back, and FFI-53 forbids an all-zero generation only on 64-bit. holes.fix_hint: Require every CAP-1 stop to build its text without allocating (a fixed per-thread buffer, with the names stored as constants), so that "out of memory" itself is always printed.

safety.notes:
The core answer to J8-18 keeps every guarantee. The test for a free slot runs before the function is moved into a block and before C is called. A full table never wraps or reuses a number, the bare declaration stops at its line, and the Result declaration returns the function. A stale handle or C number stays caught. The try_ twins that give the value back (Pool, FixedArray, ArenaMap, FixedArena, spawn) keep one owner on every path.

The holes are in the generalisation:
(1) CAP-4 removes verdict 59's count compare on 32-bit. That is sound only while every +1 is a pointer kept in memory, so an unsafe leak (MaybeUninit.write over owners) turns into a use after free. It also narrows verdict 59, which the design lists as kept.
(2) Errors now carry values, but nothing states CapacityError[T]'s thread markers or what `?` into AnyError does with the value. That is a race under today's THR-15 channel-end text, or a refusal of the twin's natural `?` under P01's J6-16 A. Separately, CapacityError[T] is an Error only when T is Debug.
(3) Lifetime ceilings the rule leaves in: an ECS Registry (Split20 on every target) stops after 2^32 creations, about 5 days at 10,000 a second. A 32-bit program's borrowed callbacks use up the table after about 4.29 billion C calls. The 64-bit table's memory grows forever with borrowed callbacks.
(4) CAP-2's closed list misses alloc_zeroed, alloc_array and alloc_uninit, the main use of the @noalloc arena. An overlay has no reporting form, an exemption because the syntax is missing. `?` into AnyError cannot pass an out-of-memory failure up.
(5) A bounded send whose receiver is on the same thread hangs, against the design's claim that "its receiver makes room".
The low holes are smaller undecided cases: CAP-4's counting against EFF-15, GpuError's cases, the once and borrowed result shapes, a discarded try_ result being only a warning, ERR-13's first sentence, reserved encodings, and the out-of-memory stop text.

Severity: no hole is high, because P01's pending lead fix J7-07 closes hole 2's race. The medium ones make broken true.

matrix.edge_cases: STD-14 (not changed) says a mutation has no twin and a world or input failure returns Result. ERR-13's first sentence (kept) says the same. P14's EFF-28 says an effect follows from the property, never from a list, yet the design gives Panic(Explicit) to CAP-1 stops by membership. EFF-16 (not changed) allows bounds and count checks under @nopanic(explicit). P08's FFI-11b and status shapes are not covered. TYP-27 writes void's value `()`.
matrix.must_compile: @nopanic(explicit) code whose push is proved to have room, as code whose index is proved in bounds compiles

matrix.guarantee: Production-ready: no known ceiling left in (checklist 7), and fault tolerant
matrix.how_kept: Running out is never corruption: no count wraps, no slot is reused, the stop is named, and the twin gives the value back.
matrix.edge_cases: Once every slot of a Registry or of a 32-bit callback table is retired, try_ returns Err forever: the twin gives no recovery. A plain push of an input-fed fixed container now stops on load with no compile-time prompt, where today's Result forced a decision.
matrix.must_compile: A server that runs for weeks creating 10,000 entities a second; a 32-bit program calling a C function with a borrowed callback 100,000 times a second

holes.program:
from std.collections import RingBuffer

struct Packet:
    id: u32
    size: u16

fn on_packet(ref mut inbox: RingBuffer[Packet, 256], owns p: Packet):
    inbox.push(owns p)          # fed from the network
holes.what_goes_wrong: STD-14 is not in the design's change list. It says a failure of the world or of input returns Result, and that 'the non-panicking twin ERR-13 asks for is an accessor's ... a mutation's caller's bug ... panics with none'. ERR-13's first sentence, which the design keeps, also says an operation whose failure depends on input returns Result. A RingBuffer fed from the network fills because of input. So by those rules push keeps today's Result (STD-7), and W2190 makes the program decide what full means. By CAP-2, push stops and gets a twin that STD-14 says a mutation does not have. The specification would say both. Under CAP-2 the program above compiles with no warning and stops the server the first time 256 packets wait; today it cannot be compiled without deciding.
holes.fix_hint: Change STD-14 and ERR-13's first sentence in the same ruling, and state the one property that decides: running out of a stated limit is its own class, neither a caller's bug nor an input failure, and it gets the stop plus the try_ twin. STD-14 then lists mutations' twins too. Put the cost to the owner plainly: the short plain form is now the one that stops under load, for every fixed container whose N meets outside data.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CAP-1 and CAP-2 say every standard-library operation that can run out comes in two forms, then CAP-2 gives a closed list ('These are:'). Array.push is on it. Array.insert and extend, Set.add, Map.insert and entry, Deque's pushes, SmallArray.push, String's push and +, Registry.emplace, Arena's alloc_uninit and alloc_slice, and jobs.submit (which the design itself makes allocate) are not. By the 'every' sentence the library is incomplete; by the list it is complete. A list deciding which operations get the twin is what P14's principle forbids. The design's real answer (try_reserve(n) first, so the next n additions need no memory) covers only growth that a reserve can cover with a count known in advance. It does not cover `copy of xs`, an f-string, `shares Player()` or an extend through a filter.
holes.fix_hint: State the property instead of a list. Every operation that adds to a value's stated limit (CAP-1's list) gets the stop and the twin. Refused memory comes back only through try_reserve(n), plus try_push for one element, which covers the next n additions of every growing operation of that container. Everything else that allocates stops (ALC-4). Then 'every' is true.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
`xs[i]` and `out.push` both stop at the line when a fixed bound is not met, and both have a twin (get, try_push). Yet `xs[i]` is RuntimeCheck(Bounds), which EFF-16 allows under @nopanic(explicit), while under the design push is Panic(Explicit), so the function is E4040.

Here the room is even proved: a range fact, and CAP-4 removes the emitted test. But EFF-15's proofs remove RuntimeCheck kinds from verdicts, not a library's Panic(Explicit). So the proved program stays refused and must write `match out.try_push(owns xs[i])` with a dead Err arm.

The compiler-made wrapper's full-table stop, and the exhaustion of a FixedArena or of a `using` arena, are neither 'panics the programmer writes' nor 'a heap allocation that fails' (EFF-16; P14's Panic(Explicit) row). Giving them Panic(Explicit) because they are CAP-1 stops is the assignment by membership that P14's EFF-28 forbids. Meanwhile a count's compare stays RuntimeCheck(Arithmetic), although CAP-1 says running out works the same everywhere. EFF-16 is not in the change list.
holes.fix_hint: Give every CAP-1 room test one effect by its property, as a bounds check has: a RuntimeCheck kind (Bounds for a fixed buffer's position, or one Room kind shared with the counts). EFF-15's proofs then remove it from verdicts, and @realtime code that must never stop asks for RuntimeCheck-free code, as it already does. If the owner wants @nopanic(explicit) to point at try_ forms, make the property 'a stop the twin would have avoided' and apply it to xs[i] and get(i) too, settled with P14.

holes.what_goes_wrong:
FFI-21's change gives the reporting form for one shape only: a bare token, `Result[Retained[ForeignCallback], CapacityError[F]]`, with F 'the callback parameter's function type'. These are left undecided:
1. A registration with a C result of its own, which FFI-11b and P08 make a tuple `(i32, Retained[...])`.
2. A `once` callback with no cancel function, which returns nothing (P08 makes a result there E5002).
3. A status registration, `Result[Retained[...], VkError]`. There CapacityError is E5002 and VkError has no case for a full table, so a program that already handles every failure of the call still stops.
4. Two callback parameters: which F, and both slots must be free before C runs.
5. A call that also hands over another value (a retained `owns body`). CAP-1 says that value comes back in the error, but CapacityError[F] holds only the function.

The FFI-53 change also says the Err holds the function for borrowed callbacks too, while the design's other cases say a borrowed one's error holds nothing.
holes.fix_hint: Write one rule over the result R that the declaration would otherwise have (a token, a tuple, nothing, or a status Result). Its reporting form is `Result[R, CapacityError[H]]`, where H is what the call was handed: every `owns` argument, as a tuple when there are several, and void for a borrowed callback. The room test covers every slot the call needs, before C runs. Settle with P08 how a status error carries it (it gains the case, or the result is nested).

holes.what_goes_wrong: On a 32-bit target this stops with the advice 'declare on_click to return Result[...]', which cannot be followed. An overlay entry's result is contract words, not a type (GRM-35's overlay_fn), so an imported registration has no reporting form at all. To get one, the program must hand-declare the same C symbol again under a second name (`try_on_click`, link_name="on_click"). That repeats the whole contract, saying it twice (checklist 5), relies on one symbol having two names (left to P07 and P28), and writes CapacityError[fn()], repeating the parameter's type. The standard library gets both forms by rule (CAP-2). C registrations, the one operation whose wrapper the compiler itself builds, are the one family where the programmer must build the twin by hand. The stop's line does not compile (checklist 9).
holes.fix_hint: The compiler already makes each registering wrapper, so it makes both forms by CAP-2's convention: `on_click` (stops) and `try_on_click` (returns Result[R, CapacityError[H]]), for imported and hand-declared functions alike, with nothing written; a clash with a real C name is reported. If the owner reads verdict 132 as forbidding a name nobody wrote, add an overlay result word instead. Either way, the stop's advice names the form that exists.

holes.program:
import std.jobs
from std.math import Vec3

@noalloc
fn step(ref mut pos: MutSpan[Vec3], vel: Span[Vec3], ref mut life: MutSpan[f32], dt: f32):
    with s = jobs.scope():
        s.submit(owns fn(): integrate(ref mut pos, vel, dt))
        s.submit(owns fn(): age(ref mut life, dt))
holes.what_goes_wrong: Today this compiles. Each job uses the caller's real variables, so its state fits the state word (CLO-10) and its slot (JOB-1); nothing allocates. The design's JOB-1 change makes every submit carry Alloc, because a job submitted to full queues is kept in memory of its own. So this @noalloc frame function, and every @realtime function that submits a job, is refused, although a scope of two submits can be counted when compiling. That contradicts CAP-3's own principle that a buffer kept for speed never changes what a program may do. The design's risk 4 names the change but not the cost to games.
holes.fix_hint: Apply CAP-3's other principle: a queue whose values each carry their own place in it has no limit. A scoped job's node (code, state, a link) lives in the scope's frame, which the scope's join outlives, and is linked into the queue, so s.submit needs no slot and no Alloc wherever the compiler can count the scope's submits (straight-line, or a counted range). Only unscoped jobs.submit, and a submit in a loop it cannot count, carry Alloc.

holes.program:
from std.ecs import Registry

struct Bullet:
    ttl: f32

fn fire(ref mut reg: Registry, n: int):     # a server: about 10,000 a second, each destroyed after 0.5 s
    for i in 0..n:
        e = reg.create()
        reg.emplace(e, Bullet(ttl=0.5))
holes.what_goes_wrong: Entity is Split20 (ECS-1): 1,048,576 slots of 4,096 generations, about 4.29 billion creations in a registry's life. After that every slot is retired (HND-3) and create() stops. At 10,000 creations a second that is about 5 days of uptime, with only about 5,000 entities ever live at once. The rule writes this stop into ECS-3 as final. try_create does not make the program fault tolerant either: once every slot is retired it returns Err on every later call, and the only recovery is a new Registry, which invalidates every entity. Verdict 115 ('not a good limit to have') and checklist 7 (no known ceiling) apply. The design defers it as open risk 2, yet its own text settles the 1,048,576 limit.
holes.fix_hint: Decide it with this rule, as the owner's question, not after it. Either a Registry's Entity is a 64-bit handle by default (32/32, as general Pool handles already are, HND-2), with Split20 only where EnTT-compatible ids are asked for, or the owner accepts the ceiling, written with its number in ECS-3.

holes.what_goes_wrong: Under FFI-21 a borrowed callback's block takes a slot for the call, and the slot is freed when the call returns. Each reuse of a slot spends one generation (FFI-53). On a 32-bit target the table holds 65,536 slots of 65,535 generations: about 4.29 billion registrations in the program's life, borrowed calls included. At 100,000 calls a second the program above stops after about 12 hours, and every later call stops too, because no slot is ever free again; the reporting form gives no recovery. The rule names the stop but leaves the ceiling (deferred as open risk 2), which checklist 7 forbids. A stale borrowed number can exist only if C kept it past the call, which breaks its vouched `callback(borrowed)` fact, and PHIL-11 already puts that outside the guarantee.
holes.fix_hint: Decide it with this rule. A slot used only for borrowed callbacks reuses its numbers once its generation wraps: the trampoline's type compare still holds, and a stale number needs C to break its contract. Retained and once slots keep retiring. Or the owner accepts the ceiling, stated with its number in FFI-53.

holes.what_goes_wrong: CAP-2 and THR-10 give thread.spawn its stop and try_spawn, but scope.spawn (THR-11) starts a thread too, and the system can refuse it just the same. It is not named, so what it does is still unstated, and so is a job worker the runtime fails to start before main.
holes.fix_hint: Name every operation that starts a thread: scope.spawn stops and has try_spawn, returning CapacityError[fn() -> R]; a refused worker at start-up stops before main with the same text.

pub fn play(ref mut q: FixedArray[Voice, 32], owns v: Voice):

audio.play(ref mut queue, owns Voice(sample=3, gain=1.0))     # line 20

In release (PRF-3: no debug info, no backtrace), the only way is a hidden caller-location argument on every library function that may stop. That is nearly all of them, since refused memory stops anywhere: a per-call cost and an ABI parameter that C does not pay. match registry.try_create():
    Ok(e):
        spawn_at(e)
    Err(CapacityError.Full):      # T = void, payload left out
        log_full()
holes.what_goes_wrong: With T = void the design writes `CapacityError.Full` with no payload, but TYP-27 spells void's value `()` (`Ok(())`). So a variant whose payload is void, written without it, is a new spelling special to void, and the grammar does not have it. Today's `Err(CapacityError.Full)` patterns (HND-3, ARN-5) also stop matching once the payload exists.
holes.fix_hint: Use the language's spelling: `CapacityError.Full(())`, and `CapacityError.Full(_)` in patterns, with `ember fmt --migrate` rewriting the old patterns.

holes.what_goes_wrong: One variant, Full, displayed as 'no room: it is full', stands for three things: a full fixed list, memory the system refused, and HEAP-8's capacity overflow. HEAP-8 says the last one panics as a bug, so it is unstated whether try_reserve(2^62) returns Err or stops, and the program cannot tell a size bug from a machine out of memory (Rust's TryReserveError separates them). The message is wrong for refused memory. The try_ forms of growing containers (Pool.try_insert, Registry.try_create, and the 64-bit callback Result form, whose block and table are allocated) do not say whether refused memory comes back as Err, although CAP-1 implies it does.
holes.fix_hint: Say in CAP-1 that every try_ form also returns refused memory as Err. Either give CapacityError a second case for refused memory (naming the bytes) with a display that fits it, or decide that capacity overflow inside a try_ form is Err as well.

fn keep_long(ref mut out: Array[String], lines: Array[String]):
    out.extend(lines.iter().filter(owns fn(l) => l.len() > 80).copy_each())
holes.what_goes_wrong: CAP-1 promises that an operation that runs out 'does none of its work: it stores nothing, takes nothing it was handed'. For a bulk addition from an iterator of unknown length that cannot hold. If memory is refused after some lines were stored and taken from the iterator, keeping the promise would mean collecting the iterator first into memory of its own (the very memory that ran out, a cost C does not pay). For the plain form the difference cannot be seen, because the program stops, but CAP-2's 'every operation has a twin' needs a try_extend whose meaning cannot be 'none of its work'. The same goes for a FixedString filled by a formatter and an ArenaArray filled from an iterator.
holes.fix_hint: Limit 'does none of its work' to operations whose room is known before they start (one value, a span or a collection of known length). A bulk addition from an iterator stores what fits, then stops, or its twin returns how many it stored and gives back the rest of the iterator.

struct Particle:

    vel: Vec3
    color: Vec4

fn emit(ref mut ps: FixedArray[Particle, 4096], owns p: Particle):

engineering.notes:
The rule's core is sound and fast: one compare where correct C has one, nothing added per trampoline call, no corruption on any path, verdicts 59 and 96 kept. It follows C++26 inplace_vector's and Rust arrayvec's push/try_push pair, and the ordinary program gets shorter. It is not finished. No hole is high; eight are medium.

1. **Contradictions left in the spec.** STD-14 and ERR-13's first sentence are not changed and still say input failures return Result and mutations have no twin. CAP-2 says 'every' operation has a twin, then gives a closed list. EFF-16 and P14's EFF-28 conflict with assigning Panic(Explicit) to every CAP-1 stop by membership. Because of that last point, a push that is proved to have room is still refused in @nopanic(explicit) code, while xs[i] is allowed there.
2. **The C side covers one result shape.** The reporting form exists only for a bare token. Tuple results, status results, once callbacks with no token, several callbacks and other handed-over values are undecided. Imported (overlay) registrations have no reporting form at all, and the stop's own advice cannot be followed for them.
3. **The JOB-1 change refuses correct @noalloc and @realtime code.** That code submits small jobs and is Alloc-free today.
4. **Two lifetime ceilings become final stops.** A correct long-running program reaches both: a Split20 Registry at about 4.29 billion creations (about 5 days at 10,000 a second, on 64-bit), and a 32-bit callback table at about 4.29 billion registrations, borrowed calls included (about 12 hours at 100,000 a second). Once every slot is retired the try_ forms return Err forever, so they give no recovery. The draft defers both (risk 2), but they should be decided with this rule (checklist 7, verdict 115).

Low items:
- scope.spawn is missing from the thread-start twins.
- 'The line of the call into a library' costs a hidden argument in release builds.
- `CapacityError.Full` is written bare for void, against TYP-27's `()`.
- One Full variant stands for refused memory and for HEAP-8's capacity overflow.
- 'Does none of its work' cannot hold for an iterator-fed extend.
- The register-return claim is wrong for a large T.

Also noted, no hole raised: GpuError has no stated case for a full GPU handle table, which CAP-2 assumes. Dropping the count compare on 32-bit targets is sound: with mem.forget gone, every owner and link takes memory, so at most 2^30 fit, below both limits. It is a code removal allowed by EFF-15, and no verdict changes.

design.rule:
Every limit in Ember has a stated number, and running out of one works the same way everywhere. Limits include a count's maximum, a Pool's or Registry's slots and generations, the callback table's slots, a fixed list's N, an arena's size, a bounded channel's capacity, and the memory, threads and stack the system gives.

When an operation needs room that is not there, it does none of its work. It stores nothing, does not take what it was handed, calls no C function, and wraps or reuses nothing a stale copy could still name. Then one of two things happens:
- **The twin hands the failure back.** The twin is named try_ plus the operation's own name, and returns Err holding what it was handed. The standard library has a twin for every operation that adds to a limit. The compiler makes one for every C function that hands C a callback (`on_click` and `try_on_click`), with nothing written. Memory the system refuses comes back through try_reserve(n), which every growing container has.
- **The plain form stops the program** at the program's own line. The message names what ran out, its number, and the twin. The test is a run-time check of the kind its property is, like a bounds check: either a position inside a buffer, or a number that must fit.

What an error gives back belongs to the line that called. A `?` into another error type ends the value at that line. So the error passed on holds nothing, needs no memory, and may go to any thread.

Three more things are settled with the rule:
- **Tables of numbers.** A table whose numbers Ember code can copy (a Pool, a Registry) never gives a number twice. A Registry's entities become the 64-bit handle, so no registry runs out over its life. The callback table's numbers are held only by C. So once every number has been given out, its retired slots come back into use. It is full only when every slot is live.
- **Buffers.** A buffer kept for speed (an inline array, a function's state word, the job queues) is not a limit. A job is a node of its own. That node sits in the scope's frame when the compiler can count the scope's submits.
- **Channel waits.** A channel wait that only the waiting thread could end stops at the line instead of hanging.

A limit the compiler can count is refused when compiling. A count's compare stays on every target (verdict 59).
design.spec_text:
Adds [CAP-1] to [CAP-6], a new section XIII.4 "Running out of room" after [ERR-13].

Changes:
- [ERR-2], [ERR-11], [ERR-13], [STD-14], [STD-7];
- [HND-3], [ECS-1], [ECS-3];
- [ARN-4], [ARN-5], [ARN-5c], [ARN-5d], [ALC-4];
- [THR-10], [THR-15], [JOB-1], [PAR-4];
- [FFI-21], [FFI-53];
- [EFF-16], [COST-3], [COST-6], [PHIL-11].

Also changes [TST-31] (the lead's) and, with P14, the X.1 row for a heap allocation that fails. Nothing is removed from verdict 59: a count's compare stays on every target.

[CAP-1] (new in 0.9.16) **A limit, and running out of it.**
A limit is the most of something a value or the program can hold, at once or over its life. Ember states each limit, with its number for each target, where the thing is defined:
- an owner count's and a weak count's maximum ([RT-7], [RC-4]);
- a Pool's or a Registry's slots and each slot's generations ([HND-2], [ECS-1], [CAP-6]);
- the callback table's slots ([FFI-53], [CAP-6]);
- the N of a FixedArray[T, N], FixedString[N] or RingBuffer[T, N] ([STD-7]), and the capacity an ArenaArray, ArenaMap or ArenaSoA is made with ([ARN-5], [SOA-4]);
- a FixedArena's bytes ([ARN-4]);
- a bounded channel's capacity ([THR-15], [CAP-5]);
- the largest Layout ([HEAP-8]).

The system keeps three more limits: the memory its allocator gives ([ALC-4]), the threads it will start ([THR-10]), and a thread's stack ([RT-12]).

An operation that needs room a limit does not have does none of its work. It stores nothing, takes nothing it was handed, calls no C function, wraps no count, and gives out no number a stale copy could still name ([CAP-6]). Then:

1. **A twin hands the failure back.** This covers a twin of [CAP-2] and an operation whose result is already a Result. A twin returns Err(CapacityError.Full(value=v)), holding what it was handed, or CapacityError.Full when it was handed nothing. An operation whose result is already a Result returns its own error, which says the room ran out.

2. **Every other operation stops the program**, in every profile, at the program's own line that asked for the room. For a library's operation, that is the line that calls it. The text names, in the program's own names:
   - what ran out, and its number;
   - for a table of generations, how many of its slots are live and how many retired;
   - the twin, where one exists ([COST-6]).

   The words that make an owner or a link (`shares`, `shares mut`, `thread_shared`, `weakref`), and a value the language makes (`Player()`, `owns Mesh(...)`), give that value, not a Result. So running out there always stops ([RC-1], verdict 59), as running out of stack does.

**The effect of a room test.** A room test is a RuntimeCheck of the kind its property is ([EFF-9]):
- **Bounds** where a position must be inside a fixed buffer: a fixed container's next element, or an arena's next bytes.
- **Arithmetic** where a number must fit before it grows: an owner or weak count, a Pool's or a Registry's slot number and generation, or the callback table's count of live callbacks.

Memory or a thread the system refuses is the X.1 row for a heap allocation that fails. A twin's own compare is the program's code and carries no effect, as `get(i)`'s compare carries none.

`std.collections` declares `enum CapacityError[T = void]`, with one variant, `Full(value: T)`.
- Its Display and Debug name the room, never the value ("no room: it is full"). So it is an Error for every T, whatever T implements.
- Its thread markers are T's ([THR-8]).
- With T = void it is written CapacityError.Full and has no size.

A program's own operation that runs out of room SHOULD use it, as [ERR-13]'s convention says.

**What an error gives back is for the line that called.** CapacityError[T], SendError[T = void] and TrySendError[T = void] give back a value their operation did not take.
- A `?` into a function whose error type is that same type hands the whole error over, value included ([ERR-7]).
- Converting such an error into any other error type (with `?`, `.context` or `F.from`) ends the value at that line, on that line's thread, and converts the same error with nothing in it.

So the error passed on needs nothing of T: no Send, no ThreadShared, no Debug, and no memory ([ERR-11]). A program that wants the value back matches before it passes the failure on.

[CAP-2] (new in 0.9.16) **Both forms.**
Every standard-library operation that adds to a limit of [CAP-1], and whose result is not already a Result, has a twin named try_ plus its own name.
- The twin does what the plain form does. It hands back every way the operation can run out: its limit, and, where the operation allocates, memory the system refuses.
- The plain form is the twin followed by the stop.

Examples, which are not a list:
- Pool.insert and try_insert;
- Registry.create and try_create;
- every adding operation of a fixed container (push, insert, extend; ArenaMap.insert) and its try_ form;
- every alloc* of an arena (alloc, alloc_array, alloc_zeroed, alloc_uninit) and its try_ form;
- thread.spawn and try_spawn.

**Memory.** Memory the system refuses is no value's stated limit. Every growing container (Array, Map, Set, Deque, SmallArray, String, a Registry's Storage[T], a growing Arena) hands it back through try_reserve(n). Once that succeeds, the next n additions of any of the container's growing operations take no memory. A growing container that has push also has try_push(owns v), which is try_reserve(1) followed by push. Every other allocation the system refuses stops ([ALC-4]).

**C registrations.** A C function whose call takes a slot of the callback table can run out of it. These are functions with a `callback(...)` parameter that has user data ([FFI-21]). The compiler already makes such a function's wrapper, so it makes both forms, imported or hand-declared, with nothing written:
- `name`, which stops;
- `try_name`, whose result is Result[R, CapacityError[H]].

R is what `name` returns: a token, a tuple of [FFI-11b], nothing, or a status Result, which is then nested. H is what the call was handed with `owns`: one value, a tuple when there are several, or void when every callback is borrowed. Before C is called, the call finds a slot for every callback it passes.

If a header or declaration already has a function named `try_name`, the program is refused when compiling, and the message names both. `rename` in the overlay gives one of them another name.

**What does not run out.** An operation whose meaning is to drop or to wait does not run out:
- push_or_drop drops ([STD-7]);
- a bounded channel's send and receive wait ([CAP-5]).

A conformance check of the standard library fails when a plain form's stop names a twin that does not exist.

[CAP-3] (new in 0.9.16) **A buffer is not a limit.**
A fixed buffer an implementation keeps for speed, and which no value states, never makes an operation stop, report, or carry an effect it would not carry without the buffer. Examples are a SmallArray's inline elements, a function value's state word ([CLO-10]), and the job queues ([JOB-1], [PAR-4]).

When such a buffer is full, the work goes on with the same result, the same effects and the same chance of finishing:
- a SmallArray moves to memory of its own, with the Alloc its push already carries;
- a job is a node of its own linked into a queue, so no queue fills ([JOB-1]).

A queue whose values each carry their own place in it has no limit. Examples are a job's node and a making thread's queue ([RC-4]).

[CAP-4] (new in 0.9.16) **Counted when compiling.**
A limit the compiler can count against is refused when compiling, and the error names the limit:
- a literal with more values than a fixed container's N;
- more types than the 32-bit type index holds ([OBJ-1]);
- nesting deeper than E0112 allows;
- a compile-time evaluation past its budget ([CT-3]).

A room test is a RuntimeCheck. So an implementation may leave out of its code a test it proves is always met, and the proofs of [EFF-15] alone decide the verdict, as they do for a bounds check.

A count's compare is emitted on every target. A count can grow with no pointer kept for it, for example a MaybeUninit written over in unsafe code ([ARN-8]). So no memory size bounds a count.

[CAP-5] (new in 0.9.16) **Waiting for room, or for a value.**
- A bounded channel's send waits while its queue is full, because its receiver makes room.
- Its receive waits while the queue is empty, because its senders send.

A wait that only the waiting thread could end never ends, and is running out. To find it, the channel keeps two marks, set when it is made:
- its receiver has stayed on the thread that made it;
- every one of its senders has stayed on that thread.

A mark is cleared for good at the first line that gives that end, or a value holding it, to another thread, a task, a job or C, or that puts it in a list, a dyn value, a shared value or a static. The compiler knows each such line from the type of what the line places.

On the making thread:
- A send that finds the queue full while the receiver's mark is set stops at the line: "`tx.send(owns i)` (line 6): the queue of `tx` is full (10), and its receiver, made with it on line 4, is on this thread, so this send would wait for ever; receive first, or use `tx.try_send(owns i)`".
- A receive that finds the queue empty while the senders' mark is set stops too: "the loop on line 7 waits for `rx`, and every sender of it is on this thread, so it would wait for ever; end the senders first: `mem.drop(owns tx)` before line 7".

Other waits keep their existing rules. A wait among several threads stays a deadlock under [PHIL-11]. A lock taken twice stays refused when compiling (verdict 43).

[CAP-6] (new in 0.9.16) **Tables of generations, over their life.**

**Pool and Registry.** A Pool's or a Registry's handle is Copy, so Ember code may hold a stale copy of it. A slot whose generation is used up therefore retires for good, so a stale handle never names a later value ([HND-1], [HND-3]). The table's life is then the count of its numbers:
- 2^64 for the 64-bit handle, a Registry's included ([ECS-1]), which no program uses up;
- about 4.29 billion for Split20, as stated where a program chooses Split20.

Insert and create stop only when every slot is live or retired.

**The callback table.** The callback table's numbers are held only by C. A Retained token is one owner on Ember's side, never a copy ([FFI-23]). So a stale number can come only from C breaking its contract ([PHIL-11]).
- A used-up slot retires while numbers remain that have never been given out.
- Once the table has given out every number it has (2^64 on a 64-bit target, 2^32 on a 32-bit one), its retired slots come back into use before any registration is refused.
- The trampoline's type compare still stops a stale number that names a function of another type.

So the callback table is full only when every slot is live: 65,536 callbacks on a 32-bit target.

answers.answer:
A full callback table is running out of a limit ([CAP-1]). On a 32-bit target the table holds 65,536 slots. A slot whose generation is used up retires, and retired slots come back into use only once the table has given out every number it has ([CAP-6]). So the table is full only when 65,536 callbacks are live at once.

When it is full, the registering call finds no free slot before C is called and does none of its work: the function is not moved into a block, C is not called, and no number is reused.
- `on_click(...)`, as declared, stops at its own line. The message names the table, its 65,536 slots and the twin.
- The compiler makes `try_on_click` beside it, with nothing written ([CAP-2]). It returns `Result[Retained[ForeignCallback], CapacityError[fn()]]`, and on a full table the function that did not fit comes back in the `Err`.

On a 64-bit target the table holds 2^48 slots, and memory runs out first. The twin hands that back too.
answers.code:
from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Hud:
    clicks: i32 = 0

unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `on_click` was given")
    unsafe fn off_click(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(off_click))
    safe fn on_click(owns cb: fn(), ud: *mut void) -> Retained[ForeignCallback]

fn main():
    hud = shares mut Hud()
    tokens: Array[Retained[ForeignCallback]] = []
    for i in 0..70000:
        tokens.push(owns on_click(owns fn() shares mut hud: hud.clicks += 1))    # line 16
    println(tokens.len())

# The program that handles a full table calls the twin the compiler made; the declarations are the same:
fn main():
    hud = shares mut Hud()
    tokens: Array[Retained[ForeignCallback]] = []
    for i in 0..70000:
        match try_on_click(owns fn() shares mut hud: hud.clicks += 1):
            Ok(token):
                tokens.push(owns token)
            Err(_):
                break
    println(tokens.len())
answers.outcome:
On a 32-bit target:
- The first program stops on the 65,537th registration, before C is called: "`on_click(...)` (line 16): no callback slot is free: C keeps 65,536 callbacks, all a 32-bit target's table holds; to handle a full table, call `try_on_click(...)`".
- The second prints 65536. The function that did not fit comes back in the error and ends with it at the end of the `Err(_)` arm, which ends its owner of `hud`.

On a 64-bit target both print 70000. A program that registers and ends callbacks for ever, kept or borrowed, never meets the table's end on either target.

other_cases.settled: insert stops at the program's line: "`pool.insert(owns t)` (line 14): this `Pool[Particle, Split20]` has no free slot: 1,048,000 of its 1,048,576 slots are live and 576 retired; use `pool.try_insert(owns t)` to handle a full pool, or `Pool[Particle]`, whose handles never run out". try_insert returns `Err(CapacityError.Full(value=t))` and gives the particle back. Handles are Copy, so retired slots stay retired ([CAP-6]): a stale handle never names a later value. The default 64-bit handle gives 2^64 numbers. Split20, which a program chooses, gives about 4.29 billion, and that number is stated.

other_cases.case: Owner and weak counts (RC-1, RC-4, RT-7)
other_cases.settled: Exactly as verdict 59 says, on every target. There is one compare before each +1, and at the limit the program stops in every profile, with the same texts (4,294,967,295, and 2,147,483,647 for thread_shared). No removal by memory size: a MaybeUninit written over in unsafe code, or an unsafe ring buffer that forgets to end what it overwrites, can raise a count with no pointer kept for it. `shares`, `weakref` and `thread_shared` give the owner or link itself, so there is no reporting form, as with Rust's Rc and Arc.

other_cases.case: A Registry's entities (ECS-1, ECS-3)
other_cases.settled: Entity becomes the 64-bit handle (a 32-bit index and a 32-bit generation). That is EnTT's own 64-bit entity and the width of every other Pool handle. A registry that creates 10,000 entities a second then never runs out (2^64 creations), and a stale entity is still always caught. Registry[Split20] keeps EnTT's default 32-bit entt::entity for a program that exchanges ids with engines using it. Its life is stated: about 4.29 billion creations, about 5 days at 10,000 a second. try_create() hands a full registry back. Options F and G give the owner the other two ways.

other_cases.case: Fixed containers: FixedArray, FixedString, RingBuffer (STD-7); ArenaArray, ArenaMap, ArenaSoA (ARN-5, SOA-4)
other_cases.settled: push, insert and extend stop at the line when the container is full. Their twins try_push, try_insert and try_extend hand the failure back with the value. That is the Pool's pair, and ERR-13's `xs[i]` and `get(i)` pair. Ordinary code drops its `.unwrap()`. A program fed from outside data (a server's RingBuffer) uses try_push where the data can fill it; option E keeps today's Result instead. push_or_drop keeps its meaning.

other_cases.case: Arenas (ARN-3, ARN-4)
other_cases.settled: Every alloc* of an arena has a twin: try_alloc, try_alloc_array, try_alloc_zeroed and try_alloc_uninit. A FixedArena's full test is RuntimeCheck(Bounds). So a @realtime or @nopanic(explicit) function that calls alloc_zeroed compiles, as one that indexes does, and a function that must never stop calls the twin. On a growing Arena the twins hand back refused memory too. try_alloc gives back the value, where today's Option ends it.

other_cases.case: Memory refused by the allocator (ALC-4, HEAP-8)
other_cases.settled: Every growing container (Array, Map, Set, Deque, SmallArray, String, a Registry's Storage[T], a growing Arena) has try_reserve(n). After it succeeds, the next n additions of any of that container's growing operations (push, insert, add, extend, entry, `+=` on a String) take no memory. A container with push also has try_push. Any other allocation the system refuses stops at the line, naming the bytes, as Rust's Box::new and Vec::clone abort. That covers `copy of xs`, an f-string and `shares Player()`.

other_cases.case: Passing a twin's failure on with `?`
other_cases.settled: `party.try_push(owns p)?` in a function returning Result[void] ends `p` at that line, on that line's thread, and passes on CapacityError.Full, which has no size, holds nothing, and is Send and ThreadShared. So it goes into AnyError with no allocation, needs nothing of p's type (no Debug, no Send), and does not fail when memory has run out. A function whose error type is CapacityError[Player] hands the whole error, player included, to its caller. A program that wants the value matches before `?`. SendError and TrySendError work the same way.

other_cases.case: C registrations of every shape (FFI-11b, FFI-16, FFI-21)
Borrowed callbacks on a 32-bit target (a ray query called 100,000 times a second)

So the program runs for ever, and the table is full only with 65,536 callbacks live at once. A stale number can arise only from C breaking its contract. If one names a callback of another function type, the trampoline's type compare still stops it.

other_cases.case: Bounded channels (THR-15)
other_cases.settled: A send waits while the queue is full, and try_send never waits: it returns TrySendError.Full or Closed, holding the value. A wait that only the waiting thread could end stops at the line ([CAP-5]): a send to a full queue whose receiver has stayed on this thread, and a receive (or a `for v in rx` loop) whose senders have all stayed on this thread. A receiver handed to a thread, or lent to a scoped task or job, clears the mark, so a correct program never stops for it.

other_cases.settled: These are buffers, not limits ([CAP-3]). When one is full, the value moves to memory of its own, with the Alloc these operations already carry. Neither ever stops by itself. If that memory is then refused, it is [ALC-4]'s stop, or try_reserve's or try_push's error.

design.prior_art:
**C++.** C++26's std::inplace_vector is the nearest shape: push_back throws bad_alloc when full, try_push_back returns a null pointer and leaves the argument untouched, and unchecked_push_back is undefined behaviour. vector throws on capacity or memory. shared_ptr's count is not checked. Its shortfalls are exceptions as the stop, an unchecked form that is undefined behaviour, and counts that can wrap.

**Rust.**
- Vec::push panics on capacity overflow and aborts on allocation failure. try_reserve exists on every growing collection: Vec, VecDeque, String, HashMap and HashSet. Ember takes this exact shape for refused memory.
- push_within_capacity (unstable) returns Err(value).
- Rc and Arc abort on count overflow, with no reporting form, on 32-bit targets too.
- arrayvec's push panics, and try_push returns Err(CapacityError<T>) holding the element. Its CapacityError<T> is Debug and Error for every T, without T's Debug. simplify() drops the element.
- With anyhow, `?` on a CapacityError<Rc<T>> does not compile until the program writes `.map_err(|e| e.simplify())`. Ember does that step at the `?` itself.
- slotmap's 32-bit versions wrap after about 2^31 reuses of a slot.
- C callbacks get Box::into_raw, an address C can call after it is freed.

**EnTT.** entt::entity is 32 bits by default (a 20-bit index and a 12-bit version), and versions wrap. A 64-bit entity (32/32) is EnTT's own configuration, which Ember makes the default (option A). Options F and G keep EnTT's default.

**Swift.** Array.append traps. A reference count that overflows its inline bits moves to a side table. C callbacks get Unmanaged.passRetained(x).toOpaque(), an address with no check.

**Go.** A full channel blocks. The runtime stops a program whose goroutines are all asleep ("all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!"), but not a partial deadlock. Ember's [CAP-5] stops the narrower case of a thread waiting for itself, whatever other threads do. Out of memory is fatal in Go.

**Ada.** Bounded containers raise Capacity_Error; memory and stack raise Storage_Error. Both are exceptions, so whether a program handles them is not visible at the call.

**Zig.** Every allocation and fixed append returns an error the caller must handle with `try`. The AssumeCapacity forms are unchecked in release builds.

**C#.** GCHandle tables grow, and a stale handle is not reliably caught.

**Where Ember lands:**
- arrayvec's pair (a stop, and a try_ twin that gives the value back) becomes one convention for every limit: the standard library, C callbacks and the language alike.
- The twin of a C registration is made by the compiler, as it makes the wrapper.
- A `?` passes the failure on without the value.
- Rust's try_reserve covers refused memory.
- A full table never hands out a number Ember code may still hold. The callback table, whose numbers only C holds, never meets an end over the program's life.
- Safe code has no unchecked form.
design.cost:
Per operation, against C:

- **Plain form of any limit.** One compare of the room used against the limit, and a branch never taken. It is the check correct C writes before storing into a fixed buffer; C that omits it overflows the buffer. It uses no memory. It is a RuntimeCheck, so an implementation may leave it out where it proves the room is there, as with a bounds check.
- **The try_ twin.** The same compare. The Result comes back in registers, and giving the value back moves its bytes, with no copy and no allocation.
- **Passing a twin's error on with `?`.** On the failure path only, the value's end (its drop) at that line. CapacityError.Full has no size, so AnyError takes no block: no allocation and no Alloc, where today's row says one allocation.
- **Counts.** Unchanged on every target (verdict 59): one compare per +1, and no memory.
- **Pool and Registry.** Unchanged: the free-slot test HND-3 already makes. A 64-bit Entity costs 4 more bytes for every entity id stored: each entry of a component storage's entity list and sparse index, and each id a program keeps. A view walks 8-byte ids instead of 4. Component data is unchanged.
- **Callback registration.** No new work per registration (FFI-53's free-slot test) and none per call: the trampoline stays at 1.02x to 1.05x of a C call through a function pointer. Retired slots come back once per 2^32 registrations on a 32-bit target, in one walk of the retired list, and never on a 64-bit target. The twin is a second small wrapper per registering function, code only.
- **Channel marks.** Two marks, one byte, in the channel's shared state. One store at each line that gives an end, or a value holding one, elsewhere. One load and compare, only when a send finds the queue full or a receive finds it empty, just before it would block in a futex wait. Nothing on the fast path.
- **Jobs.** A counted scoped submit puts its node in the scope's frame: the function value's two words and a link, 24 bytes on a 64-bit target. That is no allocation, and less work than today's copy into a queue slot. Any other submit takes one allocation for its node, which an implementation may serve from a list of the thread's freed nodes.
- **Buffers.** Zero on the fast path. When a buffer is full, the operation makes the allocation it already states.
- **Stop texts.** Built only on the stopping path.

**In total:**
- Zero per trampoline call.
- Zero per `?` of a twin's error.
- Zero memory per object.
- 4 bytes per stored entity id.
