holes.what_goes_wrong: The rule says 'one record holds on every target', but that holds only for declarations that bind the same way everywhere. The record is made on Windows, where Clang's MSVC ABI binds the enum as `@repr(c_int)`. On Linux, Clang (like GCC) gives an enum with no negative value `unsigned int`, so it binds as `@repr(c_uint)`. The form differs, and the Linux build is E5010 'changed since checked'. Running `ember bind ... --merge` on Linux then 'rewrites the overlay's line' with the Linux form only (new CLI-7), so the Windows build fails the same way: the two machines erase each other's forms. Nothing says whether the package's own build adds a new form by itself, or whether only a person may. A package whose record was made on one target gives E5010 to every consumer on another target, with no line the consumer can write.
holes.fix_hint: Key each recorded form by the configuration that produced it (target, plus the import's settings). --merge then replaces only the forms the current configuration binds and keeps the others. A form missing for this target in another package's overlay is E5010 naming the target and what that package's author runs. Drop 'one record holds on every target' from the rule, or say exactly which bindings are target-free. Leaving out only sizes and offsets does not make an enum's underlying type or an `#if`-chosen typedef target-free.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-12 makes every entry whose declaration the import lacks E5010, and FFI-30c then refuses the whole overlay. On Linux, SDL.h (through SDL_system.h) declares no SDL_Direct3D9GetAdapterIndex, so the import line is refused and the game does not build. Ember has no conditional compilation, so the import cannot choose a different overlay list per target. A published package's SDL overlay made on Windows refuses every Linux consumer, who cannot edit it. CLI-5's starter overlay, the documented first-day path (FFI-11c), produces exactly such files. Yet the entry vouches for nothing on Linux: the function is absent, and a call of it is E1061 anyway. The design lists this as open risk 4, but its own FFI-12 text is what refuses it.
holes.fix_hint: An entry whose declaration this import lacks applies nothing here, with a warning that names it and the header. A misspelt entry fails safe: the intended function stays unsafe or absent (principle 11). E5010 stays for a declaration that is present and differs from its recorded form. Alternatively, keep E5010 only for an entry that no recorded configuration has ever seen; this needs hole 1's per-configuration forms. Either way it changes FFI-12's 'cannot drift' wording, so it goes to the owner.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-12 refuses 'an entry whose path names no declaration of that import'. By FFI-6b, a function-like macro is exposed only once an overlay declares it, so it is not a declaration of the import, and the letter of the rule makes every @ffi(macro_fn) entry E5010. Today's 'do not match the header' does not have this problem. The new FFI-55 also replaces the generic 'as the importer binds it' with a closed list: 'a function's parameters and result ...; a struct's fields by name and type'. It defines no form for a macro, whose entry carries its own Ember types (ODR-147). Nor does it define one for an enum (values, underlying type), a typedef (`@ffi(handle)`, `@ffi(newtype)`, a `@ffi(safe)` function-pointer typedef, FFI-56), a global (`@ffi(immutable)`), a std::variant alias, or a class section. Whether these give E5010 is left undecided, and it depends on the kind of entry.
holes.fix_hint: Define both rules once, for every kind of entry. An entry's declaration is whatever the header declares or defines under that path, a macro included. Its fingerprint is that declaration as the importer binds it in Ember's own types (for a macro, its parameter list and replacement tokens), with the target's sizes, alignments and offsets left out. Give the two current kinds as examples, not as the list.

holes.what_goes_wrong: The new FFI-30c makes 'two overlay files that state facts about one entity' E5010, naming both files. This game is refused even though both files state the same fact. The game's author owns neither file and has no line to write: `override` works only inside one import's list. By FFI-30's letter, a C function is one entity too ('one C declaration ... whichever module, alias or overlay imports them'). So two packages that each overlay SDL.h get the same E5010 for SDL_Quit, against FFI-30a ('packages with different overlays for one header still exchange its values'). Reading the parenthesis as C++ members only makes this a rule for one construct. Nothing says what a third import of engine.hpp with no overlay sees for `lookups`: the other file's vouch (a fact its own line never stated), or none (one entity's method then being const and non-const at once).
holes.fix_hint: One general rule. A free function's facts belong to the import that applies them (FFI-30a, as today). A member's facts belong to its class, so every file stating facts about one member is merged: equal facts are one statement, and only facts that differ are E5010, naming both files and the fact (FFI-30c's own 'incompatible entries', FFI-43's disagreeing overlays). The importing package may settle a difference with its own `override` entry. Say what an import without an overlay sees.

engineering.notes:
Engineering lens on P28 (member J8-15). The core rule holds. The header, language, settings and overlay order on the import only; entries judged per import against the declaration and the record; no header-name compare. It costs nothing at run time, compiles ordinary programs unchanged, shortens the overlay head, and answers the J8-15 example and the cases about spellings, aliases, composition and dependencies correctly.

Five medium holes make it broken:
(1) 'One record holds on every target' is false wherever a described declaration binds differently per target: a C enum's underlying type is unsigned int on Linux and int under the MSVC ABI, and Vulkan's handles are pointers on 64-bit targets and uint64_t on 32-bit ones. The new CLI-7 rewrite then erases other targets' forms.
(2) An entry for a declaration present only on some targets (SDL_system.h; any CLI-5 starter overlay) refuses the whole overlay elsewhere. Ember has no conditional compilation, and the entry vouches for nothing there.
(3) The new FFI-12 wording ('names no declaration of that import') refuses every @ffi(macro_fn) entry by FFI-6b's letter, and FFI-55's fingerprint becomes a closed list of two kinds.
(4) 'Two overlay files that state facts about one entity are E5010' refuses equal facts, cannot be fixed by the program that depends on both packages, and contradicts FFI-30a if read for C functions.
(5) Verdict 121's own first clause and decision 11's 'one fingerprint per C declaration' change while the design reports 121 as kept.

Left to the safety lens, not filed here: an overlay applied to a different library whose declarations are identical (a/config.h vs b/config.h, or two static inline bodies behind one signature) passes, and a full header-identity check would have caught some of these. --merge records every import's form at once, without a person checking each configuration.

Consequence of the rule, which is a test change and not a hole: tests/conformance/FFI-12/reject_an_overlay_for_another_header.em compiles under it, since other_header.em's tally_scale(value, by) matches tally.h and its record line. I read that test folder and confirmed the stale `header = \"counter.h\"` key.

Not filed: for C, `include_paths`/`defines`/`overlay` are written per import line in every module that imports a header, while C++ centralises them in [cpp.<project>]. A `pub import` re-export (FFI-30b) already lets a program say them once.

design.rule: A fact about foreign code is written once, where it is true, and checked against what it is about. The import line, and only the import line, says which header is read, in which language (`import c` / `import cpp`), with which settings (`defines` and `include_paths`, or its `project`), and which overlays it applies, in which order. An overlay says only what is true of declarations. Its first line is `unsafe overlay:`, with no header and no language, and each entry names one declaration the way a program names it under the import (`SDL_Quit`, `engine.Grid`). Ember's record, `ember.overlays`, names no header either. For each entry it keeps every form of the declaration that a person has checked that entry against. A form is what the header gives of the declaration: everything the importer reads from it (parameters and result, a method's qualifiers, a typedef's target, an enum's values), plus its definition as written where the header has one (an inline body, a macro's tokens). It never includes how a target represents or links the declaration, so a declaration the header gives alike everywhere has one form on every target. In each import, an entry applies to the declaration its path names when that declaration's form is recorded for the entry. If the form differs, the import line is refused, and the message names the entry and the header that import reads. If the import does not declare it, the entry applies nothing there, provided some build has checked it. Something a program reaches through an import's module by name (`sdl.SDL_Quit`) has that import's facts. Something it reaches through a value, from any module (a foreign type, a member of a C++ class), is one entity for the whole build, and every overlay that states its facts must state them alike. Nothing compares header names or language words, because nothing else names them.
design.spec_text:
[GRM-35] (changed) Overlay grammar:

  overlay_decl  := ["unsafe"] "overlay" ":" NEWLINE INDENT {overlay_item} DEDENT
  overlay_item  := {attribute} (overlay_fn | "type" item_path NEWLINE | "enum" item_path NEWLINE
                   | "rename" item_path "as" IDENT NEWLINE | "hide" item_path NEWLINE | extend_decl
                   | overlay_class)
  overlay_class := "class" item_path ":" NEWLINE INDENT {{attribute} overlay_fn} DEDENT
  overlay_fn    := ["unsafe"] "fn" item_path "(" [overlay_param {"," overlay_param} [","]] ")"
                   ["->" contract {contract}] NEWLINE
  item_path     := IDENT {"." IDENT}

New text in GRM-35: "**An overlay is one file, and it says only what is true of declarations.** Which header it meets, in which language and under which settings is said once, by each import that names the file ([FFI-6], [FFI-17], [FFI-30c]). The overlay names neither, and one overlay serves every import that names it. An entry names one declaration, or a function-like macro ([FFI-6b]), by its path below the import's module, written as a program writes it after the module's name: `SDL_Quit` for `sdl.SDL_Quit`, and `engine.Grid` for `cpp.engine.Grid` ([FFI-41]: a namespace is a path segment, and an inline one adds none). A member is named by its name alone, inside its class's section (verdict 131). The import's own name (`as sdl`) is never written in an overlay. How several functions that share one name are told apart is [P07]'s rule. An overlay line that names a header or a language (`unsafe overlay c \"SDL.h\":`) is E0104: \"an overlay names no header; each import that applies it names the header: write `unsafe overlay:`\". `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites it ([CLI-20]). A second `overlay` line in one file is E0104 too, as a file is one module ([MOD-1]).\" The `override` sentence becomes: \"An item may begin with `override`. It then replaces an earlier overlay's entry for that name in the import's list ([FFI-30c], ODR-149). For a fact of a type or of a class member, it also replaces what the overlays of the packages its package depends on state of that entity ([FFI-30c]).\" The sentence \"Ember records the header each overlay was written for in `ember.overlays`, never in the overlay\" becomes: \"What each declaration an overlay describes was when a person checked the overlay is recorded by Ember in `ember.overlays`, never in the overlay ([FFI-55]).\" XVI.4's example overlay begins `unsafe overlay:`.

[FFI-12] (changed) \"An overlay entry is checked against the declaration its path names in each import that applies the overlay. That declaration is whatever the header declares or defines under that path, including a function-like macro described by an entry marked `@ffi(macro_fn)` ([FFI-6b]). An entry whose kind, parameter count or parameter names differ from that declaration is E5010. The message names the entry, the overlay and the header that import reads. An entry whose path that import does not declare applies nothing there, because there is nothing there for it to describe, and a use of the missing name is E1061, naming the header. Such an entry is E5010 when its line in the record holds nothing ([FFI-55]): no build has ever checked it against a declaration, because it is misspelt or names what no header has (\"`overlays/sdl.em` describes `SDL_Qiut` (line 3), which the `SDL.h` imported here does not declare, and which no build has checked against a declaration\"). This keeps an overlay from drifting, and an overlay for several targets builds on each. Each word of an entry is judged by the declaration it names, whatever the import's language. A word that cannot be true of that declaration is E5002 (`@ffi(const)` on a function outside a class, `@ffi(std_function)` on something that is not a `std::function`). A word that is already true of it (`@ffi(noexcept)` on a C function under `import c`) changes nothing. Nothing compares an overlay with the name of a header.\" The verdict-131 sentence (an entry outside a class section that names only members) is kept.

[FFI-17] (changed) \"… Overlays for C++ are written as for C: `unsafe overlay:`, with the grammar of [GRM-35]. A class in a namespace is named by its path, `class engine.Grid:`.\"

[FFI-30] (changed) Its first sentence becomes: \"Two imports of one C or C++ type (by Clang's USR, through typedefs) with the same layout are **one** Ember entity, its members with it, whichever module, alias or overlay imports them …\". Added: \"A function outside any class is reached through an import's module by name, so each import's is its own, with the facts its overlays state ([FFI-30a], [FFI-30c]).\"

[FFI-30c] (changed) Its last sentence becomes: \"An overlay, its own package's or another's, is applied to each import that names it, entry by entry ([FFI-12]), against its package's record ([FFI-55]). No other test decides which headers it serves. Something a program reaches through an import's module by name, such as a function outside any class, has the facts that import's overlays state, so two packages may describe `SDL_Quit` differently. Something it reaches through a value, from whichever module, is one entity for the whole build ([FFI-30]): a foreign type, and each member of a C++ class. Its facts are one statement. Every overlay that states a fact of it, through any import, states the same fact. An import whose overlays state none sees that statement, whatever the order of the build. When no overlay states the fact, the importer's own reading holds ([FFI-40a]). Two overlays that state different facts of one such entity are E5010, naming both files, both imports and the fact (\"`physics/overlays/engine.em` (line 4) says `engine.Grid.lookups` only reads its object, and `render/overlays/engine.em` (line 4) says it changes it\"). The exception is an entry marked `override` in a package whose dependency states the other fact. As within one import's list, a dependency's statement comes before the package's own, and `override` replaces it. That is the line E5010's help gives the package that depends on both. Within one import's list, files compose as above (ODR-149).\"

[FFI-55] (changed) \"**Every overlay is checked against what each declaration it describes was when a person checked it, by a record Ember keeps** (verdict 121). A package with an overlay has a file `ember.overlays` beside its `ember.toml`, written by Ember and never by hand. For each overlay it holds the overlay's file and, for each entry, a `blake3:` fingerprint of the entry and one of each **form** of the declaration that a person has checked that entry against:

  # ember.overlays: what this package's overlays were checked against.
  # Written by ember; `ember bind <header> --check <overlay> --merge` adds what a person has checked.

  [[overlay]]
  file = \"overlays/sdl.em\"
  SDL_FreeSurface = { entry = \"blake3:…\", forms = [\"blake3:…\"] }

A form is what the header gives of the declaration, as the importer reads it. It holds everything the importer reads from the declaration into the binding ([FFI-2a], [FFI-8], [FFI-11f], [FFI-24], [FFI-40], [FFI-40a], [FFI-41]): for example a function's parameters and result; a method's `const`, `static`, `virtual`, `noexcept` and ref-qualifier; a typedef's target; an enum's enumerators and their values; a struct's fields; a global's type and `const`. Where the header defines the declaration there, the form also holds its definition as written: an inline function's or method's body, and a function-like macro's parameters and replacement tokens, leaving out comments and spacing. Each type in it is named as the C or C++ standard names it (`int`, `long`, `char`, `uint64_t`, `size_t`, `std::string`). Any other typedef is resolved to what it names, with its own name kept beside it (`pool_slot`, `int32_t`), so a typedef whose meaning changes changes the form. A form leaves out how a target represents and links the declaration: sizes, alignments, offsets and packing; the integer type behind an enum whose type the header does not give; the calling convention; and the symbol's linkage, visibility and import or export attributes. Each build derives these from Clang for its own target ([FFI-2a], [FFI-9]) and checks them ([FFI-5], [FFI-5a]). So a declaration the header gives alike on every target and under every setting has one form, and one record serves every target. A declaration that a target or a setting really changes has a form for each (`VkBuffer`, which is a pointer on 64-bit targets and a `uint64_t` on 32-bit ones). A form is compared only where an entry states a fact of the declaration, which is what makes an overlay `unsafe` ([GRM-35]). An entry that states none, such as a `rename` or a `hide`, relies on nothing a form holds, so its line holds only its entry.

Every build that applies an overlay, its own package's or any other's, takes the form of each declaration the overlay describes, as the header that import reads gives it. It accepts the entry when that form is one its line holds for the entry as it is now. The package's own build writes two kinds of line itself. One is a line the record lacks, for an entry just written. The other is a line whose entry was edited, when this build gives the declaration only in forms the line holds. Both are written with the entry as it now is and those forms, and the forms that were checked against the entry as it was go. Writing an entry is checking it against the declaration in front of its writer (ODR 14.2). Any other form is E5010. The message names the overlay, the declaration as the header imported here gives it, and the way out: \"`SDL_FreeSurface` changed since `overlays/sdl.em` was checked: the `SDL.h` imported here declares `void SDL_FreeSurface(SDL_Surface*, int)`; check the overlay against it, then run `ember bind SDL.h --check overlays/sdl.em --merge`\". That command adds this build's forms to the line, beside the forms it holds for the same entry, which other targets and settings give ([CLI-7]). In another package's build nothing is written. An entry, or a form, that its package's record lacks is E5010, naming the declaration, this build's target and settings, and saying that that package checks its overlay there and records it (ODR 14.3). A change to a declaration that no entry describes changes nothing. Every program has an `ember.toml` ([MAN-9]), so the record is always beside one. An overlay in no package's folder is the importing program's own: its record is that package's, naming the overlay by its path from the package (`../vendor/sdl.em`). The record names no header: what an overlay was checked against is the declarations it describes, whichever import reads them. Nothing of this is written in the overlay or in the program.\" In the example record, the line `header = \"SDL.h\"` goes. E5010's row in the table of codes gains \"a declaration in a form no line records; two overlays that state different facts of one type or class member\".

[CLI-5] (changed) \"… and records, in that overlay's line of the package's `ember.overlays`, the forms of the declarations it describes ([FFI-55]).\"

[CLI-7] (changed) \"With `--merge`, once the overlay passes, it adds to each of the overlay's lines in `ember.overlays` the forms that this build's imports naming the overlay give, beside the forms the line holds for the same entry. For an entry edited since, it writes the entry as it now is with this build's forms, and the forms checked against the entry as it was go. With `--init --merge` ([CLI-5]), and an edited entry in the package's own build ([FFI-55]), these are the only ways a line of the record changes once written.\"

[MAN-2] (changed) \"… `ember.overlays` records what the declarations the package's overlays describe were when a person checked them ([FFI-55]) …\"

[LEX-15] (changed) \"`c` and `cpp` between `import` and a string\" (the words \"or `overlay`\" go).

answers.answer: The import decides, and only the import. The overlay's first line names no header (`unsafe overlay:`). `overlays/sdl.em` is applied to whatever header each import names, and it is judged entry by entry, against that import's declaration of each path (FFI-12) and against the record's checked forms (FFI-55). Its one entry describes `SDL_Quit`. `SDL2/SDL_video.h` does not declare `SDL_Quit` (`SDL.h` does), so the entry has nothing there to apply to. In a package where no build has ever checked that entry against a declaration, it is refused at the import line for that real reason, not because two header names differ. Where the package also imports `SDL.h` with the same overlay, so the entry is recorded, the entry simply applies nothing to the `SDL_video.h` import, and `sdl.SDL_Quit()` is refused at the call (E1061, naming the header). An import of `SDL2/SDL.h`, or of `SDL.h` where the include paths reach it, compiles under either spelling. 'Applied, refused, or ignored?' gets one answer per entry and per import: applied where its declaration is and matches a checked form; refused where it differs or was never checked; applying nothing where the import lacks a declaration that some build has checked.
answers.outcome: As written, in a package with only this import, the result is E5010 at main.em line 1: "`overlays/sdl.em` describes `SDL_Quit` (line 3), which the `SDL2/SDL_video.h` imported here does not declare, and which no build has checked against a declaration". With `import c "SDL2/SDL.h"` it compiles, and `sdl.SDL_Quit()` is safe to call. That first build writes the record line, `SDL_Quit = { entry = "blake3:…", forms = ["blake3:…"] }`. A later build where `SDL_Quit`'s declaration has changed is E5010, with the `ember bind … --check … --merge` line to run. The same record serves Windows, Linux and 32-bit builds, because `void SDL_Quit(void)` is the same declaration on each; `SDLCALL` and `DECLSPEC` are the calling convention and the linkage, and a form leaves them out. The old head, `unsafe overlay c "SDL.h":`, is E0104 with the line `unsafe overlay:` to write, and `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites it.

other_cases.case: One header spelled two ways: `import c "SDL.h"` with include path `vendor/SDL2/include/SDL2` in one module, and `import c "SDL2/SDL.h"` in another, both naming `overlays/sdl.em`.
other_cases.settled: Both apply the overlay. Their declarations give the same forms, and the record holds those forms. No header name is compared. A rule that compared the written strings would refuse the second import, and one that compared files would depend on each machine's include paths.

other_cases.case: Two different headers with the same file name, `vendor/a/config.h` and `vendor/b/config.h`, with an overlay checked against a's declarations applied to b. Today's compiler compares only the last file name, so this passes.
other_cases.settled: Each entry is checked against b's declaration of its path. If that declaration is in a form the record does not hold for the entry, the import is E5010, naming it. Nothing passes because two file names happen to be equal.

other_cases.case: Overlays split by sub-header and composed on one umbrella import: `import c "SDL.h" with (overlay = ["overlays/sdl_video.em", "overlays/sdl_audio.em"]) as sdl` (FFI-30c's list). Also the reverse: an umbrella overlay applied to an import of one sub-header.
other_cases.settled: Both compile. With the list, `SDL.h` declares every entry of both files, and composition and `override` work as ODR-149 says. With the umbrella overlay on a sub-header, each entry applies where the sub-header declares it. The other entries apply nothing there, since their declarations were checked through the umbrella import. A rule where each overlay names its own header would refuse both.

other_cases.case: One C header imported by both `import c "vulkan.h"` and `import cpp "vulkan.h" with (project = "engine")`, with one overlay.
other_cases.settled: There is no language word in the overlay to disagree. The header gives each C function alike in both modes. The `extern "C"` that the C++ mode reads is linkage, which a form leaves out, so there is one form. Each import makes its own functions: under `import cpp` a function that is not `noexcept` returns `Result` (FFI-24), unless the entry says `@ffi(noexcept)`. Under `import c` the same word is already true of a C function and changes nothing. A header that declares something else under `#ifdef __cplusplus` gives a second form, and the build adds it when the entry is written, or `--merge` adds it.

other_cases.case: A library recorded on Linux and built on Windows by an application that depends on it: `tally.h` declares `void tally_add(uint64_t amount)` and `typedef enum tally_status { TALLY_OK, TALLY_FULL } tally_status`, and `tally`'s overlay vouches `tally_add` safe and makes `tally_status` a status enum.
other_cases.settled: It compiles on both targets with one record. `uint64_t` is named as the C standard names it, so glibc's `unsigned long` and MSVC's `unsigned long long` behind it never reach the form. The enum's enumerators and values are in the form. The integer type C picks for it (`unsigned int` under GCC/Clang, `int` under MSVC) is not, since each build derives it from Clang and FFI-5 checks its size. A struct holding a `long` or a pointer is named the same way, and its sizes and offsets are checked by FFI-5 and FFI-5a on every build.

other_cases.case: A declaration that a target really changes: `vulkan_core.h` defines `VkBuffer` as `struct VkBuffer_T*` on 64-bit targets and as `uint64_t` on 32-bit ones, and the overlay says `@ffi(handle) type VkBuffer`.
other_cases.settled: There are two forms. On a 32-bit build of the package itself, the entry is E5010 until a person checks it there and runs `ember bind vulkan.h --check overlays/vulkan.em --merge`, which adds the 32-bit form beside the 64-bit one. Builds on either target then pass. In an application that depends on that package, the missing form is E5010 naming the target and saying that the package records it there (ODR 14.3).

other_cases.case: An entry for a function that only one target declares: `@ffi(no_callbacks) fn SDL_Direct3D9GetAdapterIndex(displayIndex)`, written by `ember bind --init SDL.h` on Windows, in an overlay that a Linux build applies.
other_cases.settled: On Linux it applies nothing, and `sdl.SDL_Quit()` and the rest work. Its line was written by the Windows build, so FFI-12 knows that a person checked it against a real declaration. A use of the function on Linux is E1061, naming the header. An entry no build has ever checked, such as `SDL_Qiut`, is E5010. A Linux consumer of a published package built on Windows is served the same way.

other_cases.case: A function-like macro: `#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))`, with `@ffi(macro_fn) fn SQUARE(x: i32) -> i32` in the overlay.
other_cases.settled: The entry's declaration is the macro's definition (FFI-12). Its form is the macro's parameters and replacement tokens as written. If the header changes the body (from a masked index to a raw one), the form changes, and the entry is E5010 until a person checks it again. A macro used inside the body is its own definition and is not part of this form, just as a function the body calls is not.

other_cases.case: A typedef that changes meaning: `typedef int32_t pool_slot;` becomes `typedef uintptr_t pool_slot;` under `@ffi(no_callbacks) fn pool_release(s)`.
other_cases.settled: The form names `pool_slot` resolved, `pool_slot = int32_t` before and `pool_slot = uintptr_t` after. It changes, so the result is E5010: "`pool_release` changed since `overlays/pool.em` was checked: the `pool.h` imported here declares `void pool_release(pool_slot = uintptr_t)`". The safe call `pool.pool_release(12345)` never reaches C.

other_cases.case: A C++ method whose header changes under an `@ffi(const)` entry: `int lookups() const noexcept` loses `const`, or keeps it while its inline body gains `cells_ = compacted;`.
other_cases.settled: Both changes are in the form: the receiver qualification (FFI-40), and the inline body as written. So the entry is E5010 at the import line, and the loop that walks `g.cells()` while calling `g.lookups()` is never compiled against a stale vouch. An `assert` in the body is written the same in debug and release builds, so `NDEBUG` does not split the form. The body counts as written, not as expanded.

other_cases.case: C++ namespaces: `namespace engine { class Grid { int lookups() const; }; }` and `namespace editor { class Grid {...}; }` in one header. Today's grammar allows only `class Grid:`, which matches the bare name.
other_cases.settled: The section is `class engine.Grid:` with `@ffi(const) fn lookups()` under it, which is the path the program writes (`cpp.engine.Grid`). A nested class is `class engine.Grid.Cell:`. An inline namespace adds no segment (ODR-165). An entry `class Grid:` is E5010: "`engine.hpp` declares no `Grid` at its top; it declares `engine.Grid` and `editor.Grid`".

other_cases.case: A C++ class member described through two imports of `engine.hpp`: `render.em` applies an overlay with `@ffi(const) fn lookups()`, and `tools.em` imports the header with no overlay and calls `g.lookups()` on a `raw.engine.Grid`.
other_cases.settled: The class is one entity (FFI-30), and `g.lookups()` names no module, so the method has one meaning for the whole build. It is safe and only reads its object in `tools.em` too, whichever module is built first. `ember tcb` lists the vouch under `render.em`'s overlay. If no overlay stated it, the importer's reading would hold (FFI-40a).

other_cases.case: Two packages, `physics` and `render`, each ship their own `overlays/engine.em` for `engine.hpp`, and a game imports both.
other_cases.settled: When both say `@ffi(const) fn lookups()` under `class engine.Grid:`, that is one statement and the game compiles. When one says `@ffi(const)` and the other does not (which, by verdict 132, says that the method changes its object), the result is E5010 naming both files, both imports and the fact. The help gives the game its line: an overlay of its own, applied through its own import of `engine.hpp`, with `@ffi(const)` above `override fn lookups()`. A dependency's statement comes before the package's own, as in ODR-149. Free functions are untouched: `physics.eng.f` and `render.eng.f` may have different facts, since each is reached through its own module (FFI-30a).

other_cases.case: An entry edited after it was recorded, in a package built on Windows and Linux, for a declaration whose form differs between them.
other_cases.settled: The Windows build of the package writes the line again with the entry as it now is and the Windows form. The Linux form goes, because it was checked against the old entry. The next Linux build is then E5010 until a person checks the edited entry against Linux's declaration and runs `--merge` there. Where the two forms are the same, which is the usual case, nothing more is needed.

other_cases.case: `import cpp "engine.hpp" with (project = "engine", overlay = "overlays/engine.em")`, with the project's defines and include paths.
other_cases.settled: These are already said in one place. The import names the project, and `[cpp.engine]` in the manifest defines it once, for every import of that project (`defines=` on an `import cpp` is E0104). The overlay and the record never name it. A define that changes a declaration only gives it another form.

other_cases.case: The record's own `header` key: tests/conformance/FFI-12/ember.overlays says `header = "counter.h"` above a `tally_scale` fingerprint taken from `tally.h`.
other_cases.settled: The key goes. Nothing reads it: the compiler writes it from the overlay's own line. It is already false in the repository. One overlay named by imports of two headers cannot have one true value for it.

other_cases.case: An Ember module, `src/game/physics.em`, which is module `game.physics`.
other_cases.settled: This is the precedent for the rule (MOD-1). A module's path comes from its file, and nothing inside the file restates it. An overlay's purpose comes, in the same way, from the import that names its file.

other_cases.case: `unsafe import c "./bridge.c"` (which also imports `bridge.h`), and `implementation = ["MINIAUDIO_IMPLEMENTATION"]`.
other_cases.settled: These are already in one place, and nothing changes. The header is derived from the C file (BLD-FFI-1), and the implementation is compiled once, for the one import that asks for it (E5014 for two).

other_cases.case: An overlay file that no import names.
other_cases.settled: It is never applied. `ember check` and the spec's own ```ember,overlay blocks check only its grammar. Nothing about it depends on a header.

design.prior_art: C++ names a header once per translation unit, with `#include`. Its one-definition rule says that two definitions of one entity in different translation units must be identical, and a violation is 'ill-formed, no diagnostic required', so one entity stated twice without a check ends in undefined behaviour. This rule checks exactly that case: two overlays stating different facts of one class member are E5010. Rust: a hand-written `extern \"C\" { fn SDL_Quit(); }` names no header and is never checked against one, so a mismatch is undefined behaviour. bindgen names the header once, in build.rs, but its output, layout tests included, holds for one target only, so committed bindings break on another target. This rule's forms leave the target's layout to FFI-5 for exactly that reason. cxx names the header once (`include!(\"blobstore.h\")` inside `unsafe extern \"C++\"`), and the C++ it generates is compiled against that header, so a declaration that does not match fails to compile. That is the closest to this rule: one naming, checked declaration by declaration. Swift: a module map names the headers once, `import SDL` names the module, and API notes are found by the module's name and describe declarations by name. As far as I know, an API-notes entry for a declaration the module lacks is simply never applied, with no diagnostic. This rule keeps that leniency only for an entry that some build has checked against a real declaration, and refuses one that never was. ABI checkers such as libabigail compare declarations by what they mean, per architecture, rather than by their text. That is the idea behind a form, which keeps what the header says and leaves out what a target makes of it. Zig: `@cImport(@cInclude(\"SDL.h\"))` names the header once and adds no facts; pointers stay `[*c]T`. Go: cgo's preamble `// #include <SDL.h>` names it once per file, with no contracts. Go also shows what two namings cost: a file's `package` clause need not match the last element of its import path, a known source of confusion. C#: `[DllImport(\"SDL2\")]` repeats the library on every declaration. Ada: `with Import, Convention => C` on each declaration, unchecked against any header. Where they fall short: the languages that name the header once (Zig, Go, Swift, cxx) add no checked contracts, or, in Swift's case, ignore stale ones. The ones that restate facts (C++, hand-written Rust, Ada, C#) leave a mismatch unchecked. This rule takes cxx's shape (the header named once, at the import) and checks every entry against the declaration it names, by meaning and on every target, so a fact can disagree only with a declaration, and then the import is refused.
design.cost: Zero at run time. An overlaid C call is still one `call` instruction (FFI-9), as in C, and the rule adds nothing to the image or to any value. Compile time, per entry at each import that applies it: one lookup of its path, the same hash-map lookup a program's `sdl.SDL_Quit` already does; one blake3 over its form (about 100 bytes for a declaration, the body's size for an inline one, at gigabytes per second) and one over the entry; and a compare against the few forms its line holds, usually one. Per type or class member that overlays state facts of, there is one insert into a table keyed by the entity, where equal facts merge. The compare of the header's file name goes. Forms drop sizes, offsets, calling conventions and linkage, which FFI-5 and FFI-5a check on every build anyway. Memory: the record loses its `header` line per overlay. Each line holds one entry fingerprint and usually one form; a second form appears only where a target or setting really changes the declaration. C pays nothing because C checks nothing: a C header's declarations are trusted as written, and C has no overlays.

readability.note: The program's file is unchanged, and the overlay's first line gets shorter. Someone reading the overlay on its own no longer sees the header's name in it. They find it on the import line that applies the overlay, where header and overlay already sit together, just as an Ember module's path comes from its file and not from a line inside it (MOD-1). The file's own name (`overlays/sdl.em`) or a comment can still say it. A C++ entry inside a namespace gains its namespace (`class engine.Grid:`), which is exactly how the program writes it (`cpp.engine.Grid`), and only where C++ put it in one. An entry with only the bare name cannot say which `Grid` it means. The record's shape changes, but nobody reads or writes it: Ember writes it, and its messages name the declaration and the command. A package built on several targets needs nothing more for declarations the header gives alike, which is almost every declaration.

design.compiler_does: The compiler parses `unsafe overlay:`. It refuses the old head (a header or a language word after `overlay`) and a second head in one file, giving the line to write, and `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites both. At each import that names overlays, it takes them in list order (FFI-30c) and does the following for each entry. It resolves the entry's path in the module the import is writing, with the same lookup a program's `cpp.engine.Grid` uses; a function-like macro counts as a declaration there. It checks the kind, parameter count and names (FFI-12), and judges each word by the declaration it names. It computes the declaration's form from what the importer read. Standard type names are kept, other typedefs are resolved with their names kept, and an inline body or a macro's tokens are taken as written. Sizes, offsets, packing, an enum's chosen integer type, the calling convention and linkage are left out. It then compares the form with the forms the overlay's line holds for the entry as it now is. In the package's own build, it writes a missing line, or a line whose entry was edited, from this build's forms. Any other unrecorded form is E5010 with the `--merge` line. In another package's build it writes nothing, and a missing line or form is E5010 naming the target. An entry the import does not declare applies nothing there, unless its line holds nothing, in which case it is E5010. It collects every overlay's facts about each type and each C++ class member across all imports before binding any of them. Equal facts merge. Different ones are E5010 naming both files, both imports and the fact, unless a package's `override` replaces a dependency's statement. An import with no statement of a fact uses the build's one statement, whatever the build order. Facts of a function outside any class stay with the import's own module. It never compares header names or language words. `ember bind <header> --check <overlay> --merge` adds this build's forms to the overlay's lines, keeping the forms checked against the same entry. Nothing runs while the program runs.
design.misuse: Every misuse is refused when compiling, at the import line or at the overlay's line, and none can reach run time. If an import applies an overlay whose entry it does not declare, the entry applies nothing there, and a use of the name is E1061 naming the header. If no build has ever checked the entry (a misspelling, or a function no header has), it is E5010, naming the entry, the overlay and the header the import reads. A declaration whose form changed since a person checked the entry is E5010 with the `ember bind … --check … --merge` line to run. This covers a lost `const`, a changed inline body or macro, a typedef that now names another type, and changed enum values. In another package's build, a form that package never checked (another target, other defines) is E5010 naming the target and saying that the package records it there. An entry edited in one place makes the forms checked against its old text go, so an edited contract is never accepted against a declaration nobody checked it with. The old head `unsafe overlay c \"SDL.h\":` is E0104, with `unsafe overlay:` to write, and `ember fmt --migrate` rewrites it. A word that cannot be true of the declaration it names (`@ffi(const)` on a function outside a class) is E5002. An entry that names a namespaced C++ class by its bare name is E5010, listing the paths the header declares (`engine.Grid`, `editor.Grid`). Two overlays that state different facts of one type or class member are E5010, naming both files and the fact, with the `override` line for the package that depends on both. Another package's overlay whose package has no record line is E5010 (ODR 14.3, unchanged). One mistake no compiler can catch is applying an overlay to a different library whose declarations are identical to the ones checked. The rule leaves it exactly where a header-name check would also leave it. Under any design, the import line chooses which file is parsed (through its include paths) and which library is linked, so the vouch is an asserted fact about the linked library. `ember tcb` lists that library (TCB-4).
design.verdicts:
The owner should hear three things here, plainly, as his own lines.

(1) **Verdict 121's first clause is amended, not kept.** He said: 'The header an overlay was written for is recorded by Ember in a package file of its own, `ember.overlays`, never in the overlay, and every overlay is checked against it'. It becomes: 'What each declaration an overlay describes was when a person checked it is recorded by Ember in `ember.overlays`, never in the overlay, and every overlay is checked against it.' The rest of 121 stands: a package file of its own, mandatory, never in code files, every overlay checked, the package's own included. The evidence that 'the header an overlay was written for' cannot be recorded truthfully:
  a. Nothing reads the `header` key. The compiler writes it from the overlay's own line and never compares it (cimport.rs, `check_overlay_record`).
  b. The repository's own tests/conformance/FFI-12/ember.overlays already says `header = \"counter.h\"` above a fingerprint taken from `tally.h`.
  c. One overlay named by imports of two headers (an umbrella and a sub-header, or `SDL.h` and `SDL2/SDL.h`) cannot have one true `header`.
  d. ODR 14.1, which he approved, already moved the check from the header file to each declaration.
FFI-55's bold title, which names 'the header it was written for', changes with it. Decision 11's 'one `blake3:` fingerprint per C declaration' becomes one fingerprint of the entry and one per checked form of the declaration. This is on the same line, with its reason: once a declaration may have several checked forms, a form checked against an entry's old text must stop counting when the entry is edited.

(2) **FFI-12 changes what the language does.** Today, an entry that does not match the header is always E5010. Under this rule, an entry whose declaration this import lacks applies nothing there, once some build has checked it against a real declaration. It is E5010 only when no build ever has. Without this, an overlay for several targets (a Windows-only SDL function) refuses every other target, and Ember has no conditional compilation to work around it.

(3) **A type's or class member's facts are one statement for the build.** Equal statements merge, different ones are E5010, and a package's `override` replaces what its dependencies state. This widens ODR-149 (a delegated ruling) from the files of one import's list to a package's dependencies, using ODR-149's own order: a dependency's before the package's own. It replaces the compiler's order-dependent D-879 behaviour, where a later import's entry 'states nothing'. Verdict 132 holds build-wide: an entry without `@ffi(const)` states, for the whole build, that the method changes its object.

Kept as they are: verdict 127 (every project has an ember.toml, so the record is always beside one); ODR 14.1 (a fingerprint per declaration, not per header file); ODR 14.2 (the package's own build adds a missing line, which now includes the line of an edited entry whose declaration kept a checked form, and a changed declaration stops the build until a person checks and re-records); ODR 14.3 (another package's missing line is E5010, and now a missing form too); ODR 14.4 (TOML, now with an inline table per entry). Untouched: verdicts 130, 131, 132 and 133, since entries are spelled as today and class sections now take a path; ODR-147, since a macro entry's Ember types are unchanged and its definition is now in its form; ODR-149 within one import's list. Changed as the lead's details, not as owner verdicts: decisions.md's 'FFI-55 (verdict 121)' row (the fingerprint was 'the `.embind` declaration with its layout', and a form now leaves out layout and linkage and adds an inline definition), and CLI-7's `--merge`, which now adds forms instead of rewriting the line.

options_for_owner.summary: The rule. The import is the one place that names the header and the language, and the overlay's first line is `unsafe overlay:`. Each entry is checked against that import's declaration of its path and against the record. The record names no header: it holds the forms of each declaration a person checked the entry against, with what the header says in them and nothing a target decides. A type's or class member's facts are one statement for the build.
options_for_owner.outcome: E5010: "`overlays/sdl.em` describes `SDL_Quit` (line 3), which the `SDL2/SDL_video.h` imported here does not declare, and which no build has checked against a declaration". `import c "SDL2/SDL.h"` (or `"SDL.h"`) compiles. Overlays split by sub-header compose on one import of `SDL.h`. One overlay serves C and C++ imports. One record serves Windows, Linux and 32-bit builds wherever the header says the same, and adds a form only where it does not. A header change that matters (a lost `const`, a changed typedef or inline body) is E5010.

options_for_owner.summary: Phase 2's recommendation. The overlay keeps naming its header, and that name must equal the import's; a mismatch is E5010.
options_for_owner.outcome: E5010: "`overlays/sdl.em` is written for `SDL.h`, and this import is of `SDL2/SDL_video.h`". But `import c "SDL2/SDL.h"` of the same file is refused too if the strings are compared, and depends on each machine's include paths if the files are compared. `overlay = ["overlays/sdl_video.em", "overlays/sdl_audio.em"]` on `import c "SDL.h"` is refused. One overlay cannot serve both `import c` and `import cpp`. The header stays written twice in the program's files, and a third time in the record. It still leaves open what the record holds across targets, and what two packages' overlays of one class mean.

options_for_owner.summary: The overlay is the one place. An import that applies an overlay does not name a header, and the header is read from the overlay's line.
options_for_owner.outcome: The header is named once. But `import c` then has two spellings (with a header, or without one when an overlay is given). A list of overlays must still agree on one header, which is a second naming again. main.em no longer shows which header it imports, and an overlay still cannot serve two headers.

recommendation.reason: The header is said once, where it is parsed, and the overlay is judged by what it actually describes: each declaration, by meaning and on every target, checked by FFI-12 and by the record of verdict 121. Every correct import is then accepted, whatever spelling of the header, alias, language or target it uses. Every change a vouch could rest on is refused with the changed declaration named: a lost `const`, a typedef that now means an address, a changed inline body or macro. B checks a name, which proves nothing about the file (`a/config.h` against `b/config.h`), and it refuses correct programs. C reaches one naming at the cost of two spellings of `import`. A is also the shortest to write, and it is the language's own model, since a module never restates its path (MOD-1).

owner_short.one_line: In C++ terms: the import line holds the `#include "SDL.h"`. The overlay (a file of contracts for that header's functions, like Swift's API notes for a C header) writes the header's name again on its first line, and Ember's record `ember.overlays` writes it a third time. The spec does not say which one counts, and the record's fingerprint changes from one target to another.
owner_short.step_table:
| step | thread | what happens | the value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | build | `main.em` line 1: `import c "SDL2/SDL_video.h" with (overlay = "overlays/sdl.em") as sdl` | header parsed: `SDL2/SDL_video.h` |
| 2 | build | the overlay's first line: `unsafe overlay c "SDL.h":` | header named: `SDL.h` |
| 3 | build | `ember.overlays`: `file = "overlays/sdl.em"`, `header = "SDL.h"`, fingerprints | header recorded: `SDL.h` |
| 4 | build | the spec: GRM-35 says the header is "never in the overlay", the grammar puts it there, and FFI-30c applies an overlay "only to the header it was written for" | undecided: applied, refused or ignored |
| 5 | build | today's compiler compares only the last file names | `SDL.h` against `SDL_video.h`: refused; `a/config.h` against `b/config.h`: passes |
| 6 | build | the repository's own record, tests/conformance/FFI-12/ember.overlays | `header = "counter.h"` above a fingerprint taken from `tally.h` |
| 7 | build | the fingerprint includes the target's sizes and offsets | a package recorded on Linux gives E5010 on Windows |
owner_short.today: The spec names the header in three places and says neither which counts nor what a mismatch does. The compiler compares only file names, and the repository's own record already disagrees with itself. The record's fingerprint holds for one target only.
owner_short.options:
A: the import names the header and the overlay's first line is `unsafe overlay:`. Each entry is checked against that import's declaration and against the record, which keeps what the header said of each declaration (types, `const`, typedefs, inline bodies) and nothing a target decides. The example is refused because SDL_video.h has no SDL_Quit.
B: the overlay keeps `unsafe overlay c "SDL.h":`, which must equal the import's header. The example is refused for the name, and so are correct imports that spell the header differently or combine per-header overlays.
C: the overlay names the header and the import names only the overlay. That is one naming, but `import c` gets two spellings and main.em stops showing its header.
owner_short.recommendation: A. Say the header once, where it is parsed, and judge the overlay by the declarations it describes, so correct imports are accepted on every target and real changes are refused with the real reason. Three lines in A are yours to rule, one at a time. First, verdict 121's 'the header is recorded' becomes 'what each declaration was when checked is recorded'. Second, an entry for a function this target lacks is left alone instead of refused. Third, two packages' overlays of one C++ class must agree, and the package using both may settle a disagreement with `override`.

repairs.hole: 1 (safety, high): the fingerprint was a closed list (parameters, result, struct fields). It left out a method's `const`, a macro's body, a typedef's target, an enum's values, a global's `const` and a function-pointer typedef's signature. So `lookups()` losing `const` kept an `@ffi(const)` vouch alive, and the safe loop read freed memory.
repairs.answer: A form is now defined once, for every kind of entry, as what the header gives of the declaration. It holds everything the importer reads from the declaration into the binding (FFI-2a, FFI-8, FFI-11f, FFI-24, FFI-40, FFI-40a, FFI-41) and, where the header defines it there, its definition as written: an inline function's or method's body, a macro's parameters and replacement tokens. The kinds are listed as examples, not as the definition. What is closed is the short set left out, which is how a target represents and links the declaration. Anything not in that set is fingerprinted, so forgetting a kind fails safe. Losing `const` changes the form. So does keeping `const` while the inline body starts rebuilding `cells_`, which the old list and the breaker's binding-only fix would both miss. Either change is E5010 at the import line, and the loop is never compiled against a stale vouch.

repairs.hole: 2 (safety, medium): `tally`'s record, made on Linux, fails on Windows. Its `uint64_t` was `c_ulong` there and `u64` here, and its enum was `@repr(c_uint)` there and `@repr(c_int)` here. `--merge` on one machine erased the other machine's forms.
repairs.answer: Each type in a form is named as the C or C++ standard names it, so `uint64_t` is `uint64_t` on every target, whatever glibc or MSVC typedef it to. FFI-8 need not change: `c_ulong` is an alias of `u64` on LP64 anyway, and a form never uses it. The integer type C picks for an enum whose type the header does not give is left out, since each build derives it from Clang and FFI-5 checks its size. So `tally` has one form on both targets and the application builds. Where a target really changes a declaration, the record holds a form for each. `--merge` adds this build's forms beside the others instead of rewriting the line. A dependency without the form this build needs is E5010, naming the target and saying that that package records it (ODR 14.3). I did not key forms by configuration as the hint asked. Doing that drops nothing, since the one thing a key bought (dropping stale forms) is done better by pairing forms with the entry. Configuration keys alone still miss that hazard: an entry edited on one target would be accepted on another target's old form, which nobody checked with it. Each line now holds the entry's fingerprint, and editing the entry makes the forms checked against its old text go.

repairs.hole: 3 (safety, medium): if a typedef parameter was fingerprinted by its name, `pool_slot` changing from `int32_t` to `uintptr_t` kept the vouch, and safe code freed address 12345.
repairs.answer: A form resolves every typedef that is not one the C or C++ standard names to what it names, and keeps its name beside it (`pool_slot = int32_t`, then `pool_slot = uintptr_t`). So the form changes and `pool_release` is E5010 at the import line. Together with hole 2's rule, the resolved form stays the same across targets exactly where the declaration means the same thing: `uintptr_t`, `int32_t` and `size_t` are kept by their standard names. Only an `#if`-chosen user typedef, which really differs, gives two forms.

repairs.hole: 4 (safety, medium): with `render.em`'s overlay and `tools.em`'s plain import of `engine.hpp`, it was undecided what `g.lookups()` meant on one class entity, and the answer depended on build order (D-879). The scope of 'two overlay files … one entity' was also open: it caught free functions, against FFI-30a, and could be read as refusing ODR-149's `override`.
repairs.answer: The rule is now said once, with its reason: whether the use names an import. Something reached through an import's module by name (a function outside any class) has that import's facts, so two packages may describe `SDL_Quit` differently (FFI-30a, and FFI-30 now says so). Something reached through a value from any module (a foreign type, each C++ class member) is one entity for the build, and its facts are one statement. An import that names no overlay states nothing and sees that statement. So in `tools.em`, `g.lookups()` is safe and only reads its object, whatever the build order. With no statement, the importer's reading holds. Two different statements are E5010, naming both files and both imports. ODR-149's composition within one import's list is left untouched, and the text says so.

repairs.hole: 5 (engineering, medium): 'one record holds on every target' was false for enums (`c_int` under MSVC, `c_uint` under GCC/Clang) and for `#if`-chosen typedefs such as `VkBuffer`, and `--merge` let machines erase each other's forms.
repairs.answer: The claim is now exact: a declaration the header gives alike on every target and under every setting has one form. The enum's implementation-chosen integer type is left out of the form, as are the calling convention and linkage, so SDL's `SDLCALL` and `DECLSPEC` do not split every function by target. `VkBuffer`, which really is a pointer on 64-bit targets and a `uint64_t` on 32-bit ones, gets two forms, both kept, because `--merge` adds and never erases. The package's own build on the new target is E5010 until a person checks the entry there. A consumer of another package missing that form gets E5010 naming the target and what the package's author runs. Whether a package's own build may add a new form by itself is settled too: it may not. A person adds it with `--merge`, except for the line of an entry just written or edited, which the writer has just checked.

repairs.hole: 6 (engineering, medium): the new FFI-12 refused an entry whose declaration the import lacks, so an SDL overlay made on Windows (with `SDL_Direct3D9GetAdapterIndex`) refused every Linux build, and a consumer could not fix it.
repairs.answer: FFI-12 now says this. An entry whose path this import does not declare applies nothing there, since there is nothing there for it to vouch for, and a use of the name is E1061 naming the header. It is E5010 only when its line in the record holds nothing, meaning no build has ever checked it against a real declaration: a misspelling, or a function no header has. So the Windows-made overlay builds on Linux, for its own package and for consumers, and `SDL_Qiut` is still refused. I took the record-based variant over a warning on every absent entry, because a warning on every Linux build of a correct program is noise. It needs no per-configuration keys, only the line's existence. The change to FFI-12's 'cannot drift' is a change to what the language does, so the lead takes it to the owner as its own line (verdicts, item 2). The J8-15 answer follows from it: the example is E5010 only where the entry was never checked. Where it was checked through `SDL.h`, the entry applies nothing to the `SDL_video.h` import, and the call is refused at the call.

repairs.hole: 7 (engineering, medium): FFI-12 refused 'an entry whose path names no declaration', which by FFI-6b catches every `@ffi(macro_fn)` entry. FFI-55's closed list gave no form for macros, enums, typedefs (handle, newtype, `@ffi(safe)` function pointers), globals, variant aliases or class sections.
repairs.answer: FFI-12 now says that an entry's declaration is whatever the header declares or defines under that path, including a function-like macro described by an `@ffi(macro_fn)` entry. FFI-55's form is defined once for every kind (hole 1): a macro's parameters and replacement tokens as written; a typedef's target, resolved; an enum's enumerators and values; a global's type and `const`; a function-pointer typedef's signature; a variant alias's alternatives; each class member's declaration and inline body. The list is given as examples. An entry that states no fact (`rename`, `hide`, an `extend` block) relies on nothing a form holds. Its line holds only its entry, so a library that adds a field to a renamed struct is not refused for nothing. Its path is still checked by FFI-12. Each word is judged by the declaration it names, whatever the import's language, which replaces my round-0 rule that refused C++ words under `import c` by language. `@ffi(const)` on a free function is E5002. `@ffi(noexcept)` on a C function under `import c` is already true and changes nothing, so one overlay serves both imports.

repairs.hole: 8 (engineering, medium): `physics` and `render` ship the same lines for `engine.Grid.lookups`, and the game importing both was refused with no line to write. The same reading caught `SDL_Quit` in two packages' overlays, and what a third import with no overlay sees was unsaid.
repairs.answer: Equal facts of one entity are one statement, so the game compiles. Different facts are E5010, naming both files, both imports and the fact ('… says `lookups` only reads its object, and … says it changes it'). The game gets a line to write: its own overlay, through its own import of `engine.hpp`, with `@ffi(const)` above `override fn lookups()`. A dependency's statement comes before the package's own, as ODR-149 already orders the files of one list, and `override` replaces it. Two packages neither of which depends on the other, or two imports within one package, must agree, and the package that wrote them can fix its own files. Free functions are each import's (hole 4), so two packages' `SDL_Quit` never clash. An import with no overlay sees the build's statement. The widening of ODR-149's reach is flagged for the owner (verdicts, item 3).

repairs.hole: 9 (engineering, medium): the design said 'Verdict 121 is kept' while dropping its first clause, 'the header an overlay was written for is recorded', and did not list decision 11's per-declaration count or FFI-55's title as revisited.
repairs.answer: The verdicts section now leads with this as an amendment of verdict 121's first clause, in the owner's terms: 'what each declaration an overlay describes was when a person checked it is recorded … and every overlay is checked against it.' It gives four pieces of evidence: nothing reads the key; the repository's record is already false; one overlay across two headers has no one true header; and ODR 14.1 already moved the check to declarations. On the same line it puts decision 11's count, which becomes one fingerprint of the entry and one per checked form, with the reason. It names FFI-55's bold title among the texts that change. The owner_short recommendation names it as the first of the three lines that are his to rule.

design.open_risks: 1. Three parts of A change what the language does and are the owner's, one at a time: (a) verdict 121's first clause amended, with decision 11's count; (b) FFI-12, where an entry for a declaration this import lacks applies nothing once some build has checked it, instead of E5010; (c) one statement per type and class member for the build, with `override` reaching dependencies, which widens ODR-149's reach. 2. A form includes an inline function's or method's body, and a macro's tokens, as written. Editing a described function's inline body therefore needs a re-check and `--merge`, and in a dependency it is that package's to re-record, as ODR 14.3 already makes it for a changed declaration. A header-only C++ library re-checks more often than a C one. The body is taken as written, so `NDEBUG` and `assert` never split the form. But a change inside a macro the body uses is not seen, just as a change in a function it calls is not. 3. The closed set a form leaves out (sizes, alignments, offsets, packing, an enum's chosen integer type, calling convention, linkage and visibility) is anchored to FFI-2a's derived facts and FFI-9. If a future rule makes Ember rely on one of them for a fact an entry states, it moves into the form. 4. With one statement per type for the build, a package's overlay can refuse a dependency's code in the combined build. If the game states that `lookups` changes its object, physics's loop that relies on `@ffi(const)` is E3020 in the game's build. That is correct, but it is new, and the message should name the overlay whose statement caused it. 5. FFI-30a says an overlay 'never changes a type's identity', while `@ffi(newtype)` (ODR-249) makes a typedef nominal. Under this rule a newtype is a build-wide statement about one entity, so the two rules need reconciling: the lead's, or another group's. 6. Not specified anywhere: how an import names a file inside a dependency (a git dependency's `overlays/sdl.em`). This rule settles which headers such an overlay serves, not how its path is spelled. 7. Overlap with P07: this rule owns an entry's path (namespaces, nesting) and where its facts belong. Telling apart several functions of one name, operators included, is P07's. The two compose. 8. Under every option, the safe import line chooses which file is parsed and which library is linked, so an overlay's vouch is never really scoped to one library. A header-name check (B) looks like a scope but is not one. Say this plainly to the owner rather than present it as a loss under A. 9. Tests follow the spec. tests/conformance/FFI-12/reject_an_overlay_for_another_header.em becomes an accept test: `tally_scale` is declared by `tally.h` and its form is recorded. FFI-30/reject_an_entry_for_a_member_another_import_wrote.em becomes a merge of equal facts, or E5010 for different ones. Every test overlay and the spec's own examples (XVI.4's Vulkan overlay, FFI-17) change their first line, which `ember fmt --migrate` covers. Every committed `ember.overlays` loses `header` and takes the entry-and-forms shape. The compiler's record today uses an `[overlay.declarations]` sub-table that the spec's example does not show, so the text form is the lead's to align.
